Preface: Scope and Method

This book is a work of metaphysics. It is not a commentary on Book I, and it is not a restatement
of it. It is the derivation of the metaphysical structure that Book I’s epistemology presupposes,
and the statement of the metaphysical conditions under which Book I’s framework can hold.
    The distinction is not stylistic. Book I is an epistemology: it asks what roles any complete
explanation must assign, and it answers with the four columns of explanatory cognition. Book II
is a metaphysics: it asks what must be the case in reality for those roles to be assignable, and
it answers with an ontology. Book I establishes that explanatory cognition has a four-column
structure; Book II derives what being must be like, such that the four-column structure can be
assigned to it.
    The book is written under the same commitment as Book I. Its arguments are offered to
be assessed on their own merits, and each claim is labeled with the kind of support it has and
the kind of criticism it invites. It does not draw its premises from revelation, from authority, or
from empirical data. It draws its premises from Book I, and from the philosophical arguments
that Book I established. Where it goes beyond Book I, it states the argument by which it goes
beyond, and it marks the new claim with a status label, as Book I did.


The Relation to Book I
The relation between the two books is one of derivation, not of dependence in the sense that
Book II could not stand without Book I. The relation is this: Book II presupposes Book I in
every one of its chapters, and it states the presupposition explicitly at the beginning of each
chapter, in a paragraph headed Presupposition from Book I. But the presupposition is not a mere
borrowing. Book II does not take Book I’s conclusions as a set of premises from which it deduces
a metaphysics. It takes Book I’s analytical framework as the structure whose metaphysical
conditions it must derive. The derivation is the book’s principal task.
    The derivation is not a weakness. It is the condition under which Book II can be what it
is: a metaphysics in the service of an epistemology, not a rival to it. A book that attempted to
establish both the structure of cognition and the structure of being by a single method would be
claiming more than a single method can deliver. Book I established the structure of cognition;
Book II derives the structure of being that the cognition presupposes. The two books are related
as the order of inquiry is related to the order of being; they are distinct orders, and neither
replaces the other.
    Three consequences follow, and the reader should know them before beginning.
    First consequence: no principle of Book I is reargued. Where Book II uses a principle of
Book I, it states the principle by name and number, and it states that the principle is taken as
given. It does not reargue the principle, and it does not restate the argument by which Book I
established it. The reader who wishes to assess a principle of Book I is directed to the chapter of
Book I in which the principle is established.
    Second consequence: the derivation is not a deduction. Book II does not deduce its conclusions
from Book I’s premises by a formal inference. It derives them by showing that the metaphysical
structure it describes is the condition under which Book I’s framework can be what it is.
xxiv                                                                  Preface: Scope and Method


The derivation is transcendental in form: it proceeds from the framework to its conditions of
possibility. The reader who expects a formal deduction will not find one; the reader who expects
a transcendental derivation will find it.
    Third consequence: the metaphysical claims of Book II are conditional on Book I’s core.
Book II states its claims at the strength that Book I’s core commitments support. Where a claim
of Book II would fail if a core commitment of Book I were rejected, Book II says so, and it marks
the claim with the label (D), which the next section introduces. A reader who accepts Book I’s
core should accept the claims of Book II that are marked (D); a reader who does not accept
Book I’s core has no reason to accept them, and Book II states them at exactly that strength.


The Scope of the Book
Book II is not a general introduction to metaphysics. It is the metaphysics of a particular
framework—the framework of viability—and its scope is set by Book I. It treats only those
questions that Book I’s principles raise or presuppose. It does not treat questions that Book I
declared to lie outside its method (telos, values, ethical norms), except insofar as Book I’s method
requires their metaphysical basis to be indicated.
     The scope has three levels, and each level corresponds to a way in which Book I left something
unfinished.
     The first level: what Book I presupposed without examining. Book I used the notions of
substance, essence, causation, modality, and law, but it did not analyze them. It used them as
the vocabulary of its structural description, and it deferred their analysis to the metaphysics that
would follow. Book II undertakes that analysis. It asks what substance is, such that identity can
be a mode of it; what causation is, such that light can be a conveyor of it; what law is, such
that the rules of a realm can be instances of it; what modality is, such that the modal space of
Book I can be a space of possibilities.
     The second level: what Book I left open. Book I’s chapter on the boundaries of epistemology
(Chapter 34) identified fourteen open questions. Book II addresses them, at the strength that its
own arguments support. Where a question is answered, Book II states the answer; where it is
not answered, Book II states why, and it marks the question as still open.
     The third level: what Book I made as commitments without metaphysical defense. Book I’s
Chapter 43 identified ten core commitments (C1–C10), each of which is adopted rather than
proved. Book II asks what each commitment presupposes in the order of being, and it states the
metaphysical conditions under which the commitment can hold. It does not attempt to prove
the commitment; it states the metaphysical structure that the commitment requires.
     The three levels together define the scope. Book II is the metaphysics that Book I presupposed,
left open, and made as commitments. It is not a metaphysics in general, and it does not claim to
be. It is the metaphysics of a particular framework, and its scope is exactly the scope of the
framework.


The Method
The method of Book II is the method of Book I, applied at a different level. Book I applied the
four-column framework to the analysis of explanatory cognition: fixed elements (what is related),
fluid elements (what conveys the relation), governing dynamics (the rule of the relation), and
context (the frame of the relation). Book II applies the four-column framework to the analysis of
being itself: the fixed elements of metaphysics, the fluid elements of metaphysics, the governing
dynamics of metaphysics, and the context of metaphysics.
    The four parts of Book II that follow Part I correspond to the four columns. Part II treats
the fixed elements of metaphysics: substance, essence, thisness, and the fixed elements of each
realm. Part III treats the fluid elements of metaphysics: causation, relation, light, and the fluid
Preface: Scope and Method                                                                       xxv


elements of each realm. Part IV treats the governing dynamics of metaphysics: law, necessity,
the modal space, and the dynamics of each realm. Part V treats the context of metaphysics: the
realms as contexts, the barzakhic category, non-passage, and the context of the whole.
    The method’s tools are the same as Book I’s tools. The removal test for necessity, the
reducibility test for sufficiency, the reductio, the transcendental argument, the abductive argument,
and the status labels—all of these are inherited from Book I, and Book II uses them in the same
way. The only addition is the label (D), which the next section introduces.
    The method’s aim is the same as Book I’s aim. It is not to establish metaphysics from
nothing; it is to derive the metaphysical conditions of Book I’s framework, at the strength that
Book I’s arguments support. The reader who accepts Book I’s framework should find in Book II
the metaphysical structure that the framework requires; the reader who does not accept Book I’s
framework will find Book II’s claims conditional on a framework he does not accept, and Book II
states them at that strength.


The Epistemic Status Labels
Book II uses the five status labels of Book I, with their meanings unchanged, and it adds one
new label.
    The inherited labels. (A) marks an axiom or foundational commitment—a starting point
that is adopted rather than proved. (T) marks an argued claim—a claim for which an argument
is given, typically a reductio, a transcendental argument, or an inference to the best explanation.
(E) marks an estimate—a claim that is offered as approximate and subject to revision. (Q)
marks an open philosophical question—a question that has no final answer yet, but can be
examined within the framework. (S) marks a speculation—a speculative extension, flagged for
caution.
    The new label. (D) marks a claim that is derived from Book I. It is a claim whose truth
depends on a specific principle, definition, or commitment of Book I, and whose argument in
Book II consists in showing the derivation. A (D) claim is not an independent principle; it is a
consequence that Book II derives from Book I’s commitments. A reader who accepts Book I’s
core should accept the (D) claims; a reader who does not accept Book I’s core has no reason to
accept them, and the book states them at that strength.
    The addition of (D) is not a weakening of the labels. It is a clarification. Book I used (A)
and (T) for its own claims; Book II uses (D) for claims that are neither new axioms nor new
arguments, but consequents of axioms and arguments already established. The label makes the
dependency visible, so that a reader who wishes to challenge a (D) claim knows exactly which
principle of Book I he must challenge.


The Convention of Presupposition
Every chapter of Book II opens with a paragraph headed Presupposition from Book I. The
paragraph names the principle, definition, or commitment of Book I on which the chapter
depends, summarizes it in one sentence, and states that the chapter does not restate it. The
convention is stated here, in the preface, so that the reader knows what to expect.
    The paragraph is not a formality. It is the structural element by which Book II remains a
metaphysics in the service of an epistemology rather than a rival to it. The reader who has read
Book I can follow a chapter of Book II without re-reading the corresponding chapter of Book I;
the reader who has not read Book I can use the paragraph as a pointer to the chapter of Book I
that establishes the presupposition.
    The paragraph’s form is fixed, and it is this:

      Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Principle X.Y (or
xxvi                                                                   Preface: Scope and Method


       Definition X.Y) of Book I, which establishes [summary in one sentence]. It does not
       restate the principle; it asks what the principle presupposes in the order of being.

   The paragraph is stated in every chapter, without exception. Where a chapter depends
on more than one principle of Book I, the paragraph names each principle, in the order of its
appearance in Book I.


The Reference System
References to Book I use the form [D##-m], where ## is the chapter number of Book I and m is
the number of the principle, definition, or theorem within that chapter. Thus [D12-1] refers to
the first principle of Chapter 12 of Book I, which is the definition of identity; [D15-1] refers to
the first principle of Chapter 15, which is the definition of epistemic light; and [D36-1] refers to
the first principle of Chapter 36, which is the definition of viability.
    References to sources outside Book I use the form [B2-##-m], where ## is the chapter number
of Book II and m is the number of the source within that chapter. The form is the same as
Book I’s form for its sources, and the two forms are kept apart by the initial letter: D for Book I,
B2 for Book II.
    The list of all references to Book I is collected in the Index of Cross-References to Book I at
the end of the book. The reader who wishes to see, in one place, every principle of Book I that
Book II depends on, is directed to that index.


The Structure of the Book
Book II is organized into eight parts and thirty-two chapters.
    Part I (Framework). What Book I established, what it left open, and the method of Book II.
The part includes the derivation of ontology from epistemology (Chapter 4), which is the bridge
between the two books. It states the status labels (including (D)), and the convention of
presupposition.
    Part II (Fixed Elements). The fixed elements of metaphysics: substance, essence, thisness,
and the fixed elements of each realm. The part deepens Book I’s account of identity by asking
what substance must be, such that identity can be a mode of it; what essence must be, such that
the defining invariants of Book I can be essential features; and what the fixed element of each of
the seven realms is.
    Part III (Fluid Elements). The fluid elements of metaphysics: causation, relation, light, and
the fluid elements of each realm. The part deepens Book I’s account of light by asking what
causation must be, such that light can be a conveyor of it; what relation must be, such that light
can be the condition of possibility of it; and what the fluid element of each of the seven realms is.
    Part IV (Governing Dynamics). The governing dynamics of metaphysics: law, necessity, the
modal space, and the dynamics of each realm. The part deepens Book I’s account of the rules by
asking what law must be, such that the rules of a realm can be instances of it; what necessity
must be, such that the rules of a realm can be necessary; and what the modal space is, as a
metaphysical structure derived from the framework.
    Part V (Context). The context of metaphysics: the realms as contexts, the barzakhic category,
non-passage, and the context of the whole. The part deepens Book I’s account of the context by
asking what a realm must be, such that it can serve as a context for manifestation; what the
barzakhic is, as a metaphysical category; and what the non-passage of Book I presupposes in the
order of being.
    Part VI (Divine Ground). The divine ground and the modal order. The part deepens Book I’s
three commitments about God (Principle 7.3, Principle 12.2, Principle 37.2) by asking what the
Preface: Scope and Method                                                                          xxvii


metaphysics of transcendence, creation, and providence must be. It does not attempt to prove
the commitments; it states the metaphysical structure that the commitments require.
    Part VII (Integration). Viability as the integration of the four columns. The part deepens
Book I’s definition of viability by asking what viability must be, such that it can measure the
relation between an identity and its manifestations; what the relation between viability and
essence, causation, and modality is; and what the metaphysics of viability is.
    Part VIII (Boundaries). The boundaries of metaphysics, and the conclusion. The part
answers the fourteen open questions of Book I’s Chapter 34, at the strength that Book II’s
arguments support, and it states the conclusion: Book II is a conditional metaphysics on a core
of axioms derived from Book I.
    The eight parts are ordered as the four columns are ordered in Book I, with the divine ground
stated before the integration, so that viability is presented as the consequence of the ground
rather than as an independent concept later connected to it.


What Book II Does Not Do
Book II does not restate Book I. It does not reargue Book I’s principles, and it does not repeat
Book I’s definitions. The following list states the principal things that Book II does not do, so
that the reader knows what to expect and what not to expect.
    Book II does not restate the definitions of the realms. The realms are derived in Part V from
the four columns of Book I, and their definitions are stated there. Book II does not presuppose a
prior doctrine of the realms; it derives the doctrine from the framework.
    Book II does not restate the definition of identity. The definition is given in Book I, Def-
inition 12.1. Book II refers to it, and it asks what substance and essence must be, such that
identity can be a mode of them.
    Book II does not restate the definition of manifestation. The definition is given in Book I,
Definition 13.1. Book II refers to it, and it asks what causation and relation must be, such that
a manifestation can be the product of an identity and a receiving realm.
    Book II does not restate the definition of light. The definition is given in Book I, Definition 15.1.
Book II refers to it, and it asks what the metaphysical status of light must be, such that light
can be the condition of possibility of relation.
    Book II does not restate the rules of the realms. The rules are stated in Book I, Chapters 16
and 17. Book II refers to them, and it asks what law and necessity must be, such that the rules
can be instances of them.
    Book II does not restate the definition of viability. The definition is given in Book I,
Definition 36.1. Book II refers to it, and it asks what the metaphysical conditions of viability are.
    Book II does not restate the tower model, the trans-categorical triad, or the theory of action.
These are stated in Book I, Chapters 36 to 39. Book II refers to them where it needs them, and
it asks what they presuppose in the order of being.
    The reader who has not read Book I will find Book II difficult, because Book II assumes
the vocabulary and the principles of Book I. The reader who has read Book I will find Book II
a natural continuation, because Book II undertakes exactly the questions that Book I raised
and deferred. The reader who wishes to read Book II without Book I is directed to Book I’s
Chapter 43 for the core commitments, and to Book I’s Chapter 34 for the open questions that
Book II addresses.


Reading Paths
Book II can be read in three ways.
   The full path. Read from beginning to end, in the order of the chapters. Part I establishes
the framework and derives the ontology; Parts II–V treat the four columns; Part VI states the
xxviii                                                               Preface: Scope and Method


divine ground; Part VII integrates the columns in viability; Part VIII states the boundaries.
Each part presupposes only what has come before. This is the intended path.
    The thematic path. Read Parts II–V as a unit—the four columns of metaphysics—and then
read Parts VI and VII as the ground and the integration. The reader who is interested in
one column (for example, the fixed elements) can read the corresponding part and follow the
cross-references backward to Part I. The thematic path is complete in its own terms.
    The targeted path. Enter at any part, and follow the cross-references backward to Part I. The
reader who is interested in a particular question (for example, the metaphysical status of the
barzakhic, or the metaphysics of transcendence) can enter at the corresponding part, and follow
the presupposition paragraphs to the chapters of Book I that establish the principles on which
the part depends.
    The three paths are complete in their own terms. The reader who follows the full path has the
whole architecture; the reader who follows the thematic path has one column and its integration;
the reader who follows the targeted path has one question and its presuppositions.


A Note on the Title
The title Metaphysics of Viability does not make viability a metaphysical entity. In Book I,
viability is the structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
(Definition 36.1). In Book II, viability is the measure of the metaphysical relation between being
and its expression. It remains a structural measure, not a substance, not a value, not an end.
What Book II adds is the metaphysical conditions of the relation—the conditions under which
an identity can be expressed, sustained, and recovered—and the integration of those conditions
in a single structural character.
    The concept is developed in Part VII, and it returns in Part VIII. It is a descriptive concept
throughout: it states a condition on the relation between being and its expression, and it attaches
no value, end, or good to that condition. The inquiry into value belongs to a later volume, and
Book II does not undertake it.


A Note on the Divine Ground
Book I established, as commitments, that God is the transcendent ground of the realms (Princi-
ple 7.3), that the structural light is created and is not God (Principle 12.2), and that the modal
space is grounded in God (Principle 37.2). Book II takes these commitments as given, and it
asks what the metaphysical structure of transcendence, creation, and providence must be, such
that the commitments can hold. It does not attempt to prove the commitments, and it does
not describe the divine essence. It states what the metaphysical conditions of the commitments
are, and it marks them with the label (D), because their truth depends on the truth of Book I’s
commitments.
    The reader who comes to Book II from a religious tradition will find the same structural
vocabulary as in Book I, and the same silence on the divine essence. The reader who comes
to Book II from a philosophical tradition will find the same structural arguments as in Book I,
and the same openness on the question of what lies beyond the structure. The two readers
are addressed by the same book, and the book states its claims at the strength its arguments
support.


A Note on the Method
The book is offered as a conditional metaphysics on a core of axioms. Its core is the ten
commitments of Book I’s Chapter 43 (C1–C10). Every other claim of Book II is a definition that
Preface: Scope and Method                                                                     xxix


fixes vocabulary, a consequence that follows from the core and the definitions, or a hypothesis
that can be revised without disturbing the core. Book II is not a closed system: it does not
claim that its conclusions are necessary, nor that its list of principles is complete, nor that its
models are the only ones that fit the core.
     The core is stated in Appendix A, not in the body of the book, so that the body may begin
directly with the metaphysical analysis. The appendix is not an afterthought; it is the reference
that makes the body’s dependencies visible. The reader who wishes to see, for each claim of
Book II, which core commitment it depends on, is directed to Appendix A and to the Index of
Cross-References to Book I.
     The book is offered in the hope that it helps: that it clarifies what Book I presupposed, what
it left open, and what it made as commitments; that it derives the metaphysical structure that
the framework of viability requires; and that it indicates, at its boundaries, what remains to be
done. The reader who finds the book useful has found what the book offers; the reader who does
not has located a place where the inquiry continues. The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.

Introduction: The Problem, the
Method, and the Map

Book I asked how a finite subject comes to understand the structure of what is. It answered with
the four columns of explanatory cognition: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics,
and context. It argued that any complete explanation must assign these four roles, that the roles
are distinct, and that the four are jointly necessary and (as an estimate) jointly sufficient. It
then built, on that framework, an account of identity, manifestation, light, and viability, and it
stated the boundaries beyond which its method does not reach.
    Book II asks a different question. It asks what must be the case in reality, such that the
framework of Book I can be assigned to it. It does not ask how the subject comes to understand;
it asks what the structure of being must be, given that the subject’s understanding has the
structure Book I described. The question is not a repetition of Book I’s question. It is its
metaphysical counterpart.
    The present Introduction states the question, explains why it is a different question from
Book I’s, and gives the map of the book that answers it. It presupposes the Preface, and it does
not repeat what the Preface established. The reader who has read the Preface may read this
Introduction as the first philosophical statement of the book’s problem.


A Scene
Consider two inquirers who stand before the same phenomenon. The phenomenon may be a
falling stone, a spoken sentence, or a person’s grief—the choice does not matter, because the
structure of their inquiries is the same.
     The first inquirer asks: how do we explain this? She asks what elements the explanation
must identify, what medium connects them, what rule governs the connection, and from what
frame the explanation is posed. Her question is the question of Book I. She is not asking whether
the stone really falls, or whether the sentence really has meaning, or whether the grief is real.
She takes the reality of the phenomenon as given, and she asks what an explanation of it must
contain. Her answer is the four-column framework.
     The second inquirer stands before the same phenomenon and asks a different question.
She asks: what must be the case, for this phenomenon to be explainable in the first inquirer’s
way? She does not ask what roles the explanation must assign; she asks what structure the
phenomenon must have, such that the roles can be assigned to it. If the first inquirer says that
every explanation must have a fixed element, the second inquirer asks what substance must be,
such that it can be the referent of a fixed element. If the first inquirer says that every explanation
must invoke a fluid element, the second inquirer asks what causation must be, such that a fluid
element can convey effect. If the first inquirer says that every explanation must have a governing
dynamics, the second inquirer asks what law must be, such that a rule can govern a connection.
If the first inquirer says that every explanation must have a context, the second inquirer asks
what a realm must be, such that it can serve as a context for manifestation.
     The two inquirers are not rivals. They are asking two questions about the same reality,
xxxii                                                                                 Introduction


and the second question presupposes the first. If the first inquirer’s answer is correct—if every
explanation must indeed have the four columns—then the second inquirer’s question is well-posed:
there must be something in reality that corresponds to the four columns, and the second inquirer’s
task is to say what it is. The first inquirer establishes the form of explanation; the second
establishes the being that the form presupposes.
    The scene poses the question of Book II. What must being be, such that the four-column
framework of Book I can be applied to it? The book’s answer is not a new framework. It is an
ontology: a statement of the fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and contexts
that the four columns of Book I presuppose in the order of being. The book is offered as the
metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s epistemology, and its claim is that the counterpart is real,
invariant, and describable.


The Problem
The problem of Book II can be stated in a single sentence. Book I established the analytical
structure of explanatory cognition; Book II asks what the ontological structure of the explained
must be, such that the analytical structure applies to it.
    The problem is not new. It is as old as the distinction between logic and ontology, between
the form of thought and the form of being. But the form it takes in Book II is specific, and the
specificity is what makes the book a contribution rather than a repetition.
    The specificity has three aspects, and each aspect distinguishes Book II’s problem from the
problems of other metaphysical inquiries.
    The first aspect: the problem is internal to Book I’s framework. Book II does not ask what
being is in general. It asks what being must be, such that Book I’s framework applies to it. The
question is conditioned by Book I’s answer, and it is answerable only within Book I’s vocabulary.
A metaphysics that began with the categories of Aristotle, or with the substances of Spinoza,
or with the monads of Leibniz, would be a different metaphysics. Book II begins with the four
columns of Book I, and it asks what the four columns presuppose.
    The second aspect: the problem is not the problem of grounding. Book I distinguished two
orders: the order of cognition (how a finite subject comes to understand) and the order of
grounding (what makes what is actual). Book I’s Part IX stated the order of grounding, from
the modal space Ω through the actualization chain X to the structural order R. Book II’s
problem is not the problem of grounding. It is the problem of the categories that both orders
presuppose. The order of cognition presupposes that there are fixed elements, fluid elements,
governing dynamics, and contexts; the order of grounding presupposes that there are possibilities,
actualizations, and structures. Book II asks what each of these must be, metaphysically, such
that the two orders can be stated.
    The third aspect: the problem is conditional on Book I’s core. Book II does not ask what
being must be, absolutely. It asks what being must be, given Book I’s core commitments (the
ten of Book I’s Chapter 43). The answer is conditional: it holds if the core holds, and it fails if
the core fails. The conditionality is not a weakness. It is the form of a metaphysics that is in the
service of an epistemology, not a rival to it.
    The three aspects together define the problem. Book II is an internal metaphysics of Book I’s
framework; it is not the metaphysics of grounding, but the metaphysics of the categories that
grounding presupposes; and it is conditional on Book I’s core, and it states its conditionality
openly.


What Book I Established
The reader who has read Book I knows what it established. The present section restates the
essentials, for the reader who has not read Book I, and for the reader who wishes to see the
Introduction                                                                                     xxxiii


framework in one place before Book II begins its metaphysical work.
    Book I established four things, and each is a condition of Book II’s problem.
    The four-column framework. Book I argued (Principles 3.1 and 3.2) that every explanatory
cognition requires four analytical roles: fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and
context; that the four roles are distinct; that the four are jointly necessary (by the removal test)
and (as an estimate) jointly sufficient (by the reducibility test). The framework is the analytical
structure that Book II presupposes.
    Identity, manifestation, and light. Book I defined identity as invariance under a class of
allowable transformations (Definition 12.1), manifestation as the contextually realized appearance
of an identity in a receiving context (Definition 13.1), and light as the trans-categorical condition
of possibility of legible relation (Definition 15.1). The three are the fixed and fluid elements of
Book I’s epistemology, and they are the subject of Book II’s Parts II and III.
    Viability. Book I defined viability as the structural character of the relation between an
identity and its manifestations in a context, measured by fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability
(Definition 36.1). The definition is descriptive: it states a condition on the relation, and it attaches
no value or end to the condition. Viability is the integration of the four columns, and it is the
subject of Book II’s Part VII.
    The core. Book I’s Chapter 43 identified ten core commitments (C1–C10) on which every other
claim of the framework depends. The core is the load-bearing part of Book I, and Book II states
it in Appendix A, not in the body, so that the body may begin directly with the metaphysical
analysis.
    The four things are the framework, the categories, the integration, and the core. Book II
takes each as given, and it asks what each presupposes in the order of being. The question is the
same in every case: what must being be, such that this structure can be applied to it?


What Book I Left Open
Book I did not close its inquiry. It identified, in its Chapter 34, fourteen open questions, and it
marked them as questions its method could not settle. The fourteen questions are the negative
space of Book II: they state where Book I stopped, and they indicate where Book II begins.
    The fourteen questions, restated for Book II’s purpose, are these.
    The four conceptual questions. Under what structural conditions can two viabilities be jointly
realized in one context (Q1)? Where does the reduction of viability become the singularity of
death (Q2)? What is the conceptual relation between light and expression (Q3)? What is the
mode of the relation between the structural light and its divine source (Q4)?
    The five argumentative questions. What is the relation among self-awareness, consciousness,
awareness, and the subject (Q5)? What are the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of
the balance criterion (Q6)? Can the principle of contextual manifestational capacity and the
criterion of manifestational adequacy be given independent definition and support (Q7)? What
is the exact relation among the three aspects of cost (Q8)? How can the structural description
serve as the basis for a normative prescription (Q9)?
    The five epistemic questions. What is the structural possibility and ontological standing of
realization in contexts the framework does not describe (Q10)? What are the particular direct
relations among the contexts (Q11)? Can the doctrine that identity is more than signature be
given further support (Q12)? What is the exact form of the impossibility of complete knowledge
of epistemic light for subjects who are not finite (Q13)? What is the temporal structure of
self-awareness (Q14)?
    Book II addresses the four conceptual questions in its Parts II to V, the first four of the
argumentative questions in its Parts III to VI, and the first four epistemic questions in its
Parts III to V. It does not address Q9 (the bridge to normative prescription); that question
xxxiv                                                                                 Introduction


belongs to a later volume, and Book II states its metaphysical precondition without undertaking
the metaethical inquiry itself.
    The point is not that Book II answers every question Book I left open. The point is that
Book II’s problem is defined by those questions. A reader who wants to know what Book II is
for can read Book I’s Chapter 34, and then read Book II as the systematic attempt to address
the questions it founds.


The Metaphysical Turn
Book II is a metaphysics, not an epistemology. The turn from Book I to Book II is not a change
of subject, but a change of level. Book I asked what roles an explanation must assign; Book II
asks what being must be, such that the roles can be assigned. The turn is from the form of
explanation to the form of the explained.
    The turn has three moments, and each moment is a chapter in Book II.
    The first moment: the fixed elements of metaphysics. Book I’s fixed elements are the entities
held invariant within a cognition. Book II asks what substance must be, such that an entity can
be held invariant; what essence must be, such that an entity can have defining invariants; what
thisness must be, such that an entity can be the particular entity it is. The answer is the subject
of Part II.
    The second moment: the fluid elements of metaphysics. Book I’s fluid element is the entity
that conveys effect. Book II asks what causation must be, such that an effect can be conveyed;
what relation must be, such that a conveyor can hold between two terms; what light must be,
metaphysically, such that it can be the condition of possibility of legible relation. The answer is
the subject of Part III.
    The third moment: the governing dynamics of metaphysics. Book I’s governing dynamics
is the rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements. Book II asks what law must
be, such that a rule can govern a connection; what necessity must be, such that a rule can be
necessary; what the modal space is, as a metaphysical structure derived from the framework.
The answer is the subject of Part IV.
    The three moments are ordered as the four columns are ordered in Book I. The fixed elements
come first, because the fluid elements convey between them; the fluid elements come second,
because the governing dynamics governs their operation; the context (Book II’s Part V) comes
last, because it is the frame in which the first three take their specific content. The order is not
arbitrary. It is the order of Book I, applied at the metaphysical level.


The Architecture of Book II
Book II is organized into eight parts and thirty-two chapters. The parts are organized around the
four columns of Book I, and the chapters within each part are organized around the questions
that the column raises at the metaphysical level.
    Part I (Framework). What Book I established, what it left open, and the method of Book II.
The part includes the derivation of ontology from epistemology (Chapter 4), which is the bridge
between the two books. It states the status labels (including the new label (D)), and the
convention of presupposition. Four chapters.
    Part II (Fixed Elements). The fixed elements of metaphysics: substance, essence, thisness,
and the fixed elements of each realm. The part deepens Book I’s account of identity by asking
what substance must be, such that identity can be a mode of it; what essence must be, such that
the defining invariants of Book I can be essential features; and what the fixed element of each of
the seven realms is. Four chapters.
    Part III (Fluid Elements). The fluid elements of metaphysics: causation, relation, light, and
the fluid elements of each realm. The part deepens Book I’s account of light by asking what
Introduction                                                                                   xxxv


causation must be, such that light can be a conveyor of it; what relation must be, such that light
can be the condition of possibility of it; and what the fluid element of each of the seven realms is.
Four chapters.
    Part IV (Governing Dynamics). The governing dynamics of metaphysics: law, necessity, the
modal space, and the dynamics of each realm. The part deepens Book I’s account of the rules by
asking what law must be, such that the rules of a realm can be instances of it; what necessity
must be, such that the rules of a realm can be necessary; and what the modal space is, as a
metaphysical structure derived from the framework. Four chapters.
    Part V (Context). The context of metaphysics: the realms as contexts, the barzakhic category,
non-passage, and the context of the whole. The part deepens Book I’s account of the context by
asking what a realm must be, such that it can serve as a context for manifestation; what the
barzakhic is, as a metaphysical category; and what the non-passage of Book I presupposes in the
order of being. Four chapters.
    Part VI (Divine Ground). The divine ground and the modal order. The part deepens Book I’s
three commitments about God (Principle 7.3, Principle 12.2, Principle 37.2) by asking what
the metaphysics of transcendence, creation, and providence must be. It does not attempt to
prove the commitments; it states the metaphysical structure that the commitments require. Four
chapters, plus a synthesis chapter.
    Part VII (Integration). Viability as the integration of the four columns. The part deepens
Book I’s definition of viability by asking what viability must be, such that it can measure the
relation between an identity and its manifestations; what the relation between viability and
essence, causation, and modality is; and what the metaphysics of viability is. Five chapters.
    Part VIII (Boundaries). The boundaries of metaphysics, and the conclusion. The part
answers the fourteen open questions of Book I’s Chapter 34, at the strength that Book II’s
arguments support, and it states the conclusion: Book II is a conditional metaphysics on a core
of axioms derived from Book I. Two chapters.
    The eight parts are ordered as the four columns are ordered in Book I, with the divine ground
stated before the integration, so that viability is presented as the consequence of the ground
rather than as an independent concept later connected to it.


The Relation Between the Two Books
The relation between the two books can be stated in a table, and the table is the clearest way to
see the structure.

     Book I                         Book II                        Relation
     Epistemology               Metaphysics                        Complementary orders
     Order of cognition         Order of categories                Different levels
     Four columns as roles      Four columns as structures         Analytical / ontological
     Identity as invariance     Identity as essence                Derivation
     Manifestation as product   Manifestation as causal re-        Derivation

     Light as condition         Light as medium                    Derivation
     Rules as structural con- Rules as instances of law            Derivation
     straints
     Viability as structural    Viability as metaphysical          Derivation
     Boundaries of epistemology Boundaries of metaphysics          Extension

   The table shows that the relation is not one of dependence in the sense that Book II could
not stand without Book I. The relation is one of derivation. Book I establishes the form of
explanation; Book II derives the form of the explained. The two are related as two aspects of
xxxvi                                                                                Introduction


a single inquiry are related: neither reduces to the other, and neither is complete without the
other.
    The relation has one consequence that the reader should know from the outset. Book II does
not attempt to prove Book I’s principles. It takes them as given, and it asks what they presuppose.
A reader who does not accept Book I’s principles will not be persuaded by Book II’s arguments,
because Book II’s arguments are arguments about what Book I’s principles presuppose, not
arguments for Book I’s principles. The reader who accepts Book I’s principles will find Book II
the metaphysical counterpart of the epistemology he accepted. The two readers are addressed by
the same book, and the book states its claims at the strength its arguments support.


The Order of Inquiry and the Order of Being
Book I distinguished, in its Section 1.5, two orders: the order of cognition and the order of
grounding. Book II’s relation to Book I can be stated in terms of a third order, which the two
books together make visible.
     The order of cognition. The order in which a finite subject comes to understand the structure
of what is. The order is the order of Book I’s body: the four columns, the fixed elements, the
fluid element, the governing dynamics, the arguments, the resolutions, the derivative concepts,
the boundaries. The order is the order of the subject’s inquiry, not the order of being.
     The order of grounding. The order in which what is depends on what. The order is the order
of Book I’s Part IX: from the modal space Ω through the actualization chain X to the structural
order R. The order is the order of being, not the order of the subject’s inquiry.
     The order of categories. The order of the categories that both the order of cognition and the
order of grounding presuppose. The order is the order of Book II’s Parts II to V: from the fixed
elements (substance, essence, thisness) through the fluid elements (causation, relation, light) and
the governing dynamics (law, necessity, modal space) to the context (the realms, the barzakhic,
non-passage). The order is the order of the categories that make both cognition and grounding
possible.
     The three orders are distinct, and none reduces to the others. Book I is the book of the
first two orders; Book II is the book of the third. The reader who has followed Book I has the
first two orders; the reader who follows Book II has the third. The three together are the whole
architecture, and the architecture is what the two books together establish.


The Status of Claims in Book II
Book II uses the five status labels of Book I, with their meanings unchanged, and it adds the
label (D). The Preface introduced the labels; the present section restates them in the context of
Book II’s claims, so that the reader knows what kind of claim he is reading.
    (A) — Axiom or foundational commitment. Book II has few (A) claims of its own; the core
of Book II is inherited from Book I’s Chapter 43. Where Book II makes an (A) claim, it says so,
and it states that the claim is adopted rather than proved.
    (T) — Argued. The bulk of Book II’s claims are (T): they follow from the inherited core,
from the definitions that Book II introduces, and from the arguments that Book II gives. A (T)
claim is criticized by attacking its premises or its inferential step, and the book states both.
    (E) — Estimate. Book II’s estimates are structural estimates: they say what a metaphysical
structure must be, given the framework, and they are subject to revision if a different structure
does the same explanatory work. The (E) claims are concentrated in Parts IV and V, where the
modal space and the barzakhic category are at issue.
    (Q) — Open question. Book II inherits the (Q) claims of Book I’s Chapter 34, and it adds a
small number of its own. The book states them as questions, and it does not pretend to answer
them.
Introduction                                                                                xxxvii


    (S) — Speculation. Book II’s speculations are flagged as such: they are extensions of
the framework that the framework does not require, and they are offered at the strength of
speculations.
    (D) — Derived from Book I. A (D) claim is a claim whose truth depends on a specific
principle of Book I. The (D) claim is not an independent principle; it is a consequence that
Book II derives from Book I’s commitments. A reader who accepts Book I’s core should accept
the (D) claims; a reader who does not accept Book I’s core has no reason to accept them.
    The six labels are the book’s way of being honest about what it is doing. The reader is
invited to assess each claim by the standard appropriate to its status. A (T) claim is not refuted
by saying “it is only an estimate”; an (E) claim is not refuted by saying “it is not proved”; a (D)
claim is not refuted by saying “it depends on Book I”, because that is exactly what (D) says.


The Map
The reader who follows the order of the chapters will find that each part presupposes only what
has come before. The reader who wishes to consult a particular topic may begin with the relevant
chapter and follow the cross-references backward to the foundations.
   The map is stated in the following table, which gives the part, its subject, the number of
chapters, and the corresponding part of Book I.

   Part              Subject                                 Chapters       Corresponds to
   I                 Framework                               1–4            Book I, Parts I &
                                                                            X
   II                Fixed elements                          5–8            Book I, Part III
   III               Fluid elements                          9–12           Book I, Part III
   IV                Governing dynamics                      13–16          Book I, Part II
   V                 Context                                 17–20          Book I, Part II
   VI                Divine ground                           26–29          Book I, Part VI

   VIII              Boundaries                              30–31          Book I, Part V

    The correspondence is not an identity. Book II’s Part II corresponds to Book I’s Part III,
but Book II’s Part II is not a restatement of Book I’s Part III. The correspondence is of order:
Book II treats the same column at a deeper level, and the deepening is what makes the two parts
distinct. The reader who has read Book I will find Book II’s parts familiar in their subject and
new in their treatment.


Reading Paths
Book II can be read in three ways, and each path is complete in its own terms.
    The full path. Read from beginning to end, in the order of the chapters. Part I establishes
the framework and derives the ontology; Parts II–V treat the four columns; Part VI states the
divine ground; Part VII integrates the columns in viability; Part VIII states the boundaries.
Each part presupposes only what has come before. This is the intended path.
    The thematic path. Read Parts II–V as a unit—the four columns of metaphysics—and then
read Parts VI and VII as the ground and the integration. The reader who is interested in
one column (for example, the fixed elements) can read the corresponding part and follow the
cross-references backward to Part I. The thematic path is complete in its own terms.
    The targeted path. Enter at any part, and follow the “Presupposition from Book I” paragraphs
backward to the chapters of Book I that establish the principles on which the part depends. The
xxxviii                                                                              Introduction


reader who is interested in a particular question (for example, the metaphysical status of the
barzakhic, or the metaphysics of transcendence) can enter at the corresponding part, and follow
the presuppositions to the chapters of Book I that establish the principles on which the part
depends.
   The three paths are complete in their own terms. The reader who follows the full path has the
whole architecture; the reader who follows the thematic path has one column and its integration;
the reader who follows the targeted path has one question and its presuppositions.


Concluding Remark
Book II is offered as a proposal, not as a finished system. It is the metaphysical counterpart
of Book I’s epistemology, and its worth is to be measured by its coherence with Book I, by the
discrimination its distinctions make possible, and by the strength of its own arguments.
    The reader who has followed Book I to its end has seen the four-column framework built,
applied, and bounded. The reader who follows Book II to its end will see the same framework
deepened, its categories made explicit, and its metaphysical conditions stated. The two books are
related as the form of explanation is related to the form of the explained; the first is incomplete
without the second, and the second is unintelligible without the first.
    The inquiry continues. The horizon is open. The reader who finds a claim unconvincing is
invited to strengthen the objection and continue the inquiry. The reader who finds a question
unresolved is invited to consider whether the resolution belongs to Book II, or to one of the later
volumes of the series. The reader who finds the whole proposal useful has found what the book
offers: the metaphysics that Book I presupposed, and the categories that Book I used without
analyzing.

Epistemic Status Labels

Every claim in this book is tagged with one of six epistemic-status labels. The labels tell the
reader what kind of argument is being offered, and therefore what kind of criticism is appropriate.
They are not decorations. They are the book’s way of being honest about what it is doing, and
they are the reader’s way of knowing, at a glance, what he is being asked to accept.
    The labels are inherited from Book I, with one addition. The five inherited labels—(A),
(T), (E), (Q), and (S)—are defined in Book I’s front matter, and Book II uses them with their
meanings unchanged. The new label—(D)—is defined here, because it is the label that Book II
introduces to mark the claims that are derived from Book I. The reader who has read Book I’s
front matter will recognize the five; the reader who has not will find them defined in the sections
that follow.


Why Labels at All
A claim can be made in many ways, and the way it is made determines what kind of criticism it
invites. A mathematical proof invites a check of its inferential steps; a work of history invites a
check of its sources; a poem invites a reading. A philosophical claim can be made in any of these
ways and in others besides, and the reader who does not know which way is being used cannot
know how to respond.
    The labels fix the way. They say: this claim is an axiom, adopted rather than proved; this
claim is an argument, with premises that can be attacked; this claim is an estimate, offered at
a lower strength; this claim is an open question, not yet answered; this claim is a speculation,
flagged for caution; this claim is derived from Book I, and its truth depends on Book I’s core.
    The labels are not a substitute for the arguments. The arguments are given in the chapters,
and the reader who wishes to assess a claim must read the chapter in which the argument is
given. The labels are a guide to the argument’s kind, not a replacement for it. A reader who
reads only the labels has read the map, not the territory.


The Six Labels at a Glance
The six labels, with their meaning and their place of introduction, are as follows.

               Label Meaning                                      Introduced in
               (A)      Axiom or foundational commitment          Book I, front matter
               (T)      Argued                                    Book I, front matter
               (E)      Estimate                                  Book I, front matter
               (Q)      Open philosophical question               Book I, front matter
               (S)      Speculation                               Book I, front matter
               (D)      Derived from Book I                       Book II, this chapter

    The five inherited labels are defined in the sections that follow, in the order of their introduction
in Book I. The new label (D) is defined after them, with the detail its derivation from Book I
xl                                                                       Epistemic Status Labels


requires.


(A) — Axiom or Foundational Commitment
Definition. An (A) claim is a starting point that is adopted rather than proved. Its justification
is coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness—not deduction. An (A) claim can be criticized
by showing that it is incoherent with other commitments, that a rival commitment is more
explanatory or more fruitful, or that the framework could do without it.
    Book I’s audit. In Book I’s first edition, (A) covered three different things: a primitive
commitment, a stipulated definition, and a derivable or revisable claim. The audit of Book I’s
Chapter 43 separated them. After the audit, (A) covers two of the three: the primitive
commitments (the core), and the stipulated definitions. The derivable claims became (T); the
revisable claims became (E).
    Examples from Book I. The core commitment that the subject is finite (Principle 3.1) is
(A); the commitment that philosophy describes structure, not telos (Principle 4.1) is (A); the
commitment that identity is rigid and conserved (Principle 12.1 and 12.2) is (A); the commitment
that epistemic light is trans-categorical (Principle 15.1) is (A); the commitment that category-
relative predication holds (Principle 25.1) is (A); the commitment that epistemic justification is
autonomous (Principle 4.2) is (A). The definition of identity (Definition 12.1), the definition of
manifestation (Definition 13.1), and the definition of epistemic light (Definition 15.1) are (A) in
the sense of stipulated definitions.
    How to criticize an (A) claim. An (A) claim is not refuted by saying “it is only a commitment,”
because that is exactly what (A) says. It is refuted by showing that the commitment is incoherent
with other commitments that the framework cannot do without, that a rival commitment does
the same explanatory work better, or that the framework would be more fruitful without it. The
argument against an (A) claim is an argument about the framework’s overall coherence, not an
argument about the claim in isolation.
    What (A) does not mean. (A) does not mean “certain,” “obvious,” or “beyond criticism.” It
means “adopted, not proved; assessed by coherence, not by deduction.” A reader who rejects an
(A) claim has rejected a commitment of the framework, and the framework’s other claims are
conditional on the commitment. The book states its (A) claims at the strength their adoption
supports, and it invites the reader to challenge them at that strength.


(T) — Argued
Definition. A (T) claim is one for which an argument is given in the text—typically a reductio,
a transcendental argument, an inference to the best explanation, or a direct proof from stated
premises. A (T) claim can be criticized by attacking its premises or its inferential step.
    Book I’s use. The bulk of Book I’s claims are (T). The four-column principle, in its necessity
half, is (T) (Principle 7.1); the conveyor principle is (T) (Principle 8.1); the impossibility of
super-identity is (T) (Principle 27.1); the conservation of identity is (T) (Principle 12.7); the
non-travel of light is (T) (Principle 16.2); the transcendental argument for the non-completion of
expression is (T) (Principle 38.2). The audit of Book I’s Chapter 43 reclassified fourteen claims
from (A) to (T), because they follow from other entries and definitions, and the reclassification
is the audit’s main result.
    How to criticize a (T) claim. A (T) claim is refuted by showing that a premise is false, that
an inferential step is invalid, or that the argument is circular. The book states the premises
of each (T) claim, and the reader who wishes to attack the claim is directed to the premises.
Where a (T) claim depends on an (A) commitment, the book says so; where it does not, the
book says that too. The (T) claim is as strong as its weakest premise, and the book states the
premise so that the reader can assess the strength.
Epistemic Status Labels                                                                          xli


    What (T) does not mean. (T) does not mean “proved beyond doubt.” It means “argued from
stated premises, and assessable by the argument’s strength.” A (T) claim can be challenged at
any of its premises, and the book invites the challenge. The (T) label is the book’s way of saying:
here is the argument; assess it on its merits.


(E) — Estimate
Definition. An (E) claim is one that is offered as approximate and subject to revision—typically
a structural estimate, or a modelling assumption whose rejection would leave the core of the
framework intact. An (E) claim can be criticized by showing that a different structure does the
same explanatory work, or that the specific structure is doing no explanatory work.
    Book I’s use. Book I’s (E) claims are concentrated where the framework makes structural
estimates. The sufficiency half of the four-column principle is (E) (Principle 7.1); the claim that
light is an active structure is (E) (Principle 16.1); the claim that light is the foundational fluid
element is (E) (Principle 17.2); the claim that we are encompassed in light is (E) (Principle 17.4);
the unity of the rules is (E) (Principle 13.7); the structural duality of intensity and breadth is
(E) (Principle 26.1); the claim that time is context-relative succession is (E) (Principle 32.1);
the principle of ontological economy is (E) (Principle 39.1). The audit of Book I’s Chapter 43
reclassified twelve claims from (A) to (E), because they are substantive claims whose rejection
would not disturb the core.
    How to criticize an (E) claim. An (E) claim is refuted by showing that a different structure
does the same explanatory work as well or better, or that the specific structure is doing no
explanatory work and can be replaced by a simpler one. The (E) claim is offered at a lower
strength than (A) or (T), and the book states the strength so that the reader can assess the
claim at the appropriate level. A reader who finds the estimate unconvincing has not refuted the
framework; he has found a place where the framework’s estimate could be revised.
    What (E) does not mean. (E) does not mean “unjustified” or “arbitrary.” It means “offered
as an estimate, subject to revision, and assessed by explanatory power, not by proof.” The (E)
claim is a substantive claim about the framework’s structure, and the book states it at the
strength its arguments support.


(Q) — Open Philosophical Question
Definition. A (Q) claim is a philosophical question that has no final answer yet, but can be
examined within the system. It is not handed to any other domain for measurement or testing.
A (Q) claim marks a place where the framework’s principles raise a question that the framework
does not settle.
    Book I’s use. Book I’s Chapter 34 identified fourteen open questions, and they are the
negative space of Book I: they state where the framework stops, and they indicate where Book II
(or a later volume) begins. The (Q) claims are not weaknesses of the framework; they are its
honesty about what it has not settled.
    How to criticize a (Q) claim. A (Q) claim is not refuted by saying “the question is unanswered,”
because that is exactly what (Q) says. It is refuted by showing that the question is not real—
that it dissolves upon analysis, that it is answered by the framework’s principles in a way the
framework has not noticed, or that it belongs to another domain and should not be asked within
the framework. A reader who answers a (Q) claim has extended the framework; a reader who
dissolves it has shown a limit of the framework’s formulation.
    What (Q) does not mean. (Q) does not mean “unanswerable.” It means “unanswered within
the framework as it stands.” The question is a real philosophical question, and the framework’s
principles make it visible; the framework’s silence is the framework’s honest recognition of what
it has not done.
xlii                                                                        Epistemic Status Labels


(S) — Speculation
Definition. An (S) claim is a speculative extension, flagged for caution. The framework does
not claim that the speculation is true; it claims that the speculation follows naturally from the
framework’s structure and is worth investigating.
     Book I’s use. Book I’s (S) claims are few. The second half of the infinity of contexts
(Principle 11.1) is (S): whether the infinity is countable or uncountable is a question the
framework does not settle. The consequences for fission (Chapter 12) are (S): whether an identity
can continue in more than one of the resulting systems is a question the framework does not
decide. The structural possibility of realization in contexts the framework does not describe
(Principle 17.6, second consequence) is (S): whether identities are actually realized in those
contexts is a question the framework does not answer. The conditional possibilities, or middle
knowledge, is (S): the framework neither needs nor adopts it.
     How to criticize an (S) claim. An (S) claim is not refuted by saying “it is speculative,” because
that is exactly what (S) says. It is refuted by showing that the speculation is incompatible with
the framework’s core, or that the framework’s structure does not in fact point toward it, or that
it is doing no work in the framework’s arguments. An (S) claim is offered at the lowest strength
of the six labels, and the reader should assess it at that strength.
     What (S) does not mean. (S) does not mean “false” or “unworthy of attention.” It means
“speculative, flagged for caution, offered for investigation.” The (S) claim is the book’s way of
saying: here is a direction the framework points toward, but the framework does not claim to
have established it; the reader who wishes to investigate is invited to do so.


(D) — Derived from Book I
Definition. A (D) claim is a claim whose truth depends on a specific principle, definition, or
commitment of Book I, and whose argument in Book II consists in showing the derivation. A
(D) claim is not an independent principle; it is a consequence that Book II derives from Book I’s
commitments.
    The new label. Book I did not have (D), because Book I did not depend on another book.
Book II introduces (D) because its claims are derived from Book I’s core, and the derivation
needs a label. A (D) claim is not (A), because it is not adopted; it is not (T) in the full sense,
because its argument is not a new argument but a demonstration of derivation; it is not (E),
because its truth does not depend on the framework’s explanatory power but on the truth of
Book I’s commitments. The (D) label marks the fourth kind of claim: a consequent of Book I’s
core.
    Examples from Book II. The following claims, all of which appear in Book II’s later chapters,
are (D):

    How to criticize a (D) claim. A (D) claim is not refuted by saying “it depends on Book I,”
because that is exactly what (D) says. It is refuted by showing that the derivation does not
hold—that the claim is not in fact a consequence of the principle it is said to derive from, or that
the principle of Book I on which it depends is false. The first criticism is a criticism of Book II;
the second is a criticism of Book I. The book states the derivation explicitly, so that the reader
knows which criticism is appropriate.
    What (D) does not mean. (D) does not mean “unargued” or “unjustified.” It means “argued
by demonstration of derivation, and conditional on Book I’s core.” A (D) claim is as strong as
Book I’s principle, and the book states the principle so that the reader can assess the strength.
The (D) label is the book’s way of saying: here is what Book I’s principle requires in the order of
being; if the principle is true, the claim is true; if the principle is false, the claim falls with it.
    The relation of (D) to Book I’s core. A (D) claim is conditional on the ten core commitments
of Book I’s Chapter 43 (C1–C10). Where a (D) claim depends on a core commitment, the
book says so, and the reader who rejects the core commitment has a reason to reject the (D)
claim. Where a (D) claim depends on a non-core commitment of Book I—on a definition, an
estimate, or a speculation—the book says that too, and the (D) claim is as strong as the non-core
commitment. The book’s honesty about the derivation is part of what makes the (D) claims
assessable.


The “Proposed” Status
Book I used a status that is not one of the six labels: the status “proposed.” A proposed claim is
a claim that the framework proposes but has not yet assigned a status to, because its independent
definition and support are given in a later part of the book or in a later volume.
xliv                                                                     Epistemic Status Labels


    Book I’s proposed claims. Book I proposed two claims. The principle of manifestational
adequacy (Chapter 22) was proposed, and retained only if a later part of Book I gave it
an independent definition and support. The principle of contextual manifestational capacity
(Chapter 13) was proposed, and retained only if a later part of Book I gave it an independent
account of capacity.
    The proposed status in Book II. Book II inherits the proposed status, and it uses it sparingly.
Where Book II proposes a claim without assigning it a full status, it says so, and it states what
would be needed for the claim to receive a full status. The proposed status is the book’s way of
saying: here is a claim the framework needs, but the framework has not yet established it; the
reader who wishes to develop it is invited to do so.
    The proposed status is not (Q). A proposed claim is not an open question. An open question
is a question the framework does not answer; a proposed claim is a claim the framework needs
but has not yet established. The first is a gap in the framework’s answers; the second is a gap in
the framework’s support. The book distinguishes the two, and it uses the proposed status only
for the second.


The Labels in Combination
A claim can carry more than one label, when its status is composite. The book uses the following
combinations, and the reader should know them.
    (T) relative to (A). A claim that is argued, but whose argument depends on an (A) com-
mitment. The claim is (T) given the commitment; it is not (T) independently. Examples: the
argument for the impossibility of super-identity (Book I, Chapter 27) is (T) relative to the
finitude of the subject (Principle 3.1) and the openness of relations (Principle 11.1).
    (T) relative to (D). A claim that is argued, but whose argument depends on a (D) claim.
The claim is (T) given the derivation; it is not (T) independently. Examples: Book II’s Part VII
arguments for the metaphysics of viability are (T) relative to the (D) claims of Parts II to V.
    (D) relative to (A). A claim that is derived from Book I’s core, and whose derivation is itself
a consequence of an (A) commitment. The claim is (D) relative to the (A) commitment; it is not
(D) independently. Examples: Book II’s Part VI claims about the divine ground are (D) relative
to Book I’s Principle 4.1 (Structure, Not Telos), which is (A).
    (E) relative to (D). An estimate that is conditional on a (D) claim. The estimate is (E) given
the derivation; it is not (E) independently. Examples: Book II’s estimates about the modal space
(Part IV) are (E) relative to the (D) claim that the modal space is grounded in God (Book I,
Principle 11.1).
    The combinations are the book’s way of being precise about what it is doing. The reader who
sees a combined label knows that the claim’s status is not simple, and he knows which part of
the status depends on which commitment. The combination is a guide to the claim’s structure,
not a complication for its own sake.


The Audit and the Core
The labels are related to the audit of Book I’s Chapter 43. The audit reclassified the claims
that Book I’s first edition marked (A) into four classes: ten Core commitments, twenty-four
Definitions, fourteen Consequences (relabelled (T)), and twelve Hypotheses (relabelled (E)). The
reclassification is the audit’s main result, and Book II inherits it.
    The core. The core is the ten Core commitments (C1–C10). They are stated in Book I’s
Chapter 43, and Book II restates them in Appendix A. The (D) claims of Book II are conditional
on them.
    The definitions. The twenty-four definitions are (A) in the sense of stipulated definitions.
Book II inherits them, and it uses them without rearguing them. The definitions are the
Epistemic Status Labels                                                                       xlv


vocabulary of the framework, and the (D) claims are stated in the vocabulary.
    The consequences. The fourteen consequences are (T). Book II inherits them, and it uses
them where it needs them. The consequences are the framework’s arguments, and the (D) claims
often depend on them.
    The hypotheses. The twelve hypotheses are (E). Book II inherits them, and it uses them as
the framework’s structural estimates. The hypotheses are the framework’s modelling assumptions,
and the (D) claims that depend on them are as strong as the hypotheses.
    The audit’s relevance to Book II is this: the (D) claims of Book II are conditional on the
core, on the definitions, on the consequences, and on the hypotheses of Book I, and the book
states the dependency explicitly. The reader who rejects a core commitment knows which (D)
claims fall with it; the reader who rejects a hypothesis knows which (D) claims are weakened
but not refuted. The audit is the map of the dependency, and the Index of Cross-References to
Book I is the map’s application to Book II.


A Note on Honesty
The six labels are the book’s way of being honest about what it is doing. The book does not
claim to prove what it only adopts; it does not claim to argue what it only estimates; it does not
claim to answer what it only asks; it does not claim to establish what it only speculates; it does
not claim to be independent of Book I when it derives from Book I. The labels make the book’s
honesty visible, and they make the reader’s task possible.
    The reader who accepts the book’s honesty is invited to assess each claim by the standard
appropriate to its label. A (T) claim is not refuted by saying “it is only an argument”; an (E)
claim is not refuted by saying “it is not proved”; a (Q) claim is not refuted by saying “it is
unanswered”; an (S) claim is not refuted by saying “it is speculative”; a (D) claim is not refuted
by saying “it depends on Book I.” Each label says what the claim is, and the reader who wishes
to refute the claim must refute what it is, not what it is not.
    The reader who finds a label misapplied—a claim labelled (T) that is only (E), or a claim
labelled (D) that is in fact independent—has found a place where the book’s honesty fails, and
he is invited to say so. The labels are not beyond criticism; they are the book’s way of exposing
itself to criticism at the right level.

The labels are the book’s contract with the reader: they say what kind of claim is being made, and
they invite the criticism appropriate to that kind. The reader who honors the contract will find
the book assessable; the reader who does not will find it opaque. The book is offered in the hope
that the contract is honored, and that the inquiry continues.
