              Part I

Framework of Metaphysical Inquiry
                                                                                                 3




Chapter 1

What Book I Established and What
It Left Open

Scope. This chapter opens the main body of Book II. It gives the ledger of what Book I established,
the ledger of what Book I left open, and the ledger of what Book I used without analyzing. It
then states, in one place, what Book II undertakes with respect to each ledger. Its claims are
meta-philosophical and structural: they concern what Book I did and did not do, and what
Book II will do about it. The chapter makes no new metaphysical claim; it establishes the
space in which the metaphysical claims of the later chapters will be made. Where it speaks of
“established,” “left open,” or “deferred,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter and by the status labels of Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter presupposes Book I as a whole. Its task is to
make the presupposition explicit, and to state what Book I did not settle. It does not restate
the arguments of Book I; it states what the arguments established, and what they left for the
metaphysics that follows.


1.1     A Scene
Consider a grammarian who has mastered the syntax of a language. She can parse any sentence
the language permits; she can tell a well-formed sentence from a malformed one; she can state
the rules that every sentence must obey. Her mastery is complete, in its domain. If someone asks
her whether a given string of words is a sentence of the language, she can answer with certainty.
    Now ask her a different question. What does the sentence this stone exists mean? She can
parse it: the demonstrative, the noun, the verb. She can say that it is well-formed. But if the
question is not about the syntax of the sentence but about what it says—about the stone, and
about the existence it is said to have—her grammar has nothing to say. The grammar tells her
how the sentence is built, not what the sentence is about. The two questions are different, and
the mastery of the first is not the mastery of the second.
    The scene is not about grammar in particular. It is about a general distinction, one that
Book I drew for explanatory cognition, and that Book II now draws for the relation between
epistemology and metaphysics. Book I is the grammarian of explanation: it has mastered the
syntax of explanatory cognition, and it can state the rules that every explanation must obey.
Book II asks a different question. It asks what the syntax is about—what must be the case, in
reality, for the syntax to apply.
    The grammarian in the scene is not confused, and her mastery is not in question. The point
is that a grammar is not an ontology, and that a complete account of the form of a sentence does
not deliver an account of what the sentence is about. Book I’s mastery of the form of explanation
4                                  Chapter 1. What Book I Established and What It Left Open


is complete in its domain. Book II’s question is what the form is about—and the question is a
different question, one that Book I deliberately did not undertake.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What did Book I establish, and what did it
leave to the metaphysics that follows? The answer is a ledger, and the ledger is the space in
which Book II will work.


1.2      The Question
The question of the chapter is not the question of Book II. The question of Book II is: what must
being be, such that the framework of Book I can be applied to it? The question of the present
chapter is prior to that question: what did Book I establish, what did it leave open, and what
did it use without analyzing? The chapter’s answer is a ledger, and the ledger is the statement
of the space in which Book II’s question will be posed.
    Three ledgers are distinguished, and the distinction is the chapter’s principal contribution.
    The ledger of established claims. What Book I argued, defined, or committed itself to, with
the statuses its arguments support. The ledger is the inventory of what Book II inherits, and it
is what Book II takes as given.
    The ledger of open questions. What Book I raised but did not settle. The ledger is the
inventory of what Book I’s principles make visible but do not answer, and it is what Book II
addresses at the strength its own arguments support.
    The ledger of deferred analyses. What Book I used without analyzing. The ledger is the
inventory of the concepts that Book I employed as the vocabulary of its structural descrip-
tion—substance, essence, causation, law, modality—and that it deferred to the metaphysics that
would follow. The ledger is what Book II must analyze before it can use the concepts in its own
arguments.
    The three ledgers are not the same, and the difference matters. The established claims are
what Book II can take for granted; the open questions are what Book II must address; the
deferred analyses are what Book II must undertake before it can take them for granted. The
three together define the space of Book II’s work, and the chapter’s task is to state the space.


1.3      The Ledger of Established Claims
Book I established a great deal, and the establishment is distributed across its ten parts. The
present section gives the ledger, organized by part, with representative principles and definitions.
It does not list every entry—the Index of Principles of Book I is the complete inventory—but it
gives the structure, so that the reader can see what Book II inherits.

1.3.1     The Framework (Part I of Book I)
Book I established the four-column framework of explanatory cognition. The framework consists
of:

    • the definition of explanatory cognition (Definition 1.1), which fixes the scope of the
      framework;

    • the four roles of the framework—fixed element (Definition 2.1), fluid element (Definition 2.2),
      governing dynamics (Definition 2.3), context (Definition 2.4)—which fix the analytical
      vocabulary;

    • the four-column principle (Principle 3.1), which asserts the necessity of the four roles ((T))
      and their sufficiency ((E));
1.3. The Ledger of Established Claims                                                           5


  • the distinctness of the four roles (Principle 3.2), which asserts that no role is supplied by
    another ((T));

  • the conveyor principle (Principle 4.1), which asserts that no complete explanation of how
    one thing bears on another can omit a fluid element ((T));

  • the non-sequential connectivity (Principle 4.2), which asserts that the fluid element need
    not pass through every intermediate element ((T));

  • the context-dependence principle (Principle 5.1), which asserts that fixedness and fluidity
    are roles, not essences ((T));

  • the openness of relations (Definition 5.1), which asserts that every manifestation can become
    a fixed element of a further context ((A));

  • the infinity of contexts (Principle 5.2), which asserts that the contexts in which an identity
    can be cognized are not finite in number ((T), with the countable-or-uncountable question
    marked ((S)));

  • the impossibility of super-identity (Principle 6.1), which asserts that no finite subject can
    know all manifestations of an identity in all contexts ((T));

  • the three criteria of context validity—cross-checkability (Principle 6.2), minimality (Princi-
    ple 6.3), consistency (Principle 6.4)—which discipline the plurality of contexts ((A));

  • the definition of viability (Definition 6.2), which fixes the framework’s central descriptive
    concept ((A)).

   The framework is the analytical structure that Book II presupposes in every chapter. Book II
does not reargue the framework; it asks what the framework requires in the order of being.

1.3.2   The Ontology (Part II of Book I)
Book I established the seven-realm ontology: four fundamental realms and three barzakhic realms.
The ontology consists of:

    of the realms (Principle 7.1, (A));

  • the principle of determinate capacity of realms (Principle 7.2, (T));

  • the Divine Ground (Definition 7.3, (A)), the Throne-Domain (Definition 7.4, (A)), and the
    transcendence of the Divine Ground (Principle 7.3, (A));

  • the four fundamental realms—First Determination (Definition 7.5), Structural Determi-
    nation (Definition 7.6), Relational Manifestation (Definition 7.7), Material Manifestation
    (Definition 7.8);

  • the non-necessity of downward passage (Principle 7.4, (T));

  • the definition of barzakhic realm (Definition 8.1, (A)) and mediation (Definition 8.2, (A));

  • the independent reality of the barzakhic realms (Principle 8.1, (T));

  • the mixed nature of the barzakhic realms (Definition 8.3, (A));

  • the three hubs—Hub of Decree (Definition 8.4), Hub of Signification (Definition 8.5), Hub
    of Realization (Definition 8.6).

   The ontology is the structure that Book II deepens. Book II asks what each realm must be,
metaphysically, such that it can serve as a context for manifestation; what the barzakhic is, as a
metaphysical category; and what the non-passage of Book I presupposes in the order of being.

    • the definition of manifestation (Definition 10.1, (A)) and of essential feature (Definition 10.2,

    • the proposed principle of contextual manifestational capacity (Principle 10.1, proposed);
    • the essential homogeneity of manifestation (Principle 10.2, (A));

   The fixed elements are the subject of Book II’s Part II. Book II asks what substance, essence,

1.3.5   The Governing Dynamics (Part V of Book I)
Book I established the twenty-two rules of the seven realms: thirteen rules of the four fundamental

  • the principle that rules are structural constraints (Principle 16.1, (A));

  • the three rules of the Material Manifestation—causality (Principle 16.12, (E)), temporality
    (Principle 16.13, (A)), and discreteness (Principle 16.14, (E));

  • the unity of the rules of the fundamental realms (Principle 16.15, (E));

  • the principle that rules of barzakhic realms are rules of transition (Principle 17.1, (A));

  • the three rules of the Hub of Decree—proportion (Principle 17.2, (A)), order (Principle 17.3,
    (A)), and harmony (Principle 17.4, (A));

  • the three rules of the Hub of Signification—truthfulness (Principle 17.5, (A)), accuracy
    (Principle 17.6, (A)), and fidelity (Principle 17.7, (A));

  • the three rules of the Hub of Realization—proportion in realization (Principle 17.8, (A)),
    preservation of the realized (Principle 17.9, (A)), and continuation of realization (Princi-
    ple 17.10, (A));

  • the unity of the rules of the barzakhic realms (Principle 17.11, (E)).

  The governing dynamics are the subject of Book II’s Part IV. Book II asks what law and
modality must be, such that the twenty-two rules can be instances of them.

1.3.7    The Resolutions (Part VII of Book I)
Book I resolved the apparent tensions among its principles by the principle of category-relative
predication (Principle 27.1, (A)). The resolutions include the distinction of the plurality of
manifestations from the plurality of identities (Principle 28.1, (T)), the definition of recursive
manifestation (Definition 28.3, (A)), the structural duality of expression (Principle 29.1, (E)),
the principle that tendency is not success (Principle 30.1, (T)), and the principle that function is
not dependence (Principle 31.1, (T)). The resolutions are the subject of Book II’s Part V, where
the category-relative structure is applied to the relation between a realm’s function and its mode
of existence.

    The extensions are the subject of Book II’s Part IV (the modal space) and of Part VII (the

1.3.10    The Boundaries (Part X of Book I)
Book I’s Part X fixed the boundaries of philosophy (Principle 41.1, (A); Principle 41.2, (T);
Principle 41.3, (T)) and stated the conditional character of the book (Principle 42.1, (A)). The

1.3.11    The Core
Book I’s Chapter E audited the framework’s commitments and identified the core: thirteen
commitments on which every other claim of the framework depends. The core commitments are
C1 (Finitude of the Subject), C2 (Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos), C3 (Independent
Reality of the Realms), C4 (Transcendence of the Divine Ground), C5 (Identity Conservation),
C6 (Non-Duplicability), C7 (Trans-Categorical Character of Light), C8 (Expression as Structural
Necessity), C9 (Category-Relative Predication), C10 (Autonomy of Philosophical Justification),
C11 (Openness of Relations), C12 (Totality of Possibility), and C13 (The Trans-Categorical
Triad). Book II’s (D) claims are conditional on this core, and the Index of Cross-References to
Book I states the dependency for each.


1.4      The Ledger of Open Questions
Book I did not close its inquiry. It identified, in its Chapter 41, nine open questions, and in its
Chapter 40, nine more. The eighteen are the negative space of Book I: they state where the
framework stopped, and they indicate where Book II begins.

1.4.1    The Four Conceptual Questions (Book I, Ch. 41)
The four conceptual questions are:

  • Q1: Under what structural conditions can two viabilities be jointly realized in the same
    realm? (Book I, Chapter 41, §41.7)

  • Q2: Where does a reduction of structural viability become the singularity of death? (Book I,
    Chapter 41, §41.7)

  • Q3: What exactly is the conceptual relation between light and expression? (Book I,
    Chapter 41, §41.7)

  • Q4: What is the mode of the relation between the structural light and its divine source?
    (Book I, Chapter 41, §41.7)

   The four questions are conceptual: they concern the framework’s concepts and their relations.
They are open because Book I’s principles make them visible without answering them.

1.4.2    The Five Argumentative Questions (Book I, Ch. 41)
The five argumentative questions are:

  • Q5: What is the relation among self-awareness, consciousness, awareness, and the subject?
    (Book I, Chapter 41, §41.8)
10                                 Chapter 1. What Book I Established and What It Left Open


     • Q6: What are the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and of the balance criterion?
       (Book I, Chapter 41, §41.8)

     • Q7: Can the principle of contextual manifestational capacity and the criterion of mani-
       festational adequacy be given independent definition and support? (Book I, Chapter 41,
       §41.8)

     • Q8: What is the exact relation among the three aspects of cost? (Book I, Chapter 41,
       §41.8)

     • Q9: How can the structural description serve as the basis for a normative prescription?
       (Book I, Chapter 41, §41.8)

   The five questions are argumentative: they concern the framework’s arguments and their
premises. They are open because the framework’s arguments, as given, do not settle them.

1.4.3     The Three Metaphysical Questions (Book I, Ch. 41)
The three metaphysical questions are:

     • Q10: What is the structural possibility and ontological standing of the realization of
       identities in the barzakhic realms? (Book I, Chapter 41, §41.9)

     • Q11: What are the particular direct relations among the realms? (Book I, Chapter 41,
       §41.9)

     • Q12: Can the doctrine that identity is more than signature be given further support?
       (Book I, Chapter 41, §41.9)

    The three questions are metaphysical: they concern the framework’s ontology and its structural
claims. They are open because the framework’s ontology, as given, does not settle them.

1.4.4     The Nine Questions of Book I’s Chapter 40
Book I’s Chapter 40 identified nine further open questions, all of them arising from the structural
extensions of Part IX:

     • Q40.1 (Weighting): Which measure of capacity is the right one for comparing a space’s
       gains and losses?

     • Q40.2 (Failure to act): Is the failure to act, when an action was available that would have
       expanded a space, itself a contraction?

     • Q40.3 (The infinite network): How is an action assessed in a network of affected identities
       that no finite subject can survey?

     • Q40.4 (Grounding): What is the precise structure of the grounding of the modal space and
       of the Throne-Domain in God?

     • Q40.5 (Fundamental and divine self-awareness): Is fundamental self-awareness the divine
       self-awareness, or a condition that the divine self-awareness grounds?

     • Q40.6 (Time): Is structural time a feature of the realms independent of any subject, or of
       the relation between the realms and fundamental self-awareness?

     • Q40.7 (The boundary of duty): An action that leaves a space as it is but improves the
       harmony of the space with self-awareness: duty or virtue?
1.5. The Ledger of Deferred Analyses                                                                11


   • Q40.8 (The agent of a contextual act): Can an act without deliberation have an agent?

   • Q40.9 (The attempt): What is the status of an attempt whose effect does not land?

   The nine questions are technical and specific; they arise from the particular models that
Book I’s Part IX introduces, and they are open because the models, as given, do not settle them.


1.5     The Ledger of Deferred Analyses
The third ledger is the most important for Book II’s project, and it is the one that Book I did
not state as an open question. Book I used a vocabulary that it did not analyze. The vocabulary
is the metaphysical vocabulary of the framework—substance, essence, causation, law, modality,
subsistence—and Book I used it as the medium of its structural description, but it did not
analyze it. The deferral was deliberate (as Book I’s Chapter 41 said), and Book II is the analysis
that was deferred.
    The deferred analyses fall into five families, and each family is the subject of a part of Book II.

1.5.1    The Deferred Analysis of Substance
Book I used the notion of substance in its account of the fixed element of an explanation: an
entity that can be held invariant while its relations are explained. It did not ask what substance
must be, such that it can be held invariant; it did not distinguish substance from constitution,
from essence, from modality. The distinction between a thing and its constitution—between what
a thing is and what it is made of—was not drawn by Book I; it was deferred to the metaphysics.
    The deferred analysis of substance is the subject of Book II’s Chapter 5.

1.5.2    The Deferred Analysis of Essence
Book I used the notion of essence in its definition of identity: an identity is what remains invariant
under a class of allowable transformations, and the defining invariants are the features that
constitute its determination. The definition was given, but the metaphysical question—what is
an essence, such that it can be the determination of an identity?—was not asked. Is essence the
same as the defining invariants of Book I? Is it a real feature of the thing, or a convention of the
describer? Is it compatible with the essentialism that Book I’s account of identity implies?
   The deferred analysis of essence is the subject of Book II’s Chapter 6.

1.5.3    The Deferred Analysis of Causation
Book I used the notion of causation in its conveyor principle and in its account of the rules of the
Material Manifestation. The conveyor principle was argued analytically: no complete explanation
of how one thing bears on another can omit a fluid element. The principle was established; the
metaphysical question—what is causation, such that a fluid element can be a conveyor of it?—was
not asked. Is causation a regularity, a counterfactual dependence, a disposition, a power? Is the
conveyor principle compatible with any of these accounts, or does it require one of them?
    The deferred analysis of causation is the subject of Book II’s Chapter 9.

1.5.4    The Deferred Analysis of Law
Book I used the notion of law in its twenty-two rules of the seven realms. The rules were stated
(Part V), and their unity was argued (Principle 16.15, Principle 17.11). The rules were argued to
be structural constraints on the realms’ modes of existence (Principle 16.1); the metaphysical
question—what is a law, such that a rule can be a structural constraint?—was not asked. Is a
12                                Chapter 1. What Book I Established and What It Left Open


law a regularity, a necessitation, a disposition, a power? Is the necessity of the rules metaphysical
necessity, natural necessity, or logical necessity?
   The deferred analysis of law is the subject of Book II’s Chapter 13.

1.5.5    The Deferred Analysis of Modality
Book I used the notion of modality in its Part IX, where it introduced the modal space
Ω (Principle 37.1), the actualization chain X (Definition 37.1), and the two kinds of divine
knowledge (Principle 37.4). The modal space was introduced as the space of all possibilities, and
the actualization chain as the possibilities that are actualized. The metaphysical question—what
is a possibility, such that it can be in a space? Is the space a set of possible worlds, a space
of propositions, a space of possibilities as such?—was not asked. The question of the relation
between modality and time, between modality and grounding, between modality and God, was
raised (Q40.4) but not settled.
    The deferred analysis of modality is the subject of Book II’s Chapters 14 and 15.

1.5.6    The Deferred Analysis of the Categories
Beyond the five families above, Book I used the categories of being—what there is, in the most
general sense—without analyzing them. It used the category of substance (in the fixed element),
of relation (in the fluid element and in light), of process (in the account of manifestation), of
accident (in the account of non-essential features). It used the categories without asking what a
category is, what categories there are, and how the categories of Book I relate to the classical
categories of Aristotle or Kant.
    The deferred analysis of the categories is the subject of Book II’s Chapter 6 and Chapter 7
(where substance and essence are analyzed), and of the integration in Chapter 25 (where the
categories are shown to be the metaphysical structure of the four columns).


1.6     What Book II Undertakes
The three ledgers together define Book II’s undertaking. Book II undertakes three tasks, and
each task corresponds to one ledger.
    The first task: the analysis of the deferred concepts. Book II analyzes the concepts that Book I
used without analyzing: substance, essence, causation, law, modality, and the categories. The
analysis is the subject of Book II’s Parts II, III, and IV. It is the book’s principal contribution,
because it is the analysis that Book I’s framework requires but does not give.
    The second task: the address of the open questions. Book II addresses the eighteen open
questions of Book I, at the strength that its own arguments support. It does not attempt to
answer every question; it addresses the questions that its analysis of the deferred concepts makes
tractable, and it marks the others as still open. The address is distributed across Book II’s
Parts II to VI, and it is summarized in Part VIII.
    The third task: the statement of the metaphysical conditions of the core. Book II states the
metaphysical conditions under which Book I’s core commitments can hold. It does not attempt
to prove the core commitments; it states what the commitments require in the order of being,
and it marks the (D) claims that express the requirements. The statement is the subject of
Book II’s Part VI, and the divine ground of the requirements is the subject of Part VII.
    The three tasks are distinct, and each is offered at its own strength. The first task is (T) or
(E), depending on the specific analysis; the second is (T) where the framework’s principles settle
the question, (Q) where they do not; the third is (D) throughout, because the metaphysical
conditions are conditional on Book I’s core.

1.8       What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Three things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not give the ledger of every claim of Book I. The Index of Principles
and the Index of Arguments of Book I are the complete inventories; the present chapter gives the
structure, not the full list. A reader who wishes to see the full ledger is directed to those indices,
and to the Index of Cross-References to Book I in the back matter of the present book.
    Second, the chapter does not analyze the deferred concepts. The analysis is the subject of
the later parts of Book II; the present chapter only names the concepts, and states that their
analysis is Book II’s first task. A reader who expects the analysis in this chapter has misread the
chapter’s scope; the analysis begins in Chapter 5.
    Third, the chapter does not address the open questions. The address is the subject of the
later chapters and of Part VIII. The present chapter only lists the questions, and states that
their address is Book II’s second task. A reader who expects the address in this chapter has
misread the chapter’s scope; the address begins in Chapter 5 and is summarized in Chapter 30.
    The three deferrals are not weaknesses. They are the conditions under which the chapter
is offered, and they are stated so that the reader knows what kind of claim is being made. A
reader who accepts the deferrals accepts the chapter’s scope; a reader who does not has a reason
to read the later chapters, where the deferrals are lifted.

1.10      A Question for Reflection
Consider a domain you know well—a discipline, a practice, a tradition. What did it establish,
and what did it leave open? What did it use without analyzing? If someone were to write the
metaphysics of your domain—the account of what must be the case for the domain’s claims to
hold—what would that metaphysics have to undertake? Which of its concepts would it have to
analyze, which of its open questions would it have to address, and which of its core commitments
would it have to state the conditions of?
    The answer is a model of Book II’s task. The book is the metaphysics of the framework of
viability, and its three tasks are the same three tasks that any metaphysics of any domain would
undertake: the analysis of the domain’s deferred concepts, the address of the domain’s open
questions, and the statement of the metaphysical conditions of the domain’s core commitments.
The model is offered as a way of seeing the book’s project, not as a proof of its claims.

The next chapter states the method by which Book II undertakes its three tasks. It asks how the
four-column framework of Book I can be applied to metaphysics itself, and it states the analytical
structure of the metaphysical inquiry. With the method in place, the book can begin its analysis
of the deferred concepts, in Part II.

Chapter 2

The Four-Column Framework as a
Method of Ontology

Scope. This chapter states the method by which Book II undertakes its three tasks. It argues
that metaphysical inquiry is itself a form of explanatory cognition, and that the four-column
framework of Book I therefore applies to it: every metaphysical inquiry has fixed elements, a
fluid element, governing dynamics, and a context. It defines the four columns of metaphysical
inquiry, states the removal test and the reducibility test at the metaphysical level, and—most
importantly—states the distinction between the analytical roles of metaphysical inquiry and
the ontological content that fills them. The distinction is the chapter’s principal contribution,
because it is what prevents the application from becoming a confusion of the method with the
ontology. Its claims are methodological and structural; where it speaks of “inquiry,” “method,”
“role,” or “content,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this
chapter and by the definitions of Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Principle 1.1 of Book I (the
distinction between cognitive and ontological architecture), Principle 3.1 (the four-column
principle, in its necessity and sufficiency halves), Principle 3.2 (the distinctness of the four roles),
Definitions 2.1 to 2.4 (the four columns), and Principle 4.1 (the conveyor principle). It does not
restate these principles; it asks what they require when they are applied to metaphysical inquiry
itself.


2.1     A Scene
Consider a person who asks three questions about the same thing. The thing is a stone, and the
person asks:

   1. What does the word “stone” mean?

   2. How do we know that this is a stone?

   3. What must the world be, such that there can be stones?

    The three questions are not the same, and the person who asks one is not asking the others.
The first is semantic: it asks for the meaning of a word. The second is epistemological: it asks
for the conditions under which a stone can be known. The third is metaphysical: it asks for the
conditions under which a stone can exist.
    The three questions have a common form. Each seeks to understand how something stands to
something else. The semantic question seeks to understand how the word stands to its referent.
The epistemological question seeks to understand how the knower stands to the known. The
16                          Chapter 2. The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology


metaphysical question seeks to understand how the stone stands to the conditions of its existence.
The three questions are different, but they are all questions of the same form: they are questions
of understanding how things stand.
    Now consider the person’s method for answering the third question. She does not begin with
an inventory of stones; she begins with a question about what a stone must be. She asks: what is
the fixed element in the stone—what is held invariant when we speak of it? She asks: what is the
fluid element—what conveys the effect of one stone on another, or of the stone on the observer?
She asks: what are the governing dynamics—what rules govern the behavior of stones? She asks:
what is the context—in what frame is the stone individuated as this stone rather than another?
    The four questions are the four columns of Book I, and the person is asking them about a
metaphysical question, not about an explanatory one. She is asking what the stone must be,
and she is asking it in the four-column form. The form is the same, but the subject is different:
Book I asked the four questions about explanatory cognition; the person in the scene asks them
about a metaphysical inquiry.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. If the four-column framework applies to
explanatory cognition, does it apply to metaphysical inquiry? And if it does, what does the
application consist in? The chapter’s answer is: yes, it applies, because metaphysical inquiry is a
form of explanatory cognition; and the application consists in treating the four columns as the
analytical structure of any metaphysical question, not as the ontological content of the answer.
The distinction between the analytical structure and the ontological content is the chapter’s
principal contribution.


2.2     The Question
The question of the chapter is: can the four-column framework of Book I be applied to meta-
physical inquiry itself? And if it can, what does the application establish, and what does it not
establish?
    The question is not idle. If the framework applies to metaphysical inquiry, then Book II has a
method: it can ask, of any metaphysical concept, what its fixed element is, what its fluid element
is, what its governing dynamics is, and what its context is. The method would give Book II the
same analytical discipline that Book I gave to explanatory cognition, and it would allow Book II
to organize its inquiry into the deferred concepts (Chapter 1, §5) as a systematic application of
the framework.
    But the application has a danger. If the framework is applied to metaphysical inquiry without
qualification, it may be taken to establish the framework itself—and that would be circular. The
framework would be used to justify the framework, and the justification would be empty. The
chapter must therefore distinguish two things: the application of the framework as a method,
and the justification of the framework as a claim. The first is what the chapter does; the second
is what Book I did, and what Book II does not repeat.
    Three aspects of the question must be distinguished.
    The first aspect: is metaphysical inquiry a form of explanatory cognition? If it is, then
Book I’s Principle 3.1 applies to it, and the four-column framework is the analytical structure of
metaphysical inquiry. If it is not, the framework does not apply, and Book II needs a different
method.
    The second aspect: if the framework applies, what are the four columns of metaphysical
inquiry? The columns are the same roles as in Book I—fixed element, fluid element, governing
dynamics, context—but the content that fills them is different. The chapter must state the
difference, so that the application is not a confusion of the two.
    The third aspect: what does the application establish, and what does it not establish? The
application establishes a method: it gives Book II the analytical structure of its inquiry. It does
not establish the framework itself; the framework is established by Book I, and the application is
2.3. Metaphysical Inquiry as Explanatory Cognition                                               17


not a re-justification. The chapter must state the distinction clearly, so that the reader does not
mistake the method for a proof.
    The three aspects are treated in the three sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: yes,
metaphysical inquiry is a form of explanatory cognition; the four columns of metaphysical inquiry
are the four columns of Book I, applied to a different subject; and the application is a method,
not a justification.


2.3     Metaphysical Inquiry as Explanatory Cognition
2.3.1    The Argument
The argument for the first aspect is short, and its brevity is the point.

Principle 2.1 (Metaphysical Inquiry Is Explanatory Cognition). (T) Metaphysical inquiry is a
form of explanatory cognition: it seeks to understand how some things stand to one another,
and its aim is to make the standing intelligible.

    Argument. The argument has three premises, and each is a premise that the reader can assess
on its own.

   1. Premise 1. Every inquiry that seeks to understand how some things stand to one another
      is explanatory cognition, in the sense of Book I’s Definition 1.1.

   2. Premise 2. Metaphysical inquiry seeks to understand how some things stand to one another:
      it seeks to understand how a thing stands to the conditions of its existence, how a property
      stands to its bearer, how a cause stands to its effect, how a possibility stands to its
      actualization.

   3. Premise 3. Therefore, metaphysical inquiry is explanatory cognition, in the sense of Book I’s
      Definition 1.1.

   The argument is valid, and its premises are the framework’s own definitions. Premise 1 is
Book I’s Definition 1.1, stated in the form of a general criterion. Premise 2 is the chapter’s claim
about the subject matter of metaphysics: that metaphysics asks how things stand, not merely
what words mean or how things are known. The conclusion follows by modus ponens.

2.3.2    Objections and Replies
The argument is short, and its brevity invites three objections. Each objection is stated, and the
reply is given.
    Objection 1: Metaphysics asks what is, not how things stand. The objection is that metaphysics
is the inquiry into being as being, not the inquiry into relations among beings. Its question is
“what is there?”, not “how do things stand?”.
    Reply. The objection rests on a false dichotomy. The question “what is there?” is itself a
question of how things stand: it asks how the things that are stand to the conditions of their
being. The question “what is a substance?” asks how a substance stands to its accidents, its
essence, its existence. The question “what is a cause?” asks how a cause stands to its effect. The
question “what is a possibility?” asks how a possibility stands to its actualization. In each case,
the metaphysical question is a question of standing, and the answer is an account of how the
standing works. The objection mistakes the surface grammar of the question (“what is?”) for its
logical form (“how does it stand?”). The logical form is the form of explanatory cognition.
    Objection 2: Metaphysics is not explanatory, because it does not explain particular phenomena.
The objection is that the natural sciences explain particular phenomena (why the stone fell, why
18                          Chapter 2. The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology


the water boiled), while metaphysics explains nothing in particular; it only clarifies concepts. On
this view, metaphysics is conceptual analysis, not explanation.
    Reply. The objection rests on a narrow conception of explanation. Explanation, in Book I’s
sense, is not limited to the explanation of particular phenomena; it is the making-intelligible
of how things stand. Metaphysics makes intelligible how a thing stands to the conditions of its
existence; that is an explanation, even if the thing is not a particular phenomenon. The natural
sciences explain particular phenomena by appealing to laws and causes; metaphysics explains
the laws and causes themselves, by appealing to the conditions under which they can hold. The
two are explanations at different levels, and the difference of level does not make the higher one
non-explanatory.
    Objection 3: If metaphysics is explanatory cognition, then the four-column framework applies
to it trivially, and the application establishes nothing. The objection is that the argument from
Principle 1.1 is too easy: if every explanatory cognition has four columns, and metaphysics is
explanatory cognition, then metaphysics has four columns; but this is a trivial consequence, and
a trivial consequence cannot ground a method.
    Reply. The objection is half right. The inference from Principle 1.1 to the conclusion is
indeed short, and the shortness is the point: the chapter’s contribution is not the inference but
the content of the four columns when applied to metaphysics. The inference gives the form; the
content gives the method. The content is the subject of the next section, and it is not trivial:
it requires distinguishing the four columns of metaphysical inquiry from the four columns of
explanatory cognition, and it requires stating the removal test and the reducibility test at the
metaphysical level. The objection mistakes the inference for the whole chapter; the inference is
the beginning, not the end.

2.3.3    What the Argument Establishes
The argument establishes that metaphysical inquiry has the same general form as explanatory
cognition: it is a form of understanding how things stand. The argument does not establish that
the four columns of metaphysics are the same as the four columns of Book I; it establishes that
metaphysics has some four-column structure, and it leaves the content of the columns to the
next section.
    The distinction is important. The argument establishes the applicability of the framework;
the next section establishes the content of the application. The first is (T) relative to Book I’s
Principle 1.1; the second is (A), because the content of the columns is a stipulation that the
chapter introduces, and the reader may reject it by proposing a different content.


2.4     The Four Columns of Metaphysical Inquiry
The four columns of metaphysical inquiry are the four columns of Book I, applied to the subject
matter of metaphysics. They are stated in four definitions, and the definitions are stipulations
that fix the vocabulary of the chapter and of the book.

2.4.1    The Fixed Element of Metaphysical Inquiry
Definition 2.2 (Fixed Element of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) A fixed element of a metaphysical
inquiry is an entity, kind, or category that the inquiry holds invariant while it explains the
conditions of its being. Its fixedness is methodological: it is held stable for the purpose of
explaining its conditions, and does not by itself imply that the entity is ontologically ultimate.

    The definition is the metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s Definition 2.1. In Book I, the fixed
element is an entity held invariant in an explanation of how things stand; in Book II, the fixed
element is an entity, kind, or category held invariant in an explanation of the conditions of being.
2.4. The Four Columns of Metaphysical Inquiry                                                      19


The difference is the subject matter: Book I explains relations among entities; Book II explains
the conditions under which entities can be what they are.
    Three remarks on the definition.
    Remark. The definition applies to entities, kinds, and categories alike. A metaphysical inquiry
may hold a particular entity (this stone) invariant while it explains the conditions of its being; it
may hold a kind (stones as such) invariant while it explains what it is to be a stone; it may hold
a category (substance) invariant while it explains what it is to be a substance. The three are
different fixed elements, and the inquiry may use one or more of them.
    Remark. The fixedness is methodological, not ontological. To hold a category invariant in
a metaphysical inquiry is to decide, for the purpose of the inquiry, not to vary it. It is not to
claim that the category cannot vary, or that the category is the ultimate furniture of the world.
The distinction is the same as Book I’s distinction between the methodological fixedness of an
element and the ontological invariance of an identity (Book I, §2.2).
    Remark. A fixed element of metaphysical inquiry can be a concept that the inquiry itself
introduces. The concept of “essence,” for example, is introduced by the inquiry into essence,
and the inquiry holds it invariant while it explains what an essence is. The introduction is not
a circularity, because the concept is not defined by the inquiry; it is the subject of the inquiry.
The distinction is the distinction between a concept that the inquiry uses and a concept that the
inquiry analyzes.

2.4.2    The Fluid Element of Metaphysical Inquiry
Definition 2.3 (Fluid Element of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) A fluid element of a metaphysical
inquiry is a relation, process, or medium that the inquiry invokes to explain how the conditions
of being of one fixed element bear on the conditions of being of another. It is the metaphysical
counterpart of the fluid element of Book I: it is what conveys the effect of the conditions of being
from one element to another.
     The definition is the metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s Definition 2.2. In Book I, the
fluid element is what conveys effect between fixed elements in an explanation; in Book II, the
fluid element is what conveys the effect of the conditions of being between fixed elements in a
metaphysical explanation. The examples are different: Book I’s fluid element may be a language,
a signal, a process; Book II’s fluid element may be a causal relation, a grounding relation, a
dependence relation.
     Two remarks on the definition.
     Remark. The metaphysical fluid element is the most controversial of the four columns, because
it is the one most easily taken for a metaphysical posit. The definition must be read carefully:
the fluid element is what the inquiry invokes, not what the inquiry has proved to be real. A
metaphysical inquiry that invokes causation to explain how causes bear on effects is not claiming
that causation is a metaphysical posit; it is using causation as the fluid element of its explanation,
and the reality of causation is the subject of the inquiry into causation, not its presupposition.
The distinction is the same as Book I’s distinction between the analytical role and the ontological
content (Book I, Principle 1.1).
     Remark. The fluid element of a metaphysical inquiry need not be a single relation. It may be
a family of relations, or a hierarchy of relations, or a structure of relations. The definition says
“a relation, process, or medium,” and the disjunction is intended to cover the variety.

2.4.3    The Governing Dynamics of Metaphysical Inquiry
Definition 2.4 (Governing Dynamics of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) A governing dynamics of a
metaphysical inquiry is a rule that explains how the fluid elements of the inquiry affect the fixed
elements of the inquiry. It is the metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s Definition 2.3: it is the
rule of the metaphysical explanation, the pattern that the explanation must obey.
20                          Chapter 2. The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology


     The definition is the metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s Definition 2.3. In Book I, the
governing dynamics is the rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed elements in an
explanation; in Book II, the governing dynamics is the rule that explains how the fluid elements
of the metaphysical inquiry affect the fixed elements of the inquiry. The examples are different:
Book I’s governing dynamics may be a law, a convention, a regularity; Book II’s governing
dynamics may be a law of grounding, a principle of dependence, a rule of metaphysical necessity.
     Two remarks on the definition.
     Remark. The governing dynamics of a metaphysical inquiry is itself a subject of the inquiry,
not merely a rule that the inquiry follows. The inquiry into causation asks what rule governs the
effect of causes on effects; that rule is the governing dynamics of the inquiry, and it is also the
subject of the inquiry. The reflexivity is not a circularity; it is the structure of a metaphysical
inquiry that asks about its own rules.
     Remark. The governing dynamics need not be a single rule. It may be a family of rules, or a
hierarchy of rules, or a structure of rules. The definition says “a rule,” and the indefinite article
is intended to cover the variety.

2.4.4    The Context of Metaphysical Inquiry
Definition 2.5 (Context of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) A context of a metaphysical inquiry is
the frame in which the inquiry’s fixed elements, fluid elements, and governing dynamics take
their specific content. The context determines what counts as a fixed element, what counts as
a fluid element, and which dynamics governs. It is the metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s
Definition 2.4.

    The definition is the metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s Definition 2.4. In Book I, the
context is the frame in which cognition occurs; in Book II, the context is the frame in which a
metaphysical inquiry occurs. The context may be an ontological framework (a particular ontology,
a particular tradition, a particular metaphysical system), or it may be a set of methodological
commitments (a commitment to a particular method, a commitment to a particular standard of
explanation), or it may be a combination of both.
    Three remarks on the definition.
    Remark. The context of a metaphysical inquiry is not the same as the existential context
of a manifestation (Book I, Definition 10.3). The existential context is the realm in which a
manifestation is realized; the context of a metaphysical inquiry is the frame in which the inquiry
is posed. The two are different, and the difference is the difference between the order of being
and the order of inquiry.
    Remark. The context is not chosen by the inquirer at will. It is fixed by the tradition, the
method, and the commitment that the inquiry inherits. The inquirer can revise the context,
but the revision is itself an act within a context, and the act presupposes the context it revises.
The point is the same as Book I’s point about the context-dependence of fixedness (Book I,
Principle 5.1): the context is not an arbitrary choice, but the frame in which the choice is made.
    Remark. The context of a metaphysical inquiry can be the seven realms of Book I, or it can
be a different ontological framework. The inquiry can be conducted within the framework of
Book I, or within a different framework, or in comparison between frameworks. The choice of
context is the choice of framework, and the choice determines what the inquiry can establish.

The four columns of metaphysical inquiry are stated in the following table, with the corresponding
columns of Book I.

   The table is a summary; it does not prove the definitions. The definitions are (A) stipulations

2.5    The Removal Test at the Metaphysical Level
The four columns of metaphysical inquiry are necessary only if the removal test succeeds at the
metaphysical level. The test is the same as Book I’s removal test, applied to a metaphysical
inquiry rather than to an explanatory one.

Principle 2.6 (Removal Test at the Metaphysical Level). (T, relative to the definitions of §5) If
a metaphysical inquiry omits one of the four columns, the inquiry is incomplete as a metaphysical
explanation.

   Argument. By the definitions of §5, a metaphysical inquiry says what is held invariant, by
what the conditions of being are conveyed, according to what rule, and from what frame. The
argument removes each column in turn and observes what remains.

  • Without fixed elements. There is nothing for the conditions of being to hold between. What
    remains is a flow of conditions with no terms, which is a description of a process but not of
    what the process holds. The resulting account is a recognizable metaphysical failure.

  • Without fluid elements. The fixed elements are a list, not a structure. Nothing is said about
    how the conditions of being of one element bear on the conditions of being of another. The
    resulting account is a recognizable metaphysical failure; the argument that this is so is the
    metaphysical counterpart of the conveyor principle, which the present chapter states in the
    next section.

  • Without governing dynamics. The structure is unordered: it shows that the conditions of
    being are connected, but not how the connection behaves. The resulting account cannot
    support inference from the conditions of one element to the conditions of another, and it is
    a recognizable metaphysical failure.

  • Without context. The explanation is a rule without a frame. The same elements can be
    partitioned into fixed and fluid in different ways, and the rule alone does not say which
    partition is intended. The resulting account is a recognizable metaphysical failure.

   Each removal yields a recognizable metaphysical failure. Hence each column is necessary for
a metaphysical inquiry, given the definitions of §5.
22                            Chapter 2. The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology


    Remark. The argument depends on a premise that is not itself proved: that we can recognize
a metaphysical failure when we see one. The premise is the metaphysical counterpart of Book I’s
premise that we can recognize an explanatory failure when we see one (Book I, §3.3), and it is a
commitment of the method. The framework does not claim more than the inspection delivers.
    Remark. The argument is relative to the definitions of §5. If the reader rejects the definitions,
the argument does not apply; the reader is invited to propose a different set of columns, and the
removal test will be applied to the proposed set.


2.6       The Reducibility Test at the Metaphysical Level
Sufficiency cannot be proved from the definitions, because a new kind of metaphysical inquiry
might always turn up. It is therefore offered as an estimate and supported by a test.

Principle 2.7 (Reducibility Test at the Metaphysical Level). (E) No fifth column is needed for
a metaphysical inquiry: every candidate fifth column that has been examined reduces to one of
the four.

   The test proceeds by examining the standard candidates for a fifth column, and asking, for
each, whether its role can be reassigned.

     • Candidate 1: the standard of truth. A metaphysical inquiry invokes a standard of truth
       (correspondence, coherence, pragmatic adequacy) to assess its claims. Is the standard a
       fifth column? No. The standard is part of the context: it fixes the frame in which the
       inquiry’s claims are assessed. The standard of truth is not a separate element of the inquiry;
       it is a feature of the frame.

     • Candidate 2: the inquirer. A metaphysical inquiry is conducted by an inquirer, and the
       inquirer’s perspective affects the inquiry. Is the inquirer a fifth column? No. The inquirer
       is part of the context: the inquirer’s perspective is a feature of the frame, not a separate
       element. Book I’s treatment of the perspective (Book I, Definition 10.4) is the precedent:
       the perspective is a feature of the context, not a separate column.

     • Candidate 3: the history of the inquiry. A metaphysical inquiry has a history (the tradition
       it inherits, the debates it engages). Is the history a fifth column? No. The history is part
       of the context: it fixes the frame in which the inquiry is posed, and it determines what the
       inquiry inherits and what it revises.

    These three are the standard candidates. The test would fail, and the principle would have
to be revised, if a metaphysical inquiry accepted as complete could be exhibited whose content
cannot be redistributed over the four columns in this way.
    Remark. The framework makes a risky claim, and says in advance what would refute it. A
candidate fifth column that resists reduction to the four would refute the sufficiency half of the
principle. The framework does not offer a proof that no such candidate can be found; it offers
an estimate, supported by the examination of the candidates that have been proposed, and it
invites the reader to produce a counterexample.


2.7       The Distinction Between Analytical and Ontological
The chapter’s principal contribution is the distinction between the analytical roles of metaphysical
inquiry and the ontological content that fills them. The distinction is the metaphysical counterpart
of Book I’s Principle 1.1, and it is what prevents the application from becoming a confusion of
the method with the ontology.
2.8. The Method Stated                                                                          23


Principle 2.8 (Analytical and Ontological at the Metaphysical Level). (D) The four columns of
metaphysical inquiry are four analytical roles that any complete metaphysical explanation must
assign. From the definitions of the columns alone it does not follow that reality consists of four
kinds of entity, nor that the four columns are the four categories of being, nor that the ontology
has four levels. The columns are analytical; the ontology is the content that fills them.

    Source. The principle is the metaphysical application of Book I’s Principle 1.1, which states
that the four columns of explanatory cognition are analytical roles, not ontological levels. The
application is straightforward: if the four columns of explanatory cognition are analytical, and
the four columns of metaphysical inquiry are the same four columns applied to a different subject,
then the four columns of metaphysical inquiry are analytical too.
    The distinction. The four columns are analytical roles; the ontology is the content that fills
them. When the metaphysical inquiry asks what the fixed element of a substance is, it is asking
what fills the fixed-element role in the inquiry into substance; it is not asking what the category
of substance is. The category of substance may be the content that fills the fixed-element role in
some inquiries and the fluid-element role in others; the roles and the contents are different, and
the confusion of the two is the confusion that Book I’s Principle 1.1 was stated to prevent.
    Consequence. The principle has three consequences, and the book relies on each of them.

  1. The method is not the ontology. The four columns are the method by which Book II
     organizes its metaphysical inquiry; they are not the ontology that the inquiry establishes.
     The inquiry’s result is an ontology, and the ontology is not the four columns. The distinction
     is the distinction between the method and the result.

  2. The categories of being are not the four columns. The categories of being—substance,
     quality, quantity, relation, and the others—are the content that fills the four columns in a
     particular inquiry. They are not the four columns. A metaphysical inquiry into substance
     uses the four columns to analyze substance; it does not confuse substance with one of the
     columns.

  3. The four columns of Book II are not the four columns of Book I. The two sets of columns
     have the same names (fixed element, fluid element, governing dynamics, context) and
     the same analytical role, but they apply to different subjects. Book I’s columns apply
     to explanatory cognition; Book II’s columns apply to metaphysical inquiry. The two
     applications are related, but they are not the same, and the difference is the difference of
     subject.

    What the principle does not say. The principle does not say that the four columns are
arbitrary, or that any set of columns would do. The four columns are the ones that Book I
established by the removal test and the reducibility test; their adequacy is the adequacy that
Book I’s arguments support. The principle says only that the columns are analytical, not
ontological; it does not say that the columns are optional.


2.8     The Method Stated
With the four columns in place, the removal test and the reducibility test at the metaphysical
level, and the distinction between the analytical and the ontological, the method of Book II can
be stated in a single principle.

Principle 2.9 (The Method of Book II). (A) Book II’s method is the following. For each
metaphysical concept that Book I used without analyzing, the book asks four questions: (i) what
is the fixed element of the concept—what does the concept hold invariant while it explains the
conditions of being? (ii) what is the fluid element of the concept—what does the concept invoke
24                          Chapter 2. The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology


to explain how the conditions of being of one thing bear on the conditions of being of another?
(iii) what is the governing dynamics of the concept—what rule does the concept state for the
effect of the fluid element on the fixed element? (iv) what is the context of the concept—in what
frame does the concept take its specific content? The book’s answer to the four questions is its
analysis of the concept; the analysis is offered at the strength that its arguments support, and it
is marked with a status label, as Book I marked its claims.

     The method is (A) because it is the book’s stipulation of its own procedure. Its justification is
its fruitfulness: the chapters that follow use the method to analyze substance, essence, causation,
law, modality, and the categories, and the analyses they produce are the evidence for the method’s
adequacy. A reader who accepts the method will find the chapters that follow systematic; a
reader who rejects it will find them arbitrary, because they presuppose the method. The book
states the method openly, so that the reader knows what the analyses depend on.
     Remark. The method is not the same as the four columns. The four columns are the
analytical structure; the method is the procedure by which the book applies the structure to a
particular concept. The method is the use of the four columns, not the four columns themselves.
The distinction is the same as Book I’s distinction between the four-column framework and the
method of its application (Book I, §1.4).
     Remark. The method is not the only method by which a metaphysical inquiry can be
conducted. Other methods—conceptual analysis, transcendental argument, phenomenological
description—are legitimate, and the book does not claim that its method is the only one. The
book claims that its method is the one that Book I’s framework requires, and that the method is
adequate for the book’s purpose. The claim is structural, not exclusive.


2.9     What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not apply the method to any specific concept. The application is the
subject of Parts II to IV of the book; the present chapter only states the method, and leaves its
application to the chapters that follow. The reader who expects the analysis of substance in this
chapter has misread the chapter’s scope; the analysis begins in Chapter 5.
    Second, the chapter does not prove that the four columns are the analytical structure of all
metaphysical inquiry. It proves that they are the analytical structure of the metaphysical inquiry
that Book II conducts, which is an inquiry into the conditions of being of the framework of
Book I. A different metaphysical inquiry might have a different analytical structure; the chapter
does not claim otherwise.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether metaphysical inquiry is a form of
explanatory cognition in every one of its parts. The argument of §4 establishes that the bulk
of metaphysical inquiry is explanatory; it leaves open whether some parts (for example, the
clarification of a concept, the statement of a definition) are explanatory in the same sense. The
question is a (Q) question, and the chapter marks it as such.
    Fourth, the chapter does not address the objection that the application of the four-column
framework to metaphysics is circular. The objection is addressed in §4, in the reply to Objection 3,
but the reply is brief, and the chapter does not claim to have settled the question. A reader who
finds the reply inadequate has found a place where the chapter’s argument is most vulnerable,
and is invited to develop the objection further.

2.11      A Question for Reflection
Consider a metaphysical concept you use in your own inquiry—substance, causation, identity,
truth, or another. If you were to analyze it by the method of this chapter, what would its fixed
element be? Its fluid element? Its governing dynamics? Its context? Which of the four is most
easily identified, and which is most easily overlooked? And if you were to analyze a concept
by this method, would the analysis be an explanation of the concept, or a description of the
concept’s use?
    The answer to the last question is a model of the method’s scope. The method explains the
concept by showing how the concept’s four columns work; the explanation is not a description
of how the concept is used, because the use is one thing and the conditions of the concept’s
applicability are another. The method’s aim is the second, not the first; the first is the subject of
a different inquiry (the inquiry into conceptual practice), and the method does not undertake it.

The next chapter states the epistemic status of the metaphysical claims that the method produces.
It asks what kind of claim a metaphysical claim is, and it states the statuses that the book’s claims
will carry. With the method in place and the statuses in hand, the book can begin its analysis of
the deferred concepts, in Part II.
