5.8     The Substance of Each Realm
The substance takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the
form, one realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered
at the strength that the framework’s principles support, and subject to revision if a different
form of substance in a realm does the same explanatory work.

5.8.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, substance takes the form of the extended, discrete, localized body.
The body is the ground of a material thing’s being the same one through change, and of its being
the subject of its material properties. The body is not the matter; the body is what the matter
has become, as the substance of a material thing. The distinction is the distinction of §5: the
matter is what the thing is made of; the body is what the thing is.

5.8.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, substance takes the form of the relation that is held invariant.
The relation is the ground of a relational thing’s being the same one through change—the ground
of a friendship’s being the same friendship, or a tradition’s being the same tradition. The relation
is not a bundle of relata; it is the structure that holds the relata together, and it is the substance
of the relational thing.

5.8.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, substance takes the form of the form or law that is held invariant.
The form is the ground of a structural thing’s being the same one through change—the ground
of a number’s being the same number, or a theorem’s being the same theorem. The form is not
a thing in the Material Manifestation’s sense; it is a structural invariant, and it is the substance
of the structural thing.

5.8.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, substance takes the form of pure unity. The First Determination has
no parts, no properties, no change; its substance is its unity, and its unity is its substance. The
form is the limit case of the other forms: it is what the other forms become when the multiplicity
is zero.
56                                                                          Chapter 5. Substance


5.8.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, substance takes the form of the measure—the allotment of the extent, the
limit, and the proportion within which an identity will express itself (Book I, Definition 8.4).
The measure is the ground of the apportioning’s being the same apportioning through change; it
is the substance of the apportioning.

5.8.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, substance takes the form of the sign—the structure standing as a sign
(Book I, Definition 8.5). The sign is the ground of the signification’s being the same signification
through change; it is the substance of the signification.

5.8.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, substance takes the form of the actualization—the realizing of what is
possible as something concrete (Book I, Definition 8.6). The actualization is the ground of the
realization’s being the same realization through change; it is the substance of the realization.

5.8.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

that the general definition of substance applies to all seven realms, not that the specific forms
are final.


5.9     Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: Substance is a relic of Aristotelian metaphysics; modern philosophy has abandoned
it. The objection is that substance was a central notion in Aristotle’s and in the rationalists’
metaphysics, but that modern philosophy—from Hume to the process philosophers to the
structuralists—has replaced it with notions of property, process, or structure. The framework’s
use of substance, the objection concludes, is a regression.
5.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                         57


    Reply. The objection confuses the history of the notion with the notion itself. The history of
a notion does not determine its truth; what determines its truth is whether the notion is required
by the framework that uses it. The present chapter has argued that the fixed element of Book I’s
framework presupposes a ground, and that the ground is what the framework calls substance.
If the argument is correct, the notion of substance is required by the framework, whatever its
history. The objection’s conclusion—that the notion is a regression—does not follow, because
the notion is not a regression to Aristotle; it is a metaphysical consequent of Book I’s framework.
    Objection 2: Bundle theory can do the job without substance. The objection is that a thing
can be analyzed as a bundle of properties, without a substance that underlies them. The bundle
theory—defended by Hume, by Russell, and by some contemporary metaphysicians—is simpler
than the substance theory, and it does not need the notion of a substance.
    Reply. The bundle theory cannot explain what makes the bundle one bundle. A bundle of
properties is a collection; a collection is one only if it is collected, and the collecting requires a
ground that is not another property. The ground is what the framework calls substance. The
bundle theory, therefore, presupposes substance, even when it denies it; it calls the presupposition
by a different name (the “compresence” of properties, or the “bundling relation”), but the
presupposition is the same. The objection mistakes the name for the thing; the thing is required,
whatever it is called.
    Objection 3: The chapter’s definition is circular. The definition says that substance is the
ground of a thing’s being the same one through change; but the notion of “the same one” is
Book I’s notion of identity, which Book I defined in terms of invariance. If substance is defined
in terms of identity, and identity is defined in terms of invariance, and invariance is a structural
feature, then the definition of substance is circular: it defines a metaphysical notion in terms of
a structural notion that the metaphysical notion is supposed to ground.
    Reply. The circularity is only apparent. The definition does not define substance in terms of
identity; it defines substance as the ground of identity. The distinction is the distinction between
the defined notion (substance) and the notion in terms of which it is defined (identity). The
substance is the ground of the identity; the identity is the structural feature that the substance
grounds. The two are distinct, and the definition does not identify them. The objection mistakes
the relation of grounding for a relation of identity; the reply distinguishes them.


5.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that substance exists. It argues that if the fixed element
of Book I’s framework is real, then substance is its ground; the antecedent is Book I’s, and the
chapter does not reargue it. The reader who accepts Book I’s framework accepts the antecedent,
and the chapter’s argument gives him the consequent; the reader who does not accept Book I’s
framework has no reason to accept the consequent, and the chapter states the argument at
exactly that strength.
    Second, the chapter does not analyze essence, thisness, or the relation between substance and
properties. The analyses are the subject of Chapters 6 and 7; the present chapter distinguishes
substance from essence and thisness, but it does not analyze them. The reader who expects the
analyses in this chapter has misread the chapter’s scope; the analyses begin in Chapter 6.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether there is one substance or many.
Monism, dualism, and pluralism are all compatible with the definition; the chapter does not
settle which is correct. The question is a (Q) question, and it is marked as such in the chapter’s
status table.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the form of substance in each realm at the strength of
a proof. The forms are (E) estimates; they are offered at the strength that the framework’s
principles support, and they are subject to revision. The reader who finds a form inadequate is
58                                                                         Chapter 5. Substance


invited to propose a different one; the framework’s claim is that the general definition applies,
not that the specific forms are final.

    The chapter’s claims are metaphysical and structural. The two definitions are (A) stipulations
that fix the chapter’s vocabulary; the two distinctions are (T) arguments from the definitions;
the principal claim is (D), because it depends on Book I’s definition of the fixed element; the
four-column structure is (T), because it applies the method of Chapter 2; the realm-specific forms
are (E), because they are estimates; the question of the number of substances is (Q), because the
chapter leaves it open.


5.12      A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a person, a place, a work of art, an institution. What is its
substance? Is it the material it is made of? The form it has? The history it carries? The function
it serves? Or is it the ground that these all express? And if it is the ground, what would it mean
for the thing to lose its substance? Would it cease to be the thing it is, or would it become a
different thing with the same appearance?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The substance is not the material, the
form, the history, or the function; it is the ground that these all express, and that makes them
the material, the form, the history, and the function of one thing. The reader who can state, for
a thing he knows, what its substance is, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who
cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the
difficulty further.

The next chapter analyzes essence: what it is for a thing to be the kind of thing it is, and how
essence relates to substance. With substance in place, the framework can distinguish what a thing
is (essence) from what grounds its being the thing it is (substance), and it can state the relation
between the two.
                                                                                                   59




Chapter 6

Essence and Essentialism

Scope. This chapter analyzes essence: what it is for a thing to be the kind of thing it is, and
what grounds a thing’s necessary properties. It defines essence as the constitutive what of a
thing—the determination that makes the thing the kind of thing it is, and that grounds the
features the thing cannot lose without ceasing to be the thing it is. It distinguishes essence from
substance, from thisness, and from accident; it argues that essence is what Book I’s defining
invariants (Definition 9.2) presuppose in the order of being; it states the essentialist thesis that
things have essences and gives three arguments for it; it states the four-column structure of the
inquiry into essence; it states the form that essence takes in each of the seven realms; and it
answers three standard objections. Its claims are metaphysical and structural; where it speaks of
“essence,” “kind,” “necessity,” “definition,” or “what,” these are structural terms; their sense is
fixed by the definitions in this chapter and by the framework of Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s definition of identity
(Definition 9.1), of defining invariants (Definition 9.2), of identity-preserving transformation
(Definition 9.3), and of essential feature (Definition 10.2); the principle of identity conservation
(Principle 9.5, C5); and the principle of non-duplicability (Principle 9.6, C6). It does not restate
these principles; it asks what they presuppose in the order of being. The presupposition is
stated in §6, and the chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that essence is the
presupposition.


6.1     A Scene
Consider a biologist in a field station, examining a specimen. The specimen is a small bird,
brown and undistinguished, that she has captured and measured. She writes in her notebook:
This is a sparrow. The statement is not a statement about the bird’s color (many small birds are
brown); it is not a statement about its size (many sparrows are larger, and many larger birds are
smaller); it is not a statement about its location (sparrows are found on every continent). What,
then, is the statement about? What is the sparrow that the statement names?
    The biologist’s statement is a statement about the bird’s essence—about what it is to be
the kind of bird the bird is. The essence is not the bird’s color, or its size, or its location. The
essence is the constitutive what of the bird: the determination that makes the bird a sparrow,
and that grounds the features the bird cannot lose without ceasing to be a sparrow. A bird that
lost its color, its size, or its location would still be a sparrow; a bird that lost its essence would
not be a sparrow at all—it would be a different kind of bird, or no bird at all.
    The distinction is not merely a biologist’s convention. The bird’s essence is not a label that
the biologist applies; it is the determination that the label describes. The essence is real, and the
biologist’s statement is true because the essence is what it is. The essence is also not the bird’s
substance; the bird’s substance makes the bird the same bird through time, while the bird’s
60                                                        Chapter 6. Essence and Essentialism


essence makes the bird a sparrow. The two are distinct, and the distinction is the chapter’s
principal task to state.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is essence? What is the metaphysical
ground of a thing’s being the kind of thing it is, and of its necessary properties? And what does
the framework of Book I require, in the order of being, when it speaks of the defining invariants
of an identity? The chapter’s answer is: essence. The chapter’s task is to say what essence is,
to distinguish it from the notions with which it is easily confused, and to show that it is the
metaphysical consequent of Book I’s defining invariants.


6.2     The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is essence, and what does it presuppose?
    The question is not the same as the question of Book I’s Chapter 9, and it is not the same as
the question of Chapter 5. Book I asked what identity is, and it answered: identity is invariance
under a class of allowable transformations (Definition 9.1). The answer was structural. Chapter 5
asked what grounds the invariance, and it answered: substance, the ground of a thing’s being
the same one through change. The answer was metaphysical. The present chapter asks a third
question: what grounds the thing’s being the kind of thing it is, and its necessary properties?
The answer is essence, and the answer is metaphysical.
    The three questions are distinct: identity is the structural feature, substance is the ground
of the sameness, and essence is the ground of the whatness. The three are related—a thing’s
identity is invariant because its substance grounds the sameness and its essence grounds the
whatness—but they are not the same, and the chapter must keep them apart.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of essence? The chapter must define essence, and it
must distinguish the definition from the definitions of substance (Chapter 5, Definition 5.1) and
of thisness (Chapter 7). The definition must be precise enough to be argued about, and general
enough to cover the essence of each of the seven realms.
    The second aspect: what is the relation between essence and Book I’s defining invariants?
The chapter must state how essence relates to Book I’s Definition 9.2. The relation is the
chapter’s principal contribution, because it is what makes essence a metaphysical consequent of
the framework, not a metaphysical posit alongside it.
    The third aspect: does essentialism hold? The chapter must state the essentialist thesis—the
thesis that things have essences—and it must give the arguments for it. The arguments are the
chapter’s case for the thesis, and they are what makes the chapter a metaphysical analysis, not a
mere stipulation of a definition.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: essence
is the constitutive what of a thing; it is what Book I’s defining invariants presuppose; and
essentialism holds, because without essences no thing would be any kind of thing.


6.3     The Definition of Essence
6.3.1   The Definition
Definition 6.1 (Essence). (A) An essence is the constitutive what of a thing: the determination
that makes the thing the kind of thing it is, and that grounds the features the thing cannot lose
without ceasing to be the thing it is.

   The definition has three components, and each is important.
   The first component: essence is a what. An essence answers the question “what is it?” in
the sense that identifies the kind—the species, the natural kind, the form of life, the structure
of meaning. The what is not a which: the essence does not identify the particular thing; it
6.3. The Definition of Essence                                                                     61


identifies the kind the thing belongs to. A particular sparrow is this sparrow; its essence is being
a sparrow, which it shares with every other sparrow. The what and the which are distinct, and
Chapter 7 states the distinction.
    The second component: essence makes the thing the kind of thing it is. The essence is what
makes the thing belong to its kind—the determination by which the thing is a sparrow rather
than a robin, or a violin rather than a cello. Without the essence, the thing would not be the
kind of thing it is; it would be a different kind of thing, or no kind at all.
    The third component: essence grounds the necessary properties. A necessary property is a
property that the thing cannot lose without ceasing to be the thing it is. The essence is what
grounds the necessity—the determination that makes the properties necessary. The properties
are not necessary because they are listed in a definition; they are necessary because the essence
requires them. The essence is the ground, and the necessity is what the ground grounds.
    The three components are not three definitions; they are three aspects of one definition. The
essence is the constitutive what, and the constitutive what makes the thing the kind of thing it
is and grounds the properties it cannot lose—and these are three ways of saying the same thing,
because a thing’s whatness, its kind-membership, and its necessary properties are three aspects
of its essence.

6.3.2    What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
    It does not say that essence is a thing. The essence is a what, not a thing. It is the
determination that makes the thing the kind of thing it is, not another thing in addition to the
thing. The distinction is the distinction between the what and the thing—the essence is the first,
and the thing (with its properties) is the second. The essence is not a hidden entity; it is the
determination that the thing exhibits in being what it is.
    It does not say that essence is a concept. The essence is not a concept in the mind of the
knower; it is the determination in the thing, independently of whether anyone knows it. A concept
is a mental representation; an essence is the determination that the representation represents
(when it is adequate). The two are distinct, and the distinction is the distinction between the
epistemic and the ontic—which the framework keeps throughout (Book I, Chapter 10).
    It does not say that essence is a set of properties. The essence is not a set of properties; it is
the determination that grounds the properties’ being necessary. A set of properties is a collection;
the essence is what makes the collection the properties of one kind of thing. The distinction is
the same as Chapter 5’s distinction between substance and composition: the composition is what
the thing is made of; the substance is what makes the composition the composition of one thing.
The essence is what makes the set of properties the properties of one kind.
    It does not say that essence is fixed. The essence of a thing can be discovered, refined, or
corrected. The biologist’s first classification of the bird may be wrong; a further examination
may reveal that the bird is a different species. The essence is fixed by the thing, not by the
biologist’s first classification; the classification is an approximation, and the essence is what
the classification approximates. The distinction is the same as Book I’s distinction between
identity and pseudo-identity (Book I, Definition 9.5): the essence is the identity’s whatness; the
classification is the pseudo-identity of the whatness.

6.3.3    Essence and Accident
Definition 6.2 (Essential and Accidental Properties). (A) An essential property of a thing is a
property that belongs to its essence, and that the thing cannot lose without ceasing to be the
thing it is. An accidental property of a thing is a property that does not belong to its essence,
and that the thing can lose without ceasing to be the thing it is.
62                                                          Chapter 6. Essence and Essentialism


    The distinction between essential and accidental properties is classical, and the framework
uses it. The distinction is not between two kinds of properties in themselves; it is between
two roles that a property plays relative to a thing’s essence. A property is essential to a thing
when it belongs to the thing’s essence; a property is accidental to a thing when it does not.
The same property can be essential to one thing and accidental to another—being rational,
for example, is essential to a human being and accidental to a machine that can reason. The
framework’s use of the distinction is the same as Book I’s use of the essential/non-essential
distinction (Definition 10.2): the role is analytical, and the same property can play different roles
in different things.


6.4     Essence and Substance
The first distinction that essence requires is the distinction from substance.

6.4.1    What a Thing Is Is Not the Ground of Its Being One
The distinction is the distinction between the what and the one. The essence of a thing is what
the thing is—the kind, the form, the determination. The substance of a thing is what grounds
the thing’s being the same one through change and of its being the subject of its properties. The
two are distinct: a thing can be the same one through change while its essence is unchanged (the
luthier’s violin remains a violin while its substance grounds its sameness); a thing can change its
essence while remaining the same one (a caterpillar becomes a butterfly—if we say it is the same
substance, its essence has changed).
    The distinction is the distinction between the whatness and the sameness. The whatness is
the thing’s being the kind of thing it is; the sameness is the thing’s being the same one through
change. A thing has both, and the two are related—the whatness requires the sameness, because
a what that did not persist would not be a what of anything—but they are not the same.

6.4.2    Essence Presupposes Substance
The two are not merely distinct; the essence presupposes the substance. For an essence to be the
essence of a thing, there must be a thing of which it is the essence; and for there to be a thing,
there must be a substance that grounds its being the same one. Without substance, the essence
would be a free-floating what—a form without a bearer, a kind without a member. The essence
is the what of a thing, and a thing is what its substance grounds. The essence presupposes the
substance, and the substance grounds the essence.

6.4.3    The Distinction from Chapter 5
Chapter 5’s distinction between substance and composition is not the same as the present
distinction between substance and essence. The first is the distinction between what grounds
a thing’s being one and what the thing is made of; the second is the distinction between what
grounds a thing’s being one and what the thing is. The three notions—substance, composition,
essence—are distinct, and the present chapter distinguishes essence from the other two.


6.5     Essence and Thisness
The second distinction that essence requires is the distinction from thisness. The full analysis of
thisness is the subject of Chapter 7; the present section states the distinction, and defers the
analysis.
6.6. Essence as the Presupposition of Defining Invariants                                       63


6.5.1    What a Thing Is Is Not Which Thing It Is
The essence of a thing is what the thing is—the kind, the form, the determination. The thisness
of a thing is which thing it is—the individuating feature that distinguishes the thing from every
other thing of the same kind. The two are distinct: two sparrows have the same essence (both
are sparrows) but different thisnesses (each is this sparrow, not the other); two violins have the
same essence (both are violins) but different thisnesses (each is this violin, not the other).
    The distinction is the distinction between the what and the which. The what is share-
able—many things can have the same essence. The which is not shareable—no two things can
have the same thisness. The two are distinct, and the distinction is the distinction between the
kind and the individual.

6.5.2    Essence Presupposes Thisness
The two are not merely distinct; the essence presupposes the thisness. For an essence to be the
essence of a thing, there must be a thing of which it is the essence; and for there to be a thing,
there must be a thisness that individuates the thing. Without thisness, the essence would be a
kind without an individual—a species without a specimen, a form without a bearer. The essence
is the what of a thing, and a thing is what its thisness individuates. The essence presupposes the
thisness, and the thisness individuates the essence.

6.5.3    The Distinction from Book I
Book I’s Principle 9.6 (C6, non-duplicability) is the framework’s statement of thisness at the
structural level: identity cannot be copied, because the thisness is not shareable. The present
chapter’s distinction between essence and thisness is the metaphysical analysis of what Book I’s
structural principle presupposes. The two are related: the structural principle is (A) in Book I,
and the metaphysical analysis is (D) in the present chapter, because the analysis depends on the
principle.


6.6     Essence as the Presupposition of Defining Invariants
The chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that essence is what Book I’s defining
invariants presuppose in the order of being. The demonstration has three steps.

6.6.1    Step 1: The Defining Invariants Presuppose a What
Book I’s Definition 9.2 states that the defining invariants of an identity are the features that
constitute its determination: those that distinguish it from its alternatives and are fixed by what
it is. The definition adds that the invariants are “taken as primitive in the framework”—that the
framework does not derive them from anything more basic. The primitiveness is the framework’s
methodological choice, but it is not the whole story. The defining invariants presuppose a what:
for features to be defining, there must be a what that they define; for features to constitute a
determination, there must be a determination that they constitute. The what is what the present
chapter calls essence.
     The step is a (D) claim: it is conditional on Book I’s Definition 9.2. The claim is not that
the defining invariants are the essence; the claim is that the defining invariants presuppose an
essence, and that the presupposition is the defining invariants’ metaphysical condition.

6.6.2    Step 2: The What Is Essence
The what that the defining invariants presuppose is what the chapter calls essence. The
identification is not arbitrary: it is the identification of the what with the notion that the
64                                                           Chapter 6. Essence and Essentialism


metaphysical tradition has called essence. The tradition’s notion is the notion of the constitutive
what of a thing, the determination that makes the thing the kind of thing it is; the chapter’s
definition is the same notion, stated in the framework’s vocabulary.
    The step is a (T) claim: it is argued by the analysis of the notion of essence and by the
comparison with the tradition’s notion. It is relative to the chapter’s definition (Definition 6.1),
and it is assessable by the definition’s adequacy.

6.6.3    Step 3: The Presupposition Is a Metaphysical Consequent
The presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of Book I’s framework, not an independent
metaphysical posit. The framework does not add essence to the defining invariants; it states
what the defining invariants require in the order of being. The requirement is a (D) claim, and
the (D) claim is the chapter’s principal contribution.
   The step is the synthesis of Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 establishes that the defining invariants
presuppose a what; Step 2 establishes that the what is essence; Step 3 establishes that the
presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of the framework. The three steps together establish
the chapter’s principal claim.

Principle 6.3 (Essence as the Metaphysical Consequent of Defining Invariants). (D) Essence is
the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s defining invariants: the defining invariants presuppose
a constitutive what that they define, and the what is what the chapter calls essence. The
principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Definition 9.2; it is the chapter’s principal
contribution because it states what the defining invariants require in the order of being.


6.7     Essentialism: The Argument
The chapter’s second contribution is the statement and argument for the essentialist thesis.

Principle 6.4 (The Essentialist Thesis). (T) Things have essences: for every thing that belongs
to a kind, there is a constitutive what that makes the thing the kind of thing it is, and that
grounds the properties the thing cannot lose without ceasing to be the thing it is.

    The thesis is (T): it is argued, and the argument is the chapter’s case. Three arguments are
given, and each is independent of the others.

6.7.1    First Argument: From Classification
Argument. 1. To classify a thing is to identify the kind of thing it is. 2. To identify the kind of
thing a thing is, is to identify what the thing is—the constitutive what that distinguishes it from
things of other kinds. 3. The constitutive what is what the chapter calls essence. 4. Therefore,
to classify is to presuppose an essence. 5. Since classification is pervasive (we classify things in
every domain of inquiry), essences are presupposed pervasively.
    The argument’s force is in Step 2. If classification did not identify a what—if it merely
applied a label without identifying the kind—then classification would be a convention, not a
discovery, and the argument would fail. The chapter’s claim is that classification does identify a
what; the label is a label of something, and the something is the kind. The argument is (T),
relative to the premise that classification identifies a kind.

6.7.2    Second Argument: From Necessity
Argument. 1. Some properties are necessary to a thing: the thing cannot lose them without
ceasing to be the thing it is (Book I, Definition 10.2, essential features; and Book I, Principle 9.6,
C6, thisness). 2. A necessary property requires a ground: the necessity is not arbitrary, and it is
6.8. The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Essence                                        65


not a mere regularity (a regularity would be contingent, not necessary). 3. The ground of the
necessity is the thing’s essence: the essence is what makes the properties necessary. 4. Therefore,
the necessity of the thing’s properties presupposes an essence.
    The argument’s force is in Step 2. If necessary properties did not require a ground—if they
were simply necessary without a ground—then the argument would fail. The chapter’s claim
is that necessities are always grounded; the necessity is the necessity of something, and the
something is the essence. The argument is (T), relative to the principle that necessity requires a
ground.

6.7.3    Third Argument: From the Determinacy of Change
Argument. 1. A thing can change, and its changes are not arbitrary: the thing can change in
some respects, but not in all; some changes are compatible with the thing’s being the thing it
is, and others are not. 2. The compatibility of a change with the thing’s being the thing it is,
requires a determination of what the thing is: without the determination, there would be no
basis for saying which changes are compatible and which are not. 3. The determination is what
the chapter calls essence. 4. Therefore, the determinacy of change presupposes an essence.
    The argument’s force is in Step 2. If the compatibility of a change did not require a
determination—if any change were compatible with any thing—then the argument would fail.
The chapter’s claim is that the compatibility is determinate; the determinacy is the determinacy
of something, and the something is the essence. The argument is (T), relative to the premise
that the determinacy of change requires a determination.

6.7.4    The Three Arguments Together
The three arguments are independent: one proceeds from classification, one from necessity, one
from the determinacy of change. A reader who accepts one of the arguments has a reason to
accept the essentialist thesis; a reader who rejects one has a reason to reject the thesis, but not a
reason to reject the other two. The three arguments together constitute the chapter’s case for
the thesis, and the case is offered at the strength that the arguments support.


6.8     The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Essence
With the definition of essence in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can be applied to
the inquiry into essence. The application states what the inquiry into essence holds invariant,
what it invokes as the medium of the conditions of being, what rule it follows, and in what frame
it is posed.

6.8.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Essence
The fixed element of the inquiry into essence is the essence itself, held invariant while the inquiry
explains the conditions of its being. The essence is held invariant as the subject of the inquiry—the
what whose conditions the inquiry seeks to state. The fixedness is methodological: the inquiry
decides to hold the essence invariant for the purpose of explaining its conditions, and it does not
claim that the essence cannot vary.

6.8.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Essence
The fluid element of the inquiry into essence is the relation between the essence and its in-
stances—the relation by which the instances are instances of the essence, and by which the
essence is what the instances share. The relation is the medium of the inquiry: it is what conveys
the effect of the essence’s being what it is to the instances’ being what they are. The relation is
the subject of the present chapter, and it is stated in §6.
66                                                         Chapter 6. Essence and Essentialism


6.8.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Essence
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into essence is the rule by which the essence determines
the necessary properties—the rule that explains how an essence’s being what it is determines the
properties its instances must have. The rule is the subject of §7, where the essentialist thesis is
argued.

6.8.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Essence
The context of the inquiry into essence is the realm in which the essence is realized. The seven
realms of Book I are the contexts, and the essence takes a different form in each. The form of
essence in each realm is the subject of §9.

6.8.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into essence are stated in the following table.

                 Column               In the Inquiry into Essence
                 Fixed element    The essence itself, held invariant as the
                                  subject of the inquiry
                 Fluid element    The relation between the essence and its
                                  instances
                 Governing dynam- The rule by which the essence determines
                 ics              the necessary properties

   The table is the application of Chapter 2’s method to the inquiry into essence. It is not a new
method; it is the same method, applied to a specific concept. The application is the chapter’s
contribution to the book’s systematic character.


6.9     Essence in Each Realm
The essence takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the
form, one realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered
at the strength that the framework’s principles support, and subject to revision if a different
form of essence in a realm does the same explanatory work.

6.9.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, essence takes the form of the natural kind—the species, the
chemical element, the material structure. The natural kind is the constitutive what of a material
thing; it makes the thing the kind of material thing it is, and it grounds the properties the
thing cannot lose without ceasing to be the material thing it is. The essence is not the thing’s
material composition; it is the form that the composition realizes. The distinction is the same as
Chapter 5’s distinction between substance and composition.

6.9.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, essence takes the form of the meaning-structure—the pattern of
relations that makes a relational thing the kind of relational thing it is. A friendship’s essence
is the pattern of mutual recognition, trust, and care that makes it a friendship rather than an
acquaintance or a business partnership. The essence is not the particular relations between
the two friends; it is the pattern that the particular relations realize. The distinction is the
distinction between the pattern and its instances.
6.9. Essence in Each Realm                                                                         67


6.9.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, essence takes the form of the form or law that makes a structural
thing the kind of structural thing it is. A number’s essence is the structure that makes it the
number it is (in the structural sense—the position in the number system, the relations to other
numbers). A theorem’s essence is the structure of the proof that makes it the theorem it is. The
essence is not the particular symbol or notation; it is the structure that the symbol or notation
expresses.

6.9.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, essence takes the form of pure unity. The First Determination has
no multiplicity, no properties, no change; its essence is its unity, and its unity is its essence.
The form is the limit case of the other forms: it is what the other forms become when the
multiplicity is zero. The First Determination’s essence is not distinct from its substance, and not
distinct from its existence, in the way that a material thing’s essence, substance, and existence
are distinct; the distinction is a feature of the realms of multiplicity, and the First Determination
is the limit case where the distinction collapses.

6.9.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, essence takes the form of the measure—the allotment that makes an
apportioning the kind of apportioning it is. The measure is the ground of the apportioning’s
necessary features; it is the essence of the apportioning.

6.9.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, essence takes the form of the sign—the structure that makes a
signification the kind of signification it is. The sign is the ground of the signification’s necessary
features; it is the essence of the signification.

6.9.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, essence takes the form of the actualization—the realizing that makes
a realization the kind of realization it is. The actualization is the ground of the realization’s
necessary features; it is the essence of the realization.

6.9.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

                 First Determina-      Pure unity (limit case)
                 tion
                 Hub of Decree         Measure (allotment)
                 Structural Deter-     Form (law)
                 mination
                 Hub of Significa-     Sign (structure as sign)
                 tion

                 festation

    The table is the chapter’s map of essence across the seven realms. It is an (E) claim, and it
is offered at the strength that the framework’s principles support. A reader who finds a different
form of essence in a realm more adequate is invited to propose it; the framework’s claim is that
the general definition of essence applies to all seven realms, not that the specific forms are final.


6.10     Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: Essentialism is incompatible with modern biology. The objection is that modern
biology has abandoned the notion of fixed species essences; species evolve, and the boundaries
between species are not sharp. Essentialism, the objection concludes, is a relic of pre-Darwinian
biology.
    Reply. The objection confuses species essentialism with essentialism tout court. The chapter
does not claim that biological species have fixed essences in the pre-Darwinian sense; it claims
that things have essences—that a thing’s constitutive what makes it the kind of thing it is. The
essence of a biological organism may be a developmental structure that is realized differently
in different environments, and the structure may not correspond to a fixed species boundary.
The objection’s conclusion—that essentialism is obsolete—does not follow, because the chapter’s
essentialism is not species essentialism. The chapter’s essentialism is the thesis that things have
constitutive whats, and the thesis is compatible with an evolutionary biology that recognizes
developmental structures rather than fixed species boundaries.
    Objection 2: Essences are not observable, and what is not observable is not real. The objection
is that essences cannot be observed, and that the framework’s epistemology (Book I) is committed
to the observability of what it posits. Essentialism, the objection concludes, is incompatible with
the framework’s epistemology.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the framework’s epistemology for an empiricism. Book I’s
epistemology is not an empiricism; it is a structural account of explanatory cognition (Book I,
Chapter 1), and its account of what is real is not limited to what is observable. The essence is
real, in the framework’s sense, because it is required by the framework’s principles (the defining
invariants presuppose a what, and the what is the essence). The essence is not observable as a
separate thing, but it is observable in the thing’s properties and behavior—the observable features
are the observable manifestations of the essence, and the essence is what the manifestations
manifest. The objection’s premise—that what is not observable is not real—is not the framework’s
premise; the framework’s premise is that what is required by the principles is real, and the
essence is required.
6.11. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                        69


    Objection 3: The chapter’s definition of essence is circular. The definition says that essence
is the constitutive what; but the notion of “what” is the notion of essence, and the definition
defines essence in terms of itself. The objection is that the definition is circular and therefore
uninformative.
    Reply. The circularity is only apparent. The definition does not define essence in terms
of the word “essence”; it defines essence in terms of the notion of the constitutive what—the
determination that makes the thing the kind of thing it is. The notion of the constitutive what
is not the same as the notion of essence; it is the notion that the definition uses to characterize
essence. The definition is informative because it states what essence is in terms of the constitutive
what, the kind-membership, and the necessary properties, and these are not the same as the
word “essence”. The objection mistakes the semantic circularity (the word “essence” appears in
the explanans) for a substantive circularity; the reply distinguishes them.


6.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that every thing has an essence. It argues that things
have essences, in the sense that the things that belong to a kind have a constitutive what; the
argument does not apply to things that do not belong to any kind, and the chapter does not
settle whether there are such things. The question is a (Q) question, and it is marked as such in
the chapter’s status table.
    Second, the chapter does not analyze thisness. The analysis is the subject of Chapter 7; the
present chapter distinguishes essence from thisness, but it does not analyze thisness. The reader
who expects the analysis in this chapter has misread the chapter’s scope; the analysis begins in
Chapter 7.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the essence of a thing is knowable.
The question is epistemic, and it is the subject of Book I’s account of pseudo-identity (Book I,
Definition 9.5) and of the impossibility of super-identity (Book I, Principle 6.1). The present
chapter states the metaphysical structure of essence, and it leaves the epistemic question to
Book I’s epistemology.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the form of essence in each realm at the strength of a proof.
The forms are (E) estimates; they are offered at the strength that the framework’s principles
support, and they are subject to revision. The reader who finds a form inadequate is invited to
propose a different one; the framework’s claim is that the general definition applies, not that the
specific forms are final.

6.13      A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a person, a place, a work of art, an institution. What is its
essence? What is the constitutive what that makes it the kind of thing it is, and that grounds
the features it cannot lose without ceasing to be the thing it is? Is the essence what the thing is,
or is it what we say the thing is? And if the essence is real, what would it mean for a thing to
lose its essence? Would it become a different kind of thing, or would it cease to be at all?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The essence is not the thing’s properties,
or its material, or its history; it is the constitutive what that grounds the properties’ being the
properties of one kind, the material’s being the material of one kind, and the history’s being
the history of one kind. The reader who can state, for a thing he knows, what its essence is,
has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the
distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

The next chapter analyzes thisness: what it is for a thing to be this thing rather than another of
the same kind. With essence and thisness in place, the framework can distinguish the what from
the which, and it can state the relation between the two. The analysis is the subject of Chapter 7.
                                                                                                   71




Chapter 7

Identity and Thisness, Deepened

Scope. This chapter analyzes thisness: what it is for a thing to be this thing rather than another
thing of the same kind, and what grounds the numerical distinctness of things that share all
their qualitative features. It defines thisness as the non-qualitative individuating feature of a
thing—the feature that makes the thing the particular thing it is, and that cannot be shared
by another thing. It distinguishes thisness from essence, from substance, and from signature; it
argues that thisness is what Book I’s principle of non-duplicability (Principle 9.6, C6) presupposes
in the order of being; it states the doctrine of primitive thisness and gives three arguments for it;
it states the four-column structure of the inquiry into thisness; it states the form that thisness
takes in each of the seven realms; and it answers four standard objections, including the objection
from Black’s two spheres and the objection from Quine’s skepticism about de re modality. Its
claims are metaphysical and structural; where it speaks of “thisness,” “individuation,” “feature,”
“haecceity,” or “distinctness,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in
this chapter and by the framework of Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s definition of identity
(Definition 9.1), of signature (Definition 9.4), of pseudo-identity (Definition 9.5), and of non-
duplicability (Principle 9.6, C6); the principle of identity conservation (Principle 9.5, C5); and
the argument from the logic of numerical identity (Book I, §23.4). It does not restate these
principles; it asks what they presuppose in the order of being. The presupposition is stated in §7,
and the chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that thisness is the presupposition.


7.1     A Scene
Consider a potter in a workshop, holding two cups she has just made. The cups are identical in
every qualitative respect: the same clay, the same shape, the same glaze, the same size, the same
weight, the same texture. If you held one cup in each hand and closed your eyes, you could not
tell which was which. The two cups are exact qualitative duplicates.
    The potter sets one cup on the shelf and keeps the other in her hand. She says: This is the
cup I made first. The statement is not a statement about the cup’s qualitative features; the two
cups share every qualitative feature. It is not a statement about the cup’s position; the other
cup is on the shelf, and the potter could have kept the other one. It is not a statement about
the cup’s history; the two cups were made in the same firing, from the same clay, by the same
hands. What, then, is the statement about? What is the this cup that the potter’s demonstrative
names?
    The potter’s statement is a statement about the cup’s thisness— about what makes the cup
this cup rather than the other. The thisness is not the cup’s qualitative features; the two cups
share them. It is not the cup’s essence; the two cups share it. It is not the cup’s substance;
each cup has its own substance, but the substance is what grounds the cup’s being the same
72                                                  Chapter 7. Identity and Thisness, Deepened


cup through time, not what distinguishes it from the other cup at a time. The thisness is what
individuates the cup—what makes it the particular thing it is, and what makes the other cup a
different particular thing even though the two are qualitatively indistinguishable.
    The potter’s demonstrative is not a figure of speech. She can point to one cup and not the
other; she can say this one and mean it; she can make a claim about the cup that is true of the
cup she is holding and false of the cup on the shelf, even though every qualitative predicate she
applies to the one she applies equally to the other. The thisness is real, in the framework’s sense,
because without it the demonstrative would have no referent—it would pick out neither cup, or
both, and the potter’s claim would be unintelligible.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is thisness? What is the metaphysical
ground of a thing’s being this thing rather than another of the same kind? And what does
the framework of Book I require, in the order of being, when it asserts the non-duplicability of
identity (Principle 9.6)? The chapter’s answer is: thisness. The chapter’s task is to say what
thisness is, to distinguish it from the notions with which it is easily confused, and to show that it
is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s non-duplicability.


7.2     The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is thisness, and what does it presuppose?
    The question is not the same as the question of Book I’s Chapter 9, and it is not the same as
the questions of Chapters 5 and 6. Book I asked what identity is, and it answered: identity is
invariance under a class of allowable transformations (Definition 9.1). The answer was structural.
Chapter 5 asked what grounds the invariance, and it answered: substance, the ground of the
thing’s being the same one through change. The answer was metaphysical. Chapter 6 asked
what grounds the thing’s being the kind of thing it is, and it answered: essence, the constitutive
what. The answer was metaphysical. The present chapter asks a fourth question: what grounds
the thing’s being this thing rather than another of the same kind? The answer is thisness, and
the answer is metaphysical.
    The four questions are distinct: identity is the structural feature, substance is the ground of
the sameness, essence is the ground of the whatness, and thisness is the ground of the whichness.
The four are related—a thing’s identity is invariant because its substance grounds the sameness,
its essence grounds the whatness, and its thisness grounds the whichness—but they are not the
same, and the chapter must keep them apart.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of thisness? The chapter must define thisness, and it
must distinguish the definition from the definitions of substance (Chapter 5), essence (Chapter 6),
and signature (Book I, Definition 9.4). The definition must be precise enough to be argued about,
and general enough to cover the thisness of each of the seven realms.
    The second aspect: what is the relation between thisness and Book I’s non-duplicability?
The chapter must state how thisness relates to Book I’s Principle 9.6 (C6). The relation is the
chapter’s principal contribution, because it is what makes thisness a metaphysical consequent of
the framework, not a metaphysical posit alongside it.
    The third aspect: does the doctrine of primitive thisness hold? The chapter must state the
doctrine—the thesis that thisness is a non-qualitative, primitive individuating feature—and it
must give the arguments for it. The arguments are the chapter’s case for the doctrine, and they
are what makes the chapter a metaphysical analysis, not a mere stipulation of a definition.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: thisness
is the non-qualitative individuating feature of a thing; it is what Book I’s non-duplicability
presupposes; and the doctrine of primitive thisness holds, because without it no thing would be
this thing rather than another.
7.3. The Definition of Thisness                                                                  73


7.3     The Definition of Thisness
7.3.1    The Definition
Definition 7.1 (Thisness). (A) The thisness of a thing is the non-qualitative individuating
feature that makes the thing the particular thing it is, and that cannot be shared by another
thing. It is the ground of the thing’s being this thing rather than another thing of the same kind,
and it is distinct from every qualitative feature the thing has.

    The definition has three components, and each is important.
    The first component: thisness is a feature. The thisness is a feature of the thing—it is
something the thing has, not something the thing is. The distinction is the distinction between
the thing and its features; the thisness is a feature, and the thing is what has it. The feature is
not a qualitative feature; it is not a color, a shape, a size, a mass, or any other property that
could be shared by another thing of the same kind. It is a non-qualitative feature—a feature
that individuates without describing.
    The second component: thisness individuates. The thisness makes the thing the particular
thing it is; it grounds the thing’s numerical distinctness from every other thing, including every
other thing of the same kind. Two things of the same kind share their essence; their thisnesses
distinguish them. The thisness is what makes the potter’s two cups two cups, and not one cup
counted twice.
    The third component: thisness is not shareable. The thisness cannot be shared by another
thing. This is the feature that distinguishes thisness from essence: an essence is shareable (many
things can have the same essence), and a thisness is not. The non-shareability is the ground of
the framework’s principle of non-duplicability (Book I, Principle 9.6): identity cannot be copied,
because the thisness cannot be copied.
    The three components are not three definitions; they are three aspects of one definition. The
thisness is the non-qualitative individuating feature, and the non-qualitative individuation is the
ground of the thing’s being the particular thing it is—and these are three ways of saying the
same thing, because the feature’s non-qualitative character, its individuating function, and its
non-shareability are three aspects of its being a thisness.

7.3.2    What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
    It does not say that thisness is a property. The thisness is a feature, but not a property in
the sense of a qualitative characteristic. A property, in the framework’s sense, is a qualitative
feature that can be shared; the thisness is a non-qualitative feature that cannot be shared. The
distinction is the distinction between the quality and the haecceity—the “thisness” that the
tradition has called by that name. The thisness is not another quality alongside the qualities; it
is the individuation that the qualities presuppose.
    It does not say that thisness is a thing. The thisness is a feature, not a thing. It is not a
hidden entity that underlies the properties; it is the individuating feature that the thing has.
The distinction is the distinction between the feature and the thing; the thisness is the first, and
the thing (with its qualities and its thisness) is the second.
    It does not say that thisness is knowable. The thisness may be inaccessible to a finite
subject—the potter cannot, by inspecting the two cups, tell which is which, because the thisness
is not qualitative and the qualitative inspection cannot distinguish them. The inaccessibility
is not a defect of thisness; it is a feature of the relation between a finite subject and a non-
qualitative individuator. The distinction is the same as Book I’s distinction between identity
and pseudo-identity (Book I, Definition 9.5): the thisness is the identity’s individuation; the
pseudo-identity is the finite subject’s reconstruction, and the reconstruction cannot reach the
thisness.
74                                                  Chapter 7. Identity and Thisness, Deepened


    It does not say that thisness is simple. A thisness can be the thisness of a composite thing,
and the composite thing can have parts. The thisness is the individuation of the whole, not the
individuation of the parts; the parts are individuated by their own thisnesses, and the whole
is individuated by its own. The distinction is the distinction between the individuation of the
whole and the individuation of the parts; the two are related, but they are not the same.

7.3.3    Thisness and Signature
Definition 7.2 (Thisness and Signature). (A) A thing’s signature is the structural description
of its invariance: what can be read off, compared, recorded, and reproduced about the pattern
(Book I, Definition 9.4). A thing’s thisness is the non-qualitative individuation that the signature
cannot capture. The signature is shareable; the thisness is not.

    The distinction between thisness and signature is the distinction between the describable and
the individuating. The signature is what can be said about the thing—its pattern, its structure,
its reproducible features. The thisness is what cannot be said—the individuation that makes
the thing this thing, and that no description can reach. The signature is the thing’s what in the
broad sense; the thisness is the thing’s which. The two are distinct, and the distinction is the
distinction between the describable and the individuating.


7.4     Thisness and Essence
The first distinction that thisness requires is the distinction from essence.

7.4.1    What a Thing Is Is Not Which Thing It Is
The essence of a thing is what the thing is—the kind, the form, the determination (Chapter 6,
Definition 6.1). The thisness of a thing is which thing it is—the individuating feature that
distinguishes the thing from every other thing of the same kind. The two are distinct: two things
of the same kind share their essence but not their thisness. The potter’s two cups share their
essence (both are cups) but have different thisnesses (each is this cup, not the other).
    The distinction is the distinction between the what and the which. The what is shareable;
the which is not. The what answers the question “what is it?”; the which answers the question
“which one is it?”. The two questions are distinct, and the answers are distinct.

7.4.2    Essence and Thisness Are Related
The two are not merely distinct; they are related. The essence is the what of the thing, and
the thisness is the which of the thing; the two are aspects of the same thing, and neither is
complete without the other. A thing without an essence would be a which without a what—an
individuated thing that is no kind of thing; a thing without a thisness would be a what without
a which—a kind without an individual. The essence and the thisness are the two halves of the
thing’s being a thing.

7.4.3    The Distinction from Chapter 6
Chapter 6’s distinction between essence and substance is not the same as the present distinction
between essence and thisness. The first is the distinction between the what and the ground
of the sameness; the second is the distinction between the what and the which. The three
notions—substance, essence, thisness—are distinct, and the present chapter distinguishes thisness
from the other two.
7.5. Thisness and Substance                                                                      75


7.5     Thisness and Substance
The second distinction that thisness requires is the distinction from substance.

7.5.1    The Ground of Sameness Is Not the Ground of Individuation
The substance of a thing is what grounds the thing’s being the same one through change
(Chapter 5, Definition 5.1). The thisness of a thing is what grounds the thing’s being this thing
rather than another. The two are distinct: a thing can be the same one through change while its
thisness is unchanged (the luthier’s violin remains the same violin, and its thisness is unchanged,
while its substance grounds the sameness through time); a thing can be individuated by its
thisness while its substance is composite and changeable (the violin’s substance is composed of
many parts, and the parts change, but the violin’s thisness is unchanged).
    The distinction is the distinction between the sameness and the whichness. The sameness is
the thing’s being the same one through change; the whichness is the thing’s being this thing
rather than another. A thing has both, and the two are related—the sameness requires the
whichness, because a thing that is not this thing cannot be the same one through change—but
they are not the same.

7.5.2    Thisness Presupposes Substance
The two are not merely distinct; the thisness presupposes the substance. For a thisness to be
the thisness of a thing, there must be a thing of which it is the thisness; and for there to be a
thing, there must be a substance that grounds the thing’s being the same one through change.
Without substance, the thisness would be a free-floating individuation—a which without a one,
an individuation without an individuated. The thisness is the which of a thing, and a thing is
what its substance grounds. The thisness presupposes the substance, and the substance grounds
the thisness.

7.5.3    The Distinction from Chapter 5
Chapter 5’s distinction between substance and composition is not the same as the present
distinction between substance and thisness. The first is the distinction between what grounds
the thing’s being one and what the thing is made of; the second is the distinction between what
grounds the thing’s being one and what individuates the thing. The three notions—substance,
composition, thisness—are distinct, and the present chapter distinguishes thisness from the other
two.


7.6     Thisness as the Presupposition of Non-Duplicability
The chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that thisness is what Book I’s principle
of non-duplicability (Principle 9.6, C6) presupposes in the order of being. The demonstration
has three steps.

7.6.1    Step 1: Non-Duplicability Presupposes a Non-Shareable
Book I’s Principle 9.6 states that identity cannot be copied—that signatures, pseudo-identities,
and information can be duplicated, but identity cannot. The principle is (A): it is a commitment
of the framework, and its argument is the argument from the logic of numerical identity (Book I,
§23.4) together with the doctrine of primitive thisness (Book I, §23.7). The argument’s force is
that numerical duplication of an identity would require two distinct things to be the same identity,
which the logic of identity excludes. But the logic of identity excludes only numerical duplication;
it does not explain why an exact qualitative duplicate is not a numerical duplicate. The
76                                                   Chapter 7. Identity and Thisness, Deepened


explanation is that the identity is individuated by a non-shareable feature—by a thisness—and
that the feature cannot be copied. The non-shareable feature is what the chapter calls thisness.
    The step is a (D) claim: it is conditional on Book I’s Principle 9.6. The claim is not that
the thisness is the principle; the claim is that the principle presupposes a thisness, and that the
presupposition is the principle’s metaphysical condition.

7.6.2    Step 2: The Non-Shareable Is Thisness
The non-shareable feature that the principle presupposes is what the chapter calls thisness. The
identification is not arbitrary: it is the identification of the non-shareable individuator with
the notion that the metaphysical tradition has called thisness (or haecceity). The tradition’s
notion is the notion of the non-qualitative individuating feature that makes a thing this thing;
the chapter’s definition is the same notion, stated in the framework’s vocabulary.
   The step is a (T) claim: it is argued by the analysis of the notion of thisness and by the
comparison with the tradition’s notion. It is relative to the chapter’s definition (Definition 7.1),
and it is assessable by the definition’s adequacy.

7.6.3    Step 3: The Presupposition Is a Metaphysical Consequent
The presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of Book I’s framework, not an independent
metaphysical posit. The framework does not add thisness to the non-duplicability; it states what
the non-duplicability requires in the order of being. The requirement is a (D) claim, and the (D)
claim is the chapter’s principal contribution.
    The step is the synthesis of Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 establishes that non-duplicability presupposes
a non-shareable; Step 2 establishes that the non-shareable is thisness; Step 3 establishes that
the presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of the framework. The three steps together
establish the chapter’s principal claim.

Principle 7.3 (Thisness as the Metaphysical Consequent of Non-Duplicability). (D) Thisness is
the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s principle of non-duplicability: the principle presupposes
a non-shareable individuator, and the individuator is what the chapter calls thisness. The
principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principle 9.6; it is the chapter’s principal
contribution because it states what the non-duplicability requires in the order of being.


7.7     The Doctrine of Primitive Thisness
The chapter’s second contribution is the statement and argument for the doctrine of primitive
thisness.

Principle 7.4 (The Doctrine of Primitive Thisness). (T) Thisness is primitive and non-qualitative:
it is not derived from the thing’s qualitative features, and it is not a species of the qualitative; it
is the non-qualitative individuator that grounds the thing’s numerical distinctness from every
other thing. The doctrine is the chapter’s thesis about the nature of thisness, and it is (T)
because it is argued, not stipulated.

    The doctrine is the framework’s most contested commitment about identity, and the chapter’s
case for it is offered at the strength that the arguments support. Three arguments are given, and
each is independent of the others.

7.7.1    First Argument: From Numerical Distinctness
Argument. 1. Two things can share all their qualitative features. 2. The two things are
distinct—they are two, not one. 3. What distinguishes them cannot be a qualitative feature
7.8. The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Thisness                                         77


(by hypothesis, they share all qualitative features). 4. Therefore, what distinguishes them is a
non-qualitative feature. 5. This feature is what the chapter calls thisness. 6. Therefore, thisness
is primitive and non-qualitative.
    The argument’s force is in Step 1. If two things could not share all their qualitative features—if
every difference between things were a qualitative difference—then the argument would fail,
because there would be no need for a non-qualitative individuator. The chapter’s claim is that
two things can share all their qualitative features; the argument is (T), relative to the possibility
of qualitative duplicates.

7.7.2    Second Argument: From the Logic of Identity
Argument. 1. Identity is strict sameness: if a is identical with b, then a is b (Leibniz’s law; Book I,
§23.4). 2. An exact qualitative duplicate of a is not a; it is a distinct thing that shares all of a’s
qualitative features. 3. The distinctness of the duplicate from a cannot be a qualitative difference
(by hypothesis, they share all qualitative features). 4. Therefore, the distinctness is grounded in
a non-qualitative individuator. 5. This individuator is what the chapter calls thisness.
    The argument’s force is in Step 2. If an exact qualitative duplicate were identical with the
original—if copying the qualitative features were sufficient for copying the identity—then the
argument would fail, because there would be no distinctness to be grounded. The chapter’s claim
is that the duplicate is distinct; the argument is (T), relative to the doctrine of non-duplicability
(which the chapter has argued in §7).

7.7.3    Third Argument: From the Possibility of Indiscernibles
Argument. 1. There are possible worlds in which two things are exactly similar—they share
all their qualitative features. 2. In such a world, the two things are two, not one. 3. What
distinguishes them is a non-qualitative individuator. 4. The individuator is what the chapter
calls thisness. 5. Therefore, thisness is primitive and non-qualitative.
    The argument’s force is in Step 1. If no possible world contained exactly similar things—if
exact similarity entailed identity—then the argument would fail, because there would be no
possible case for the thisness to individuate. The chapter’s claim is that such worlds are
possible; the argument is (T), relative to the possibility of indiscernibles. The argument is the
framework’s response to Black’s two spheres (Black, “The Identity of Indiscernibles,” Mind 61
(1952): 153–164), and it is stated more fully in §11, where the objection is addressed.

7.7.4    The Three Arguments Together
The three arguments are independent: one proceeds from numerical distinctness, one from the
logic of identity, one from the possibility of indiscernibles. A reader who accepts one of the
arguments has a reason to accept the doctrine; a reader who rejects one has a reason to reject
the doctrine, but not a reason to reject the other two. The three arguments together constitute
the chapter’s case for the doctrine, and the case is offered at the strength that the arguments
support.


7.8     The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Thisness
With the definition of thisness in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can be applied to
the inquiry into thisness. The application states what the inquiry into thisness holds invariant,
what it invokes as the medium of the conditions of being, what rule it follows, and in what frame
it is posed.
78                                                 Chapter 7. Identity and Thisness, Deepened


7.8.1   The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Thisness
The fixed element of the inquiry into thisness is the thisness itself, held invariant while the
inquiry explains the conditions of its being. The thisness is held invariant as the subject of the
inquiry—the which whose conditions the inquiry seeks to state. The fixedness is methodological:
the inquiry decides to hold the thisness invariant for the purpose of explaining its conditions,
and it does not claim that the thisness cannot vary.

7.8.2   The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Thisness
The fluid element of the inquiry into thisness is the relation between the thisness and its
bearer—the relation by which the thisness is the thisness of a thing, and by which the thing is
the thing the thisness individuates. The relation is the medium of the inquiry: it is what conveys
the effect of the thisness’s being what it is to the thing’s being the particular thing it is.

7.8.3   The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Thisness
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into thisness is the rule by which the thisness individu-
ates—the rule that explains how a thisness makes a thing the particular thing it is, and how it
distinguishes the thing from every other thing. The rule is the subject of §6, where the relation
between essence and thisness is stated.

7.8.4   The Context of the Inquiry into Thisness
The context of the inquiry into thisness is the realm in which the thisness is realized. The seven
realms of Book I are the contexts, and the thisness takes a different form in each. The form of
thisness in each realm is the subject of §10.

7.8.5   The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into thisness are stated in the following table.

                 Column               In the Inquiry into Thisness
