7.9     Thisness in Each Realm
The thisness takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the
form, one realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered
at the strength that the framework’s principles support, and subject to revision if a different
form of thisness in a realm does the same explanatory work.
7.9. Thisness in Each Realm                                                                       79


7.9.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, thisness takes the form of the material individual—the particular
body, the particular lump of matter, the particular physical thing. The material individual is
individuated by its spatiotemporal position: no two material individuals can occupy the same
place and time, and the position individuates the individual. The position is a non-qualitative
individuator: it is not a qualitative feature (many things share qualitative features), but it
is a spatiotemporal coordinate that distinguishes the individual from every other individual.
The framework’s thisness in the Material Manifestation is the material individuation that the
spatiotemporal position provides.

7.9.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, thisness takes the form of the relational individual—the par-
ticular relation, the particular community, the particular tradition. The relational individual
is individuated by its history: no two relational individuals can have the same history, and the
history individuates the individual. The history is a non-qualitative individuator: it is not a
qualitative feature (many relations share qualitative features), but it is a historical trajectory
that distinguishes the individual from every other individual.

7.9.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, thisness takes the form of the structural individual—the
particular number, the particular theorem, the particular structure. The structural individual
is individuated by its position in the structure: no two structural individuals can occupy the
same position, and the position individuates the individual. The position is a non-qualitative
individuator: it is not a qualitative feature (many structures share qualitative features), but it is
a structural coordinate that distinguishes the individual from every other individual.

7.9.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, thisness takes the form of pure unity—the thisness of the one, which
is its unity. The First Determination has no parts, no properties, no change; its thisness is its
unity, and its unity is its thisness. The form is the limit case of the other forms: it is what the
other forms become when the multiplicity is zero. The First Determination’s thisness is not
distinct from its essence or its substance in the way that a material thing’s thisness, essence, and
substance are distinct; the distinction is a feature of the realms of multiplicity, and the First
Determination is the limit case where the distinction collapses.

7.9.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, thisness takes the form of the measure—the particular allotment that
individuates the apportioning. The measure is the ground of the apportioning’s being the
particular apportioning it is; it is the thisness of the apportioning.

7.9.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, thisness takes the form of the sign—the particular structure that
individuates the signification. The sign is the ground of the signification’s being the particular
signification it is; it is the thisness of the signification.
80                                                   Chapter 7. Identity and Thisness, Deepened


7.9.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, thisness takes the form of the actualization—the particular realizing
that individuates the realization. The actualization is the ground of the realization’s being the
particular realization it is; it is the thisness of the realization.

7.9.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

                 Realm                 The Form of Thisness
                 First Determina-      Pure unity (limit case)
                 tion
                 Hub of Decree         Measure (particular allotment)
                 Structural Deter-     Structural position
                 mination
                 Hub of Significa-     Sign (particular structure)
                 tion

                 festation

    The table is the chapter’s map of thisness across the seven realms. It is an (E) claim, and it
is offered at the strength that the framework’s principles support. A reader who finds a different
form of thisness in a realm more adequate is invited to propose it; the framework’s claim is that
the general definition of thisness applies to all seven realms, not that the specific forms are final.


7.10      Objections and Replies
Four objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: The doctrine of primitive thisness is unintelligible. The objection is that a
non-qualitative feature is unintelligible: every feature we can understand is qualitative, and a
“non-qualitative feature” is a contradiction in terms. The doctrine, the objection concludes, is
not a metaphysical thesis but a pseudo-thesis.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the limits of our qualitative vocabulary for the limits of reality.
A non-qualitative feature is not a feature that is “nothing”; it is a feature that individuates
without describing. The demonstrative “this” is the paradigm of a non-qualitative individuator: it
picks out the thing without describing it, and it succeeds because the thing has a thisness that the
demonstrative tracks. The objection’s premise—that every intelligible feature is qualitative—is
not established; the framework’s claim is that the non-qualitative feature is required by the logic
of identity, and that the demonstrative is the evidence that we can grasp it.
    Objection 2: Bundle theory can do without thisness. The objection is that a thing can
be analyzed as a bundle of properties, without a non-qualitative individuator. The bundle
theory—defended by Hume, Russell, and some contemporary metaphysicians—is simpler than
the primitive thisness theory, and it does not need the notion of a non-qualitative feature.
    Reply. The bundle theory cannot explain what makes the bundle one bundle. A bundle of
properties is a collection; a collection is one only if it is collected, and the collecting requires
an individuator that is not another property (if it were another property, it would be part of
the bundle, and the collection would not be one). The individuator is what the framework calls
7.11. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                         81


thisness. The bundle theory, therefore, presupposes thisness, even when it denies it; it calls the
presupposition by a different name (the “compresence” of properties, or the “bundling relation”),
but the presupposition is the same. The objection mistakes the name for the thing; the thing is
required, whatever it is called.
    Objection 3: Black’s two spheres refute the doctrine. The objection is that Black (1952)
described a possible world with two exactly similar spheres, and that the description shows
that the two spheres do not need a non-qualitative individuator to be two. The two spheres
are two because they are spatially separated; their spatial separation individuates them, and no
non-qualitative feature is needed.
    Reply. Black’s two spheres do not refute the doctrine; they illustrate it. The two spheres
are two, and their being two requires an individuator. The spatial separation is a qualitative
feature—the spheres differ in their relational properties (their positions), even though they share
their intrinsic properties. But the spatial separation is itself an individuator only if the positions
are individuated; and the positions are individuated by their thisness (the thisness of this position
and the thisness of that position). The spatial separation thus presupposes thisness; it does not
replace it. The objection mistakes the illustration for a refutation; the illustration is a case of
thisness, not a counterexample to it.
    Objection 4: Quine’s skepticism about de re modality undermines the doctrine. The objection
is that Quine argued that de re modality—necessity as a feature of things, not of statements—is
unintelligible, and that the doctrine of primitive thisness is a form of de re modality. The
doctrine, the objection concludes, inherits Quine’s critique.
    Reply. The objection confuses two distinct issues. Quine’s critique of de re modality is a
critique of necessity in rebus—the claim that some things have necessary properties independently
of how they are described. The doctrine of primitive thisness is not a doctrine about necessary
properties; it is a doctrine about individuation. The thisness is not a necessary property of the
thing; it is the individuator that makes the thing this thing. The two issues are distinct, and
the doctrine of primitive thisness does not inherit Quine’s critique. The objection mistakes the
individuator for a modal property; the reply distinguishes them.


7.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that thisness exists in every realm. It argues that thisness is
what Book I’s non-duplicability presupposes; the argument is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 9.6,
and it is offered at the strength that the principle supports. A reader who accepts the principle
accepts the argument; a reader who does not has no reason to accept the conclusion, and the
chapter states the argument at exactly that strength.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether thisness is knowable. The question
is epistemic, and it is the subject of Book I’s account of pseudo-identity (Book I, Definition 9.5)
and of the impossibility of super-identity (Book I, Principle 6.1). The present chapter states the
metaphysical structure of thisness, and it leaves the epistemic question to Book I’s epistemology.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether thisness is simple or composite.
The question is metaphysical, and it is the subject of Chapter 7’s further development (if the book
treats it), or of a further volume. The present chapter states the definition and the arguments
for the doctrine, and it leaves the question of simplicity to a further analysis.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the form of thisness in each realm at the strength of
a proof. The forms are (E) estimates; they are offered at the strength that the framework’s
principles support, and they are subject to revision. The reader who finds a form inadequate is
invited to propose a different one; the framework’s claim is that the general definition applies,
not that the specific forms are final.

7.13      A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a person, a place, a work of art, an institution. What is its
thisness? What makes it this thing rather than another thing of the same kind? Is it the thing’s
position in space and time? Its history? Its relation to other things? Or is it a non-qualitative
individuator that no description can reach? And if the thisness is real, what would it mean for
the thing to lose its thisness? Would it cease to be the thing it is, or would it become a different
thing with the same appearance?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The thisness is not the thing’s properties,
its essence, or its substance; it is the non-qualitative individuator that makes the thing this thing,
and that no description can reach. The reader who can state, for a thing he knows, what its
thisness is, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place
where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

With this chapter, Part II of Book II is complete. The fixed elements of metaphysics—substance,
essence, and thisness—are stated, and their relations to Book I’s fixed element, defining invariants,
and non-duplicability are argued. The next part turns to the fluid elements of metaphysics:
causation, relation, light, and the fluid elements of each realm. The first analysis is causation,
which is the subject of Chapter 9.

Chapter 8

The Fixed Elements of Each Realm

Scope. This chapter synthesizes the analyses of Chapters 5, 6, and 7 into a single account of the
fixed elements of the seven realms. It states the triad of fixed elements—substance, essence, and
thisness—as a structural whole, and it states the realm-dependent structure of the triad: the
pattern of collapse, partial coincidence, and full distinction that the triad exhibits across the
seven realms. It argues that the pattern is not accidental, but tracks the ontological architecture
of Book I; it states the fixed element of each realm as a single structure (rather than as three
separate analyses); and it states what Part II has and has not established. Its claims are
metaphysical and structural; where it speaks of “triad,” “pattern,” “collapse,” “coincidence,” or
“distinction,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and
by the analyses of the preceding three chapters.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given the definitions and principles
that Chapters 5, 6, and 7 established as the metaphysical consequents of Book I’s fixed element
(Definition 2.1), defining invariants (Definition 9.2), and non-duplicability (Principle 9.6, C6). It
does not reargue those chapters; it asks what the three analyses, taken together, establish, and it
states the structural pattern that the three exhibit across the seven realms.


8.1     A Scene
Consider a will, signed and witnessed in a lawyer’s office. The will is a single document: a sheet
of paper, ink, a signature, a date, two witnesses. But the will is also a single act: the testator’s
disposition of her property, the witness’s attestation, the lawyer’s supervision. And the will is a
single instrument: a legal object with a certain force, a certain kind, and a certain history.
    Three things, and each is different. The sheet of paper is the will’s material; it can be replaced
(the lawyer might transcribe the will onto new paper) without the will changing. The testator’s
act is the will’s substance; it grounds the will’s being the same will through the transcription,
and it grounds the will’s being the disposition of this testator. The legal kind is the will’s essence;
it makes the will a will rather than a deed or a contract, and it grounds the features a will cannot
lose without ceasing to be a will (a disposition of property, an intention to take effect at death, a
revocable form). And the particular signature is the will’s thisness; it makes the will this will
rather than another will of the same testator, on the same day, with the same terms.
    The three elements are distinct, and the three are related. The substance grounds the
sameness; the essence grounds the whatness; the thisness grounds the whichness. The will is one
thing, and the three elements are three aspects of its being one thing—three ways in which the
will’s unity is articulated.
    Now consider a forged will. The forgery has the same material (a sheet of paper, ink, a
signature), the same essence (it is, in form, a will), and the same thisness (it is this particular
document, not another). But it does not have the same substance: the act is not the testator’s
84                                               Chapter 8. The Fixed Elements of Each Realm


act, but the forger’s. The forgery shows that the three elements are distinct: the substance can
be wrong while the essence and the thisness are intact, and the legal invalidity of the forgery is
the invalidity of the substance, not the invalidity of the essence or the thisness.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. The three elements of the fixed element—substance,
essence, thisness—are distinct in the will, and their distinctness is what makes the will a complex
thing. But the distinctness is not the same in every realm. In some realms, the three elements
collapse into one; in others, they coincide partially; in others, they are fully distinguished. What
is the pattern of the distinctness? And what does the pattern tell us about the seven realms?


8.2     The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is the structure of the triad of fixed elements, and how does
the structure vary across the seven realms?
    The question is not the same as the questions of Chapters 5, 6, and 7. Each of those chapters
analyzed one element of the triad: Chapter 5 analyzed substance, Chapter 6 analyzed essence,
Chapter 7 analyzed thisness. Each analysis was of one element, in all seven realms, but the
analysis was organized around the element, not around the realm. The present chapter inverts
the organization: it asks what the triad, as a whole, looks like in each realm, and what the
variation across realms tells us about the realms themselves.
    The inversion is the chapter’s principal contribution. It is not a summary of the three preceding
chapters; it is a reorganization of their results into a single structure, and the reorganization
reveals something that the three analyses, taken separately, did not reveal: the pattern of collapse,
partial coincidence, and full distinction.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the triad of fixed elements? The chapter must state the triad as a
structural whole—not as three separate elements, but as one structure with three components.
The statement is the chapter’s contribution to the systematic character of Part II.
    The second aspect: what is the realm-dependent structure of the triad? The chapter must
state the pattern of variation across the seven realms. The pattern is the chapter’s principal
contribution, because it is what makes the synthesis a genuine chapter, not a summary.
    The third aspect: what does the pattern tell us about the realms? The chapter must state
the implication of the pattern: the fixed element of a realm is the realm’s mode of being as a
structure of substance, essence, and thisness, and the variation of the structure is what makes
the realms structurally distinct at the level of fixed elements. The implication is the chapter’s
contribution to the framework’s ontology.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: the triad is
a structural whole; its structure varies across the seven realms according to a pattern of collapse,
partial coincidence, and full distinction; and the variation is what makes the realms structurally
distinct at the level of fixed elements.


8.3     The Triad of Fixed Elements
8.3.1    The Triad
Definition 8.1 (The Triad of Fixed Elements). (A) The triad of fixed elements is the structure
of substance, essence, and thisness, taken together. The substance is the ground of a thing’s
being the same one through change (Chapter 5, Definition 5.1); the essence is the constitutive
what that makes the thing the kind of thing it is (Chapter 6, Definition 6.1); and the thisness
is the non-qualitative individuator that makes the thing the particular thing it is (Chapter 7,
Definition 7.1). The triad is the structure of the thing’s being a thing, and it is the metaphysical
content of the fixed element of Book I’s framework.
8.4. The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Triad                                                   85


    The definition states the triad as a structural whole. The three elements are not three
separate things; they are three aspects of one structure—the structure of a thing’s being a thing.
The substance grounds the sameness; the essence grounds the whatness; the thisness grounds the
whichness. The three together make the thing the thing it is: a same one, of a certain kind, that
is this one rather than another.
    The triad is not a list. It is a structure, and the structure is what the definition captures.
The three elements are related: the substance requires the essence (a thing’s being the same
one requires that it be some kind of thing); the essence requires the thisness (a thing’s being
the kind of thing it is requires that it be this thing, not another); and the thisness requires the
substance (a thing’s being this thing requires that it be the same one through change). The
three are mutually requiring, and the mutual requirement is what makes them a triad.

8.3.2    The Triad and the Four Columns
The triad is the metaphysical content of the fixed element of Book I’s framework. It is not a fifth
column; it is the content that fills the first column. The distinction is the analytical/ontological
distinction of Chapter 2: the fixed element is the analytical role; the triad is the ontological
content that the role presupposes.
    The triad relates to the other three columns as follows. The substance is what the fixed
element holds invariant; the essence is what the fixed element’s invariant is; the thisness is what
distinguishes the fixed element from other fixed elements. The fluid element (Chapter 9) is
what conveys the effect of the substance on the substance of another; the governing dynamics
(Chapter 13) is the rule by which the essence determines the properties; the context (Chapter 17)
is the realm in which the thisness is realized. The four columns and the triad are not the same
structure; they are related structures, and the relation is what the later parts of Book II will
state.

8.3.3    The Triad and the Realm
The triad is not the same in every realm. In each realm, the triad takes a different form, and the
form is what the present chapter states. The form is the realm’s articulation of the triad—the
specific way in which substance, essence, and thisness are distinct, coincident, or collapsed in
that realm.
   The distinction is the chapter’s principal contribution. A chapter that merely listed the
substance, essence, and thisness of each realm would be a summary of Chapters 5, 6, and 7.
A chapter that states the pattern of their articulation across the realms is a genuine synthesis,
because the pattern is not visible from any single realm and is not stated in any single analysis.


8.4     The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Triad
8.4.1    The Three Patterns
The triad exhibits three patterns of articulation across the seven realms.
    The pattern of collapse. In the First Determination, the three elements of the triad collapse
into one. The substance of the First Determination is its unity; its essence is its unity; its
thisness is its unity. The three are not distinct, because there is no multiplicity in the First
Determination—no parts, no properties, no change—and the distinction of the triad is a distinction
of multiplicity. The First Determination is the limit case of the triad: it is what the triad becomes
when the multiplicity is zero.
    The pattern of partial coincidence. In the barzakhic realms (the Hubs of Decree, Signification,
and Realization), two elements of the triad coincide and the third distinguishes. The substance
and the essence coincide: the Hub of Decree’s substance is its measure, and its essence is its
86                                                Chapter 8. The Fixed Elements of Each Realm


measure; the Hub of Signification’s substance is its sign, and its essence is its sign; the Hub
of Realization’s substance is its actualization, and its essence is its actualization. The thisness
distinguishes: the Hub of Decree’s thisness is its particular allotment, the Hub of Signification’s
thisness is its particular sign, the Hub of Realization’s thisness is its particular actualization. The
coincidence is not an accident; it is a feature of the barzakhic mode of existence. The barzakhic
realm is a level whose mode of existence includes mediating, transforming, or regulating relations
between other realms (Book I, Definition 8.1); its being is its function, and its substance (the
ground of its being) and its essence (its what) are the same, because the realm is its function.
The thisness remains distinct, because the particular realm is this realm, not another.
    The pattern of full distinction. In the fundamental realms of multiplicity (the Structural
Determination, the Relational Manifestation, and the Material Manifestation), the three elements
of the triad are fully distinguished. The substance grounds the sameness; the essence grounds
the whatness; the thisness grounds the whichness. The three are distinct, and the distinction is
what makes the realm a realm of multiplicity: the realm has many things, each with its own
substance, essence, and thisness, and the three elements are what make the things things.

8.4.2    The Pattern as a Principle
The three patterns are not accidental; they are the articulation of a single principle, and the
principle is the chapter’s principal contribution.

Principle 8.2 (The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Triad). (E) The triad of fixed elements
is articulated differently in each realm, and the articulation is a function of the realm’s position
in the ontological architecture. In the First Determination, the triad collapses into unity. In the
barzakhic realms, substance and essence coincide, and thisness distinguishes. In the fundamental
realms of multiplicity, the triad is fully distinguished. The pattern tracks the realm’s mode of
existence: the more a realm is a realm of multiplicity, the more the triad is articulated.

    The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the analysis of
the seven realms supports. Its justification is that the pattern is visible in the seven realms and
that a different pattern would do the same explanatory work less well. Its refutation would be
a realm whose articulation does not fit the pattern, or a different pattern that does the same
explanatory work as well or better.

8.4.3    The Pattern and Book I
The pattern is not a new principle; it is the metaphysical articulation of Book I’s Principle 7.1
(C3, independent reality of the realms) and of Book I’s Principle 27.1 (C9, category-relative
predication). The first states that the realms are independently real, with modes of existence of
their own; the second states that metaphysical predicates are defined relative to a realm. The
pattern is the articulation of the two: the triad’s structure is relative to the realm, and the
relativity is what makes the realms independently real at the level of fixed elements.
    The pattern is (D) relative to Book I’s Principles 7.1 and 27.1. The chapter’s claim is not
that the pattern is a new principle; the claim is that the pattern is what Book I’s principles
require in the order of being, and the requirement is a metaphysical consequent of the principles.


8.5     The Fixed Elements of the Seven Realms
With the pattern in place, the fixed element of each realm can be stated as a single structure,
rather than as three separate analyses. The statements are (E) claims, offered at the strength
that the framework’s principles support.
8.5. The Fixed Elements of the Seven Realms                                                         87


8.5.1    The First Determination
The fixed element of the First Determination is pure unity, in which substance, essence, and
thisness collapse. The realm is what it is; its being is its unity; its what is its unity; its which is
its unity. The collapse is the limit case of the triad, and it is what the triad becomes when the
multiplicity is zero.

8.5.2    The Hub of Decree
The fixed element of the Hub of Decree is the measure that apportions, in which substance and
essence coincide and thisness distinguishes. The realm’s substance is its measure; its essence is
its measure; its thisness is its particular allotment. The coincidence is the barzakhic pattern: the
realm’s being is its function, and its substance and essence are the same, because the realm is its
measure.

8.5.3    The Structural Determination
The fixed element of the Structural Determination is the form or law that is held invariant, in
which the three elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s substance is the form (the ground
of the form’s being the same form through change); its essence is the law (the constitutive what
of the form); its thisness is the structural position (the non-qualitative individuator of the form).
The distinction is the fundamental-realm pattern: the realm is a realm of multiplicity, and the
three elements are what make the forms many.

8.5.4    The Hub of Signification
The fixed element of the Hub of Signification is the sign that signifies, in which substance and
essence coincide and thisness distinguishes. The realm’s substance is its sign; its essence is its
sign; its thisness is its particular sign. The coincidence is the barzakhic pattern: the realm’s
being is its function, and its substance and essence are the same, because the realm is its sign.

8.5.5    The Relational Manifestation
The fixed element of the Relational Manifestation is the relation that is held invariant, in which
the three elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s substance is the relation (the ground of
the relation’s being the same relation through change); its essence is the meaning-structure (the
constitutive what of the relation); its thisness is the historical trajectory (the non-qualitative
individuator of the relation). The distinction is the fundamental-realm pattern: the realm is a
realm of multiplicity, and the three elements are what make the relations many.

8.5.6    The Hub of Realization
The fixed element of the Hub of Realization is the actualization that realizes, in which substance
and essence coincide and thisness distinguishes. The realm’s substance is its actualization; its
essence is its actualization; its thisness is its particular actualization. The coincidence is the
barzakhic pattern: the realm’s being is its function, and its substance and essence are the same,
because the realm is its actualization.

8.5.7    The Material Manifestation
The fixed element of the Material Manifestation is the extended, discrete body, in which the three
elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s substance is the body (the ground of the body’s
being the same body through change); its essence is the natural kind (the constitutive what of
the body); its thisness is the spatiotemporal position (the non-qualitative individuator of the
88                                                Chapter 8. The Fixed Elements of Each Realm


body). The distinction is the fundamental-realm pattern: the realm is a realm of multiplicity,
and the three elements are what make the bodies many.

8.6     The Fixed Element and the Realm
8.6.1    The Fixed Element as the Realm’s Mode of Being
The table shows more than the substance, essence, and thisness of each realm; it shows that the
fixed element of a realm is the realm’s mode of being. The fixed element is not a thing in the
realm; it is the realm’s articulation of the triad, and the articulation is what makes the realm
the realm it is. The Material Manifestation is the realm in which the triad is articulated as body,
kind, and position; the Structural Determination is the realm in which the triad is articulated as
form, law, and position; the First Determination is the realm in which the triad is collapsed into
unity. The articulation is the realm’s mode of being, and the mode of being is the realm’s fixed
element.
    The identification is the chapter’s contribution to Book I’s Principle 7.1 (C3, independent
reality of the realms). Book I stated that each realm has a mode of existence of its own; the
present chapter states what the mode of existence is at the level of fixed elements. The mode of
existence is the articulation of the triad, and the articulation is what makes the realm independent
at the level of fixed elements.

8.6.2    The Fixed Element and the Realm’s Independence
The independence of the realm is the independence of its articulation. The Material Manifestation
is not reducible to the Structural Determination because its articulation of the triad (body, kind,
position) is not reducible to the Structural Determination’s articulation (form, law, position).
The First Determination is not reducible to the Material Manifestation because its collapse of the
triad is not reducible to the Material Manifestation’s distinction of the triad. The independence
is the independence of the articulation, and the articulation is what the table states.
8.7. The Four-Column Structure of the Synthesis                                                   89


Principle 8.3 (The Fixed Element as the Realm’s Mode of Being). (T) The fixed element
of a realm is the realm’s mode of being as an articulation of the triad of substance, essence,
and thisness. The articulation is what makes the realm independently real at the level of fixed
elements, and the independence is the independence of the articulation.

   The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the seven realms in §6 and by the
observation of the table. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 7.1, because the principle’s truth
depends on the independent reality of the realms.


8.7     The Four-Column Structure of the Synthesis
The synthesis itself has a four-column structure, and the structure is stated here.

8.7.1    The Fixed Element of the Synthesis
The fixed element of the synthesis is the triad of fixed elements itself, held invariant while the
synthesis explains the conditions of its articulation across the seven realms. The triad is held
invariant as the subject of the synthesis—the structure whose articulation the synthesis seeks to
state.

8.7.2    The Fluid Element of the Synthesis
The fluid element of the synthesis is the relation between the triad and the realm—the relation
by which the realm articulates the triad, and by which the triad is realized in the realm. The
relation is the medium of the synthesis: it is what conveys the effect of the realm’s mode of
existence to the triad’s articulation.

8.7.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Synthesis
The governing dynamics of the synthesis is the rule by which the realm’s position in the ontological
architecture determines the triad’s articulation—the rule that the more a realm is a realm of
multiplicity, the more the triad is articulated. The rule is the principle of §4 (8.2).

8.7.4    The Context of the Synthesis
The context of the synthesis is the framework of Book I, in which the seven realms are indepen-
dently real and the triads are category-relative. The context is the frame in which the synthesis
is posed, and it is what makes the synthesis a synthesis of the framework, not a synthesis in
general.

8.8     What Part II Establishes
Part II has established four things.
    The definition of substance (Chapter 5, Definition 5.1), and the argument that substance is
the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s fixed element (Chapter 5, Principle 5.3).
    The definition of essence (Chapter 6, Definition 6.1), the argument that essence is the
metaphysical consequent of Book I’s defining invariants (Chapter 6, Principle 6.3), and the
essentialist thesis with its three arguments (Chapter 6, Principle 6.4).
    The definition of thisness (Chapter 7, Definition 7.1), the argument that thisness is the
metaphysical consequent of Book I’s non-duplicability (Chapter 7, Principle 7.3), and the doctrine
of primitive thisness with its three arguments (Chapter 7, Principle 7.4).
    The synthesis of the triad across the seven realms (the present chapter, Definition 8.1 and
Principle 8.2), and the principle that the fixed element of a realm is the realm’s mode of being
as an articulation of the triad (the present chapter, Principle 8.3).
    The four establishments are the contribution of Part II. They are the metaphysical analysis
of Book I’s fixed element, and they are what Book II’s later parts will presuppose.


8.9     What Part II Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from Part II are deliberately deferred.
    First, Part II does not analyze the fluid elements of metaphysics. The fluid element—causation,
relation, light—is the subject of Part III. The present part has analyzed the fixed elements in
isolation from the fluid elements, and the isolation is deliberate: it makes the fixed elements
visible before the fluid elements are introduced.
    Second, Part II does not settle the question of whether the triad is exhaustive. The triad
(substance, essence, thisness) is the chapter’s analysis of the fixed element; whether a fourth
element is needed, or whether one of the three can be derived from the others, is a question the
present part leaves open. The question is marked (Q) in the chapter’s status table.
    Third, Part II does not state the relation between the triad and the governing dynamics. The
relation is the subject of Part IV, where the governing dynamics of metaphysics is analyzed. The
present part has stated the fixed elements; the relation to the governing dynamics is deferred.
    Fourth, Part II does not state the relation between the triad and the context. The relation is
the subject of Part V, where the context of metaphysics is analyzed. The present part has stated
the fixed elements; the relation to the context is deferred.
    The four deferrals are the conditions under which Part II is offered, and they are stated so
that the reader knows what kind of claim is being made. A reader who accepts the deferrals
accepts the part’s scope; a reader who does not has a reason to read the later parts, where the
deferrals are lifted.

8.11      A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a person, a place, a work of art, an institution—and consider
the realm in which it is realized. Is the thing’s substance, essence, and thisness fully distinguished,
or do two of them coincide, or do all three collapse? What does the answer tell you about the
realm in which the thing is realized, and about the thing’s mode of being?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The triad is not the same in every realm;
its articulation is a function of the realm’s position in the ontological architecture. The reader
who can state, for a thing he knows, the articulation of its triad, has understood the chapter’s
distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and
is invited to develop the difficulty further.

With this chapter, Part II of Book II is complete. The fixed elements of metaphysics—substance,
essence, and thisness—are analyzed, synthesized into the triad, and shown to be articulated
differently in each of the seven realms. The next part turns to the fluid elements of metaphysics:
causation, relation, light, and the fluid elements of each realm. The first analysis is causation,
which is the subject of Chapter 9.

Chapter 9

Causation

Scope. This chapter opens Part III with the analysis of causation. It defines causation as the
real transfer of effect from a cause to an effect through a medium, and it argues that causation
is what Book I’s conveyor principle (Principle 4.1, C8) presupposes in the order of being. It
distinguishes causation from regularity, from counterfactual dependence, from the manifestation
of a power, and from process, and it states what the four standard theories of causation share; it
states the relation between causation and the fluid element of Book I’s framework; it states the
four-column structure of the inquiry into causation; it states the form that causation takes in
each of the seven realms; and it answers three standard objections. Its claims are metaphysical
and structural; where it speaks of “cause,” “effect,” “transfer,” “medium,” or “regularity,” these
are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and by the framework
of Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s definition of the fluid
element (Definition 2.2), the conveyor principle (Principle 4.1), the non-sequential connectivity
(Principle 4.2), the principle that every explanation requires a conveyor (Principle 15.3), the
causality rule of the Material Manifestation (Principle 16.12), and the principle of category-
relative predication (Principle 27.1, C9). It does not restate these principles; it asks what they
presuppose in the order of being. The presupposition is stated in §6, and the chapter’s principal
contribution is the demonstration that causation is the presupposition.


9.1     A Scene
Consider a violinist in a small studio, teaching a student. The teacher takes her bow and plays a
phrase. She plays it slowly, then again, then again, each time with the same slight emphasis, the
same pause before the last note, the same leaning into the string. She puts the bow down. She
says: Now you.
    The student plays the phrase. Her first attempt is different: the emphasis is elsewhere, the
pause is gone, the leaning is absent. The teacher does not say a word; she takes the bow again,
and she plays the phrase once more, and she looks at the student. The student plays again. Her
second attempt is different from her first: the emphasis is closer, the pause is almost there, the
leaning has begun. The teacher nods.
    Something has passed between the teacher and the student. The sound has traveled through
the air; the student’s ears have received it; her fingers have responded. But the sound is not
what has passed: the student can hear a recording of the phrase, and she will not learn it from
the recording. What has passed is the way of playing—the technique, the emphasis, the pause,
the leaning. The way of playing is not the sound, and it is not the bow, and it is not the air. It
is what the sound carries, and what the student’s fingers receive, and what the teacher’s playing
has caused in the student’s playing.
96                                                                           Chapter 9. Causation


    What has happened between the teacher and the student is causation. The teacher’s playing
has caused the student’s playing, and the causation has been conveyed through a medium—the
sound, the room, the teacher’s presence, the student’s attention. The causation is not physical
impact; the teacher has not touched the student’s fingers. The causation is not logical entailment;
the student’s second attempt does not follow from the teacher’s playing as a theorem follows
from an axiom. The causation is motivational: the teacher’s playing has moved the student to
play differently, and the moving has been conveyed through the medium of the lesson.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is causation? Is it the physical impact of
one body on another, the logical entailment of one proposition from another, the regularity of
one event following another, or the manifestation of a power? And what does the framework
of Book I require, in the order of being, when it says that every explanation of how one thing
bears on another must invoke a fluid element—a conveyor? The chapter’s answer is: causation is
the real transfer of effect through a medium, and it is what the fluid element presupposes. The
chapter’s task is to say what causation is, to distinguish it from the notions with which it is easily
confused, and to show that it is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s conveyor principle.


9.2     The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is causation, and what does it presuppose?
    The question is not the same as the question of Book I’s Chapter 4. Book I asked what an
explanation of how one thing bears on another must contain, and it answered: a fluid element—a
carrier, medium, signal, or process by which the effect passes (Principle 4.1). The answer was
analytical: it said what an explanation must contain, not what reality must contain. The present
chapter asks the metaphysical counterpart: what must be the case in reality, such that a fluid
element can convey an effect? What must causation be, such that a conveyor can be a conveyor?
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of causation? The chapter must define causation,
and it must distinguish the definition from the definitions of substance (Chapter 5), essence
(Chapter 6), thisness (Chapter 7), and relation (Chapter 10). The definition must be precise
enough to be argued about, and general enough to cover the causation of each of the seven
realms.
    The second aspect: what is the relation between causation and Book I’s conveyor principle?
The chapter must state how causation relates to Book I’s Principle 4.1. The relation is the
chapter’s principal contribution, because it is what makes causation a metaphysical consequent
of the framework, not a metaphysical posit alongside it.
    The third aspect: what is the relation between causation and the standard theories? The chapter
must state the four standard theories of causation—regularity, counterfactual dependence, powers,
and process—and it must state what they share. The statement is the chapter’s contribution to
the philosophical debate, and it is what makes the chapter a metaphysical analysis, not a mere
stipulation of a definition.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: causation
is the real transfer of effect through a medium; it is what Book I’s conveyor principle presupposes;
and the four standard theories share the notion of transfer, which the framework calls the causal
medium.


9.3     The Definition of Causation
9.3.1    The Definition
Definition 9.1 (Causation). (A) Causation is the real transfer of effect from a cause to an effect
through a medium. The transfer is what the cause does to the effect; the medium is what the
9.3. The Definition of Causation                                                                   97


transfer passes through; the effect is what the transfer produces.

     The definition has three components, and each is important.
     The first component: causation is a real transfer. The transfer is not a figure of speech;
it is a real relation between the cause and the effect. The cause does something to the effect,
and the doing is what the definition calls the transfer. The transfer is not the regularity of the
effect’s following the cause (a regularity is a pattern, not a transfer); it is not the counterfactual
dependence of the effect on the cause (a dependence is a modal relation, not a transfer); it is
not the manifestation of a power (a manifestation is the actualization of a disposition, not a
transfer). The transfer is the real relation by which the cause produces its effect.
     The second component: the transfer passes through a medium. The transfer is not immediate;
it is conveyed through a medium. The medium is what the transfer passes through; it is the
condition under which the transfer is possible. The medium is not the cause, and it is not the
effect; it is the third thing—the condition of the transfer. The medium is what the framework
calls the causal medium, and it is what Chapter 11 will identify with light.
     The third component: the effect is what the transfer produces. The effect is the result of the
transfer; it is the change that the transfer has brought about in the effect. The effect is not the
cause, and it is not the medium; it is the third thing—the product of the transfer. The effect is
what the transfer has made different, and the difference is what the transfer has produced.
     The three components are not three definitions; they are three aspects of one definition. The
causation is the real transfer, the transfer passes through a medium, and the transfer produces
the effect—and these are three ways of saying the same thing, because the transfer’s reality, its
medium, and its product are three aspects of its being a transfer.

9.3.2    What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
    It does not say that causation is physical impact. The transfer is not the collision of two
bodies; it is the transfer of effect, and the effect can be physical, motivational, formal, or of
another kind. The teacher’s playing has caused the student’s playing, and the causation is not a
collision; it is a transfer of a way of playing through the medium of the lesson. The physical
impact is one mode of the transfer; it is not the transfer itself.
    It does not say that causation is a regularity. A regularity is a pattern of events; the transfer
is the relation that the pattern exhibits. The pattern is the observable side of the transfer; the
transfer is the real relation that the pattern manifests. The distinction is the distinction between
the pattern and the transfer; the causation is the transfer, not the pattern.
    It does not say that causation is a counterfactual dependence. A counterfactual dependence
is a modal relation between events (if the cause had not occurred, the effect would not have
occurred); the transfer is the real relation that the dependence tracks. The dependence is the
modal side of the transfer; the transfer is the real relation that the dependence manifests. The
distinction is the distinction between the modal relation and the real relation; the causation is
the real relation, not the modal one.
    It does not say that causation is a power. A power is a disposition to produce an effect;
the transfer is the actualization of the disposition. The power is the source of the transfer; the
transfer is what the power does when it is actualized. The distinction is the distinction between
the disposition and its actualization; the causation is the actualization, not the disposition alone.
    It does not say that causation is a process. A process is a spatiotemporal sequence of events;
the transfer is the relation that the sequence carries. The process is the vehicle of the transfer;
the transfer is what the vehicle carries. The distinction is the distinction between the vehicle
and the carried; the causation is the carried, not the vehicle alone.
98                                                                            Chapter 9. Causation


9.3.3    Causation and Effect
Definition 9.2 (Cause and Effect). (A) A cause is what produces an effect; an effect is what
a cause produces. The cause and the effect are the relata of the causation; the transfer is the
relation between them; the medium is what the relation passes through.
    The distinction between cause and effect is classical, and the framework uses it. The distinction
is not between two kinds of things; it is between two roles that a thing plays relative to a causation.
The same thing can be a cause in one causation and an effect in another—the teacher’s playing
is the effect of her practice and the cause of the student’s playing. The framework’s use of the
distinction is the same as Book I’s use of the fixed-fluid distinction (Book I, Principle 5.1): the
role is analytical, and the same thing can play different roles in different causations.


9.4     Causation and the Standard Theories
The chapter’s first contribution to the philosophical debate is the statement of what the four
standard theories of causation share.

9.4.1    The Four Theories
Four theories of causation are standard in the contemporary debate.
    Regularity theory. Causation is constant conjunction: the cause is the event that is regularly
followed by the effect (Hume; Mackie’s INUS conditions). The theory’s virtue is its empiricism:
it does not posit unobservable relations. Its difficulty is that regularity does not distinguish
causation from mere correlation, and that it does not explain why the regularity holds.
    Counterfactual theory. Causation is counterfactual dependence: the cause is the event such
that, if it had not occurred, the effect would not have occurred (Lewis). The theory’s virtue
is its sensitivity to the difference between causes and mere conditions. Its difficulty is that
counterfactual dependence is a modal relation, and the theory must explain what grounds the
dependence.
    Powers theory. Causation is the manifestation of a power: the cause is the thing whose power
is actualized in the effect (Mumford; Molnar; Ellis). The theory’s virtue is that it explains why
the regularity holds. Its difficulty is that powers are unobservable, and the theory must explain
what a power is.
    Process theory. Causation is a physical process: the cause is the event that initiates a process
which transmits a mark to the effect (Salmon; Dowe). The theory’s virtue is its attention to the
mechanism of transmission. Its difficulty is that it is limited to physical causation, and it does
not cover the causation of non-physical realms.

9.4.2    What the Theories Share
The four theories differ on what causation is, but they share a common structure. Each theory
posits a transfer of something from the cause to the effect, and each theory explains what the
transfer is in its own terms.
Principle 9.3 (What the Theories Share). (T) The four standard theories of causation—regularity,
counterfactual dependence, powers, and process—share the notion of a transfer of effect from
the cause to the effect. The theories differ on what the transfer is (a regularity of a transfer, a
counterfactual dependence of a transfer, a manifestation of a transfer, a physical process of a
transfer), but they all presuppose that there is a transfer. The transfer is what the chapter calls
the causal medium.
   The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the four theories. Its argument is the
observation that each theory, in its own vocabulary, posits something by which the cause produces
9.5. Causation as the Presupposition of the Fluid Element                                          99


its effect in the effect, and that the something is what the framework calls the transfer. The
regularity theory’s constant conjunction is a pattern of transfers; the counterfactual theory’s
dependence is a modal tracking of transfers; the powers theory’s manifestation is the actualization
of a transfer; the process theory’s physical process is the vehicle of a transfer. The four theories
are four ways of describing the same structure—the transfer—and the framework’s contribution
is to name the structure and to identify it with the causal medium.

9.4.3    The Framework’s Position
The framework does not choose one of the four theories over the others. Its claim is that
the four theories are partial descriptions of the transfer, and that the framework’s definition
(Definition 9.1) is the general structure that the four theories describe in their own terms.

Principle 9.4 (The Framework’s Position on the Theories). (E) The framework does not adopt
one of the four standard theories of causation; it identifies the general structure—the transfer
through a medium—that the four theories describe in their own terms. The framework’s position
is compatible with all four theories, and it is incompatible with none of them; it is the general
structure that the theories instantiate.

   The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the analysis of
the four theories supports. Its justification is that the general structure is visible in all four
theories and that it does the same explanatory work as any one of them, without committing
the framework to the specific claims of any one. Its refutation would be a theory of causation
that does not presuppose a transfer, or a general structure that does not fit the four theories.


9.5     Causation as the Presupposition of the Fluid Element
The chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that causation is what Book I’s conveyor
principle presupposes in the order of being. The demonstration has three steps.

9.5.1    Step 1: The Fluid Element Presupposes a Transfer
Book I’s Definition 2.2 states that the fluid element is an entity that conveys effect. The definition
is analytical: it names the role the fluid element plays in an explanation. But the role presupposes
a transfer: for the fluid element to convey effect, there must be an effect to be conveyed, and
the conveyance must be a real relation between the fluid element and the effect. The transfer is
what the fluid element’s role presupposes; without the transfer, the role would be empty.
    The step is a (D) claim: it is conditional on Book I’s Definition 2.2. The claim is not that
the fluid element is a transfer; the claim is that the fluid element presupposes a transfer, and
that the presupposition is the fluid element’s metaphysical condition.

9.5.2    Step 2: The Transfer Is Causation
The transfer that the fluid element presupposes is what the chapter calls causation. The
identification is not arbitrary: it is the identification of the transfer with the notion that the
metaphysical tradition has called causation. The tradition’s notion is the notion of the real
relation by which a cause produces its effect; the chapter’s definition is the same notion, stated
in the framework’s vocabulary.
    The step is a (T) claim: it is argued by the analysis of the notion of causation and by the
comparison with the tradition’s notion. It is relative to the chapter’s definition (Definition 9.1),
and it is assessable by the definition’s adequacy.
100                                                                         Chapter 9. Causation


9.5.3    Step 3: The Presupposition Is a Metaphysical Consequent
The presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of Book I’s framework, not an independent
metaphysical posit. The framework does not add causation to the fluid element; it states what
the fluid element requires in the order of being. The requirement is a (D) claim, and the (D)
claim is the chapter’s principal contribution.
    The step is the synthesis of Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 establishes that the fluid element
presupposes a transfer; Step 2 establishes that the transfer is causation; Step 3 establishes that
the presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of the framework. The three steps together
establish the chapter’s principal claim.
Principle 9.5 (Causation as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Conveyor Principle). (D)
Causation is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s conveyor principle: the conveyor principle
presupposes a real transfer of effect from the cause to the effect, and the transfer is what the
chapter calls causation. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principle 4.1
(C8); it is the chapter’s principal contribution because it states what the conveyor principle
requires in the order of being.

9.5.4    The Conveyor Principle and Book I’s Other Principles
The principle connects Book I’s conveyor principle (Principle 4.1) to Book I’s other principles.
    The non-sequential connectivity (Book I, Principle 4.2). The non-sequential connectivity
states that the conveyor need not pass through every intermediate element. The present chapter’s
definition is compatible with the principle: the transfer can be direct (through a medium that
does not pass through every intermediate) or sequential (through a medium that does). The
distinction is the distinction between two modes of the transfer, not two kinds of transfer.
    Every explanation requires a conveyor (Book I, Principle 15.3). The principle states that every
explanation requires a conveyor. The present chapter’s claim is that every conveyor presupposes
a causation; the two together yield the conclusion that every explanation presupposes a causation.
The conclusion is the chapter’s contribution to Book I’s account of explanation: the explanation’s
conveyor is the manifestation of the causation in the order of explanation.
    The causality rule of the Material Manifestation (Book I, Principle 16.12). Book I stated
that the Material Manifestation has the rule of causality: every material event has a cause, and
every cause produces an effect. The present chapter’s claim is that this rule is the Material
mode of the general causal structure—the mode in which the transfer takes the form of physical
causation. The distinction is the distinction between the general structure (the transfer through
a medium) and the Material mode (physical causation); the present chapter states the general
structure, and the Material mode is one of its seven modes.
Principle 9.6 (The Material Manifestation’s Causality Is a Mode). (D) Book I’s causality
rule of the Material Manifestation (Principle 16.12) is the Material mode of the general causal
structure: the general structure is the transfer of effect through a medium, and the Material
mode is the transfer as physical causation. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on
Book I’s Principle 16.12 and on the principle of category-relative predication (Principle 27.1, C9).
    The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the application of Book I’s category-
relative predication to the specific case of causation. The application shows that the general
structure is the same across the realms, and that the differences are the differences of the mode,
not of the structure.


9.6     The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Causation
With the definition of causation in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can be applied
to the inquiry into causation.
9.7. Causation in Each Realm                                                                   101


9.6.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Causation
The fixed element of the inquiry into causation is the cause and the effect, held invariant while
the inquiry explains the conditions of the transfer. The cause and the effect are held invariant as
the relata of the causation—the terms whose transfer the inquiry seeks to explain.

9.6.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Causation
The fluid element of the inquiry into causation is the transfer itself—the relation by which the
cause produces its effect through a medium. The transfer is the medium of the inquiry: it is
what conveys the effect of the cause’s being what it is to the effect’s being what it is.

9.6.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Causation
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into causation is the rule by which the transfer oper-
ates—the rule that explains how the cause produces its effect, and under what conditions the
transfer is possible. The rule is the subject of §4, where the standard theories are analyzed; each
theory states a different rule, and the framework’s claim is that the rule is the general structure
that the theories describe in their own terms.

9.6.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Causation
The context of the inquiry into causation is the realm in which the causation occurs. The seven
realms of Book I are the contexts, and causation takes a different form in each. The form of
causation in each realm is the subject of §8.

9.6.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into causation are stated in the following table.

                 Column               In the Inquiry into Causation
                 Fixed element    The cause and the effect, held invariant as
                                  the relata of the transfer
                 Fluid element    The transfer itself, through which the effect
                                  is conveyed
                 Governing dynam- The rule by which the transfer operates
                 ics
                 Context          The realm in which the causation occurs

   The table is the application of Chapter 2’s method to the inquiry into causation. The
application is the chapter’s contribution to the book’s systematic character.


9.7     Causation in Each Realm
Causation takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the form,
one realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered at the
strength that the framework’s principles support, and subject to revision if a different form of
causation in a realm does the same explanatory work.
102                                                                         Chapter 9. Causation


9.7.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, causation takes the form of physical causation—the transfer of
energy, momentum, force, or another physical quantity from one material thing to another. The
fire’s heat causes the wood’s ignition; the stone’s impact causes the glass’s breakage. The physical
causation is the Material mode of the general causal structure, and it is the mode that Book I’s
Principle 16.12 describes.

9.7.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, causation takes the form of motivational causation—the transfer
of a reason, a meaning, or a significance from one relational thing to another. The teacher’s
playing causes the student’s playing; the argument’s force causes the listener’s change of mind;
the friend’s presence causes the friend’s comfort. The motivational causation is the Relational
mode of the general causal structure, and it is the mode that the scene of the teacher and student
exhibits.

9.7.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, causation takes the form of formal causation—the transfer of
necessity from a premise to its consequence. The axiom causes the theorem; the definition causes
the entailment; the law causes the instance. The formal causation is the Structural mode of the
general causal structure, and it is the mode that logical entailment exhibits. The framework’s
claim is that the formal causation is a mode of the transfer, not a different kind of relation; the
necessity is what the transfer carries in the Structural Determination, as the physical quantity is
what the transfer carries in the Material Manifestation.

9.7.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, there is no causation. The First Determination has no multiplicity,
no change, no succession (Book I, Definition 7.5); causation requires a change from the cause to
the effect, and the First Determination has no change. The absence of causation is not a defect;
it is a feature of the First Determination’s mode of existence. The form is the limit case of the
other forms: it is what causation becomes when there is nothing to change.

9.7.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, causation takes the form of apportioning causation—the transfer of the
measure from the unified source to the multiple forms. The measure causes the apportioning; the
source causes the form. The apportioning causation is the mode of the general causal structure
in the Hub of Decree.

9.7.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, causation takes the form of signification causation—the transfer of
significance from the structure to the sign. The structure causes its meaning; the law causes its
signification. The signification causation is the mode of the general causal structure in the Hub
of Signification.

9.7.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, causation takes the form of realization causation—the transfer of
actuality from the possible to the concrete. The possibility causes its actualization; the meaning
9.8. Objections and Replies                                                                       103


causes its realization. The realization causation is the mode of the general causal structure in
the Hub of Realization.

9.7.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

                  Realm                The Form of Causation
                  First Determina-     No causation (limit case)
                  tion
                  Hub of Decree        Apportioning causation (measure)
                  Structural Deter-    Formal causation (entailment)
                  mination
                  Hub of Significa-    Signification causation (sign)
                  tion
                  Relational Mani-     Motivational causation (reason)
                  festation
                  Hub of Realiza-      Realization causation (actualization)
                  tion
                  Material Manifes-    Physical causation (energy)
                  tation

     The table is the chapter’s map of causation across the seven realms. It is an (E) claim, and
it is offered at the strength that the framework’s principles support.


9.8     Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: Causation is a physical relation; the framework’s “motivational causation” is
not causation. The objection is that causation is the transfer of physical quantities (energy,
momentum, force), and that the teacher’s playing causing the student’s playing is not causation
but influence, or persuasion, or teaching—something other than causation.
    Reply. The objection confuses physical causation with causation tout court. The framework’s
definition of causation is the real transfer of effect through a medium; the physical causation
is one mode of the transfer, not the whole of it. The teacher’s playing is a real transfer of a
real effect (the way of playing) through a real medium (the lesson); the transfer is what makes
the causation causation, and the mode (motivational rather than physical) is what makes it
the mode it is. The objection’s premise—that only physical transfers are causation—is not the
framework’s premise; the framework’s premise is that every real transfer of effect is causation,
and the physical transfer is one of its modes. The distinction is the distinction between the
general structure and its modes; the framework states the general structure, and the modes are
its seven forms.
    Objection 2: Hume showed that causation is just constant conjunction; the framework’s
“transfer” is a metaphysical posit that Hume refuted. The objection is that Hume’s analysis of
causation as constant conjunction shows that there is no real transfer, only a regularity, and that
the framework’s “transfer” is a relic of pre-Humean metaphysics.
    Reply. The objection confuses Hume’s epistemology of causation with his metaphysics of
causation. Hume’s argument is about how we know causation—he argued that we do not perceive
the necessary connection, and that we infer it from custom. But Hume did not deny that there
is a real regularity; his regularity theory posits a real constant conjunction. The framework’s
“transfer” is not a denial of the regularity; it is the analysis of what the regularity is—the pattern
104                                                                         Chapter 9. Causation


that a real transfer exhibits. The regularity is the observable side of the transfer; the transfer
is the real relation that the observable side manifests. The framework’s claim is metaphysical,
not epistemological; the objection’s Hume is the epistemological Hume, not the metaphysical
one. The two are distinct, and the framework’s analysis is compatible with the epistemological
Hume’s conclusions.
    Objection 3: The definition is circular. The definition says that causation is the transfer of
effect; the effect is what the transfer produces; and the transfer is the causation. The three terms
are defined in terms of one another, and the definition is circular.
    Reply. The circularity is only apparent. The definition does not define the effect as “what the
transfer produces”; it defines the effect as the relatum of the causation that the transfer produces.
The transfer is the primitive notion; the cause and the effect are the relata of the transfer; the
medium is what the transfer passes through. The definition’s structure is: transfer (primitive) +
relata (cause, effect) + medium (condition) = causation (the structure). The three terms are not
defined in terms of one another; they are three aspects of one structure, and the structure is the
definition. The objection mistakes the structural definition for a semantic circularity; the reply
distinguishes them.


9.9     What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that causation is a real relation. It argues that causation
is what Book I’s conveyor principle presupposes; the argument is (D) relative to Book I’s
Principle 4.1, and it is offered at the strength that the principle supports. A reader who rejects
the conveyor principle has a reason to reject the conclusion; the chapter states the argument at
exactly that strength.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of which of the four standard theories is
correct. The chapter’s claim is that the four theories are partial descriptions of the transfer, and
that the framework’s general structure is compatible with all four; the choice among the four is a
further question, and the chapter leaves it open. The question is marked (Q) in the chapter’s
status table.
    Third, the chapter does not analyze relation. Relation is the subject of Chapter 10; the
present chapter distinguishes causation from relation where the distinction is needed, but it
does not analyze relation. The reader who expects the analysis in this chapter has misread the
chapter’s scope; the analysis begins in Chapter 10.
    Fourth, the chapter does not identify causation with light. The identification is the subject
of Chapter 11; the present chapter states that causation presupposes a medium, but it does not
identify the medium with light. The identification is deferred to Chapter 11, where the medium
is analyzed as light.

9.11      A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you caused something—a word that changed someone’s mind, a
gesture that comforted someone, a decision that set something in motion. What was the transfer?
What was the medium? Was the transfer physical, motivational, formal, or of another kind?
And if the transfer was real, what would it mean for the transfer to be caused by the medium
rather than by the cause?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The cause is what produces the effect; the
medium is what the transfer passes through; the effect is what the transfer produces. The three
are distinct, and the distinction is what makes the causation a causation rather than a mere
regularity. The reader who can state, for a causation he knows, what the cause, the medium,
and the effect are, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a
place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

The next chapter analyzes relation: what it is for two things to stand in a relation, and how
relation relates to causation. With causation in place, the framework can distinguish the transfer
of effect (causation) from the connection of terms (relation), and it can state the relation between
the two—the relation that the medium presupposes, and that the causation presupposes as its
field. The analysis is the subject of Chapter 10.
