Chapter 10

Relation

Scope. This chapter analyzes relation. It defines relation as the real connection between two
or more terms, distinct from the terms themselves and distinct from the transfer of effect that
causation names. It distinguishes relation from causation, from property, and from trope; it states
the four standard theories of relation—realism, anti-realism, trope theory, and structuralism—and
it states what they share; it argues that relation is what Book I’s account of the Relational
Manifestation (Definition 7.7) and the fluid element (Definition 2.2) presuppose in the order
of being; it addresses Bradley’s regress and shows that Book I’s Principle 12.3—light as the
condition of possibility of relation—is the framework’s response to the regress; it states the
four-column structure of the inquiry into relation; it states the form that relation takes in each
of the seven realms; and it answers three standard objections. Its claims are metaphysical
and structural; where it speaks of “relation,” “connection,” “relatum,” or “regress,” these are
structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and by the framework of
Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s definition of the fluid
element (Definition 2.2), the principle that light is the condition of possibility of relation
(Principle 12.3), the definition of the Relational Manifestation (Definition 7.7) and its rules
(Principles 16.9 and 16.10), and the principle of category-relative predication (Principle 27.1,
C9). It does not restate these principles; it asks what they presuppose in the order of being. The
presupposition is stated in §5 and §6, and the chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration
that relation is the presupposition, and that Book I’s account of light is the framework’s response
to Bradley’s regress.


10.1      A Scene
Consider a family at a dinner table. There are four people: a mother, a father, a daughter, a son.
The four are related to one another: the mother is married to the father; the daughter is the
child of both; the son is the sibling of the daughter. The relations are real: they make the four a
family, not four strangers who happen to share an address. The relations are not the people:
the mother is not her marriage; the daughter is not her childhood. And the relations are not
the dinner: the dinner is what the relations have occasioned, and the dinner may end while the
relations continue.
    What, then, are the relations? The mother’s marriage to the father is not a fifth person at
the table; it is not a physical object in the room; it is not a sound or a color. It is the connection
between the mother and the father—the connection that makes the two of them a couple. The
connection is real, and it is distinct from the two it connects. The daughter’s childhood is not a
thing the daughter carries around; it is the connection between the daughter and her parents—the
108                                                                           Chapter 10. Relation


connection that makes her their child. The connection is real, and it is distinct from the three it
connects.
     The scene is not about families in particular. It is about a general structure, and the structure
is this: a relation connects two or more terms, and the connection is neither of the terms nor a
third term alongside them. The connection is what makes the terms related; it is the condition
under which the terms are the terms of a relation.
     Now consider a harder case. Consider a relation between a relation and its terms. The
marriage connects the mother and the father; but does the marriage itself need to be connected
to the mother and the father? If the marriage is a thing, and the mother and father are things,
then something must connect the marriage to the mother, and that connection must be a further
thing, and that further thing needs a connection to the marriage, and so on without end. This is
Bradley’s regress, and it has been the central difficulty for any theory that treats relations as
real.
     The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is a relation? Is it a thing, a property, a
trope, a pattern, or a condition? And what does the framework of Book I require, in the order of
being, when it says that light is the condition of possibility of relation (Principle 12.3)? The
chapter’s answer is: relation is the real connection between terms, distinct from the terms and
distinct from causation; and Book I’s account of light is the framework’s response to Bradley’s
regress—light is not a relation, but the condition under which relation is possible, and the
condition does not enter the regress. The chapter’s task is to say what relation is, to distinguish
it from the notions with which it is easily confused, and to show that Book I’s account of light is
the framework’s solution to the regress.


10.2      The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is relation, and what does it presuppose?
    The question is not the same as the question of Chapter 9. Chapter 9 asked what causation is,
and it answered: causation is the real transfer of effect from a cause to an effect through a medium.
The answer was about transfer. The present chapter asks a different question: what is a relation,
and what does it presuppose? The answer is about connection. The two notions—transfer and
connection—are distinct: a transfer is what a cause does to an effect; a connection is what makes
two terms related, whether or not any transfer is involved. The teacher’s playing causes the
student’s playing (a transfer); the teacher and the student are related as teacher and student (a
connection). The two are distinct, and the chapter must keep them apart.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of relation? The chapter must define relation, and
it must distinguish the definition from the definitions of causation (Chapter 9, Definition 9.1),
substance (Chapter 5, Definition 5.1), and essence (Chapter 6, Definition 6.1). The definition
must be precise enough to be argued about, and general enough to cover the relation of each of
the seven realms.
    The second aspect: what is the relation between relation and Book I’s account of light? The
chapter must state how relation relates to Book I’s Principle 12.3 (light as the condition of
possibility of relation). The relation is the chapter’s principal contribution, because it is what
makes Book I’s account of light the framework’s response to Bradley’s regress.
    The third aspect: what is the relation between relation and the standard theories? The chapter
must state the four standard theories—realism, anti-realism, trope theory, and structuralism—and
it must state what they share. The statement is the chapter’s contribution to the philosophical
debate, and it is what makes the chapter a metaphysical analysis, not a mere stipulation of a
definition.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: relation is
the real connection between terms; it is what Book I’s account of light and of the Relational
10.3. The Definition of Relation                                                                   109


Manifestation presupposes; and the four standard theories share the notion of connection, which
the framework calls relation.


10.3      The Definition of Relation
10.3.1    The Definition
Definition 10.1 (Relation). (A) A relation is the real connection between two or more terms,
distinct from the terms themselves and distinct from the transfer of effect that causation names.
The relation is what makes the terms related; it is the condition under which the terms are the
terms of a relation.
     The definition has three components, and each is important.
     The first component: a relation is a real connection. The connection is not a figure of speech;
it is a real feature of the world. The mother’s marriage is real; the daughter’s childhood is real;
the son’s siblinghood is real. The connection is not the observer’s projection; it is what the
observer’s projection tracks. The distinction is the distinction between the real connection and
the observed pattern; the relation is the first, not the second.
     The second component: a relation is distinct from its terms. The relation connects the terms,
and it is not one of the terms. The mother’s marriage is not the mother; the daughter’s childhood
is not the daughter; the son’s siblinghood is not the son. The relation is real, and it is distinct
from the terms it relates. The distinction is the distinction between the relation and the relata;
the relation is the first, and the relata are the second.
     The third component: a relation is distinct from causation. The relation connects the terms;
causation transfers the effect. The two are distinct: the teacher and the student are related (a
relation), and the teacher’s playing causes the student’s playing (a causation). The relation is
the connection; the causation is the transfer. The two are not the same, and the chapter must
keep them apart.
     The three components are not three definitions; they are three aspects of one definition. The
relation is the real connection, distinct from its terms and distinct from causation—and these
are three ways of saying the same thing, because the connection’s reality, its distinctness from
the relata, and its distinctness from causation are three aspects of its being a connection.

10.3.2    What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
     It does not say that relation is a thing. The relation is a connection, not a thing. It is not a
fifth person at the table; it is not a physical object in the room. The relation is the connection
between the terms, and the connection is not a further term alongside the terms. The distinction
is the distinction between the connection and the connected; the relation is the first, not the
second.
     It does not say that relation is a property. A property is a feature of a single thing; a relation
is a feature of two or more things. The mother’s kindness is a property; the mother’s marriage
to the father is a relation. The two are distinct: the property belongs to one thing; the relation
holds between two. The distinction is the distinction between the monadic and the polyadic; the
property is monadic, and the relation is polyadic.
     It does not say that relation is causation. Causation is the transfer of effect; relation is the
connection of terms. The two are distinct: a relation can hold without any transfer (the mother
and the father are related as spouses whether or not any effect passes between them), and a
causation can occur without a relation that is not itself a causal relation (the teacher’s playing
causes the student’s playing, and the causation is one relation among many that hold between
them). The distinction is the distinction between the connection and the transfer; the relation is
the first, and the causation is the second.
110                                                                           Chapter 10. Relation


    It does not say that relation is a trope. A trope is a particular property; the relation is
a connection. The trope theorist says that the mother’s marriage is a particular trope—a
relation-trope—that exists at a particular place and time. The framework’s definition is neutral
about the trope theory; it says that the relation is the real connection, and it leaves open whether
the connection is a trope, a universal, or a condition. The trope theory is one of the standard
theories, and the chapter states it in §4 without adopting it.
    It does not say that relation is internal or external. An internal relation is one that holds by
the natures of the relata; an external relation is one that holds independently of the natures of
the relata. The mother’s marriage is (at least partly) external: the mother and the father could
have existed without being married. The daughter’s childhood is (at least partly) internal: the
daughter could not have existed as the daughter without being the child of her parents. The
framework’s definition is neutral about the internal and the external; it says that the relation
is the real connection, and it leaves open whether the connection is internal or external. The
distinction is the subject of §4, where the standard theories are analyzed.

10.3.3     Relation and Relatum
Definition 10.2 (Relatum). (A) A relatum is a term of a relation; the relata are the terms that
the relation connects. The relation holds between the relata; the relata are what the relation
holds between.

    The distinction between relation and relatum is classical, and the framework uses it. The
distinction is not between two kinds of things; it is between two roles that a thing plays relative
to a relation. The same thing can be a relatum in one relation and a relation in another—the
mother is a relatum of the marriage and the relation of the daughter. The framework’s use of
the distinction is the same as Book I’s use of the fixed-fluid distinction (Book I, Principle 5.1):
the role is analytical, and the same thing can play different roles in different relations.


10.4      Relation and the Standard Theories
The chapter’s first contribution to the philosophical debate is the statement of what the four
standard theories of relation share.

10.4.1     The Four Theories
Four theories of relation are standard in the contemporary debate.
     Realism about relations. Relations are real features of the world, distinct from the relata
(Russell; Armstrong). The theory’s virtue is that it takes the reality of relations seriously. Its
difficulty is Bradley’s regress: if relations are real and distinct from the relata, what connects the
relations to the relata?
     Anti-realism about relations. Relations are not real features of the world; they are projections
of the observer, or patterns that the observer imposes (the empiricist tradition; some versions of
Hume). The theory’s virtue is that it avoids Bradley’s regress. Its difficulty is that it cannot
explain the difference between a real connection (the mother’s marriage) and an observed pattern
(a similarity between two colors).
     Trope theory. Relations are particular tropes—relation-tropes that exist at particular places
and times, and that are not reducible to the relata (Williams; Campbell; Maurin). The theory’s
virtue is that it takes the reality of relations seriously while avoiding the universals that realism
posits. Its difficulty is that relation-tropes are strange entities, and it is not clear how they
connect to their relata without a further regress.
     Structuralism. Relations are the fundamental features of the world; the relata are nodes in a
structure of relations (Ladyman; Ross; French). The theory’s virtue is that it takes relations as
10.5. Relation as the Presupposition of the Relational Manifestation                             111


primary, and it avoids the difficulty of explaining how relations connect to antecedently existing
relata. Its difficulty is that it must explain how the structure is individuated, and it may collapse
into a form of anti-realism.

10.4.2    What the Theories Share
The four theories differ on what relation is, but they share a common structure. Each theory
posits a connection between the terms, and each theory explains what the connection is in its
own terms.

Principle 10.3 (What the Theories Share). (T) The four standard theories of relation—realism,
anti-realism, trope theory, and structuralism—share the notion of a connection between the terms.
The theories differ on what the connection is (a real feature of a connection, a projection of a
connection, a trope of a connection, a structural node of a connection), but they all presuppose
that there is a connection. The connection is what the chapter calls relation.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the four theories. Its argument is the
observation that each theory, in its own vocabulary, posits something by which the terms are
related, and that the something is what the framework calls the connection. The realist’s
real relation is a connection; the anti-realist’s projection is a projection of a connection; the
trope theorist’s relation-trope is a trope of a connection; the structuralist’s structural node is
a node of a connection. The four theories are four ways of describing the same structure—the
connection—and the framework’s contribution is to name the structure and to identify it with
relation.

10.4.3    The Framework’s Position
The framework does not choose one of the four theories over the others. Its claim is that the
four theories are partial descriptions of the connection, and that the framework’s definition
(Definition 10.1) is the general structure that the four theories describe in their own terms.

Principle 10.4 (The Framework’s Position on the Relation Theories). (E) The framework does
not adopt one of the four standard theories of relation; it identifies the general structure—the
connection between the terms—that the four theories describe in their own terms. The frame-
work’s position is compatible with all four theories, and it is incompatible with none of them; it
is the general structure that the theories instantiate.

   The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the analysis of
the four theories supports. Its justification is that the general structure is visible in all four
theories and that it does the same explanatory work as any one of them, without committing
the framework to the specific claims of any one.


10.5     Relation as the Presupposition of the Relational Manifes-
         tation
The chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that relation is what Book I’s account
of the Relational Manifestation presupposes in the order of being. The demonstration has three
steps.

10.5.1    Step 1: The Relational Manifestation Presupposes a Connection
Book I’s Definition 7.7 states that the Relational Manifestation is the fundamental realm of
relational multiplicity, whose mode of existence is that of things that exist in relation to one
112                                                                          Chapter 10. Relation


another through meaning and significance. The definition is analytical: it names the mode of
existence of the realm. But the mode of existence presupposes a connection: for the things to exist
in relation to one another, there must be a real connection between them, and the connection
must be a real feature of the realm. The connection is what the Relational Manifestation’s mode
of existence presupposes; without the connection, the mode of existence would be empty.
    The step is a (D) claim: it is conditional on Book I’s Definition 7.7. The claim is not that
the Relational Manifestation is a connection; the claim is that the Relational Manifestation
presupposes a connection, and that the presupposition is the realm’s metaphysical condition.

10.5.2    Step 2: The Connection Is Relation
The connection that the Relational Manifestation presupposes is what the chapter calls relation.
The identification is not arbitrary: it is the identification of the connection with the notion that
the metaphysical tradition has called relation. The tradition’s notion is the notion of the real
connection between terms; the chapter’s definition is the same notion, stated in the framework’s
vocabulary.
   The step is a (T) claim: it is argued by the analysis of the notion of relation and by the
comparison with the tradition’s notion. It is relative to the chapter’s definition (Definition 10.1),
and it is assessable by the definition’s adequacy.

10.5.3    Step 3: The Presupposition Is a Metaphysical Consequent
The presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of Book I’s framework, not an independent
metaphysical posit. The framework does not add relation to the Relational Manifestation; it
states what the realm requires in the order of being. The requirement is a (D) claim, and the
(D) claim is the chapter’s principal contribution.
    The step is the synthesis of Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 establishes that the Relational Manifestation
presupposes a connection; Step 2 establishes that the connection is relation; Step 3 establishes
that the presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of the framework. The three steps together
establish the chapter’s principal claim.

Principle 10.5 (Relation as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Relational Manifestation). (D)
Relation is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s account of the Relational Manifestation:
the realm’s mode of existence presupposes a real connection between the things that exist in
relation to one another, and the connection is what the chapter calls relation. The principle is
(D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Definition 7.7; it is the chapter’s principal contribution
because it states what the Relational Manifestation requires in the order of being.


10.6      Relation and Bradley’s Regress
The chapter’s second contribution is the analysis of Bradley’s regress and the demonstration
that Book I’s Principle 12.3—light as the condition of possibility of relation—is the framework’s
response to the regress.

10.6.1    Bradley’s Regress
Bradley’s regress is the classical difficulty for any theory that treats relations as real. The
argument is the following.

   1. A relation is a real connection between two terms.

   2. The relation is distinct from the two terms.
10.6. Relation and Bradley’s Regress                                                              113


   3. Therefore, the relation must be connected to the first term by a further relation, and to
      the second term by a further relation.

   4. These further relations are themselves real, and they must be connected to the first relation
      by further relations, and so on.

   5. The regress is vicious: it never terminates, and it shows that the relation cannot be a real
      connection after all.

     The argument’s force is in Step 3. If a relation were a thing that needs to be connected to its
relata, then the regress would be vicious. The standard responses to the regress are:
     Response 1: Relations are not things. Relations are “unsaturated”—they are not things that
need to be connected to their relata, because they are the connecting. The relation is what
connects the relata; it is not a third thing that needs a further connecting. The response’s
difficulty is that it must explain what the “unsaturated” relation is, without reifying it.
     Response 2: The regress is not vicious. The regress is a benign infinite regress: it is a
description of the structure of relation, not a defect. The response’s difficulty is that it must
explain why the regress is benign, and that the explanation may be ad hoc.
     Response 3: Relations are internal. The relation is not a connection between the relata; it is
a feature of the relata’s natures. The mother’s marriage is not a connection between the mother
and the father; it is a feature of the mother’s and the father’s natures. The response’s difficulty is
that it cannot explain external relations, and that the mother and the father could have existed
without being married.

10.6.2    Book I’s Response: Light as the Condition of Possibility
Book I’s Principle 12.3 states that light is the condition of possibility of relation. The principle
is the framework’s response to Bradley’s regress, and the response is the following.

Principle 10.6 (Bradley’s Regress and Light). (D) Book I’s Principle 12.3 (light as the condition
of possibility of relation) is the framework’s response to Bradley’s regress: the regress presupposes
that a relation is a thing that needs to be connected to its relata, and the presupposition is false
because light is not a relation but the condition under which relation is possible. The condition
does not enter the regress, because the condition is not a thing that needs to be connected to
the terms it conditions.

    The response’s structure is the following. The regress assumes that the relation is a thing
that needs to be connected to the relata. Book I’s response is that the relation is not a thing
that needs to be connected; the relation is the connection, and the condition under which the
connection is possible is light. Light is not a relation; light is the condition under which relation
is possible. The condition does not need to be connected to the terms it conditions, because the
condition is not a term in a relation; it is the structural condition under which the terms can be
related.
    The response is not a denial of the regress; it is a diagnosis of the regress’s premise. The
regress’s premise is that the relation is a thing that needs to be connected; the premise is false,
because the relation is a connection, not a thing, and the condition of the connection is light,
not a further relation. The regress dissolves once the premise is rejected, and the rejection is
Book I’s Principle 12.3.

10.6.3    The Response and the Standard Responses
Book I’s response is related to the three standard responses, and the relation is worth stating.
   The response and Response 1 (relations are not things). Book I’s response agrees with
Response 1 that relations are not things, but it goes further: it states what the relation is (a
114                                                                            Chapter 10. Relation


connection) and what the condition of the connection is (light). Response 1 is a denial; Book I’s
response is a positive account.
    The response and Response 2 (the regress is not vicious). Book I’s response disagrees with
Response 2: the regress is vicious if its premise is granted, and Book I’s response is to reject the
premise rather than to accept the regress as benign. The rejection is the response.
    The response and Response 3 (relations are internal). Book I’s response disagrees with
Response 3: the framework’s account of relation is compatible with both internal and external
relations, and the condition of possibility of relation (light) is what makes both possible. The
internal/external distinction is a feature of the relation; the condition of the relation is not.
    The response is the framework’s contribution to the debate, and it is offered at the strength
that Book I’s Principle 12.3 supports.


10.7      The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Relation
With the definition of relation in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can be applied to
the inquiry into relation.

10.7.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Relation
The fixed element of the inquiry into relation is the relata, held invariant while the inquiry explains
the conditions of the relation. The relata are held invariant as the terms of the relation—the
things whose connection the inquiry seeks to explain.

10.7.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Relation
The fluid element of the inquiry into relation is the connection itself—the relation by which the
terms are connected. The connection is the medium of the inquiry: it is what conveys the effect
of one term’s being what it is to the other term’s being what it is.

10.7.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Relation
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into relation is the rule by which the connection holds—the
rule that explains how the terms are related, and under what conditions the relation is possible.
The rule is the subject of §4, where the standard theories are analyzed; each theory states a
different rule, and the framework’s claim is that the rule is the general structure that the theories
describe in their own terms.

10.7.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Relation
The context of the inquiry into relation is the realm in which the relation occurs. The seven
realms of Book I are the contexts, and relation takes a different form in each. The form of
relation in each realm is the subject of §8.

10.7.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into relation are stated in the following table.
10.8. Relation in Each Realm                                                                      115

10.8      Relation in Each Realm
Relation takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the form,
one realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered at the
strength that the framework’s principles support, and subject to revision if a different form of
relation in a realm does the same explanatory work.

10.8.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, relation takes the form of spatial and temporal relation—the
relation of one material thing to another by position, distance, duration, or succession. The
stone is two meters from the tree; the rain follows the wind; the planets are in gravitational
relation. The spatial and temporal relation is the Material mode of the general relation, and it is
the mode that the Material Manifestation’s discreteness (Book I, Principle 16.14) presupposes.

10.8.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, relation takes the form of meaning-relation—the relation of one
manifestation to another by significance, recognition, or care. The teacher’s words are related to
the student’s understanding; the friend’s presence is related to the friend’s comfort; the tradition’s
texts are related to the practitioner’s practice. The meaning-relation is the Relational mode of
the general relation, and it is the mode that Book I’s Definition 7.7 describes.

10.8.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, relation takes the form of logical relation—the relation of one
proposition to another by entailment, contradiction, or equivalence. The axiom is related to
the theorem by entailment; the definition is related to the instance by subsumption; the law is
related to the case by application. The logical relation is the Structural mode of the general
relation, and it is the mode that Book I’s universality and formality (Principles 16.6 and 16.8)
presuppose.

10.8.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, relation takes the form of pure identity. The First Determination
has no multiplicity, no change, no succession (Book I, Definition 7.5); its relation is its unity, and
its unity is its relation. The form is the limit case of the other forms: it is what relation becomes
when there are no distinct terms to be related.
116                                                                          Chapter 10. Relation


10.8.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, relation takes the form of apportioning relation—the relation of the
measure to the multiple forms. The measure is related to the form by the apportioning; the
source is related to the manifestation by the allotment. The apportioning relation is the mode of
the general relation in the Hub of Decree.

10.8.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, relation takes the form of signification relation—the relation of the
structure to the sign. The law is related to its signification by the sign; the structure is related
to its meaning by the signification. The signification relation is the mode of the general relation
in the Hub of Signification.

10.8.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, relation takes the form of realization relation—the relation of the
possible to the concrete. The possibility is related to its actualization by the realizing; the
meaning is related to its realization by the actualization. The realization relation is the mode of
the general relation in the Hub of Realization.

10.8.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

is offered at the strength that the framework’s principles support.


10.9     Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: Bradley’s regress shows that relations are not real. The objection is that the
regress is vicious, and that the only way to avoid it is to deny that relations are real.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the regress for a refutation. The regress is an argument, and
like every argument it has premises. The premise is that a relation is a thing that needs to be
connected to its relata. The premise is false, because the relation is a connection, not a thing,
and the condition of the connection is light, not a further relation. Once the premise is rejected,
10.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                      117


the regress dissolves. The framework’s response is the rejection of the premise, and the rejection
is Book I’s Principle 12.3. The objection’s conclusion—that relations are not real—does not
follow, because the regress’s premise is false.
    Objection 2: The framework’s “light as condition of possibility” is a deus ex machina. The
objection is that the framework appeals to light to solve Bradley’s regress, and that the appeal
is ad hoc—light is introduced solely to solve the regress, without independent justification.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the framework’s method for an ad hoc move. Light is not
introduced to solve the regress; light is introduced by Book I’s Principle 12.1 (the trans-categorical
character of light) and Principle 12.3 (light as the condition of possibility of relation), and the
introduction is justified by the argument of Book I’s Chapter 12 (the deadlock of the four
categories). The regress’s solution is a consequence of Book I’s account of light, not a motivation
for it. The framework’s response is not ad hoc; it is the application of Book I’s account of light
to a problem that the account solves. The objection’s charge of ad hocness is based on a false
chronology; the reply corrects it.
    Objection 3: The definition is circular. The definition says that relation is the connection
between terms; the terms are what the relation connects; and the connection is the relation. The
three terms are defined in terms of one another, and the definition is circular.
    Reply. The circularity is only apparent. The definition does not define the terms as “what
the relation connects”; it defines the terms as the relata of the connection that the relation is.
The relation is the primitive notion; the terms are the relata of the relation; the connection
is what the relation is. The definition’s structure is: relation (primitive) + relata (terms) =
connection (the relation). The three terms are not defined in terms of one another; they are
three aspects of one structure, and the structure is the definition. The objection mistakes the
structural definition for a semantic circularity; the reply distinguishes them.


10.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that relation is real. It argues that relation is what Book I’s
account of the Relational Manifestation presupposes; the argument is (D) relative to Book I’s
Definition 7.7, and it is offered at the strength that the definition supports. A reader who
rejects the Relational Manifestation has a reason to reject the conclusion; the chapter states the
argument at exactly that strength.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the four standard theories of
relation are correct. The chapter’s claim is that the four theories are partial descriptions of the
connection, and that the framework’s general structure is compatible with all four; the choice
among the four is a further question, and the chapter leaves it open. The question is marked (Q)
in the chapter’s status table.
    Third, the chapter does not analyze light. Light is the subject of Chapter 11; the present
chapter appeals to Book I’s Principle 12.3 (light as the condition of possibility of relation) to
solve Bradley’s regress, but it does not analyze what light is. The reader who expects the analysis
in this chapter has misread the chapter’s scope; the analysis begins in Chapter 11.
    Fourth, the chapter does not settle the question of whether relations are internal or external.
The question is a further development of the theory of relation, and the chapter leaves it open.
The framework’s account is compatible with both internal and external relations, and the choice
between them is a separate question.

10.12      A Question for Reflection
Consider a relation you know well—a friendship, a marriage, a professional relation, a relation to
a place. What is the connection? Is it a thing, a property, a trope, or a condition? Is it internal
to the relata, or external? And if the connection is real, what would it mean for the connection
to be conditioned by something that is not itself a relation—by light, as Book I says?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The relation is the connection; the relata
are what the relation connects; the condition of the connection is light, not a further relation.
The reader who can state, for a relation he knows, what the connection, the relata, and the
condition are, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place
where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

The next chapter analyzes light as the metaphysical medium. With causation and relation in
place, the framework can state what light is —the condition under which causation and relation
can function as the fluid element. The analysis is the subject of Chapter 11, which reconsiders
Book I’s account of light in the light of the metaphysical analyses of Part II and of the present
Part.

Chapter 11

Light as Metaphysical Medium,
Reconsidered

Scope. This chapter reconsiders Book I’s account of light in the light of the metaphysical analyses
of Part II and of Chapters 9 and 10. It does not restate Book I’s account; it asks what kind of
being light is, given the metaphysical structure of substance (Chapter 5), causation (Chapter 9),
and relation (Chapter 10). It defines light as a metaphysical medium—the structural condition
under which causation and relation can function as the fluid element of an explanation—and it
argues that the term “trans-categorical substance” of Book I (Principle 12.1, C7) is an analogical
use of “substance” whose analogy Book II can now unpack. It distinguishes light from substance,
from relation, and from process; it states the relation between light and causation, and between
light and relation; it states the four-column structure of the inquiry into light; it states the form
that light takes in each of the seven realms; and it answers three standard objections. Its claims
are metaphysical and structural; where it speaks of “light,” “medium,” “substance,” “condition,”
or “conveyance,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter
and by the framework of Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s Principle 12.1 (the
trans-categorical character of light, C7), Principle 12.3 (light as the condition of possibility of
relation), Principle 13.1 (light as an active connection structure), Principle 13.2 (the non-travel
of light), Principle 14.2 (light as the foundational fluid element), and Principle 14.3 (appearance
in the mode of the apparatus). It also takes as given Book I’s Remark 12.6, which states that
“substance” is used analogically when applied to light. It does not restate the principles; it asks
what they require, given the metaphysical analyses of Part II and of Chapters 9 and 10. The
reconsideration is stated in §6, and the chapter’s principal contribution is the unpacking of the
analogy.


11.1      A Scene
Consider a prism on a windowsill. A beam of white light falls on it, and on the wall beyond, a
spectrum appears: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet. The spectrum is not in the
prism, and it is not in the white light. The spectrum is what the white light becomes when it
passes through the prism, and its form is determined by the prism’s structure—the angle of its
faces, the refractive index of its glass, the orientation of its axis.
    The scene is not about the physics of refraction. It is about a metaphysical structure, and
the structure is this. The prism does not carry the light from one side to the other; it does
not travel with the light. The prism is the condition under which the white light manifests as
a spectrum—the structural condition that determines the form the manifestation takes. The
120                                  Chapter 11. Light as Metaphysical Medium, Reconsidered


white light is what it is; the spectrum is what it becomes; the prism is what makes the becoming
possible, and what gives the becoming its form.
    Now consider a harder case. Consider a prism that is itself made of light—a prism whose
structure is a structure of light, whose faces are faces of light, whose refractive index is the
refractive index of light. What would it mean for the light to pass through such a prism? The
light would not pass through the prism; the light would be the prism, and the prism would be the
light. The distinction between the medium and the conveyed would collapse, and the structure
would be one structure—the structure of light as the condition of its own manifestation.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. Book I called light a “trans-categorical substance”
(Principle 12.1, C7)—a substance that comes before the distinction between substance, accident,
process, and relation. But the analyses of Part II have given us a precise notion of substance
(Chapter 5, Definition 5.1), and the analyses of Chapters 9 and 10 have given us precise notions
of causation and relation. Is light a substance in that precise sense? Is it a relation? Is it a
process? Or is the word “substance” in Book I an analogical use, whose analogy the metaphysical
analyses now allow us to unpack? The chapter’s answer is: the word “substance” in Book I is
analogical, and the precise notion is medium. Light is the metaphysical medium—the structural
condition under which causation and relation can function as the fluid element of an explanation.


11.2      The Question
The question of the chapter is: what kind of being is light, given the metaphysical analyses of
substance (Chapter 5), causation (Chapter 9), and relation (Chapter 10)?
     The question is not the same as the question of Book I’s Chapter 12. Book I asked what
light is, and it answered: light is a trans-categorical substance, the condition of possibility of
relation. The answer was (according to Book I’s own remark, Remark 12.6) analogical: the word
“substance” was used because light is not a substance, but is substance-like in being the condition
of possibility of the categories. The present chapter asks the metaphysical question that Book I
deferred: what is the positive structure that the analogical use of “substance” gestures at? What
is light, in terms of the metaphysical notions that Part II and Chapters 9–10 have established?
     The question has three aspects.
     The first aspect: is light a substance in the sense of Chapter 5? Chapter 5 defined substance
as the ground of a thing’s being the same one through change, and of its being the subject of
its properties. Is light such a ground? The chapter’s answer is: no. Light is not the ground
of a thing’s sameness; light is the condition under which things can be conveyed between one
another. The notion of substance that Chapter 5 defined is not the notion that fits light, and
the “substance” of Book I’s Principle 12.1 is a different, analogical notion.
     The second aspect: if light is not a substance, what is it? The chapter’s answer is: light is a
medium. It is the structural condition under which causation and relation can function as the
fluid element. The medium is not a substance (it is not a ground of sameness); it is not a relation
(it is not a connection between two things); it is not a process (it is not a becoming); it is not
an accident (it is not a property of a substance). It is the condition of possibility of these—the
structural condition under which the fluid element can be the fluid element.
     The third aspect: what does the reconsideration establish, and what does it not establish? The
reconsideration establishes that Book I’s analogical use of “substance” can be unpacked: the
analogy was pointing at the medium, and the medium is what Book II can now state positively.
The reconsideration does not establish that light is unreal; it establishes what kind of real thing
light is—a structural condition, not a substance, not a relation, not a process.
     The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: light is
not a substance in the sense of Chapter 5; it is a metaphysical medium, the structural condition
under which causation and relation can function as the fluid element; and the reconsideration
unpacks Book I’s analogical use of “substance.”
11.3. Light and Substance                                                                       121


11.3      Light and Substance
11.3.1    The Substance of Chapter 5 Does Not Fit Light
Chapter 5 defined substance as the ground of a thing’s being the same one through change, and
of its being the subject of its properties (Definition 5.1). Does light satisfy the definition?
    First, is light the ground of a thing’s being the same one through change? No. Light is not
the ground of any thing’s sameness; light is what conveys the effect of one thing on another. The
violin’s substance grounds its sameness through the replacement of its parts; light conveys the
sound of the violin from the strings to the listener. The substance is what makes the violin the
same violin; light is what carries the sound from the violin to the ear. The two are different roles,
and the definition of substance does not fit light.
    Second, is light the subject of its properties? No. Light has no properties in the sense in
which a substance has properties—the properties of a substance are the accidents that the
substance has, and that can be removed without the substance ceasing to be the substance it is
(Definition 5.2). Light has no accidents; it is not a thing to which accidents can attach. The
properties of light (wavelength, frequency, intensity) are not accidents of a substance; they are
the structural features of the medium. The distinction is the distinction between the accident of
a substance and the feature of a condition.
    The conclusion is: light is not a substance in the sense of Chapter 5. The word “substance”
in Book I’s Principle 12.1 is used in a different, analogical sense—the sense in which light is
substance-like, not the sense in which a violin or a stone is a substance. Book I’s Remark 12.6
explicitly noted that the use was analogical; the present chapter unpacks what the analogy was
pointing at.

11.3.2    The Analogy and Its Unpacking
The analogy in Book I is the analogy between the way a substance underlies its accidents
and the way light underlies the categories. A substance is what remains when the accidents
are removed; light is what remains when the categories are removed—the condition that the
categories presuppose. The analogy is: as substance is to accident, so light is to category. The
analogy is not an identity; the two relations are similar, not the same.
    The present chapter’s contribution is the unpacking of the analogy. The relation that the
analogy points at is not the substance-accident relation; it is the condition-conditioned relation.
Light is the condition of the categories; the categories are what the condition conditions. The
condition is not a substance in the substance-accident sense; it is a medium—a structural
condition under which the categories can be what they are.

Principle 11.1 (The Analogy of “Substance” in Book I). (T) The word “substance” in Book I’s
Principle 12.1 is an analogical use, whose analogy is the analogy between the substance-accident
relation and the condition-conditioned relation. The analogy points at the medium: light is the
structural condition under which the categories can be what they are, not a substance in the
substance-accident sense.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of Book I’s Remark 12.6 and by the analysis
of the definition of substance in Chapter 5. Its argument is the demonstration that light does
not satisfy the definition of substance, and that the analogical use of “substance” gestures at a
different relation—the relation between a condition and what it conditions.
122                                    Chapter 11. Light as Metaphysical Medium, Reconsidered


11.4      The Definition of Light as Metaphysical Medium
11.4.1     The Definition
Definition 11.2 (Light as Metaphysical Medium). (A) Light is a metaphysical medium: the
structural condition under which causation and relation can function as the fluid element of
an explanation. It is not a substance, not a relation, not a process, not an accident. It is the
condition of possibility of these—the structural condition that the categories presuppose, and
that the fluid element requires.

    The definition has three components, and each is important.
    The first component: light is a structural condition. A structural condition is what makes
something else possible; it is not itself the thing it conditions. Light is the condition under
which the categories can be what they are; it is not a category, and it is not something that has
categories. The distinction is the distinction between the condition and the conditioned; light is
the first, and the categories are the second.
    The second component: light is the condition of causation and relation. Chapters 9 and 10
established that causation and relation are what the fluid element invokes. The present chapter
establishes that light is what causation and relation presuppose: without light, causation would
be a regularity without a medium, and relation would be a connection without a conveyor. Light
is the medium through which causation and relation can be what they are—the fluid element’s
metaphysical ground.
    The third component: light is not a substance, a relation, a process, or an accident. The
definition states the negative characterization that Book I’s Principle 12.1 also stated. The
negative characterization is the same: light is trans-categorical. The present chapter adds the
positive characterization: light is a medium, and the medium is the condition of possibility of
the categories.
    The three components together define light. Light is the trans-categorical condition—the
medium—under which the fluid element can be the fluid element, and under which the categories
can be the categories.

11.4.2     What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
    It does not say that light is unreal. The medium is real; its reality is the reality of a structural
condition, not the reality of a substance. The distinction is the distinction between the reality of
a condition and the reality of a thing; the medium is the first, not the second. The distinction
is the same as Book I’s distinction between the reality of the structure and the reality of the
explained (Book I, Chapter 6, §6.6): the structure is real, and the medium is the structure’s
most general form.
    It does not say that light is unknowable. The medium is knowable, but its knowledge is the
knowledge of a condition—the knowledge of what the categories presuppose, not the knowledge
of a substance. The distinction is the distinction between the knowledge of a condition and the
knowledge of a thing; the first is the knowledge of the medium, and the second is the knowledge
of the substance. Book I stated that the knowledge of light is partial (Book I, Principle 14.5);
the present chapter adds that the partiality is the partiality of the knowledge of a condition, not
of a thing.
    It does not say that light is passive. The medium is active: it is the active structure that
Book I’s Principle 13.1 described. The distinction is the distinction between the passivity of a
substance that merely has properties and the activity of a condition that makes things possible;
the medium is the second, not the first.
    It does not say that light is one. The medium is one in the sense of being a single structural
condition; it is not one in the sense of being a single substance among substances. The distinction
11.5. Light and Causation                                                                     123


is the distinction between the unity of a condition and the unity of a thing; the medium is the
first, not the second. The medium’s unity is the unity of the condition under which the categories
can be the categories—a unity that is compatible with the plurality of the things it conditions.

11.4.3    Light and the Fluid Element
The definition of light as medium is the metaphysical ground of Book I’s definition of the fluid
element. Book I defined the fluid element as the entity that conveys effect (Definition 2.2). The
definition was structural: it named the role the fluid element plays in an explanation. The
present chapter adds the metaphysical ground: the fluid element can convey effect because light
is the medium—the structural condition under which conveyance is possible.
    The relation is the relation between the analytical role and the metaphysical condition. The
fluid element is the analytical role; the medium is the metaphysical condition that the role
presupposes. The distinction is the same as the distinction between the fixed element and
substance (Chapter 5, §7): the fixed element is the role, and substance is the condition. The
medium is the fluid element’s condition, and the fluid element is the medium’s analytical role.


11.5     Light and Causation
11.5.1    Causation Presupposes a Medium
Chapter 9 established that causation is the metaphysical ground of the conveyor: the conveyor is
what causation requires to convey effect from one thing to another. The present chapter asks:
what does causation presuppose, such that it can convey? The answer is: the medium.
    The argument is the following. Causation is the relation by which one thing produces an
effect in another. For the effect to be conveyed, there must be something through which the
effect is conveyed—a condition under which the production is possible. The condition is the
medium. Without the medium, causation would be a production without a vehicle—a cause that
acts, but whose effect is not conveyed. The medium is what makes the conveyance possible.
Principle 11.3 (Causation Presupposes the Medium). (D) Causation presupposes light as the
metaphysical medium: the conveyance of an effect from one thing to another requires a structural
condition under which the conveyance is possible, and the condition is what the chapter calls
light. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s C7 (the trans-categorical
character of light) and on Chapter 9’s analysis of causation.
    The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the demonstration that Book I’s C7
and Chapter 9’s analysis jointly require the medium. The demonstration has two premises: the
premise that causation requires a vehicle (Chapter 9), and the premise that the vehicle requires
a condition (the present section). The conclusion follows: causation presupposes the medium.

11.5.2    The Medium Is Not the Cause
The principle must not be read as saying that light is the cause of anything. Light is not a cause;
light is the medium through which causation operates. The distinction is the distinction between
the cause and the medium: the cause is what produces the effect; the medium is what makes the
production possible. The sun causes the warmth of the stone; the light is the medium through
which the sun’s warmth reaches the stone. The sun is the cause; the light is the medium. The
two are different, and the distinction is the distinction between production and conveyance.
    The distinction is important because it blocks the inference from the medium to the cause.
The medium is not the cause; the medium is what makes the cause’s effect reach its recipient.
Without the medium, the cause would act, but its effect would not be conveyed; with the medium,
the cause acts and its effect is conveyed. The medium is the condition of conveyance, not the
source of the effect.
124                                  Chapter 11. Light as Metaphysical Medium, Reconsidered


11.6      Light and Relation
11.6.1    Relation Presupposes a Condition of Possibility
Chapter 10 established that relation is a category: it is a structural feature of things, not a mere
appearance or a projection. The present chapter asks: what does relation presuppose, such that
it can be a category? The answer is: the condition of possibility of relation—what Book I’s
Principle 12.3 called light.
    Book I’s argument was the regress argument: if light were a relation, it would need another
relation to connect it to the terms it relates, and that relation would need another, and so
on. The regress is avoided only if light is not a relation, but the condition of possibility of
relation. The present chapter’s contribution is the re-examination of the argument in the light of
Chapter 10’s analysis of relation.
    The re-examination is the following. Chapter 10 distinguished three aspects of relation: the
relata, the connecting feature, and the context in which the relation obtains. The connecting
feature is what the relata have in common; the context is what makes the relation possible. The
medium is the structural condition under which the context can be a context and the connecting
feature can connect—the condition of possibility of the relation’s being a relation.

Principle 11.4 (Relation Presupposes the Medium). (D) Relation presupposes light as the
metaphysical medium: for a relation to obtain between two things, there must be a structural
condition under which the relation is possible, and the condition is what Book I’s Principle 12.3
calls light. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principle 12.3 and on
Chapter 10’s analysis of relation.

    The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the re-examination of Book I’s
regress argument in the light of Chapter 10. The re-examination shows that the regress is avoided
by the medium, and the medium is what the regress argument was pointing at.

11.6.2    The Medium Is Not the Relation
The principle must not be read as saying that light is the relation. Light is not a relation; light
is the condition of possibility of relation. The distinction is the distinction between the relation
and its condition: the relation is between two things; the condition is what makes the relation
possible. The friendship is a relation; the medium through which the friendship is legible is the
condition. The friendship is the relation; the medium is the condition. The two are different,
and the distinction is the distinction between the connected and the condition of connection.
    The distinction is important because it blocks the inference from the medium to the relation.
The medium is not the relation; the medium is what makes the relation legible. Without the
medium, the relation would not be a relation (it would be a collection of relata without a
connection); with the medium, the relation is a relation. The medium is the condition of relation,
not the relation itself.


11.7      The Reconsideration of Principle 12.1
The chapter’s principal contribution is the reconsideration of Book I’s Principle 12.1 in the light
of the metaphysical analyses of Part II and of Chapters 9–10.

11.7.1    What Principle 12.1 Stated
Book I’s Principle 12.1 stated that light goes beyond the existing philosophical categories—substance,
accident, process, relation—and that a new category is needed: the trans-categorical substance
(Book I, Principle 12.1, C7). The principle’s status was (A): it was a commitment of Book I,
11.8. The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Light                                          125


supported by the deadlock of the four categories. Book I’s Remark 12.6 explicitly noted that
“substance” was used analogically: light is not a substance among substances, but the precondition
for any substance to be related to another.

11.7.2     What the Reconsideration Adds
The reconsideration adds three things, and each is important.
     First, the positive definition of the medium. Book I’s Principle 12.1 was mostly negative:
it said what light is not (substance, accident, process, relation), and it introduced a new label
(“trans-categorical substance”) without unpacking the positive structure. The present chapter’s
definition (Definition 11.2) gives the positive structure: light is the medium—the structural
condition under which causation and relation can function as the fluid element.
     Second, the unpacking of the analogy. Book I used “substance” analogically; the present
chapter unpacks the analogy. The analogy is the analogy between the substance-accident relation
and the condition-conditioned relation. Light is not a substance in the substance-accident sense;
it is a condition in the condition-conditioned sense. The distinction is the distinction between
the two relations, and the present chapter states it.
     Third, the relation to causation and relation. Book I stated that light is the condition of
possibility of relation (Principle 12.3), but it did not state the relation between light and causation.
The present chapter states the relation: causation presupposes the medium (Principle 11.3), and
relation presupposes the medium (Principle 11.4). The two presuppositions are the chapter’s
contribution to the systematic character of Part III.

11.7.3     What the Reconsideration Does Not Change
The reconsideration does not change the substance of Book I’s Principle 12.1. The principle
stated that light is trans-categorical; the reconsideration confirms the statement, and it unpacks
the positive structure. The principle stated that light is the condition of possibility of relation;
the reconsideration confirms the statement, and it adds the relation to causation. The principle
stated that God is the source of all light (Book I, Principle 12.2); the reconsideration confirms
the statement, and it states what the statement requires in the order of being (the medium is
created and grounded in God, as Book I’s Principle 12.2 states).
    The reconsideration is a deepening, not a revision. Book I’s Principle 12.1 is (A) in Book I;
the present chapter’s definition and principles are (D) in Book II, because they depend on
Book I’s Principle 12.1. The (D) label marks the dependency; the deepening is the consequence
of the dependency.
Principle 11.5 (The Reconsideration of Light). (D) Book I’s Principle 12.1 (the trans-categorical
character of light) is deepened, not revised, by the metaphysical analyses of Part II and of
Chapters 9 and 10: light is the metaphysical medium, the structural condition under which
causation and relation can function as the fluid element. The deepening is (D) because its truth
depends on Book I’s Principle 12.1; it is the chapter’s principal contribution because it gives the
positive structure that Book I’s analogical use of “substance” gestured at.


11.8      The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Light
With the definition of light as medium in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can be
applied to the inquiry into light.

11.8.1     The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Light
The fixed element of the inquiry into light is light itself, held invariant while the inquiry explains
the conditions of its being. The light is held invariant as the subject of the inquiry—the medium
126                                   Chapter 11. Light as Metaphysical Medium, Reconsidered


whose conditions the inquiry seeks to state.

11.8.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Light
The fluid element of the inquiry into light is the relation between light and the categories—the
relation by which light is the condition of the categories, and by which the categories are what
light conditions. The relation is the medium of the inquiry: it is what conveys the effect of light’s
being what it is to the categories’ being what they are.

11.8.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Light
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into light is the rule by which light conditions the
categories—the rule that explains how the medium makes the categories possible. The rule is
the subject of §4 and §5, where the relations between light and causation, and between light and
relation, are stated.

11.8.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Light
The context of the inquiry into light is the realm in which light is realized. The seven realms of
Book I are the contexts, and light takes a different form in each. The form of light in each realm
is the subject of §8.

11.8.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into light are stated in the following table.

11.9      Light in Each Realm
Light takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the form, one
realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered at the
strength that the framework’s principles support, and subject to revision if a different form of
light in a realm does the same explanatory work.

11.9.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, light takes the form of the physical medium—the electromagnetic
field, the wave, the photon. The physical medium is what conveys the effect of one material
thing on another: the light of the sun conveys the sun’s warmth to the stone; the light of a lamp
conveys the lamp’s illumination to the wall. The physical medium is the descended version of
the medium—the medium in the mode of the Material Manifestation (Book I, Principle 14.3).
11.9. Light in Each Realm                                                                     127


11.9.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, light takes the form of the meaning-relation—the structure of
significance through which one manifestation is legible to another. The meaning-relation is what
conveys the effect of one relational thing on another: the word’s meaning conveys the speaker’s
intent to the hearer; the symbol’s significance conveys the tradition’s content to the participant.
The meaning-relation is the medium in the mode of the Relational Manifestation.

11.9.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, light takes the form of the law-structure—the pattern of
entailment through which one structural thing follows from another. The law-structure is what
conveys the effect of one structural thing on another: the axiom’s content conveys the theorem’s
content; the definition’s content conveys the consequence’s content. The law-structure is the
medium in the mode of the Structural Determination.

11.9.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, light takes the form of pure unity—the unity that precedes the
distinction between the medium and the conveyed. The First Determination has no multiplicity,
no change, no succession; its medium is its unity, and its unity is its medium. The form is the
limit case of the other forms: it is what the other forms become when the multiplicity is zero.

11.9.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, light takes the form of the measure—the allotment through which the
apportioning is conveyed. The measure is the medium in the mode of the Hub of Decree.

11.9.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, light takes the form of the sign—the structure through which the
signification is conveyed. The sign is the medium in the mode of the Hub of Signification.

11.9.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, light takes the form of the actualization—the realizing through
which the realization is conveyed. The actualization is the medium in the mode of the Hub of
Realization.

11.9.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

11.10      Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: The reconsideration contradicts Book I. Book I called light a “trans-categorical
substance”; the present chapter calls it a “medium.” The objection is that the two terms are
incompatible, and that the reconsideration is a revision, not a deepening.
    Reply. The reconsideration is a deepening, not a revision. Book I used “substance” analogically,
and Book I’s Remark 12.6 explicitly noted the analogy. The present chapter unpacks the analogy:
light is not a substance in the substance-accident sense; it is a condition in the condition-
conditioned sense. The two statements are compatible: the “substance” of Book I is the
analogical name for what the present chapter calls the “medium.” The reconsideration does not
change Book I’s Principle 12.1; it states what the principle’s analogical language presupposed.
    Objection 2: “Medium” is vague. The objection is that the notion of a medium is less precise
than the notion of a substance, and that the reconsideration trades precision for a metaphor.
    Reply. The notion of a medium is not vaguer than the notion of a substance; it is a different
notion, with its own precision. The definition of the medium (Definition 11.2) states three
components: it is a structural condition; it is the condition of causation and relation; it is not a
substance, relation, process, or accident. The three components are as precise as the components
of the definition of substance (Chapter 5, Definition 5.1). The objection mistakes the difference
of the notion for a lack of precision; the reply distinguishes them.
    Objection 3: If light is not a substance, is it unreal? The objection is that only substances
are real, and that a medium that is not a substance is a mere figure of speech.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the reality of substance for the whole of reality. The medium
is real; its reality is the reality of a structural condition, not the reality of a substance. The
condition is real because it is required by the framework’s principles (the fluid element requires a
medium, as the present chapter has argued); the condition is not a substance because it is not
the ground of sameness. The distinction is the distinction between the reality of a condition and
the reality of a substance; the medium is the first, not the second. The objection’s premise—that
only substances are real—is not the framework’s premise; the framework’s premise is that what
is required by the principles is real, and the medium is required.
11.11. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                   129


11.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that light is unreal as a substance. It argues that light is
not a substance in the sense of Chapter 5; the argument is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 12.1,
and it is offered at the strength that the principle supports. A reader who rejects the analogical
use of “substance” in Book I has a reason to reject the reconsideration; the chapter states the
reconsideration at exactly that strength.
    Second, the chapter does not state the relation between light and the other elements of the
framework. The relation is the subject of Part V (where light is analyzed as a context) and
Part VI (where light is related to viability). The present chapter has stated the relation to
causation and relation; the relation to the other elements is deferred.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the medium is one or many. The
medium is one in the sense of being a single structural condition; whether it is one in the sense
of being a single entity among entities is a question the chapter leaves open. The question is
marked (Q) in the chapter’s status table.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the form of light in each realm at the strength of a proof.
The forms are (E) estimates; they are offered at the strength that the framework’s principles
support, and they are subject to revision.

11.13      A Question for Reflection
Consider a moment in which you understood something through a medium—a conversation
through which you understood a friend, a book through which you understood a tradition, a
piece of music through which you understood a feeling. Was the medium itself the thing you
understood, or was it the condition under which the thing was understood? What would it
mean to understand the medium as such? And if the medium is the condition of possibility of
understanding, can any understanding of the medium be complete?
130                                 Chapter 11. Light as Metaphysical Medium, Reconsidered


     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The medium is not the thing it conveys;
it is the condition under which the thing is conveyed. The reader who can state, for a medium
he knows, what the medium is and what it conveys, has understood the chapter’s distinction;
the reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to
develop the difficulty further.

The next chapter synthesizes the analyses of Chapters 9, 10, and 11 into a single account of the
fluid elements of the seven realms. With the medium in place, the framework can state the fluid
element of each realm as the medium in that realm’s mode—the law-structure of the Structural
Determination, the meaning-relation of the Relational Manifestation, the physical medium of the
Material Manifestation, and the corresponding forms of the barzakhic realms.
