Chapter 12

The Fluid Elements of Each Realm

Scope. This chapter synthesizes the analyses of Chapters 9, 10, and 11 into a single account of
the fluid elements of the seven realms. It states the triad of fluid elements—light, causation,
relation—as a structural whole, and it states the realm-dependent structure of the triad: the
pattern of collapse, partial coincidence, and full distinction that the triad exhibits across the
seven realms. It argues that the pattern is not accidental, but tracks the ontological architecture
of Book I; it states the fluid element of each realm as a single structure (rather than as three
separate analyses); it states the relation between the fluid triad and the fixed triad of Part II; and
it states what Part III has and has not established. Its claims are metaphysical and structural;
where it speaks of “triad,” “pattern,” “collapse,” “coincidence,” “distinction,” or “passage,” these
are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and by the analyses of
the preceding three chapters.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given the definitions and principles that
Chapters 9, 10, and 11 established as the metaphysical consequents of Book I’s fluid element
(Definition 2.2), conveyor principle (Principle 4.1), account of light (Principle 12.3), and account
of the Relational Manifestation (Definition 7.7). It also takes as given Book I’s Principle 7.1 (C3,
independent reality of the realms) and Principle 27.1 (C9, category-relative predication). It does
not reargue those chapters; it asks what the three analyses, taken together, establish, and it
states the structural pattern that the three exhibit across the seven realms.


12.1      A Scene
Consider an orchestra playing a symphony. The conductor raises her baton; the strings begin;
the woodwinds answer; the brass enters; the percussion punctuates. Three things are happening
at once, and each is different.
    The first is the transfer of effect. The conductor’s gesture causes the first violin’s bow to
move; the violin’s sound causes the listener’s attention to shift; the cello’s entrance causes the
harmonic balance to change. The transfer is real; it is not a figure of speech. The conductor’s
gesture is not merely followed by the violin’s motion; it produces it, through the medium of the
orchestra’s shared attention.
    The second is the connection of terms. The musicians are related to one another: the first
violin is related to the second violin by their shared part; the strings are related to the woodwinds
by their counterpoint; the orchestra is related to the conductor by their mutual attention. The
connection is real; it is not a projection. The first violin is not merely near the second violin; the
two are bound together by their common task.
    The third is the medium. The sound is what carries the transfer and the connection; the
concert hall is what makes the sound possible; the shared musical tradition is what makes the
score legible. The medium is what makes both the transfer and the connection possible. Without
132                                               Chapter 12. The Fluid Elements of Each Realm


the sound, the conductor’s gesture would not reach the musicians; without the tradition, the
score would not be a score.
     Three things, and each is different. But in other scenes, the three seem to be one. Consider a
conversation. One person speaks; the other listens; the meaning passes from speaker to hearer.
Is the passing a transfer (causation), a connection (relation), or a medium (light)? In the
conversation, the three seem to be the same: the meaning that passes is also the connection
between the speakers, and the language that carries it is the medium of both. The distinctions
that the orchestra exhibits are collapsed in the conversation, and the collapse is not a confusion;
it is a feature of the conversational mode of the fluid triad.
     Now consider a harder case. Consider a conversation in which the two speakers do not share
a language. One speaks; the other does not understand; the meaning does not pass. The transfer
has failed, and the connection has failed, and the medium has failed. The three failures are not
the same: the transfer failed because the medium was absent; the connection failed because the
transfer failed; the medium failed because the speakers did not share it. The three are distinct,
and their distinctness is what the failure reveals.
     The scene poses the question of the chapter. The fluid triad—transfer, connection, medium—is
distinct in the orchestra, collapsed in the conversation, and distinct again in the failed conversation.
What is the pattern of the triad’s articulation across the seven realms? And what does the
pattern tell us about the fluid element of each realm?


12.2      The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is the structure of the triad of fluid elements, and how does
the structure vary across the seven realms?
    The question is not the same as the questions of Chapters 9, 10, and 11. Each of those
chapters analyzed one element of the triad: Chapter 9 analyzed causation, Chapter 10 analyzed
relation, Chapter 11 analyzed light as the medium. Each analysis was of one element, in all seven
realms, but the analysis was organized around the element, not around the realm. The present
chapter inverts the organization: it asks what the triad, as a whole, looks like in each realm, and
what the variation across realms tells us about the realms themselves.
    The inversion is the chapter’s principal contribution. It is not a summary of the three preceding
chapters; it is a reorganization of their results into a single structure, and the reorganization
reveals something that the three analyses, taken separately, did not reveal: the pattern of collapse,
partial coincidence, and full distinction.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the triad of fluid elements? The chapter must state the triad as a
structural whole—not as three separate elements, but as one structure with three components.
The statement is the chapter’s contribution to the systematic character of Part III.
    The second aspect: what is the realm-dependent structure of the triad? The chapter must
state the pattern of variation across the seven realms. The pattern is the chapter’s principal
contribution, because it is what makes the synthesis a genuine chapter, not a summary.
    The third aspect: what is the relation between the fluid triad and the fixed triad of Part II?
The chapter must state the relation between the triad of fluid elements and the triad of fixed
elements (Chapter 8, Definition 8.1). The relation is the chapter’s contribution to the framework’s
overall architecture, because it shows how the two triads together make the seven realms a single
system.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: the fluid
triad is a structural whole; its structure varies across the seven realms according to a pattern of
collapse, partial coincidence, and full distinction; and the variation is what makes the realms
structurally distinct at the level of fluid elements, in a way that mirrors and completes the
distinction at the level of fixed elements.
12.3. The Triad of Fluid Elements                                                                   133


12.3      The Triad of Fluid Elements
12.3.1     The Triad
Definition 12.1 (The Triad of Fluid Elements). (A) The triad of fluid elements is the structure of
light, causation, and relation, taken together. Light is the metaphysical medium—the structural
condition under which causation and relation can function (Chapter 11, Definition 11.2); causation
is the real transfer of effect from a cause to an effect through a medium (Chapter 9, Definition 9.1);
and relation is the real connection between two or more terms (Chapter 10, Definition 10.1).
The triad is the structure of the fluid element of Book I’s framework, and it is the metaphysical
content of the second column.

    The definition states the triad as a structural whole. The three elements are not three
separate things; they are three aspects of one structure—the structure of the fluid element. The
light is the medium; the causation is the transfer; the relation is the connection. The three
together make the fluid element the fluid element: the condition under which, the transfer by
which, and the connection in which things bear on one another.
    The triad is not a list. It is a structure, and the structure is what the definition captures. The
three elements are related, but the relation is not symmetric: light is the condition of the other
two. Causation and relation both presuppose the medium (Chapter 11, Principles 11.3 and 11.4);
the medium does not presuppose them. The asymmetry is the triad’s distinctive feature, and it
distinguishes the fluid triad from the fixed triad of Part II, whose three elements are peers.

12.3.2     The Triad and the Four Columns
The triad is the metaphysical content of the fluid element of Book I’s framework. It is not a fifth
column; it is the content that fills the second column. The distinction is the analytical/ontological
distinction of Chapter 2: the fluid element is the analytical role; the triad is the ontological
content that the role presupposes.
    The triad relates to the other three columns as follows. The light is the medium through
which the fixed elements (Part II) are related; the causation is the transfer by which the fixed
elements affect one another; the relation is the connection in which the fixed elements stand. The
governing dynamics (Chapter 13) is the rule by which the transfer and the connection operate;
the context (Chapter 17) is the realm in which the triad is realized. The four columns and the
fluid triad are not the same structure; they are related structures, and the relation is what the
later parts of Book II will state.

12.3.3     The Triad and the Fixed Triad
The fluid triad is not the same as the fixed triad (Chapter 8, Definition 8.1). The fixed triad is the
structure of substance, essence, and thisness; the fluid triad is the structure of light, causation,
and relation. The two are related: the fixed triad is what the fluid triad relates; the fluid triad is
what relates the fixed triad. The two triads together make the seven realms a single system, and
the relation between the two is the subject of §7.


12.4      The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Triad
12.4.1     The Three Patterns
The fluid triad exhibits three patterns of articulation across the seven realms.
    The pattern of collapse. In the First Determination, the three elements of the triad collapse
into unity. The First Determination has no multiplicity, no change, no succession (Book I,
Definition 7.5); its light is its unity, its causation is its unity, its relation is its unity. The three
134                                              Chapter 12. The Fluid Elements of Each Realm


are not distinct, because there is no multiplicity in the First Determination—no terms to be
connected, no effect to be transferred, no medium distinct from what it conveys. The First
Determination is the limit case of the triad: it is what the triad becomes when the multiplicity is
zero.
    The pattern of partial coincidence. In the barzakhic realms (the Hubs of Decree, Signification,
and Realization), causation and relation coincide in the passage, and light distinguishes as the
mode of the passage. The Hub of Decree’s apportioning is simultaneously a transfer of the
measure (causation) and a connection between the source and the multiple forms (relation); the
Hub of Signification’s signification is simultaneously a transfer of the structure (causation) and a
connection between the structure and its sign (relation); the Hub of Realization’s actualization is
simultaneously a transfer of actuality (causation) and a connection between the possible and
the concrete (relation). The coincidence is not an accident; it is a feature of the barzakhic
mode of existence. The barzakhic realm is a level whose mode of existence includes mediating,
transforming, or regulating relations between other realms (Book I, Definition 8.1); its being is
its passage, and its causation and relation are the same, because the passage is the transfer and
the connection at once. The light distinguishes: the light is the mode of the passage, the specific
way in which the passage is possible.
    The pattern of full distinction. In the fundamental realms of multiplicity (the Structural
Determination, the Relational Manifestation, and the Material Manifestation), the three elements
of the triad are fully distinguished. The light is the medium; the causation is the transfer;
the relation is the connection. The three are distinct, and the distinction is what makes the
realm a realm of multiplicity: the realm has many things, and the things bear on one another
through three distinct structures—the condition of bearing, the bearing as transfer, the bearing
as connection.

12.4.2    The Pattern as a Principle
The three patterns are not accidental; they are the articulation of a single principle, and the
principle is the chapter’s principal contribution.

Principle 12.2 (The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Fluid Triad). (E) The triad of fluid
elements is articulated differently in each realm, and the articulation is a function of the realm’s
position in the ontological architecture. In the First Determination, the triad collapses into unity.
In the barzakhic realms, causation and relation coincide in the passage, and light distinguishes as
the mode of the passage. In the fundamental realms of multiplicity, the triad is fully distinguished.
The pattern tracks the realm’s mode of existence: the more a realm is a realm of passage, the
more its causation and relation coincide; the more a realm is a realm of multiplicity, the more
the triad is articulated.

    The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the analysis of
the seven realms supports. Its justification is that the pattern is visible in the seven realms and
that a different pattern would do the same explanatory work less well. Its refutation would be
a realm whose articulation does not fit the pattern, or a different pattern that does the same
explanatory work as well or better.

12.4.3    The Pattern and Book I
The pattern is not a new principle; it is the metaphysical articulation of Book I’s Principle 7.1
(C3, independent reality of the realms) and of Book I’s Principle 27.1 (C9, category-relative
predication). The first states that the realms are independently real, with modes of existence of
their own; the second states that metaphysical predicates are defined relative to a realm. The
pattern is the articulation of the two: the fluid triad’s structure is relative to the realm, and the
relativity is what makes the realms independently real at the level of fluid elements.
12.5. The Fluid Elements of the Seven Realms                                                     135


   The pattern is (D) relative to Book I’s Principles 7.1 and 27.1. The chapter’s claim is not
that the pattern is a new principle; the claim is that the pattern is what Book I’s principles
require in the order of being, and the requirement is a metaphysical consequent of the principles.

12.4.4    The Pattern and the Fixed Pattern
The fluid pattern is not the same as the fixed pattern (Chapter 8, Principle 8.2). The fixed
pattern’s barzakhic case has substance and essence coinciding, and thisness distinguishing
(Chapter 8, §4.1). The fluid pattern’s barzakhic case has causation and relation coinciding, and
light distinguishing. The two patterns are parallel but not identical: in the fixed pattern, the
coincidence is between the grounds (substance and essence); in the fluid pattern, the coincidence
is between the operations (causation and relation). The parallel is not an accident; it is a feature
of the barzakhic mode of existence, which makes both the fixed ground and the fluid operation
collapse into the realm’s passage. The relation between the two patterns is the subject of §7.


12.5      The Fluid Elements of the Seven Realms
With the pattern in place, the fluid element of each realm can be stated as a single structure,
rather than as three separate analyses. The statements are (E) claims, offered at the strength
that the framework’s principles support.

12.5.1    The First Determination
The fluid element of the First Determination is pure unity, in which light, causation, and relation
collapse. The realm is what it is; its medium is its unity; its transfer is its unity; its connection
is its unity. The collapse is the limit case of the triad, and it is what the triad becomes when the
multiplicity is zero.

12.5.2    The Hub of Decree
The fluid element of the Hub of Decree is the apportioning, in which causation and relation
coincide and light distinguishes. The realm’s causation is its apportioning (the transfer of the
measure from the source to the forms); its relation is its apportioning (the connection between the
source and the forms); its light is its measure (the mode of the apportioning). The coincidence is
the barzakhic pattern: the realm’s being is its passage, and its causation and relation are the
same, because the passage is the transfer and the connection at once.

12.5.3    The Structural Determination
The fluid element of the Structural Determination is the law that entails, in which the three
elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s light is the law-structure (the medium of entailment);
its causation is the formal causation (the transfer of necessity from the premise to the consequence);
its relation is the logical relation (the connection of the premise to the consequence). The
distinction is the fundamental-realm pattern: the realm is a realm of multiplicity, and the three
elements are what make the entailments many.

12.5.4    The Hub of Signification
The fluid element of the Hub of Signification is the signification, in which causation and relation
coincide and light distinguishes. The realm’s causation is its signification (the transfer of the
structure to the sign); its relation is its signification (the connection between the structure and
the sign); its light is its sign (the mode of the signification). The coincidence is the barzakhic
pattern.
136                                             Chapter 12. The Fluid Elements of Each Realm


12.5.5    The Relational Manifestation
The fluid element of the Relational Manifestation is the meaning-relation, in which the three
elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s light is the meaning-relation as medium (the
condition under which meanings are legible); its causation is the motivational causation (the
transfer of a reason from one manifestation to another); its relation is the meaning-relation as
connection (the connection of one manifestation to another by significance). The distinction is
the fundamental-realm pattern.

12.5.6    The Hub of Realization
The fluid element of the Hub of Realization is the actualization, in which causation and relation
coincide and light distinguishes. The realm’s causation is its actualization (the transfer of
actuality from the possible to the concrete); its relation is its actualization (the connection
between the possible and the concrete); its light is its actualization (the mode of the actualizing).
The coincidence is the barzakhic pattern.

12.5.7    The Material Manifestation
The fluid element of the Material Manifestation is the physical medium, in which the three
elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s light is the physical medium (the field, the wave,
the photon); its causation is the physical causation (the transfer of energy, momentum, or force);
its relation is the spatial-temporal relation (the connection of one thing to another by position,
distance, or succession). The distinction is the fundamental-realm pattern.

12.5.8    The Seven Realms Together
The fluid elements of the seven realms are stated in the following table.

12.6      The Fluid Element and the Realm
12.6.1    The Fluid Element as the Realm’s Mode of Operation
The table shows more than the light, causation, and relation of each realm; it shows that the
fluid element of a realm is the realm’s mode of operation. The fluid element is not a thing in the
realm; it is the realm’s articulation of the triad, and the articulation is what makes the realm the
realm it is. The Material Manifestation is the realm in which the triad is articulated as physical
medium, physical causation, and spatial-temporal relation; the Structural Determination is the
realm in which the triad is articulated as law-structure, formal causation, and logical relation;
the First Determination is the realm in which the triad is collapsed into unity. The articulation
is the realm’s mode of operation, and the mode of operation is the realm’s fluid element.
    The identification is the chapter’s contribution to Book I’s Principle 7.1 (C3, independent
reality of the realms). Book I stated that each realm has a mode of existence of its own; the
present chapter states what the mode of existence is at the level of fluid elements. The mode
of operation is the articulation of the triad, and the articulation is what makes the realm
independent at the level of fluid elements.

12.6.2    The Fluid Element and the Realm’s Independence
The independence of the realm is the independence of its articulation. The Material Mani-
festation is not reducible to the Structural Determination because its articulation of the fluid
triad (physical medium, physical causation, spatial-temporal relation) is not reducible to the
Structural Determination’s articulation (law-structure, formal causation, logical relation). The
First Determination is not reducible to the Material Manifestation because its collapse of the fluid
triad is not reducible to the Material Manifestation’s distinction of the triad. The independence
is the independence of the articulation, and the articulation is what the table states.
Principle 12.3 (The Fluid Element as the Realm’s Mode of Operation). (T) The fluid element
of a realm is the realm’s mode of operation as an articulation of the triad of light, causation,
and relation. The articulation is what makes the realm independently real at the level of fluid
elements, and the independence is the independence of the articulation.
   The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the seven realms in §5 and by the
observation of the table. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 7.1, because the principle’s truth
depends on the independent reality of the realms.


12.7      The Relation Between the Two Triads
The chapter’s final contribution is the statement of the relation between the fluid triad and the
fixed triad.

12.7.1    The Two Triads
The two triads are the fixed triad of Part II (substance, essence, thisness) and the fluid triad of
Part III (light, causation, relation). The fixed triad is the structure of the fixed element; the
fluid triad is the structure of the fluid element. The two triads are related, and the relation is
the framework’s architecture at the level of the triads.
    The relation is the following. The fixed triad is what the fluid triad relates: the substance,
essence, and thisness of the things that bear on one another are the terms of the causation and
the relata of the relation. The fluid triad is what relates the fixed triad: the light, causation, and
relation are the medium, the transfer, and the connection through which the things bear on one
another. The two triads are not the same; they are the two sides of one structure—the structure
of the seven realms as a system of things in relation.
138                                             Chapter 12. The Fluid Elements of Each Realm


12.7.2    The Parallelism and the Asymmetry
The two triads exhibit a parallelism and an asymmetry.
    The parallelism. Both triads have three elements, and both exhibit the pattern of collapse,
partial coincidence, and full distinction across the seven realms. The parallelism is what makes
the seven realms a single system: the same pattern of articulation governs both the fixed and
the fluid elements, and the pattern is what makes the realms structurally distinct at both levels.
    The asymmetry. The fixed triad’s three elements are peers—each is a ground of a different
aspect of the thing (substance for sameness, essence for whatness, thisness for whichness)—and
none is the condition of the others. The fluid triad’s three elements are not peers—light is
the condition of causation and relation, and causation and relation are the conditioned. The
asymmetry is what makes the fluid triad a hierarchy, and the hierarchy is what makes the medium
the framework’s most fundamental fluid structure.
    The parallelism and the asymmetry together are the framework’s architecture at the level
of the triads. The architecture is what the present chapter states, and the architecture is what
makes Book II’s Part II and Part III a single contribution rather than two separate analyses.

Principle 12.4 (The Relation Between the Two Triads). (T) The fixed triad and the fluid triad
are related as the related and the relating: the fixed triad is what the fluid triad relates, and
the fluid triad is what relates the fixed triad. The two triads exhibit a parallelism (both have
three elements and both exhibit the same pattern of articulation) and an asymmetry (the fixed
triad’s elements are peers; the fluid triad’s elements are a hierarchy, with light as the condition
of causation and relation). The parallelism and the asymmetry together make the seven realms a
single system.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the two triads in Part II and Part III
and by the observation of their relation. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 7.1, because the
system it describes is the system of the independently real realms.


12.8     The Four-Column Structure of the Synthesis
The synthesis itself has a four-column structure, and the structure is stated here.

12.8.1    The Fixed Element of the Synthesis
The fixed element of the synthesis is the fluid triad itself, held invariant while the synthesis
explains the conditions of its articulation across the seven realms. The triad is held invariant as
the subject of the synthesis—the structure whose articulation the synthesis seeks to state.

12.8.2    The Fluid Element of the Synthesis
The fluid element of the synthesis is the relation between the triad and the realm—the relation
by which the realm articulates the triad, and by which the triad is realized in the realm. The
relation is the medium of the synthesis: it is what conveys the effect of the realm’s mode of
operation to the triad’s articulation.

12.8.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Synthesis
The governing dynamics of the synthesis is the rule by which the realm’s position in the ontological
architecture determines the triad’s articulation—the rule that the more a realm is a realm of
passage, the more its causation and relation coincide; the more a realm is a realm of multiplicity,
the more the triad is articulated. The rule is the principle of §4 (12.2).
12.9. What Part III Establishes                                                                139


12.8.4    The Context of the Synthesis
The context of the synthesis is the framework of Book I, in which the seven realms are indepen-
dently real and the triads are category-relative. The context is the frame in which the synthesis
is posed, and it is what makes the synthesis a synthesis of the framework, not a synthesis in
general.

12.8.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the synthesis are stated in the following table.

synthesis (Chapter 12). The method is the same at every level, and the same at every level is
what makes the book a systematic work.


12.9     What Part III Establishes
Part III has established five things.
    The definition of causation (Chapter 9, Definition 9.1), the argument that causation is
the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s conveyor principle (Chapter 9, Principle 9.5), and the
demonstration that the four standard theories of causation share the notion of transfer (Chapter 9,
Principle 9.3).
    The definition of relation (Chapter 10, Definition 10.1), the argument that relation is the
metaphysical consequent of Book I’s account of the Relational Manifestation (Chapter 10,
Principle 10.5), and the solution to Bradley’s regress by Book I’s Principle 12.3 (Chapter 10,
Principle 10.6).
    The definition of light as metaphysical medium (Chapter 11, Definition 11.2), the unpacking
of Book I’s analogical use of “substance” (Chapter 11, Principle 11.1), and the demonstration
that causation and relation presuppose the medium (Chapter 11, Principles 11.3 and 11.4).
    The synthesis of the fluid triad across the seven realms (the present chapter, Definition 12.1
and Principle 12.2), and the principle that the fluid element of a realm is the realm’s mode of
operation as an articulation of the triad (the present chapter, Principle 12.3).
    The relation between the two triads (the present chapter, Principle 12.4), and the demon-
stration that the seven realms are a single system at the level of both the fixed and the fluid
elements.
    The five establishments are the contribution of Part III. They are the metaphysical analysis
of Book I’s fluid element, and they are what Book II’s later parts will presuppose.


12.10      What Part III Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from Part III are deliberately deferred.
140                                             Chapter 12. The Fluid Elements of Each Realm


    First, Part III does not analyze the governing dynamics of metaphysics. The governing
dynamics—law, modality, the modal space—is the subject of Part IV. The present part has
analyzed the fluid elements in isolation from the governing dynamics, and the isolation is
deliberate: it makes the fluid elements visible before the governing dynamics is introduced.
    Second, Part III does not settle the question of whether the fluid triad is exhaustive. The
triad (light, causation, relation) is the chapter’s analysis of the fluid element; whether a fourth
element is needed, or whether one of the three can be derived from the others, is a question the
present part leaves open. The question is marked (Q) in the chapter’s status table.
    Third, Part III does not state the relation between the fluid triad and the context. The
relation is the subject of Part V, where the context of metaphysics is analyzed. The present part
has stated the fluid elements; the relation to the context is deferred.
    Fourth, Part III does not state the relation between the fluid triad and viability. The relation
is the subject of Part VI, where viability is analyzed as the integration of the four columns. The
present part has stated the fluid elements; the relation to viability is deferred.
    The four deferrals are the conditions under which Part III is offered, and they are stated so
that the reader knows what kind of claim is being made. A reader who accepts the deferrals
accepts the part’s scope; a reader who does not has a reason to read the later parts, where the
deferrals are lifted.

12.12      A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a person, a place, a work of art, an institution—and consider
the realm in which it is realized. Is the thing’s light, causation, and relation fully distinguished,
or do causation and relation coincide, or do all three collapse? What does the answer tell you
about the realm in which the thing is realized, and about the thing’s mode of operation?
12.12. A Question for Reflection                                                              141


     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The fluid triad is not the same in every
realm; its articulation is a function of the realm’s position in the ontological architecture. The
reader who can state, for a thing he knows, the articulation of its fluid triad, has understood
the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most
difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

With this chapter, Part III of Book II is complete. The fluid elements of metaphysics—light,
causation, and relation—are analyzed, synthesized into the triad, and shown to be articulated
differently in each of the seven realms. The next part turns to the governing dynamics of
metaphysics: law, modality, the modal space, and the dynamics of each realm. The first analysis
is law, which is the subject of Chapter 13.

             Part IV

Governing Dynamics of Metaphysics

Chapter 13

Law

Scope. This chapter opens Part IV with the analysis of law. It defines law as the structural
pattern that grounds the regularity, necessity, and formality of a realm’s rules, and it argues that
law is what Book I’s twenty-two rules of the seven realms (Principles 16.2 to 17.10) presuppose
in the order of being. It distinguishes law from regularity, from necessity, from disposition, and
from the other two governing-dynamics notions; it states the four standard theories of law and
what they share; it states the relation between law and causation, and between law and relation;
it states the four-column structure of the inquiry into law; it states the form that law takes in
each of the seven realms; and it answers three standard objections. Its claims are metaphysical
and structural; where it speaks of “law,” “rule,” “pattern,” “necessity,” or “regularity,” these are
structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and by the framework of
Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s principle that the
rules of the realms are structural constraints (Principle 16.1), the twenty-two rules themselves
(Principles 16.2 to 17.10), the unity of the rules of the fundamental realms (Principle 16.15),
the unity of the rules of the barzakhic realms (Principle 17.11), and the principle of category-
relative predication (Principle 27.1, C9). It does not restate these principles; it asks what they
presuppose in the order of being. The presupposition is stated in §6, and the chapter’s principal
contribution is the demonstration that law is the presupposition, and that the unity of the rules
(Principles 16.15 and 17.11) is a consequence of it.


13.1     A Scene
Consider a chess player studying a position. The board is set; the pieces are placed; the player
considers her move. Three things are present to her at once, and each is different.
    The first is the rules of the game. The player knows that the bishop moves diagonally, that
the knight moves in an L, that the king moves one square at a time. The rules are what make
the position a chess position; without them, the pieces would be a collection of carved shapes
with no relations.
    The second is the pattern of the position. The player sees that her bishop is pinned to her
king, that her opponent’s queen is attacking the kingside, that her rook is passive. The pattern
is what the position is at the strategic level; it is what the player must understand to choose her
move well. The pattern is not the rules; the rules are the same in every game, but the pattern
differs from position to position.
    The third is the playing of the game. The player’s move transfers the effect of her intention to
the board; her opponent’s response transfers the effect of the position back to her. The playing is
what the rules and the pattern make possible; without the rules, there is no legal move; without
the pattern, there is no reason to choose one move over another.
146                                                                               Chapter 13. Law


     Three things, and each is different. The rules are the laws of the game; the pattern is what
the laws make possible in this position; the playing is what the players do within the laws and
the pattern. The three are related, but they are not the same, and the player must keep them
apart.
     Now consider a harder case. Consider a game whose rules change as the game is played—a
game in which the bishop’s move is different after ten moves, or in which the king may move two
squares in the endgame. The game has a rule of rule-change, a higher-order rule that specifies
how the lower-order rules are altered. The rule of rule-change is not itself a rule of the game; it is
the law that makes the rules what they are at each stage. The distinction between the rules and
the law is the distinction between what the rules say and what makes them the rules they are.
     The scene poses the question of the chapter. Book I stated twenty-two rules of the seven
realms, and it argued that the rules are structural constraints of the realms’ modes of existence
(Principle 16.1). But what makes a rule a law? What is the metaphysical ground of the rules’
regularity, necessity, and formality? Is it a regularity (the rules are what they are because
they are observed to hold), a necessitation (the rules are what they are because a relation of
necessitation holds between universals), a disposition (the rules are what they are because the
realm’s nature disposes it to behave so), or a best system (the rules are what they are because
they are the axioms of the best systematization)? The chapter’s answer is: law is the structural
pattern that grounds the rules’ regularity, necessity, and formality, and law is distinct from all
four standard theories while being compatible with each. The chapter’s task is to say what law
is, to distinguish it from the notions with which it is easily confused, and to show that it is the
metaphysical consequent of Book I’s Principle 16.1.


13.2      The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is law, and what does it presuppose?
    The question is not the same as the question of Book I’s Chapter 16 or Chapter 17. Book I
asked what the rules of the realms are, and it answered: the thirteen rules of the fundamental
realms (Principles 16.2 to 16.14) and the nine rules of the barzakhic realms (Principles 17.2
to 17.10). The answer was analytical: it said what the rules are, not what makes them laws. The
present chapter asks the metaphysical counterpart: what must be the case in reality, such that a
rule can be a law? What is the ground of the rules’ regularity, necessity, and formality?
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of law? The chapter must define law, and it must
distinguish the definition from the definitions of substance (Chapter 5), essence (Chapter 6),
causation (Chapter 9), relation (Chapter 10), and light (Chapter 11). The definition must be
precise enough to be argued about, and general enough to cover the law of each of the seven
realms.
    The second aspect: what is the relation between law and Book I’s twenty-two rules? The
chapter must state how law relates to Book I’s Principle 16.1 and to the twenty-two rules. The
relation is the chapter’s principal contribution, because it is what makes law a metaphysical
consequent of the framework, not a metaphysical posit alongside it.
    The third aspect: what is the relation between law and the four standard theories? The
chapter must state the four standard theories—regularity, necessitation, disposition, and best
system—and it must state what they share. The statement is the chapter’s contribution to
the philosophical debate, and it is what makes the chapter a metaphysical analysis, not a mere
stipulation of a definition.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: law is the
structural pattern that grounds the rules’ regularity, necessity, and formality; it is what Book I’s
Principle 16.1 presupposes; and the four standard theories share the notion of pattern, which the
framework calls law.
13.3. The Definition of Law                                                                       147


13.3      The Definition of Law
13.3.1    The Definition
Definition 13.1 (Law). (A) A law is the structural pattern that grounds the regularity, necessity,
and formality of a realm’s rules. The pattern is what makes the rules the rules they are; it is the
condition under which a rule is a law, and not a mere description or a contingent regularity.

    The definition has three components, and each is important.
    The first component: law is a structural pattern. The pattern is not a regularity (a regularity
is a pattern of events; the pattern is what the regularity exhibits); it is not a necessitation (a
necessitation is a relation between universals; the pattern is what the relation tracks); it is not a
disposition (a disposition is a power of a thing; the pattern is what the power’s manifestation
exhibits). The pattern is the structural feature that the regularity, the necessitation, and the
disposition all presuppose.
    The second component: law grounds the regularity, necessity, and formality. The three are
the marks of a law that Book I’s Structural Determination (Principles 16.6 to 16.8) identified:
universality (the law applies to all instances), necessity (the law could not be otherwise), formality
(the law concerns the form, not the content). The law is the ground of the three: the pattern is
what makes the law universal, necessary, and formal.
    The third component: law makes a rule a law. A rule is a statement of what must be the
case; a law is what makes the statement a statement of what must be the case. The distinction is
the distinction between the rule and the law: the rule is the formulation; the law is the structure
that the formulation formulates. A rule that is not grounded in a law is a mere description or a
contingent regularity; a rule that is grounded in a law is a law.
    The three components are not three definitions; they are three aspects of one definition. The
law is the structural pattern, and the pattern grounds the regularity, necessity, and formality—and
these are three ways of saying the same thing, because the pattern’s being structural, its grounding
the three marks, and its making the rule a law are three aspects of its being a law.

13.3.2    What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
    It does not say that law is a command. The law is not a command issued by a legislator; it
is a structural pattern of the realm. The distinction is the distinction between a legal law (a
command of a sovereign) and a metaphysical law (a pattern of a realm). The framework’s law is
the second, not the first.
    It does not say that law is a description. The law is not a description of the regularity; it
is the structure that the description describes. The distinction is the distinction between the
description and the described; the law is the second, not the first. A description can be true or
false; a law is what makes a description true or false.
    It does not say that law is a regularity. The law is not the regularity of events; it is the
pattern that grounds the regularity. The regularity is the observable side of the law; the law is
the structural side. The distinction is the distinction between the observable and the structural;
the law is the second, not the first.
    It does not say that law is a necessity. The law is not the necessity of the rule; it is the
pattern that grounds the necessity. The necessity is the modal side of the law; the law is the
structural side. The distinction is the distinction between the modal and the structural; the
law is the second, not the first. Chapter 14 (on necessity and modality) will state the relation
between law and necessity more fully.
    It does not say that law is a disposition. The law is not the power of a thing; it is the pattern
that the power’s manifestation exhibits. The disposition is the source of the manifestation; the
148                                                                              Chapter 13. Law


law is the pattern that the manifestation follows. The distinction is the distinction between the
source and the pattern; the law is the second, not the first.

13.3.3    Law and Rule
Definition 13.2 (Rule and Law). (A) A rule is a formulation of what must be the case in a
realm; a law is the structural pattern that the formulation formulates. The rule is the formulation;
the law is the structure. A rule is a law if and only if it is grounded in a law of the realm.

    The distinction between rule and law is the distinction between the formulation and the
structure. The rule is what is stated; the law is what makes the statement a statement of what
must be the case. Book I’s twenty-two rules (Principles 16.2 to 17.10) are formulations; the
present chapter asks what makes them laws. The answer is: the structural patterns that the
formulations formulate.
    The distinction is the same as the distinction between a theorem and its proof: the theorem is
the formulation; the proof is the structure that makes the formulation a theorem. A rule without
a law is a formulation without a proof—a statement that might be true, but whose truth is not
grounded. The law is the ground, and the rule is the formulation of the ground.


13.4      Law and the Standard Theories
The chapter’s first contribution to the philosophical debate is the statement of what the four
standard theories of law share.

13.4.1    The Four Theories
Four theories of law are standard in the contemporary debate.
    Regularity theory. Laws are regularities: a law is a true universal generalization that describes
a regularity in nature (Hume; Ramsey; Lewis’s best-system variant is sometimes classified here).
The theory’s virtue is its empiricism: it does not posit unobservable necessities. Its difficulty is
that it cannot explain the difference between a law and an accidental generalization, and that it
cannot explain why the regularity holds.
    Necessitation theory. Laws are relations of necessitation between universals: a law is a second-
order relation between two universals, such that the first necessitates the second (Armstrong;
Dretske; Tooley). The theory’s virtue is that it explains the necessity of laws. Its difficulty is
that it posits unobservable relations, and that it must explain what a relation of necessitation is.
    Dispositional theory. Laws are the manifestations of dispositions: a law is the regular
manifestation of a thing’s disposition to behave in a certain way (Bird; Mumford; Ellis). The
theory’s virtue is that it grounds laws in the natures of things. Its difficulty is that dispositions
are unobservable, and that the theory must explain what a disposition is.
    Best-system theory. Laws are the axioms of the best deductive system: a law is a statement
that appears as an axiom in the systematization of all truths that best balances simplicity and
strength (Lewis). The theory’s virtue is that it is empirically adequate and it avoids unobservable
necessities. Its difficulty is that it makes laws depend on our standards of systematization, and
that it is not clear that the best system is unique.

13.4.2    What the Theories Share
The four theories differ on what law is, but they share a common structure. Each theory posits
a pattern that grounds the regularity of the law, and each theory explains what the pattern is in
its own terms.
13.5. Law and Causation, Law and Relation                                                         149


Principle 13.3 (What the Theories Share). (T) The four standard theories of law—regularity,
necessitation, disposition, and best system—share the notion of a pattern that grounds the
regularity of the law. The theories differ on what the pattern is (a pattern of regularities, a
pattern of necessitation, a pattern of dispositions, a pattern of systematization), but they all
presuppose that there is a pattern. The pattern is what the chapter calls law.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the four theories. Its argument is the
observation that each theory, in its own vocabulary, posits something by which the regularity
is grounded, and that the something is what the framework calls the pattern. The regularity
theory’s universal generalization is a pattern of regularities; the necessitation theory’s relation of
necessitation is a pattern of necessitation; the disposition theory’s manifestation is a pattern
of dispositions; the best-system theory’s systematization is a pattern of systematization. The
four theories are four ways of describing the same structure—the pattern—and the framework’s
contribution is to name the structure and to identify it with law.

13.4.3    The Framework’s Position
The framework does not choose one of the four theories over the others. Its claim is that
the four theories are partial descriptions of the pattern, and that the framework’s definition
(Definition 13.1) is the general structure that the four theories describe in their own terms.

Principle 13.4 (The Framework’s Position on the Law Theories). (E) The framework does not
adopt one of the four standard theories of law; it identifies the general structure—the structural
pattern that grounds the regularity—that the four theories describe in their own terms. The
framework’s position is compatible with all four theories, and it is incompatible with none of
them; it is the general structure that the theories instantiate.

   The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the analysis of
the four theories supports. Its justification is that the general structure is visible in all four
theories and that it does the same explanatory work as any one of them, without committing
the framework to the specific claims of any one.


13.5      Law and Causation, Law and Relation
The chapter’s second contribution is the distinction of law from the other two elements of the
fluid triad—causation (Chapter 9) and relation (Chapter 10)—and the statement of how the
three relate.

13.5.1    Law Is Not Causation
Causation is the real transfer of effect from a cause to an effect through a medium (Chapter 9,
Definition 9.1). Law is not the transfer; it is the pattern that the transfer follows. The distinction
is the distinction between the transfer and the pattern of the transfer: the fire’s heat causes the
wood’s ignition (a transfer); the law of combustion is the pattern that the transfer follows (a
law). The two are distinct: the transfer is one event; the pattern is what makes the event an
instance of a kind. The transfer presupposes the pattern; the pattern is what makes the transfer
intelligible as a transfer of a kind.
    The distinction is important because it blocks the inference from the transfer to the law. The
law is not the transfer; the law is what makes the transfer an instance of the law. Without the
law, the transfer would be a singular event with no kind; with the law, the transfer is an instance
of a kind. The law is the condition of the transfer’s intelligibility, not the transfer itself.
150                                                                               Chapter 13. Law


13.5.2    Law Is Not Relation
Relation is the real connection between two or more terms (Chapter 10, Definition 10.1). Law is
not the connection; it is the pattern that the connection follows. The distinction is the distinction
between the connection and the pattern of the connection: the mother and the father are related
as spouses (a connection); the law of marriage is the pattern that the connection follows (a law).
The two are distinct: the connection is one relation; the pattern is what makes the relation
an instance of a kind. The connection presupposes the pattern; the pattern is what makes the
connection intelligible as a connection of a kind.

13.5.3    Law, Causation, and Relation
The three—law, causation, relation—are related as pattern, transfer, and connection. The law
is the pattern that both the transfer and the connection follow; the causation is the transfer;
the relation is the connection. The three are distinct, and the distinction is what makes the
fluid element a triad: the medium (light) makes the transfer and the connection possible; the
transfer (causation) and the connection (relation) are what the medium conveys and connects;
the pattern (law) is what the transfer and the connection follow.
    The relation is the relation between the three elements of the fluid triad, and it is stated in
the following principle.

Principle 13.5 (Law, Causation, and Relation). (T) Law, causation, and relation are related as
pattern, transfer, and connection: the law is the pattern that the transfer (causation) and the
connection (relation) follow; the transfer and the connection are what the law patterns. The
three are distinct, and the distinction is what makes the fluid element a triad.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the three elements and by the observation
of their relation. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 16.1 and to Chapters 9 and 10.


13.6      Law as the Presupposition of the Rules
The chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that law is what Book I’s twenty-two
rules presuppose in the order of being. The demonstration has three steps.

13.6.1    Step 1: The Rules Presuppose a Pattern
Book I’s Principle 16.1 states that the rules of the realms are structural constraints of the realms’
modes of existence—they are not imposed from without, but they are what the realms are. The
principle is (A): it is a commitment of Book I. But the commitment presupposes a pattern: for
the rules to be structural constraints, there must be a structure that they constrain, and the
structure must be a pattern that the rules articulate. The pattern is what makes the rules the
rules they are; without the pattern, the rules would be arbitrary formulations with no ground.
    The step is a (D) claim: it is conditional on Book I’s Principle 16.1. The claim is not that
the rules are laws; the claim is that the rules presuppose a pattern, and that the presupposition
is the rules’ metaphysical condition.

13.6.2    Step 2: The Pattern Is Law
The pattern that the rules presuppose is what the chapter calls law. The identification is not
arbitrary: it is the identification of the pattern with the notion that the metaphysical tradition
has called law. The tradition’s notion is the notion of the structural pattern that grounds the
regularity, necessity, and formality of the rules; the chapter’s definition is the same notion, stated
in the framework’s vocabulary.
13.7. The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Law                                         151


    The step is a (T) claim: it is argued by the analysis of the notion of law and by the comparison
with the tradition’s notion. It is relative to the chapter’s definition (Definition 13.1), and it is
assessable by the definition’s adequacy.

13.6.3    Step 3: The Presupposition Is a Metaphysical Consequent
The presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of Book I’s framework, not an independent
metaphysical posit. The framework does not add law to the rules; it states what the rules require
in the order of being. The requirement is a (D) claim, and the (D) claim is the chapter’s principal
contribution.
    The step is the synthesis of Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 establishes that the rules presuppose a
pattern; Step 2 establishes that the pattern is law; Step 3 establishes that the presupposition is
a metaphysical consequent of the framework. The three steps together establish the chapter’s
principal claim.

Principle 13.6 (Law as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Rules). (D) Law is the metaphysical
consequent of Book I’s rules of the realms: the rules presuppose a structural pattern that grounds
their regularity, necessity, and formality, and the pattern is what the chapter calls law. The
principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principle 16.1; it is the chapter’s principal
contribution because it states what the rules require in the order of being.

13.6.4    The Unity of the Rules as a Consequence
The chapter’s second principal contribution is the demonstration that the unity of the rules
(Book I, Principles 16.15 and 17.11) is a consequence of law.
    Book I argued, as an estimate (E), that the rules of the fundamental realms are related by a
single structure (Principle 16.15), and that the rules of the barzakhic realms are related by the
structure of the transition from unity to multiplicity (Principle 17.11). The two arguments were
structural estimates: they showed that the rules are related, but they did not state the ground of
the relation. The present chapter states the ground: the relation is a consequence of law. The
rules are related because they are the articulations of a single pattern—the law of the realm—in
the different modes of the realm. The law is what makes the rules one pattern, and the unity of
the rules is the unity of the pattern.

Principle 13.7 (The Unity of the Rules as a Consequence of Law). (D) The unity of the rules
of the realms (Book I, Principles 16.15 and 17.11) is a consequence of law: the rules are related
because they are the articulations of a single pattern—the law of the realm—in the different
modes of the realm. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principles 16.15
and 17.11 and on the definition of law (Definition 13.1).

    The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the demonstration that Book I’s
estimates of the unity of the rules are consequences of the present chapter’s definition of law.
The demonstration shows that the unity is not an accident of the rules; it is the unity of the law
that the rules articulate.


13.7     The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Law
With the definition of law in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can be applied to the
inquiry into law.
152                                                                               Chapter 13. Law


13.7.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Law
The fixed element of the inquiry into law is the law itself, held invariant while the inquiry explains
the conditions of its being. The law is held invariant as the subject of the inquiry—the pattern
whose conditions the inquiry seeks to state.

13.7.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Law
The fluid element of the inquiry into law is the relation between the law and its instances—the
relation by which the instances are instances of the law, and by which the law is what the
instances follow. The relation is the medium of the inquiry: it is what conveys the effect of the
law’s being what it is to the instances’ being what they are.

13.7.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Law
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into law is the rule by which the law grounds the
instances—the rule that explains how the pattern makes the instances necessary, universal, and
formal. The rule is the subject of §4, where the standard theories are analyzed; each theory
states a different rule, and the framework’s claim is that the rule is the general structure that
the theories describe in their own terms.

13.7.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Law
The context of the inquiry into law is the realm in which the law operates. The seven realms of
Book I are the contexts, and law takes a different form in each. The form of law in each realm is
the subject of §8.

13.7.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into law are stated in the following table.

                 Column                In the Inquiry into Law
                 Fixed element    The law itself, held invariant as the subject

                 Fluid element    The relation between the law and its in-
                                  stances
                 Governing dynam- The rule by which the law grounds the

    The table is the application of Chapter 2’s method to the inquiry into law. The application

13.8      Law in Each Realm
Law takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the form, one
realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered at the
strength that the framework’s principles support, and subject to revision if a different form of
law in a realm does the same explanatory work.
13.8. Law in Each Realm                                                                          153


13.8.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, law takes the form of physical law—the pattern that grounds the
regularity of material events. The law of combustion grounds the regularity of fire’s ignition of
wood; the law of gravitation grounds the regularity of bodies’ falling; the law of thermodynamics
grounds the regularity of heat’s flow. The physical law is the Material mode of the general law,
and it is the mode that Book I’s causality, temporality, and discreteness rules (Principles 16.12
to 16.14) formulate.

13.8.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, law takes the form of meaning law—the pattern that grounds
the regularity of meaning relations. The law of signification grounds the regularity of a word’s
meaning a concept; the law of recognition grounds the regularity of a face’s being recognized as
the same face; the law of care grounds the regularity of a friend’s being comforted by a friend’s
presence. The meaning law is the Relational mode of the general law, and it is the mode that
Book I’s relationality, contextuality, and awareness rules (Principles 16.9 to 16.11) formulate.

13.8.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, law takes the form of logical law—the pattern that grounds
the regularity of logical entailment. The law of non-contradiction grounds the regularity of
a proposition’s not being both true and false; the law of identity grounds the regularity of a
proposition’s being the same proposition through reformulation; the law of modus ponens grounds
the regularity of a consequence’s following from its premises. The logical law is the Structural
mode of the general law, and it is the mode that Book I’s universality, necessity, and formality
rules (Principles 16.6 to 16.8) formulate.

13.8.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, law takes the form of pure unity. The First Determination has
no multiplicity, no change, no succession (Book I, Definition 7.5); its law is its unity, and its
unity is its law. The form is the limit case of the other forms: it is what law becomes when the
multiplicity is zero. The First Determination’s four rules (invariance, atemporality, indivisibility,
unity) are all modes of the unity that the law is; the law of the First Determination is the unity
that the rules articulate.

13.8.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, law takes the form of measure law—the pattern that grounds the regularity
of apportioning. The law of proportion grounds the regularity of the apportioning’s preserving
the unity of the source; the law of order grounds the regularity of the apportioning’s following
the articulation of the realms; the law of harmony grounds the regularity of the apportioning’s
producing a coherent multiplicity. The measure law is the mode of the general law in the Hub of
Decree.

13.8.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, law takes the form of signification law— the pattern that grounds the
regularity of signification. The law of truthfulness grounds the regularity of the signification’s
carrying the structural features of the structure; the law of accuracy grounds the regularity of
the signification’s preserving the distinctions; the law of fidelity grounds the regularity of the
signification’s preserving the identity. The signification law is the mode of the general law in the
Hub of Signification.
154                                                                              Chapter 13. Law


13.8.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, law takes the form of realization law—the pattern that grounds
the regularity of actualization. The law of proportion in realization grounds the regularity
of the realization’s distributing the conditions proportionally; the law of preservation of the
realized grounds the regularity of the realization’s preserving the structural conditions; the law
of continuation of realization grounds the regularity of the realization’s preserving the conditions
across stages. The realization law is the mode of the general law in the Hub of Realization.

13.8.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

13.9     Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
     Objection 1: Law is a Humean posit; the framework’s “structural pattern” is a metaphysical
fiction. The objection is that Hume showed that laws are just regularities, and that the
framework’s “structural pattern” is a relic of pre-Humean metaphysics.
     Reply. The objection mistakes Hume’s epistemology of law for his metaphysics of law. Hume
argued that we do not perceive the necessary connection, and that we infer it from custom.
But Hume did not deny that there is a regularity; his regularity theory is itself a metaphysical
position (the position that laws are regularities). The framework’s “pattern” is not a denial
of the regularity; it is the analysis of what the regularity is—the pattern that the regularity
exhibits. The regularity is the observable side of the pattern; the pattern is the structural
side. The framework’s claim is metaphysical, not epistemological; the objection’s Hume is the
epistemological Hume, not the metaphysical one. The two are distinct, and the framework’s
analysis is compatible with the epistemological Hume’s conclusions.
     Objection 2: Law is a physical notion; the framework’s “law of the Structural Determination”
is a metaphor. The objection is that laws are laws of nature—physical laws that govern the
behavior of physical things—and that the framework’s “law of the Structural Determination” is
a metaphor, not a law.
13.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                     155


    Reply. The objection confuses physical law with law tout court. The framework’s definition
of law is the structural pattern that grounds the regularity, necessity, and formality of a realm’s
rules; the physical law is one mode of the pattern, not the whole of it. The logical law of the
Structural Determination is a real pattern (it grounds the regularity of entailment); the meaning
law of the Relational Manifestation is a real pattern (it grounds the regularity of signification);
the measure law of the Hub of Decree is a real pattern (it grounds the regularity of apportioning).
The objection’s premise—that only physical regularities are laws—is not the framework’s premise;
the framework’s premise is that every realm has its law, and the physical law is one of the
seven modes. The distinction is the distinction between the general structure and its modes; the
framework states the general structure, and the modes are its seven forms.
    Objection 3: The definition is circular. The definition says that law is the structural pattern
that grounds the rules; the rules are what the law grounds; and the pattern is the law. The three
terms are defined in terms of one another, and the definition is circular.
    Reply. The circularity is only apparent. The definition does not define the rules as “what
the law grounds”; it defines the rules as the formulations of what must be the case, and the
law as the pattern that the formulations formulate. The pattern is the primitive notion; the
rules are the formulations of the pattern; the law is the pattern that the formulations formulate.
The definition’s structure is: pattern (primitive) + formulations (rules) = law (the pattern that
the rules formulate). The three terms are not defined in terms of one another; they are three
aspects of one structure, and the structure is the definition. The objection mistakes the structural
definition for a semantic circularity; the reply distinguishes them.


13.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that law is a real feature of the world. It argues that law is
what Book I’s Principle 16.1 presupposes; the argument is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 16.1,
and it is offered at the strength that the principle supports. A reader who rejects Principle 16.1
has a reason to reject the conclusion; the chapter states the argument at exactly that strength.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of which of the four standard theories is
correct. The chapter’s claim is that the four theories are partial descriptions of the pattern, and
that the framework’s general structure is compatible with all four; the choice among the four is a
further question, and the chapter leaves it open. The question is marked (Q) in the chapter’s
status table.
    Third, the chapter does not analyze necessity and modality. Necessity and modality are the
subjects of Chapter 14; the present chapter distinguishes law from necessity, but it does not
analyze necessity. The reader who expects the analysis in this chapter has misread the chapter’s
scope; the analysis begins in Chapter 14.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the relation between law and the modal space. The relation
is the subject of Chapter 15, where the modal space is analyzed. The present chapter has stated
the relation between law and the twenty-two rules; the relation to the modal space is deferred.
