13.12      A Question for Reflection
Consider a law you know well—a physical law, a logical law, a moral law, a law of a practice.
What is the pattern that grounds it? Is the pattern a regularity, a necessitation, a disposition, or
a systematization? What would it mean for the law to be a law and not merely a description?
And if the law is the pattern that grounds the regularity, what would it mean for the pattern to
change?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The law is the pattern; the regularity is
the observable side; the rule is the formulation. The reader who can state, for a law he knows,
what the pattern, the regularity, and the rule are, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the
reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to
develop the difficulty further.

The next chapter analyzes necessity and modality: what it is for a law to be necessary, and how
necessity relates to law. With law in place, the framework can distinguish the pattern (law) from
the modal status of the pattern (necessity), and it can state the relation between the two—the
relation that Book I’s Principle 16.7 (necessity of the structural laws) presupposes. The analysis
is the subject of Chapter 14.
                                                                                                157




Chapter 14

Necessity and Modality

Scope. This chapter analyzes necessity and modality. It defines necessity as the modal status of
a proposition that cannot be otherwise, and modality as the structure of the possible, the actual,
and the necessary. It distinguishes four kinds of necessity—logical, metaphysical, natural, and
normative—and it argues that the four are grounded in different structures: logical necessity in
the form of propositions, metaphysical necessity in essence (Chapter 6), natural necessity in law
(Chapter 13), and normative necessity in the structure of the good (Part VI). It states the relation
between necessity and Book I’s modal space Ω (Principle 37.1), and it argues that Book I’s
principle that the structural laws are necessary (Principle 16.7) is a principle of metaphysical
necessity grounded in essence. It states the four-column structure of the inquiry into necessity; it
states the form that necessity takes in each of the seven realms; and it answers three standard
objections, including the objection from Quine’s skepticism about de re modality. Its claims are
metaphysical and structural; where it speaks of “necessity,” “possibility,” “modality,” “ground,”
or “essence,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and
by the framework of Book I.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s principle that the
structural laws are necessary (Principle 16.7, within the Structural Determination), the principle
that the modal space Ω is real and is the totality of possibilities (Principle 37.1, C12), the
definition of the three layers of the ontological architecture (Definition 37.1), and the principle
that Ω is grounded in God (Principle 37.2). It does not restate these principles; it asks what they
presuppose in the order of being. The presupposition is stated in §6 and §7, and the chapter’s
principal contribution is the demonstration that necessity is not one thing but four, and that the
four are grounded in different structures.


14.1      A Scene
Consider a logician, a physicist, and a metaphysician in conversation. Each says: It cannot be
otherwise. And each means something different.
    The logician says: A proposition cannot be both true and false. Her “cannot” is logical
necessity: the negation of her statement would be a contradiction, and a contradiction is not
a possible state of affairs. The necessity is grounded in the form of propositions; it does not
depend on what the world is like, and it holds in every possible world.
    The physicist says: A body cannot accelerate beyond the speed of light. Her “cannot” is natural
necessity: the negation of her statement would not be a contradiction, and it is conceivable that
a body accelerates beyond the speed of light—but the laws of nature exclude it. The necessity is
grounded in the laws of the physical realm; it depends on what the world is like, and it holds in
this world, and in every world with the same laws.
158                                                          Chapter 14. Necessity and Modality


    The metaphysician says: A human being cannot fail to be a rational animal. Her “cannot”
is metaphysical necessity: the negation of her statement would not be a contradiction (it is
conceivable that a human being is not rational), and it is not excluded by the laws of nature (a
non-rational human being would not violate a physical law)—but it is excluded by the essence
of a human being. The necessity is grounded in essence; it depends on what the human being
essence is, and it holds in every world in which the essence is instantiated.
    Three “cannot”s, and each is different. The three are not the same kind of necessity, and
the three are grounded in different structures. The logician’s necessity is grounded in the form
of propositions; the physicist’s in the laws of nature; the metaphysician’s in essence. The three
are related—logical necessity is a condition of every other kind, and metaphysical necessity is
the ground of natural necessity—but they are not the same, and the conversation reveals their
distinctness.
    Now consider a fourth speaker, a moral philosopher. She says: A promise cannot be broken
without a reason. Her “cannot” is normative necessity: the negation of her statement would
not be a contradiction, and it is not excluded by the laws of nature—but it is excluded by the
structure of the good. The normative necessity is grounded in the structure of value, and it holds
in every world in which the structure obtains.
    Four speakers, four “cannot”s, four kinds of necessity. The scene poses the question of the
chapter. What is necessity? Is it one thing, with four modes, or four things, with a common
name? And what does Book I’s principle that the structural laws are necessary (Principle 16.7)
assert—is it logical, metaphysical, natural, or normative necessity?
    The chapter’s answer is: necessity is not one thing; it is four kinds, grounded in four different
structures (form, essence, law, good). The four kinds are not reducible to one another, and
the framework’s claim is that Book I’s Principle 16.7 is a principle of metaphysical necessity,
grounded in essence. The chapter’s task is to define the four kinds, to distinguish them, to state
their grounding, and to show that Book I’s claims about necessity are clarified by the distinction.


14.2      The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is necessity, and what does it presuppose?
     The question is not the same as the question of Chapter 13. Chapter 13 asked what law
is, and it answered: law is the structural pattern that grounds the regularity, necessity, and
formality of a realm’s rules. The answer named necessity as one of the three marks of law, but
it did not analyze necessity itself. The present chapter asks a different question: what is the
necessity that law grounds? What is the modal status of a law’s assertion, and what structure
grounds it?
     The question is also not the same as the question of Book I’s Chapter 37. Book I’s Chapter 37
introduced the modal space Ω (Principle 37.1, C12) and the actualization chain X (Definition 37.1);
it stated that Ω is grounded in God (Principle 37.2). The present chapter does not reargue those
claims; it asks what necessity is within Ω—what distinguishes the necessary from the merely
possible, and what grounds the distinction.
     The question has three aspects.
     The first aspect: what is the definition of necessity and of modality? The chapter must
define necessity and modality, and it must distinguish the definitions from the definitions of law
(Chapter 13), essence (Chapter 6), and causation (Chapter 9).
     The second aspect: what kinds of necessity are there? The chapter must distinguish logical,
metaphysical, natural, and normative necessity, and it must state what grounds each.
     The third aspect: what is the relation between necessity and Book I’s claims about necessity?
The chapter must state how necessity relates to Book I’s Principle 16.7 (the structural laws are
necessary) and to Book I’s modal space Ω (Principle 37.1). The relation is the chapter’s principal
contribution, because it is what makes necessity a metaphysical consequent of the framework,
14.3. The Definition of Necessity and Modality                                                      159


not a metaphysical posit alongside it.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: necessity
is four kinds, grounded in four structures; the four kinds are not reducible to one another; and
Book I’s Principle 16.7 is a principle of metaphysical necessity grounded in essence.


14.3      The Definition of Necessity and Modality
14.3.1     The Definitions
Definition 14.1 (Modality). (A) Modality is the structure of the possible, the actual, and the
necessary. The possible is what could be; the actual is what is; the necessary is what cannot be
otherwise. The three are the three modal statuses, and they are distinct: a thing can be possible
without being actual; a thing can be actual without being necessary; a thing can be necessary
without being actual (in the sense of being instantiated in this world—the necessary holds in
every world).

Definition 14.2 (Necessity). (A) Necessity is the modal status of a proposition, state of affairs,
or thing that cannot be otherwise. A proposition is necessary if its negation is impossible; a state
of affairs is necessary if its non-obtaining is impossible; a thing is necessary if its non-existence is
impossible. The “cannot” is the modal operator, and its sense is fixed by the kind of necessity in
question (logical, metaphysical, natural, or normative).

    The definitions have three components, and each is important.
    The first component: modality is a structure of three statuses. The three statuses—possible,
actual, necessary—are not three things; they are three statuses that a thing or proposition can
have. The distinction is the distinction between the status and the thing: the status is what the
thing has; the thing is what has the status. The same thing can be possible in one world and
actual in another, and necessary in every world; the statuses are the modal profiles of the thing.
    The second component: necessity is the modal status of what cannot be otherwise. The
“cannot” is not a single operator; it is a family of operators, and each kind of necessity has its
own. The logical “cannot” is the impossibility of contradiction; the metaphysical “cannot” is the
impossibility of violating essence; the natural “cannot” is the impossibility of violating law; the
normative “cannot” is the impossibility of violating the good. The four “cannot”s are different,
and the chapter’s task is to distinguish them.
    The third component: the sense of the “cannot” is fixed by the kind of necessity. The definition
does not say which kind of necessity is at issue; it says that the kind is what determines the
sense of the “cannot”. The distinction is the distinction between the general notion (necessity as
the modal status of what cannot be otherwise) and the specific kinds (the four “cannot”s). The
general notion is what the definition captures; the specific kinds are what the chapter’s §4 states.

14.3.2     What the Definitions Do Not Say
The definitions are stipulations, and it is important to state what they do not say.
    They do not say that necessity is one thing. The definitions state the general notion of
necessity; they do not state that the general notion is a single kind. The chapter’s principal
contribution is the demonstration that the general notion has four kinds, and that the kinds are
not reducible to one another.
    They do not say that necessity is a property of propositions alone. Necessity can be a property
of propositions (a proposition is necessary), of states of affairs (a state of affairs is necessary), or
of things (a thing is necessary). The three are related but distinct: the proposition’s necessity is
the necessity of the state of affairs it expresses; the state of affairs’ necessity is the necessity of
the thing’s being what it is. The definitions state the general notion, and the chapter’s later
sections state the specific applications.
160                                                            Chapter 14. Necessity and Modality


    They do not say that necessity is knowable. The definitions state what necessity is; they do
not state how it is known. The knowledge of necessity is an epistemic question, and it is the
subject of Book I’s account of explanation and of pseudo-identity. The present chapter states the
metaphysical structure of necessity, and it leaves the epistemic question to Book I’s epistemology.
    They do not say that necessity is absolute. The definitions state the modal status of what
cannot be otherwise; they do not state that the “cannot” is the same in every kind. The four
kinds are different, and the “cannot” of each is fixed by the kind. The distinction is the distinction
between the general notion and its kinds; the definitions state the general notion, and the kinds
are the chapter’s §4.

14.3.3    Necessity and Possibility
Definition 14.3 (Possibility). (A) Possibility is the modal status of what could be. A proposition
is possible if its negation is not necessary; a state of affairs is possible if its non-obtaining is not
necessary; a thing is possible if its non-existence is not necessary. The possible is the complement
of the necessary, in the sense that what is not necessary is possible (when the possibility is not
excluded by another modal status).

    The distinction between necessity and possibility is classical, and the framework uses it.
The two are interdefinable in classical modal logic: a proposition is necessary if and only if its
negation is not possible; a proposition is possible if and only if its negation is not necessary. The
framework’s use of the interdefinability is standard; the chapter’s contribution is the distinction
of the four kinds, not the modal logic.


14.4      The Four Kinds of Necessity
The chapter’s principal contribution is the distinction of the four kinds of necessity and the
statement of what grounds each.

14.4.1    Logical Necessity
Definition 14.4 (Logical Necessity). (A) Logical necessity is the modal status of a proposition
that is true in virtue of its logical form alone. A logically necessary proposition is one whose
negation is a logical contradiction; the necessity is grounded in the form of the proposition, not
in what the world is like.

     Logical necessity is the necessity of the laws of logic. A proposition cannot be both true and
false is logically necessary; if all men are mortal and Socrates is a man, then Socrates is mortal
is logically necessary. The necessity is grounded in the form of the proposition; the form is what
makes the negation a contradiction.
     The framework’s claim is that logical necessity is the most general kind: every other kind
of necessity presupposes logical necessity, because every other kind of necessity operates within
the space of logical possibility. The logical necessity is the form of the space of possibilities; the
other kinds are the specific constraints within the space.

14.4.2    Metaphysical Necessity
Definition 14.5 (Metaphysical Necessity). (A) Metaphysical necessity is the modal status of a
proposition, state of affairs, or thing that is necessary in virtue of essence. A metaphysically
necessary proposition is one whose negation is incompatible with the essence of some thing; the
necessity is grounded in essence (Chapter 6), not in law (Chapter 13) and not in form alone.
14.4. The Four Kinds of Necessity                                                                   161


    Metaphysical necessity is the necessity of essence. A human being cannot fail to be a rational
animal is metaphysically necessary; a triangle cannot fail to have three sides is metaphysically
necessary. The necessity is grounded in essence; the essence is what makes the negation
incompatible with what the thing is.
    The framework’s claim is that Book I’s Principle 16.7 (the structural laws are necessary) is a
principle of metaphysical necessity. The structural laws of the realms are necessary because they
are grounded in the essence of the realms—the essence is what makes the laws what they are,
and the essence is what makes the laws necessary. The distinction is the distinction between
the law (Chapter 13) and the essence (Chapter 6); the law is the pattern, and the essence is
what grounds the pattern’s necessity. The present chapter’s contribution is the statement of the
distinction.

Principle 14.6 (The Structural Laws Are Metaphysically Necessary). (D) Book I’s Principle 16.7
(the structural laws are necessary) is a principle of metaphysical necessity grounded in essence:
the laws are necessary because they are grounded in the essence of the realms, and the essence
is what makes the laws necessary. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s
Principle 16.7 and on the definition of metaphysical necessity (Definition 14.5) and of essence
(Chapter 6, Definition 6.1).

   The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the clarification of Book I’s
Principle 16.7. Book I stated that the structural laws are necessary; the present chapter states
what kind of necessity the principle asserts, and what grounds it.

14.4.3     Natural Necessity
Definition 14.7 (Natural Necessity). (A) Natural necessity is the modal status of a proposition
or state of affairs that is necessary in virtue of the laws of nature. A naturally necessary
proposition is one whose negation is incompatible with the laws of the physical realm; the
necessity is grounded in law (Chapter 13), not in essence and not in form alone.

     Natural necessity is the necessity of physical law. A body cannot accelerate beyond the speed
of light is naturally necessary; water cannot fail to boil at 100 °C at sea level is naturally necessary.
The necessity is grounded in the laws of nature; the laws are what make the negation incompatible
with the physical realm.
     The framework’s claim is that natural necessity is a mode of metaphysical necessity in the
Material Manifestation. The physical laws are the Material mode of the structural laws; the
physical necessity is the Material mode of the metaphysical necessity. The distinction is the
distinction between the general structure (the structural laws and their metaphysical necessity)
and the Material mode (the physical laws and their natural necessity); the present chapter states
the general structure, and the Material mode is one of its seven modes.

Principle 14.8 (Natural Necessity Is a Mode of Metaphysical Necessity). (D) Natural necessity
is the Material mode of metaphysical necessity: the physical laws are the Material mode of the
structural laws, and the natural necessity is the Material mode of the metaphysical necessity. The
principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principle 16.12 (the Material Manifestation’s
causality rule) and on the principle of category-relative predication (Principle 27.1, C9).

14.4.4     Normative Necessity
Definition 14.9 (Normative Necessity). (A) Normative necessity is the modal status of a
proposition or state of affairs that is necessary in virtue of the structure of the good. A
normatively necessary proposition is one whose negation is incompatible with the good; the
necessity is grounded in the good (Part VI), not in essence, not in law, and not in form alone.
162                                                           Chapter 14. Necessity and Modality


    Normative necessity is the necessity of the good. A promise cannot be broken without a reason
is normatively necessary; a person cannot be treated merely as a means is normatively necessary.
The necessity is grounded in the structure of the good; the good is what makes the negation
incompatible with what ought to be.
    The framework’s claim is that normative necessity is a posterior kind: it presupposes the
other three kinds, and it is grounded in the good. The chapter does not develop the structure of
the good; the development is the subject of Part VI. The chapter’s claim is only that normative
necessity is a distinct kind, and that it is not reducible to the other three.

14.4.5     The Four Kinds Together
The four kinds are stated in the following table.

             Kind               What It Is                  What Grounds It
             Logical            The negation is a contra-   The form of the proposition
                                diction
             Metaphysical       The negation is incom-      The essence of the thing
                                patible with essence
             Natural            The negation is incom-      The law of the realm
                                patible with law
             Normative          The negation is incom-      The structure of the good
                                patible with the good

    The table is the chapter’s map of the four kinds. It is an (A) claim: the four kinds are
the framework’s stipulation, and the reader may reject the four kinds by proposing a different
taxonomy. The framework’s justification is that the four kinds are the kinds that the conversation
of the scene revealed, and that they are distinct in their grounds.


14.5      The Relation Among the Four Kinds
The four kinds are not independent; they are related, and the relation is worth stating.

14.5.1     Logical Necessity as the Form of the Space
Logical necessity is the form of the space of possibilities: every other kind of necessity operates
within the space, and the space is logically structured. The logical necessity is the most general
kind; the other three are the specific kinds, and each is a constraint within the space.
    The relation is not a reduction: logical necessity does not entail metaphysical necessity
(a proposition can be logically consistent and metaphysically impossible: water is not H2 O is
logically consistent, because its negation is not a contradiction, but it is metaphysically impossible
if the essence of water is H2 O). The distinction is the distinction between the form of the space
and the constraints within it.

14.5.2     Metaphysical Necessity as the Ground of Natural Necessity
Metaphysical necessity is the ground of natural necessity: the natural laws are necessary because
they are grounded in essence, and the essence is what makes them necessary. The natural
necessity is the Material mode of the metaphysical necessity; the material law is the Material
mode of the structural law; the material essence is the Material mode of the general essence.
    The relation is a relation of grounding: the metaphysical necessity grounds the natural
necessity; the natural necessity is what the metaphysical necessity becomes in the Material Mani-
festation. The distinction is the distinction between the ground and its mode; the metaphysical
necessity is the ground, and the natural necessity is the mode.
14.6. Necessity and the Modal Space                                                               163


14.5.3    Normative Necessity as Posterior
Normative necessity is posterior to the other three: it presupposes the logical, metaphysical, and
natural kinds, and it is grounded in the good. The normative necessity is not a constraint of the
space of possibilities in the same sense as the other three; it is a constraint of the good, and the
good is what ought to be, not what is.
     The relation is a relation of dependence: the normative necessity depends on the other three
(it operates within the space they define), and it is grounded in the good (which is the subject of
Part VI). The distinction is the distinction between the constraints of what is (the first three
kinds) and the constraint of what ought to be (the fourth kind); the two are distinct, and the
fourth is posterior.

14.5.4    The Four Kinds Together
The four kinds are stated in the following principle.

Principle 14.10 (The Relation Among the Four Kinds). (T) The four kinds of necessity are
related as form, ground, mode, and posterior: logical necessity is the form of the space of
possibilities; metaphysical necessity is the ground of natural necessity; natural necessity is the
Material mode of metaphysical necessity; and normative necessity is posterior to the other three
and grounded in the good. The four kinds are not reducible to one another, and the relation
among them is a relation of grounding, not of identity.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the four kinds and by the observation of
their relation. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 16.7 and to Chapters 6, 13, and the modal
space of Book I’s Part IX.


14.6      Necessity and the Modal Space
The chapter’s second contribution is the statement of the relation between necessity and Book I’s
modal space Ω.

14.6.1    The Modal Space Revisited
Book I’s Principle 37.1 (C12) states that there is a space Ω of all possibilities, and that it is real.
The space is the totality of what could be; the actualization chain X is the possibilities that are
actualized (Book I, Definition 37.1). The present chapter asks: what is the relation between Ω
and necessity?
    The answer is: Ω is the space of what is possible, and necessity is the status of what is in
every subset of Ω that is closed under the relevant constraints. The necessary is what is in every
such subset; the possible is what is in at least one. The distinction is the distinction between the
space of possibilities and the modal statuses within the space; Ω is the space, and necessity is a
status within it.
    The relation is not a reduction: Ω is not the necessary; Ω is the space in which the necessary
and the possible are distinguished. The distinction is the distinction between the space and the
statuses within it; the space is the framework’s most general modal notion, and the statuses are
what the space distinguishes.

14.6.2    The Grounding of Necessity
The necessary, within Ω, is not a primitive status; it is grounded. The grounding is the subject
of the four kinds: the logical necessary is grounded in the form of propositions; the metaphysical
necessary in essence; the natural necessary in law; the normative necessary in the good. The
164                                                         Chapter 14. Necessity and Modality


grounding is what distinguishes the necessary from the merely possible; without the grounding,
the necessary would be a status with no basis.
    The framework’s claim is that the grounding of necessity is the framework’s most important
contribution to the modal ontology. The space Ω (Book I, Principle 37.1) gives the extent of the
possible; the four kinds give the structure of the necessary within the extent. The two together
are the framework’s account of modality.

Principle 14.11 (The Grounding of Necessity). (T) The necessary, within the modal space Ω,
is not a primitive status; it is grounded in the four structures—form, essence, law, and good.
The grounding distinguishes the necessary from the merely possible, and the four structures are
the framework’s account of the structure of the necessary within the extent of the possible.

  The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the four kinds and by the analysis of the
modal space. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 37.1 and to Chapters 6 and 13.

14.6.3    The Grounding of Ω and the Grounding of Necessity
Book I’s Principle 37.2 states that Ω is grounded in God. The present chapter’s claim is that
necessity is grounded in the four structures, and that the four structures are themselves grounded
in God, through the framework’s Part VII (the Divine Ground). The two groundings are related:
the grounding of Ω is the grounding of the space; the grounding of necessity is the grounding of
the statuses within the space. The two are not the same; the first is the grounding of the extent,
the second is the grounding of the structure. Part VII will state the relation more fully.


14.7     The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Necessity
With the definitions of necessity and modality in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2
can be applied to the inquiry into necessity.

14.7.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Necessity
The fixed element of the inquiry into necessity is the necessary proposition or state of affairs,
held invariant while the inquiry explains the conditions of its necessity. The necessary is held
invariant as the subject of the inquiry—the status whose conditions the inquiry seeks to state.

14.7.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Necessity
The fluid element of the inquiry into necessity is the grounding relation between the necessary
and its ground—the relation by which the necessary is grounded in form, essence, law, or good.
The relation is the medium of the inquiry: it is what conveys the effect of the ground’s being
what it is to the necessary’s being what it is.

14.7.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Necessity
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into necessity is the rule by which the grounding operates—
the rule that explains how the form, essence, law, or good makes the necessary necessary. The
rule is the subject of §4, where the four kinds are analyzed; each kind states a different rule, and
the framework’s claim is that the rule is the general structure that the four kinds describe in
their own terms.
14.8. Necessity in Each Realm                                                                    165


14.7.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Necessity
The context of the inquiry into necessity is the realm in which the necessary is realized. The
seven realms of Book I are the contexts, and necessity takes a different form in each. The form
of necessity in each realm is the subject of §9.

14.7.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into necessity are stated in the following table.

                 Column                In the Inquiry into Necessity
                 Fixed element    The necessary, held invariant as the subject
                                  of the inquiry
                 Fluid element    The grounding relation between the neces-
                                  sary and its ground
                 Governing dynam- The rule by which the grounding operates
                 ics
                 Context          The realm in which the necessary is real-
                                  ized
   The table is the application of Chapter 2’s method to the inquiry into necessity. The
application is the chapter’s contribution to the book’s systematic character.


14.8     Necessity in Each Realm
Necessity takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the form,
one realm at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered at the
strength that the framework’s principles support.

14.8.1    The Material Manifestation
In the Material Manifestation, necessity takes the form of natural necessity—the necessity of the
physical laws. The laws of physics are the Material mode of the structural laws; the physical
necessity is the Material mode of the metaphysical necessity. The necessity holds within the
Material Manifestation, and it is the mode that Book I’s Principle 16.12 (causality) and 16.14
(discreteness) presuppose.

14.8.2    The Relational Manifestation
In the Relational Manifestation, necessity takes the form of meaning-necessity—the necessity of
the meaning laws. The laws of signification, recognition, and care are the Relational mode of
the structural laws; the meaning-necessity is the Relational mode of the metaphysical necessity.
The necessity holds within the Relational Manifestation, and it is the mode that Book I’s
Principle 16.9 (relationality) and 16.10 (contextuality) presuppose.

14.8.3    The Structural Determination
In the Structural Determination, necessity takes the form of logical necessity—the necessity of the
logical laws. The laws of logic are the Structural mode of the structural laws; the logical necessity
is the Structural mode of the metaphysical necessity. The necessity holds within the Structural
Determination, and it is the mode that Book I’s Principle 16.6 (universality) and 16.7 (necessity)
presuppose. The present chapter’s claim is that the necessity of the Structural Determination is
the most general mode of the metaphysical necessity, because the Structural Determination is
the realm of form and law.
166                                                            Chapter 14. Necessity and Modality


14.8.4    The First Determination
In the First Determination, necessity takes the form of pure unity. The First Determination has
no multiplicity, no change, no succession; its necessity is its unity, and its unity is its necessity.
The form is the limit case of the other forms: it is what necessity becomes when the multiplicity
is zero. The First Determination is necessary in the most radical sense: it cannot be otherwise,
because there is no alternative to it.

14.8.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, necessity takes the form of measure necessity— the necessity of the measure
laws. The laws of proportion, order, and harmony are the mode of the structural laws in the
Hub of Decree; the measure necessity is the mode of the metaphysical necessity.

14.8.6    The Hub of Signification
In the Hub of Signification, necessity takes the form of signification necessity—the necessity of the
signification laws. The laws of truthfulness, accuracy, and fidelity are the mode of the structural
laws in the Hub of Signification; the signification necessity is the mode of the metaphysical
necessity.

14.8.7    The Hub of Realization
In the Hub of Realization, necessity takes the form of realization necessity—the necessity of
the realization laws. The laws of proportion in realization, preservation of the realized, and
continuation of realization are the mode of the structural laws in the Hub of Realization; the
realization necessity is the mode of the metaphysical necessity.

The seven forms are stated in the following table.

14.9. Objections and Replies                                                                    167


14.9      Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: Quine showed that de re modality is unintelligible; the framework’s metaphysical
necessity is a relic of pre-Quinean metaphysics. The objection is that Quine’s critique of de re
modality—the argument that necessity in rebus is unintelligible because it depends on how the
thing is described—shows that the framework’s metaphysical necessity is not a coherent notion.
    Reply. The objection mistakes Quine’s critique for a refutation. Quine’s critique is an
argument, and like every argument it has premises. The premise is that necessity is a property of
propositions, and that de re necessity is a confused projection of de dicto necessity onto things.
The framework’s claim is that the premise is false: necessity is not a property of propositions
alone; it is a status that things have in virtue of their essence. The essence is what the necessity
is grounded in, and the essence is what the description describes—the description is not the
essence, and the necessity is not the description. The framework’s response is the rejection of
the premise, and the rejection is the framework’s distinction between the essence (Chapter 6)
and the description. The objection’s conclusion—that de re modality is unintelligible— does
not follow, because the framework’s notion of essence makes it intelligible. (The same objection
was addressed in Chapter 7, in the context of primitive thisness; the present chapter applies the
same response to necessity.)
    Objection 2: The four kinds of necessity are arbitrary. Why four, and not three or five? The
objection is that the four kinds are a convention, and a convention can be otherwise.
    Reply. The four kinds are not arbitrary. They are the kinds that the conversation of the
scene revealed, and they are the kinds that the framework’s principles require. The logical kind
is required by the form of the space of possibilities; the metaphysical kind by the essence; the
natural kind by the law; the normative kind by the good. The four kinds are the kinds that the
framework’s analyses of essence (Chapter 6), law (Chapter 13), and the good (Part VI) jointly
require. The objection mistakes the labels for a decorative classification; the labels are the book’s
contract with the reader, and the contract is not arbitrary.
    Objection 3: The definition of necessity is circular. The definition says that necessity is
the modal status of what cannot be otherwise; the “cannot be otherwise” is the definition of
necessity; and the definition is circular.
    Reply. The circularity is only apparent. The definition does not define the “cannot be
otherwise” in terms of necessity; it defines necessity in terms of the “cannot be otherwise,” and
the “cannot be otherwise” is the explanandum, not the explanans. The definition’s structure is:
“cannot be otherwise” (primitive) = necessity (the modal status). The primitive is the “cannot
be otherwise”; the definiendum is necessity. The four kinds are the four specifications of the
primitive; each kind specifies what the “cannot be otherwise” means. The objection mistakes the
primitive for the definiendum; the reply distinguishes them.


14.10       What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not prove that any particular proposition is necessary. It argues that
necessity is four kinds, grounded in four structures; the argument is (D) relative to Book I’s
Principle 16.7 and to Chapters 6 and 13, and it is offered at the strength that the principles
support.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the four kinds are exhaustive.
The four kinds are the ones the chapter identifies; whether a fifth kind is needed, or whether one
of the four can be derived from the others, is a question the chapter leaves open. The question is
marked (Q) in the chapter’s status table.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the structure of the good. The normative necessity is
168                                                        Chapter 14. Necessity and Modality


grounded in the good; the development of the good is the subject of Part VI. The present chapter
states that normative necessity is a distinct kind, and it leaves the development of the good to
Part VI.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the relation between necessity and God. The relation is the
subject of Part VII (the Divine Ground); the present chapter states the grounding of necessity in
the four structures, and it points to Part VII for the grounding of the four structures in God.

14.12      A Question for Reflection
Consider a “cannot” you know well—a logical “cannot,” a physical “cannot,” a metaphysical
“cannot,” a moral “cannot.” What kind of necessity does it express? What grounds it? And if the
necessity is grounded in essence, what would it mean for the essence to change? If the necessity
is grounded in law, what would it mean for the law to change? If the necessity is grounded in
the good, what would it mean for the good to change?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The necessity is four kinds, grounded
in four structures; the kinds are not reducible to one another, and the relation among them
is a relation of grounding. The reader who can state, for a “cannot” he knows, what kind of
necessity it expresses and what grounds it, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader
14.12. A Question for Reflection                                                             169


who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop
the difficulty further.

The next chapter analyzes the modal space: what is the space of possibilities, and how does it
relate to the four kinds of necessity? With the four kinds in place, the framework can state the
structure of the modal space as the space in which the kinds are distinguished. The analysis is
the subject of Chapter 15, which reconsiders Book I’s account of the modal space (Principle 37.1)
in the light of the present chapter’s distinction of the four kinds.

Chapter 15

The Modal Space Ω Derived

Scope
This chapter derives the modal space Ω from the governing dynamics of Book I. It does not
restate Book I’s account of Ω; it asks what kind of reality Ω must have, such that the governing
dynamics of Book I can be what they are. It argues that Ω is not a flat set of possible worlds,
nor a set of abstract propositions, but a stratified modal structure whose strata are the four
kinds of necessity derived in Chapter 14—logical, metaphysical, natural, and normative—and
whose reality is the reality of the essences and laws that ground the strata. It argues that the
grounding of Ω in God is not one relation but a family of analogous relations, each corresponding
to a stratum of Ω. It distinguishes Ω from the realms, from the actualization chain X, and from
the context of the whole; it states the relation between Ω and light; it states the four-column
structure of the inquiry into Ω; and it answers three standard objections, including the objection
from modal realism and the objection from the grounding of the possible.
    The chapter’s claims are metaphysical and structural. Where it speaks of “space,” “stratum,”
“grounding,” or “possible,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in
this chapter and by the framework of Book I.

     Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given the governing dynamics
     of Book I (Definition 6.3), the rules of the realms (Chapters 16 and 17), the principle
     that the rules are structural constraints (Principle 13.1), and the openness of relations
     (Principle 11.1). It also takes as given the four kinds of necessity derived in Chapter 14
     of the present book. It does not restate these; it asks what they presuppose in the order
     of being. The derivation is stated in §15.3, and the chapter’s principal contribution is
     the unpacking of Ω’s internal structure and of its grounding relation.


15.1      A Scene: The Library at Night
Consider a library at night. The shelves are full; the lights are off; the building is closed. The
books are there—their pages, their words, their arguments—but no one is reading them. Now
consider a scholar who enters in the morning, takes a book from the shelf, and reads it. Something
has changed: the book is now read, and the reading is an event in the library’s history. But
what has not changed is the book: its words, its arguments, its structure were there before the
reading, and they remain after.
    The scene is not about libraries in particular. It is about a general structure, and the structure
is this. The possible is like the library at night: it is there, fully formed, before any reading, and
the actualization is like the scholar’s reading: it selects one book from the shelf and brings it into
the light. The possible is not created by the reading; the possible is what the reading selects.
The reading is an event; the possible is a condition of the event.
172                                                      Chapter 15. The Modal Space Ω Derived


     Now consider a harder case. Consider a library whose catalogue is itself a book in the library.
The catalogue lists every book on the shelves; but the catalogue is one of the books, and so it
must list itself. When it lists itself, the listing is a new entry, and the catalogue is no longer the
catalogue it was—it is a catalogue that lists itself. The catalogue cannot be complete, because
every attempt to complete it generates a new entry.
     The scene poses the question of the chapter. What must the possible be, such that the
governing dynamics of Book I can be what they are? What kind of reality must Ω have? Is
it a set of concrete possible worlds (as the modal realist says), a set of abstract propositions
(as some propositionalists say), or a structure of possible configurations (as the framework will
argue)? Is it flat, or does it have internal structure? And what is the relation between Ω and the
actualization chain X—is the actualization a selection from Ω, or a creation of new possibilities?
     The chapter’s answer is: Ω is not flat and not a set of concrete worlds; it is a stratified modal
structure whose strata are the four kinds of necessity derived in Chapter 14, and whose reality is
the reality of the essences and laws that ground the strata. The actualization is a selection from
Ω, not a creation of new possibilities—but the selection does not exhaust Ω, and the possible
remains possible after the selection. The chapter’s task is to state this structure, to distinguish
it from the standard accounts, and to show that it is what Book I’s governing dynamics require
in the order of being.


15.2      The Question
The governing dynamics of Book I is the rule that explains how fluid elements affect fixed
elements (Definition 6.3). The rules of the realms are the structural constraints of the realms’
modes of existence (Principle 13.1). The rules are necessary: they hold in every case to which
they apply, not merely in the cases that have been observed (Chapter 14, §??).
     The present chapter asks: what must be the case in reality, such that the rules can be
necessary? What must the possible be, such that the rules can hold in every case to which they
apply? The framework’s answer is: the modal space Ω, the space of all possibilities, within which
the rules hold and from which the actual is selected. The chapter asks what kind of reality Ω
must have.
     The question has three aspects.
     The first aspect: what kind of reality does Ω have? The chapter must distinguish three
standard accounts: modal realism (Ω is a set of concrete possible worlds), propositionalism (Ω is
a set of abstract propositions), and configurationalism (Ω is a structure of possible configurations
of essences and laws). The chapter argues for the third, as the account that Book I’s governing
dynamics requires.
     The second aspect: what is Ω’s internal structure? The chapter must state whether Ω is flat
(all possibilities are on the same level) or stratified (some possibilities are grounded in others, and
the grounding gives Ω an internal structure). The chapter argues for the second, and identifies
the strata with the four kinds of necessity of Chapter 14.
     The third aspect: what is the structure of Ω’s grounding? The chapter must state how Ω
depends on God, as the framework’s Part VI will state. The chapter argues that the grounding
is not one relation but a family of analogous relations, each corresponding to a stratum of Ω.
     The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: Ω is a
stratified modal structure derived from the governing dynamics; its strata are the four kinds
of necessity; its grounding in God is a family of analogous relations. The derivation deepens
Book I’s account; it does not revise it.
15.3. The Derivation of Ω                                                                         173


15.3      The Derivation of Ω
15.3.1    Step 1: The Rules Presuppose Necessity
The rules of the realms are structural constraints (Principle 13.1). For the rules to be constraints,
they must hold in every case to which they apply: they must be necessary, not merely regular.
A regularity is a pattern that happens to hold; a constraint is a pattern that must hold. The
necessity is what distinguishes a rule from a mere regularity.
    The step is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 13.1 and to Chapter 14’s derivation of meta-
physical necessity. The claim is not that the rules are necessary in the sense of logical necessity;
the claim is that they are necessary in the sense of metaphysical necessity—necessary in virtue
of the essences of the realms.

15.3.2    Step 2: Necessity Presupposes a Space of Possibilities
For the rules to be necessary, there must be a space of possibilities within which they hold. The
necessity is the necessity of a rule that holds in every possible case; the "possible case" is a case
within the space of possibilities. The space is what the necessity presupposes: without the space,
the necessity would have nothing to range over.
    The step is (D) relative to Chapter 14’s derivation of metaphysical necessity. The claim is
not that the space is a separate entity; the claim is that the space is the condition of possibility
of the necessity. The space is Ω.

15.3.3    Step 3: The Space Is the Modal Space
The space that the necessity presupposes is what the chapter calls the modal space Ω: the space
of all possibilities, within which the rules of the realms hold and from which the actual is selected.
The identification is not arbitrary: it is the identification of the space with the notion that Book I
introduced as the totality of possibilities (Principle 11.1), stated in the framework’s vocabulary.
    The step is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the notion of necessity and by the comparison
with Book I’s notion of Ω. It is relative to the chapter’s definition of Ω, and it is assessable by
the definition’s adequacy.

15.3.4    The Result of the Derivation
The three steps yield the derivation: the rules of the realms are necessary, the necessity presupposes
a space of possibilities, and the space is the modal space Ω. The derivation is (D) throughout: it
is the demonstration that the governing dynamics of Book I presupposes Ω.

Principle 15.1 (The Modal Space as the Condition of Necessity). (D) The modal space Ω is
the condition of possibility of the necessity of the rules of the realms. Without Ω, the rules could
not be necessary; with Ω, the rules are necessary within the space of possibilities. The principle
is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principle 13.1 and on Chapter 14’s derivation of
metaphysical necessity.


15.4      The Ontological Status of Ω
15.4.1    The Three Standard Accounts
Three accounts of the ontological status of Ω are standard in the contemporary debate.
    Modal realism (Lewis). Ω is a set of concrete possible worlds. Each world is a spatiotemporal
system, as concrete as the actual world, and the actual world is one of them. The possible worlds
are not abstract; they are as real as the actual. The theory’s virtue is that it takes the reality of
174                                                      Chapter 15. The Modal Space Ω Derived


the possible seriously. Its difficulty is that it posits an enormous plurality of concrete worlds,
and that it must explain what makes one world actual rather than another.
    Propositionalism (Plantinga, Adams). Ω is a set of abstract propositions. A possible world is
a maximal consistent proposition; the actual world is the maximal consistent proposition that is
true. The theory’s virtue is that it avoids the plurality of concrete worlds. Its difficulty is that it
must explain what makes a proposition true, and that it must explain how abstract propositions
can be about concrete things.
    Configurationalism (the framework). Ω is a structure of possible configurations of essences
and laws. A possibility is a configuration of essences (Chapter 6) and laws (Chapter 13); the
space of possibilities is the space of all configurations that the essences and laws admit. The
theory’s virtue is that it grounds the possible in the essences and laws that the framework has
already derived. Its difficulty is that it must explain what a configuration is, and that it must
explain how the space of configurations is related to the actual.

15.4.2    The Framework’s Position
The framework adopts configurationalism, and the adoption is the chapter’s contribution.

Principle 15.2 (The Framework’s Position on Ω). (D) Ω is a structure of possible configurations
of essences and laws: a possibility is a configuration of essences (Chapter 6) and laws (Chapter 13),
and the space of possibilities is the space of all configurations that the essences and laws admit.
The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Principle 11.1 (the openness of
relations) and on the framework’s accounts of essence and law.

    The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the specification of what Book I’s
governing dynamics requires, given the framework’s accounts of essence and law. The specification
has three components.
    The first component: essences are the "matter" of Ω. Essences are what the possible is about;
a possibility is a way the essences can be configured. The essence of water is the "matter" of the
possibility that water is H2 O; the essence of a triangle is the "matter" of the possibility that a
triangle has three sides.
    The second component: laws are the "form" of Ω. Laws are what constrains the configurations;
a possibility is a configuration that the laws admit. The law of non-contradiction is the "form" of
the possibility that a proposition is not both true and false; the law of combustion is the "form"
of the possibility that fire ignites wood.
    The third component: configurations are the "content" of Ω. A configuration is a specific
arrangement of essences and laws; a possibility is a configuration that is admitted by the laws.
The configuration is what the possible is—the specific way that the essences and laws are
arranged.
    The three components together yield the framework’s account. Ω is not a set of concrete
worlds (contra Lewis); it is not a set of abstract propositions (contra Plantinga); it is a structure
of configurations of essences and laws. The structure is what the possible is; the essences and
laws are what ground the structure; the configurations are what the structure contains.

15.4.3    The Relation to Book I’s Principle 11.1
The framework’s position is the specification of Book I’s Principle 11.1, not a revision of it.
Book I stated that the contexts are not finite in number; the framework states what the contexts
are contexts of. Book I stated that every manifestation can become a fixed element of a further
context; the framework states what makes the manifestation possible—the configuration of
essences and laws. Book I stated that no possibility is created by an action; the framework states
why—the possibility is a configuration of essences and laws, and the configuration is not created
by the action, because the essences and laws are not created by the action.
15.5. The Internal Structure of Ω                                                                175


   The specification is the chapter’s contribution to the framework’s modal ontology. It makes
Ω a structure that the framework can analyze, rather than a bare posit. The analysis is what
the later sections of the chapter will develop.


15.5      The Internal Structure of Ω
15.5.1    Flat or Stratified?
The question of Ω’s internal structure is whether Ω is flat (all possibilities are on the same level)
or stratified (some possibilities are grounded in others, and the grounding gives Ω an internal
structure). The standard accounts differ: modal realism treats Ω as a set of concrete worlds,
and a set has no internal structure beyond membership; propositionalism treats Ω as a set of
propositions, and a set of propositions has only the structure of logical relations. The framework
argues for stratification.
    The argument is the following. Chapter 14 derived four kinds of necessity—logical, metaphys-
ical, natural, and normative. The four kinds are not the same; each is grounded in a different
structure (form, essence, law, good). If Ω were flat, the four kinds would be indistinguishable
within it—the logical necessary, the metaphysical necessary, the natural necessary, and the
normative necessary would be on the same level, and the distinctions of Chapter 14 would be
lost. Since the distinctions are real (Chapter 14), Ω must be stratified: the four kinds occupy
different strata, and the strata are ordered by grounding.
Principle 15.3 (The Stratification of Ω). (T) Ω is not flat; it is stratified, and the strata are the
four kinds of necessity of Chapter 14. The logical stratum is the most general; the metaphysical
stratum is grounded in essence; the natural stratum is grounded in law; the normative stratum
is grounded in the good. The strata are ordered by grounding: the logical stratum underlies the
metaphysical, the metaphysical underlies the natural, and the normative is posterior to the other
three.
   The principle is (T): it is argued by the distinction of the four kinds (Chapter 14) and
by the requirement that the distinctions be preserved within Ω. It is (D) relative to Book I’s
Principle 11.1 and to Chapter 14.

15.5.2    The Strata
The four strata are stated in the following table.

              Stratum            What It Contains            What Grounds It
              Logical            The logically possible      The form of propositions
              Metaphysical       The metaphysically pos-     The essences of things
                                 sible
              Natural            The naturally possible      The laws of the realms
              Normative          The normatively possi-      The structure of the
                                 ble                         good

    The table is the chapter’s map of the strata. Each stratum contains the possibilities of
the corresponding kind; each stratum is grounded in the corresponding structure. The strata
are nested: the metaphysical stratum is within the logical stratum (every metaphysically
possible proposition is logically possible, but not conversely); the natural stratum is within the
metaphysical stratum (every naturally possible state of affairs is metaphysically possible, but
not conversely); the normative stratum is posterior to the other three (the normatively possible
is what is compatible with the good, and the good operates within the space the other three
define).
176                                                    Chapter 15. The Modal Space Ω Derived


15.5.3    The Stratification and the Possible
The stratification has a consequence for the notion of the possible: the possible is not a single
modal status; it is four, corresponding to the four strata. The logically possible is what is
not logically excluded; the metaphysically possible is what is not metaphysically excluded; the
naturally possible is what is not naturally excluded; the normatively possible is what is not
normatively excluded. The four are nested, and the nesting is what gives Ω its internal structure.
   The consequence is the chapter’s contribution to the modal ontology. Book I stated that the
contexts are not finite in number; the present chapter states that the possibilities are not all of
one kind—they are four kinds, and the four kinds structure Ω.


15.6     The Grounding of Ω in God
15.6.1    The Question of the Grounding
The framework’s Part VI will state that the divine ground is the metaphysical condition of the
realms (Chapter 26). The present section asks: what is the structure of Ω’s grounding in God?
Is it one relation, or a family of analogous relations?
    Book I’s Chapter 34 stated the question: "What is the precise structure of the grounding of
Ω and of the context of the whole in God: one relation or a family of analogous relations?" The
present section answers the question: a family of analogous relations.

15.6.2    The Family of Analogous Relations
The argument for the answer is the following. The grounding of Ω in God is the grounding of
a stratified structure. Each stratum is grounded in a different structure (form, essence, law,
good), and each structure is grounded in God through a different mode. The grounding of
the logical stratum is the grounding of the form of propositions in God; the grounding of the
metaphysical stratum is the grounding of essences in God; the grounding of the natural stratum
is the grounding of laws in God; the grounding of the normative stratum is the grounding of the
good in God. The four groundings are not the same; they are analogous—each is a mode of the
grounding relation, and the modes are related by analogy, not by identity.
Principle 15.4 (The Grounding of Ω). (D) The grounding of Ω in God is not one relation
but a family of analogous relations, each corresponding to a stratum of Ω: the logical stratum
is grounded in God through the form of propositions; the metaphysical stratum through the
essences of things; the natural stratum through the laws of the realms; the normative stratum
through the good. The four groundings are modes of one grounding relation, and the modes are
related by analogy, not by identity. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s
Principle 4.1 (structure, not telos) and on the framework’s accounts of essence (Chapter 6), law
(Chapter 13), and the good (Chapter 25).
   The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the answer to Book I’s Q4, and the
answer is the framework’s specification of what the divine ground requires. The specification is
the chapter’s principal contribution to the debate on the grounding of the possible.

15.6.3    The Relation to the Context of the Whole
The framework’s Chapter 20 states that the context of the whole is the encompassing order in
which all the realms stand. The present section states the relation between Ω and the context of
the whole.
    The relation is the following. The context of the whole is the encompassing order of the
realms; Ω is the space of possibilities from which the realms are actualized. The two are not
the same: the context of the whole is the order, and Ω is the space. The context of the whole is
15.7. Ω and Light                                                                                   177


what the realms are in; Ω is what the realms are selected from. The two are related: both are
derived from the framework, both are grounded in God, and the relation between them is the
relation between the order of actualization and the space of actualization.
    The relation is stated in the following principle.
Principle 15.5 (The Relation Between Ω and the Context of the Whole). (E) Ω is the space of
possibilities from which the realms are actualized; the context of the whole is the encompassing
order in which the realms are situated. The two are distinct—the space and the order—and they
are related as the condition of actualization and the order of actualization. Both are derived
from the framework, and both are grounded in God.
    The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the framework’s
derivation supports. The estimate is the framework’s contribution to the relation between the
modal order and the ontological order.


15.7      Ω and Light
The chapter’s final contribution is the statement of the relation between Ω and light (Book I,
Definition 15.1, and Chapter 11 of the present book).

15.7.1     The Relation
Ω is the space of possibilities; light is the medium through which the possibilities are actualized.
The two are distinct: Ω is the what of the possible; light is the how of the actualization. The
distinction is the distinction between the space and the medium: Ω is the space of configurations;
light is the condition under which a configuration is actualized.
    The relation is the following. The actualization of a possibility is the selection of a configuration
from Ω and the realization of the configuration in a realm. The selection is the work of fundamental
self-awareness (Book I, Chapter 20); the realization is the work of light. The light is the medium
through which the selected configuration is realized; the configuration is what the light realizes.
The two are related as the medium and the realized: light is the how, the configuration is the
what.

15.7.2     The Analogous Grounding
The relation between Ω and light extends to the grounding. Both Ω and light are derived from
the framework (Chapter 11 for light, the present chapter for Ω), and both are grounded in God.
The two groundings are analogous modes of the same grounding relation. Ω is grounded in God
as the space of possibilities; light is grounded in God as the medium of actualization. The two
are not the same grounding; they are analogous modes, and the analogy is the analogy between
the space and the medium—the condition of possibility and the condition of actualization.
    The relation is stated in the following principle.
Principle 15.6 (The Relation Between Ω and Light). (D) Ω and light are related as the space
of possibilities and the medium of actualization: Ω is the what of the possible; light is the how of
the actualization. Both are derived from the framework, and both are grounded in God, and
the two groundings are analogous modes of the same grounding relation. The principle is (D)
because its truth depends on Book I’s Definition 15.1 (epistemic light) and on Chapter 11 of the
present book.
    The principle is (D): it is the framework’s contribution to the relation between the modal
order and the medium of actualization. It is the answer to Book I’s Q3: "What is the conceptual
relation between light and expression?" The answer: the relation is analogous to the relation
between the space and the medium.

15.8     The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Ω
With the derivation of Ω’s status, structure, and grounding in place, the four-column method of
Chapter 2 can be applied to the inquiry into Ω.

15.8.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Ω
The fixed element of the inquiry into Ω is Ω itself, held invariant while the inquiry explains the
conditions of its being. The Ω is held invariant as the subject of the inquiry—the space whose
conditions the inquiry seeks to state.

15.8.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Ω
The fluid element of the inquiry into Ω is the relation between Ω and the strata—the relation by
which the strata are the strata of Ω, and by which Ω is what the strata structure. The relation
is the medium of the inquiry: it is what conveys the effect of the strata’s being what they are to
Ω’s being what it is.

15.8.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Ω
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into Ω is the rule by which the strata are ordered—the
rule that explains how the four kinds of necessity are related, and under what conditions the
grounding of each stratum operates. The rule is the subject of §15.5 and §15.6.

15.8.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Ω
The context of the inquiry into Ω is the framework of Book I, in which the realms are real and
the rules are necessary. The context is the frame in which the inquiry is posed, and it is what
makes the inquiry an inquiry into Ω, not an inquiry in general.

Ω takes a different form in each of the seven realms. The present section states the form, one

In the First Determination, Ω takes the form of pure unity. The First Determination has no
multiplicity, no change, no succession; its space is its unity, and its unity is its space. The form
is the limit case of the other forms: it is what Ω becomes when the multiplicity is zero.

15.9.5    The Hub of Decree
In the Hub of Decree, Ω takes the form of the space of apportioning configurations—the

In the Hub of Realization, Ω takes the form of the space of realization configurations—the
configurations of actualization that the realization admits. The space is the mode of the general
Ω in the Hub of Realization.

15.10      Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: The framework’s configurationalism is a form of modal realism. The objection
is that configurationalism treats the possible as real, and that any realism about the possible is a
form of modal realism (Lewis’s view). The framework, the objection concludes, has not escaped
the difficulties of modal realism.
    Reply. The objection confuses realism about the possible with realism about concrete possible
worlds. Modal realism is the view that possible worlds are concrete spatiotemporal systems
as real as the actual world. The framework’s configurationalism is the view that possibilities
are configurations of essences and laws—not concrete worlds, not abstract propositions, but
structures of essences and laws. The configurations are real, but their reality is the reality of the
essences and laws that ground them; they are not a plurality of concrete worlds. The objection
mistakes the realism of the framework for the realism of Lewis; the reply distinguishes them.
    Objection 2: The stratification of Ω is arbitrary. Why four strata, and not three or five? The
objection is that the four strata are a convention, and a convention can be otherwise.
    Reply. The four strata are not arbitrary. They are the four kinds of necessity of Chapter 14,
and the four kinds are the kinds that the framework’s analyses of essence, law, and the good jointly
require. The logical kind is required by the form of the space of possibilities; the metaphysical
kind by essence; the natural kind by law; the normative kind by the good. The four strata
are the kinds that the framework’s analyses require, and the requirement is not a convention.
The objection mistakes the labels for a decorative classification; the labels are the framework’s
structure, and the structure is not arbitrary.
    Objection 3: The grounding of Ω in God is unintelligible. The objection is that the grounding
of a space of possibilities in God is unintelligible: how can a space be grounded in a being? The
framework, the objection concludes, has not explained what grounding is.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the grounding relation for a spatial relation. The grounding is
not a spatial containment; it is a relation of ontological dependence—the space of possibilities is
what it is because God is what God is. The grounding of Ω in God is the same kind of relation as
the grounding of the realms in God (Chapter 26), and the grounding of the realms is a relation
of ontological dependence, not of spatial containment. The objection mistakes the ontological
relation for a spatial relation; the reply distinguishes them.


15.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
15.12. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                181


    First, the chapter does not prove that Ω is real. It derives Ω from the governing dynamics
of Book I; the derivation is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 13.1 and to Chapter 14, and it is
offered at the strength that the principles support.
    Second, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the four strata are exhaustive.
The four strata are the kinds that the framework’s analyses require; whether a fifth stratum is
needed, or whether one of the four can be derived from the others, is a question the chapter
leaves open. The question is marked (Q) in the chapter’s status table.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the structure of the good. The normative stratum is
grounded in the good; the development of the good is the subject of Part VII. The present
chapter states that the normative stratum is a distinct stratum, and it leaves the development of
the good to Part VII.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the relation between Ω and the actualization chain X
beyond what the derivation states. The relation is the selection of a configuration from Ω; the
structure of the selection is the subject of Chapter 29. The full account is deferred.

15.13      A Question for Reflection
Consider a possibility you know well—a possibility for your life, for a project, for a relationship.
What kind of possibility is it? Is it logically possible, metaphysically possible, naturally possible,
or normatively possible? Is the possibility grounded in your essence, in the laws of the situation,
in the good, or in all three? And if the possibility is real, what does its reality depend on?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The possibility is not a bare modal status;
it is a stratified configuration of essences and laws, and its reality is the reality of the essences
and laws that ground it. The reader who can state, for a possibility he knows, what kind of
possibility it is and what grounds it, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who
cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the
difficulty further.

governs its possibilities.
