Chapter 16

The Governing Dynamics of Each
Realm

Scope. This chapter synthesizes the analyses of Chapters 13, 14, and 15 into a single account
of the governing dynamics of the seven realms. It states the triad of governing dynamics—law,
necessity, and modal space—as a structural whole, and it states the realm-dependent structure of
the triad: the pattern of collapse, partial coincidence, and full distinction that the triad exhibits
across the seven realms. It argues that the pattern is not accidental, but tracks the ontological
architecture of Book I; it states the governing dynamics of each realm as a single structure (rather
than as three separate analyses); it states the relation between the governing-dynamics triad and
the fluid triad of Part III; and it states what Part IV has and has not established. Its claims
are metaphysical and structural; where it speaks of “triad,” “pattern,” “collapse,” “coincidence,”
“distinction,” or “modal space,” these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions
in this chapter and by the analyses of the preceding three chapters.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given the definitions and principles that
Chapters 13, 14, and 15 established as the metaphysical consequents of Book I’s rules of the
realms (Principles 16.1 to 17.10), of Book I’s necessity rule (Principle 16.7), and of Book I’s modal
space Ω (Principle 37.1, C12). It also takes as given Book I’s Principle 7.1 (C3, independent
reality of the realms) and Principle 27.1 (C9, category-relative predication). It does not reargue
those chapters; it asks what the three analyses, taken together, establish, and it states the
structural pattern that the three exhibit across the seven realms.


16.1      A Scene
Consider a constitutional court on the morning of a difficult decision. The court has before it a
question that the constitution does not explicitly answer: whether a certain exercise of state
power is permitted. Three things are present to the justices, and each is different.
    The first is the text of the constitution. The constitution contains clauses, principles, amend-
ments, a history of interpretation. The text is what the court must apply; it is the pattern within
which the court’s decision must fall. The text is the law, in the framework’s sense: it is the
structural pattern that the decision must follow.
    The second is the binding force of the constitution. The court does not merely consult the
constitution; it is bound by it. The binding force is the necessity of the constitution: the clauses
are not suggestions, they are requirements; the court cannot decide as if the clauses did not exist.
The binding force is the modal status of the constitution—the “cannot be otherwise” that the
court acknowledges.
    The third is the space of possible interpretations. The constitution admits many readings,
and the court must choose among them. The space of readings is the modal space of the
184                                       Chapter 16. The Governing Dynamics of Each Realm


constitution—the space within which the court’s decision must fall. The space is not the text;
the text is what is interpreted; the space is the range of interpretations the text admits.
    Three things, and each is different. The text is the law; the binding force is the necessity; the
space of readings is the modal space. But in other cases, the three seem to be one. Consider a
case in which the constitution is absolutely clear—a clause that admits only one reading, that is
binding without qualification, and that leaves no room for interpretation. In such a case, the
text, the binding force, and the space of readings collapse into one: the law is its own necessity,
and its necessity exhausts the space.
    Now consider a harder case. Consider a case in which the constitution is silent—a question the
text does not address, and that the court must nevertheless decide. In such a case, the text fails,
but the binding force does not: the court is bound to decide within the constitution’s principles,
even when the text is silent. The space of readings is not the space of the text’s readings; it is
the space of the principles’ implications. The three are distinct, and their distinctness is what
the hard case reveals.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. The governing triad—law, necessity, modal
space—is collapsed in the clear case, distinct in the hard case, and partially coincident in the
ordinary case. What is the pattern of the triad’s articulation across the seven realms? And what
does the pattern tell us about the governing dynamics of each realm?


16.2      The Question
The question of the chapter is: what is the structure of the triad of governing dynamics, and
how does the structure vary across the seven realms?
    The question is not the same as the questions of Chapters 13, 14, and 15. Each of those
chapters analyzed one element of the triad: Chapter 13 analyzed law, Chapter 14 analyzed
necessity, Chapter 15 analyzed the modal space. Each analysis was of one element, in all seven
realms, but the analysis was organized around the element, not around the realm. The present
chapter inverts the organization: it asks what the triad, as a whole, looks like in each realm, and
what the variation across realms tells us about the realms themselves.
    The inversion is the chapter’s principal contribution. It is not a summary of the three preceding
chapters; it is a reorganization of their results into a single structure, and the reorganization
reveals something that the three analyses, taken separately, did not reveal: the pattern of collapse,
partial coincidence, and full distinction.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the triad of governing dynamics? The chapter must state the triad as
a structural whole—not as three separate elements, but as one structure with three components.
The statement is the chapter’s contribution to the systematic character of Part IV.
    The second aspect: what is the realm-dependent structure of the triad? The chapter must
state the pattern of variation across the seven realms. The pattern is the chapter’s principal
contribution, because it is what makes the synthesis a genuine chapter, not a summary.
    The third aspect: what is the relation between the governing-dynamics triad and the fluid triad
of Part III? The chapter must state the relation between the triad of governing dynamics and the
triad of fluid elements (Chapter 12, Definition 12.1). The relation is the chapter’s contribution
to the framework’s overall architecture, because it shows how the two triads together make the
seven realms a single system.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: the
governing triad is a structural whole; its structure varies across the seven realms according to
a pattern of collapse, partial coincidence, and full distinction; and the variation is what makes
the realms structurally distinct at the level of governing dynamics, in a way that mirrors and
completes the distinctions at the level of fixed and fluid elements.
16.3. The Triad of Governing Dynamics                                                           185


16.3      The Triad of Governing Dynamics
16.3.1    The Triad
Definition 16.1 (The Triad of Governing Dynamics). (A) The triad of governing dynamics is the
structure of law, necessity, and modal space, taken together. Law is the structural pattern that
grounds the regularity, necessity, and formality of a realm’s rules (Chapter 13, Definition 13.1);
necessity is the modal status of what cannot be otherwise, and the four kinds of necessity are
logical, metaphysical, natural, and normative (Chapter 14, Definition 14.2); and the modal space
Ω is the stratified space of configurations of essences and laws (Chapter 15, Principle ??). The
triad is the structure of the governing dynamics of Book I’s framework, and it is the metaphysical
content of the third column.

    The definition states the triad as a structural whole. The three elements are not three
separate things; they are three aspects of one structure—the structure of the governing dynamics.
The law is the pattern; the necessity is the modal status of the pattern; the modal space is the
extent within which the pattern and its necessity operate.
    The triad is not a list. It is a structure, and the structure is what the definition captures.
The three elements are related, and the relation is a three-level hierarchy: the modal space Ω
is the extent; the law is the pattern within the extent; the necessity is the modal status of the
pattern. The hierarchy is what distinguishes the governing triad from the fixed triad of Part II
(whose elements are peers) and from the fluid triad of Part III (whose elements are a two-level
hierarchy, with light as the condition of causation and relation).
    The hierarchy has three levels, and the three levels are the three elements of the triad. The
modal space is the most general; the law is the specific pattern within the space; the necessity
is the modal status of the pattern. The three are related by grounding: the space grounds the
possibility of the pattern; the pattern grounds the necessity of its instances; the necessity is what
the pattern is, in the space.

16.3.2    The Triad and the Four Columns
The triad is the metaphysical content of the governing dynamics of Book I’s framework. It
is not a fifth column; it is the content that fills the third column. The distinction is the
analytical/ontological distinction of Chapter 2: the governing dynamics is the analytical role;
the triad is the ontological content that the role presupposes.
    The triad relates to the other three columns as follows. The law is the rule by which the fluid
elements (Part III) affect the fixed elements (Part II); the necessity is the modal force of the
rule; the modal space is the extent within which the rule operates. The fixed elements are what
the law governs; the fluid elements are what the law governs through; the context (Chapter 17)
is the realm in which the triad is realized. The four columns and the governing triad are not the
same structure; they are related structures, and the relation is what the later parts of Book II
will state.

16.3.3    The Triad and the Fluid Triad
The governing triad is not the same as the fluid triad (Chapter 12, Definition 12.1). The fluid
triad is the structure of light, causation, and relation; the governing triad is the structure of
law, necessity, and modal space. The two are related: the fluid triad is what the governing triad
governs; the governing triad is what governs the fluid triad. The two triads together make the
seven realms a single system, and the relation between the two is the subject of §7.
186                                         Chapter 16. The Governing Dynamics of Each Realm


16.4      The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Triad
16.4.1    The Three Patterns
The governing triad exhibits three patterns of articulation across the seven realms.
     The pattern of collapse. In the First Determination, the three elements of the triad collapse
into unity. The First Determination has no multiplicity, no change, no succession (Book I,
Definition 7.5); its law is its unity, its necessity is its unity, its modal space is its unity. The
three are not distinct, because there is no multiplicity in the First Determination—no pattern to
be distinguished from the space, no necessity to be distinguished from the pattern. The First
Determination is the limit case of the triad: it is what the triad becomes when the multiplicity is
zero.
     The pattern of partial coincidence. In the barzakhic realms (the Hubs of Decree, Signification,
and Realization), law and necessity coincide, and the modal space distinguishes as the space
of the passage. The Hub of Decree’s law is its measure (proportion, order, harmony), and its
necessity is its measure—the measure is necessary just because it is what the passage is. The
Hub of Signification’s law is its signification (truthfulness, accuracy, fidelity), and its necessity is
its signification—the signification is necessary just because it is what the passage is. The Hub
of Realization’s law is its actualization (proportion in realization, preservation, continuation),
and its necessity is its actualization—the actualization is necessary just because it is what the
passage is. The coincidence is not an accident; it is a feature of the barzakhic mode of existence.
The barzakhic realm is a level whose mode of existence includes mediating, transforming, or
regulating relations between other realms (Book I, Definition 8.1); its being is its passage, and
its law and necessity are the same, because the passage is its own law and its own necessity. The
modal space distinguishes: the modal space is the space of the passage’s possibility—the range
of configurations that the passage admits.
     The pattern of full distinction. In the fundamental realms of multiplicity (the Structural
Determination, the Relational Manifestation, and the Material Manifestation), the three elements
of the triad are fully distinguished. The law is the pattern; the necessity is the modal status of
the pattern; the modal space is the extent within which the pattern and its necessity operate.
The three are distinct, and the distinction is what makes the realm a realm of multiplicity: the
realm has many things, and the things are governed by patterns whose modal status and whose
space are distinct from the patterns themselves.

16.4.2    The Pattern as a Principle
The three patterns are not accidental; they are the articulation of a single principle, and the
principle is the chapter’s principal contribution.

Principle 16.2 (The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Governing Triad). (E) The triad of
governing dynamics is articulated differently in each realm, and the articulation is a function
of the realm’s position in the ontological architecture. In the First Determination, the triad
collapses into unity. In the barzakhic realms, law and necessity coincide in the passage, and the
modal space distinguishes as the space of the passage. In the fundamental realms of multiplicity,
the triad is fully distinguished. The pattern tracks the realm’s mode of existence: the more a
realm is a realm of passage, the more its law and necessity coincide; the more a realm is a realm
of multiplicity, the more the triad is articulated.

    The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the analysis of
the seven realms supports. Its justification is that the pattern is visible in the seven realms and
that a different pattern would do the same explanatory work less well. Its refutation would be
a realm whose articulation does not fit the pattern, or a different pattern that does the same
explanatory work as well or better.
16.5. The Governing Dynamics of the Seven Realms                                                   187


16.4.3     The Pattern and Book I
The pattern is not a new principle; it is the metaphysical articulation of Book I’s Principle 7.1
(C3, independent reality of the realms) and of Book I’s Principle 27.1 (C9, category-relative
predication). The first states that the realms are independently real, with modes of existence of
their own; the second states that metaphysical predicates are defined relative to a realm. The
pattern is the articulation of the two: the governing triad’s structure is relative to the realm, and
the relativity is what makes the realms independently real at the level of governing dynamics.
    The pattern is (D) relative to Book I’s Principles 7.1 and 27.1. The chapter’s claim is not
that the pattern is a new principle; the claim is that the pattern is what Book I’s principles
require in the order of being, and the requirement is a metaphysical consequent of the principles.

16.4.4     The Pattern and the Patterns of Parts II and III
The governing pattern is not the same as the fixed pattern (Chapter 8, Principle 8.2) or the
fluid pattern (Chapter 12, Principle 12.2). The fixed pattern’s barzakhic case has substance and
essence coinciding, and thisness distinguishing. The fluid pattern’s barzakhic case has causation
and relation coinciding, and light distinguishing. The governing pattern’s barzakhic case has law
and necessity coinciding, and the modal space distinguishing.
    The three patterns are parallel but not identical. The parallel is that in each, the barzakhic
case has two elements coinciding and one distinguishing. The difference is which two coincide:
in the fixed pattern, the grounds coincide (substance and essence); in the fluid pattern, the
operations coincide (causation and relation); in the governing pattern, the pattern and its modal
status coincide (law and necessity). The three patterns together are the framework’s architecture
of the barzakhic mode of existence: the barzakhic realm is a passage in which the ground is the
operation, and the pattern is its necessity. The relation among the three patterns is the subject
of §7.


16.5      The Governing Dynamics of the Seven Realms
With the pattern in place, the governing dynamics of each realm can be stated as a single
structure, rather than as three separate analyses. The statements are (E) claims, offered at the
strength that the framework’s principles support.

16.5.1     The First Determination
The governing dynamics of the First Determination is pure unity, in which law, necessity, and
modal space collapse. The realm is what it is; its pattern is its unity; its necessity is its unity; its
space is its unity. The collapse is the limit case of the triad, and it is what the triad becomes
when the multiplicity is zero. The First Determination’s four rules (invariance, atemporality,
indivisibility, unity) are all modes of the unity that the law, the necessity, and the modal space
are.

16.5.2     The Hub of Decree
The governing dynamics of the Hub of Decree is the apportioning, in which law and necessity
coincide and the modal space distinguishes. The realm’s law is its measure (proportion, order,
harmony); its necessity is its measure (the measure is necessary just because it is what the passage
is); its modal space is the space of the apportioning’s possibility (the range of configurations
that the apportioning admits). The coincidence is the barzakhic pattern.
188                                          Chapter 16. The Governing Dynamics of Each Realm


16.5.3     The Structural Determination
The governing dynamics of the Structural Determination is the law that entails, in which the three
elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s law is the logical pattern (universality, necessity,
formality); its necessity is the logical necessity (the modal status of the pattern); its modal space
is the space of the logical configurations (the logically possible configurations). The distinction is
the fundamental-realm pattern.

16.5.4     The Hub of Signification
The governing dynamics of the Hub of Signification is the signification, in which law and necessity
coincide and the modal space distinguishes. The realm’s law is its signification (truthfulness,
accuracy, fidelity); its necessity is its signification (the signification is necessary just because it is
what the passage is); its modal space is the space of the signification’s possibility (the range of
configurations that the signification admits). The coincidence is the barzakhic pattern.

16.5.5     The Relational Manifestation
The governing dynamics of the Relational Manifestation is the meaning law, in which the three
elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s law is the meaning pattern (relationality, contextu-
ality, awareness); its necessity is the meaning-necessity (the modal status of the pattern); its
modal space is the space of the meaning configurations (the meaningfully possible configurations).
The distinction is the fundamental-realm pattern.

16.5.6     The Hub of Realization
The governing dynamics of the Hub of Realization is the actualization, in which law and necessity
coincide and the modal space distinguishes. The realm’s law is its actualization (proportion
in realization, preservation, continuation); its necessity is its actualization (the actualization is
necessary just because it is what the passage is); its modal space is the space of the actualization’s
possibility (the range of configurations that the actualization admits). The coincidence is the
barzakhic pattern.

16.5.7     The Material Manifestation
The governing dynamics of the Material Manifestation is the physical law, in which the three
elements are fully distinguished. The realm’s law is the physical pattern (causality, temporality,
discreteness); its necessity is the natural necessity (the modal status of the pattern); its modal
space is the space of the physical configurations (the physically possible configurations). The
distinction is the fundamental-realm pattern.

16.5.8     The Seven Realms Together
The governing dynamics of the seven realms are stated in the following table.

16.6     The Governing Dynamics and the Realm
16.6.1    The Governing Dynamics as the Realm’s Mode of Governance
The table shows more than the law, necessity, and modal space of each realm; it shows that the
governing dynamics of a realm is the realm’s mode of governance. The governing dynamics is
not a thing in the realm; it is the realm’s articulation of the triad, and the articulation is what
makes the realm the realm it is. The Material Manifestation is the realm in which the triad
is articulated as physical law, natural necessity, and the space of physical configurations; the
Structural Determination is the realm in which the triad is articulated as logical law, logical
necessity, and the space of logical configurations; the First Determination is the realm in which
the triad is collapsed into unity. The articulation is the realm’s mode of governance, and the
mode of governance is the realm’s governing dynamics.
    The identification is the chapter’s contribution to Book I’s Principle 7.1 (C3, independent
reality of the realms). Book I stated that each realm has a mode of existence of its own; the
present chapter states what the mode of existence is at the level of governing dynamics. The
mode of governance is the articulation of the triad, and the articulation is what makes the realm
independent at the level of governing dynamics.

16.6.2    The Governing Dynamics and the Realm’s Independence
The independence of the realm is the independence of its articulation. The Material Manifestation
is not reducible to the Structural Determination because its articulation of the governing
triad (physical law, natural necessity, the space of physical configurations) is not reducible to
the Structural Determination’s articulation (logical law, logical necessity, the space of logical
configurations). The First Determination is not reducible to the Material Manifestation because
its collapse of the governing triad is not reducible to the Material Manifestation’s distinction of
190                                        Chapter 16. The Governing Dynamics of Each Realm


the triad. The independence is the independence of the articulation, and the articulation is what
the table states.

Principle 16.3 (The Governing Dynamics as the Realm’s Mode of Governance). (T) The
governing dynamics of a realm is the realm’s mode of governance as an articulation of the triad
of law, necessity, and modal space. The articulation is what makes the realm independently real
at the level of governing dynamics, and the independence is the independence of the articulation.

   The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the seven realms in §5 and by the
observation of the table. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 7.1, because the principle’s truth
depends on the independent reality of the realms.


16.7     The Relation Between the Governing Triad and the Fluid
         Triad
The chapter’s final contribution is the statement of the relation between the governing triad and
the fluid triad.

16.7.1    The Two Triads
The two triads are the fluid triad of Part III (light, causation, relation) and the governing triad
of Part IV (law, necessity, modal space). The fluid triad is the structure of the fluid element; the
governing triad is the structure of the governing dynamics. The two triads are related, and the
relation is the framework’s architecture at the level of the triads.
    The relation is the following. The fluid triad is what the governing triad governs: the light,
causation, and relation are what the law governs, what the necessity makes necessary, and what
the modal space contains as possible. The governing triad is what governs the fluid triad: the
law is the pattern the fluid elements follow; the necessity is the modal status of the pattern; the
modal space is the extent within which the fluid elements operate. The two triads are not the
same; they are the two sides of one structure—the structure of the seven realms as a system of
things that bear on one another according to laws.

16.7.2    The Parallelism and the Asymmetry
The two triads exhibit a parallelism and an asymmetry.
    The parallelism. Both triads have three elements, and both exhibit the pattern of collapse,
partial coincidence, and full distinction across the seven realms. The parallelism is what makes
the seven realms a single system: the same pattern of articulation governs both the fluid and the
governing elements, and the pattern is what makes the realms structurally distinct at both levels.
    The asymmetry. The fluid triad has a two-level hierarchy (light is the condition of causation
and relation); the governing triad has a three-level hierarchy (modal space is the extent; law is
the pattern within the extent; necessity is the modal status of the pattern). The asymmetry is
what makes the governing triad the more structured of the two: it has an additional level, and
the level is the level of the modal space.
    The parallelism and the asymmetry together are the framework’s architecture at the level
of the triads. The architecture is what the present chapter states, and the architecture is what
makes Book II’s Parts II, III, and IV a single contribution rather than three separate analyses.

Principle 16.4 (The Relation Between the Governing Triad and the Fluid Triad). (T) The fluid
triad and the governing triad are related as the governed and the governing: the fluid triad is
what the governing triad governs, and the governing triad is what governs the fluid triad. The
two triads exhibit a parallelism (both have three elements and both exhibit the same pattern of
articulation) and an asymmetry (the fluid triad has a two-level hierarchy; the governing triad
16.8. The Four-Column Structure of the Synthesis                                                191


has a three-level hierarchy). The parallelism and the asymmetry together make the seven realms
a single system.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the two triads in Parts III and IV and by
the observation of their relation. It is (D) relative to Book I’s Principle 7.1, because the system
it describes is the system of the independently real realms.


16.8     The Four-Column Structure of the Synthesis
The synthesis itself has a four-column structure, and the structure is stated here.

16.8.1    The Fixed Element of the Synthesis
The fixed element of the synthesis is the governing triad itself, held invariant while the synthesis
explains the conditions of its articulation across the seven realms. The triad is held invariant as
the subject of the synthesis—the structure whose articulation the synthesis seeks to state.

16.8.2    The Fluid Element of the Synthesis
The fluid element of the synthesis is the relation between the triad and the realm—the relation
by which the realm articulates the triad, and by which the triad is realized in the realm. The
relation is the medium of the synthesis: it is what conveys the effect of the realm’s mode of
governance to the triad’s articulation.

16.8.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Synthesis
The governing dynamics of the synthesis is the rule by which the realm’s position in the ontological
architecture determines the triad’s articulation—the rule that the more a realm is a realm of
passage, the more its law and necessity coincide; the more a realm is a realm of multiplicity, the
more the triad is articulated. The rule is the principle of §4 (16.2).

16.8.4    The Context of the Synthesis
The context of the synthesis is the framework of Book I, in which the seven realms are indepen-
dently real and the triads are category-relative. The context is the frame in which the synthesis
is posed, and it is what makes the synthesis a synthesis of the framework, not a synthesis in
general.

16.9     What Part IV Establishes
Part IV has established five things.
    The definition of law (Chapter 13, Definition 13.1), the argument that law is the metaphysical
consequent of Book I’s rules of the realms (Chapter 13, Principle 13.6), the demonstration that
the four standard theories of law share the notion of pattern (Chapter 13, Principle 13.3), and the
demonstration that the unity of the rules (Book I, Principles 16.15 and 17.11) is a consequence
of law (Chapter 13, Principle 13.7).
    The definitions of the four kinds of necessity (Chapter 14, Definitions 14.4 to 14.9), the
argument that the structural laws of the realms are metaphysically necessary (Chapter 14,
Principle 14.6), and the argument that natural necessity is a mode of metaphysical necessity
(Chapter 14, Principle 14.8).
    The framework’s position on Ω (Chapter 15, Principle ??), the stratification of Ω (Chapter 15,
Principle ??), the grounding of Ω in God as a family of analogous relations (Chapter 15,
Principle ??), and the relation between Ω and light (Chapter 15, Principle ??).
    The synthesis of the governing triad across the seven realms (the present chapter, Defini-
tion 16.1 and Principle 16.2), and the principle that the governing dynamics of a realm is the
realm’s mode of governance as an articulation of the triad (the present chapter, Principle 16.3).
    The relation between the governing triad and the fluid triad (the present chapter, Princi-
ple 16.4), and the demonstration that the seven realms are a single system at the levels of the
fixed, fluid, and governing elements.
    The five establishments are the contribution of Part IV. They are the metaphysical analysis
of Book I’s governing dynamics, and they are what Book II’s later parts will presuppose.


16.10      What Part IV Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from Part IV are deliberately deferred.
    First, Part IV does not analyze the context of metaphysics. The context—the realms as
contexts, the barzakhic as category, the non-passage—is the subject of Part V. The present part
has analyzed the governing dynamics in isolation from the context, and the isolation is deliberate:
it makes the governing dynamics visible before the context is introduced.
    Second, Part IV does not settle the question of whether the governing triad is exhaustive. The
triad (law, necessity, modal space) is the chapter’s analysis of the governing dynamics; whether
a fourth element is needed, or whether one of the three can be derived from the others, is a
question the present part leaves open. The question is marked (Q) in the chapter’s status table.
    Third, Part IV does not state the relation between the governing triad and viability. The
relation is the subject of Part VI, where viability is analyzed as the integration of the four
columns. The present part has stated the governing dynamics; the relation to viability is deferred.
    Fourth, Part IV does not state the relation between the governing triad and the divine
ground. The relation is the subject of Part VII. The present part has stated the stratification
and grounding of Ω (Chapter 15); the fuller account of the divine ground is deferred to Part VII.
    The four deferrals are the conditions under which Part IV is offered, and they are stated so
that the reader knows what kind of claim is being made. A reader who accepts the deferrals
accepts the part’s scope; a reader who does not has a reason to read the later parts, where the
deferrals are lifted.

16.12      A Question for Reflection
Consider a thing you know well—a person, a place, a work of art, an institution—and consider
the realm in which it is realized. Is the thing’s law, necessity, and modal space fully distinguished,
or do law and necessity coincide, or do all three collapse? What does the answer tell you about
the realm in which the thing is realized, and about the thing’s mode of governance?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The governing triad is not the same in every
realm; its articulation is a function of the realm’s position in the ontological architecture. The
reader who can state, for a thing he knows, the articulation of its governing triad, has understood
the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most
difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

With this chapter, Part IV of Book II is complete. The governing dynamics of metaphysics—law,
necessity, and modal space—are analyzed, synthesized into the triad, and shown to be articulated
differently in each of the seven realms. The next part turns to the context of metaphysics: the
realms as contexts, the barzakhic as a metaphysical category, non-passage and presence, and
the context of the whole. The first analysis is the realms as contexts, which is the subject of
Chapter 17.

Chapter 17

Realms as Contexts, Derived

Scope
This chapter opens Part V with the derivation of the realm as a context. It asks what a realm
must be, such that it can serve as a context for manifestation, and it answers by deriving the
realm from the context column of Book I. It defines a realm, as a context, as a mode of existence
with a determinate capacity—a structural range of what can appear in it and what cannot—and
it argues that a realm is not a container (a "where" things are) but a condition (a "how" things
can be). It distinguishes the realm-as-context from the cognitive context, from the container
metaphor, and from the mode of existence considered in abstraction from its capacity. It states
the relation between the realm’s capacity and the realm’s mode of existence, and it derives the
openness of the realm from Book I’s openness of relations. It states the four-column structure of
the inquiry into the realm, and it states the form that capacity takes in each of the realms.
    The chapter’s claims are metaphysical and structural. Where it speaks of "realm," "context,"
"condition," "container," or "capacity," these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the
definitions in this chapter and by the framework of Book I.

     Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given the context column of
     Book I (Definition 6.4), the context-dependence principle (Principle 10.1), the two
     kinds of context (Definition 14.1 and Definition 14.2), the definition of manifestation
     (Definition 13.1), and the openness of relations (Principle 11.1). It does not restate
     these principles; it asks what they require in the order of being. The derivation is
     stated in §17.3, and the chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that the
     realm-as-context is the presupposition of the context column, and that the realm is a
     condition of actualization, not a container of things.


17.1     A Scene: The Doorway
Consider a person standing at a doorway. On one side, a room: a temperature, a light, a sound,
a set of objects at rest. On the other side, another room: a different temperature, a different
light, a different sound, a different set of objects. The person crosses the threshold. Something
has changed. But what has changed is not the person—she is the same woman she was a moment
ago—and it is not the rooms, because the rooms were what they are before she crossed. What
has changed is the condition under which things appear to her: the air she breathes, the light
she sees, the sound she hears, the objects she can touch.
    The threshold is not a container. It does not hold the person the way a box holds a marble.
The threshold is the condition of being in one room rather than another; it is the structural
boundary at which the conditions of appearance change. The two rooms are contexts, and the
contexts are not the things in them; the contexts are the conditions under which things appear.
198                                                    Chapter 17. Realms as Contexts, Derived


    Now consider a harder case. Consider a person who crosses a threshold not of space but
of state: a person who falls asleep, or who falls ill, or who enters a religious ceremony. The
threshold is not spatial; it is a transition between two conditions of appearance. The person
does not move from one place to another; she moves from one mode of appearance to another.
The context is not a location; it is a condition. And the person can be the same person in both
contexts—the same woman, before and after—even though what appears to her, and how it
appears, is different.
    The scene is not about rooms or states in particular. It is about a general structure, and the
structure is this: a context is not a container in which things are placed; it is a condition under
which things appear. The context determines what can appear in it, and how it appears, and
the context is distinct from the things it conditions.
    Now consider a third case, the hardest. Consider a context that is itself in flux—a room
whose walls are being raised, whose light is changing, whose air is being altered. The context is
not a fixed frame; it is a condition that itself changes, and the change in the condition changes
what can appear. The context is real, and its reality is the reality of a condition, not the reality
of a thing. The context is what the framework calls a realm, and the realm’s reality is the reality
of a mode of existence with a determinate capacity.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What must a realm be, such that it can serve as
a context for manifestation? What is a mode of existence? What is it for a mode of existence to
have a capacity? And is the realm a container or a condition? The chapter’s answer is: the realm
is a condition—a mode of existence with a determinate capacity, which is a structural range of
what can appear in it and what cannot. The realm-as-context is not a "where" things are; it
is a "how" things can be. The chapter’s task is to derive the realm from the context column of
Book I, and to state the realm’s structure.


17.2     The Question
The context column of Book I is the frame in which the fixed elements, fluid elements, and
governing dynamics take their specific content (Definition 6.4). The context is what determines
what counts as a fixed element, what counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics governs.
The context-dependence principle states that the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on
the cognitive context, not on the element’s essence (Principle 10.1).
    The present chapter asks: what must be the case in reality, such that the context column
can be what it is? What must a context be, such that it can determine what counts as a fixed
element, what counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics governs? The framework’s answer
is: a realm, the mode of existence with a determinate capacity, within which manifestations are
realized. The chapter asks what kind of reality the realm must have.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of realm-as-context? The chapter must define realm-
as-context, and it must distinguish the definition from the definitions of the cognitive context
(Definition 14.1) and the existential context (Definition 14.2). The definition must be precise
enough to be argued about, and general enough to cover the realm of each of the modes.
    The second aspect: what is the relation between the realm’s capacity and its mode of existence?
The chapter must state what the capacity is, metaphysically, and how it relates to the mode
of existence. The answer is the chapter’s principal contribution, because it is what makes the
realm-as-context a condition of actualization, not a container.
    The third aspect: what is the relation between the realm-as-context and Book I’s openness of
relations? Book I’s Principle 11.1 states that every manifestation can become a fixed element
of a further context—that the process of re-contextualization never terminates. The chapter
must state the existential counterpart of that openness. The answer is the chapter’s second
contribution: the realm’s capacity is open in the sense that it is a structural range, not a finite
17.3. The Derivation of the Realm                                                                   199


list.
     The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: realm-
as-context is a mode of existence with a determinate capacity; the capacity is the structural
range of what the mode admits; and the range is open in the sense that it is a structure, not an
enumeration.


17.3      The Derivation of the Realm
17.3.1     Step 1: The Context Presupposes a Condition
The context column of Book I is the frame in which an explanation is posed. The frame determines
what counts as a fixed element, what counts as a fluid element, and which dynamics governs. For
the frame to determine these things, there must be a condition under which the determination is
possible: a structural framework within which realization can occur. The condition is what the
realm-as-context captures; without the condition, the frame would be a container, not a context.
    The step is (D) relative to Book I’s Definition 6.4 and to the context-dependence principle
(Principle 10.1). The claim is not that the context is a condition; the claim is that the context
presupposes a condition, and that the presupposition is the context’s metaphysical structure.

17.3.2     Step 2: The Condition Is Realm-as-Context
The condition that the context presupposes is what the chapter calls realm-as-context: the
mode of existence with a determinate capacity, within which manifestations are realized. The
identification is not arbitrary: it is the identification of the condition with the notion that the
metaphysical tradition has called a realm, stated in the framework’s vocabulary. The realm is
the mode; the mode is the condition; the capacity is the mode’s range.
   The step is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the notion of realm-as-context and by the
comparison with the tradition’s notion. It is relative to the chapter’s definition, and it is assessable
by the definition’s adequacy.

17.3.3     Step 3: The Presupposition Is a Derived Consequent
The presupposition is a derived consequent of Book I’s framework, not an independent metaphys-
ical posit. The framework does not add the condition to the context; it states what the context
requires in the order of being. The requirement is a (D) claim, and the (D) claim is the chapter’s
principal contribution.
    The step is the synthesis of Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 establishes that the context presupposes a
condition; Step 2 establishes that the condition is realm-as-context; Step 3 establishes that the
presupposition is a derived consequent of the framework. The three steps together establish the
chapter’s principal claim.

Principle 17.1 (Realm-as-Context as the Derived Consequent of the Context). (D) Realm-
as-context is the derived consequent of Book I’s context column: the context presupposes a
structural condition under which realization can occur, and the condition is what the chapter
calls realm-as-context. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Definition 6.4
and on the context-dependence principle (Principle 10.1); it is the chapter’s principal contribution
because it states what the context requires in the order of being.

    The principle is (D): it is the demonstration that the context column of Book I presupposes
the realm-as-context. A reader who accepts the context column has a reason to accept the
realm-as-context; a reader who does not has no reason to accept it, and the derivation states this
at exactly that strength.
200                                                    Chapter 17. Realms as Contexts, Derived


17.4      The Definition of Realm as Context
17.4.1    The Definition
Definition 17.2 (Realm as Context). (A) A realm, as a context, is a mode of existence with a
determinate capacity: a structural range of what can appear in it and what cannot. The realm
is not a container (a "where" things are); it is a condition (a "how" things can be). The condition
determines what can appear (the capacity of the realm) and what cannot (the constraints of the
realm).

    The definition has three components, and each is important.
    The first component: a realm is a mode of existence. A mode of existence is a way of being—a
structural character that makes the things that are in it the things they are. The Material
Manifestation is the mode of existence in which things are extended, discrete, and localized; the
Structural Determination is the mode in which things are formal, universal, and necessary; the
First Determination is the mode in which there is no multiplicity at all. The mode of existence
is what the realm is, and the mode is distinct from the things that are in the realm.
    The second component: a realm has a determinate capacity. The capacity is not a quantity
of "space" that can be filled; it is a structural range of what can appear and what cannot. The
capacity of the Material Manifestation is the range of physical configurations that material
things can take; the capacity of the Structural Determination is the range of logical forms that
structural things can have; the capacity of the Relational Manifestation is the range of meanings
that relational things can carry. The capacity is structural, not quantitative; it is a range of
kinds, not a count of instances.
    The third component: a realm is a condition, not a container. A container is a "where"—a
spatial or quasi-spatial region in which things are placed. A condition is a "how"—a structural
framework under which things can be what they are. The realm is the second, not the first. The
realm is not a place that things fill; it is a framework that things presuppose. The distinction is
the distinction between the container and the condition, and the realm is the condition.
    The three components are not three definitions; they are three aspects of one definition. The
realm is the mode of existence, and the mode of existence is a condition with a determinate
capacity—and these are three ways of saying the same thing, because the realm’s being a mode,
its having a capacity, and its being a condition are three aspects of its being a realm-as-context.

17.4.2    What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
    It does not say that a realm is a substance. A substance is the ground of a thing’s sameness
through change (Chapter 5, Definition 5.1); a realm is a mode of existence, not a ground of a
thing. The distinction is the distinction between the substance and the mode; the realm is the
mode, not the substance.
    It does not say that a realm is a relation. A relation is a real connection between two or
more terms (Chapter 10, Definition 10.1); a realm is a mode of existence, not a connection. The
distinction is the distinction between the relation and the mode; the realm is the mode, not the
relation.
    It does not say that a realm is a law. A law is a structural pattern that grounds the regularity,
necessity, and formality of a realm’s rules (Chapter 13, Definition 13.1); a realm is a mode of
existence, not a pattern. The distinction is the distinction between the law and the mode; the
realm is the mode, not the law.
    It does not say that a realm is a cognitive context. A cognitive context is a frame fixed
by the question being asked (Definition 14.1); a realm is a mode of existence fixed by the
structure of being. The distinction is the distinction between the cognitive and the existential
(Definition 14.2); the realm is the existential, not the cognitive.
17.5. Realm and Capacity                                                                        201


    It does not say that a realm is a container. The definition explicitly denies this: the realm
is a condition, not a container. The container metaphor is a projection of the material realm’s
spatiality onto the other realms; the projection is useful for illustration and misleading for
analysis. The realm is the condition, not the container.

17.4.3    Realm and Existential Context
Definition 17.3 (Realm as Existential Context). (A) The existential context of a manifestation
is the realm in which the manifestation is realized, with the capacity and the constraints of that
realm (Book I, Definition 14.2). The realm is the existential context; the existential context is
the realm considered as the condition of the manifestation’s realization.
    The distinction between the realm and the existential context is the distinction between the
mode of existence and the mode considered as a condition. The realm is the mode; the existential
context is the mode considered as what it conditions. The two are the same thing under two
descriptions: the realm is the mode; the existential context is the mode as conditioning. The
distinction is useful because it keeps separate two things that are easily confused: the mode
of existence (what the realm is) and the condition of realization (what the realm does for the
manifestation).

17.4.4    Realm and Cognitive Context
The distinction between the existential and the cognitive context was drawn in Book I’s Defini-
tion 14.1 and Definition 14.2: the existential context is the realm in which a manifestation is
realized; the cognitive context is the frame in which something is cognized. The present chapter
derives the distinction.
    The existential context is fixed by the realm, not by the question. The realm is what it is,
and its capacity is what it is, independently of any inquirer. The cognitive context is fixed by
the question, not by the realm. The frame is what the inquirer asks, and the frame’s elements
are individuated by the question. The two contexts are distinct, and neither is reducible to the
other.
    The distinction is the distinction between the order of being and the order of inquiry. The
realm is the order of being; the cognitive context is the order of inquiry. The realm is what
the inquirer finds; the cognitive context is what the inquirer brings. The two are related (the
cognitive context is the inquirer’s way of accessing the realm), but they are not the same, and
the chapter keeps them apart.


17.5     Realm and Capacity
17.5.1    The Capacity Is Structural, Not Quantitative
Book I’s Principle 10.1 states that the fixedness or fluidity of an element depends on the cognitive
context. The present chapter asks: what is the capacity of the realm, metaphysically? The
answer is: the capacity is the structural range of what the mode of existence admits. The range
is not a quantity; it is a structure—a set of kinds that the mode admits and a set of kinds that it
excludes.
    The Material Manifestation admits extended, discrete, localized configurations; it excludes
non-extended, non-discrete, non-localized configurations. The range is the set of admissible kinds,
and the set is structural, not quantitative.
Principle 17.4 (The Capacity Is Structural). (D) The capacity of a realm is the structural
range of what the mode of existence admits; it is not a quantitative limit of how much can appear.
The capacity is a set of kinds, not a count of instances. The principle is (D) because its truth
depends on Book I’s Definition 6.4 and on the definition of realm-as-context (Definition 17.2).
202                                                   Chapter 17. Realms as Contexts, Derived


    The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the metaphysical specification of
the context column. The specification is the chapter’s contribution to the analysis of the realm.

17.5.2    The Capacity and the Mode of Existence
The capacity is not something added to the mode of existence; it is the mode of existence
considered as a range. The mode of existence is what the realm is; the capacity is what the mode
admits. The two are the same thing under two descriptions: the mode is the being; the capacity
is the being’s range. The distinction is the distinction between the mode and the range; the
realm is the mode, and the capacity is the mode’s range.
     The relation has a consequence: the capacity cannot be changed without changing the mode
of existence. If the realm’s capacity were altered, the realm’s mode of existence would be altered,
and the realm would no longer be the realm it is. The capacity is fixed by the mode; the mode
is fixed by the realm. The capacity is not a contingent feature of the realm; it is the realm’s
structural character.

17.5.3    The Capacity and the Openness of the Realm
The capacity is open in the sense that it is a structural range, not an enumeration. The range
is the set of kinds that the mode admits; the range is not a finite list of instances. The realm
can admit an indefinite number of instances of the kinds it admits, and the indefiniteness is the
openness of the realm.
    The openness is the existential counterpart of Book I’s openness of relations (Principle 11.1).
Book I’s openness stated that every manifestation can become a fixed element of a further
context; the existential openness states that every realm can admit indefinitely many instances
of the kinds it admits. The two are distinct—the first is about cognitive contexts, the second
about the realm’s capacity—but they are parallel: both are about the range of what can be, not
the count of what is.

Principle 17.5 (The Existential Openness of the Realm). (T) The capacity of a realm is open
in the sense that it is a structural range, not a finite enumeration. The realm can admit an
indefinite number of instances of the kinds it admits, and the indefiniteness is the openness of
the realm. The principle is (T): it is argued from the definition of the capacity (Definition 17.2)
and from Book I’s Principle 11.1.


17.6     Realm and Mode of Existence
17.6.1    The Mode of Existence Is a Condition
The mode of existence is what the realm is; the condition is what the realm does. The two are
related: the mode is the condition, considered as what it is; the condition is the mode, considered
as what it does. The relation is the relation between the being and its operation: the realm’s
mode of existence is its being; the realm’s condition is its operation.
    The mode of existence is a condition in the sense that it is the framework within which the
manifestations can be realized. The mode is not a thing that manifestations are attached to;
the mode is the structure that the manifestations presuppose. The distinction is the distinction
between the thing and the framework; the mode is the framework, not the thing.

17.6.2    The Mode of Existence and the Four Columns
The mode of existence is related to the four columns. The fixed element (Part II) is what the
mode admits; the fluid element (Part III) is what the mode conveys; the governing dynamics
(Part IV) is what the mode rules; the context (Part V) is what the mode is. The four columns
17.7. The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Realm                                       203


are the four ways the mode of existence is articulated: as what, as how, as rule, as frame. The
mode is one; the articulations are four; the four are the realm’s being a realm in the framework.

17.6.3    The Mode of Existence and the Realm’s Independence
The realm’s independence is the independence of its mode of existence. The Material Manifestation
is not reducible to the Structural Determination because its mode of existence (extended, discrete,
localized) is not reducible to the Structural Determination’s mode (formal, universal, necessary).
The independence is the independence of the mode, not the independence of the capacity—the
capacity is the mode’s range, and the mode is what the realm is.


17.7     The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into Realm
With the definition of realm-as-context in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can be
applied to the inquiry into realm.

17.7.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into Realm
The fixed element of the inquiry into realm is the realm itself, held invariant while the inquiry
explains the conditions of its being. The realm is held invariant as the subject of the inquiry—the
mode whose conditions the inquiry seeks to state.

17.7.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into Realm
The fluid element of the inquiry into realm is the relation between the realm and its manifestations—
the relation by which the manifestations are the manifestations of the realm, and by which the
realm is what the manifestations are in. The relation is the medium of the inquiry: it is what
conveys the effect of the realm’s being what it is to the manifestations’ being what they are.

17.7.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into Realm
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into realm is the rule by which the realm’s mode of
existence determines its capacity—the rule that explains how the mode admits some kinds and
excludes others. The rule is the subject of §17.5 and §17.6.

17.7.4    The Context of the Inquiry into Realm
The context of the inquiry into realm is the framework of Book I, in which the realms are real
and their capacities are determinate. The context is the frame in which the inquiry is posed, and
it is what makes the inquiry an inquiry into the realm, not an inquiry in general.

17.7.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into realm are stated in the following table.

                 Column               In the Inquiry into Realm
                 Fixed element    The realm itself, held invariant as the sub-
                                  ject of the inquiry
                 Fluid element    The relation between the realm and its

                 Governing dynam- The rule by which the mode of existence

17.8     Realm in Each Realm
The form of the realm-as-context—the form of the determinate capacity—takes a different shape
in each of the realms. The present section states the form, one realm at a time. The statements
are (E) claims: they are structural estimates, offered at the strength that the framework’s
principles support.

17.8.1    The Material Manifestation
The capacity of the Material Manifestation is the range of physical configurations that extended,
discrete, localized things can take. The range includes positions, durations, masses, energies, and
their combinations; the range excludes non-extended, non-discrete, non-localized configurations.
The capacity is the Material mode of the general capacity, and it is the mode that Book I’s rules
of the Material Manifestation presuppose.

17.8.2    The Relational Manifestation
The capacity of the Relational Manifestation is the range of meaning-configurations that relational
things can carry. The range includes meanings, significances, recognitions, and their combinations;
the range excludes meaningless configurations. The capacity is the Relational mode of the general
capacity.

17.8.3    The Structural Determination
The capacity of the Structural Determination is the range of logical forms that structural things
can have. The range includes universals, necessities, formal relations, and their combinations;
the range excludes non-formal configurations. The capacity is the Structural mode of the general
capacity.

17.8.4    The First Determination
The capacity of the First Determination is pure unity—the range of what the First Determination
admits, which is nothing but itself. The First Determination has no multiplicity, no change,
no succession; its capacity is its unity, and its unity is its capacity. The form is the limit case
of the other forms: it is what the capacity becomes when the multiplicity is zero. The First
Determination admits only itself, because there is nothing else to admit.

17.8.5    The Hub of Decree
The capacity of the Hub of Decree is the range of apportioning configurations that the measure
admits. The range includes proportions, orders, harmonies, and their combinations; the range
excludes disproportions, disorders, and disharmonies. The capacity is the mode of the general
capacity in the Hub of Decree.

17.8.6    The Hub of Signification
The capacity of the Hub of Signification is the range of signification configurations that the
sign admits. The range includes truths, accuracies, fidelities, and their combinations; the range
excludes untruths, inaccuracies, and infidelities. The capacity is the mode of the general capacity
in the Hub of Signification.
17.9. Objections and Replies                                                                    205


17.8.7    The Hub of Realization
The capacity of the Hub of Realization is the range of realization configurations that the
actualization admits. The range includes proportional realizations, preservations, continuations,
and their combinations; the range excludes disproportionate realizations, failures to preserve, and
failures to continue. The capacity is the mode of the general capacity in the Hub of Realization.

17.8.8    The Seven Forms Together
The seven forms are stated in the following table.

                Realm                   The Form of Capacity
                First Determination     Pure unity (limit case)
                Hub of Decree           Range of apportioning configurations
                Structural Determi-     Range of logical forms

    The table is the chapter’s map of the realm-as-context across the seven realms. It is an (E)

17.9      Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: The realm is a container, not a condition. The objection is that the realm is a
"where"—a place or a region in which things are located—and that the framework’s "condition"
is a figure of speech. The realm, the objection concludes, is a container in the ordinary sense.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the container metaphor for the thing. The container is a
feature of the Material Manifestation: things are in places, and the places are "containers" in the
ordinary sense. But the container is a mode of the realm’s conditionality, not its definition. The
realm is a condition—a structural framework under which things can appear—and the condition
takes the form of a container in the Material Manifestation because the Material Manifestation’s
condition is spatial. The other realms have other forms: the Structural Determination’s condition
is formal, not spatial; the Relational Manifestation’s condition is meaningful, not spatial. The
objection mistakes one form of the condition for the condition itself; the reply distinguishes them.
    Objection 2: The distinction between cognitive and existential context is arbitrary. The
objection is that all contexts are constructed by the inquirer, and that the framework’s "existential
context" is a covert cognitive context.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the epistemic access for the ontological structure. The
existential context is accessed through a cognitive context; the access is the inquirer’s, and the
inquirer’s access is always framed by the question. But the existential context is not the access;
the existential context is the realm, and the realm is what it is independently of any inquirer.
The Material Manifestation was the Material Manifestation before any inquirer asked about it,
and it will be after; the realm’s capacity is what it is, not what the inquirer says it is. The
distinction is the distinction between the epistemic and the ontic, and the framework keeps them
apart.
206                                                  Chapter 17. Realms as Contexts, Derived


    Objection 3: The capacity is a limit, not a structure. The objection is that the capacity is
the quantity of what a realm can hold, and that the framework’s "structural range" is a way of
avoiding the question of quantity.
    Reply. The objection mistakes the quantity for the structure. The capacity is not a quantity;
it is a set of kinds. The Material Manifestation can hold an indefinite number of physical
configurations; the number is not the capacity, the range is. The range is the set of kinds the
realm admits, and the kinds are what the realm is. A realm that admitted a different range of
kinds would be a different realm, not the same realm with a different quantity. The objection
mistakes the count for the kind; the reply distinguishes them.


17.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not analyze the barzakhic realm as a metaphysical category. The
analysis is the subject of Chapter 18; the present chapter derives the realm as a context, and
it applies the derivation to the barzakhic realms in §17.8 without analyzing what makes the
barzakhic a distinct category.
    Second, the chapter does not analyze non-passage and presence. The analysis is the subject
of Chapter 19; the present chapter derives the realm as a condition, not a container, but it does
not analyze what it is for an identity to be present in a realm without passing through the
intermediate realms.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the realms are exhaustive. The
realms are derived from the four columns; whether a further realm is possible is a question the
present chapter leaves open.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the relation between the realm and the modal space Ω.
The relation is the subject of Chapter 15; the present chapter derives the realm as a context,
and it leaves the relation to the modal space to the earlier chapter.

17.12      A Question for Reflection
Consider a context you know well—a place, a tradition, a community, a practice. Is the context a
container (a "where" things are) or a condition (a "how" things can be)? What is the capacity of
the context—the range of what can appear in it and what cannot? And if the context’s capacity
is structural, not quantitative, what would it mean for the context to change?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The context is the condition; the condition
is the mode of existence with a determinate capacity; the capacity is the structural range. The
reader who can state, for a context he knows, what the condition, the mode, and the capacity
are, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the
distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

The next chapter (Chapter 18) derives the barzakhic realm as a metaphysical category: what
makes the barzakhic a distinct category, and how does the barzakhic serve as a context for the
manifestations that pass through it? With the realm-as-context in place, the framework can
distinguish the fundamental realm’s conditionality (fixed) from the barzakhic realm’s conditionality
(passage), and it can state what the barzakhic’s capacity is.
