Chapter 18

The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical
Category, Derived

Scope
This chapter derives the barzakhic as a metaphysical category. It asks what the barzakhic
must be, such that it can serve as a context of transition between realms, and it answers by
deriving the barzakhic from the context column of Book I and from the fluid element. It defines
the barzakhic, as a category, as a mode of existence whose being is the passage between two
other modes—not a being that passes, but the passage itself, considered as a level of being. It
distinguishes the barzakhic category from the function of mediation, from relation, from process,
and from composite; it states the standard accounts of what makes a category and what they
share; it argues that the barzakhic is what the context column and the fluid element presuppose
in the order of being; it answers Book I’s Q10 (the ontological standing of realization in the
barzakhic realms); it states the four-column structure of the inquiry into the barzakhic; it states
the form that the barzakhic category takes in each of the three hubs; and it answers three
standard objections.
    The chapter’s claims are metaphysical and structural. Where it speaks of "passage," "category,"
"function," or "passage-level," these are structural terms; their sense is fixed by the definitions in
this chapter and by the framework of Book I.

      Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given the context column of
      Book I (Definition 6.4), the two kinds of context (Definition 14.1 and Definition 14.2),
      the non-necessity of downward passage (derived in Chapter 17), the definition of
      manifestation (Definition 13.1), the definition of epistemic light (Definition 15.1),
      and the openness of relations (Principle 11.1). It also takes as given the answer to
      Book I’s Q10, which the present chapter derives. It does not restate these; it asks
      what they presuppose in the order of being. The derivation is stated in §18.3, and the
      chapter’s principal contribution is the demonstration that the barzakhic is a category
      of passage, and that the passage is not a function but a mode of existence.


18.1      A Scene: The Customs House
Consider a customs house at a border. Two countries lie on either side; a road runs between
them; the customs house stands at the crossing. Goods come from one country, pass through
the customs house, and enter the other. The customs house has officials, rules, procedures, a
building, a seal. It has a history; it has a bureaucracy; it has a budget. It is, in every ordinary
sense, a real institution.
210                            Chapter 18. The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category, Derived


     Now ask: what is the customs house? It is not the goods; the goods are what pass through it.
It is not the country of origin; the country of origin is where the goods come from. It is not the
country of destination; the country of destination is where the goods go. It is not the road; the
road is what the goods travel on. The customs house is none of these. The customs house is the
passage—the formal process by which the goods cross from one country to another.
     The customs house is real, and its reality is not the reality of the goods. The goods are
physical things; the customs house is a formal structure. The goods can be destroyed and the
customs house can continue; the customs house can be abolished and the goods can continue
(through another crossing). The two are distinct, and the distinction is the distinction between
the passage and the things that pass.
     The customs house is also not a mere function. A function is what a thing does—the role
it plays, the service it provides. The customs house is not merely the function of crossing; the
customs house is the crossing, considered as an institution. The function is what the customs
house does; the customs house is what the passage is. The distinction is the distinction between
the operation and the mode of existence—between what a thing does and what a thing is.
     Now consider a harder case. Consider a customs house that has no building—a customs
procedure conducted entirely in the cloud, with no physical location, no officials present, no
building to stand at the border. The customs procedure is still the passage; it still has rules,
procedures, a reality. But its reality is even more clearly the reality of a passage, not the reality
of a place. The passage is what the customs procedure is; the passage is its mode of existence.
     The scene poses the question of the chapter. What must the barzakhic be, such that it can
serve as a context of transition between realms? What is a mode of existence that includes
mediating? Is the barzakhic a function (a thing that does the mediating), a relation (a connection
between the realms it mediates), a process (a sequence of mediations), or a composite (a whole
made of the realms it mediates)? Or is the barzakhic a distinct category—a mode of existence
whose being is the passage itself, considered as a level of being? The chapter’s answer is: the
barzakhic is a distinct category, the category of passage. The chapter’s task is to derive the
category from the context column and the fluid element, and to show that the derivation yields
the category.


18.2      The Question
The context column of Book I is the frame in which the fixed elements, fluid elements, and
governing dynamics take their specific content (Definition 6.4). The realms, derived in Chapter 17,
are the modes of existence that the context presupposes. The non-necessity of downward passage
(derived in Chapter 17) states that the presence of an identity in one realm does not require
its passage through every intermediate realm. The fluid element is the medium of relation
(Definition 15.1).
    The present chapter asks: what must the case in reality be, such that the realms can be
related to one another, and such that a manifestation in one realm can be conveyed to another?
The framework’s answer is: the barzakhic, the mode of existence whose being is the passage
between two other modes. The chapter asks what kind of category the barzakhic is.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of the barzakhic as a category? The chapter must
define the barzakhic as a category, and it must distinguish the definition from the definitions of
the realms (Chapter 17) and of relation (Chapter 10). The definition must be precise enough to
be argued about, and general enough to cover the three hubs.
    The second aspect: what is the relation between the barzakhic and the non-necessity of
downward passage? The chapter must state how the barzakhic relates to the non-passage derived
in Chapter 17. The relation is the chapter’s principal contribution, because it is what makes the
barzakhic a category, not a function.
18.3. The Derivation of the Barzakhic                                                           211


    The third aspect: what is the ontological standing of realization in the barzakhic realms?
Book I’s Chapter 34, Q10, stated the question and did not answer it. The present chapter answers
it by deriving the answer from the framework: identities are present through the barzakhic, not
realized in it. The answer is the chapter’s second contribution.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: the
barzakhic is a category of passage; the category is derived from the context column and the fluid
element; and identities are present through the barzakhic, not realized in it.


18.3     The Derivation of the Barzakhic
18.3.1    Step 1: The Realms Presuppose a Passage
The realms, derived in Chapter 17, are the modes of existence that the context presupposes. For
the realms to be related—for a manifestation in one realm to be conveyed to another—there
must be a mode of existence that carries the relation: a passage between the realms. The passage
is what the realms’ relatedness presupposes; without the passage, the realms would be isolated,
and a manifestation in one realm could not reach another.
    The step is (D) relative to Book I’s Definition 6.4 and to the derivation of the realms in
Chapter 17. The claim is not that the passage is a separate thing; the claim is that the realms’
relatedness presupposes the passage.

18.3.2    Step 2: The Passage Is the Barzakhic
The passage that the realms’ relatedness presupposes is what the chapter calls the barzakhic:
the mode of existence whose being is the passage between two other modes. The identification is
not arbitrary: it is the identification of the passage with the notion that the tradition has called
the barzakhic, stated in the framework’s vocabulary. The barzakhic is not a being that passes; it
is the passage itself, considered as a level of being.
    The step is (T): it is argued by the analysis of the notion of the barzakhic and by the
comparison with the tradition’s notion. It is relative to the chapter’s definition, and it is
assessable by the definition’s adequacy.

18.3.3    Step 3: The Presupposition Is a Derived Consequent
The presupposition is a derived consequent of Book I’s framework, not an independent metaphys-
ical posit. The framework does not add the barzakhic to the realms; it states what the realms
require in the order of being. The requirement is a (D) claim, and the (D) claim is the chapter’s
principal contribution.
    The step is the synthesis of Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 establishes that the realms presuppose
a passage; Step 2 establishes that the passage is the barzakhic; Step 3 establishes that the
presupposition is a derived consequent of the framework. The three steps together establish the
chapter’s principal claim.

Principle 18.1 (The Barzakhic as the Derived Consequent of the Realms). (D) The barzakhic
is the derived consequent of the realms: the realms’ relatedness presupposes a mode of existence
whose being is the passage between them, and the mode is what the chapter calls the barzakhic.
The principle is (D) because its truth depends on Book I’s Definition 6.4 and on the derivation
of the realms in Chapter 17; it is the chapter’s principal contribution because it states what the
realms require in the order of being.

   The principle is (D): it is the demonstration that the realms presuppose the barzakhic. A
reader who accepts the derivation of the realms has a reason to accept the barzakhic; a reader
who does not has no reason to accept it, and the derivation states this at exactly that strength.
212                            Chapter 18. The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category, Derived


18.4      The Definition of the Barzakhic Category
18.4.1    The Definition
Definition 18.2 (The Barzakhic Category). (A) The barzakhic, as a category, is the mode of
existence whose being is the passage between two other modes—not a being that passes, but the
passage itself, considered as a level of being. The passage is real; its reality is the reality of a
mode of existence, not the reality of a thing. The passage has its own structure (its rules, its
capacity, its determinations), and the structure is what makes the passage the passage it is.

     The definition has three components, and each is important.
     The first component: the barzakhic is a mode of existence. A mode of existence is a way
of being—a structural character that makes what is in it what it is. The barzakhic’s mode of
existence is the passage: the being of the barzakhic is the passing, not a thing that passes. The
distinction is the distinction between the being and the passing: the barzakhic is the passing,
and the things that pass are the identities that are realized in the realms the barzakhic mediates.
     The second component: the barzakhic is the passage between two other modes. The passage
is not a passage in general; it is the passage between two specific modes. The Hub of Decree
is the passage between the First Determination and the Structural Determination; the Hub of
Signification between the Structural Determination and the Relational Manifestation; the Hub of
Realization between the Relational Manifestation and the Material Manifestation. The passage
is specific to the modes it mediates; a passage between other modes would be a different passage,
and a different barzakhic.
     The third component: the passage is a level of being. The passage is not an event in a realm;
it is a level whose mode of existence is the passage. The barzakhic is a level in the framework’s
ontology; it is the level whose being is the passage. The distinction is the distinction between the
level and the event: the barzakhic is the level, and the passages that occur in it are the events.
     The three components are not three definitions; they are three aspects of one definition. The
barzakhic is a mode of existence, and the mode is the passage between two other modes, and
the passage is a level of being—and these are three ways of saying the same thing, because the
barzakhic’s being a mode, its being a passage, and its being a level are three aspects of its being
a barzakhic category.

18.4.2    What the Definition Does Not Say
The definition is a stipulation, and it is important to state what it does not say.
    It does not say that the barzakhic is a thing. The barzakhic is a mode of existence, not a thing.
It is not a place that things are in; it is the passage that things are through. The distinction is
the distinction between the thing and the mode; the barzakhic is the mode, not the thing.
    It does not say that the barzakhic is a function. A function is what a thing does; the barzakhic
is what a level is. The function of mediation is what the barzakhic does; the barzakhic is the
passage. The distinction is the distinction between the operation and the mode of existence—
between what a thing does and what a thing is. This distinction is the chapter’s principal
contribution, and it is what makes the barzakhic a category, not a role.
    It does not say that the barzakhic is a relation. A relation is a real connection between two
or more terms (Chapter 10, Definition 10.1); the barzakhic is the passage between two modes.
The distinction is the distinction between the connection and the passage: a relation connects
terms; a passage takes a thing from one mode to another. The barzakhic is the passage, not
the connection—though the passage presupposes both the relation (the connection between the
modes) and the causation (the transfer through the modes).
    It does not say that the barzakhic is a process. A process is a sequence of events; the barzakhic
is the level whose being is the passage. The distinction is the distinction between the sequence
18.5. The Barzakhic and the Standard Accounts of Category                                       213


and the level: the process is the sequence of passages; the barzakhic is the level in which the
passages occur. The barzakhic is the level, not the sequence.
    It does not say that the barzakhic is a composite. A composite is a whole made of parts;
the barzakhic is a level whose being is the passage. The barzakhic is not made of the realms
it mediates; it is the passage between them. The distinction is the distinction between the
composite and the level: the barzakhic is the level, not the composite.

18.4.3    The Barzakhic and the Category of Transition
The framework’s derivation of the barzakhic yields a category of transition: a level H between
two realms Xa and Xb , such that the level H is not determined by the composite Xa → Xb . The
present chapter’s definition is the metaphysical articulation of the derivation.
    The relation between the two is the relation between the derivation and the category. The
derivation yields the category; the category is the metaphysical content that the derivation yields.
The present chapter does not replace the derivation; it gives the category that the derivation
yields.


18.5     The Barzakhic and the Standard Accounts of Category
The chapter’s first contribution to the philosophical debate is the statement of what the standard
accounts of a metaphysical category share, and of how the barzakhic fits them.

18.5.1    The Standard Accounts
Four accounts of what makes a category are standard in the contemporary debate.
     The substance-attribute account. A category is a most general kind of substance or attribute—
a way of being that is not a species of a more general way. The category of substance, of quality,
of relation, of quantity—each is a category in this sense. The account’s virtue is its clarity: a
category is the most general kind. Its difficulty is that it is tailored to the substance-attribute
framework, and it may not fit modes of existence that are not substance or attribute.
     The kind-account. A category is a most general kind of entity—a kind that is not a species of
a more general kind. The account is similar to the substance-attribute account, but it is broader:
it applies to any entity, not only to substances and attributes. The account’s virtue is its breadth.
Its difficulty is that it may be too broad: if every most general kind is a category, the number of
categories is indefinite.
     The mode-of-being account. A category is a mode of existence—a way of being that is not
reducible to another way of being. The account is ontological: it is about what there is, not
about what can be said. The account’s virtue is that it captures the framework’s notion of the
realm: each realm is a mode of existence, and the realms are categories. Its difficulty is that it
must explain what a mode of existence is, and how modes are distinguished.
     The structural-role account. A category is a structural role that an entity can play—a position
in a structure that is not reducible to the entity’s intrinsic properties. The account is structural:
it is about the position, not the entity. The account’s virtue is that it captures the framework’s
notion of the barzakhic: the barzakhic is a structural role (the role of passage), not a substance
or an attribute. Its difficulty is that it must explain what a structural role is, and how roles are
distinguished from functions.

18.5.2    The Framework’s Position
The framework adopts a combination of the mode-of-being account and the structural-role
account, and the combination is the chapter’s contribution.
214                             Chapter 18. The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category, Derived


Principle 18.3 (The Framework’s Position on the Category of Barzakhic). (E) The barzakhic
is a category in the mode-of-being sense (it is a mode of existence, not a substance or an
attribute) and in the structural-role sense (its mode of existence is a structural role, not an
intrinsic property). The framework’s position is that the barzakhic is a category of passage—a
mode of existence whose being is the passage—and that the category is not reducible to the
substance-attribute account or to the kind-account alone.

    The principle is (E): it is a structural estimate, offered at the strength that the analysis of the
standard accounts supports. Its justification is that the barzakhic is visible in the framework’s
derivation as a mode of existence, and that the mode is a structural role. Its refutation would
be a category of passage that is not a mode of existence, or a barzakhic that is reducible to a
function.

18.5.3    The Barzakhic as a Category of Passage
The framework’s position is that the barzakhic is a category of passage. The category has three
marks, and the three marks are what distinguish it from the other categories.
    The first mark: the barzakhic is a mode of existence. The barzakhic is not a substance (a
ground of sameness), not an attribute (a property of a substance), not a relation (a connection
between terms), not a process (a sequence of events). It is a mode of existence: a way of being
whose being is the passage. The mark distinguishes the barzakhic from the fundamental realms’
categories (substance, attribute, relation, process) and from the other modes of existence (the
fixed, the fluid, the governing).
    The second mark: the barzakhic is a structural role. The barzakhic is not an intrinsic property
of a thing; it is a position in a structure—the position of passage between two modes. The mark
distinguishes the barzakhic from the fundamental realms, which are positions of being-in rather
than positions of passage.
    The third mark: the barzakhic is the passage itself. The barzakhic is not a being that passes;
the barzakhic is the passage considered as a level of being. The mark distinguishes the barzakhic
from a function (which is what a thing does) and from a process (which is a sequence of events).
The barzakhic is the passage, not the passing.
    The three marks together are the chapter’s definition of the barzakhic category. The definition
is (A): it is the framework’s stipulation of what the category is. Its justification is that it fits the
standard accounts (the mode-of-being and the structural-role accounts), and that it does the
work that the derivation of the realms requires.


18.6      The Barzakhic and Function
The chapter’s second contribution is the distinction between the barzakhic and a function.

18.6.1    The Function of Mediation
The function of mediation is the structural regulation, conditioning, or transformation of a
relation between two realms by a realm whose mode of existence includes that function. The
function is analytical: it names the role the barzakhic plays in the relation. But the role
presupposes a mode of existence: for the barzakhic to mediate, there must be a level whose being
is the passage, and the level must be what the definition of the barzakhic category captures.
    The distinction is the distinction between the function and the mode of existence. The
function is what the barzakhic does; the mode is what the barzakhic is. The two are distinct: a
function can be described without describing the mode, and a mode can be described without
describing the function. The distinction is what makes the barzakhic a category, not a role.
18.7. The Barzakhic and Relation                                                                215


18.6.2    The Argument for the Distinction
The argument for the distinction has three steps.

   1. A function is what a thing does; a mode of existence is what a thing is.

   2. A thing can lose its function without ceasing to be the thing it is; a thing cannot lose its
      mode of existence without ceasing to be the thing it is.

   3. The barzakhic can lose its function of mediation (if the realms it mediates were reorganized)
      without ceasing to be the barzakhic; but the barzakhic cannot lose its mode of existence
      (the passage) without ceasing to be the barzakhic.

    The conclusion follows: the barzakhic is a mode of existence, not a function. The argument
is (T): it is argued by the distinction between the function and the mode, and by the application
of the distinction to the barzakhic.

Principle 18.4 (The Barzakhic Is a Mode of Existence, Not a Function). (D) The barzakhic is
a mode of existence, not a function: the barzakhic can lose its function of mediation without
ceasing to be the barzakhic, but it cannot lose its mode of existence (the passage) without ceasing
to be the barzakhic. The principle is (D) because its truth depends on the derivation of the
barzakhic in §18.3 and on the derivation of the realms in Chapter 17.

18.6.3    The Barzakhic and the Functional Reduction
The objection from the functional reduction is that the barzakhic can be reduced to a function
of the fundamental realms—that the mediation can be performed by the fundamental realms
themselves, without a distinct level. The framework’s reply is that the barzakhic is not a function;
it is a mode of existence, and the mode is what the function presupposes.
     The argument has three steps.

   1. The fundamental realms’ modes of existence are being-in (the realm is a place where things
      are); the barzakhic’s mode of existence is passage (the realm is a level through which things
      pass).

   2. The being-in and the passage are distinct modes; the one is not reducible to the other.

   3. Therefore, the barzakhic’s mode of existence is not reducible to the fundamental realms’
      mode of existence; and the barzakhic is not reducible to a function of the fundamental
      realms.

   The conclusion follows: the barzakhic is a distinct category, not a function. The argument is
(D): it is conditional on the derivation of the barzakhic and on the derivation of the realms.


18.7     The Barzakhic and Relation
The chapter’s third contribution is the distinction between the barzakhic and a relation.

18.7.1    The Relation and the Passage
A relation is a real connection between two or more terms (Chapter 10, Definition 10.1); the
barzakhic is the passage between two modes. The two are distinct: a relation connects terms; a
passage takes a thing from one mode to another. The relation is a connection; the passage is a
transformation.
216                            Chapter 18. The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category, Derived


    The distinction is the distinction between the connection and the transformation. The
barzakhic is the transformation, not the connection. The connection is what the barzakhic
presupposes (the two modes must be connected for the passage to be possible); the transformation
is what the barzakhic is.

18.7.2    The Barzakhic and the Relation-Passage Distinction
The distinction between the barzakhic and relation is the framework’s response to an objection:
if the barzakhic is a relation, then it can be reduced to the relation between the fundamental
realms, and the barzakhic is not a distinct level. The framework’s response is that the barzakhic
is not a relation; it is the passage, and the passage is distinct from the relation.
    The argument has three steps.

  1. A relation connects terms; a passage transforms terms.

  2. The connection and the transformation are distinct; a term can be connected to another
     term without being transformed by the connection.

  3. Therefore, the barzakhic is not a relation; it is the passage, and the passage is distinct from
     the relation.

   The conclusion follows: the barzakhic is a category of passage, not a category of relation. The
argument is (T): it is argued by the distinction between the connection and the transformation,
and by the application of the distinction to the barzakhic.

Principle 18.5 (The Barzakhic Is a Passage, Not a Relation). (D) The barzakhic is a passage,
not a relation: a relation connects terms; a passage transforms terms. The two are distinct,
and the barzakhic is the passage, not the connection. The principle is (D) because its truth
depends on the derivation of the barzakhic in §18.3 and on the definition of relation (Chapter 10,
Definition 10.1).


18.8     The Answer to Q10
The chapter’s fourth contribution is the answer to Book I’s Q10.

18.8.1    The Question Stated
Book I’s Chapter 34, Q10, stated the question: "What is the structural possibility and ontological
standing of realization in contexts the framework does not describe?" The question is: are
identities realized in the barzakhic realms as they are realized in the fundamental realms, or is
the realization something else?
     The question is not idle. If the barzakhic is a level of being (as the derivation of the realms
states), then identities might be realized in it as they are realized in the fundamental realms. But
if the barzakhic is the passage (as the present chapter derives), then identities are not realized in
it in the same way; they are present through it.

18.8.2    The Answer
The answer is: identities are not realized in the barzakhic as they are in the fundamental
realms; they are present through the barzakhic, in the sense that the passage is what makes their
realization in the lower realm possible.
    The answer has three components.
    The first component: the barzakhic’s mode of existence is not being-in. The fundamental
realms’ mode of existence is being-in (the realm is a place where things are); the barzakhic’s
18.9. The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into the Barzakhic                                 217


mode of existence is passage (the realm is a level through which things pass). The identity’s
realization in a fundamental realm is its being in the realm; the identity’s presence through the
barzakhic is its passing through the level.
    The second component: the presence-through is not a realization. A realization is the identity’s
having a manifestation in the realm; a presence-through is the identity’s being conveyed through
the level. The two are distinct: a realization is the identity’s being in a realm; a presence-through
is the identity’s being through a level.
    The third component: the presence-through is what makes the realization in the lower realm
possible. The passage is the structural condition under which the identity can be realized in
the lower realm. The identity’s presence through the barzakhic is the passage that the identity
makes; the identity’s realization in the lower realm is what the passage produces.

Principle 18.6 (The Answer to Q10). (D) Identities are not realized in the barzakhic realms
as they are realized in the fundamental realms; they are present through the barzakhic realms,
in the sense that the passage is what makes their realization in the lower realm possible. The
principle is (D) because its truth depends on the derivation of the barzakhic in §18.3 and on the
derivation of the realms in Chapter 17.

    The principle is (D): it is not an independent claim; it is the answer to Book I’s Q10. The
answer is the chapter’s contribution to the framework’s account of the barzakhic realms, and it
is what makes the barzakhic a category of passage, not a category of being-in.

18.8.3    The Answer and the Three Hubs
The answer applies to the three hubs, and the application is the chapter’s contribution to the
understanding of each hub.
    The Hub of Decree. The identity’s presence through the Hub of Decree is its passage from the
First Determination’s unity to the Structural Determination’s form. The identity is not realized
in the Hub of Decree; it is present through the hub, in the sense that the hub’s apportioning is
what makes the identity’s realization in the Structural Determination possible.
    The Hub of Signification. The identity’s presence through the Hub of Signification is its
passage from the Structural Determination’s form to the Relational Manifestation’s meaning. The
identity is not realized in the Hub of Signification; it is present through the hub, in the sense that
the hub’s signification is what makes the identity’s realization in the Relational Manifestation
possible.
    The Hub of Realization. The identity’s presence through the Hub of Realization is its passage
from the Relational Manifestation’s meaning to the Material Manifestation’s matter. The identity
is not realized in the Hub of Realization; it is present through the hub, in the sense that the hub’s
actualization is what makes the identity’s realization in the Material Manifestation possible.
    The three applications together are the chapter’s contribution to the understanding of the
three hubs. The hubs are not places where identities are; they are passages through which
identities are. The distinction is the distinction between the place and the passage, and the hubs
are the passage.


18.9      The Four-Column Structure of the Inquiry into the Barza-
          khic
With the definition of the barzakhic category in place, the four-column method of Chapter 2 can
be applied to the inquiry into the barzakhic.
218                           Chapter 18. The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category, Derived


18.9.1    The Fixed Element of the Inquiry into the Barzakhic
The fixed element of the inquiry into the barzakhic is the barzakhic itself, held invariant while
the inquiry explains the conditions of its being. The barzakhic is held invariant as the subject of
the inquiry—the passage whose conditions the inquiry seeks to state.

18.9.2    The Fluid Element of the Inquiry into the Barzakhic
The fluid element of the inquiry into the barzakhic is the relation between the barzakhic and the
modes it mediates—the relation by which the barzakhic is the passage between the modes, and
by which the modes are the modes the barzakhic passes between. The relation is the medium of
the inquiry: it is what conveys the effect of the barzakhic’s being what it is to the modes’ being
what they are.

18.9.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Inquiry into the Barzakhic
The governing dynamics of the inquiry into the barzakhic is the rule by which the barzakhic’s
passage operates—the rule that explains how the passage transforms the identity, and under
what conditions the passage is possible. The rule is the subject of §18.4 and §18.6.

18.9.4    The Context of the Inquiry into the Barzakhic
The context of the inquiry into the barzakhic is the framework of Book I, in which the realms
are real and their relation is mediated. The context is the frame in which the inquiry is posed,
and it is what makes the inquiry an inquiry into the barzakhic, not an inquiry in general.

18.9.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the inquiry into the barzakhic are stated in the following table.

18.10      The Barzakhic in Each of the Three Hubs
The barzakhic category takes a different form in each of the three hubs. The present section
states the form, one hub at a time. The statements are (E) claims: they are structural estimates,
offered at the strength that the framework’s principles support.

18.10.1    The Hub of Decree
The barzakhic category in the Hub of Decree is the passage from unity to form. The passage
is the apportioning of the unity into the forms; the passage’s rules are proportion, order, and
harmony; the passage’s capacity is the range of apportioning configurations that the measure
admits. The passage is the hub’s mode of existence; the apportioning is what the passage does.
18.11. Objections and Replies                                                                    219


18.10.2     The Hub of Signification
The barzakhic category in the Hub of Signification is the passage from form to meaning. The
passage is the signification of the forms into meanings; the passage’s rules are truthfulness,
accuracy, and fidelity; the passage’s capacity is the range of signification configurations that the
sign admits. The passage is the hub’s mode of existence; the signification is what the passage
does.

18.10.3     The Hub of Realization
The barzakhic category in the Hub of Realization is the passage from meaning to matter. The
passage is the actualization of the meanings into matter; the passage’s rules are proportion in
realization, preservation of the realized, and continuation of realization; the passage’s capacity is
the range of realization configurations that the actualization admits. The passage is the hub’s
mode of existence; the actualization is what the passage does.

18.10.4     The Three Forms Together
The three forms are stated in the following table.

                Hub                     The Form of the Barzakhic Category
                Hub of Decree           Passage from unity to form (apportioning)
                Hub of Signification    Passage from form to meaning (significa-
                                        tion)
                Hub of Realization      Passage from meaning to matter (actual-
                                        ization)

    The table is the chapter’s map of the barzakhic category across the three hubs. It is an (E)
claim, and it is offered at the strength that the framework’s principles support. The table also
shows the relation between the barzakhic category and the three hubs’ rules: each hub’s form of
the category is the passage that the hub’s rules regulate.


18.11      Objections and Replies
Three objections are stated, and the replies are given.
    Objection 1: The barzakhic is a function, not a category. The objection is that the barzakhic
is what the fundamental realms do when they mediate; it is a function of the fundamental realms,
not a distinct level of being. The framework, the objection concludes, has dressed a function in
the language of a category.
    Reply. The objection confuses the function with the mode of existence. The function of
mediation is what the barzakhic does; the mode of existence (the passage) is what the barzakhic
is. The two are distinct, as the argument of §18.6 established: the barzakhic can lose its function
without ceasing to be the barzakhic, but it cannot lose its mode of existence without ceasing to
be the barzakhic. The objection mistakes the operation for the mode; the reply distinguishes
them.
    Objection 2: The barzakhic is a relation, not a category. The objection is that the barzakhic
is the relation between the fundamental realms; it is a connection, not a level. The framework,
the objection concludes, has reified a relation.
    Reply. The objection confuses the connection with the passage. A relation connects terms; a
passage transforms terms. The two are distinct, as the argument of §18.7 established: a term can
be connected to another term without being transformed by the connection. The barzakhic is
the passage, not the connection; the passage is what the connection presupposes, and the passage
220                           Chapter 18. The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category, Derived


is not reducible to the connection. The objection mistakes the connection for the passage; the
reply distinguishes them.
    Objection 3: The barzakhic is a composite, not a category. The objection is that the barzakhic
is made of the two fundamental realms it mediates; it is a composite of the two, not a distinct
level. The framework, the objection concludes, has reified a composite.
    Reply. The objection confuses the composite with the level. A composite is a whole made
of parts; the barzakhic is a level whose being is the passage. The barzakhic is not made of the
two realms; it is the passage between them. The distinction is the distinction between the whole
and the level: the barzakhic is the level, not the whole. The objection mistakes the parts for the
level; the reply distinguishes them.


18.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not analyze non-passage and presence. The analysis is the subject of
Chapter 19; the present chapter derives the barzakhic category, and it leaves the fuller account
of non-passage to the next chapter.
    Second, the chapter does not analyze the context of the whole. The analysis is the subject of
Chapter 20; the present chapter derives the barzakhic as a category, and it leaves the question of
the whole to the later chapter.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the three hubs are exhaustive.
The three hubs are derived from the passage between the fundamental realms; whether a fourth
hub is possible is a question the present chapter leaves open.
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the relation between the barzakhic and the fixed, fluid,
and governing triads of Parts II, III, and IV. The relation is the subject of Chapter 20; the
present chapter derives the barzakhic as a category, and it leaves the relation to the triads to the
later chapter.

18.14      A Question for Reflection
Consider a passage you know well—a rite of passage, a translation, a conversion, a crossing. Is
the passage a thing, a function, a relation, a process, or a composite? Or is it the passage itself,
a mode of existence whose being is the passing? What would it mean for the passage to have its
own reality, distinct from the things that pass through it?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The passage is the mode of existence; the
mode is the being of the passage; the being is what the passage is. The reader who can state, for
a passage he knows, what the mode, the being, and the passing are, has understood the chapter’s
distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and
is invited to develop the difficulty further.

The next chapter (Chapter 19) derives non-passage and presence: what is it for an identity to be
present in a realm without passing through the intermediate realms, and how does the barzakhic’s
category of passage make the non-passage possible? With the barzakhic category in place, the
framework can state what the non-necessity of downward passage presupposes in the order of
being.

Chapter 19

Non-Passage and Presence

Scope
This chapter states and argues the metaphysical principle of non-passage: the principle that
the presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm does not require that the identity pass
existentially through every realm that lies between. It draws on the epistemological principle of
non-sequential connectivity (Book I, Chapter 9) and on the framework’s account of realms as
contexts (Chapter ??), and it develops the metaphysical correlate of the epistemological principle:
presence as a structural relation, not a spatial or temporal one. It distinguishes passage from
presence, mediation from itinerary, and descent from travel. It argues that the barzakhic realms
mediate without requiring passage; it states what the principle does not say and what would
refute it; and it marks the boundary of what the chapter establishes. Its claims are metaphysical;
where it speaks of “presence,” “passage,” “mediation,” “descent,” “travel,” or “route,” these are
structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


19.1     A Scene
Consider an apple on a table. It is red. The redness is present in the apple: it is what we see
when we look at the apple, it is what we describe when we say “the apple is red,” it is what the
apple shares with other red things.
    Now ask: how did the redness come to be present in the apple? One answer is that the
redness traveled from a realm of forms, through every intermediate realm, and arrived in the
apple. The redness would then be the last stage of a long process, and the process would have to
be described in detail. The other answer is that the redness is present in the apple directly: the
apple participates in the redness, and the participation is not a journey. The redness is present
in the apple without having passed through every intermediate realm.
    The first answer has a difficulty: no such process is described, and the redness in the apple
does not seem to depend on the details of the process. The second answer has a different difficulty:
if the redness is present directly in the apple, how can it also be present in other red things?
The direct presence seems to make the redness many, one in each red thing.
    The two answers are not the only options. The framework’s answer is that the redness
is present in the apple directly, without passage through intermediate realms, and that the
directness is compatible with the redness being one. The redness is a form; the apple is a material
instance; the presence of the form in the instance is a structural relation, not a journey. The
relation is what the framework calls presence without passage.
    The scene poses a question. What is the structure of presence without passage? How can an
identity be present in a lower realm without having passed through every intermediate realm?
And what does the presence require, if it does not require passage?
224                                                      Chapter 19. Non-Passage and Presence


Remark 19.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question at
work in a familiar case. It does not prove the principle; it makes the principle intelligible before
it is stated. The principle is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and the scene carries
no weight in them. The redness is an example; the principle is about identities and realms in
general.


19.2     The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have developed the framework’s account of realms as contexts
(Chapter ??) and of the barzakhic realms as a metaphysical category (Chapter ??). The present
chapter turns to a principle that the framework has used but not yet stated in its metaphysical
form: the principle of non-passage.
    The question is: what does it mean for an identity to be present in a realm? Does presence
require passage through every intermediate realm, or can presence be direct? The framework’s
answer is that presence can be direct: the presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm
does not require that the identity pass existentially through every realm that lies between.
The principle is the metaphysical correlate of the epistemological principle of non-sequential
connectivity (Book I, Chapter 9), and it is the subject of this chapter.
    The question is not idle. If presence required passage, then every manifestation in a lower
realm would require the identity to be present in every intermediate realm, and the framework’s
account of the barzakhic realms would be mistaken: the hubs would be stations through which
every manifestation must pass, not mediators that regulate the relation without requiring passage.
The present chapter argues that the framework’s account is the second, and it states the principle
that makes the account coherent.
    The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the principle. It distinguishes passage from
presence, and mediation from itinerary. It states presence as a structural relation. It argues for
the principle. It states the relation between the principle and the barzakhic realms. It states
what the principle does not say, and what would refute it. And it marks what the chapter does
not establish.
Remark 19.2 (The Question Is About Presence, Not About the Realms). The question is about
presence, not about the realms. The realms have been stated in Chapter ??; the barzakhic
realms have been stated in Chapter ??. The present chapter asks what it is for an identity to be
present in a realm, and whether the presence requires passage. The question presupposes the
account of the realms; it does not restate it.


19.3     The Principle Stated
Principle 19.3 (Non-Passage). (T) The presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm does
not require that the identity pass existentially through every realm that lies between. The
relation between realms is not confined to a single sequential route.

    The principle is stated as a claim about presence and effect. It does not say that the
intermediate realms are idle or dispensable; it says that the presence of an identity in a lower
realm does not require that the identity be present in each intermediate realm in turn. The
intermediate realms may still regulate, condition, or transform the relation (Chapter ??); what
they do not do is require the identity to traverse them.
    The principle is (T): it is argued from the framework’s account of realms (Chapter ??), of the
barzakhic realms (Chapter ??), and of the manifestation relation (Chapter ??). The argument is
given in Section 19.7. The principle’s status is therefore the status of its premises; a reader who
accepts the premises should accept the principle, and a reader who rejects one of the premises
has a reason to reject the principle.
19.4. Passage and Presence Distinguished                                                       225


Remark 19.4 (The Principle Is the Metaphysical Correlate of Non-Sequential Connectivity).
The principle is the metaphysical correlate of the epistemological principle of non-sequential
connectivity (Book I, Chapter 9). The epistemological principle says that the conveyor principle
does not require the connection between two fixed elements to pass through all intermediate fixed
elements. The metaphysical principle says that the presence of an identity in a lower realm does
not require the identity to pass through all intermediate realms. The two are related: the first is
about the structure of explanation; the second is about the structure of being. The framework’s
claim is that the two principles are compatible, and that the second is the metaphysical form of
the first.
Remark 19.5 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Mediation). The principle is not a denial
of mediation. The barzakhic realms mediate the relation between the fundamental realms
(Chapter ??); the principle says that the mediation does not require passage. The distinction is
the distinction between mediation and itinerary; the framework keeps it throughout. A reader
who takes the principle as a denial of mediation has misread it; a reader who takes it as a denial
of the necessity of passage has read it correctly.


19.4      Passage and Presence Distinguished
The principle turns on a distinction between two things that are easily run together: passage
and presence. The distinction is stated in two definitions.

Definition 19.6 (Passage). Passage is the existential traversal of a realm by an identity: the
identity is present in the realm as such, in the course of moving from its realm of origin to a
lower realm.

Definition 19.7 (Presence). Presence is the structural relation in which an identity is realized,
or its effect is realized, in a realm. Presence does not require that the identity have been present
in the intermediate realms; it requires only that the identity be realized in the realm in question.

    The two definitions are different, and the difference is the difference between a route and a
realization. Passage is a route: the identity goes through the realm. Presence is a realization:
the identity is in the realm, whether or not it passed through the intermediate ones.
Remark 19.8 (The Distinction Is Structural, Not Verbal). The distinction is structural, not
verbal. If passage and presence were the same, the principle of non-passage would be false by
definition: every presence would be a passage. But the distinction shows that presence can
obtain without passage: the identity can be realized in the lower realm without having traversed
the intermediate ones. The distinction is what makes the principle stateable.
Remark 19.9 (The Distinction Is Not the Distinction Between the Real and the Unreal). The
distinction is not the distinction between the real and the unreal. Both passage and presence are
real; the question is which one the relation between realms requires. The framework’s claim is
that presence is required and passage is not; it does not claim that passage never occurs, and it
does not claim that presence is a lesser form of reality.
Remark 19.10 (The Table of the Distinction). The distinction is summarized in the following
table.


 Aspect                         Passage                                                Presence
 What it is                     Existential traversal of a realm                       Realization in a realm
 What it requires               The identity is present in each intermediate realm     The identity is realized in t
 What it is not                 A structural relation                                  A route
 What the framework holds       Not required                                           Required
226                                                        Chapter 19. Non-Passage and Presence


    The table is a summary, not a new argument. Its purpose is to locate the distinction in the
framework’s architecture: passage is the route; presence is the realization. The framework’s
claim is that presence is required and passage is not.


19.5      Presence as a Structural Relation
The principle of non-passage turns on the concept of presence. The present section states what
presence is, and what it is not.
     Presence is not spatial location. A material object is present in a place by occupying it; an
identity is not present in a realm by occupying it. The identity is not a thing that can be located
in a region; it is a structural determination that can be realized in a realm.
     Presence is not temporal simultaneity. A material event is present at a time by occurring
then; an identity is not present in a realm by occurring at a time. The identity is not an event;
it is a structural determination that can be realized in a realm, with the temporality that the
realm permits.
     Presence is the realization of the identity, or of its effect, in the realm. The realization is the
identity’s being what it is in the mode of the realm; it is the identity’s taking the form that the
realm’s capacity permits. The realization is not a copy of the identity, and it is not the identity
itself; it is the identity in the mode of the realm.

Principle 19.11 (Presence as Structural Realization). (T) The presence of an identity in a
realm is the structural realization of the identity, or of its effect, in the realm, according to
the realm’s capacity. Presence is not spatial location and not temporal simultaneity; it is the
realization of the identity in the mode of the realm.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the framework’s account of realms (Chapter ??) and of
the manifestation relation (Chapter ??). The realization is the identity’s taking the form the
realm permits; the presence is the realization.
Remark 19.12 (Presence Is Indexed to the Realm). Presence is indexed to the realm. The same
identity can be present in different realms in different modes; the presence in each realm is the
realization of the identity in that realm’s mode. The identity is one; the presences are many; the
many presences are the identity’s presence in the many realms.
Remark 19.13 (Presence Is Compatible with Non-Passage). Presence is compatible with non-
passage. The identity can be realized in a lower realm without having been present in the
intermediate realms; the realization does not require the route. The principle of non-passage is
the statement of this compatibility.
Remark 19.14 (Presence Is Not a Relation Among Realms). Presence is not a relation among
realms; it is a relation between an identity and a realm. The relation among realms is the order
of the realms and the mediation of the barzakhic realms; the relation between the identity and
the realm is the realization. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.


19.6      Mediation Is Not Itinerary
The principle is easily confused with a stronger claim that it does not entail: the claim that
the relation between realms is immediate, with no mediation at all. The confusion is worth
distinguishing.
    Mediation is the structural regulation, conditioning, or transformation of a relation between
two realms by a third realm whose mode of existence includes that function (Chapter ??).
Mediation is the presence of the hub as a condition, not the presence of the identity as a term.
The identity does not have to be present in the hub for the hub to mediate the relation.
19.7. The Argument                                                                                 227


    Itinerary is the route that the identity takes from its realm of origin to its destination. The
itinerary is a sequence of realms through which the identity passes. The principle of non-passage
says that the presence of the identity in the destination realm does not require an itinerary; it
does not say that the relation has no mediation.
    The distinction is the distinction between mediation and itinerary. The barzakhic realms
mediate; the identity does not have to pass through them. The mediation is the condition; the
itinerary is the route. The framework’s claim is that the condition is required and the route is
not.
Remark 19.15 (The Distinction Is the Distinction Between the Hub and the Station). The hub is
the level at which the relation is regulated; the station is the level at which the identity is present
in the course of passage. The hub is not a station; the identity does not have to be present in
the hub for the hub to mediate the relation. The distinction is structural, and the framework
keeps it throughout.
Remark 19.16 (The Distinction Resolves an Apparent Tension). The distinction resolves an
apparent tension between the mediation of the barzakhic realms and the non-passage of the
identity. If mediation required passage, the barzakhic realms would be stations through which
every manifestation must pass, and the framework’s account of the hubs as mediators would be
mistaken. The distinction shows that mediation does not require passage: the hubs mediate
the relation without requiring the identity to traverse them. The tension is dissolved by the
distinction.


19.7      The Argument
The argument for the principle proceeds in three steps.

Argument for Non-Passage.      1. By the framework’s account of realms (Chapter ??), each
     realm has a determinate capacity: its mode of existence permits certain manifestations
     and constrains others. The form that an identity takes in a realm is fixed by the identity
     and that realm’s capacity, not by what the identity became in the intermediate realms.

   2. By the framework’s account of the barzakhic realms (Chapter ??), the hubs mediate the
      relation between the fundamental realms. The mediation is the regulation, conditioning, or
      transformation of the relation; it is not the traversal of the identity through the hub.

   3. By the framework’s account of the manifestation relation (Chapter ??), the manifestation
      of an identity in a realm is the product of the identity and the receiving realm. It does not
      require that the identity have been manifested in every intermediate realm.

   4. Therefore the presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm does not require that the
      identity pass existentially through every realm that lies between.

    The argument’s force is in step 1. If the form an identity takes in a lower realm were fixed by
what the identity became in the intermediate realms, then the intermediate realms would be
necessary for the presence, and the principle would be false. But the form is fixed by the identity
and the receiving realm; the intermediate realms do not contribute to the form. The principle
follows.
Remark 19.17 (The Argument Is Relative to Its Premises). The argument depends on the
framework’s accounts of realms, of the barzakhic realms, and of the manifestation relation. A
reader who rejects one of these accounts has a reason to reject the principle; the framework does
not pretend otherwise. The argument’s value is not that it proves the principle from nothing; it
is that it shows what the principle depends on, and what would refute it.
228                                                     Chapter 19. Non-Passage and Presence


Remark 19.18 (The Argument Is Not a Proof That Intermediate Realms Are Irrelevant). The
argument does not show that the intermediate realms are irrelevant. The barzakhic realms have
functions of their own (Chapter ??); the fundamental realms have rules of their own (Chapter ??);
the intermediate realms may regulate, condition, or transform the relation without requiring
passage. The argument shows only that the relation does not require passage; it does not show
that the relation is unmediated.


19.8     The Relation to the Barzakhic Realms
The principle of non-passage is related to the framework’s account of the barzakhic realms
(Chapter ??), and the relation is worth stating.
    The barzakhic realms mediate the relation between the fundamental realms. The mediation
is the regulation, conditioning, or transformation of the relation by a realm whose mode of
existence includes that function. The mediation does not require the identity to pass through
the hub; it requires the hub to be present as a condition of the relation.
    The principle of non-passage says that the identity does not have to pass through the hub
for the hub to mediate the relation. The principle is compatible with the mediation, and the
mediation is compatible with the principle. The two are different: the mediation is the condition;
the non-passage is the absence of the requirement of passage.
Remark 19.19 (The Hubs Are Conditions, Not Stations). The hubs are conditions of the relation,
not stations through which the identity passes. The hub is present as a condition; the identity
is present as a term. The distinction is the distinction between the condition and the term;
the framework keeps it throughout. A reader who takes the hubs as stations has misread the
framework’s account; a reader who takes them as conditions has read it correctly.
Remark 19.20 (The Principle Is Compatible with the Mediation). The principle is compatible
with the mediation. The principle says that the identity does not have to pass through the hub;
the mediation says that the hub regulates the relation. The two are different claims, and they
are compatible. The framework’s claim is that the mediation is required and the passage is not;
the principle is the statement of the second claim.
Remark 19.21 (The Relation Is Not Sequential). The relation between the realms is not sequential
in the sense that the identity must pass through every realm in turn. The relation is structural:
the realms are ordered by the order of expression (Chapter ??), and the barzakhic realms mediate
the transitions. The order of expression is not a route; it is the order of the realms’ generality.
The principle of non-passage is the statement that the order of expression does not impose a
route.


19.9     What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that the intermediate realms are idle. The barzakhic realms have
functions of their own; the fundamental realms have rules of their own. The intermediate realms
may regulate, condition, or transform the relation without requiring passage.
    The principle does not say that the relation is immediate, with no mediation. The barzakhic
realms mediate the relation; the principle says that the mediation does not require passage.
The two are different: the mediation is the condition; the non-passage is the absence of the
requirement of passage.
    The principle does not say that passage never occurs. The principle says that passage is not
required. In some cases, an identity may be present in every intermediate realm; in others, it
may not. The framework does not decide in advance which case holds; it states the principle
19.10. What Would Refute the Principle                                                        229


that the relation does not require passage, and it leaves the question of what actually occurs to
the inquiry.
    The principle does not deny direct action. The principle is a claim about the relation between
realms; it does not claim that every effect must be mediated by the realms. A direct effect—an
effect that comes from beyond the architecture itself—is not excluded by the principle. The
framework’s claim is that the architecture does not require passage; it does not claim that the
architecture is the whole of what is.
Remark 19.22 (The Principle Leaves Direct Action Open). The principle leaves direct action
open. It says that the relation between realms does not require passage; it does not say that
every effect must be mediated by the realms. The distinction is the distinction between the
architecture and what lies beyond it; the framework keeps it throughout. A reader who takes
the principle as a denial of direct action has misread it; a reader who takes it as a claim about
the architecture has read it correctly.
Remark 19.23 (No Conflict with the Manifestation Relation). The manifestation relation is
compatible with the principle of non-passage. An identity appears in a lower realm in a form
suited to that realm; the form is fixed by the identity and the receiving realm. Nothing in this
requires that the identity have appeared in each intermediate realm on the way. The manifestation
relation says what the appearance is; the non-passage principle says what the appearance does
not require.


19.10      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in Section 19.7. What would refute it is worth
stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that the form an identity takes in a lower realm is
fixed by what the identity became in the intermediate realms. If such a showing could be made,
the intermediate realms would be necessary for the presence, and the principle would be false.
The framework’s claim is that the form is fixed by the identity and the receiving realm, and that
the intermediate realms do not contribute to the form.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the barzakhic realms require the identity
to pass through them for the mediation to occur. If such a showing could be made, the mediation
would require passage, and the principle would be false. The framework’s claim is that the
mediation is the presence of the hub as a condition, not the presence of the identity as a term;
the two claims are different, and the principle is the second.
Remark 19.24 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the framework’s account of the form; the second challenges the framework’s account of
mediation. The two challenges require different responses, and the framework responds to each in
its own terms. The first is answered by the framework’s account of manifestation (Chapter ??);
the second by the framework’s account of mediation (Chapter ??).


19.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the order of grounding. The order of grounding—the
order in which what is depends on what—is stated in a later part of the book (Part VI); the
present chapter states the principle of non-passage, which is part of the order of cognition.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the barzakhic realms. The barzakhic
realms are stated in Chapter ??; the present chapter states the principle of non-passage, which
is related to the account of the barzakhic realms but does not develop it.
230                                                       Chapter 19. Non-Passage and Presence


    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of which identities are present in which realms.
The principle states that the presence does not require passage; it does not state which identities
are present in which realms. The question of which identities are present in which realms is a
matter for the inquiry, not for the principle.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the principle. It claims to
have described the principle, and the principle points beyond itself to its ground. The question
of what grounds the principle is left to a later part of the book, and the present chapter is silent
on it by method, not by denial.
Remark 19.25 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
stated the principle of non-passage, as the metaphysical correlate of the epistemological principle
of non-sequential connectivity. It has distinguished passage from presence, and mediation from
itinerary. It has stated presence as a structural relation. It has argued for the principle, from the
framework’s accounts of realms, of the barzakhic realms, and of the manifestation relation. And
it has stated the relation between the principle and the barzakhic realms, and what would refute
the principle.
Remark 19.26 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter ??). The chapter prepares Chapter ??, which
states the context of the whole. The principle of non-passage states that the presence of an
identity in a realm does not require passage through every intermediate realm. Chapter ?? states
the context in which the realms stand—the whole of the realms as a context—and the relation
between the whole and its parts. The two chapters together state the framework’s account of
the relation between the realms: the realms are distinct, ordered, and mediated, and their order
does not impose a route.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a case in which an identity is present in a lower realm—a law in a particular case, a
color in a particular object, a meaning in a particular utterance. Did the identity have to pass
through every intermediate realm to be present in the lower one? What would it mean to say
that it did? What does your answer tell you about the relation between presence and passage,
and about the principle of non-passage?

relation between the realms; the next chapter states the context in which the realms stand.
