Chapter 20

The Context of the Whole

Scope
This chapter states the framework’s account of the context of the whole: the encompassing
context in which all the realms stand. It defines the context of the whole, argues that it is
not a realm, distinguishes it from the contexts of the parts, and states the relation between
the whole and its parts. It connects the context of the whole to the divine ground, which
Part VI develops, and to the order of grounding, which Part VI states. It does not develop the
divine ground in detail; it states the context that the divine ground encompasses. Its claims are
metaphysical; where it speaks of “the whole,” “context,” “part,” “encompassing,” or “order,”
these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter.


20.1     A Scene
Consider a library. Each book in the library is in its place. The place of a book is its shelf, its
room, its floor. But the library itself is not a book, and it is not a shelf, or a room, or a floor.
The library is the order in which the books, the shelves, the rooms, and the floors stand. The
order is not a book; it is the context in which the books are placed.
    Now ask: where is the library? The library is not in a place in the way a book is. The library
is the encompassing order in which the places are. To ask “where is the library?” is to ask for
the place of the order of places, and the order of places is not itself in a place.
    The scene is not about libraries. It is about the relation between a whole and its parts. The
whole is not a part of itself; it is the order in which the parts stand. The order is the context of
the parts. And the order is not in a place the way a part is; it is the encompassing context of
the places.
    The scene poses a question. What is the context of the whole? The whole of the realms is
like the library; the realms are like the books. The context of the whole is the order in which the
realms stand. It is not a realm; it is the encompassing context of the realms.
Remark 20.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the relation
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them.


20.2     The Question
The previous chapters of Part V have developed the framework’s account of realms as contexts
(Chapter ??), of the barzakhic realms as a metaphysical category (Chapter ??), and of non-
passage and presence (Chapter ??). The present chapter turns to a question that these chapters
234                                                       Chapter 20. The Context of the Whole


have prepared but not yet stated: what is the context of the whole?
    The question is: is there a context in which all the realms stand, and if so, what is it? The
framework’s answer is that there is: the context of the whole is the encompassing order in which
the realms stand. It is not a realm; it is the context of the realms. The framework calls it the
Throne-Domain, and it is the subject of this chapter.
    The question is not idle. If there were no context of the whole, the realms would be a plurality
without an order, and the framework’s claim that the realms are ordered would be unsupported.
If the context of the whole were a realm, it would be one of the realms, and the framework’s
claim that the realms are not the whole would be false. The present chapter argues that there is
a context of the whole, that it is not a realm, and that it is the encompassing order in which the
realms stand.
    The chapter proceeds as follows. It defines the context of the whole. It argues that the
context of the whole is not a realm. It distinguishes the context of the whole from the contexts
of the parts. It states the relation between the whole and its parts. It connects the context of
the whole to the divine ground. It states what the principle does not say, and what would refute
it. And it marks what the chapter does not establish.
Remark 20.2 (The Question Presupposes the Realms). The question presupposes the realms.
The realms have been stated in Chapter ??; the barzakhic realms have been stated in Chapter ??.
The present chapter asks what the context of the whole is, given the realms; it does not restate
the realms, and it does not argue for their existence.


20.3      The Context of the Whole Defined
The context of the whole is defined in a definition.

Definition 20.3 (Context of the Whole). The context of the whole is the encompassing order in
which all the realms stand. It is not a realm, and it is not a part of any realm; it is the context
in which the realms are situated, the order of their standing, and the condition of their being
together.

     The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
     The first part: the context of the whole is an order. It is not a thing, not a realm, not a part;
it is the order in which the realms stand. The order is real; it is what makes the realms a whole,
rather than a plurality of unrelated realms.
     The second part: the context of the whole is encompassing. It encompasses the realms; the
realms stand within it. The encompassing is not spatial; it is the order of the realms’ standing.
The realms are not in the context the way books are in a library; they are in the context the way
books are in the order that the library is.
     The third part: the context of the whole is the condition of the realms’ being together. Without
the context, the realms would be unrelated; with the context, they are a whole. The context is
what makes the whole a whole.
Remark 20.4 (The Context of the Whole Is Not the Sum of the Realms). The context of the
whole is not the sum of the realms. The sum of the realms would be a collection; the context of
the whole is the order of the collection. The order is not the collection; it is what makes the
collection a whole. A reader who takes the context of the whole as the sum of the realms has
misread the definition; a reader who takes it as the order of the realms has read it correctly.
Remark 20.5 (The Context of the Whole Is Not a Realm). The context of the whole is not a
realm. The realms are the levels of being; the context of the whole is the order in which the levels
stand. The order is not a level; it is the context of the levels. The distinction is the distinction
between the levels and the order of the levels; the framework keeps it throughout.
20.4. The Whole Is Not a Realm                                                                     235


20.4      The Whole Is Not a Realm
The definition states that the context of the whole is not a realm. The present section argues for
the claim.
Principle 20.6 (The Whole Is Not a Realm). (T) The context of the whole is not a realm. It is
not one of the seven realms, and it is not an eighth realm. It is the encompassing order in which
the seven realms stand.
   The principle is (T): it is argued from the definition of the context of the whole (Definition 20.3)
and from the framework’s account of realms (Chapter ??). The argument is given below.

Argument for the Principle.   1. A realm is an independently real mode of existence, with its
     own capacity and its own rules (Chapter ??).
   2. The context of the whole is the order in which the realms stand (Definition 20.3). It does
      not have a mode of existence of its own; it has the mode of existence of the order of the
      realms.
   3. If the context of the whole were a realm, it would have a mode of existence of its own, and
      the realms would stand in a realm among realms. But the context of the whole is the order
      of the realms, not a realm among them.
   4. Therefore the context of the whole is not a realm.

    The argument’s force is in step 2. If the context of the whole had a mode of existence of
its own, it would be a realm; but it is the order of the realms, and the order is not a mode of
existence among the modes. The principle follows.
Remark 20.7 (The Context of the Whole Is Created). The context of the whole is created. It is
not God, and it is not a part of God. The framework’s account is that God is the transcendent
Creator and ground of the whole (Book I, Principle 7.3), and the context of the whole is the
encompassing order of the created realms. The distinction is the distinction between the Creator
and the created order; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 20.8 (The Context of the Whole Is Not an Eighth Realm). The context of the whole is
not an eighth realm. The framework’s account has seven realms (Chapter ??); the context of
the whole is the order of the seven, not an additional realm. A reader who takes the context of
the whole as an eighth realm has misread the framework’s account; a reader who takes it as the
order of the seven has read it correctly.


20.5      The Context of the Whole and the Contexts of the Parts
The context of the whole is related to the contexts of the parts, and the relation is worth stating.
    Each realm is a context (Chapter ??): the realm is the existential context in which manifes-
tations are realized. The context of the whole is the context in which the realms stand. The two
are different: the realm is the context of the parts; the context of the whole is the context of the
contexts.
    The relation is the relation between the whole and its parts. The whole is not the sum of the
parts; it is the order in which the parts stand. The context of the whole is not the sum of the
contexts of the parts; it is the order in which the contexts of the parts stand.
Principle 20.9 (The Context of the Whole Is the Condition of the Contexts of the Parts). (T)
The context of the whole is the condition of possibility of the contexts of the parts. Without the
context of the whole, the contexts of the parts would not be a plurality of ordered realms; they
would be a plurality of unrelated contexts. The context of the whole is what makes the plurality
a whole.
236                                                     Chapter 20. The Context of the Whole


   The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of the context of the whole and from the
framework’s account of realms. The argument is that the realms are ordered (Chapter ??), and
the order is the context of the whole; without the order, the realms would not be ordered.
Remark 20.10 (The Context of the Whole Is Not the Context of Any Realm). The context of the
whole is not the context of any realm. The context of a realm is the realm itself; the context of
the whole is the order in which the realms stand. The two are different: the first is a realm; the
second is the order of the realms. The framework keeps them apart.
Remark 20.11 (The Context of the Whole Is Not the Cognitive Context). The context of the
whole is not the cognitive context. The cognitive context is the frame in which cognition occurs
(Book I, Chapter 6); the context of the whole is the order in which the realms stand. The two
are different: the first is a frame of inquiry; the second is an order of being. The framework
keeps them apart.


20.6     The Whole and Its Parts
The relation between the whole and its parts is worth stating in its own place.
    The whole is not the sum of its parts. The sum of the parts would be a collection; the whole
is the order of the collection. The order is what makes the collection a whole.
    The whole is not a part of itself. The whole is the order of the parts, and the order is not
a part. The whole is not in the parts the way a part is in the whole; the whole is the order in
which the parts stand.
    The whole is not prior to the parts in time. The parts and the whole are simultaneous; the
whole is the order of the parts, and the order is not a stage that comes after the parts. The
whole is the order of the parts, and the order is what the parts are as a whole.
Principle 20.12 (The Whole Is the Order of the Parts). (T) The whole is the order of the parts,
not the sum of the parts, not a part of itself, and not a stage that comes after the parts. The
whole is what the parts are as a whole.
   The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of the context of the whole and from the
framework’s account of realms. The argument is that the realms are ordered, and the order is
the whole; the whole is not the sum, not a part, and not a stage.
Remark 20.13 (The Whole Is Not a Substance). The whole is not a substance. A substance is a
thing with properties; the whole is the order in which the things stand. The distinction is the
distinction between a thing and an order; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 20.14 (The Whole Is Not an Accident). The whole is not an accident. An accident
is a property of a substance; the whole is the order of the substances. The distinction is the
distinction between a property and an order; the framework keeps it throughout.


20.7     The Context of the Whole and the Divine Ground
The context of the whole is related to the divine ground, and the relation is worth stating.
    The context of the whole is the encompassing order of the created realms. The divine ground
is God, the transcendent Creator and ground of the whole (Book I, Principle 7.3). The two are
different: the context of the whole is created; the divine ground is the Creator. The context of
the whole points beyond itself to the divine ground.
    The context of the whole is not God. It is not the divine essence, not a part of God, and not
an aspect of God. It is the order of the created realms, and the order is created.
    The divine ground is not the context of the whole. God is not a context; God is the ground
of every context. The context of the whole is the order of the realms; the divine ground is the
ground of the order. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
20.8. What the Principle Does Not Say                                                         237


Principle 20.15 (The Context of the Whole Points Beyond Itself). (T) The context of the
whole points beyond itself to the divine ground. The context is the order of the created realms;
it is not self-grounded. The divine ground is the ground of the order.

   The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of the context of the whole and from the
framework’s account of the divine ground (Book I, Principle 7.3). The argument is that the
context of the whole is created, and the created order points beyond itself to its Creator.
Remark 20.16 (The Context of the Whole Is Not the Divine Ground). The context of the whole is
not the divine ground. The context is created; the divine ground is the Creator. The distinction
is the distinction between the created order and its Creator; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 20.17 (The Divine Ground Is Not a Context). The divine ground is not a context.
God is not a frame, not an order, not a realm. God is the ground of every frame, every order,
every realm. The distinction is the distinction between the ground and what is grounded; the
framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 20.18 (The Context of the Whole Is the Throne-Domain). The context of the whole
is what Book I calls the Throne-Domain (Book I, Definition 7.4). The Throne-Domain is the
encompassing order of divine sovereignty and governance within which the sevenfold architecture
of created existence is situated. The context of the whole is the same order, stated in the
metaphysical vocabulary of the present volume.


20.8     What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that the context of the whole is unreal. The context is real; it is
the order in which the realms stand. The principle says that the context is not a realm; it does
not say that the context is nothing.
    The principle does not say that the realms are unreal. The realms are real; the context is the
order of the realms. The principle says that the context is not a realm; it does not say that the
realms are not real.
    The principle does not say that the context is dispensable. The context is the condition of
the realms’ being together; without the context, the realms would not be a whole. The principle
says that the context is not a realm; it does not say that the context is not needed.
    The principle does not say that God is the context. God is the ground of the context; the
context is the created order. The principle says that the context is not a realm; it does not say
that the context is God.
Remark 20.19 (The Principle Leaves the Divine Ground Open). The principle leaves the divine
ground open. It says that the context of the whole is not a realm; it does not say what the divine
ground is. The divine ground is the subject of Part VI; the present chapter states the context of
the whole, and it leaves the divine ground to its place.
Remark 20.20 (No Conflict with the Manifestation Relation). The manifestation relation is
compatible with the context of the whole. A manifestation is realized in a realm; the realm is a
context; the context of the whole is the order of the contexts. The manifestation relation says
what the appearance is; the context of the whole says what the order of the appearances is. The
two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.


20.9     What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
238                                                       Chapter 20. The Context of the Whole


    The principle would be refuted by showing that the context of the whole is a realm. If such a
showing could be made, the context would be one of the realms, and the principle would be false.
The framework’s claim is that the context is the order of the realms, not a realm among them.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that there is no context of the whole. If such
a showing could be made, the realms would be a plurality without an order, and the principle
would be false. The framework’s claim is that the realms are ordered (Chapter ??), and the
order is the context of the whole.
Remark 20.21 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the framework’s account of the context; the second challenges the framework’s account
of the realms. The two challenges require different responses, and the framework responds to
each in its own terms.


20.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the divine ground. The divine ground is the subject of
Part VI; the present chapter states the context of the whole, and it leaves the divine ground to
its place.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the order of grounding. The order of grounding is the
order in which what is depends on what; it is stated in Part VI. The present chapter states the
context of the whole, and it connects the context to the divine ground, but it does not develop
the order of grounding.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of what the context of the whole is in itself.
The principle states that the context is not a realm; it does not state what the context is in itself.
The question of what the context is in itself is left to a later part of the book.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the whole. It claims to have described
the context of the whole; the whole is more than its context, and the chapter is silent on what
lies beyond the context by method, not by denial.
Remark 20.22 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
defined the context of the whole. It has argued that the context of the whole is not a realm. It
has stated the relation between the whole and its parts, and the relation between the context of
the whole and the contexts of the parts. And it has connected the context of the whole to the
divine ground, and stated what would refute the principle.
Remark 20.23 (The Chapter Closes Part V). The chapter closes Part V. Part V has developed
the framework’s account of the context of metaphysics: the realms as contexts (Chapter ??),
the barzakhic realms as a metaphysical category (Chapter ??), non-passage and presence
(Chapter ??), and the context of the whole (the present chapter). Part VII turns from the
context to the viability of the metaphysical order: the integration of the structural character of
viability (Book I, Chapter 36) with the metaphysical order of the realms, of the fixed elements,
of the fluid elements, and of the governing dynamics.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a whole you know—a family, a tradition, a practice, a body of work. Is the whole the
sum of its parts, or the order in which the parts stand? What would it mean to say that the
whole is a part of itself? What does your answer tell you about the relation between the whole
and its parts, and about the context of the whole?
Part V is complete. Part VII turns from the context of metaphysics to the viability of the
metaphysical order: the integration of the structural character of viability (Book I, Chapter 36)
with the metaphysical order of the realms, of the fixed elements, of the fluid elements, and of the
governing dynamics. The reader who has followed Part V has the vocabulary; Part VII puts it to
work.

From Context to Integration

Scope
This chapter is the transition between Part V (Context) and Part VI (Divine Ground). It asks
how the four columns of metaphysics—fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and
context—converge in a realm, and it argues that the convergence is what the framework calls
viability. It states the three components of viability (fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability)
as the components of the convergence, and it shows that they are derived from the four columns,
not stipulated independently. It then states that the convergence points beyond itself to its
ground—the divine ground—which Part VI will state.
    The chapter’s claims are metaphysical and structural. Where it speaks of “convergence,”
“integration,” “viability,” “fidelity,” “sustainability,” or “recoverability,” these are structural terms;
their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and by the framework of Book I.

      Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given the four-column frame-
      work of Book I (Principles 7.1 and 7.2), the conveyor principle (Principle 8.1), the
      non-sequential connectivity (Principle 9.1), the context-dependence principle (Princi-
      ple 10.1), the openness of relations (Principle 11.1), and the definition of viability
      (Definition 36.1). It also takes as given the derivations of the fixed elements (Part II),
      the fluid elements (Part III), the governing dynamics (Part IV), and the contexts
      (Part V). It does not restate these; it asks how they converge, and it argues that the
      convergence is what the framework calls viability.


20.12       A Scene: The Four Rivers
Consider four rivers that flow from four different sources and converge in a single lake. The first
river comes from the mountains; it is cold, clear, and fast. The second comes from the forests; it
is warm, dark, and slow. The third comes from the plains; it is broad, shallow, and steady. The
fourth comes from the springs; it is deep, still, and constant.
    Each river is real, and each is distinct. The first is not the second; the third is not the fourth.
But in the lake, the four rivers are one. The lake is not the first river, nor the second, nor the
third, nor the fourth. The lake is the convergence of the four.
    The scene is not about rivers in particular. It is about a general structure, and the structure
is this: four distinct things can converge in a single reality, and the reality is not any of the four,
but the convergence of the four. The convergence is real, and its reality is the reality of the
relation among the four, not the reality of any one of them.
    Now consider a harder case. Consider a lake whose water is not the same at any two points.
The water near the mountain river is cold and clear; the water near the forest river is warm
and dark; the water near the plain river is broad and shallow; the water near the spring is deep
and still. The lake is one, but its water is not uniform. The unity of the lake is the unity of a
convergence, not the unity of a homogeneous substance.
    The lake is what the framework calls a realm, and the four rivers are what the framework
calls the four columns: the fixed elements, the fluid elements, the governing dynamics, and
242                                                                    From Context to Integration


the context. The lake is the convergence of the four columns, and the convergence is what the
framework calls viability.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. How do the four columns converge in a
realm? What is the structure of their convergence? And why is “viability” the only adequate
description of their convergence? The chapter’s answer is: the four columns converge as the
fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
in the realm, and viability is the name of that convergence.


20.13       The Question
Parts II to V have derived the four columns of metaphysics: the fixed elements (substance,
essence, thisness), the fluid elements (causation, relation, light), the governing dynamics (law,
necessity, the modal space), and the contexts (the realms, the barzakhic category, non-passage).
Each part has derived its column from the corresponding column of Book I, and each has stated
the column’s structure.
     The present chapter asks: how do the four columns converge in a realm? The question is not
what each column is; the previous parts have said that. The question is how the four columns
are related in the concrete reality of a realm, and what the structure of their relation is.
     The question has three aspects.
     The first aspect: what is the convergence of the four columns? The chapter must state what
it is for the four columns to converge, and it must distinguish the convergence from the mere
co-presence of the four columns.
     The second aspect: why is “viability” the name of the convergence? The chapter must argue
that viability—the structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
in a context (Book I, Definition 36.1)—is the only adequate description of the convergence. The
argument is the chapter’s principal contribution.
     The third aspect: what does the convergence point beyond itself to? The chapter must state
that the convergence is not self-grounded, and that it points beyond itself to its ground. The
pointing is the transition to Part VI (Divine Ground).
     The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: the four
columns converge as the fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability of the relation between an
identity and its manifestations; viability is the name of that convergence; and the convergence
points beyond itself to the divine ground.


20.14       The Convergence of the Four Columns
20.14.1     The Four Columns Are Not Separate
The first thing to be said about the convergence is that the four columns are not separate. They
are not four independent structures that happen to be found together; they are four aspects of
one structure—the structure of a realm’s reality. The fixed elements are what the realm holds
invariant; the fluid elements are what conveys the relation among them; the governing dynamics
is what rules the relation; the context is what frames the relation. The four are aspects of one
structure, and the structure is the realm.
    The distinction is the distinction between the columns as analytical roles and the columns as
aspects of one reality. As analytical roles, the columns are distinct (Book I, Principle 7.2); as
aspects of one reality, the columns are inseparable. The convergence is what the framework calls
the realm’s viability.
20.15. Why Viability Is the Name of the Convergence                                               243


20.14.2     The Convergence Is the Relation
The second thing to be said about the convergence is that the convergence is the relation among
the four columns, not the columns themselves. The relation is not a fifth thing added to the
four; it is what the four are in their togetherness. The relation is the fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability of the identity’s expression in the realm.
    The distinction is the distinction between the columns and the relation among them. The
columns are the terms; the relation is what the terms are in their togetherness. The relation is
what the framework calls viability.

20.14.3     The Convergence Is Derived from the Four Columns
The third thing to be said about the convergence is that the convergence is derived from the four
columns, not stipulated independently. The three components of viability—fidelity, sustainability,
and recoverability—are derived from the four columns as follows.
    Fidelity is derived from the fixed elements. The fixed elements are what the realm holds
invariant. For the fixed elements to be held invariant, the manifestations of the identity must
preserve the identity’s essential determination. The preservation is what the framework calls
fidelity.
    Sustainability is derived from the fluid elements and the governing dynamics. The fluid
elements convey the relation; the governing dynamics rules the relation. For the relation to be
maintained, the cost of the conveyance and the rule must not exceed what the realm can bear.
The condition is what the framework calls sustainability.
    Recoverability is derived from the context. The context is the realm in which the identity is
manifested. For the identity to retain its capacity to manifest, the realm must not have crossed
the singularity at which restoring the manifestation would cost more than producing a new one.
The condition is what the framework calls recoverability.
    The three derivations are the chapter’s principal contribution. They show that viability is
not a fifth column added to the four; it is the convergence of the four, derived from the four.

Principle 20.24 (The Convergence of the Four Columns). (T) The four columns converge in a
realm as the fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability of the relation between an identity and its
manifestations. The convergence is not a fifth column; it is the relation among the four. Fidelity
is derived from the fixed elements; sustainability from the fluid elements and the governing
dynamics; recoverability from the context. The principle is (T): it is argued by the derivations of
the four columns in Parts II to V, and by the analysis of the relation among them.

   The principle is (T): it is argued, and its argument is the derivation of the three components
from the four columns. It is the chapter’s principal contribution.


20.15      Why Viability Is the Name of the Convergence
20.15.1     The Convergence Is the Structural Character
The convergence of the four columns is the structural character of the relation between an
identity and its manifestations in a realm. The character is not the identity, and it is not the
manifestation; it is the relation between them, considered under its structural aspect.
    The character has three components: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. The compo-
nents are not independent; they are three aspects of one character. A relation that satisfies all
three is what the framework calls viable. A relation that fails one of the three is not fully viable.
244                                                                  From Context to Integration


20.15.2     Viability Is the Only Adequate Name
The question is: why is “viability” the only adequate name for the convergence? The answer is
that the convergence is the structural character of the relation, and viability is the name that
Book I gives to that character (Definition 36.1). The name is not arbitrary; it is the name that
the framework uses for the relation’s structural character, and it is the only name that captures
the three components of the convergence.
    The argument has three steps.

   1. The convergence of the four columns is the structural character of the relation between an
      identity and its manifestations in a realm.

   2. Book I defines viability as the structural character of the relation between an identity and
      its manifestations in a context (Definition 36.1).

   3. Therefore, viability is the name of the convergence.

   The conclusion follows: viability is the only adequate name for the convergence, because it is
the name that Book I gives to the structural character of the relation, and the convergence is
that character.

20.15.3     Viability Is Not a Fifth Column
The objection is that viability is a fifth column, added to the four. The reply is that viability is
not a column; it is the relation among the columns. The columns are the terms; viability is what
the terms are in their togetherness. The distinction is the distinction between the terms and the
relation, and the framework keeps it.

Principle 20.25 (Viability as the Name of the Convergence). (T) Viability is the name of the
convergence of the four columns. It is not a fifth column; it is the structural character of the
relation among the four. The name is not arbitrary; it is the name that Book I gives to the
structural character of the relation, and it is the only name that captures the three components
of the convergence.

   The principle is (T): it is argued by the derivation of the convergence and by the analysis of
the name. It is the chapter’s second contribution.


20.16      The Convergence Points Beyond Itself
20.16.1     The Convergence Is Not Self-Grounded
The convergence of the four columns is real, and its reality is the reality of the relation among
the four. But the convergence is not self-grounded. It depends on something beyond itself: the
identity that is expressed, the realm in which it is manifested, and the ground of both. The
convergence is not the whole of what is; it is the structural character of a relation that points
beyond itself to its ground.
    The pointing is the transition to Part VI. The convergence of the four columns is the structural
character of the relation; the ground of the relation is the divine ground, which Part VI will
state.

20.16.2     The Ground of the Convergence
The ground of the convergence is not another column; it is the condition under which the columns
can be what they are. The condition is the divine ground: the transcendent reality that grounds
20.17. The Structure of Part VI                                                                245


the realms, the identities, and the relations among them. Part VI will state the structure of the
ground; the present chapter states that the convergence points beyond itself to it.
    The distinction is the distinction between the convergence and its ground. The convergence
is the structural character of the relation; the ground is what makes the relation possible. The
two are distinct, and the framework keeps them apart.
Principle 20.26 (The Convergence Points Beyond Itself). (T) The convergence of the four
columns is not self-grounded; it points beyond itself to its ground. The ground is the condition
under which the columns can be what they are, and it is the subject of Part VI. The principle is
(T): it is argued by the analysis of the convergence and by the framework’s commitment to the
divine ground.
   The principle is (T): it is argued, and its argument is the analysis of the convergence and the
framework’s commitment to the divine ground. It is the chapter’s third contribution, and it is
the transition to Part VI.


20.17      The Structure of Part VI
Part VI states the divine ground of the convergence. It has four chapters and a synthesis chapter.
    Chapter 21: The Metaphysics of Transcendence. The chapter derives the transcendence of
the divine ground from the framework’s commitments: God is not a realm, a level, or a part of
the sevenfold architecture; God is the transcendent Creator and ground of the whole.
    Chapter 22: Creation and Sustaining. The chapter derives the two acts by which the
transcendent relation is established: creation (the giving of being) and sustaining (the giving of
being at every moment).
    Chapter 23: The Modal Space as Created. The chapter derives the createdness of the modal
space from the framework’s derivation of the modal space (Chapter 15) and from the framework’s
commitment to the divine ground.
    Chapter 24: Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered. The chapter reconsiders
the three questions in the light of the createdness of the modal space, and it states what the
createdness adds to the three questions.
    Chapter 25: Return to the Architecture. The synthesis chapter returns to the four-column
architecture and shows how the divine ground illuminates the necessity of the four columns.
    The five chapters together state the divine ground of the convergence. They do not prove
the existence of God; they state the metaphysical structure that the framework’s commitments
require. The present chapter has stated that the convergence points beyond itself to the ground;
Part VI states the ground.


20.18      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
     First, the chapter does not develop the three components of viability in detail. The components
are derived in §20.14; their detailed development is the subject of Part VII.
     Second, the chapter does not develop the divine ground. The ground is the subject of Part VI;
the present chapter states that the convergence points beyond itself to the ground, and it leaves
the ground to Part VI.
     Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the convergence is the only possible
structure of the relation among the four columns. The convergence is the structure that the
framework derives; whether a different structure is possible is a question the chapter leaves open.
     Fourth, the chapter does not prove that the convergence is real. It derives the convergence
from the four columns; the derivation is (T) relative to the derivations of the four columns, and
it is offered at the strength that the derivations support.
246                                                                  From Context to Integration


20.19      Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter
                 Claim                                         Status
                 The convergence of the four columns           (T)
                 (Pr. 20.24)
                 Viability as the name of the convergence      (T)

                 (Pr. 20.26)

                 The question of whether the convergence       (Q)

   The chapter’s claims are metaphysical and structural. The three (T) claims are argued in the
chapter; the (A) claim is a stipulation of the structure of Part VI; the (Q) claim is a question

20.20      A Question for Reflection
Consider a relation you know well—a person and their actions, a law and its applications, a form
and its instances. Is the relation viable in the sense of the chapter? Does the relation satisfy
the three components of fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability? And does the relation point
beyond itself to a ground that is not the relation?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The convergence is the relation; the
relation is viable when it satisfies the three components; and the relation points beyond itself
to its ground. The reader who can state, for a relation he knows, what the convergence, the
viability, and the ground are, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot
has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty
further.

Part V is complete. Part VI (Divine Ground) states the ground to which the convergence points.
The reader who has followed Part V has the convergence; Part VI states the ground.

           Part VI

Divine Ground and Modal Order
                                                                                                249




Chapter 21

The Metaphysics of Transcendence

Scope. This chapter states the metaphysics of transcendence. It recalls Book I’s three com-
mitments about God—that God is not a realm, a level, or a part of the sevenfold architecture
(Principle 7.3), that the structural light is created and is not God (Principle 12.2), and that the
modal space is grounded in God (Principle 37.2)—and it asks what the metaphysical structure of
transcendence must be, such that the three commitments can hold. It defines transcendence as
the relation of ontological dependence of the created order on God; it distinguishes transcendence
from spatial separation, from categorical distinction, and from hierarchical superiority; it states
the modes of transcendence; and it states how the transcendent relation relates to the four
columns of the framework. It does not prove the three commitments, and it does not describe
the divine essence. It states the metaphysical structure that the commitments require, and it
marks its claims with the label (D) where their truth depends on Book I’s commitments. It
prepares the transition to Chapter 22 (Creation and Sustaining).

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s Principle 7.3 (the
transcendence of the Divine Ground), Principle 12.2 (God is the source of all light), Principle 37.2
(the modal space is grounded in God), Definition 7.3 (the Divine Ground), Definition 7.4 (the
Throne-Domain), and Principle 36.1 (the Throne-Domain as the encompassing created order). It
also takes as given the four-column framework of Book I, Chapter 6. It does not reargue these
commitments; it asks what they presuppose in the order of being.


21.1      A Scene
Consider a lighthouse on a cliff, and the light it casts on the sea. The light on the sea is not the
lighthouse; the lighthouse is not in the light. The lighthouse is the source of the light; the light
depends on the lighthouse. But the lighthouse is not a part of the light, and the light is not the
lighthouse. The lighthouse is transcendent to the light it casts: it is the source, not the light; it
is the condition, not the conditioned.
    Now consider the sailors on the sea. They see the light; they do not see the lighthouse. The
light reaches them; the lighthouse does not. And yet the light is from the lighthouse; the light is
what the lighthouse gives, in the form that the distance and the atmosphere permit. The sailors’
relation to the lighthouse is mediated by the light; but the lighthouse is not the light, and the
light is not the lighthouse.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is the relation between God and the
created order? Is it spatial (God is “above” the created order)? Is it categorical (God is in a
different category from the created order)? Is it hierarchical (God is at the top of a hierarchy of
being)? Or is it something else—a relation of ontological dependence that is not captured by any
of these three?
250                                              Chapter 21. The Metaphysics of Transcendence


    The framework’s answer is: the relation is one of ontological dependence, and it is not spatial,
not categorical, and not hierarchical. The transcendent relation is the relation of the created to
its Creator; it is the relation of what is made to what makes it. The scene of the lighthouse is
not an analogy for this relation; the relation is more radical than any analogy. The lighthouse is
created; God is not. The light is created; God is not. The relation of the created to the Creator
is the relation that the chapter’s definition states.
Remark 21.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow,
and the scene carries no weight in them. The lighthouse is an example; the account is about
transcendence in general.


21.2      The Question
Book I committed itself to three claims about God, and each was stated as (A): God is not
a realm, a level, or a part of the sevenfold architecture (Principle 7.3); the structural light is
created and is not God (Principle 12.2); the modal space is grounded in God (Principle 37.2).
The three claims are the framework’s answer to the question of what God is not; they are not a
description of the divine essence, and the framework does not attempt one.
    The present chapter asks: what is the metaphysical structure of transcendence, such that the
three claims can hold? The question is not what God is; it is what the relation between God
and the created order must be, such that God is not a realm, not a level, not a part, and yet the
created order depends on God. The relation is what the chapter calls transcendence.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of transcendence? The chapter must define transcen-
dence, and it must distinguish the definition from the definitions of spatial separation, categorical
distinction, and hierarchical superiority. The distinction is the chapter’s contribution, because
the three false conceptions of transcendence are common, and each misleads.
    The second aspect: what are the modes of transcendence? The chapter must state the modes
in which the created order depends on God. The modes are not the same; each is a different
respect in which the created order is from God. The three modes are the ontological, the
epistemic, and the relational modes.
    The third aspect: how does the transcendent relation relate to the four columns? The chapter
must state how the transcendent relation relates to the fixed elements, the fluid element, the
governing dynamics, and the context. The relation is not one of the four columns; it is the
condition of all four, and the chapter states the distinction.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: transcen-
dence is the relation of ontological dependence of the created order on God; it is not spatial, not
categorical, not hierarchical; it has three modes (ontological, epistemic, relational); and it is the
condition of the four columns, not one of them.
Remark 21.2 (The Question Presupposes Book I’s Commitments). The question presupposes
Book I’s commitments. The three commitments (Principles 7.3, 12.2, 37.2) are stated in Book I,
and the present chapter does not reargue them. It asks what the three commitments presuppose
in the order of being; the answer is the metaphysical structure of transcendence. The reader who
has not read Book I will find the present chapter compressed; the reader who has read Book I
will find the present chapter the metaphysical completion of what Book I committed itself to.


21.3      What Book I Committed
Book I committed itself to three claims about God, and the present chapter asks what the three
presuppose. The three are worth restating, because the present chapter’s argument depends on
21.4. The Definition of Transcendence                                                            251


them.
    The first commitment: God is not a realm. Book I’s Principle 7.3 states that God is the
transcendent Creator and ontological ground of the entire created order; God is not a realm,
a category, or a level within the sevenfold architecture; the seven realms do not contain God,
delimit Him, or constitute levels within the divine essence. The commitment is (A): it is adopted,
not proved, and its support is that it keeps the distinction between Creator and creature without
which the architecture would be incoherent.
    The second commitment: the structural light is created. Book I’s Principle 12.2 states that
God is the source of all the light of existence; that the structural light is created; that it is not
God, not a part of God, not the Throne-Domain; and that its being and its mediating function
are given by God. The commitment is (T) relative to the first: if God is the Creator of all that
is not God, and the structural light is not God, then the structural light is created.
    The third commitment: the modal space is grounded in God. Book I’s Principle 37.2 states
that the modal space Ω is created and grounded in God; that the relation is one of grounding,
not of containment and not of identity; and that Ω is not a part of the divine essence. The
commitment is (T) relative to the first: if God is the Creator of all that is not God, and Ω is not
God, then Ω is created and grounded in God.
    The three commitments together state what God is not: not a realm, not the light, not the
modal space. The present chapter asks what the three commitments together require: what is
the relation between God and the created order, such that the three commitments can hold?
Remark 21.3 (The Three Commitments Are Not Three Arguments). The three commitments
are not three arguments for God’s existence. They are three claims about what God is not;
they presuppose that God is, and they state the structure of the relation between God and the
created order. The present chapter does not argue for God’s existence; it asks what the three
commitments require in the order of being.
Remark 21.4 (The Three Commitments Are Consistent). The three commitments are consistent
with one another. The first says that God is not a realm; the second says that the light is
not God; the third says that Ω is not God. The three are three applications of one principle:
God is the Creator, and everything else is created. The present chapter states the metaphysical
structure of the principle.


21.4      The Definition of Transcendence
The definition of transcendence is stated here.
Definition 21.5 (Transcendence). Transcendence is the relation of ontological dependence of
the created order on God. The created order depends on God for its being, its intelligibility, and
its relations; God does not depend on the created order for anything. The relation is not spatial,
not categorical, and not hierarchical; it is the relation of what is made to what makes it.
    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what transcen-
dence is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for
the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength. Its support is Book I’s three commitments;
its development is the present chapter.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the created order depends on God. The created order is all that is not God:
the seven realms, the light, the modal space, the Throne-Domain, and everything in them. The
dependence is ontological: the created order would not be if God were not. The dependence is
not a dependence of one thing on another thing; it is the dependence of what is made on what
makes it.
    The second part: God does not depend on the created order. God is not enriched, diminished,
or affected by the created order. The relation is asymmetrical: the created order depends on God;
252                                              Chapter 21. The Metaphysics of Transcendence


God does not depend on the created order. The asymmetry is what distinguishes transcendence
from other relations of dependence (a relation of mutual dependence is not transcendence).
    The third part: the relation is not spatial, categorical, or hierarchical. The relation is not
spatial (God is not “above” the created order in a place); it is not categorical (God is not in a
different category from the created order, because the categories are created); it is not hierarchical
(God is not at the top of a hierarchy of being, because a hierarchy is an order of created things).
The relation is the relation of what is made to what makes it, and this relation is not captured
by any of the three.
Remark 21.6 (Transcendence Is Not a Relation Among Created Things). Transcendence is not a
relation among created things. The relation between a cause and its effect is a relation among
created things; both the cause and the effect are created. The relation between God and the
created order is not of this kind: God is not a created thing, and the created order is not a
second created thing alongside God. The distinction is the distinction between the relation of
the created to the Creator and the relation of one created thing to another; the framework keeps
it throughout.
Remark 21.7 (Transcendence Is Not a Spatial Relation). Transcendence is not a spatial relation.
To say that God is “transcendent” is not to say that God is in a place called “above” the created
order; it is to say that the relation between God and the created order is not a relation of place
at all. The spatial vocabulary (“above,” “beyond,” “outside”) is a figure; the figure points to the
relation, and the relation is not the figure.
Remark 21.8 (Transcendence Is Not a Categorical Distinction). Transcendence is not a categorical
distinction. To say that God is “transcendent” is not to say that God is in a different category
from the created order; it is to say that the categories themselves are created, and that God is
not within any of them. The distinction is the distinction between the Creator and the created
categories; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 21.9 (Transcendence Is Not a Hierarchical Superiority). Transcendence is not a hierar-
chical superiority. To say that God is “transcendent” is not to say that God is at the top of a
hierarchy of being, higher than the highest realm; it is to say that the hierarchy itself is created,
and that God is not a level within it. The distinction is the distinction between the Creator and
the created hierarchy; the framework keeps it throughout.


21.5      The Modes of Transcendence
The relation of transcendence has three modes, and the three are worth stating. Each mode is a
different respect in which the created order depends on God.

21.5.1    The Ontological Mode
The ontological mode is the dependence of the created order on God for its being. The created
order would not be if God were not; it is not self-grounded; its existence is given by God at every
moment. The ontological mode is the most fundamental of the three; it is the ground of the
other two.

Principle 21.10 (The Ontological Mode). (D) The created order depends on God for its being:
it would not be if God were not, and its existence is given by God. The ontological mode is the
ground of the other modes of transcendence.

   The principle is (D): it is the metaphysical form of Book I’s Principle 7.3. The argument is
that God is the Creator of all that is not God (Book I, Principle 7.3); the created order is all
that is not God; therefore the created order depends on God for its being.
21.5. The Modes of Transcendence                                                                    253


21.5.2     The Epistemic Mode
The epistemic mode is the dependence of the created order on God for its intelligibility. The
created order is intelligible because God gives it its order; the order is not self-given, and it is
not given by the created order to itself. The intelligibility of the created order is the epistemic
mode of its dependence on God.
Principle 21.11 (The Epistemic Mode). (D) The created order depends on God for its intelligi-
bility: it is intelligible because God gives it its order. The epistemic mode is distinct from the
ontological mode; the first concerns the being of the created order, the second its intelligibility.
    The principle is (D): it is the metaphysical form of Book I’s Principle 37.2 (the modal space
is grounded in God), read in its epistemic aspect. The argument is that the modal space is the
order of the possible (Book I, Principle 37.1); the order is given by God (Book I, Principle 37.2);
the intelligibility of the created order is the intelligibility of the order; therefore the created order
depends on God for its intelligibility.

21.5.3     The Relational Mode
The relational mode is the dependence of the created order on God for its relations. The created
order is a network of relations; the relations are not self-given; they are given by God as part of
the order of the created order. The relational mode is the dependence of the relations on God.
Principle 21.12 (The Relational Mode). (D) The created order depends on God for its relations:
the relations are given by God as part of the order of the created order. The relational mode
is distinct from the ontological and epistemic modes; the first concerns being, the second
intelligibility, the third relations.
    The principle is (D): it is the metaphysical form of Book I’s Principle 12.2 (God is the source
of all light). The argument is that the light is the medium of relation (Book I, Principle 12.1);
the light is created and is given by God (Book I, Principle 12.2); the relations of the created
order are carried by the light; therefore the created order depends on God for its relations.

21.5.4     The Three Modes Together
The three modes are stated in the following table.

             Mode               What It Is                      What It Grounds
             Ontological        Dependence of the created       The other two modes
                                order for its being
             Epistemic          Dependence of the created       The order of the possible
                                order for its intelligibility
             Relational         Dependence of the created       The network of relations
                                order for its relations

    The table is the chapter’s map of the three modes. The three are not independent; the onto-
logical mode grounds the other two, and the epistemic and relational modes are the intelligibility
and the network of the being that the ontological mode gives.
Remark 21.13 (The Three Modes Are Not Three Arguments). The three modes are not three
arguments for God’s existence; they are three respects in which the created order depends on
God. The distinction is the distinction between the modes of the relation and the arguments for
the relation; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 21.14 (The Three Modes Are Not Three Godheads). The three modes are not three
Godheads; they are three modes of one relation. The distinction is the distinction between the
modes and the relation; the framework keeps it throughout.
254                                            Chapter 21. The Metaphysics of Transcendence


21.6     The Relation to the Four Columns
The relation of transcendence is not one of the four columns of the framework; it is the condition
of all four. The present section states the relation.
    The four columns are the fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, and the
context (Book I, Chapter 6). The four columns are analytical roles of any complete explanation;
they describe the structure of an explanation, not the structure of being. The relation of
transcendence is a relation in the order of being: it is the relation of the created order to God.
The relation is not one of the four columns; it is the condition under which the four columns can
describe the created order.
    Transcendence and the fixed elements. The fixed elements are the identity and its manifesta-
tions (Book I, Chapter 6). The identities and their manifestations are created; their being is
given by God. The transcendent relation is the condition under which the identities can be what
they are: without God, they would not be.
    Transcendence and the fluid element. The fluid element is light (Book I, Principle 12.1). The
light is created; its being and its mediating function are given by God (Book I, Principle 12.2).
The transcendent relation is the condition under which the light can mediate: without God, the
light would not be.
    Transcendence and the governing dynamics. The governing dynamics are the rules of the
realms (Book I, Chapter 6). The rules are created; their being is given by God. The transcendent
relation is the condition under which the rules can govern: without God, the rules would not be.
    Transcendence and the context. The context is the realm in which manifestations are realized
(Book I, Chapter 6). The realms are created; their being is given by God. The transcendent
relation is the condition under which the realms can be contexts: without God, the realms would
not be.

Principle 21.15 (Transcendence Is the Condition of the Four Columns). (D) Transcendence is
not one of the four columns; it is the condition under which the four columns can describe the
created order. The fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, and the context
are all created; their being is given by God; the transcendent relation is the condition under
which they can be what they are.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 7.3 (God is the Creator of all that
is not God) and from the four-column framework (Book I, Chapter 6). The argument is that
the four columns describe the created order; the created order depends on God; therefore the
four columns describe a created order that depends on God, and the transcendent relation is the
condition under which the four columns can describe it.
Remark 21.16 (The Relation Is Not a Fifth Column). The transcendent relation is not a fifth
column. The four columns are analytical roles of any complete explanation; the transcendent
relation is not an analytical role, and it is not a term in any explanation of the created order.
It is the condition of the created order, and the condition is not one of the roles by which the
created order is explained.
Remark 21.17 (The Relation Is Not a Part of the Framework). The transcendent relation is not a
part of the framework; it is the condition of the framework. The framework describes the created
order; the created order depends on God; the dependence is not a part of the description, but
the condition under which the description is possible. The distinction is the distinction between
the description and the condition of the description; the framework keeps it throughout.


21.7     What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
21.8. What Would Refute the Principle                                                             255


    The principle does not say that God is a realm. God is not a realm, not a level, not a part
(Book I, Principle 7.3). The principle says that the created order depends on God; it does not
say that God is one of the created things.
    The principle does not say that the created order is unreal. The created order is real; it is
created by God. The principle says that the created order depends on God; it does not say that
the created order is unreal.
    The principle does not say that the created order is God. The created order is not God; it is
created by God. The principle says that the created order depends on God; it does not say that
the created order is God.
    The principle does not say that the relation of transcendence is spatial or categorical or
hierarchical. The relation is ontological; it is not spatial, not categorical, not hierarchical. The
principle says that the relation is ontological; it does not say that the relation is one of the three
false conceptions.
Remark 21.18 (The Principle Leaves the Divine Essence Open). The principle leaves the divine
essence open. It states the metaphysical structure of the relation between God and the created
order; it does not describe the divine essence. The distinction is the distinction between
the relation and the essence; the framework keeps it throughout, and it is stated in Book I,
Remark 7.10.
Remark 21.19 (No Conflict with the Three Commitments). The principle is compatible with
Book I’s three commitments. God is not a realm (Principle 7.3); the light is not God (Princi-
ple 12.2); the modal space is not God (Principle 37.2). The principle says that the created order
depends on God; it does not say that any of the three commitments is mistaken.


21.8      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (D), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that the created order does not depend on God.
If such a showing could be made, the created order would be self-grounded, and the transcendent
relation would be a redundant concept. The framework’s claim is that the created order depends
on God; the dependence is the metaphysical structure that Book I’s three commitments require.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the transcendent relation is a relation of
mutual dependence. If such a showing could be made, God would depend on the created order,
and the relation would not be transcendence but mutual dependence. The framework’s claim is
that the relation is asymmetrical: the created order depends on God; God does not depend on
the created order.
Remark 21.20 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the dependence of the created order on God; the second challenges the asymmetry of
the relation. The two challenges require different responses, and the framework responds to each
in its own terms.


21.9      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not prove God’s existence. It states the metaphysical structure of
the relation between God and the created order, given Book I’s three commitments. The three
commitments are (A); the present chapter does not reargue them.
    Second, the chapter does not describe the divine essence. It states the structure of the
relation; it does not describe what God is in God’s self. The distinction is the distinction between
the relation and the essence; the framework keeps it throughout.
256                                             Chapter 21. The Metaphysics of Transcendence


    Third, the chapter does not develop the modes of transcendence in detail. The three modes
are stated in their general form; their development is the work of the chapters that treat creation
(Chapter 22), the modal space (Chapter 23), and providence (Chapter 24).
    Fourth, the chapter does not state the relation between transcendence and the Throne-Domain
in detail. The Throne-Domain is the encompassing created order (Book I, Definition 7.4); the
transcendence is the relation of the created order to God. The relation is stated in Chapter 22
(Creation and Sustaining); the present chapter states the structure of transcendence.
Remark 21.21 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
stated the definition of transcendence. It has distinguished transcendence from spatial separation,
from categorical distinction, and from hierarchical superiority. It has stated the three modes
of transcendence (ontological, epistemic, relational). And it has stated the relation between
transcendence and the four columns.
Remark 21.22 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter 22). The chapter prepares Chapter 22 (Creation
and Sustaining). The definition of transcendence states the relation between God and the created
order; the next chapter states the two acts by which the relation is established: creation (the
giving of being) and sustaining (the giving of being at every moment). The two acts are the two
modes of the ontological mode of transcendence.
