21.11      A Question for Reflection
Consider a relation of dependence you know well—a child and a parent, a student and a teacher,
a creature and its source. Is the relation spatial? Is it categorical? Is it hierarchical? Or is it
something else—a relation of what is made to what makes it? What does your answer tell you
about the relation between the created order and God, and about the metaphysical structure of
transcendence?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The relation of dependence you know
well is a relation among created things; the relation between the created order and God is not a
21.11. A Question for Reflection                                                                257


relation among created things. The reader who can state, for the relation he knows, why it is not
the transcendent relation, and what the transcendent relation is, has understood the chapter’s
distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and
is invited to develop the difficulty further.
The next chapter (Chapter 22) states the two acts by which the transcendent relation is established:
creation and sustaining. Creation is the giving of being; sustaining is the giving of being at every
moment. The two are the two modes of the ontological mode of transcendence, and the chapter
states their metaphysical structure. The reader who has followed the present chapter has the
definition of transcendence; the next chapter puts it to work.
258   Chapter 21. The Metaphysics of Transcendence
                                                                                                 259




Chapter 22

Creation and Sustaining

Scope. This chapter states the two acts by which the transcendent relation of Chapter 21 is
established: creation, the giving of being, and sustaining, the giving of being at every moment. It
defines the two, distinguishes them from one another and from emanation, from mere causation,
and from pantheism, states their relation, and states how each relates to the four columns of
the framework. It does not prove God’s existence, and it does not describe the divine essence.
Its claims are metaphysical; where it speaks of “creation,” “sustaining,” “being,” “act,” or
“dependence,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter
and in the chapters to which it refers. It prepares the transition to Chapter 23 (The Modal
Space as Created).

Presupposition from Book I and Chapter 21. This chapter takes as given Book I’s
Principle 7.3 (God is the transcendent Creator and sustaining ground of the created order),
Book I’s Principle 12.2 (God is the source of all light), Book I’s Principle 37.2 (the modal space
is grounded in God), and Chapter 21’s definition of transcendence as the relation of ontological
dependence of the created order on God. It does not reargue these; it asks what the two acts by
which the relation is established must be, such that the relation can hold.


22.1      A Scene
Consider a fire and the light it casts. The light is not the fire; the fire is not the light. The
fire gives the light; the light depends on the fire. Now ask: did the fire give the light once, at
the beginning, and then the light continues on its own? Or does the fire give the light at every
moment, so that if the fire were to cease, the light would cease at once?
    The first answer treats the relation as a relation of creation: the fire gives the light once, and
the light then continues by itself. The second answer treats the relation as a relation of creation
and sustaining: the fire gives the light once, and it gives the light at every moment, so that the
continuation is as much a gift as the beginning.
    The scene is small, but the question is not. If the relation between God and the created order
is a relation of creation alone, then the created order, once given, would be self-sustaining; it
would depend on God for its beginning but not for its continuation. If the relation is a relation
of creation and sustaining, then the created order depends on God for its beginning and for its
continuation; it is not self-sustaining at any moment.
    The framework’s answer is the second: creation and sustaining are not two separate acts,
but two modes of one relation—the relation of ontological dependence that Chapter 21 called
transcendence. Creation is the mode in which the relation is established; sustaining is the mode
in which the relation is maintained. Neither is a separate event; both are aspects of the one
relation by which the created order depends on God.
260                                                        Chapter 22. Creation and Sustaining


    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is creation, and what is sustaining? How
are they distinct, and how are they related? And how does the distinction between them bear
on the framework’s account of the relation between God and the created order?
Remark 22.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them. The fire and the light are examples; the account is about
creation and sustaining in general.


22.2     The Question
The previous chapter stated the metaphysics of transcendence: the relation of ontological
dependence of the created order on God, with three modes (ontological, epistemic, relational).
The present chapter turns to the two acts by which the ontological mode of the relation is
established: creation and sustaining.
    The question is: what are creation and sustaining? How are they distinct, and how are they
related? And how does the distinction between them bear on the framework’s account of the
relation between God and the created order?
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of creation? The chapter must define creation, and
it must distinguish the definition from emanation, from mere causation, and from pantheism.
The distinction is the chapter’s contribution, because the three false conceptions of creation are
common, and each misleads.
    The second aspect: what is the definition of sustaining? The chapter must define sustaining,
and it must distinguish the definition from a series of separate acts over time, from a mere
conservation of what already is, and from a deistic withdrawal. The distinction is the chapter’s
contribution, because the three false conceptions of sustaining are common, and each misleads.
    The third aspect: how are creation and sustaining related? The chapter must state the
relation. The framework’s answer is: the two are not two separate acts, but two modes of one
relation—the relation of ontological dependence that Chapter 21 called transcendence. The
relation is the same; the modes are different.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: creation
is the giving of being; sustaining is the giving of being at every moment; the two are the two
modes of the ontological mode of transcendence; and the two modes are not two separate acts
but two aspects of one relation.
Remark 22.2 (The Question Presupposes Chapter 21). The question presupposes Chapter 21.
The definition of transcendence is stated there; the three modes of transcendence are stated there.
The present chapter does not restate them; it states the two acts by which the ontological mode of
the relation is established. The reader who has not read Chapter 21 will find the present chapter
compressed; the reader who has read it will find the present chapter the natural development of
the ontological mode.


22.3     What Chapter 26 Established
Chapter 21 established three things, and the present chapter develops the third.
    The definition of transcendence. Transcendence is the relation of ontological dependence of
the created order on God; the created order depends on God for its being, its intelligibility, and
its relations; God does not depend on the created order for anything.
    The three modes of transcendence. The ontological mode is the dependence of the created
order on God for its being; the epistemic mode is the dependence of the created order on God
22.4. The Definition of Creation                                                                261


for its intelligibility; the relational mode is the dependence of the created order on God for its
relations.
    Transcendence is the condition of the four columns. Transcendence is not one of the four
columns; it is the condition under which the four columns can describe the created order. The
fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, and the context are all created; their
being is given by God.
    The present chapter develops the ontological mode. The ontological mode has two acts:
creation (the giving of being) and sustaining (the giving of being at every moment). The two
acts are the two modes of the ontological mode; the chapter states their structure.
Remark 22.3 (The Two Acts Are Not Two Modes of Transcendence). The two acts (creation
and sustaining) are not two modes of transcendence; they are two modes of the ontological
mode of transcendence. The distinction is the distinction between the modes of the relation
(ontological, epistemic, relational) and the modes of the ontological mode (creation, sustaining);
the framework keeps it throughout.


22.4      The Definition of Creation
The definition of creation is stated here.
Definition 22.4 (Creation). Creation is the act by which God gives being to the created order.
It is not a change in God, and it is not a change in a pre-existing material; it is the giving of
being to what did not have being. The created order depends on God for its being; creation is
the mode in which the dependence is established.
    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what creation
is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for
the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength. Its support is Book I’s Principle 7.3; its
development is the present chapter.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: creation is the giving of being. God gives being to the created order. The
giving is not a transfer of being from God to the created order (God does not lose being in
creating); it is the establishment of the created order in being. The created order is what it is
because God gives it being.
    The second part: creation is not a change in God. The act of creation does not change God;
God is the same before and after creation. The act is a relation, not a change; the relation is
established by God’s giving, and the giving does not modify God.
    The third part: creation is not a change in a pre-existing material. The created order is not
made from a pre-existing material; it is given being. The giving is not a shaping of what was
already there; it is the establishment of what was not. The created order depends on God for its
being; the dependence is total, and it is established by creation.
Remark 22.5 (Creation Is Not Emanation). Creation is not emanation. Emanation is the flowing
of the created order from God as a necessary consequence of God’s nature; the emanation is
necessary, and the created order is a necessary overflowing of the divine. Creation is the giving of
being by God’s free act; the giving is free, and the created order is not a necessary overflowing of
the divine. The distinction is the distinction between the necessary and the free; the framework
keeps it throughout.
Remark 22.6 (Creation Is Not Mere Causation). Creation is not mere causation. Causation is
the relation between a cause and its effect, where both are within the created order; the cause
gives the effect a form, and the effect depends on the cause for its form. Creation is the giving of
being, not the giving of form; the created order depends on God for its being, not only for its
form. The distinction is the distinction between the giving of form and the giving of being; the
framework keeps it throughout.
262                                                         Chapter 22. Creation and Sustaining


Remark 22.7 (Creation Is Not Pantheism). Creation is not pantheism. Pantheism identifies
the created order with God; the created order is God in another form. Creation distinguishes
the created order from God; the created order is not God, and God is not the created order.
The distinction is the distinction between the Creator and the creature; the framework keeps it
throughout, and it is stated in Book I, Principle 7.3.


22.5     The Definition of Sustaining
The definition of sustaining is stated here.

Definition 22.8 (Sustaining). Sustaining is the act by which God gives being to the created order
at every moment. It is not a series of separate acts over time; it is the continuous dependence of
the created order on God. The created order depends on God for its being at every moment;
sustaining is the mode in which the dependence is maintained.

    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what sustaining
is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the
concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength. Its support is Book I’s Principle 7.3 (God is
the sustaining ground); its development is the present chapter.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: sustaining is the giving of being at every moment. The created order depends
on God at every moment, not only at the beginning. The giving is continuous; the dependence is
continuous. The created order would not be if God were not giving it being at every moment.
    The second part: sustaining is not a series of separate acts over time. The sustaining is
not a series of acts, one for each moment; it is one act, in the mode of continuous giving. The
distinction is the distinction between the act and the series of its effects; the framework keeps it
throughout.
    The third part: sustaining is the mode in which the dependence is maintained. The dependence
is the same dependence that creation establishes; the sustaining is the mode in which the
dependence is maintained. The two are not two dependencies; they are two modes of one
dependence.
Remark 22.9 (Sustaining Is Not a Series of Separate Acts). Sustaining is not a series of separate
acts over time. The sustaining is one act; its effect is the continuous being of the created order.
If the sustaining were a series of acts, the created order would depend on God at each moment
for a new act, and the dependence would be a series of dependencies. The framework’s claim is
that the dependence is one, and that the sustaining is the mode in which it is maintained.
Remark 22.10 (Sustaining Is Not Mere Conservation). Sustaining is not mere conservation.
Conservation is the preservation of what already is; the conserved thing could, in principle,
continue without the conservator. Sustaining is the giving of being at every moment; the sustained
thing could not continue without the sustainer. The distinction is the distinction between the
preservation of what is and the giving of what is; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 22.11 (Sustaining Is Not Deistic Withdrawal). Sustaining is not deistic withdrawal.
Deism holds that God created the world and then withdrew, leaving it to run on its own.
Sustaining holds that God gives being to the world at every moment; the world does not run on
its own. The distinction is the distinction between the withdrawal and the continuous giving;
the framework keeps it throughout.


22.6     The Relation Between Creation and Sustaining
The relation between creation and sustaining is stated here.
22.7. Creation and the Four Columns                                                            263


    The two are not two separate acts; they are two modes of one relation. The relation is the
relation of ontological dependence of the created order on God (Chapter 21); the modes are the
modes in which the relation is established (creation) and maintained (sustaining). The relation
is the same; the modes are different.
    The two are not sequential. The relation does not begin with creation and continue with
sustaining; the two are simultaneous aspects of one relation. The created order depends on God
for its being (creation) and for its being at every moment (sustaining); the two are not two stages
of the dependence, but two aspects of it.
    The two are not separable. The created order depends on God for its being; the dependence
is not separable into a beginning and a continuation. The creation without the sustaining would
be an establishment of being that is not maintained; the sustaining without the creation would
be a maintenance of being that is not established. The two are not separable; they are aspects of
one relation.
Principle 22.12 (Creation and Sustaining Are Two Modes of One Relation). (D) Creation
and sustaining are not two separate acts; they are two modes of one relation—the relation of
ontological dependence of the created order on God. The relation is the same; the modes are
different. The two are not sequential, and they are not separable.
    The principle is (D): it follows from Chapter 21’s definition of transcendence and from the
definitions of creation and sustaining (Definitions 22.4 and 22.8). The argument is that the
relation is one (the dependence of the created order on God); the modes are two (the establishment
and the maintenance of the dependence); the modes are modes of the relation, not separate
relations.
Remark 22.13 (The Two Modes Are Not Two Dependencies). The two modes are not two
dependencies. The dependence is one; the modes are two. The distinction is the distinction
between the relation and its modes; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 22.14 (The Two Modes Are Not Two Gods). The two modes are not two Gods. There is
one God; the modes are two modes of one relation between God and the created order. The
distinction is the distinction between the modes and the relation, and between the relation and
God; the framework keeps it throughout.


22.7     Creation and the Four Columns
Creation is related to the four columns, and the relation is worth stating.
    The four columns are the fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, and the
context (Book I, Chapter 6). The four columns are analytical roles of any complete explanation;
they describe the structure of an explanation, not the structure of being. Creation is not one of
the four columns; it is the act by which the created order that the four columns describe is given
being.
    Creation and the fixed elements. The fixed elements are the identity and its manifestations.
The identities and their manifestations are created; their being is given by God. Creation is the
act by which they are given being.
    Creation and the fluid element. The fluid element is light. The light is created; its being and
its mediating function are given by God (Book I, Principle 12.2). Creation is the act by which
the light is given being.
    Creation and the governing dynamics. The governing dynamics are the rules of the realms.
The rules are created; their being is given by God. Creation is the act by which they are given
being.
    Creation and the context. The context is the realm in which manifestations are realized. The
realms are created; their being is given by God. Creation is the act by which they are given
being.
264                                                        Chapter 22. Creation and Sustaining


Principle 22.15 (Creation Is the Act That Establishes the Created Order). (D) Creation is the
act by which the created order that the four columns describe is given being. It is not one of the
four columns; it is the act that establishes the created order that the four columns describe.
    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 7.3 (God is the Creator of all that is
not God) and from the four-column framework (Book I, Chapter 6). The argument is that the
four columns describe the created order; the created order depends on God for its being; creation
is the act by which the dependence is established.
Remark 22.16 (Creation Is Not a Fifth Column). Creation is not a fifth column. The four
columns are analytical roles of any complete explanation; creation is an act in the order of being.
The distinction is the distinction between the analytical roles and the act; the framework keeps
it throughout.


22.8     Sustaining and the Four Columns
Sustaining is related to the four columns, and the relation is worth stating.
    Sustaining is not one of the four columns; it is the act by which the created order that the
four columns describe is maintained in being.
    Sustaining and the fixed elements. The identities and their manifestations are sustained; their
being is given by God at every moment. Sustaining is the act by which they are maintained in
being.
    Sustaining and the fluid element. The light is sustained; its being and its mediating function
are given by God at every moment. Sustaining is the act by which the light is maintained in
being.
    Sustaining and the governing dynamics. The rules are sustained; their being is given by God
at every moment. Sustaining is the act by which they are maintained in being.
    Sustaining and the context. The realms are sustained; their being is given by God at every
moment. Sustaining is the act by which they are maintained in being.
Principle 22.17 (Sustaining Is the Act That Maintains the Created Order). (D) Sustaining is
the act by which the created order that the four columns describe is maintained in being. It is
not one of the four columns; it is the act that maintains the created order that the four columns
describe.
    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 7.3 (God is the sustaining ground of
the created order) and from the four-column framework (Book I, Chapter 6). The argument is
that the four columns describe the created order; the created order depends on God for its being
at every moment; sustaining is the act by which the dependence is maintained.
Remark 22.18 (Sustaining Is Not a Fifth Column). Sustaining is not a fifth column. The four
columns are analytical roles of any complete explanation; sustaining is an act in the order of
being. The distinction is the distinction between the analytical roles and the act; the framework
keeps it throughout.


22.9     What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that the created order is a part of God. The created order is not
a part of God; it is created by God (Book I, Principle 7.3). The principle says that the created
order depends on God; it does not say that the created order is God or a part of God.
    The principle does not say that God is a part of the created order. God is not a part of the
created order; God is the Creator. The principle says that God gives being to the created order;
it does not say that God is one of the things in the created order.
22.10. What Would Refute the Principle                                                              265


    The principle does not say that creation is a change in God. Creation is the giving of being
to the created order; it is not a change in God. The principle says that creation is an act; it does
not say that the act changes God.
    The principle does not say that sustaining is a series of acts over time. Sustaining is one act
in the mode of continuous giving; it is not a series of acts. The principle says that sustaining is
the mode in which the dependence is maintained; it does not say that the mode is a series.
Remark 22.19 (The Principle Leaves the Divine Act Open). The principle leaves the divine act
open. It states the structure of the act; it does not describe the divine act in itself. The distinction
is the distinction between the structure and the act; the framework keeps it throughout, and it is
stated in Chapter 21, Remark 21.18.
Remark 22.20 (No Conflict with Book I’s Three Commitments). The principle is compatible
with Book I’s three commitments. God is not a realm (Principle 7.3); the light is not God
(Principle 12.2); the modal space is not God (Principle 37.2). The principle says that the created
order depends on God for its being; it does not say that any of the three commitments is mistaken.


22.10       What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (D), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that the created order does not depend on God
for its being. If such a showing could be made, the created order would be self-grounded, and
creation would be a redundant concept. The framework’s claim is that the created order depends
on God for its being; the dependence is the metaphysical structure that Book I’s Principle 7.3
requires.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the created order depends on God for
its beginning but not for its continuation. If such a showing could be made, sustaining would be
a redundant concept, and the relation would be a relation of creation alone. The framework’s
claim is that the created order depends on God for its being at every moment; the dependence is
the metaphysical structure that Book I’s Principle 7.3 requires.
Remark 22.21 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the dependence of the created order on God; the second challenges the continuous
character of the dependence. The two challenges require different responses, and the framework
responds to each in its own terms.


22.11       What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not prove God’s existence. It states the metaphysical structure of the
two acts by which the transcendent relation is established, given Book I’s three commitments.
The three commitments are (A); the present chapter does not reargue them.
    Second, the chapter does not describe the divine essence. It states the structure of the acts;
it does not describe what God is in God’s self. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure and the essence; the framework keeps it throughout.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the relation between creation and sustaining and the
modal space. The modal space is the subject of Chapter 23; the present chapter states the two
acts by which the created order is established and maintained, and it leaves the modal space to
its place.
    Fourth, the chapter does not settle the question of whether creation is temporal. The created
order is given being; the question of whether the giving is a temporal event is a question the
266                                                        Chapter 22. Creation and Sustaining


chapter leaves open. Book I’s Principle 37.1 states that the modal space is real; the question of
the temporality of the giving is the subject of a different inquiry.
Remark 22.22 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
stated the definition of creation and the definition of sustaining. It has distinguished the two
from emanation, from mere causation, from pantheism, from a series of separate acts, from mere
conservation, and from deistic withdrawal. It has stated the relation between the two: they are
two modes of one relation. And it has stated the relation between the two and the four columns.
Remark 22.23 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter 23). The chapter prepares Chapter 23 (The Modal
Space as Created). The modal space is the space of possibilities (Book I, Principle 37.1); it is
created; its being is given by God. The present chapter states the two acts by which the created
order is established and maintained; the next chapter states the modal space as a created order,
and the relation between the modal space and the divine ground.

22.13      A Question for Reflection
Consider a gift you have received. Was the gift given once, at the beginning, and then it continued
on its own? Or was it given at every moment, so that the continuation was as much a gift as the
beginning? What does your answer tell you about the relation between creation and sustaining,
and about the metaphysical structure of the dependence of the created order on God?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. Creation and sustaining are not two
separate acts; they are two modes of one relation. The reader who can state, for a gift he
knows, why the gift is not the transcendent relation, and what the transcendent relation is,
has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the
distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.
22.13. A Question for Reflection                                                             267


The next chapter (Chapter 23) states the modal space as created: the space of possibilities is
created, and its being is given by God. The present chapter has stated the two acts by which the
created order is established and maintained; the next chapter states the modal space as a created
order, and the relation between the modal space and the divine ground. The reader who has
followed the present chapter has the structure of the two acts; the next chapter puts it to work.

Chapter 23

The Modal Space as Created

Scope. This chapter states the createdness of the modal space Ω. It takes as given Chapter ??’s
stratification of Ω into four strata (logical, metaphysical, natural, normative), Chapter 21’s
account of transcendence, and Chapter 22’s account of creation and sustaining. It defines the
created modal space, states the four modes of its createdness, and addresses the central difficulty:
if Ω is created, and if Ω contains necessary truths, how can the necessary be both necessary
and created? The chapter answers that the necessary is the form of the created order, and
that the createdness of the necessary is a claim about grounding, not about modal status. It
distinguishes the position from modal realism, from Platonism about possibilities, from the
doctrine that possibilities are divine ideas, and from fictionalism. It states the relation of the
created modal space to the four columns of the framework. Its claims are metaphysical; where it
speaks of “modal space,” “stratum,” “necessity,” “createdness,” “grounding,” or “form,” these
are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the chapters
to which it refers. It prepares the transition to Chapter 24 (Providence, Knowledge, and Choice
Reconsidered).

Presupposition from Book I and Chapters ??, 21, 22. This chapter takes as given
Book I’s Principle 37.1 (the totality of possibility, C12), Principle 37.2 (the modal space is
grounded in God), Definition 37.1 (the three layers of the ontological architecture), Chapter ??’s
stratification of Ω into four strata, Chapter 21’s definition of transcendence, and Chapter 22’s
definitions of creation and sustaining. It does not reargue these; it asks what the createdness of
Ω must be, such that the commitments can hold.


23.1      A Scene
Consider a library whose catalogue is itself a book in the library. The catalogue lists every book
on the shelves; the catalogue is one of the books; the catalogue must list itself. Now ask: when
the library was founded, was the catalogue founded with the books, or was it somehow already
there?
    The first answer is: the catalogue was founded with the books. The founder ordered the
shelves, acquired the books, and wrote the catalogue. The catalogue is not prior to the books; it
is the order of the books, and the order is given along with the books.
    The second answer is: the catalogue was somehow already there. It was not founded with
the books; it is the order of the possible books, and the possible books are not the actual books.
The catalogue is the space of possibilities, and the space is not created with the actual.
    The two answers are not about libraries in particular. They are about the modal space. The
modal space is the catalogue of what can be; the actual is what is. The question is: is the modal
space created along with the actual, or is it somehow prior to the actual?
270                                                    Chapter 23. The Modal Space as Created


    The framework’s answer is: the modal space is created along with the actual. It is not prior
to the actual; it is not the space of what could have been, independent of what is. It is the space
of what can be, given the created essences and the created laws; and the created essences and
the created laws are created along with the actual.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What does it mean for Ω to be created? What
are the modes of its createdness? And how can the necessary be both necessary and created?
Remark 23.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them. The library is an example; the account is about the modal
space in general.


23.2      The Question
Chapter ?? stated the stratification of Ω into four strata: the logical (the form of propositions),
the metaphysical (the essences of things), the natural (the laws of the realms), and the normative
(the good). The chapter stated that the four strata are the framework’s account of what the
modal space contains, and that the four kinds of necessity (Chapter 14) are the framework’s
account of what the modal statuses are. The chapter did not say whether the modal space is
created or uncreated; that was left to Part VI.
    The present chapter asks: is the modal space created? The framework’s answer is: yes, the
modal space is created, and its being is given by God. The createdness of Ω is the metaphysical
form of Book I’s Principle 37.2, which states that the modal space is grounded in God. The
present chapter states the structure of the grounding.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of the created modal space? The chapter must define
what it means for Ω to be created, and it must distinguish the definition from the definitions of
the uncreated modal space (modal realism, Platonism).
    The second aspect: what are the modes of the createdness of Ω? The chapter must state the
modes of the createdness, corresponding to the four strata.
    The third aspect: how can the necessary be both necessary and created? The chapter must
address the central difficulty: if Ω contains necessary truths, and if Ω is created, is the necessary
contingent? The chapter answers that the necessary is the form of the created order, and that
its createdness is a claim about grounding, not about modal status.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: Ω is
created; its createdness has four modes, corresponding to the four strata; the necessary is the
form of the created order, and its createdness is grounded in God without being contingent in
the sense of “could have been otherwise in an arbitrary way.”
Remark 23.2 (The Question Presupposes Chapter ??). The question presupposes Chapter ??.
The stratification of Ω is stated there; the four strata are stated there. The present chapter does
not restate them; it states the createdness of the modal space. The reader who has not read
Chapter ?? will find the present chapter compressed; the reader who has read it will find the
present chapter the natural development of the stratification.


23.3      What Chapters 15, 26, and 27 Established
Chapters ??, 21, and 22 established three things, and the present chapter integrates them.
    The stratification of Ω. Chapter ?? established that Ω is not a flat set of possible worlds, nor
a set of abstract propositions, but a stratified modal structure whose strata are the four kinds
of necessity. The logical stratum is the form of propositions; the metaphysical stratum is the
23.4. The Definition of the Created Modal Space                                                  271


essences of things; the natural stratum is the laws of the realms; the normative stratum is the
good.
    Transcendence. Chapter 21 established that transcendence is the relation of ontological
dependence of the created order on God; that the relation is not spatial, not categorical, and not
hierarchical; and that the relation has three modes (ontological, epistemic, relational).
    Creation and sustaining. Chapter 22 established that creation is the giving of being, that
sustaining is the giving of being at every moment, and that the two are two modes of one
relation—the relation of ontological dependence.
    The present chapter integrates the three. The stratification of Ω is the structure of the modal
space; the transcendence is the relation of the modal space to God; the creation and sustaining
are the two acts by which the relation is established and maintained. The createdness of Ω is the
metaphysical form of the integration.
Remark 23.3 (The Three Are Not Independent). The three are not independent. The stratification
is the structure; transcendence is the relation; creation and sustaining are the acts. The three
together are the framework’s account of the modal space; the present chapter states what the
three together require.


23.4      The Definition of the Created Modal Space
The definition of the created modal space is stated here.
Definition 23.4 (The Created Modal Space). The created modal space Ω is the stratified
structure of possible configurations of essences and laws whose being, intelligibility, and relations
are given by God. Its strata are the four kinds of necessity (Chapter 14); its being is given
by God (Chapter 22, creation); its being is maintained by God (Chapter 22, sustaining); its
intelligibility is given by God (Chapter 21, epistemic mode); its relations are given by God
(Chapter 21, relational mode).
    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what the created
modal space is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s
proposal for the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength. Its support is Book I’s
Principle 37.2; its development is the present chapter.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the modal space is stratified. The modal space is not flat; it has four strata
(Chapter ??). The stratification is the structure of the modal space; it is not a feature added to
a flat space.
    The second part: the modal space is created. The modal space is created; its being is given
by God (Chapter 22). The createdness is not a feature added to a pre-existing modal space; it is
the relation of the modal space to God.
    The third part: the createdness has modes. The createdness of the modal space has four
modes, corresponding to the four strata: the logical stratum is created; the metaphysical stratum
is created; the natural stratum is created; the normative stratum is created. The four modes are
the framework’s account of what the createdness contains.
Remark 23.5 (The Modal Space Is Not God). The modal space is not God. The modal space
is created; God is the Creator. The modal space is not a part of God, not the divine essence,
and not the divine ideas. The distinction is the distinction between the Creator and the created
order; the framework keeps it throughout, and it is stated in Book I, Principle 37.2.
Remark 23.6 (The Modal Space Is Not a Fictional Space). The modal space is not a fictional
space. A fictional space is a space of what could be imagined or stipulated; it has no being
apart from the imagination or the stipulation. The modal space has being; its being is given by
God. The distinction is the distinction between the real and the fictional; the framework keeps it
throughout.

23.5      The Four Modes of the Createdness of the Modal Space
The createdness of the modal space has four modes, corresponding to the four strata. Each mode
is a different respect in which the stratum is created.

23.5.1     The Createdness of the Logical Stratum
The logical stratum is the form of propositions. Its createdness is the giving of the form by God.
The form is not God; it is the form of the created order. The logical stratum is created because
the form is given; it is necessary because the form is the form of the created order, and the form
is what it is.

Principle 23.7 (The Createdness of the Logical Stratum). (D) The logical stratum is created:
the form of propositions is given by God. The form is not God; it is the form of the created
order. The logical stratum is necessary because it is the form of the created order, not because it
is independent of God.

   The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 37.2 (the modal space is grounded in
God) and from Chapter ??’s stratification (the logical stratum is the form of propositions). The
argument is that the modal space is created; the logical stratum is a stratum of the modal space;
therefore the logical stratum is created.

23.5.2     The Createdness of the Metaphysical Stratum
The metaphysical stratum is the essences of things. Its createdness is the giving of the essences
by God. The essences are not God; they are the essences of created things. The metaphysical
stratum is created because the essences are given; it is necessary because the essences are what
they are.

Principle 23.8 (The Createdness of the Metaphysical Stratum). (D) The metaphysical stratum
is created: the essences of things are given by God. The essences are not God; they are the
essences of created things. The metaphysical stratum is necessary because it is the essences of
created things, not because it is independent of God.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 37.2 and from Chapter ??’s stratification
(the metaphysical stratum is the essences of things). The argument is the same as for the logical
stratum.

23.5.3     The Createdness of the Natural Stratum
The natural stratum is the laws of the realms. Its createdness is the giving of the laws by God.
The laws are not God; they are the laws of created realms. The natural stratum is created
because the laws are given; it is necessary because the laws are what they are.

Principle 23.9 (The Createdness of the Natural Stratum). (D) The natural stratum is created:
the laws of the realms are given by God. The laws are not God; they are the laws of created
realms. The natural stratum is necessary because it is the laws of created realms, not because it
is independent of God.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 37.2 and from Chapter ??’s stratification
(the natural stratum is the laws of the realms). The argument is the same.

23.5.4     The Createdness of the Normative Stratum
The normative stratum is the good. Its createdness is the giving of the good by God. The good
is not God; it is the good of the created order. The normative stratum is created because the
good is given; it is necessary because the good is what it is.

Principle 23.10 (The Createdness of the Normative Stratum). (D) The normative stratum is
created: the good is given by God. The good is not God; it is the good of the created order.
The normative stratum is necessary because it is the good of the created order, not because it is
independent of God.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 37.2 and from Chapter ??’s stratification
(the normative stratum is the good). The argument is the same.

Remark 23.11 (The Four Modes Are Not Four Creations). The four modes are not four creations.

23.6      The Createdness of the Necessary
The central difficulty of the chapter is stated here, and its answer is given.
    The difficulty. If Ω is created, and if Ω contains necessary truths (the logical stratum contains
logical necessities; the metaphysical stratum contains metaphysical necessities), then how can
the necessary be both necessary and created? If the necessary is created, is it contingent? If it is
contingent, is it necessary?
    The framework’s answer has three parts.
    The first part: createdness is a claim about grounding, not about modal status. To say that
the necessary is created is to say that its being is given by God; it is not to say that its modal
status is contingent. The necessary is necessary (in its stratum); it is created (because its being
is given). The two claims are compatible: the necessary is both necessary and created.
    The second part: the necessary is the form of the created order. The logical necessity is the
form of propositions; the metaphysical necessity is the essence of things; the natural necessity
is the law of the realms; the normative necessity is the good. Each is the form of the created
order, and the form is what it is because God gives it. The necessary is necessary because it is
the form of the created order; it is created because the form is given.
274                                                     Chapter 23. The Modal Space as Created


    The third part: the createdness of the necessary does not make it arbitrary. The form is not
arbitrary; it is given by God’s wisdom (Book I, Principle 7.3). The createdness does not make
the necessary "could have been otherwise in an arbitrary way"; it makes the necessary dependent
on God for its being. The necessary is necessary (in its stratum) because it is the form of the
created order; it is created because the form is given by God.
Principle 23.12 (The Createdness of the Necessary). (D) The necessary is created: its being
is given by God. The createdness is a claim about grounding, not about modal status. The
necessary is necessary (in its stratum) because it is the form of the created order; it is created
because the form is given by God. The createdness does not make the necessary arbitrary; the
form is given by God’s wisdom, not by an arbitrary fiat.
   The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 37.2 and from Chapter ??’s stratification.
The argument is that the modal space is created; the necessary is a stratum of the modal space;
therefore the necessary is created. The createdness is not a denial of the necessity; it is a claim
about the grounding of the necessity.
Remark 23.13 (The Distinction Between Createdness and Contingency). The distinction between
createdness and contingency is essential. A thing can be created and necessary; a thing can be
created and contingent; a thing can be uncreated and necessary (if there is such a thing). The
createdness is about the grounding of the thing’s being; the contingency is about the modal
status of the thing’s truth. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 23.14 (The Distinction Between Createdness and Arbitrariness). The distinction between
createdness and arbitrariness is essential. A thing can be created and not arbitrary; a thing can
be created and arbitrary; a thing can be uncreated and arbitrary (if there is such a thing). The
createdness is about the grounding of the thing’s being; the arbitrariness is about the form of
the thing’s truth. The form of the created order is given by God’s wisdom, not by an arbitrary
fiat; the necessary is necessary because it is the form of the created order, and the form is what
it is because God is wise.
Remark 23.15 (No Conflict with the Modal Status of the Necessary). The principle is compatible
with the modal status of the necessary. The necessary is necessary (in its stratum); the createdness
does not change the modal status. The two claims are about different things: the modal status
is about the truth of the necessary; the createdness is about the being of the necessary. The
framework’s claim is that both can be true.


23.7      Distinctions from False Conceptions
The createdness of the modal space is easily confused with four false conceptions, and the
distinctions are worth stating.
    Modal realism. Modal realism (Lewis) treats the possible worlds as concrete spatiotemporal
systems, as real as the actual world. The modal space is not created; it is the plurality of the
concrete worlds. The framework’s position is different: the modal space is not a plurality of
concrete worlds; it is a stratified structure of possible configurations of essences and laws. The
modal space is created; its being is given by God. The distinction is the distinction between the
created stratification and the uncreated plurality; the framework keeps it throughout.
    Platonism about possibilities. Platonism about possibilities treats the possible as an abstract
realm, independent of the actual and independent of God. The modal space is not created; it is
the abstract realm of the possible. The framework’s position is different: the modal space is not
an abstract realm; it is a created structure of essences and laws. The modal space is created; its
being is given by God. The distinction is the distinction between the created structure and the
uncreated abstract realm; the framework keeps it throughout.
    The doctrine that possibilities are divine ideas. The doctrine treats the possible as the content
of God’s mind; the modal space is the divine ideas. The framework’s position is different: the
23.8. The Relation to the Four Columns                                                            275


modal space is not the divine ideas; it is a created order. The distinction is the distinction
between the created order and the divine mind; the framework keeps it throughout, and it is
stated in Book I, Principle 37.2 (the modal space is grounded in God, not identical with God).
    Fictionalism about possibilities. Fictionalism treats the possible as a useful fiction; the modal
space is a fiction, not a reality. The framework’s position is different: the modal space is real; its
being is given by God. The distinction is the distinction between the real and the fictional; the
framework keeps it throughout.

Principle 23.16 (The Created Modal Space Is Not Any of the Four). (D) The created modal
space is not the modal realist’s plurality of concrete worlds, not the Platonist’s abstract realm,
not the divine ideas, and not a fiction. It is a created structure of essences and laws; its being is
given by God; it is real.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Chapter ??’s stratification and from the definition of the
created modal space. The argument is that the modal space is created; the four false conceptions
treat the modal space as uncreated or as unreal; the framework’s position is different.
Remark 23.17 (The Four Are Not Equally Wrong). The four false conceptions are not equally
wrong. Modal realism and Platonism about possibilities treat the modal space as uncreated;
the doctrine of divine ideas treats the modal space as identical with God; fictionalism treats
the modal space as unreal. The framework’s position is that the modal space is created and
real; each of the four false conceptions misses one of the two features. The distinction is the
distinction between the created and the uncreated, and between the real and the unreal; the
framework keeps both.


23.8      The Relation to the Four Columns
The created modal space is related to the four columns, and the relation is worth stating.
    The four columns are the fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, and the
context (Book I, Chapter 6). The four columns are analytical roles of any complete explanation;
they describe the structure of an explanation, not the structure of being. The created modal
space is not one of the four columns; it is the order in which the four columns describe the
created order.
    The created modal space and the fixed elements. The fixed elements are the identity and its
manifestations. The identities and their manifestations are possible in the modal space; their
possibility is grounded in the strata of the modal space. The created modal space is the order of
the possible identities and manifestations.
    The created modal space and the fluid element. The fluid element is light. The light is the
medium of the relation between the identity and its manifestations; the light is possible in the
modal space; its possibility is grounded in the strata of the modal space. The created modal
space is the order of the possible lights.
    The created modal space and the governing dynamics. The governing dynamics are the rules
of the realms. The rules are possible in the modal space; their possibility is grounded in the
natural stratum of the modal space. The created modal space is the order of the possible rules.
    The created modal space and the context. The context is the realm in which manifestations
are realized. The realms are possible in the modal space; their possibility is grounded in the
strata of the modal space. The created modal space is the order of the possible realms.

Principle 23.18 (The Created Modal Space Is the Order of the Four Columns). (D) The created
modal space is not one of the four columns; it is the order in which the four columns describe the
created order. The fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, and the context
are all possible in the modal space; their possibility is grounded in the strata of the modal space;
the created modal space is the order of the possible configurations of the four columns.
276                                                   Chapter 23. The Modal Space as Created


    The principle is (D): it follows from the four-column framework (Book I, Chapter 6) and
from the definition of the created modal space. The argument is that the four columns describe
the created order; the created order is possible in the modal space; the modal space is the order
of the possible; therefore the modal space is the order in which the four columns describe the
created order.
Remark 23.19 (The Modal Space Is Not a Fifth Column). The modal space is not a fifth column.
The four columns are analytical roles of any complete explanation; the modal space is the order
of the possible. The distinction is the distinction between the analytical roles and the order of
the possible; the framework keeps it throughout.


23.9     What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
     The principle does not say that the modal space is God. The modal space is created; God is
the Creator. The principle says that the modal space is created; it does not say that the modal
space is God.
     The principle does not say that the modal space is a part of God. The modal space is created;
it is not a part of God. The principle says that the modal space is created; it does not say that
the modal space is a part of God.
     The principle does not say that the necessary is contingent. The necessary is necessary (in
its stratum); it is created. The principle says that the necessary is created; it does not say that
the necessary is contingent.
     The principle does not say that the necessary is arbitrary. The necessary is necessary because
it is the form of the created order; the form is given by God’s wisdom, not by an arbitrary fiat.
The principle says that the necessary is created; it does not say that the necessary is arbitrary.
Remark 23.20 (The Principle Leaves the Divine Wisdom Open). The principle leaves the divine
wisdom open. It states that the form of the created order is given by God’s wisdom; it does
not describe what the divine wisdom is in itself. The distinction is the distinction between the
structure and the wisdom; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 23.21 (No Conflict with the Three Commitments). The principle is compatible with
Book I’s three commitments. God is not a realm (Principle 7.3); the light is not God (Princi-
ple 12.2); the modal space is not God (Principle 37.2). The principle says that the modal space
is created; it does not say that any of the three commitments is mistaken.


23.10      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (D), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that the modal space is uncreated. If such a
showing could be made, the modal space would be independent of God, and the createdness
would be a redundant concept. The framework’s claim is that the modal space is created; the
createdness is the metaphysical form of Book I’s Principle 37.2.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the createdness of the necessary makes
the necessary contingent. If such a showing could be made, the necessary would not be necessary,
and the framework’s account of the four kinds of necessity (Chapter 14) would be mistaken. The
framework’s claim is that the necessary is necessary in its stratum and created in its grounding;
the two are compatible.
Remark 23.22 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the createdness of the modal space; the second challenges the compatibility of the
23.11. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                   277


createdness with the necessity. The two challenges require different responses, and the framework
responds to each in its own terms.


23.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not prove God’s existence. It states the createdness of the modal
space, given Book I’s three commitments. The three commitments are (A); the present chapter
does not reargue them.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the modal status of the created order in detail. The
four kinds of necessity are stated in Chapter 14; the stratification of Ω is stated in Chapter ??;
the present chapter states the createdness of the modal space, and it leaves the modal status to
the chapters that treat it.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the modal space is created in time
or in eternity. The createdness of the modal space is a claim about its grounding; the question of
the temporality of its creation is a question the chapter leaves open, and it is the subject of a
different inquiry.
    Fourth, the chapter does not describe the divine wisdom. It states that the form of the
created order is given by God’s wisdom; it does not describe what the divine wisdom is in itself.
The distinction is the distinction between the structure and the wisdom; the framework keeps it
throughout.
Remark 23.23 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
stated the definition of the created modal space. It has stated the four modes of the createdness,
corresponding to the four strata. It has addressed the central difficulty of the chapter—how the
necessary can be both necessary and created—and has given the answer. And it has distinguished
the created modal space from modal realism, from Platonism about possibilities, from the
doctrine that possibilities are divine ideas, and from fictionalism.
Remark 23.24 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter 24). The chapter prepares Chapter 24 (Providence,
Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered). The modal space is the space of the possible; the
actualization chain X is the subset of the possible that is actualized (Book I, Definition 37.1).
The present chapter states the createdness of the modal space; the next chapter states the
relation between the modal space and the actualization chain, and it reconsiders the questions of
providence, divine knowledge, and creaturely choice in the light of the createdness of the modal
space.

23.13      A Question for Reflection
Consider a necessary truth you know—a truth of logic, a truth of mathematics, a truth of essence.
Is the truth created? Is it necessary? If it is both, how can it be both? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between the createdness and the necessity, and about the metaphysical
structure of the modal space?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The necessary is necessary (in its stratum)
and created (in its grounding); the two are compatible. The reader who can state, for a necessary
truth he knows, why it is both, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot
has found a place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty
further.

chain, and it reconsiders the three questions in the light of the createdness. The reader who has
followed the present chapter has the created modal space; the next chapter puts it to work.
