Chapter 24

Providence, Knowledge, and Choice
Reconsidered

Scope. This chapter reconsiders three questions in the light of the createdness of the modal
space (Chapter 23): providence, the governance of the created order by God; divine knowledge,
the knowledge by which God knows the possible and the actualized; and creaturely choice,
the selection by which a creature actualizes one possibility rather than another. It recalls
Book I’s Principle 37.4 (two kinds of divine knowledge) and Theorem 37.2 (compatibility of
divine knowledge and creaturely choice), and it states what the createdness of the modal space
adds to the recall. It distinguishes its position from determinism, from open theism, from
Molinism, from occasionalism, and from deism. It states the modal status of the future, and it
states what is not resolved—notably the problem of evil. Its claims are metaphysical; where it
speaks of “providence,” “knowledge,” “choice,” “selection,” or “actualization,” these are structural
terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the chapters to which it
refers. It prepares the transition to Part VIII.

Presupposition from Book I and Chapters 21–23. This chapter takes as given Book I’s
Principle 37.1 (the totality of possibility, C12), Principle 37.2 (the modal space is grounded in
God), Definition 37.1 (the three layers of the ontological architecture), Principle 37.4 (two kinds
of divine knowledge), Theorem 37.2 (compatibility of divine knowledge and creaturely choice),
and the account of middle knowledge as a speculation (Book I, Definition 37.2). It also takes as
given Chapter 21’s account of transcendence, Chapter 22’s account of creation and sustaining,
and Chapter 23’s account of the created modal space. It does not reargue these; it asks what the
createdness of the modal space adds to the three questions.


24.1     A Scene
Consider a playwright and a play. The playwright writes the play; the play has scenes, characters,
and a plot. The playwright knows the play; the playwright wrote it. Now ask: do the characters
choose? Do they act freely, or are they determined by the playwright’s script?
    The first answer is: the characters are determined by the script; they have no freedom. This
is determinism: the playwright’s writing determines what the characters do.
    The second answer is: the characters are not determined; they choose freely, and the playwright
does not know what they will do. This is open theism: the playwright’s knowledge is limited by
the characters’ freedom.
    The third answer is: the characters choose freely, and the playwright knows what they will
choose, because the playwright wrote a play in which they freely choose. This is the classical
answer: divine knowledge and creaturely choice are compatible, because the playwright’s knowing
is not a cause of the characters’ choosing.
280                              Chapter 24. Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered


    The framework’s answer is the third, with a refinement: the playwright not only wrote the
play; the playwright also wrote the space of possible plays. The characters’ choices are selections
within that space; the playwright knows what they will choose, not because the playwright forces
the choice, but because the playwright knows the space and knows the selection. The knowing is
not the causing; the space is created; the selection is the creature’s.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is providence? What is divine knowledge?
What is creaturely choice? And how do the three relate in the light of the createdness of the
modal space?
Remark 24.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them. The playwright and the play are examples; the account is
about providence, knowledge, and choice in general.


24.2      The Question
Book I stated the framework’s position on divine knowledge and creaturely choice in Theorem 37.2:
given Principle 37.4 (two kinds of divine knowledge—natural knowledge of Ω and free knowledge
of X, with the knowing being explanatorily posterior to the selection), the infallible divine
knowledge of the actualized chain is compatible with the selection’s being a creature’s own.
Book I also stated that middle knowledge (Molinism) is a speculation (Definition 37.2), not
required by the framework, and that the problem of evil is not resolved by the framework but
supported structurally.
    The present chapter reconsiders the three questions in the light of Chapter 23’s account of
the createdness of the modal space. The createdness adds something that Book I did not state:
the modal space is not an uncreated abstract realm, but a created order. The possible is created;
the selection is the creature’s; the knowing is God’s. The createdness changes the picture of the
three questions.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is providence? The chapter must define providence, and it must
distinguish it from determinism, from deism, from occasionalism, and from open theism.
    The second aspect: what is divine knowledge? The chapter must state the two kinds of divine
knowledge (natural and free), recall Book I’s argument for the compatibility of divine knowledge
and creaturely choice, and state what the createdness of the modal space adds to the argument.
    The third aspect: what is creaturely choice? The chapter must state what creaturely choice
is, given the createdness of the modal space, and how it relates to the selection within the
actualization chain.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: providence
is the governance of the created order by God; divine knowledge is the two kinds of knowledge
(natural and free); creaturely choice is the selection within the created modal space; and the three
are compatible because the createdness of the modal space makes the knowing, the creating, and
the selecting three distinct acts, not one.
Remark 24.2 (The Question Presupposes Book I and Chapters 21–23). The question presupposes
Book I’s Principle 37.4 and Theorem 37.2, and it presupposes Chapters 21–23. The present
chapter does not reargue them; it reconsiders the three questions in the light of the createdness of
the modal space. The reader who has not read the earlier chapters will find the present chapter
compressed; the reader who has read them will find the present chapter the natural completion
of the account.
24.3. What Book I and Chapters 26–28 Established                                                281


24.3      What Book I and Chapters 26–28 Established
Book I and Chapters 21–23 established four things, and the present chapter integrates them.
     The two kinds of divine knowledge. Book I’s Principle 37.4 established that God knows (i)
every possibility (natural knowledge of Ω) and (ii) the actualized chain X (free knowledge), and
that the knowing of X is explanatorily posterior to the selection: God knows the chain because
it is what is selected, and the selection is not what it is because God knows it.
     The compatibility of divine knowledge and creaturely choice. Book I’s Theorem 37.2 established
that the infallible divine knowledge of the actualized chain is compatible with the selection’s
being a creature’s own. The argument has two replies: the objection from necessity (infallible
knowledge does not turn the selection into a necessity) and the objection from the fixed past
(there is no such belief, because the knowing is not at a time).
     Transcendence. Chapter 21 established that transcendence is the relation of ontological
dependence of the created order on God, with three modes (ontological, epistemic, relational).
     Creation and sustaining. Chapter 22 established that creation is the giving of being, that
sustaining is the giving of being at every moment, and that the two are two modes of one relation.
     The created modal space. Chapter 23 established that Ω is created, that its createdness has
four modes, and that the necessary is the form of the created order, not arbitrary.
     The present chapter integrates the five. Providence is the governance of the created order by
God; divine knowledge is the two kinds of knowledge; creaturely choice is the selection within
the created modal space. The createdness of the modal space is what makes the integration
possible: because the modal space is created, the knowing, the creating, and the selecting are
three distinct acts, not one.
Remark 24.3 (The Five Are Not Independent). The five are not independent. The two kinds
of divine knowledge presuppose the reality of Ω; the compatibility of divine knowledge and
creaturely choice presupposes the reality of X; the transcendence is the relation of Ω and X
to God; the creation and sustaining are the two acts by which the relation is established; the
createdness of the modal space is the metaphysical form of the relation. The five together are
the framework’s account of the relation between God and the created order; the present chapter
integrates them.


24.4      The Definition of Providence
The definition of providence is stated here.

Definition 24.4 (Providence). Providence is the governance of the created order by God. It
is the act by which God orders the created order toward the ends that God wills, without
determining the creature’s selection within the created modal space. The governance is not
a force imposed from without; it is the order of the created order, established by God and
maintained by God.

    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what providence
is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal for the
concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength. Its support is Book I’s three commitments
(Principles 7.3, 12.2, 37.2); its development is the present chapter.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: providence is the governance of the created order. God governs the created
order; the governance is not a governance of an uncreated order, and it is not a governance of a
part of the created order. The governance is the order of the whole.
    The second part: providence orders the created order toward the ends that God wills. The
created order is ordered; the order is toward the ends that God wills. The ends are not given by
282                               Chapter 24. Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered


the created order to itself; they are given by God. The governance is the establishment of the
order.
    The third part: providence does not determine the creature’s selection. The governance orders
the created order toward its ends; it does not determine the creature’s selection within the modal
space. The distinction is the distinction between the order of the created order and the selection
within the order; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 24.5 (Providence Is Not Determinism). Providence is not determinism. Determinism
holds that every event is determined by prior causes; the creature’s selection is not free. Providence
holds that the created order is ordered toward the ends that God wills; the creature’s selection is
free within the order. The distinction is the distinction between the order and the determination;
the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 24.6 (Providence Is Not Deism). Providence is not deism. Deism holds that God created
the world and withdrew; the world runs on its own. Providence holds that God governs the
world at every moment; the world does not run on its own. The distinction is the distinction
between the withdrawal and the continuous governance; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 24.7 (Providence Is Not Occasionalism). Providence is not occasionalism. Occasionalism
holds that God is the only cause; the creature’s acts are occasions for God’s causation. Providence
holds that the creature’s selection is real; the creature selects, and God governs the order in
which the selection occurs. The distinction is the distinction between the only cause and the
governance of the order; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 24.8 (Providence Is Not Open Theism). Providence is not open theism. Open theism
holds that God does not know the future, because the future is not yet determinate. Providence
holds that God knows the actualized chain (free knowledge); the knowledge does not determine
the chain. The distinction is the distinction between the ignorance and the knowledge; the
framework keeps it throughout, and it is stated in Book I, Theorem 37.2.


24.5      The Modes of Providence
Providence has three modes, and the three are worth stating.

24.5.1    The Ordering Mode
The ordering mode is the establishment of the order of the created order. God orders the created
order toward the ends that God wills; the order is the structure of the created order, and the
structure is given by God. The ordering mode is the most fundamental of the three; it is the
ground of the other two.
Principle 24.9 (The Ordering Mode of Providence). (D) Providence orders the created order
toward the ends that God wills. The order is the structure of the created order; the structure is
given by God. The ordering mode is the ground of the other modes of providence.
    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 7.3 (God is the Creator and sustaining
ground) and from Chapter 22’s account of creation and sustaining. The argument is that God
creates the order; the order is the structure of the created order; therefore God orders the created
order.

24.5.2    The Sustaining Mode
The sustaining mode is the maintenance of the order at every moment. God sustains the created
order at every moment (Chapter 22); the sustaining is the maintenance of the order, not a new
ordering. The sustaining mode is the continuation of the ordering mode; the order is not a
one-time establishment, but a continuous giving.
24.6. Divine Knowledge                                                                        283


Principle 24.10 (The Sustaining Mode of Providence). (D) Providence sustains the order of
the created order at every moment. The sustaining is the maintenance of the order, not a new
ordering. The sustaining mode is the continuation of the ordering mode.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Chapter 22’s account of sustaining. The argument is that
God sustains the created order; the created order is ordered; the sustaining is the maintenance
of the order; therefore God sustains the order.

24.5.3    The Directing Mode
The directing mode is the direction of the created order toward its ends. God directs the
created order toward the ends that God wills; the direction is the orientation of the order, not
the determination of the selection. The directing mode is the completion of the ordering and
sustaining modes; the order is not only established and maintained, but also directed.

Principle 24.11 (The Directing Mode of Providence). (D) Providence directs the created order
toward its ends. The direction is the orientation of the order, not the determination of the
selection. The directing mode is the completion of the ordering and sustaining modes.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 7.3 and from Chapter 22’s account of
creation and sustaining. The argument is that God wills the ends; the ends are the orientation
of the order; therefore God directs the created order.

24.5.4    The Three Modes Together
The three modes are stated in the following table.

            Mode              What It Is                    What It Grounds
            Ordering          Establishment of the order   The other two modes
            Sustaining        Maintenance of the order     The continuation of the
                                                           order
            Directing         Orientation of the order to- The completion of the
                              ward its ends                order

    The table is the chapter’s map of the three modes. The three are not independent; the
ordering grounds the other two, and the sustaining and directing are the maintenance and the
orientation of the order that the ordering establishes.
Remark 24.12 (The Three Modes Are Not Three Providences). The three modes are not three
providences; they are three modes of one providence. The distinction is the distinction between
the modes and the providence; the framework keeps it throughout.


24.6     Divine Knowledge
The two kinds of divine knowledge are recalled here, with the addition that the createdness of
the modal space makes.

24.6.1    The Two Kinds of Divine Knowledge
Book I’s Principle 37.4 states two kinds of divine knowledge.
    Natural knowledge. God knows every possibility, because God knows the modal space Ω. The
knowledge is not of the actualized chain; it is of the possible. The knowledge is what Book I
called natural knowledge.
284                              Chapter 24. Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered


   Free knowledge. God knows the actualized chain X, because God knows what is selected.
The knowledge is explanatorily posterior to the selection: God knows the chain because it is
what is selected, not because the knowing determines the selection. The knowledge is not an
event in time.
   The two kinds of knowledge are distinct, and the distinction is the framework’s account of
how God knows the possible and the actualized.

24.6.2    What the Createdness of the Modal Space Adds
Chapter 23 established that Ω is created. The createdness adds something to the two kinds of
knowledge: the knowledge of Ω is knowledge of a created order, not knowledge of an uncreated
abstract realm. The natural knowledge is the knowledge of the created order; the free knowledge
is the knowledge of the actualized chain within the created order. The two kinds of knowledge
are not the knowledge of an abstract realm; they are the knowledge of a created order.
    The createdness also adds a distinction between the two kinds of knowledge and the creation
itself. The creation is the act by which the created order is given being; the knowledge is the act
by which God knows the created order. The two are distinct: God creates the order; God knows
the order; the creation is not the knowing, and the knowing is not the creation. The distinction
is the distinction between the creating and the knowing; the framework keeps it throughout.

Principle 24.13 (Divine Knowledge of the Created Modal Space). (D) The two kinds of divine
knowledge (natural and free) are the knowledge of the created modal space, not the knowledge of
an uncreated abstract realm. The natural knowledge is the knowledge of the created order; the
free knowledge is the knowledge of the actualized chain within the created order. The knowledge
is distinct from the creation: God creates the order; God knows the order; the creation is not
the knowing, and the knowing is not the creation.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Principle 37.4 and from Chapter 23’s account of
the created modal space. The argument is that Ω is created; the two kinds of knowledge are the
knowledge of Ω; therefore the two kinds of knowledge are the knowledge of the created order; the
knowledge is distinct from the creation.

24.6.3    The Compatibility of Divine Knowledge and Creaturely Choice
Book I’s Theorem 37.2 established the compatibility. The createdness of the modal space does
not change the argument; it clarifies it. The argument has two replies to the objection.
    The objection from necessity. Infallible knowledge that p entails that p; it does not entail
that p is necessary. From “necessarily, if God knows p then p” one cannot infer “if God knows p
then necessarily p.” The first is the necessity of the consequence; the second is the necessity of
the consequent, and the argument from knowledge to necessity commits the fallacy of passing
from the first to the second.
    The objection from the fixed past. The argument requires a belief of God’s at an earlier time,
which is then a past fact that no one can now alter. By Principle 37.4 there is no such belief: the
knowing is not at a time, and the time at which the selection occurs is posterior to Ω (Chapter 23,
the created modal space). The argument has no premise to begin from.
    The createdness of the modal space clarifies the replies. The two kinds of knowledge are
the knowledge of a created order; the knowing is not the creating, and the creating is not the
determining of the selection. The creature’s selection is within the created order; the selection is
real; the knowing does not determine it.
Remark 24.14 (The Createdness Does Not Change the Argument). The createdness does not
change the argument; it clarifies it. The argument is the same as Book I’s Theorem 37.2; the
createdness makes the clarification possible, because it distinguishes the created order from the
uncreated abstract realm.
24.7. Creaturely Choice                                                                            285


Remark 24.15 (Middle Knowledge Is Not Required). Middle knowledge (Molinism) is not required
by the framework. Book I states it as a speculation (Definition 37.2), and the present chapter
does not adopt it. The two kinds of knowledge (natural and free) are sufficient for the framework’s
account of divine knowledge and creaturely choice.


24.7      Creaturely Choice
Creaturely choice is stated here.
Definition 24.16 (Creaturely Choice). Creaturely choice is the selection by which a creature
actualizes one possibility rather than another within the created modal space. The selection
is the creature’s own; it is not determined by God’s knowledge, and it is not determined by
the created order. The selection is the realization of the creature’s fundamental self-awareness
(Book I, Principle 37.3) in the created modal space.
    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what creaturely
choice is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal
for the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength. Its support is Book I’s Principle 37.3
(fundamental self-awareness as the condition of choice); its development is the present chapter.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the selection is the creature’s own. The creature selects; the selection is the
creature’s act. The selection is not God’s; it is not the order’s; it is the creature’s. The distinction
is the distinction between the selection and the order; the framework keeps it throughout.
    The second part: the selection is not determined by God’s knowledge. The knowledge is not
the determination; the selection is the creature’s. The distinction is the distinction between the
knowing and the determining; the framework keeps it throughout, and it is stated in Book I,
Theorem 37.2.
    The third part: the selection is the realization of fundamental self-awareness. The selection
is the act of fundamental self-awareness (Book I, Principle 37.3) in the created modal space. The
self-awareness is the condition of the selection; the selection is the realization of the condition in
the created order.
Remark 24.17 (Creaturely Choice Is Not a Threat to Providence). Creaturely choice is not a
threat to providence. Providence orders the created order toward its ends; the creature’s selection
is within the order; the selection is real, and the order is real. The distinction is the distinction
between the order and the selection; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 24.18 (Creaturely Choice Is Not an Illusion). Creaturely choice is not an illusion. The
selection is the creature’s act; the act is real; the act is the realization of fundamental self-
awareness. The framework does not claim that the selection is an illusion; it claims that the
selection is real, and that it is compatible with providence and divine knowledge.


24.8      The Modal Status of the Future
The modal status of the future is stated here.
    The future is the part of the actualization chain X that has not yet been actualized. Its modal
status is not the status of the possible (the possible is in Ω); it is not the status of the actual
(the actual is in X and has been selected); it is the status of the selected-but-not-yet-actualized.
    The future is selected by the creature’s choice; the selection is within the created modal space;
the selection is not determined by the possible, and it is not determined by the past. The future
is real; its reality is the reality of the selected chain, and the selected chain is the creature’s own.
Principle 24.19 (The Modal Status of the Future). (D) The future is the selected-but-not-yet-
actualized part of the actualization chain X. Its modal status is not the status of the possible
286                               Chapter 24. Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered


(which is in Ω) and not the status of the actual (which has been selected). The future is real; its
reality is the reality of the selected chain; the selected chain is the creature’s own.

    The principle is (D): it follows from Book I’s Definition 37.1 (the three layers of the ontological
architecture) and from the present chapter’s account of creaturely choice. The argument is that
the future is part of X; X is selected within Ω; the selection is the creature’s; therefore the future
is selected and real.
Remark 24.20 (The Future Is Not Determined by the Past). The future is not determined by the
past. The past is the part of X that has been selected; the future is the part of X that has not
yet been selected. The past constrains the future; the past does not determine the future. The
distinction is the distinction between the constraint and the determination; the framework keeps
it throughout.
Remark 24.21 (The Future Is Not an Open Set of Possibilities). The future is not an open set of
possibilities. The future is the selected chain; the selected chain is real, even though it has not
yet been actualized. The distinction is the distinction between the possible (which is in Ω) and
the selected (which is in X); the framework keeps it throughout.


24.9      What Is Not Resolved
The chapter states what is not resolved.
    The problem of evil. The framework does not resolve the problem of evil. It supports the
structure of the free-will defence: God grounds the possibility of evil in Ω, and the actualization
of evil is the creature’s selection. But it does not resolve the problem of evil; it states the
structure, and it leaves the problem to the inquiry that undertakes it. Book I, Remark 37.11
states the position; the present chapter restates it.
    Middle knowledge. The framework does not adopt middle knowledge. Book I states it as
a speculation (Definition 37.2), and the present chapter does not adopt it. The two kinds of
knowledge (natural and free) are sufficient for the framework’s account.
    The amount of evil. The framework does not state why the amount of evil is what it is. The
framework’s account is structural; the amount of evil is a question of the actualized chain, and
the framework does not claim to settle it.
    The eternal destiny. The framework does not state the eternal destiny of the creature. The
creature’s selection is within the created order; the eternal destiny is beyond the created order,
and the framework does not describe it.
Remark 24.22 (The Limits Are Not Deficiencies). The limits are not deficiencies of the chapter.
They are the conditions under which the chapter’s claims are offered; the chapter states them so
that the reader knows what kind of claim is being made. A reader who accepts the limits may
still accept the chapter; a reader who rejects the limits is invited to show that the chapter can
resolve what it does not.


24.10       What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that God is the author of evil. God grounds the possibility of evil;
the actualization of evil is the creature’s selection. The distinction is the distinction between the
possibility and the actualization; the framework keeps it throughout.
    The principle does not say that the creature’s choice is an illusion. The choice is real; it
is the creature’s act; it is the realization of fundamental self-awareness. The distinction is the
distinction between the real and the illusory; the framework keeps it throughout.
24.11. What Would Refute the Principle                                                           287


    The principle does not say that God does not know the future. God knows the future (free
knowledge); the knowledge does not determine the selection. The distinction is the distinction
between the knowing and the determining; the framework keeps it throughout.
    The principle does not say that providence is a force. Providence is the governance of the
created order by God; the governance is the order of the created order, not a force imposed from
without. The distinction is the distinction between the order and the force; the framework keeps
it throughout.
Remark 24.23 (The Principle Leaves the Problem of Evil Open). The principle leaves the problem
of evil open. It states the structure of the free-will defence; it does not resolve the problem. The
distinction is the distinction between the structure and the resolution; the framework keeps it
throughout.
Remark 24.24 (No Conflict with Book I’s Commitments). The principle is compatible with
Book I’s commitments. God is not a realm (Principle 7.3); the light is not God (Principle 12.2);
the modal space is not God (Principle 37.2). The principle says that providence is the governance
of the created order; it does not say that any of the three commitments is mistaken.


24.11      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (D), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that providence determines the creature’s selection.
If such a showing could be made, the creature’s choice would be an illusion, and the framework’s
account of creaturely choice (Definition 24.16) would be mistaken. The framework’s claim is
that providence orders the created order without determining the selection; the order and the
selection are distinct.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that divine knowledge determines the
selection. If such a showing could be made, the creature’s choice would be an illusion, and
Book I’s Theorem 37.2 would be mistaken. The framework’s claim is that the knowledge does
not determine the selection; the knowing and the determining are distinct.
Remark 24.25 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the relationship between providence and creaturely choice; the second challenges the
relationship between divine knowledge and creaturely choice. The two challenges require different
responses, and the framework responds to each in its own terms.


24.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not resolve the problem of evil. It states the structure of the free-will
defence; it does not resolve the problem. The distinction is the distinction between the structure
and the resolution; the framework keeps it throughout.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the relation between providence and the four columns
in detail. The four columns are the fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics,
and the context (Book I, Chapter 6); providence is the governance of the created order that the
four columns describe. The relation is stated in Chapter 21 (transcendence is the condition of
the four columns); the present chapter states the three modes of providence, and it leaves the
relation to the four columns to the earlier chapter.
    Third, the chapter does not develop the eternal destiny of the creature. The eternal destiny is
beyond the created order; the framework does not describe it. The distinction is the distinction
between the created order and what lies beyond it; the framework keeps it throughout.
288                              Chapter 24. Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered


    Fourth, the chapter does not develop the relation between providence and the problem of evil
in detail. The structure is stated; the development is the work of the inquiry that undertakes the
problem of evil. The present chapter states the position, and it leaves the development to that
inquiry.
Remark 24.26 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It
has stated the definition of providence, with three modes (ordering, sustaining, directing). It
has recalled the two kinds of divine knowledge and the compatibility of divine knowledge and
creaturely choice, with the clarification that the createdness of the modal space adds. It has
stated the definition of creaturely choice and the modal status of the future. And it has stated
what is not resolved—notably the problem of evil, middle knowledge, the amount of evil, and
the eternal destiny.
Remark 24.27 (The Chapter Completes Part VI). The chapter completes Part VI. The part has
developed the metaphysics of transcendence (Chapter 21), creation and sustaining (Chapter 22),
the created modal space (Chapter 23), and the three questions of providence, knowledge, and
choice (the present chapter). The part is complete; the next part (Part VIII) states the boundaries
of metaphysics and the conclusion.

24.14      A Question for Reflection
Consider a choice you have made—a choice that mattered, a choice that shaped what followed.
Was the choice yours? Was it known? Was it governed? If it was all three, how can it be all
24.14. A Question for Reflection                                                              289


three? What does your answer tell you about the relation between providence, divine knowledge,
and creaturely choice, and about the metaphysical structure of the three?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The choice is yours (the selection is the
creature’s); the choice is known (the knowledge is God’s); the choice is governed (the order is
God’s). The three are distinct, and the framework’s claim is that they are compatible. The
reader who can state, for a choice he knows, why the three are compatible, has understood the
chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a place where the distinction is most
difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.
Part VI is complete. The next part (Part VIII) states the boundaries of metaphysics and the
conclusion. The reader who has followed Part VI has the vocabulary of transcendence, creation,
sustaining, the created modal space, and the three questions of providence, knowledge, and choice;
the next part puts the vocabulary to work in stating the boundaries of the framework.

Return to the Architecture

Scope
This chapter is the synthesis of Part VI. It returns to the four-column architecture of Parts II
to V and asks how the divine ground, stated in Chapters 21–24, illuminates the architecture. It
argues that the ground is not a fifth column; it is the condition under which the four columns
can be what they are. It states the three illuminations of the ground: the ground illuminates
the necessity of the columns, the unity of the columns, and the limits of the columns. It then
transitions to Part VII (Integration) by stating that the ground is the condition of possibility of
viability.
    The chapter’s claims are metaphysical and structural. Where it speaks of “ground,” “archi-
tecture,” “illumination,” “necessity,” “unity,” or “limit,” these are structural terms; their sense is
fixed by the definitions in this chapter and by the framework of Book I.

     Presupposition from Parts II–VI. This chapter takes as given the four-column
     architecture of Parts II to V (the fixed elements, the fluid elements, the governing
     dynamics, and the context), and the divine ground of Part VI (transcendence, creation
     and sustaining, the created modal space, and providence). It does not reargue them; it
     asks how the ground illuminates the architecture, and it states the three illuminations.
     The chapter is the bridge between the architecture and the integration.


24.15      A Scene: The Cathedral and the Light
Consider a cathedral. It has four walls, a floor, a ceiling, and a window. The four walls are the
structure; the floor and the ceiling are the frame; the window is the opening through which the
light enters. The cathedral is not the light, and the light is not the cathedral. But the light is
what makes the cathedral visible; without the light, the cathedral would be a structure in the
dark.
    Now consider a harder case. Consider a cathedral whose window is not a single opening but
a rose window, with many panes of colored glass. The light enters through the rose window, and
the light is not the same as the glass. The glass is the condition through which the light enters;
the light is what the glass admits. The two are distinct, and the light is what makes the glass
visible.
    The scene is not about cathedrals in particular. It is about a general structure, and the
structure is this: a ground is not a part of the structure it grounds; it is the condition under
which the structure can be what it is. The ground illuminates the structure, and the illumination
is not a part of the structure.
    The cathedral is what the framework calls the four-column architecture, and the light is what
the framework calls the divine ground. The ground is not a fifth column; it is the condition
under which the four columns can be what they are. The ground illuminates the architecture,
and the illumination is what the present chapter states.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. How does the divine ground illuminate the
four-column architecture? What does the ground add to the architecture that the architecture
292                                                                     Return to the Architecture


does not contain? The chapter’s answer is: the ground illuminates the necessity, the unity, and
the limits of the architecture, and the illumination is the condition of possibility of viability.


24.16      The Question
Parts II to V have derived the four columns of metaphysics: the fixed elements (substance,
essence, thisness), the fluid elements (causation, relation, light), the governing dynamics (law,
necessity, the modal space), and the contexts (the realms, the barzakhic category, non-passage).
Part VI has stated the divine ground of the convergence: transcendence (Chapter 21), creation
and sustaining (Chapter 22), the created modal space (Chapter 23), and providence (Chapter 24).
    The present chapter asks: how does the ground illuminate the architecture? The question is
not what the ground is; Part VI has said that. The question is what the ground adds to the
architecture, and how the addition illuminates the architecture’s necessity, unity, and limits.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: the necessity of the columns. The ground shows that the four columns are
not contingent features of the framework; they are the conditions under which the ground can be
what it is. The ground illuminates the necessity of the columns.
    The second aspect: the unity of the columns. The ground shows that the four columns are not
four separate structures; they are four aspects of one structure, and the structure is grounded in
the ground. The ground illuminates the unity of the columns.
    The third aspect: the limits of the columns. The ground shows that the four columns are not
the whole of what is; they are the structure of the relation between the created order and the
ground, and the relation points beyond itself to the ground. The ground illuminates the limits of
the columns.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: the ground
illuminates the necessity, the unity, and the limits of the architecture, and the illumination is the
condition of possibility of viability.


24.17      The Ground Illuminates the Necessity of the Columns
24.17.1     The Columns Are Not Contingent
The first illumination is the necessity of the columns. Without the ground, the four columns
would be contingent features of the framework: they would be the way the framework happens
to describe the world, but they would not be the way the world must be. With the ground, the
columns are necessary: they are the conditions under which the ground can be what it is.
    The argument has three steps.

   1. The ground is the condition under which the created order can be what it is (Chapter 21).

   2. The created order is the structure of the four columns (Parts II to V).

   3. Therefore, the four columns are the conditions under which the ground can be what it is,
      and they are necessary.

   The conclusion follows: the ground illuminates the necessity of the columns. Without the
ground, the columns would be contingent; with the ground, the columns are necessary.

24.17.2     The Necessity Is Not Logical
The necessity that the ground illuminates is not logical necessity. It is not the necessity of a
theorem that follows from axioms by inference rules. It is the necessity of a condition: the
24.18. The Ground Illuminates the Unity of the Columns                                         293


columns are the conditions under which the ground can be what it is, and the conditions are
necessary because the ground is what it is.
    The distinction is the distinction between logical necessity and metaphysical necessity. The
ground illuminates the metaphysical necessity of the columns, not their logical necessity.

Principle 24.28 (The Ground Illuminates the Necessity of the Columns). (T) The divine ground
illuminates the necessity of the four columns: the columns are the conditions under which the
ground can be what it is, and they are necessary because the ground is what it is. The necessity
is metaphysical, not logical.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the derivation of the ground in Part VI and by the
derivation of the columns in Parts II to V. It is the chapter’s first contribution.


24.18      The Ground Illuminates the Unity of the Columns
24.18.1     The Columns Are Not Separate
The second illumination is the unity of the columns. Without the ground, the four columns
would be four separate structures that happen to be found together; there would be no reason
why the fixed elements, the fluid elements, the governing dynamics, and the context should be
related as they are. With the ground, the columns are one structure: they are the four aspects
of the relation between the created order and the ground, and the relation is one.
    The argument has three steps.

   1. The ground is the condition under which the created order can be what it is (Chapter 21).

   2. The created order is the structure of the four columns (Parts II to V).

   3. Therefore, the four columns are the four aspects of one relation between the created order
      and the ground, and they are one structure.

   The conclusion follows: the ground illuminates the unity of the columns. Without the ground,
the columns would be separate; with the ground, the columns are one.

24.18.2     The Unity Is Not Homogeneity
The unity that the ground illuminates is not homogeneity. The columns are distinct (Book I,
Principle 7.2); they are not the same column under different names. The unity is the unity of a
relation, not the unity of a substance; the columns are distinct, and their distinctness is what
makes the relation what it is.
    The distinction is the distinction between the unity of a relation and the unity of a substance.
The ground illuminates the unity of the relation, not the homogeneity of the columns.

Principle 24.29 (The Ground Illuminates the Unity of the Columns). (T) The divine ground
illuminates the unity of the four columns: the columns are the four aspects of one relation
between the created order and the ground, and they are one structure. The unity is the unity of
a relation, not the homogeneity of the columns.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the derivation of the ground in Part VI and by the
derivation of the columns in Parts II to V. It is the chapter’s second contribution.
294                                                                      Return to the Architecture


24.19      The Ground Illuminates the Limits of the Columns
24.19.1     The Columns Are Not the Whole
The third illumination is the limits of the columns. Without the ground, the four columns would
appear to be the whole of what is: the framework would describe the structure of the world, and
there would be nothing beyond the structure. With the ground, the columns are the structure
of the relation between the created order and the ground, and the relation points beyond itself
to the ground. The columns are not the whole; they are the structure of a relation that points
beyond itself.
    The argument has three steps.

   1. The ground is the condition under which the created order can be what it is (Chapter 21).
   2. The created order is the structure of the four columns (Parts II to V).
   3. Therefore, the four columns are the structure of a relation that points beyond itself to the
      ground, and they are not the whole of what is.

    The conclusion follows: the ground illuminates the limits of the columns. Without the ground,
the columns would appear to be the whole; with the ground, the columns are the structure of a
relation that points beyond itself.

24.19.2     The Limits Are Not a Defect
The limits that the ground illuminates are not a defect of the columns. The columns are the
structure of the relation, and the structure is real; the fact that the structure points beyond itself
to the ground is not a failure of the structure, but the condition under which the structure can
be what it is. The limits are the framework’s way of marking where the structure ends and the
ground begins.
    The distinction is the distinction between a limit and a defect. The ground illuminates the
limits of the columns as the condition of their intelligibility, not as a failure of their adequacy.
Principle 24.30 (The Ground Illuminates the Limits of the Columns). (T) The divine ground
illuminates the limits of the four columns: the columns are the structure of a relation that points
beyond itself to the ground, and they are not the whole of what is. The limits are not a defect;
they are the condition under which the structure can be what it is.
    The principle is (T): it is argued by the derivation of the ground in Part VI and by the
derivation of the columns in Parts II to V. It is the chapter’s third contribution.


24.20      The Ground as the Condition of Possibility of Viability
24.20.1     The Transition to Part VII
The three illuminations together yield the transition to Part VII. The ground illuminates the
necessity, the unity, and the limits of the columns; the columns are the structure of the relation
between the created order and the ground; and the relation is what Part VII calls viability. The
ground is the condition of possibility of viability.
   The argument has three steps.

   1. The ground illuminates the necessity, the unity, and the limits of the columns (Sections 24.17–
      24.19).
   2. The columns are the structure of the relation between the created order and the ground
      (Parts II to V and Part VI).
24.21. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                      295


  3. Therefore, the ground is the condition of possibility of the relation, and the relation is what
     Part VII calls viability.

   The conclusion follows: the ground is the condition of possibility of viability. Part VII states
the viability of the relation; the present chapter states the ground of the relation.

24.20.2     What Part VII Will State
Part VII states the viability of the relation between an identity and its manifestations in a realm.
It has five chapters.
    Chapter 25: From Structural to Metaphysical Viability. The chapter states the transition from
the structural concept of viability (Book I) to the metaphysical concept of viability (Book II).
    Chapter 26: Viability and Essence. The chapter applies metaphysical viability to essence.
    Chapter 27: Viability and Causation. The chapter applies metaphysical viability to causation.
    Chapter 28: Viability and Modality. The chapter applies metaphysical viability to modality.
    Chapter 29: The Metaphysics of Viability. The chapter states the metaphysics of viability as
a whole.
    The five chapters together state the viability of the relation. The present chapter has stated
the ground of the relation; Part VII states the relation.

Principle 24.31 (The Ground as the Condition of Possibility of Viability). (T) The divine
ground is the condition of possibility of viability: the ground illuminates the necessity, the unity,
and the limits of the columns, and the columns are the structure of the relation that Part VII
calls viability.

    The principle is (T): it is argued by the three illuminations and by the framework’s derivation
of viability. It is the chapter’s fourth contribution, and it is the transition to Part VII.


24.21      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred.
    First, the chapter does not reargue the divine ground. The ground is the subject of Chapters 21–
24; the present chapter states the illuminations, and it leaves the ground to its place.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the three illuminations in detail. The illuminations are
stated at the strength of the framework’s derivations; their detailed development is the subject
of the chapters that follow, if they are developed at all.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the illuminations are the only
illuminations the ground provides. The illuminations are the ones the framework derives; whether
a fourth illumination is possible is a question the chapter leaves open.
    Fourth, the chapter does not prove that the ground is real. It derives the illuminations from
the framework’s derivation of the ground; the derivations are (T) relative to the framework’s
commitments, and they are offered at the strength that the commitments support.

24.23      A Question for Reflection
Consider a structure you know well—a legal system, a scientific theory, a work of art. What is
the ground of the structure? Is the ground a part of the structure, or is it the condition under
which the structure can be what it is? What does the ground add to the structure that the
structure does not contain?
     The answer is a model of the chapter’s distinction. The ground is not a part of the structure;
it is the condition of the structure. The ground illuminates the necessity, the unity, and the limits
of the structure. The reader who can state, for a structure he knows, what the ground is and
what it illuminates, has understood the chapter’s distinction; the reader who cannot has found a
place where the distinction is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.

Part VI is complete. Part VII (Integration) states the viability of the relation that the ground
makes possible. The reader who has followed Part VI has the ground; Part VII states the relation.

        Part VII

Chapter 25

From Structural to Metaphysical
Viability

Scope
This chapter opens Part VII by stating the transition from the structural concept of viability
developed in Book I to the metaphysical concept of viability developed in the present volume.
It recalls the structural concept, states the distinction between the cognitive context and the
existential context on which the transition depends, argues for the metaphysical extension of
the three components (fidelity, sustainability, recoverability), defines metaphysical viability, and
states the relation between structural and metaphysical viability. It does not yet apply the
concept to essence, causation, or modality; those applications are the work of Chapters 26, 27,
and ??. Its claims are metaphysical; where it speaks of “viability,” “structural,” “metaphysical,”
“fidelity,” “sustainability,” “recoverability,” “context,” or “realm,” these are structural terms, and
their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in Book I.


25.1      A Scene
Consider a bridge. It is built across a river. The bridge is a material structure; its parts are
steel, concrete, and stone. The bridge is also a relation: it connects two banks, and it carries
what passes from one bank to the other. The bridge is not the sum of its parts; it is the order in
which the parts stand, and the order is what makes the bridge a bridge.
    Now ask: what makes the bridge viable? One answer is that the bridge is viable because it
satisfies the criteria of the engineer: it bears the load, it resists the wind, it lasts the years. The
criteria are structural; they describe the relation between the bridge and the river, the bridge
and the load, the bridge and the years.
    The other answer is that the bridge is viable because it is what a bridge is: it connects, it
carries, it stands. The viability is not a property added to the bridge; it is the structural character
of the bridge’s relation to the river, to the load, to the years. The viability is metaphysical: it is
the character of the bridge’s being what it is.
    The two answers are not the same. The first is an engineering answer; the second is a
metaphysical answer. The first describes the criteria; the second describes the character of the
relation that the criteria measure. The framework’s claim is that the two answers are compatible,
and that the second is the metaphysical form of the first.
    The scene poses a question. What is the relation between the structural viability of Book I
and the metaphysical viability of the present volume? Is metaphysical viability a different concept,
or is it the same concept applied to a different context? And if it is the same concept, what is
the context to which it is applied?
300                                       Chapter 25. From Structural to Metaphysical Viability


Remark 25.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question at
work in a familiar case. It does not prove the transition; it makes the transition intelligible before
it is stated. The transition is argued in the sections that follow, and the scene carries no weight
in them. The bridge is an example; the transition is about the concept of viability in general.


25.2      The Question
Book I developed the concept of viability as the epistemic structural character of the relation
between an identity and its manifestations in a cognitive context (Book I, Chapter 36). The
concept has three components: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. The components were
stated in their epistemic form; the chapters that follow applied them to the epistemic economy
of cognition.
    The present volume is a metaphysics. It asks what the structure of being is; it does not ask
what the structure of explanatory cognition is. The question of the present chapter is: is there a
metaphysical concept of viability, and if so, how is it related to the structural concept of Book I?
    The framework’s answer is that there is: metaphysical viability is the structural character
of the relation between an identity and its manifestations in an existential context, with the
same three components as structural viability but understood metaphysically. The answer is the
subject of this chapter.
    The question is not idle. If there were no metaphysical concept of viability, the framework of
Book I would be confined to epistemology, and the present volume would have no concept of
viability to develop. If the metaphysical concept were a different concept, the framework’s unity
would be lost, and the concept of viability would be two concepts under one name. The present
chapter argues that the metaphysical concept is the same concept applied to a different context,
and that the unity of the framework is preserved.
    The chapter proceeds as follows. It recalls the structural concept. It states the distinction
between the cognitive context and the existential context on which the transition depends. It
argues for the metaphysical extension of the three components. It defines metaphysical viability.
It states the relation between structural and metaphysical viability. It states what the principle
does not say, and what would refute it. And it marks what the chapter does not establish.
Remark 25.2 (The Question Presupposes Book I). The question presupposes Book I. The
structural concept of viability is stated in Book I, Chapter 36; the present chapter recalls it,
but it does not restate it. The reader who has not read Book I will find the present chapter
compressed; the reader who has read Book I will find the present chapter a natural extension of
the concept.


25.3      The Structural Concept Recalled
The structural concept of viability is stated in Book I, Chapter 36. The present section recalls it,
so that the transition can be stated precisely.
Definition 25.3 (Structural Viability (Recalled)). (Book I, Definition 36.1) The structural
viability of an identity in a cognitive context is the structural character of the relation between
the identity and its manifestations in that context, in three respects: fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability.
   The definition has three components, and each is recalled here in its structural form.
   Fidelity. The manifestation preserves the essential determination of the identity, so that
the cognition records an appearance of that identity and not of another (Book I, Chapter 37;
developed in Book I, Chapter 38).
   Sustainability. The cost of producing and maintaining the manifestation does not exceed
what the receiving cognitive context can bear (Book I, Chapter 39).
25.4. The Distinction Between Cognitive and Existential Context                                   301


    Recoverability. The identity retains its structural capacity to manifest in the context; the
singularity at which restoring a manifestation would cost more than producing a new one has
not been crossed (Book I, Chapter 40).
    The three components are aspects of one structural character. They are not independent;
they are the character of the relation between the identity and its manifestations, considered
under its epistemic aspect.
Remark 25.4 (The Structural Concept Is Epistemic). The structural concept is epistemic. It
describes the relation between an identity and its manifestations in a cognitive context, with
the capacities and the constraints that the context imposes on cognition. The concept is not a
metaphysical claim about what the identity is; it is a claim about the character of the relation
between the identity and its manifestations, as the relation is cognized.
Remark 25.5 (The Structural Concept Is Not a Value). The structural concept is not a value. It
states a condition on the relation between an identity and its manifestations, and it attaches no
value, end, or good to the condition. The framework’s claim is that the condition is a structural
character; it does not claim that the character is valuable or that it is the good.


25.4      The Distinction Between Cognitive and Existential Context
The transition from structural to metaphysical viability depends on a distinction that Book I
states and that the present volume develops: the distinction between the cognitive context and
the existential context. The distinction is worth restating.

Definition 25.6 (Cognitive Context (Recalled)). (Book I, Definition 10.1) A cognitive context
is the frame in which something is cognized: the question asked, the elements held fixed, the rule
applied, and the standpoint from which the partition into fixed and fluid is made. A cognitive
context is fixed by the question, and there are indefinitely many of them.

Definition 25.7 (Existential Context (Recalled)). (Book I, Definition 10.2) An existential
context is the setting in which a manifestation is realized, with the capacity and the constraints
of that setting. An existential context is fixed by the identity and the receiving setting, not by
the question.

    The two definitions are different, and the difference is the difference between the order of
inquiry and the order of being. The cognitive context is the order through which what is becomes
intelligible; the existential context is the order of what is. The two are distinct, and neither is
reducible to the other; but the first is the condition of possibility of the second.

Principle 25.8 (The Transition Is From the Cognitive to the Existential). (T) The transition
from structural to metaphysical viability is the transition from the viability of the relation in a
cognitive context to the viability of the relation in an existential context. The three components
are the same; the context is different.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the definitions of structural viability and of the two kinds
of context. The argument is that the structural concept of viability is stated for the cognitive
context, and the metaphysical concept is stated for the existential context; the components are
the same, and the context is what distinguishes the two concepts.
Remark 25.9 (The Transition Is Not a Change of Concept). The transition is not a change of
concept. The concept of viability is the same; the context to which it is applied is different.
The structural concept describes the relation in the cognitive context; the metaphysical concept
describes the relation in the existential context. The two are the same concept, applied to two
kinds of context.
302                                      Chapter 25. From Structural to Metaphysical Viability


Remark 25.10 (The Transition Is Not a Reduction). The transition is not a reduction. It does
not say that the metaphysical concept is the structural concept in disguise, or that the structural
concept is the metaphysical concept in disguise. It says that the two concepts are the same
concept, applied to two kinds of context, and that the two contexts are distinct.


25.5      The Metaphysical Extension of the Three Components
The three components of viability are stated in their structural form in Book I. The present
section states their metaphysical form.
    Fidelity (metaphysical). The manifestation preserves the essential determination of the
identity, as that determination is determined by the realm’s mode of existence. The manifestation
is not a copy of the identity; it is the identity’s taking the form that the realm’s capacity permits
(Chapter ??). The fidelity is the extent to which the form preserves the identity’s essential
determination, as the realm’s mode of existence permits.
    Sustainability (metaphysical). The cost of producing and maintaining the manifestation does
not exceed what the realm can bear. The cost is the demand that the manifestation makes on
the realm’s ontological capacity; the capacity is what the realm’s mode of existence permits
(Chapter ??). The sustainability is the condition under which the cost does not exceed the
capacity.
    Recoverability (metaphysical). The identity retains its structural capacity to manifest in the
realm; the singularity at which restoring a manifestation would cost more than producing a new
one has not been crossed. The singularity is the threshold of the manifestation’s restoration; the
recoverability is the condition under which the identity’s capacity to manifest in the realm is
retained.
Principle 25.11 (The Three Components in Their Metaphysical Form). (T) The three compo-
nents of viability—fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability—are the same in their metaphysical
form as in their structural form; what differs is the context to which they are applied. In the
metaphysical form, the context is the existential context (the realm), not the cognitive context.
    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (given in the next
section) and from the distinction between the cognitive and the existential context (Section 25.4).
The argument is that the three components are stated for the relation between an identity and
its manifestations; the relation is the same in both forms; the context is what distinguishes the
forms.
Remark 25.12 (The Three Components Are Not Restated). The three components are not
restated in their metaphysical form; they are recalled and re-applied. The recall is in Section 25.3;
the re-application is in the present section. The reader who wishes to see the components in
their structural form is directed to Book I, Chapters 37–40; the reader who wishes to see them
in their metaphysical form is directed to the present section and to Chapters 26–??.
Remark 25.13 (The Metaphysical Form Is Not a Different Concept). The metaphysical form
is not a different concept. It is the same concept, applied to the existential context. The
framework’s claim is that the concept of viability is one concept, and that the two forms are the
two applications of the concept to the two kinds of context.


25.6      The Definition of Metaphysical Viability
The definition of metaphysical viability is stated here.
Definition 25.14 (Metaphysical Viability). The metaphysical viability of an identity in an
existential context (a realm) is the structural character of the relation between the identity and
its manifestations in that realm, in three respects: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.
25.7. The Relation Between Structural and Metaphysical Viability                                 303


    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what meta-
physical viability is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s
proposal for the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the identity. The identity is the invariant that an explanatory cognition holds
fixed across a class of allowable transformations of its manifestations (Book I, Chapter 12). The
identity is not a substance; it is a structural determination. The identity’s manifestations in a
realm are the realizations of the identity in the realm’s mode (Chapter ??).
    The second part: the existential context (the realm). The realm is the existential context in
which the identity is manifested (Chapter ??). The realm’s mode of existence determines what
can appear in it and what it constrains (Book I, Principle 7.2).
    The third part: the three components. The three components are fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability; they are the same components as in the structural concept (Book I, Chapter 37),
applied to the existential context.
Remark 25.15 (Metaphysical Viability Is Not Structural Viability). Metaphysical viability is not
structural viability. The structural concept describes the relation in the cognitive context; the
metaphysical concept describes the relation in the existential context. The two are the same
concept, applied to two kinds of context; the two are not the same, and the framework keeps
them apart.
Remark 25.16 (Metaphysical Viability Is Not a Value). Metaphysical viability is not a value.
It states a condition on the relation between an identity and its manifestations in a realm; it
attaches no value, end, or good to the condition. The framework’s claim is that the condition is
a structural character; it does not claim that the character is valuable or that it is the good.
Remark 25.17 (Metaphysical Viability Is Not a Definition of Identity). Metaphysical viability is
not a definition of identity. Identity is defined in Book I, Chapter 12, as the invariant that an
explanatory cognition holds fixed across a class of allowable transformations of its manifestations.
Metaphysical viability is the character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
in a realm, not the identity itself. The two are related, but they are not the same, and the
framework keeps them apart.


25.7      The Relation Between Structural and Metaphysical Viabil-
          ity
The relation between structural and metaphysical viability is worth stating.
    The two are the same concept, applied to two kinds of context. The structural concept
describes the relation in the cognitive context; the metaphysical concept describes the relation in
the existential context. The two contexts are distinct; the two concepts are the same concept.
    The two are not reducible to each other. The structural concept cannot be derived from
the metaphysical concept, and the metaphysical concept cannot be derived from the structural
concept. The two are distinct applications of the same concept, and neither is a substitute for
the other.
    The two are related. The metaphysical viability is the character of the relation in the realm;
the structural viability is the character of the relation as it is cognized. The first is the order of
being; the second is the order of inquiry. The two are distinct, and neither is reducible to the
other; but the first is the condition of possibility of the second.
Principle 25.18 (The Relation Between Structural and Metaphysical Viability). (T) Structural
viability and metaphysical viability are the same concept applied to two kinds of context. The
structural concept applies to the cognitive context; the metaphysical concept applies to the
existential context. The two are not reducible to each other, and the first is the condition of
possibility of the second.
304                                       Chapter 25. From Structural to Metaphysical Viability


    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of the two concepts and from the distinction
between the two kinds of context. The argument is that the concept of viability is one concept,
and the contexts are two kinds; the same concept applies to both, and the two applications are
distinct.
Remark 25.19 (The Relation Is One of Condition, Not of Reduction). The relation is one of
condition, not of reduction. The metaphysical viability is the condition of possibility of the
structural viability; the structural viability is the intelligibility of the metaphysical viability. The
two are related as the order of being is related to the order of inquiry; the first is the condition,
and the second is the intelligibility.
Remark 25.20 (The Relation Is Not a Hierarchy). The relation is not a hierarchy. The metaphysical
concept is not more important than the structural concept; the structural concept is not more
important than the metaphysical concept. The two are the same concept, applied to two kinds
of context, and the two are equally needed for the framework.


25.8      What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that the structural concept is false. The structural concept is
true of the cognitive context; the metaphysical concept is true of the existential context. The
principle says that the two concepts are the same concept, applied to two kinds of context; it
does not say that either is false.
    The principle does not say that the metaphysical concept is a different concept. The
metaphysical concept is the same concept as the structural concept; the difference is the context,
not the concept.
    The principle does not say that the metaphysical concept is more fundamental. The two
concepts are equally fundamental; the difference is the context, not the fundamentality.
    The principle does not say that the metaphysical concept is a value. The concept states a
condition on the relation; it attaches no value, end, or good to the condition.
Remark 25.21 (The Principle Leaves the Applications Open). The principle leaves the applications
open. It states the transition from structural to metaphysical viability; it does not state how
the concept applies to essence, causation, or modality. Those applications are the work of
Chapters 26, 27, and ??.
Remark 25.22 (No Conflict with the Three Components). The principle is compatible with the
three components. The components are the same in both forms; the context is what distinguishes
the forms. The framework’s claim is that the concept of viability is one concept, with three
components, applied to two kinds of context.


25.9      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that the metaphysical concept of viability is a
different concept from the structural concept. If such a showing could be made, the framework’s
unity would be lost, and the concept of viability would be two concepts under one name. The
framework’s claim is that the two concepts are the same concept, applied to two kinds of context.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the existential context is not a context
in which viability can be applied. If such a showing could be made, the metaphysical concept
would have no application, and the principle would be false. The framework’s claim is that the
existential context is a context in which the concept applies, and that the application is the
subject of Chapters 26–??.
25.10. What This Chapter Does Not Establish                                                      305


Remark 25.23 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the unity of the concept; the second challenges the applicability of the concept to the
existential context. The two challenges require different responses, and the framework responds
to each in its own terms.


25.10      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
     First, the chapter does not develop the applications of metaphysical viability. The applications
are the work of Chapters 26–??; the present chapter states the transition and the definition, and
it leaves the applications to their place.
     Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the existential context. The existential
context is stated in Chapter ??; the present chapter recalls the distinction between the cognitive
and the existential context, and it leaves the full account to its place.
     Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the concept of viability applies
to all realms in the same way. The concept applies to the relation between an identity and its
manifestations in a realm; the question of how the concept applies to each realm is a matter for
the inquiry, not for the chapter.
     Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the concept. It claims
to have described the concept and its transition; the concept points beyond itself to its ground.
The question of what grounds the concept is left to a later part of the book.
Remark 25.24 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
recalled the structural concept of viability. It has stated the distinction between the cognitive
and the existential context, on which the transition depends. It has argued for the metaphysical
extension of the three components. And it has defined metaphysical viability, and stated the
relation between structural and metaphysical viability.
Remark 25.25 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter 26). The chapter prepares Chapter 26, which
applies metaphysical viability to essence. The present chapter states the concept; Chapter 26
states the application to essence; Chapter 27 states the application to causation; Chapter ??
states the application to modality; and Chapter ?? states the metaphysics of viability as a whole.
The five chapters of Part VII together state the framework’s metaphysical account of viability.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a relation you know between a thing and its manifestations—a person and their actions,
a law and its applications, a form and its instances. Is the relation viable in the structural sense
of Book I? Is it viable in the metaphysical sense of the present chapter? What does the difference
tell you about the transition from structural to metaphysical viability, and about the relation
between the two concepts?
The next chapter (Chapter 26) applies metaphysical viability to essence. The present chapter
has stated the transition and the definition; the next chapter states what the concept makes of
essence, and how the concept applies to the essence of an identity in a realm.
