Chapter 26

Viability and Essence

Scope
This chapter applies the metaphysical concept of viability (Chapter 25) to essence. It recalls the
framework’s account of essence (Chapter ??), states the relation between essence and viability,
defines viable essence, and argues that the three components of viability—fidelity, sustainability,
and recoverability—apply to essence in its metaphysical form. It distinguishes the essence of an
identity from its accidental features, argues that essence is not a static list of properties but a
structural determination that is expressed in a realm, and states the conditions under which an
essence is viable in a realm. It does not yet apply the concept to causation or to modality; those
applications are the work of Chapters 27 and ??. Its claims are metaphysical; where it speaks
of “essence,” “essentialism,” “viability,” “fidelity,” “sustainability,” “recoverability,” “accident,”
or “determination,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this
chapter and in the chapters to which it refers.


26.1      A Scene
Consider a seed. It is a small thing, hard and dry, with a coat that protects what is inside. What
is inside? Not a tree; the tree is not in the seed the way a chair is in a room. What is inside is
the determination of the tree: the structure that makes the seed a seed of this kind, and that,
when the conditions are right, becomes a tree of this kind.
     Now ask: what is the essence of the seed? One answer is that the essence is the list of
properties that every seed of this kind has: the shape, the coat, the embryo, the stored food.
The list is accurate; it describes what a seed of this kind is. But the list is not the essence; the
essence is what makes the list the list it is. The essence is the structural determination that the
list describes, and that the seed expresses when it becomes a tree.
     The other answer is that the essence is the determination itself: the structure that the seed
carries, and that the tree expresses. The essence is not the list of properties; it is what the
properties are properties of. The essence is the structural determination of the seed, and it is
what the seed is when it is a seed, and what the tree is when it is a tree.
     The two answers are not the same. The first is a list; the second is a determination. The
framework’s claim is that the second is the essence, and that the first is the description of the
essence’s expression in a realm.
     The scene poses a question. What is the relation between essence and viability? Is the essence
viable in the seed? Is it viable in the tree? And what would it mean for an essence to be viable,
or not viable, in a realm?
Remark 26.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
308                                                             Chapter 26. Viability and Essence


the scene carries no weight in them. The seed is an example; the account is about essence and
viability in general.


26.2      The Question
The previous chapter stated the transition from structural to metaphysical viability, and defined
metaphysical viability as the structural character of the relation between an identity and its
manifestations in a realm (Chapter 25). The present chapter applies the concept to essence.
    The question is: what is the relation between essence and viability? Is essence subject to
viability, or is essence prior to viability? And if essence is subject to viability, what does it mean
for an essence to be viable in a realm?
    The framework’s answer is that essence is subject to viability, and that the viability of an
essence is the structural character of the relation between the essence and its manifestations in a
realm, in the three respects of fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. The essence is not prior
to viability; it is the identity that viability characterizes. The essence is what is expressed; the
viability is the character of its expression.
    The question is not idle. If essence were prior to viability, the essence would be what it is
regardless of its expression, and the framework’s account of manifestation (Book I, Chapter 13)
would be mistaken. If essence were subject to viability, the essence is what it is, and its expression
is what is viable or not. The present chapter argues that the second is the framework’s account,
and it states what the account implies for the concept of essence.
    The chapter proceeds as follows. It recalls the framework’s account of essence. It states the
relation between essence and viability. It defines viable essence. It states the three components
in their application to essence. It states the relation between essence and accident. It states
what the principle does not say, and what would refute it. And it marks what the chapter does
not establish.
Remark 26.2 (The Question Presupposes the Account of Essence). The question presupposes
the account of essence. The account is stated in Chapter ??; the present chapter recalls it, but
it does not restate it. The reader who has not read Chapter ?? will find the present chapter
compressed; the reader who has read it will find the present chapter a natural application of the
account.


26.3      The Framework’s Account of Essence Recalled
The framework’s account of essence is stated in Chapter ??. The present section recalls it, so
that the application to viability can be stated precisely.
Definition 26.3 (Essence (Recalled)). (Chapter ??, Definition ??) The essence of an identity
is the structural determination that constitutes it: the determination that makes the identity
the identity it is, and that distinguishes it from its alternatives. The essence is not a list of
properties; it is the structural principle that the properties express.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The essence is a structural determination. It is not a list; it is the principle that distinguishes
the identity and holds it one. The list of properties is the description of the essence’s expression
in a realm; the essence is what the description is a description of.
    The essence constitutes the identity. It is what makes the identity the identity it is. Without
the essence, the identity would not be the identity; it would be another identity, or no identity
at all.
    The essence distinguishes the identity from its alternatives. It is what makes the identity
different from other identities. The essence is the principle of distinction; it is what makes the
identity one and not another.
26.4. The Relation Between Essence and Viability                                                    309


Remark 26.4 (The Essence Is Not a List of Properties). The essence is not a list of properties.
The list is the description of the essence’s expression; the essence is the structural determination
that the description describes. A reader who takes the essence as the list has misread the account;
a reader who takes it as the structural determination has read it correctly.
Remark 26.5 (The Essence Is Not a Substance). The essence is not a substance. A substance is
a thing with properties; the essence is the determination that makes the thing the thing it is.
The distinction is the distinction between a thing and its determination; the framework keeps it
throughout.


26.4      The Relation Between Essence and Viability
The relation between essence and viability is stated in a principle.

Principle 26.6 (Essence Is Subject to Viability). (T) Essence is subject to viability. The essence
is the identity that is expressed; the viability is the structural character of the relation between
the essence and its manifestations in a realm. The essence is not prior to viability; it is the
identity that viability characterizes.

   The principle is (T): it is argued from the framework’s account of essence (Chapter ??) and
of metaphysical viability (Chapter 25). The argument is given below.

Argument for the Principle.     1. The essence is the structural determination that constitutes
     the identity (Definition 26.3).

   2. The essence is expressed in manifestations in a realm (Book I, Chapter 13; Chapter ??).

   3. The viability is the structural character of the relation between the identity and its
      manifestations in a realm (Definition 25.14).

   4. The essence is the identity that the relation is between; the viability is the character of
      the relation. The essence is not prior to the relation; it is the identity that the relation is
      about.

   5. Therefore essence is subject to viability: the essence is what it is, and its expression is what
      is viable or not.

    The argument’s force is in step 4. If the essence were prior to the relation, the essence would
be what it is regardless of its expression, and the viability would be an external addition to the
essence. But the essence is the identity that the relation is about; the viability is the character
of the relation. The essence is not prior to the relation; it is what the relation is about. The
principle follows.
Remark 26.7 (Essence Is Not Prior to Viability). Essence is not prior to viability. The essence is the
identity; the viability is the character of the relation between the identity and its manifestations.
The essence is what it is; the viability is the character of its expression. The two are related, but
they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 26.8 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Essence). The principle is not a denial of essence.
It affirms the essence; it says that the essence is subject to viability. The essence is real, invariant,
and describable; the viability is the character of the essence’s expression. The two are different,
and the framework keeps them apart.
310                                                            Chapter 26. Viability and Essence


26.5      Viable Essence Defined
The definition of viable essence is stated here.

Definition 26.9 (Viable Essence). The viable essence of an identity in a realm is the essence
whose relation to its manifestations in the realm satisfies the three components of metaphysical
viability: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.

    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what viable
essence is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal
for the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the essence. The essence is the structural determination that constitutes the
identity (Definition 26.3). The essence is not a list of properties; it is the principle that the
properties express.
    The second part: the relation to its manifestations in the realm. The relation is the relation
between the essence and its manifestations in the realm (Book I, Chapter 13). The relation is
what the three components characterize.
    The third part: the three components. The components are fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability (Chapter 25). The viable essence is the essence whose relation to its manifestations
satisfies the three components.
Remark 26.10 (Viable Essence Is Not the Same as Essence). Viable essence is not the same as
essence. The essence is the structural determination; the viable essence is the essence whose
relation to its manifestations satisfies the three components. The essence is what it is; the viable
essence is the essence in a viable relation to its manifestations. The two are related, but they are
not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 26.11 (Viable Essence Is Not a Degree of Essence). Viable essence is not a degree of
essence. The essence does not admit of degrees; the viable essence does. The essence is what it is;
the viable essence is the essence in a viable relation. The distinction is the distinction between
the identity and the character of its expression; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 26.12 (Viable Essence Is Not a Value). Viable essence is not a value. It states a condition
on the relation between the essence and its manifestations in a realm; it attaches no value, end,
or good to the condition. The framework’s claim is that the condition is a structural character;
it does not claim that the character is valuable or that it is the good.


26.6      Fidelity and Essence
The first component of viability is fidelity. The present section states what fidelity is in its
application to essence.

Principle 26.13 (Fidelity of Essence). (T) The fidelity of an essence in a realm is the extent to
which the manifestations of the essence in the realm preserve the essential determination of the
essence. The fidelity is the first component of the viable essence; without it, the manifestations
are not manifestations of the essence, and the relation is not viable.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Definition 25.14)
and from the definition of essence (Definition 26.3). The argument is that the fidelity is the
preservation of the essential determination; the essence is the essential determination; the fidelity
is what the relation between the essence and its manifestations must satisfy.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: fidelity preserves the essential determination. The manifestations of the
essence in the realm preserve the essential determination of the essence. The preservation is not
26.7. Sustainability and Essence                                                                 311


a copy; it is the identity’s taking the form that the realm’s capacity permits (Chapter ??). The
manifestation that is high in fidelity preserves the essential determination; the manifestation
that is low in fidelity preserves it less completely; the manifestation that is at the limit of zero
fidelity does not preserve it at all.
    The second part: fidelity is the first component. Without fidelity, the manifestations are not
manifestations of the essence; they are manifestations of another identity, or of no identity at all.
The fidelity is the condition under which the manifestations are manifestations of the essence.
    The third part: fidelity is not a degree of essence. The essence does not admit of degrees;
the fidelity does. The essence is what it is; the fidelity is the extent to which the manifestations
preserve the essence’s essential determination. The two are different, and the framework keeps
them apart.
Remark 26.14 (Fidelity Is Not Identity). Fidelity is not identity. The identity is the invariant
that the essence is; the fidelity is the extent to which the manifestations preserve the identity’s
essential determination. The identity is what it is; the fidelity is the character of the relation
between the identity and its manifestations. The two are different, and the framework keeps
them apart.
Remark 26.15 (Fidelity Is Not a Degree of Essence). Fidelity is not a degree of essence. The
essence is rigid (Chapter ??); the fidelity is graded. The essence is what it is; the fidelity is the
extent to which the manifestations preserve the essence’s essential determination. The two are
different, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 26.16 (Fidelity Is Not a Value). Fidelity is not a value. It states a condition on the
relation between the essence and its manifestations; it attaches no value, end, or good to the
condition. The framework’s claim is that the condition is a structural character; it does not
claim that the character is valuable or that it is the good.


26.7      Sustainability and Essence
The second component of viability is sustainability. The present section states what sustainability
is in its application to essence.

Principle 26.17 (Sustainability of Essence). (T) The sustainability of an essence in a realm is
the condition under which the cost of expressing the essence in the realm does not exceed what
the realm can bear. The sustainability is the second component of the viable essence; without it,
the expression of the essence exhausts the realm’s capacity, and the relation is not viable.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Definition 25.14)
and from the framework’s account of the cost of cognition (Book I, Chapter 39), read in its
metaphysical form. The argument is that the cost is the demand that the expression makes on
the realm’s capacity; the sustainability is the condition under which the cost does not exceed the
capacity.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: sustainability is a condition on the cost. The cost is the demand that the
expression of the essence makes on the realm’s capacity. The sustainability is the condition
under which the cost does not exceed the capacity. The expression that is sustainable is the
expression that the realm can bear; the expression that is not sustainable is the expression whose
cost exceeds the realm’s capacity.
    The second part: sustainability is the second component. Without sustainability, the expression
of the essence exhausts the realm’s capacity, and the essence cannot continue to be expressed.
The sustainability is the condition under which the expression can continue.
    The third part: sustainability is not cheapness. The expression that is cheap is not thereby
sustainable; the expression that is expensive is not thereby unsustainable. The sustainability is
312                                                             Chapter 26. Viability and Essence


the condition under which the cost does not exceed the capacity, not the condition under which
the cost is low.
Remark 26.18 (Sustainability Is Not Fidelity). Sustainability is not fidelity. The expression can
be fidelious and unsustainable (if the preservation of the essence’s determination costs more than
the realm can bear); the expression can be sustainable and not fidelious (if the expression is
cheap but distorts the essence). The two are different components of the viable essence, and the
framework keeps them apart.
Remark 26.19 (Sustainability Is Not the Cost Alone). Sustainability is not the cost alone. The
cost is what the expression demands of the realm’s capacity; the sustainability is whether the
cost exceeds the capacity. The two are related, but they are not the same, and the framework
keeps them apart.
Remark 26.20 (Sustainability Is Not Recoverability). Sustainability is not recoverability. The
expression can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the realm’s capacity has been
exhausted; the expression is not recoverable if the cost of restoring it would exceed the cost of
producing a new one. The two are different components of the viable essence, and the framework
keeps them apart.


26.8      Recoverability and Essence
The third component of viability is recoverability. The present section states what recoverability
is in its application to essence.
Principle 26.21 (Recoverability of Essence). (T) The recoverability of an essence in a realm is
the condition under which the essence retains its structural capacity to manifest in the realm;
the singularity at which restoring a manifestation would cost more than producing a new one
has not been crossed. The recoverability is the third component of the viable essence; without it,
the essence has lost its capacity to manifest in the realm, and the relation is not viable.
    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Definition 25.14)
and from the framework’s account of the singularity (Book I, Chapter 40). The argument is that
the recoverability is the retention of the essence’s capacity to manifest; the singularity is the
threshold beyond which the capacity is lost; the recoverability is the condition under which the
capacity is retained.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: recoverability is about the essence’s capacity. The essence retains its structural
capacity to manifest in the realm. The capacity is not the manifestation; it is the structural
possibility of the manifestation. The recoverability is the retention of the capacity, not the
presence of the manifestation.
    The second part: recoverability is the third component. Without recoverability, the essence
has lost its capacity to manifest in the realm, and the expression cannot be restored. The
recoverability is the condition under which the expression can be restored if it ceases.
    The third part: recoverability is not a promise of restoration. The recoverability is the
retention of the capacity; the restoration is contingent on the essence’s decision and on the
realm’s conditions. The recoverability is the capacity; the restoration is the act.
Remark 26.22 (Recoverability Is Not Sustainability). Recoverability is not sustainability. The
expression can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the realm’s capacity has been
exhausted; if the cost of restoring the expression exceeds the cost of producing a new one, the
expression is not recoverable, even though it was sustainable. The two are different components
of the viable essence, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 26.23 (Recoverability Is Not Identity Conservation). Recoverability is not identity
conservation. The identity conservation says that the essence is invariant under all temporal
26.9. The Relation Between Essence and Accident                                                    313


transformations of its manifestations (Book I, Chapter 9); the recoverability says that the essence
retains its structural capacity to manifest in a realm. The two are different, and the framework
keeps them apart.
Remark 26.24 (Recoverability Is Not a Promise). Recoverability is not a promise of restoration.
The essence retains the capacity; the restoration is contingent on the essence’s decision and on
the realm’s conditions. The framework’s claim is that the essence retains the capacity; it does
not claim that the restoration will occur.


26.9      The Relation Between Essence and Accident
The present section states the relation between essence and accident, in the light of the viability
of essence.
Definition 26.25 (Accident). An accident of an identity is a feature that does not belong to
the essence, and that may vary among the manifestations of the identity without altering the
essence’s determination.
    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what an
accident is. The accident is the feature that is not essential; the essence is the feature that is.
    The relation between essence and accident is the relation between the essential determination
and the non-essential features. The essence is the determination that constitutes the identity;
the accident is the feature that may vary without altering the essence. The essence is subject
to viability; the accident is not. The viable essence is the essence in a viable relation to its
manifestations; the accident is a feature of the manifestations that does not affect the essence’s
viability.
Principle 26.26 (The Essence Is Subject to Viability; the Accident Is Not). (T) The essence is
subject to viability; the accident is not. The essence is the identity that is expressed; the viability
is the character of the relation between the essence and its manifestations. The accident is a
feature of the manifestations that may vary without altering the essence; it does not affect the
essence’s viability.
    The principle is (T): it follows from the definitions of essence and accident and from the
definition of viable essence. The argument is that the essence is the identity that the relation is
about; the viability is the character of the relation; the accident is a feature of the manifestations.
The essence is subject to viability; the accident is not.
Remark 26.27 (The Distinction Is Not the Distinction Between the Real and the Unreal). The
distinction is not the distinction between the real and the unreal. The accident is real; it is a
feature of the manifestations. The essence is real; it is the determination that the manifestations
express. The distinction is the distinction between the determination and the feature; the
framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 26.28 (The Distinction Is Not a Ranking). The distinction is not a ranking. The essence
is not more important than the accident; the accident is not less important than the essence. The
essence is the determination that constitutes the identity; the accident is the feature that may
vary without altering the essence. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.


26.10       What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
   The principle does not say that the essence is unreal. The essence is real; it is the determination
that the manifestations express. The principle says that the essence is subject to viability; it
does not say that the essence is unreal.
314                                                             Chapter 26. Viability and Essence


    The principle does not say that the accident is unreal. The accident is real; it is a feature of
the manifestations. The principle says that the accident is not subject to viability; it does not
say that the accident is unreal.
    The principle does not say that the essence is a value. The essence is a determination; the
viable essence is the essence in a viable relation. The principle says that the essence is subject to
viability; it does not say that the essence is valuable.
    The principle does not say that the viable essence is the good. The viable essence is a
structural character of the relation; it is not the good. The principle says that the essence is
subject to viability; it does not say that the viable essence is the good.
Remark 26.29 (The Principle Leaves the Application Open). The principle leaves the application
open. It states the relation between essence and viability; it does not state how the relation
applies to causation or to modality. Those applications are the work of Chapters 27 and ??.
Remark 26.30 (No Conflict with the Account of Essence). The principle is compatible with the
account of essence. The essence is the structural determination; the viability is the character of
the relation between the essence and its manifestations. The two are different, and the framework
keeps them apart. The principle is the framework’s account of the relation, not a denial of the
essence.


26.11       What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that the essence is prior to viability. If such a
showing could be made, the essence would be what it is regardless of its expression, and the
viability would be an external addition to the essence. The framework’s claim is that the essence
is the identity that the relation is about; the viability is the character of the relation; the essence
is not prior to the relation.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the viable essence is a degree of essence.
If such a showing could be made, the essence would admit of degrees, and the framework’s
account of the rigidity of essence (Chapter ??) would be mistaken. The framework’s claim is
that the essence does not admit of degrees; the viable essence is the essence in a viable relation,
not a degree of the essence.
Remark 26.31 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The
first challenges the relation between essence and viability; the second challenges the distinction
between the essence and the viable essence. The two challenges require different responses, and
the framework responds to each in its own terms.


26.12       What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the application to causation. The application is the work
of Chapter 27; the present chapter states the application to essence, and it leaves the application
to causation to its place.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the application to modality. The application is the work
of Chapter ??; the present chapter states the application to essence, and it leaves the application
to modality to its place.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of what the essence is in itself. The chapter
states the essence as the structural determination that constitutes the identity; the question of
what the determination is in itself is a matter for the inquiry, not for the chapter.
26.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                                 315


   Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the essence. It claims to
have described the essence and its viability; the essence points beyond itself to its ground. The
question of what grounds the essence is left to a later part of the book.
Remark 26.32 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
recalled the framework’s account of essence. It has stated the relation between essence and
viability. It has defined viable essence, and stated the three components in their application to
essence. And it has stated the relation between essence and accident, and what would refute the
principle.
Remark 26.33 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter 27). The chapter prepares Chapter 27, which
applies metaphysical viability to causation. The present chapter states the application to essence;
the next chapter states the application to causation; the chapter after that states the application
to modality; and the chapter after that states the metaphysics of viability as a whole. The five
chapters of Part VII together state the framework’s metaphysical account of viability.

A Question for Reflection
Consider an essence you know—the essence of a person, a practice, a tradition, a form. Is
the essence subject to viability in the realm in which it is manifested? Does the manifestation
preserve the essential determination (fidelity)? Is the cost of the manifestation sustainable, given
the realm’s capacity (sustainability)? Does the essence retain its capacity to manifest in the
realm (recoverability)? What does your answer tell you about the relation between essence and
viability, and about the concept of the viable essence?
The next chapter (Chapter 27) applies metaphysical viability to causation. The present chapter
has stated the application to essence; the next chapter states the application to causation, and
shows how the three components of viability apply to the causal relation between an identity and
its manifestations in a realm.

Chapter 27

Viability and Causation

Scope
This chapter applies the metaphysical concept of viability (Chapter 25) to causation. It recalls
the framework’s account of causation (Chapter ??), states the relation between causation and
viability, defines viable causation, and argues that the three components of viability—fidelity,
sustainability, and recoverability—apply to the causal relation in its metaphysical form. It
distinguishes causation from the mere succession of events, argues that the causal relation is
a relation of expression between an identity and its manifestations in a realm, and states the
conditions under which a causal relation is viable in a realm. It does not yet apply the concept
to modality; that application is the work of Chapter ??. Its claims are metaphysical; where it
speaks of “causation,” “cause,” “effect,” “viability,” “fidelity,” “sustainability,” “recoverability,”
or “expression,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this
chapter and in the chapters to which it refers.


27.1      A Scene
Consider a lamp and a room. The lamp is switched on; the room is illuminated. The illumination
is the effect; the switching on is the cause. The relation between the two is a causal relation: the
lamp’s being switched on brings about the room’s being illuminated.
    Now ask: what makes the causal relation viable? One answer is that the relation is viable
because it satisfies the conditions of the physicist: the lamp emits light, the light propagates,
the light reaches the surfaces, the surfaces reflect the light. The conditions are structural; they
describe the relation between the lamp, the light, and the room.
    The other answer is that the relation is viable because it is a relation of expression: the
lamp’s being what it is expresses itself in the room’s being illuminated, and the expression is
what the relation is. The viability is not a property added to the relation; it is the character of
the relation between the lamp’s identity and its manifestation in the room.
    The two answers are not the same. The first is a description of the mechanism; the second is
a description of the expression. The framework’s claim is that the second is the metaphysical
account, and that the first is the description of the mechanism through which the expression
occurs.
    The scene poses a question. What is the relation between causation and viability? Is the
causal relation subject to viability? And what would it mean for a causal relation to be viable,
or not viable, in a realm?
Remark 27.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
318                                                           Chapter 27. Viability and Causation


the scene carries no weight in them. The lamp is an example; the account is about causation
and viability in general.


27.2      The Question
The previous chapter applied metaphysical viability to essence, and defined the viable essence
as the essence whose relation to its manifestations in a realm satisfies the three components of
viability (Chapter 26). The present chapter applies the concept to causation.
     The question is: what is the relation between causation and viability? Is the causal relation
subject to viability, or is causation prior to viability? And if the causal relation is subject to
viability, what does it mean for a causal relation to be viable in a realm?
     The framework’s answer is that the causal relation is subject to viability, and that the viability
of a causal relation is the structural character of the relation between a cause and its effect in a
realm, in the three respects of fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. Causation is not prior
to viability; it is the relation that viability characterizes. The cause is what expresses itself; the
effect is the manifestation; the viability is the character of the expression.
     The question is not idle. If causation were prior to viability, the causal relation would be
what it is regardless of its expression, and the framework’s account of manifestation (Book I,
Chapter 13) would be mistaken. If the causal relation is subject to viability, the cause is what it
is, and its expression is what is viable or not. The present chapter argues that the second is the
framework’s account, and it states what the account implies for the concept of causation.
     The chapter proceeds as follows. It recalls the framework’s account of causation. It states
the relation between causation and viability. It defines viable causation. It states the three
components in their application to causation. It distinguishes causation from mere succession. It
states what the principle does not say, and what would refute it. And it marks what the chapter
does not establish.
Remark 27.2 (The Question Presupposes the Account of Causation). The question presupposes
the account of causation. The account is stated in Chapter ??; the present chapter recalls it,
but it does not restate it. The reader who has not read Chapter ?? will find the present chapter
compressed; the reader who has read it will find the present chapter a natural application of the
account.


27.3      The Framework’s Account of Causation Recalled
The framework’s account of causation is stated in Chapter ??. The present section recalls it, so
that the application to viability can be stated precisely.

Definition 27.3 (Causation (Recalled)). (Chapter ??, Definition ??) Causation is the structural
relation in which an identity, through its manifestation in a realm, brings about a change in
another identity’s manifestation in the same realm or in another. The causal relation is a relation
of expression: the cause expresses itself in the effect, and the effect is the manifestation of the
cause’s expression.

    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    Causation is a structural relation. It is not a mere succession of events; it is the relation
in which one identity, through its manifestation, brings about a change in another identity’s
manifestation. The relation is structural; it is what makes the cause a cause and the effect an
effect.
    Causation is a relation of expression. The cause expresses itself in the effect; the effect is the
manifestation of the cause’s expression. The expression is not a copy; it is the identity’s taking
the form that the receiving realm’s capacity permits (Book I, Chapter 13; Chapter ??).
27.4. The Relation Between Causation and Viability                                                319


    Causation is mediated by the fluid element. The causal relation is carried by the fluid
element—epistemic light in its metaphysical form (Chapter ??; Chapter ??). The fluid element
is the medium through which the cause’s expression reaches the effect.
Remark 27.4 (Causation Is Not Mere Succession). Causation is not mere succession. The mere
succession of events is a temporal ordering; causation is the structural relation in which one
identity, through its manifestation, brings about a change in another. The distinction is the
distinction between the order of events and the relation of expression; the framework keeps it
throughout.
Remark 27.5 (Causation Is Not a Thing). Causation is not a thing. It is a structural relation;
it is what makes the cause a cause and the effect an effect. The distinction is the distinction
between a thing and a relation; the framework keeps it throughout.


27.4      The Relation Between Causation and Viability
The relation between causation and viability is stated in a principle.
Principle 27.6 (Causation Is Subject to Viability). (T) Causation is subject to viability. The
causal relation is the relation of expression between a cause and its effect; the viability is
the structural character of the relation, in the three respects of fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability. Causation is not prior to viability; it is the relation that viability characterizes.
   The principle is (T): it is argued from the framework’s account of causation (Chapter ??)
and of metaphysical viability (Chapter 25). The argument is given below.

Argument for the Principle.    1. Causation is the structural relation in which an identity,
     through its manifestation in a realm, brings about a change in another identity’s manifes-
     tation (Definition 27.3).
   2. The causal relation is a relation of expression: the cause expresses itself in the effect
      (Definition 27.3).
   3. The viability is the structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifes-
      tations in a realm (Definition 25.14).
   4. The causal relation is the relation between the cause’s expression and its effect; the viability
      is the character of the expression. The causal relation is not prior to the expression; it is
      the relation that the expression is.
   5. Therefore causation is subject to viability: the cause is what it is, and its expression is
      what is viable or not.

    The argument’s force is in step 4. If causation were prior to the expression, the causal relation
would be what it is regardless of its expression, and the viability would be an external addition to
the relation. But the causal relation is the relation of expression; the viability is the character of
the relation. Causation is not prior to the expression; it is what the expression is. The principle
follows.
Remark 27.7 (Causation Is Not Prior to Viability). Causation is not prior to viability. The
causal relation is the relation of expression; the viability is the character of the relation. The
cause is what it is; the viability is the character of its expression. The two are related, but they
are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 27.8 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Causation). The principle is not a denial of
causation. It affirms causation; it says that the causal relation is subject to viability. The causal
relation is real, structural, and describable; the viability is the character of the causal relation.
The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
320                                                          Chapter 27. Viability and Causation


27.5      Viable Causation Defined
The definition of viable causation is stated here.

Definition 27.9 (Viable Causation). The viable causation of an identity in a realm is the causal
relation whose expression in the realm satisfies the three components of metaphysical viability:
fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.

    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what viable
causation is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s
proposal for the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the causal relation. The causal relation is the relation of expression between
the cause and its effect (Definition 27.3). The relation is what the three components characterize.
    The second part: the expression in the realm. The expression is the cause’s manifestation
in the effect, according to the realm’s capacity (Chapter ??). The expression is what the three
components measure.
    The third part: the three components. The components are fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability (Chapter 25). The viable causation is the causal relation whose expression satisfies
the three components.
Remark 27.10 (Viable Causation Is Not the Same as Causation). Viable causation is not the
same as causation. Causation is the relation of expression; viable causation is the relation of
expression whose character satisfies the three components. The causation is what the relation is;
the viable causation is the character of the relation. The two are related, but they are not the
same, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 27.11 (Viable Causation Is Not a Degree of Causation). Viable causation is not a degree
of causation. Causation does not admit of degrees; the viable causation does. Causation is the
relation; the viable causation is the character of the relation. The distinction is the distinction
between the relation and the character of the relation; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 27.12 (Viable Causation Is Not a Value). Viable causation is not a value. It states
a condition on the causal relation; it attaches no value, end, or good to the condition. The
framework’s claim is that the condition is a structural character; it does not claim that the
character is valuable or that it is the good.


27.6      Fidelity and Causation
The first component of viability is fidelity. The present section states what fidelity is in its
application to causation.

Principle 27.13 (Fidelity of Causation). (T) The fidelity of a causal relation in a realm is the
extent to which the effect preserves the essential determination of the cause. The fidelity is the
first component of viable causation; without it, the effect is not an effect of the cause, and the
relation is not viable.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Definition 25.14)
and from the definition of causation (Definition 27.3). The argument is that the fidelity is the
preservation of the essential determination; the cause is the essential determination; the fidelity
is what the causal relation must satisfy.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: fidelity preserves the essential determination. The effect preserves the essential
determination of the cause. The preservation is not a copy; it is the cause’s taking the form that
the receiving realm’s capacity permits (Chapter ??). The effect that is high in fidelity preserves
27.7. Sustainability and Causation                                                                 321


the essential determination; the effect that is low in fidelity preserves it less completely; the effect
that is at the limit of zero fidelity does not preserve it at all.
    The second part: fidelity is the first component. Without fidelity, the effect is not an effect
of the cause; it is an effect of another cause, or of no cause at all. The fidelity is the condition
under which the effect is an effect of the cause.
    The third part: fidelity is not a degree of causation. Causation does not admit of degrees;
the fidelity does. Causation is the relation; the fidelity is the extent to which the effect preserves
the cause’s essential determination. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 27.14 (Fidelity Is Not the Effect Itself). Fidelity is not the effect itself. The effect is the
manifestation of the cause’s expression in the receiving realm; the fidelity is the extent to which
the effect preserves the cause’s essential determination. The effect is what it is; the fidelity is the
character of the effect’s relation to the cause. The two are different, and the framework keeps
them apart.
Remark 27.15 (Fidelity Is Not a Degree of the Cause). Fidelity is not a degree of the cause. The
cause is rigid (Chapter ??); the fidelity is graded. The cause is what it is; the fidelity is the
extent to which the effect preserves the cause’s essential determination. The two are different,
and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 27.16 (Fidelity Is Not a Value). Fidelity is not a value. It states a condition on the
causal relation; it attaches no value, end, or good to the condition. The framework’s claim is
that the condition is a structural character; it does not claim that the character is valuable or
that it is the good.


27.7      Sustainability and Causation
The second component of viability is sustainability. The present section states what sustainability
is in its application to causation.

Principle 27.17 (Sustainability of Causation). (T) The sustainability of a causal relation in a
realm is the condition under which the cost of the effect does not exceed what the realm can bear.
The sustainability is the second component of viable causation; without it, the effect exhausts
the realm’s capacity, and the causal relation is not viable.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Definition 25.14)
and from the framework’s account of the cost of cognition (Book I, Chapter 39), read in its
metaphysical form. The argument is that the cost is the demand that the effect makes on the
realm’s capacity; the sustainability is the condition under which the cost does not exceed the
capacity.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: sustainability is a condition on the cost. The cost is the demand that the
effect makes on the realm’s capacity. The sustainability is the condition under which the cost
does not exceed the capacity. The effect that is sustainable is the effect that the realm can bear;
the effect that is not sustainable is the effect whose cost exceeds the realm’s capacity.
    The second part: sustainability is the second component. Without sustainability, the effect
exhausts the realm’s capacity, and the causal relation cannot continue. The sustainability is the
condition under which the relation can continue.
    The third part: sustainability is not cheapness. The effect that is cheap is not thereby
sustainable; the effect that is expensive is not thereby unsustainable. The sustainability is the
condition under which the cost does not exceed the capacity, not the condition under which the
cost is low.
Remark 27.18 (Sustainability Is Not Fidelity). Sustainability is not fidelity. The effect can be
fidelious and unsustainable (if the preservation of the cause’s determination costs more than the
322                                                          Chapter 27. Viability and Causation


realm can bear); the effect can be sustainable and not fidelious (if the effect is cheap but distorts
the cause). The two are different components of viable causation, and the framework keeps them
apart.
Remark 27.19 (Sustainability Is Not the Cost Alone). Sustainability is not the cost alone. The
cost is what the effect demands of the realm’s capacity; the sustainability is whether the cost
exceeds the capacity. The two are related, but they are not the same, and the framework keeps
them apart.
Remark 27.20 (Sustainability Is Not Recoverability). Sustainability is not recoverability. The
effect can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the realm’s capacity has been
exhausted; the effect is not recoverable if the cost of restoring it would exceed the cost of
producing a new one. The two are different components of viable causation, and the framework
keeps them apart.


27.8     Recoverability and Causation
The third component of viability is recoverability. The present section states what recoverability
is in its application to causation.
Principle 27.21 (Recoverability of Causation). (T) The recoverability of a causal relation in a
realm is the condition under which the cause retains its structural capacity to produce the effect
in the realm; the singularity at which restoring the effect would cost more than producing a new
one has not been crossed. The recoverability is the third component of viable causation; without
it, the cause has lost its capacity to produce the effect, and the relation is not viable.
    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Definition 25.14)
and from the framework’s account of the singularity (Book I, Chapter 40). The argument is that
the recoverability is the retention of the cause’s capacity to produce the effect; the singularity is
the threshold beyond which the capacity is lost; the recoverability is the condition under which
the capacity is retained.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: recoverability is about the cause’s capacity. The cause retains its structural
capacity to produce the effect in the realm. The capacity is not the effect; it is the structural
possibility of the effect. The recoverability is the retention of the capacity, not the presence of
the effect.
    The second part: recoverability is the third component. Without recoverability, the cause
has lost its capacity to produce the effect, and the causal relation cannot be restored. The
recoverability is the condition under which the relation can be restored if it ceases.
    The third part: recoverability is not a promise of restoration. The recoverability is the
retention of the capacity; the restoration is contingent on the cause’s expression and on the
realm’s conditions. The recoverability is the capacity; the restoration is the act.
Remark 27.22 (Recoverability Is Not Sustainability). Recoverability is not sustainability. The
effect can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the realm’s capacity has been
exhausted; if the cost of restoring the effect exceeds the cost of producing a new one, the effect
is not recoverable, even though it was sustainable. The two are different components of viable
causation, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 27.23 (Recoverability Is Not Causal Determinism). Recoverability is not causal deter-
minism. The recoverability is the retention of the cause’s capacity to produce the effect; it does
not claim that the effect will be produced. The effect is contingent on the cause’s expression and
on the realm’s conditions; the recoverability is the capacity, not the necessity.
Remark 27.24 (Recoverability Is Not a Promise). Recoverability is not a promise of restoration.
The cause retains the capacity; the restoration is contingent on the cause’s expression and on the
27.9. Causation Is Not Mere Succession                                                            323


realm’s conditions. The framework’s claim is that the cause retains the capacity; it does not
claim that the restoration will occur.


27.9      Causation Is Not Mere Succession
The present section states the distinction between causation and mere succession, in the light of
the viability of causation.
    Mere succession is the temporal ordering of events: one event follows another. The succession
is a fact about the order of events; it is not a causal relation. Two events can succeed one another
without one causing the other; two events can be causally related without one succeeding the
other in time (if the cause is not in time, or if the effect is not in time).
    Causation is the structural relation in which the cause expresses itself in the effect. The
relation is not the succession; it is the expression. The expression can be accompanied by
succession (in the material realm, the effect follows the cause), or it can occur without succession
(in the realms in which time is not the order of events).
    The viability of causation is the character of the expression. The fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability are the conditions on the expression; they are not conditions on the succession.
The succession is a fact about the order of events; the viability is a character of the expression.
Principle 27.25 (Causation Is Not Mere Succession). (T) Causation is not mere succession.
The causal relation is the relation of expression between the cause and the effect; the succession
is the temporal ordering of events. The two are different, and the viability of causation is the
character of the expression, not of the succession.
    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of causation (Definition 27.3) and from the
definition of viable causation (Definition 27.9). The argument is that causation is the relation of
expression; the succession is the order of events; the viability is the character of the expression,
not of the succession.
Remark 27.26 (The Distinction Is Structural). The distinction is structural. It is not the
distinction between the real and the unreal; both causation and succession are real. The
distinction is the distinction between the relation of expression and the order of events; the
framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 27.27 (The Distinction Is Not a Denial of Succession). The distinction is not a denial of
succession. The succession is real; it is the order of events in the realm. The distinction is the
distinction between the succession and the causation; the framework keeps it apart.


27.10      What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that causation is unreal. Causation is real; it is the relation of
expression between the cause and the effect. The principle says that causation is subject to
viability; it does not say that causation is unreal.
    The principle does not say that succession is unreal. Succession is real; it is the order of
events. The principle says that causation is not mere succession; it does not say that succession
is unreal.
    The principle does not say that the effect is a copy of the cause. The effect is the manifestation
of the cause’s expression in the receiving realm; the manifestation is not a copy, it is the cause’s
taking the form that the realm’s capacity permits (Chapter ??). The principle says that the
causal relation is subject to viability; it does not say that the effect is a copy.
    The principle does not say that the viable causation is the good. The viable causation is a
structural character of the causal relation; it is not the good. The principle says that the causal
relation is subject to viability; it does not say that the viable causation is the good.
324                                                          Chapter 27. Viability and Causation


Remark 27.28 (The Principle Leaves the Application Open). The principle leaves the application
open. It states the relation between causation and viability; it does not state how the relation
applies to modality. That application is the work of Chapter ??.
Remark 27.29 (No Conflict with the Account of Causation). The principle is compatible with
the account of causation. Causation is the relation of expression; the viability is the character of
the relation. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart. The principle is the
framework’s account of the relation, not a denial of causation.


27.11      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that causation is prior to viability. If such a
showing could be made, the causal relation would be what it is regardless of its expression,
and the viability would be an external addition to the relation. The framework’s claim is that
causation is the relation of expression; the viability is the character of the relation; causation is
not prior to the relation.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the viable causation is a degree of
causation. If such a showing could be made, causation would admit of degrees, and the framework’s
account of the relation of expression (Chapter ??) would be mistaken. The framework’s claim is
that causation is the relation; the viable causation is the character of the relation, not a degree
of causation.
Remark 27.30 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the relation between causation and viability; the second challenges the distinction
between causation and viable causation. The two challenges require different responses, and the
framework responds to each in its own terms.


27.12      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the application to modality. The application is the work of
Chapter ??; the present chapter states the application to causation, and it leaves the application
to modality to its place.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the full account of the fluid element. The fluid element
is stated in Chapter ?? and Chapter ??; the present chapter states the causal relation as a
relation carried by the fluid element, and it leaves the full account to its place.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of what the cause is in itself. The chapter
states the cause as the identity that expresses itself in the effect; the question of what the cause
is in itself is a matter for the inquiry, not for the chapter.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of causation. It claims to
have described the causal relation and its viability; the causal relation points beyond itself to its
ground. The question of what grounds the causal relation is left to a later part of the book.
Remark 27.31 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
recalled the framework’s account of causation. It has stated the relation between causation and
viability. It has defined viable causation, and stated the three components in their application to
causation. And it has distinguished causation from mere succession, and what would refute the
principle.
Remark 27.32 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter ??). The chapter prepares Chapter ??, which
applies metaphysical viability to modality. The present chapter states the application to
causation; the next chapter states the application to modality; and the chapter after that
27.13. Epistemic Status of Claims in This Chapter                                              325


states the metaphysics of viability as a whole. The five chapters of Part VII together state the
framework’s metaphysical account of viability.

A Question for Reflection
Consider a causal relation you know—a lamp illuminating a room, a word affecting a hearer, a
cause producing an effect. Is the relation subject to viability in the realm in which it occurs?
Does the effect preserve the essential determination of the cause (fidelity)? Is the cost of the
effect sustainable, given the realm’s capacity (sustainability)? Does the cause retain its capacity
to produce the effect (recoverability)? What does your answer tell you about the relation between
causation and viability, and about the concept of viable causation?
The next chapter (Chapter ??) applies metaphysical viability to modality. The present chapter
has stated the application to causation; the next chapter states the application to modality, and
shows how the three components of viability apply to the modal relation between an identity and
its possible manifestations in a realm.
