Chapter 28

Viability and Modality

Scope. This chapter applies the metaphysical concept of viability (Chapter ??) to modality. It
recalls the framework’s account of modality (Chapter 14) and of the modal space Ω (Chapter ??),
states the relation between modality and viability, defines viable modality, and argues that the
three components of viability—fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability—apply to the modal
relation in its metaphysical form. It distinguishes modal status from modal viability, argues
that the modal relation is a relation between a possibility and its actualization in a realm, and
states the conditions under which a modal relation is viable in a realm. It does not develop the
metaphysics of viability as a whole; that synthesis is the work of Chapter 29. Its claims are
metaphysical; where it speaks of “modality,” “possibility,” “necessity,” “actualization,” “viability,”
“fidelity,” “sustainability,” or “recoverability,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed
by the definitions in this chapter and in the chapters to which it refers.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s Principle 37.1 (the
totality of possibility, C12), Principle 37.2 (the modal space is grounded in God), Definition 37.1
(the three layers of the ontological architecture), and Principle 16.7 (the structural laws are
necessary). It also takes as given the four kinds of necessity of Chapter 14 (logical, metaphysical,
natural, normative) and the stratification of Ω of Chapter ??. It does not restate these; it asks
what they presuppose in the order of being, and it states the metaphysical conditions under
which a modal relation can be viable.


28.1      A Scene
Consider a seed and a stone. Both could become something: the seed could become a tree; the
stone could become a sculpture. Neither is what it could become; each is what it is, and each
could be otherwise.
    Now ask: which of the two possibilities is more viable? The question is not about which is
more likely, and it is not about which is more valuable. It is about the structural character of
the relation between the possibility and its actualization. The seed’s possibility of becoming a
tree is grounded in the seed’s essence; the stone’s possibility of becoming a sculpture is grounded
in the sculptor’s intention and in the stone’s capacity to be carved. The two possibilities are
different, and their difference is a difference in the structure of their relation to actualization.
    The seed’s possibility is viable in a specific sense: its actualization would preserve the seed’s
essential determination, its cost would not exceed what the soil and the climate can bear, and the
seed would retain its capacity to become a tree even if the present conditions were unfavorable.
The stone’s possibility is viable in a different sense: its actualization would preserve the stone’s
essence as a material thing, its cost would not exceed what the sculptor’s tools and time can
bear, and the stone would retain its capacity to be carved even if the present attempt failed.
328                                                            Chapter 28. Viability and Modality


    The two possibilities are both viable, but not in the same way. The seed’s viability is grounded
in its essence; the stone’s viability is grounded in its essence and in the sculptor’s intention and
in the laws of the material realm. The difference is the difference between the strata of the
modal space (Chapter ??): the seed’s possibility belongs to the metaphysical stratum; the stone’s
possibility belongs to the metaphysical stratum and to the natural stratum, and it is actualized
through the normative stratum of the sculptor’s choice.
    The scene poses a question. What is the relation between modality and viability? Is modality
subject to viability, or is modality prior to viability? And if modality is subject to viability, what
does it mean for a modal relation to be viable in a realm?
Remark 28.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them. The seed and the stone are examples; the account is about
modality and viability in general.


28.2      The Question
The previous chapters of Part VII have applied metaphysical viability to essence (Chapter ??)
and to causation (Chapter ??). The present chapter applies the concept to modality.
    The question is: what is the relation between modality and viability? Is the modal relation
subject to viability, or is modality prior to viability? And if the modal relation is subject to
viability, what does it mean for a modal relation to be viable in a realm?
    The framework’s answer is that the modal relation is subject to viability, and that the viability
of a modal relation is the structural character of the relation between a possibility (or a necessity)
and its actualization in a realm, in the three respects of fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.
Modality is not prior to viability; it is the relation that viability characterizes. The possibility is
what can be actualized; the actualization is the manifestation; the viability is the character of
the relation between them.
    The question is not idle. If modality were prior to viability, the modal relation would be
what it is regardless of its actualization, and the framework’s account of manifestation (Book I,
Chapter 13) would be mistaken. If the modal relation is subject to viability, the possibility is
what it is, and its actualization is what is viable or not. The present chapter argues that the
second is the framework’s account, and it states what the account implies for the concept of
modality.
    The chapter proceeds as follows. It recalls the framework’s account of modality and of the
modal space. It states the relation between modality and viability. It defines viable modality.
It states the three components in their application to modality. It distinguishes modal status
from modal viability. It states what the principle does not say, and what would refute it. And it
marks what the chapter does not establish.
Remark 28.2 (The Question Presupposes the Accounts of Chapters 14 and 15). The question
presupposes the accounts of Chapters 14 and ??. The four kinds of necessity are stated in
Chapter 14; the stratification of Ω is stated in Chapter ??. The present chapter recalls these
accounts, but it does not restate them. The reader who has not read the two chapters will find
the present chapter compressed; the reader who has read them will find the present chapter a
natural application of their accounts.


28.3      The Framework’s Account of Modality Recalled
The framework’s account of modality is stated in Chapter 14, and its account of the modal space
is stated in Chapter ??. The present section recalls the two, so that the application to viability
can be stated precisely.
28.4. The Relation Between Modality and Viability                                                   329


Definition 28.3 (Modality (Recalled)). (Chapter 14, Definition 14.1) Modality is the structure
of the possible, the actual, and the necessary. The possible is what could be; the actual is what
is; the necessary is what cannot be otherwise.
Definition 28.4 (The Modal Space Ω (Recalled)). (Chapter ??, Principle ??) Ω is a stratified
modal structure whose strata are the four kinds of necessity: the logical stratum (the form of
propositions), the metaphysical stratum (the essences of things), the natural stratum (the laws
of the realms), and the normative stratum (the good).
    The two definitions are the framework’s account of modality. The first states the three modal
statuses; the second states the internal structure of the modal space. The two together are the
framework’s answer to the question: what is the modal relation?
    The framework’s answer is that the modal relation is not a single relation; it is a family of
relations, corresponding to the four strata. Each stratum has its own modal statuses, and each
modal status is grounded in a different structure. The four strata are the framework’s account of
what the modal space contains, and the four kinds are its account of what the modal statuses
are.


28.4      The Relation Between Modality and Viability
The relation between modality and viability is stated in a principle.
Principle 28.5 (Modality Is Subject to Viability). (T) Modality is subject to viability. The
modal relation is the relation between a possibility (or a necessity) and its actualization in a
realm; the viability is the structural character of the relation, in the three respects of fidelity,
sustainability, and recoverability. Modality is not prior to viability; it is the relation that viability
characterizes.
   The principle is (T): it is argued from the framework’s account of modality (Chapter 14) and
of metaphysical viability (Chapter ??). The argument is given below.

Argument for the Principle.    1. Modality is the structure of the possible, the actual, and the
     necessary (Definition 28.3).
   2. The modal relation is the relation between a possibility (or a necessity) and its actualization
      in a realm (Chapter ??, the relation between Ω and light).
   3. The viability is the structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifes-
      tations in a realm (Chapter ??, Definition ??).
   4. The modal relation is the relation between the possibility and its actualization; the viability
      is the character of the actualization. The modal relation is not prior to the actualization;
      it is the relation that the actualization is.
   5. Therefore modality is subject to viability: the possibility is what it is, and its actualization
      is what is viable or not.

    The argument’s force is in step 4. If modality were prior to the actualization, the modal
relation would be what it is regardless of its actualization, and the viability would be an external
addition to the relation. But the modal relation is the relation between the possibility and
its actualization; the viability is the character of the relation. Modality is not prior to the
actualization; it is what the actualization is. The principle follows.
Remark 28.6 (Modality Is Not Prior to Viability). Modality is not prior to viability. The modal
relation is the relation between the possibility and its actualization; the viability is the character
of the relation. The possibility is what it is; the viability is the character of its actualization.
The two are related, but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
330                                                          Chapter 28. Viability and Modality


Remark 28.7 (The Principle Is Not a Denial of Modality). The principle is not a denial of
modality. It affirms modality; it says that the modal relation is subject to viability. The modal
relation is real, structural, and describable; the viability is the character of the modal relation.
The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.


28.5     Viable Modality Defined
The definition of viable modality is stated here.

Definition 28.8 (Viable Modality). The viable modality of an identity in a realm is the modal
relation whose actualization in the realm satisfies the three components of metaphysical viability:
fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.

    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what viable
modality is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the framework’s proposal
for the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the modal relation. The modal relation is the relation between a possibility (or
a necessity) and its actualization (Definition 28.3). The relation is what the three components
characterize.
    The second part: the actualization in the realm. The actualization is the realization of the
possibility in the realm, according to the realm’s capacity (Chapter ??, the relation between Ω
and light). The actualization is what the three components measure.
    The third part: the three components. The components are fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability (Chapter ??). The viable modality is the modal relation whose actualization
satisfies the three components.
Remark 28.9 (Viable Modality Is Not the Same as Modality). Viable modality is not the same
as modality. Modality is the structure of the possible, the actual, and the necessary; viable
modality is the modal relation whose actualization satisfies the three components. The modality
is what the relation is; the viable modality is the character of the relation. The two are related,
but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 28.10 (Viable Modality Is Not a Degree of Modality). Viable modality is not a degree of
modality. Modality does not admit of degrees; the viable modality does. Modality is the relation;
the viable modality is the character of the relation. The distinction is the distinction between
the relation and the character of the relation; the framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 28.11 (Viable Modality Is Not a Value). Viable modality is not a value. It states
a condition on the modal relation; it attaches no value, end, or good to the condition. The
framework’s claim is that the condition is a structural character; it does not claim that the
character is valuable or that it is the good.


28.6     Fidelity and Modality
The first component of viability is fidelity. The present section states what fidelity is in its
application to modality.

Principle 28.12 (Fidelity of Modality). (T) The fidelity of a modal relation in a realm is
the extent to which the actualization preserves the essential determination of the possibility.
The fidelity is the first component of viable modality; without it, the actualization is not the
actualization of the possibility, and the relation is not viable.
28.7. Sustainability and Modality                                                                  331


    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Chapter ??)
and from the definition of modality (Definition 28.3). The argument is that the fidelity is the
preservation of the essential determination; the possibility is the essential determination; the
fidelity is what the modal relation must satisfy.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: fidelity preserves the essential determination. The actualization preserves the
essential determination of the possibility. The preservation is not a copy; it is the possibility’s
taking the form that the receiving realm’s capacity permits (Chapter 19). The actualization that
is high in fidelity preserves the essential determination; the actualization that is low in fidelity
preserves it less completely; the actualization that is at the limit of zero fidelity does not preserve
it at all.
    The second part: fidelity is the first component. Without fidelity, the actualization is not the
actualization of the possibility; it is the actualization of another possibility, or of no possibility
at all. The fidelity is the condition under which the actualization is the actualization of the
possibility.
    The third part: fidelity is not a degree of modality. Modality does not admit of degrees; the
fidelity does. The modality is the relation; the fidelity is the extent to which the actualization
preserves the possibility’s essential determination. The two are different, and the framework
keeps them apart.
Remark 28.13 (Fidelity Is Not Modal Status). Fidelity is not modal status. The modal status is
the status of the possibility (possible, actual, necessary); the fidelity is the extent to which the
actualization preserves the possibility’s essential determination. The modal status is what the
possibility is; the fidelity is the character of the actualization. The two are different, and the
framework keeps them apart.
Remark 28.14 (Fidelity Is Not a Degree of the Possibility). Fidelity is not a degree of the
possibility. The possibility is what it is; the fidelity is the extent to which the actualization
preserves the possibility’s essential determination. The two are different, and the framework
keeps them apart.
Remark 28.15 (Fidelity Is Not a Value). Fidelity is not a value. It states a condition on the
modal relation; it attaches no value, end, or good to the condition. The framework’s claim is
that the condition is a structural character; it does not claim that the character is valuable or
that it is the good.


28.7      Sustainability and Modality
The second component of viability is sustainability. The present section states what sustainability
is in its application to modality.

Principle 28.16 (Sustainability of Modality). (T) The sustainability of a modal relation in
a realm is the condition under which the cost of the actualization does not exceed what the
realm can bear. The sustainability is the second component of viable modality; without it, the
actualization exhausts the realm’s capacity, and the modal relation is not viable.

   The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Chapter ??)
and from the framework’s account of the cost of cognition (Book I, Chapter 39), read in its
metaphysical form. The argument is that the cost is the demand that the actualization makes
on the realm’s capacity; the sustainability is the condition under which the cost does not exceed
the capacity.
   The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
   The first part: sustainability is a condition on the cost. The cost is the demand that the
actualization makes on the realm’s capacity. The sustainability is the condition under which
332                                                           Chapter 28. Viability and Modality


the cost does not exceed the capacity. The actualization that is sustainable is the actualization
that the realm can bear; the actualization that is not sustainable is the actualization whose cost
exceeds the realm’s capacity.
    The second part: sustainability is the second component. Without sustainability, the actual-
ization exhausts the realm’s capacity, and the modal relation cannot continue. The sustainability
is the condition under which the relation can continue.
    The third part: sustainability is not cheapness. The actualization that is cheap is not thereby
sustainable; the actualization that is expensive is not thereby unsustainable. The sustainability
is the condition under which the cost does not exceed the capacity, not the condition under
which the cost is low.
Remark 28.17 (Sustainability Is Not Fidelity). Sustainability is not fidelity. The actualization
can be fidelious and unsustainable (if the preservation of the possibility’s determination costs
more than the realm can bear); the actualization can be sustainable and not fidelious (if the
actualization is cheap but distorts the possibility). The two are different components of viable
modality, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 28.18 (Sustainability Is Not the Cost Alone). Sustainability is not the cost alone. The
cost is what the actualization demands of the realm’s capacity; the sustainability is whether the
cost exceeds the capacity. The two are related, but they are not the same, and the framework
keeps them apart.
Remark 28.19 (Sustainability Is Not Recoverability). Sustainability is not recoverability. The
actualization can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the realm’s capacity has been
exhausted; the actualization is not recoverable if the cost of restoring it would exceed the cost of
producing a new one. The two are different components of viable modality, and the framework
keeps them apart.


28.8      Recoverability and Modality
The third component of viability is recoverability. The present section states what recoverability
is in its application to modality.
Principle 28.20 (Recoverability of Modality). (T) The recoverability of a modal relation in a
realm is the condition under which the possibility retains its structural capacity to be actualized
in the realm; the singularity at which restoring the actualization would cost more than producing
a new one has not been crossed. The recoverability is the third component of viable modality;
without it, the possibility has lost its capacity to be actualized, and the relation is not viable.
    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of metaphysical viability (Chapter ??) and
from the framework’s account of the singularity (Book I, Chapter 40). The argument is that the
recoverability is the retention of the possibility’s capacity to be actualized; the singularity is the
threshold beyond which the capacity is lost; the recoverability is the condition under which the
capacity is retained.
    The principle has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: recoverability is about the possibility’s capacity. The possibility retains its
structural capacity to be actualized in the realm. The capacity is not the actualization; it is the
structural possibility of the actualization. The recoverability is the retention of the capacity, not
the presence of the actualization.
    The second part: recoverability is the third component. Without recoverability, the possibility
has lost its capacity to be actualized, and the modal relation cannot be restored. The recoverability
is the condition under which the relation can be restored if it ceases.
    The third part: recoverability is not a promise of restoration. The recoverability is the
retention of the capacity; the restoration is contingent on the possibility’s actualization and on
the realm’s conditions. The recoverability is the capacity; the restoration is the act.
28.9. Modal Status and Modal Viability Distinguished                                              333


Remark 28.21 (Recoverability Is Not Sustainability). Recoverability is not sustainability. The
actualization can be sustainable for a season and then fail, because the realm’s capacity has
been exhausted; if the cost of restoring the actualization exceeds the cost of producing a new
one, the actualization is not recoverable, even though it was sustainable. The two are different
components of viable modality, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 28.22 (Recoverability Is Not Modal Necessity). Recoverability is not modal necessity.
The recoverability is the retention of the possibility’s capacity to be actualized; it does not claim
that the actualization will occur. The actualization is contingent on the possibility’s actualization
and on the realm’s conditions; the recoverability is the capacity, not the necessity.
Remark 28.23 (Recoverability Is Not a Promise). Recoverability is not a promise of restoration.
The possibility retains the capacity; the restoration is contingent on the possibility’s actualization
and on the realm’s conditions. The framework’s claim is that the possibility retains the capacity;
it does not claim that the restoration will occur.


28.9      Modal Status and Modal Viability Distinguished
The distinction between modal status and modal viability is worth stating, because the two are
easily run together.
    Modal status is the status of the possibility: the possible, the actual, the necessary. Modal
viability is the character of the relation between the possibility and its actualization: the extent
to which the actualization preserves the possibility’s essential determination, the sustainability
of the cost, and the recoverability of the capacity.
    The two are different, and neither entails the other. A possibility can be possible and not viable
(a possibility whose actualization would distort its essential determination); a possibility can be
possible and viable (a possibility whose actualization would preserve its essential determination,
sustain the cost, and retain the capacity). The modal status is what the possibility is; the modal
viability is the character of the actualization.

Principle 28.24 (Modal Status Is Not Modal Viability). (T) Modal status is not modal viability.
The modal status is the status of the possibility (possible, actual, necessary); the modal viability
is the character of the relation between the possibility and its actualization. The two are different,
and neither entails the other.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the definition of modality (Definition 28.3) and from the
definition of viable modality (Definition 28.8). The argument is that the modal status is a status;
the modal viability is a character of the relation. The two are different, and the framework keeps
them apart.
Remark 28.25 (The Distinction Is Structural). The distinction is structural. It is not the
distinction between the real and the unreal; both the modal status and the modal viability are
real. The distinction is the distinction between the status and the character of the relation; the
framework keeps it throughout.
Remark 28.26 (The Distinction Is Not a Denial of Modal Status). The distinction is not a denial
of modal status. The modal status is real; the modal viability is real; the two are different. The
framework does not claim that one is more important than the other; it claims that they are
different, and that the framework uses both.


28.10       The Four Kinds of Necessity and Viable Modality
The four kinds of necessity (Chapter 14) are related to viable modality, and the relation is worth
stating.
334                                                           Chapter 28. Viability and Modality


    Each kind of necessity has its own modal viability. The logical necessity’s viability is the
extent to which the actualization preserves the logical form; the metaphysical necessity’s viability
is the extent to which the actualization preserves the essence; the natural necessity’s viability is
the extent to which the actualization respects the laws of the realm; the normative necessity’s
viability is the extent to which the actualization is compatible with the good.
    The four kinds of viability are not the same; each is grounded in a different structure. The
logical viability is grounded in the form; the metaphysical viability in the essence; the natural
viability in the law; the normative viability in the good. The four are related as the four kinds of
necessity are related: the logical is the most general; the metaphysical underlies the natural; the
normative is posterior to the other three.

Principle 28.27 (The Four Kinds of Viable Modality). (T) Each kind of necessity has its
own modal viability. The logical necessity’s viability is the preservation of the logical form;
the metaphysical necessity’s viability is the preservation of the essence; the natural necessity’s
viability is the respect for the laws of the realm; the normative necessity’s viability is the
compatibility with the good. The four are related as the four kinds of necessity are related.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the four kinds of necessity (Chapter 14) and from the
definition of viable modality (Definition 28.8). The argument is that each kind of necessity
is grounded in a different structure; the viability of each kind is the character of the relation
between the kind and its actualization; the four kinds are related as the four grounds are related.
Remark 28.28 (The Four Kinds Are Not Reducible). The four kinds of viable modality are not
reducible to one another. Each is grounded in a different structure; each has its own modal
viability. The logical viability is not the metaphysical viability; the metaphysical viability is not
the natural viability; the natural viability is not the normative viability. The four are related,
but they are not the same, and the framework keeps them apart.
Remark 28.29 (The Four Kinds Are Related as the Four Kinds of Necessity). The four kinds of
viable modality are related as the four kinds of necessity are related. The logical is the most
general; the metaphysical underlies the natural; the normative is posterior to the other three.
The relation is the relation of grounding, not of identity.


28.11      What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that modality is unreal. Modality is real; it is the structure of the
possible, the actual, and the necessary. The principle says that modality is subject to viability;
it does not say that modality is unreal.
    The principle does not say that the modal status is unreal. The modal status is real; it is the
status of the possibility. The principle says that the modal status is subject to viability; it does
not say that the modal status is unreal.
    The principle does not say that the possible is a copy of the actual. The possible is the
possibility; the actual is the actualization. The possibility is what can be actualized; the
actualization is what is. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
    The principle does not say that the viable modality is the good. The viable modality is a
structural character of the modal relation; it is not the good. The principle says that the modal
relation is subject to viability; it does not say that the viable modality is the good.
Remark 28.30 (The Principle Leaves the Application Open). The principle leaves the application
open. It states the relation between modality and viability; it does not state how the relation
applies to the four kinds of necessity in detail. The application is the work of the chapters that
treat each kind; the present chapter states the general structure.
28.12. What Would Refute the Principle                                                           335


Remark 28.31 (No Conflict with the Account of Modality). The principle is compatible with the
account of modality. Modality is the structure of the possible, the actual, and the necessary; the
viability is the character of the relation between the possibility and its actualization. The two
are different, and the framework keeps them apart. The principle is the framework’s account of
the relation, not a denial of modality.


28.12      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that modality is prior to viability. If such a
showing could be made, the modal relation would be what it is regardless of its actualization,
and the viability would be an external addition to the relation. The framework’s claim is that
modality is the relation between the possibility and its actualization; the viability is the character
of the relation; modality is not prior to the relation.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the viable modality is a degree of modality.
If such a showing could be made, modality would admit of degrees, and the framework’s account
of the modal status (Chapter 14) would be mistaken. The framework’s claim is that modality is
the relation; the viable modality is the character of the relation, not a degree of modality.
Remark 28.32 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the relation between modality and viability; the second challenges the distinction
between modality and viable modality. The two challenges require different responses, and the
framework responds to each in its own terms.


28.13      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
     First, the chapter does not develop the four kinds of viable modality in detail. Each kind is
grounded in a different structure, and its development is the work of the chapters that treat the
corresponding kind of necessity (Chapters 14 and ??). The present chapter states the general
structure.
     Second, the chapter does not develop the application of viable modality to the metaphysics
of viability as a whole. That synthesis is the work of Chapter 29. The present chapter states
the relation between modality and viability; the next chapter states the integration of the four
columns in viability.
     Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the four kinds of viable modality
are exhaustive. The four kinds are the kinds that the framework’s analyses require; whether a
fifth kind is needed, or whether one of the four can be derived from the others, is a question the
chapter leaves open.
     Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of the modal relation. It
claims to have described the modal relation and its viability; the modal relation points beyond
itself to its ground. The question of what grounds the modal relation is left to a later part of the
book.
Remark 28.33 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
recalled the framework’s account of modality and of the modal space. It has stated the relation
between modality and viability. It has defined viable modality, and stated the three components
in their application to modality. And it has distinguished modal status from modal viability,
and stated the four kinds of viable modality and their relation.
Remark 28.34 (The Chapter Prepares Chapter 29). The chapter prepares Chapter 29, which
states the metaphysics of viability as a whole. The present chapter states the application to
336                                                          Chapter 28. Viability and Modality


modality; the next chapter states the synthesis of the four columns in viability. The four chapters
of Part VII (Chapters ?? to 29) together state the framework’s metaphysical account of viability.

   The statuses are those introduced in the front matter. The (T) claims are argued in this
chapter; the (A) claims are the framework’s stipulations of its vocabulary and its commitments
about the character of the concept.


28.15      A Question for Reflection
Consider a possibility you know well—a possibility for your life, for a project, for a relationship.
Is the possibility subject to viability in the realm in which it would be actualized? Does the
actualization preserve the essential determination of the possibility (fidelity)? Is the cost of the
actualization sustainable, given the realm’s capacity (sustainability)? Does the possibility retain
its capacity to be actualized (recoverability)? What does your answer tell you about the relation
between modality and viability, and about the concept of viable modality?
The next chapter (Chapter 29) states the metaphysics of viability as a whole: the integration of
the four columns in viability, the relation between viability and essence, causation, and modality,
and the metaphysical conditions of viability. The present chapter has stated the application to
modality; the next chapter states the synthesis.

Chapter 29

The Metaphysics of Viability

Scope. This chapter states the metaphysics of viability as a whole. It recalls what Part VII has
established in Chapters ?? to 28—the transition from structural to metaphysical viability, and the
application of viability to essence, causation, and modality—and it integrates the four columns of
the framework (fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, context) in a single account
of the metaphysical conditions of viability. It states the definition of the metaphysics of viability,
the integration of the four columns, the relation of viability to the three domains of essence,
causation, and modality, and the four-column structure of the inquiry into the metaphysics of
viability. It prepares the transition to Part VI. Its claims are metaphysical; where it speaks of
“viability,” “condition,” “column,” “domain,” “essence,” “causation,” or “modality,” these are
structural terms, and their sense is fixed by the definitions in this chapter and in the chapters to
which it refers.

Presupposition from Book I. This chapter takes as given Book I’s Principle 37.1 (the
totality of possibility, C12), Principle 37.2 (the modal space is grounded in God), Definition 37.1
(the three layers of the ontological architecture), and Principle 16.7 (the structural laws are
necessary). It also takes as given the four-column framework of Book I, Chapter 6, the definition
of viability of Book I, Definition 6.2, and the metaphysical applications of Chapters ?? to 28.
It does not restate these; it asks what they require when they are brought together as a single
account.


29.1      A Scene
Consider a bridge. It is built of stone and steel; it spans a river; it carries what passes from one
bank to the other. The bridge is a material structure; it is also a relation; it is also a work of
engineering; it is also an institution. The four descriptions are not four bridges; they are four
aspects of one bridge.
    Now ask: what is the metaphysics of the bridge? The question is not what the bridge is made
of, and it is not what the bridge is for. It is the question of what must be the case for the bridge
to be a bridge at all—for the bridge to be the kind of thing that can be built, can span, can
carry, and can last. The metaphysics of the bridge is the account of the conditions under which
the bridge can be what it is.
    The framework’s answer is: the metaphysics of the bridge is the account of the conditions
under which the bridge can be viable. The viability of the bridge is the structural character of
the relation between the bridge’s identity and its manifestations in the material realm, in the
relational realm, and in the other realms in which it appears. The conditions of that viability
are the conditions of the bridge’s being what it is.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is the metaphysics of viability? What are
the conditions under which an identity can be viable in the realms in which it is manifested? And
338                                                     Chapter 29. The Metaphysics of Viability


how do the four columns of the framework—fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics,
context—integrate in the account of those conditions?
Remark 29.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar case. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them. The bridge is an example; the account is about viability
and its metaphysical conditions in general.


29.2      The Question
Part VII has developed the metaphysical concept of viability through a sequence of applications.
The transition from structural to metaphysical viability was stated in Chapter ??; the application
to essence in Chapter ??; the application to causation in Chapter ??; and the application to
modality in Chapter 28. Each application states the relation between viability and one domain
of metaphysics; each is offered at the strength that the framework’s principles support.
    The present chapter asks: what is the metaphysics of viability as a whole? The question
is not the same as the question of any single application. Each application states the relation
between viability and one domain; the present chapter states the integration of the applications
in a single account. The integration is what makes viability a metaphysical concept, not only a
concept in each domain.
    The question has three aspects.
    The first aspect: what is the definition of the metaphysics of viability? The chapter must
state what the metaphysics of viability is, as distinct from the applications of viability to each
domain.
    The second aspect: how do the four columns integrate in the account of viability? The chapter
must state how the fixed elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, and context of the
framework integrate in the metaphysical conditions of viability.
    The third aspect: what are the metaphysical conditions of viability? The chapter must state
the conditions under which an identity can be viable in the realms in which it is manifested.
    The three aspects are treated in the sections that follow. The chapter’s answer is: the
metaphysics of viability is the account of the conditions under which an identity can be viable
in the realms in which it is manifested; the four columns integrate as the four aspects of those
conditions; and the conditions are the fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability of the relation
between the identity and its manifestations in each realm.
Remark 29.2 (The Question Presupposes Chapters 21–24). The question presupposes the analyses
of Chapters ?? to 28. The transition from structural to metaphysical viability is stated in
Chapter ??; the applications to essence, causation, and modality are stated in Chapters ??, ??,
and 28. The present chapter integrates these analyses; it does not restate them. The reader who
has not read the four chapters will find the present chapter compressed; the reader who has read
them will find the present chapter the natural completion of their account.


29.3      What Part VI Has Established
Part VII has established four things, and the present chapter integrates them.
    The transition from structural to metaphysical viability. Chapter ?? established that the
structural viability of Book I (the epistemic structural character of the relation between an
identity and its manifestations in a cognitive context) has a metaphysical form: the metaphysical
viability is the character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations in an existential
context (a realm). The three components—fidelity, sustainability, recoverability—are the same
in both forms; what differs is the context.
29.4. The Definition of the Metaphysics of Viability                                              339


    The application to essence. Chapter ?? established that the essence is subject to viability:
the essence is the identity that is expressed, and the viability is the character of the relation
between the essence and its manifestations. The viable essence is the essence whose relation to
its manifestations satisfies the three components.
    The application to causation. Chapter ?? established that the causal relation is subject to
viability: the causal relation is the relation of expression between a cause and its effect, and
the viability is the character of the relation. The viable causation is the causal relation whose
expression satisfies the three components.
    The application to modality. Chapter 28 established that the modal relation is subject
to viability: the modal relation is the relation between a possibility (or a necessity) and its
actualization in a realm, and the viability is the character of the relation. The viable modality is
the modal relation whose actualization satisfies the three components.
    The four establish the concept of viability as a metaphysical concept that applies to the three
domains of essence, causation, and modality. The present chapter asks what they establish when
they are brought together as a single account.
Remark 29.3 (The Four Are Not Independent). The four applications are not independent.
Each applies viability to a domain; each presupposes the definition of metaphysical viability
(Chapter ??) and the three components. The four together are the framework’s account of
viability across the domains; the present chapter states what the four together establish.


29.4      The Definition of the Metaphysics of Viability
The definition of the metaphysics of viability is stated here.

Definition 29.4 (The Metaphysics of Viability). The metaphysics of viability is the account of
the conditions under which an identity can be viable in the realms in which it is manifested. The
conditions are the fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability of the relation between the identity
and its manifestations in each realm; the account states how the conditions integrate across the
realms and across the four columns of the framework.

    The definition is stated as a stipulation of the framework’s vocabulary: it says what the
metaphysics of viability is. It is not derived from the framework’s other principles; it is the
framework’s proposal for the concept, and it is stated at exactly that strength.
    The definition has three parts, and each is worth marking.
    The first part: the conditions. The conditions are the fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability
of the relation between the identity and its manifestations in each realm. The conditions are the
three components of metaphysical viability (Chapter ??), read across the realms.
    The second part: the integration across the realms. The conditions are not independent for
each realm; they integrate across the realms. The integration is what makes the metaphysics of
viability an account of the identity’s viability across its manifestations, not only in a single realm.
    The third part: the integration across the four columns. The conditions are stated by the
four columns: the fixed elements (the identity and its manifestations), the fluid element (light,
the medium of the relation), the governing dynamics (the rules of the realms), and the context
(the realms). The integration across the columns is what makes the metaphysics of viability a
systematic account.
Remark 29.5 (The Metaphysics of Viability Is Not One Application). The metaphysics of viability
is not one application of viability. It is the integration of the applications. The applications state
the relation between viability and one domain; the metaphysics of viability states the integration
of the applications in a single account. The distinction is the distinction between the parts and
the whole; the framework keeps it throughout.
340                                                   Chapter 29. The Metaphysics of Viability


Remark 29.6 (The Metaphysics of Viability Is Not a Value). The metaphysics of viability is not
a value. It states the conditions under which an identity can be viable; it attaches no value,
end, or good to the conditions. The framework’s claim is that the conditions are a structural
character of the relation between the identity and its manifestations; it does not claim that the
conditions are valuable or that they are the good.


29.5     The Integration of the Four Columns
The integration of the four columns in the metaphysics of viability is stated here.
    The four columns of the framework are the fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing
dynamics, and the context. In the metaphysics of viability, each column contributes to the
account of the conditions under which an identity can be viable.
    The fixed elements: the identity and its manifestations. The identity is the invariant that the
metaphysics of viability characterizes; its manifestations are the appearances in the realms. The
fixed elements contribute the subject of the conditions: what is viable, and what the viability is
measured by.
    The fluid element: light. Light is the medium of the relation between the identity and
its manifestations (Book I, Principle 12.1; Chapter 11). Light contributes the medium of the
conditions: how the identity reaches its manifestations, and how the manifestations are related
to the identity.
    The governing dynamics: the rules of the realms. The rules are the constraints that govern
what is possible in each realm (Chapter 13; Chapter 16). The rules contribute the form of the
conditions: what the identity can be in each realm, and what the realms can bear.
    The context: the realms. The realms are the existential contexts in which the identity is
manifested (Chapter ??). The realms contribute the setting of the conditions: where the identity
is manifested, and what the realms contribute to the relation.
    The four columns together yield the account of the conditions. The conditions are not stated
by any one column alone; each column contributes one aspect, and the integration of the four is
what makes the account systematic.

Principle 29.7 (The Integration of the Four Columns). (T) The four columns integrate in the
metaphysics of viability as the four aspects of the conditions under which an identity can be
viable. The fixed elements contribute the subject of the conditions; the fluid element contributes
the medium; the governing dynamics contribute the form; the context contributes the setting.
The four are not independent; they are the four aspects of one account.

   The principle is (T): it follows from the four-column framework of Book I, Chapter 6, and
from the definition of the metaphysics of viability (Definition 29.4). The argument is that the
four columns are the analytical roles of any complete explanation (Book I, Principle 3.1); the
metaphysics of viability is a complete explanation of the conditions of viability; therefore the
metaphysics of viability assigns the four roles.
Remark 29.8 (The Integration Is Not a Reduction). The integration is not a reduction. The
four columns are not reducible to one another; each contributes its own aspect to the account.
The integration is the coordination of the four aspects, not the reduction of one to another.
The framework’s claim is that the four columns are analytical roles, and that the roles are not
interchangeable (Book I, Principle 3.2).
Remark 29.9 (The Integration Is Not a Hierarchy). The integration is not a hierarchy. No column
is more fundamental than another; each contributes an aspect, and the aspects are equally
needed for the account. The distinction is the distinction between the roles, not of the roles; the
framework keeps it throughout.
29.6. Viability and the Three Domains                                                             341


29.6      Viability and the Three Domains
The three domains to which viability has been applied—essence, causation, and modality—are
related in the metaphysics of viability, and the relation is worth stating.
    Essence (Chapter ??) is the structural determination that constitutes the identity. The viable
essence is the essence whose relation to its manifestations satisfies the three components.
    Causation (Chapter ??) is the relation of expression between a cause and its effect. The
viable causation is the causal relation whose expression satisfies the three components.
    Modality (Chapter 28) is the relation between a possibility (or a necessity) and its actualization
in a realm. The viable modality is the modal relation whose actualization satisfies the three
components.
    The three domains are related as the three aspects of the identity’s manifestation. The
essence is what the identity is; causation is how the identity reaches its manifestations; modality
is whether and how the identity can be manifested. The three aspects are distinct, and each is
subject to viability; the metaphysics of viability is the account of the three aspects together.

Principle 29.10 (The Three Domains Are Three Aspects of One Relation). (T) Essence,
causation, and modality are three aspects of one relation: the relation between an identity and
its manifestations. The essence is what the identity is; causation is how the identity reaches its
manifestations; modality is whether and how the identity can be manifested. The three aspects
are distinct, and each is subject to viability; the metaphysics of viability is the account of the
three aspects together.

   The principle is (T): it follows from the applications of viability to the three domains
(Chapters ??, ??, and 28) and from the definition of the metaphysics of viability (Definition 29.4).
The argument is that the three domains are the three aspects of the relation between the identity
and its manifestations; the metaphysics of viability is the account of the relation; therefore the
metaphysics of viability is the account of the three aspects together.
Remark 29.11 (The Three Aspects Are Not Reducible). The three aspects are not reducible to
one another. The essence is not the causation; the causation is not the modality; the modality is
not the essence. Each is a distinct aspect of the relation; the metaphysics of viability keeps them
apart.
Remark 29.12 (The Three Aspects Are Related). The three aspects are related. The essence is
the ground of the causation; the causation is the expression of the essence; the modality is the
space in which the essence is expressed through the causation. The relation is the relation of
grounding, not of identity; the metaphysics of viability keeps it throughout.


29.7      The Metaphysical Conditions of Viability
The metaphysical conditions of viability are stated here, as the synthesis of the three components
across the four columns and the three domains.
    The conditions are the three components of metaphysical viability: fidelity, sustainability, and
recoverability. The components are stated in Chapter ??; the applications to the three domains
are stated in Chapters ?? to 28. The present section states the conditions as the metaphysics of
viability’s account of the relation between the identity and its manifestations.
    Fidelity (across the domains). The actualization preserves the essential determination of the
possibility; the essence preserves its determination in the causation; the causation preserves the
essential determination of the cause in the effect. The fidelity is the first condition, and it is the
same across the domains, though its application differs.
    Sustainability (across the domains). The cost of the actualization does not exceed the
realm’s capacity; the cost of the causation does not exceed the realm’s capacity; the cost of the
342                                                    Chapter 29. The Metaphysics of Viability


manifestation does not exceed the realm’s capacity. The sustainability is the second condition,
and it is the same across the domains.
    Recoverability (across the domains). The possibility retains its capacity to be actualized; the
essence retains its capacity to be manifested; the causation retains its capacity to produce the
effect. The recoverability is the third condition, and it is the same across the domains.
    The three conditions are the metaphysical conditions of viability. They are the conditions
under which an identity can be viable in the realms in which it is manifested; they are the
conditions under which the identity’s essence, causation, and modality can be what they are.

Principle 29.13 (The Metaphysical Conditions of Viability). (T) The metaphysical conditions
of viability are the fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability of the relation between an identity
and its manifestations in each realm. The conditions are the same across the domains of
essence, causation, and modality; their application differs, but the conditions are the same. The
metaphysics of viability is the account of the conditions as they integrate across the four columns
and the three domains.

    The principle is (T): it follows from the three components of metaphysical viability (Chap-
ter ??) and from the applications to the three domains (Chapters ?? to 28). The argument is
that the conditions are the three components; the components are the same across the domains;
the integration of the components across the columns and domains is the metaphysics of viability.
Remark 29.14 (The Conditions Are Not a Formula). The conditions are not a formula. They
state the three components of the relation; the assessment of the components in a given case is
the work of the inquiry, not of a formula. The framework offers the conditions as the standard
the inquiry aims at, and it leaves the assessment to the inquiry.
Remark 29.15 (The Conditions Are Not a Ranking). The conditions are not a ranking. No
condition is more important than another; each is a distinct aspect of the relation, and each
must be satisfied for the relation to be fully viable. The framework’s claim is that the three are
the components of one character, not three separate standards.


29.8     The Four-Column Structure of the Metaphysics of Viability
With the definition and the conditions in place, the four-column method of Book I, Chapter 6,
can be applied to the metaphysics of viability itself.

29.8.1    The Fixed Element of the Metaphysics of Viability
The fixed element of the metaphysics of viability is the identity and its manifestations, held
invariant while the account explains the conditions under which the identity can be viable. The
fixed elements are the subject of the account; the conditions are the conditions of the relation
between them.

29.8.2    The Fluid Element of the Metaphysics of Viability
The fluid element of the metaphysics of viability is light, the medium of the relation between the
identity and its manifestations. The fluid element is what conveys the effect of the identity to its
manifestations; it is the medium through which the conditions are realized.

29.8.3    The Governing Dynamics of the Metaphysics of Viability
The governing dynamics of the metaphysics of viability is the rules of the realms, the constraints
that govern what is possible in each realm. The rules are the form of the conditions; they
determine what the identity can be in each realm, and what the realms can bear.
29.9. What the Principle Does Not Say                                                           343


29.8.4    The Context of the Metaphysics of Viability
The context of the metaphysics of viability is the realms, the existential settings in which the
identity is manifested. The realms are the setting of the conditions; they determine where the
identity is manifested, and what they contribute to the relation.

29.8.5    The Four Columns Together
The four columns of the metaphysics of viability are stated in the following table.

                 Column               In the Metaphysics of Viability
                 Fixed element    The identity and its manifestations, held
                                  invariant as the subject
                 Fluid element    Light, the medium of the relation between
                                  the identity and its manifestations
                 Governing dynam- The rules of the realms, the form of the

   The table is the application of Book I’s four-column method to the metaphysics of viability.
The application is the chapter’s contribution to the book’s systematic character.
Remark 29.16 (The Metaphysics of Viability Is Not the Four Columns). The metaphysics of
viability is not the four columns. The four columns are the analytical roles of any complete
explanation (Book I, Principle 3.1); the metaphysics of viability is a complete explanation of the
conditions of viability. The distinction is the distinction between the roles and the account; the
framework keeps it throughout.


29.9     What the Principle Does Not Say
The principle is easily misread, and the misreadings are worth distinguishing.
    The principle does not say that viability is a substance. Viability is a structural character of
the relation between an identity and its manifestations; it is not a substance, not a thing, not a
posit. The principle says that viability is a structural character, not that it is a substance.
    The principle does not say that the conditions are a definition of the identity. The identity
is what it is; the conditions are the conditions of the relation between the identity and its
manifestations. The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
    The principle does not say that the conditions are a value. The conditions are a structural
character; they attach no value, end, or good to the relation. The framework’s claim is that the
conditions are the conditions of the relation, not that they are the good.
    The principle does not say that the conditions are complete. The conditions are the frame-
work’s account of the relation; the framework does not claim that the conditions exhaust what
the relation is, and it does not claim that nothing lies beyond them.
Remark 29.17 (The Principle Leaves the Application Open). The principle leaves the application
open. It states the definition and the conditions; it does not state how the conditions apply to
each domain in detail. The application is the work of the chapters that treat each domain; the
present chapter states the integration.
Remark 29.18 (No Conflict with the Four-Column Framework). The principle is compatible
with the four-column framework. The four columns are the analytical roles of any complete
explanation; the metaphysics of viability is a complete explanation of the conditions of viability.
The two are different, and the framework keeps them apart.
344                                                   Chapter 29. The Metaphysics of Viability


29.10      What Would Refute the Principle
The principle is (T), and its argument is given in the previous sections. What would refute it is
worth stating, so that the reader knows where to press.
    The principle would be refuted by showing that the three conditions are not the same across
the domains. If such a showing could be made, the conditions would be different in each domain,
and the metaphysics of viability would not be one account. The framework’s claim is that the
conditions are the same across the domains; their application differs, but the conditions are the
same.
    The principle would also be refuted by showing that the four columns do not integrate in the
account of the conditions. If such a showing could be made, the account would not be systematic,
and the metaphysics of viability would not be a complete explanation. The framework’s claim is
that the four columns are the analytical roles of any complete explanation (Book I, Principle 3.1),
and that the metaphysics of viability is a complete explanation of the conditions of viability.
Remark 29.19 (The Two Refutations Are Different). The two refutations are different. The first
challenges the unity of the conditions across the domains; the second challenges the systematic
character of the account. The two challenges require different responses, and the framework
responds to each in its own terms.


29.11      What This Chapter Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this chapter are deliberately deferred or declined.
    First, the chapter does not develop the application of the conditions to each domain in detail.
The applications are the work of Chapters ?? to 28; the present chapter states the integration of
the applications.
    Second, the chapter does not develop the metaphysics of the divine ground. The divine
ground is the subject of Part VI; the present chapter states the metaphysics of viability, and it
leaves the divine ground to its place.
    Third, the chapter does not settle the question of whether the three conditions exhaust the
metaphysics of viability. The three conditions are the ones the framework has identified; whether
a fourth condition is needed, or whether one of the three can be derived from the others, is a
question the chapter leaves open.
    Fourth, the chapter does not claim to have described the ground of viability. It claims to
have described the structure of viability; the structure points beyond itself to its ground. The
question of what grounds viability is left to Part VI.
Remark 29.20 (The Chapter’s Contributions). The chapter has contributed four things. It has
stated the definition of the metaphysics of viability. It has stated the integration of the four
columns. It has stated the relation of viability to the three domains of essence, causation,
and modality. And it has stated the metaphysical conditions of viability and the four-column
structure of the metaphysics of viability.
Remark 29.21 (The Chapter Completes Part VII). The chapter completes Part VII. The part has
developed the metaphysical concept of viability through a sequence of applications; the present
chapter has integrated the applications in a single account. The part is complete; the next part
(Part VI) states the divine ground of the whole.

29.13       A Question for Reflection
Consider an identity you know well—a person, a practice, a tradition, a work. What are the
metaphysical conditions under which the identity can be viable in the realms in which it is
manifested? Does the relation between the identity and its manifestations satisfy the conditions
of fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability? And how do the four columns of the framework—
the identity and its manifestations, the medium of light, the rules of the realms, the realms
themselves—integrate in your answer?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s account. The metaphysics of viability is the account of
the conditions under which the identity can be viable; the conditions are the fidelity, sustainability,
and recoverability of the relation; the four columns are the aspects of the conditions. The reader
who can state, for an identity he knows, the conditions of its viability and the integration of the
four columns, has understood the chapter’s account; the reader who cannot has found a place
where the account is most difficult, and is invited to develop the difficulty further.
Part VII is complete. Part VI turns to the divine ground and the modal order: the metaphysics
of transcendence, creation and sustaining, the modal space as created, and providence, knowledge,
and choice reconsidered. The reader who has followed Part VII has the vocabulary; Part VI puts
it to work.
