        Part VIII

Boundaries and Conclusion
                                                                                                349




Chapter 30

The Boundaries of Metaphysics

Scope
This chapter states the boundaries of the metaphysical framework developed in this book. It
says what the framework can and cannot establish, what questions it leaves open, and how it
relates to other domains of inquiry. It states the coherence of the framework, the framework’s
role as a conceptual foundation, the three principles of the boundary, and the open questions
the framework leaves in three groups (conceptual, argumentative, and metaphysical). It mirrors,
for metaphysics, the task that Book I’s Chapter 34 performed for epistemology. Its claims are
metaphysical and meta-philosophical; where it speaks of “boundary,” “coherence,” “foundation,”
“autonomy,” “open question,” or “domain,” these are structural terms, and their sense is fixed by
the definitions in this chapter. The chapter’s silence on questions of value, of the divine essence,
and of revelation is not a denial of their reality; it is the recognition that the metaphysical
description is not the whole of what can be said.

      Presupposition from Book I and Parts II–VII. This chapter takes as given
      Book I’s Principle 4.1 (philosophy describes structure, not telos), Book I’s Princi-
      ples 34.1–34.3 (the three principles of the epistemic boundary), and the metaphysical
      analyses of Parts I–VII. It does not reargue them; it applies the boundary of Book I to
      the metaphysical domain, and it states the open questions that the framework leaves.


30.1      A Scene: The Map of the Ocean
Consider a map of the ocean. The map shows the coastlines, the depths, the currents, and
the islands. It is accurate in its own terms, and it is drawn for a purpose. The map has
a boundary—the edge of the sheet, the region it covers, the features it represents—and the
boundary is not a defect. It is what makes the map useful.
     Now consider the map of a map. Someone draws a map that represents the first map: its
edges, its scale, its conventions. The second map is accurate too, and it is drawn for a different
purpose. But the second map cannot represent the territory the first map represents; it can only
represent the first map’s representation of the territory. The second map’s boundary is the first
map’s boundary, plus the first map’s frame.
     Now consider a third map, of the map of the map. Each map has a boundary, and each
boundary is the condition under which the map is useful. But no map, at any level, is the ocean.
     The scene is not about maps in particular. It is about the structure of description. A
description is not the thing described; it is a representation, drawn for a purpose, with a
boundary that is the condition of its usefulness. The same is true of a philosophical description:
it is not the world it describes; it is a description of the world, drawn for a purpose, with a
boundary that is the condition of its precision.
350                                                 Chapter 30. The Boundaries of Metaphysics


    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What is the boundary of the metaphysical
framework developed in this book? What can it establish, and what can it not? What does it
leave open, and to what inquiry does it leave it?


30.2     The Question
The preceding parts of the book have developed the metaphysical framework. Part I stated the
method and the derivation of ontology from epistemology; Parts II to V treated the four columns
of metaphysics; Part VI stated the divine ground and the modal order; Part VII integrated the
four columns in viability. The framework is now in place.
    The present chapter asks: what is the boundary of the framework? The question is not
what the framework claims; the preceding parts have said what it claims. The question is what
the framework is for, and what it is not for; what it can establish, and what it leaves to other
inquiries; what it makes possible, and what it leaves open.
    The question has two aspects.
    The coherence aspect. What can be said of the framework as a whole? The chapter states
what can be said: the framework is coherent, its definitions are fixed, its arguments state their
premises, and its statuses are declared. The statement is not a claim that the framework is
closed or beyond revision; it is a claim about what the framework has achieved, at the strength
its arguments support.
    The boundary aspect. What are the framework’s limits? The chapter states three principles
that fix the boundary—the autonomy of philosophical justification, the internal definition of the
framework’s concepts, and the non-export of meaning. It states the relation between metaphysics
and other domains, and it identifies the open questions the framework leaves.
    The chapter proceeds as follows. It states the coherence of the existing architecture. It states
the framework’s role as a conceptual foundation. It states the three principles of the boundary.
It states the relation between metaphysics and other domains. It identifies the open questions in
three groups: conceptual, argumentative, and metaphysical. It states the future of metaphysics,
as the framework sees it. It closes with what it does not establish and with the epistemic status
of its claims.


30.3     The Coherence of the Framework
Over thirty chapters, the book has built a metaphysical framework. What can be said of it is
that it is coherent: its definitions are fixed, its arguments state their premises, and its statuses
are declared. This is not a claim that it is closed or beyond revision. A metaphysical framework
is always open to correction, and the present chapter says what that means and what remains
open.
    The coherence of the framework is not a claim that every principle is true. It is a claim that
the principles are mutually consistent, that each is stated with its status, and that the arguments
for each are given in the chapters that establish them. A reader who rejects a principle has a
reason to reject the corresponding part of the framework; the framework states the principles
and their statuses, so that the reader knows which parts are in question.
    Remark. Coherence is not completeness. The framework is coherent in the sense that its
principles are mutually consistent and its arguments are stated; it is not complete in the sense
that every question it raises is answered. The open questions that this chapter identifies are the
questions the framework raises but does not settle. The framework’s coherence is compatible
with its incompleteness; the two are different virtues, and the framework has the first without
claiming the second.
    Remark. Coherence is not finality. A coherent framework can be revised; a framework that is
not coherent cannot be revised, because there is no single structure to revise. The framework’s
30.4. The Framework as a Conceptual Foundation                                                  351


coherence is what makes revision possible; it is not a claim that no revision will ever be needed.
The reader who finds a principle unpersuasive has a reason to revise the framework; the framework
invites the revision, and its coherence is what makes the invitation meaningful.
     Remark. Coherence is relative to the framework’s scope. The framework is coherent as a
metaphysical framework, for the scope it declares (Chapter 1). It is not a claim of coherence
with other frameworks, or with the whole of what is. The distinction is the distinction between
coherence within the framework and coherence with other domains; the framework claims the
first, not the second.


30.4     The Framework as a Conceptual Foundation
The framework supplies primitives, abstractions, and invariants for the metaphysical description
of being. The supply is the framework’s role, and the role is stated in a remark.
    Primitives. The framework’s primitives are substance, essence, identity, thisness, causation,
relation, light, law, necessity, modality, viability, and the divine ground. Each is defined in
its proper place; each is used throughout the framework as a term whose sense is fixed by its
definition.
    Abstractions. The framework’s abstractions are the realms, the barzakhic category, the four
strata of the modal space, the four modes of the createdness of the modal space, the three modes
of providence, and the metaphysics of viability. Each is a structural concept that the framework
introduces to describe a class of relations; each is defined by the framework’s principles.
    Invariants. The framework’s invariants are the transcendence of the divine ground, the
createdness of the modal space, the createdness of light, the non-reducibility of the realms, the
non-necessity of downward passage, the stratification of the modal space, and the compatibility
of divine knowledge and creaturely choice. Each is a structural principle that the framework
establishes; each is used as a fixed point in the framework’s arguments.
    Remark. The role of the framework is to give fundamental principles and distinctions for the
metaphysical description of being. The phrase “metaphysical operating system” would suggest
a directive role; the structural role described above is the foundational role, and it is to be
distinguished from any directive role. Value, normativity, ethics, and the divine essence belong
to other inquiries.
    Remark. The framework’s role is foundational, not directive. It describes the structure
of being; physics, chemistry, biology, and the other empirical inquiries answer their specific
questions by their own methods. The framework states the conditions under which the inquiries
can develop; the authority of those inquiries comes from their own methods. The distinction is
structural: the framework’s role is foundational, and the inquiries it describes answer the specific
questions by the methods proper to them.
    Remark. The framework describes structure; it does not prescribe conduct. The distinction
has been stated at the outset of the book (Preface, Chapter 1), and it is restated here because
it bears on the framework’s role as a conceptual foundation. A structural description is not a
normative prescription, but neither is it irrelevant to one. The description of the structure of
being provides an ontological basis on which a normative prescription may be built; it does not
itself supply that prescription, and it does not replace it.


30.5     The Three Principles of the Boundary
Three principles fix the boundary of the framework. They are stated here, with their statuses,
and they are the framework’s declaration of what it does and does not do. The three are
the metaphysical analogues of Book I’s three principles of the epistemic boundary (Book I,
Principles 34.1–34.3).
352                                                Chapter 30. The Boundaries of Metaphysics


Principle 30.1 (Autonomy of Philosophical Justification). (A) The validity of a metaphysical
principle, within the domain of philosophy, does not depend on confirmation from outside
philosophy.

    The principle was stated in Book I’s Principle 4.2, and it has been observed throughout. Its
statement here is its formal declaration in the metaphysical domain, and its role is to fix the
boundary: metaphysical justification is internal to philosophy, and no principle of the framework
is justified by appeal to an outside authority.
    The principle separates two things that are easily run together: autonomy and exclusivity.
Autonomy says that philosophy’s justification is internal to philosophy; exclusivity would say
that philosophy is the only domain of valid discourse. The framework holds the first and denies
the second. Philosophy is autonomous in its own domain; it does not claim that its domain is
the whole of reality. The question of telos, the question of the divine essence, and the question
of revelation belong to other domains; the framework neither subordinates those domains to
philosophy nor subordinates philosophy to them.

Principle 30.2 (Internal Definition). (T) The concepts of the framework are defined and justified
within its own system, from its premises.

    The principle states what the framework’s practice has been: every technical term is defined
within the book, and no argument depends on the reader’s acquaintance with any tradition. The
principle’s role is to fix the boundary of the framework’s vocabulary: the framework’s terms have
the sense the framework gives them, and no outside use of the terms determines their sense here.

Principle 30.3 (Meaning Is Not Exported). (T) The use of a word or concept in another domain
does not determine its metaphysical sense here.

    The principle states what the framework’s practice has been: where a word has a use in
another domain, that use does not enter the framework’s definitions. The principle’s role is to
fix the boundary of the framework’s vocabulary against the vocabulary of other domains: the
framework’s terms are not hostage to the uses of the same words elsewhere.
    Remark. Philosophy and other fields of inquiry are different undertakings, each answerable to
its own standards. The book does not subordinate a field to philosophy or philosophy to a field.
What is said in it is to be judged by the coherence, the discriminating power, and the strength
of its own arguments. The relation is one of coexistence, not of hierarchy.
    Remark. If someone judges that a metaphysical principle here is mistaken, the ground for
revising it is a philosophical one: incoherence with other commitments, a better rival commitment,
or the showing that the principle does no work. A principle is not revised because a statement
made outside philosophy appears to differ from it. The framework does not claim that philosophy
is immune to criticism from outside; it claims that the criticism, to be effective, must engage the
framework’s own standards.


30.6     Metaphysics and Other Domains
The three principles of the boundary have a consequence for the relation between metaphysics
and other domains, and the consequence is worth stating.
   Metaphysics and epistemology. Book I established the epistemological framework; Book II
inherits its core and extends it to the metaphysical domain. The relation is one of derivation:
Book II presupposes Book I’s principles, and it asks what they require in the order of being. The
two books are distinct, and neither replaces the other.
   Metaphysics and science. The framework does not draw its premises from empirical data,
and it does not claim that its principles are confirmed by empirical inquiry. Its principles are
metaphysical, and they are assessed by philosophical standards. The framework may speak of
30.7. The Open Questions: Conceptual                                                          353


science, but only as a coherence test, never as a ground of justification. The distinction is the
distinction between the framework’s autonomy and its coherence with the inquiries it does not
depend on.
    Metaphysics and ethics. The framework describes the structure of being; it does not prescribe
conduct. The questions of ethics, value, and guidance belong to a different inquiry, and the
framework is silent on them by method, not by denial. The framework’s description of the
structure of being provides an ontological basis on which a normative prescription may be built;
it does not itself supply that prescription, and it does not replace it.
    Metaphysics and revelation. The framework describes the structure of being; it does not
describe the content of any revelation. The question of revelation belongs to a different inquiry,
and the framework neither affirms nor denies any particular revelation. The framework’s silence
on revelation is not a denial of its possibility; it is the recognition that the framework’s method
is the method of philosophical inquiry, and that the content of revelation is not the content of
philosophical inquiry.
    Metaphysics and the divine essence. The framework describes the relation between the created
order and God; it does not describe the divine essence. The distinction is the distinction between
the relation and the essence; the framework keeps it throughout, and it is stated in Chapter 26.
    Remark. The domains are distinct, not rival. Each is answerable to its own standards, and
each has its own kind of claim. The framework’s claim is that the distinction is structural, not
that one domain is superior to the others. A reader who reads the chapter as a ranking of
domains has misread it; a reader who reads it as a statement of distinction has read it correctly.
    Remark. The boundary between metaphysics and other domains is a threshold, not a wall.
It marks the point at which metaphysical description gives way to other kinds of description,
and the other kinds of description are not lesser forms of knowledge but different forms. The
framework’s silence on other domains is not a denial of their reality; it is the recognition that
the metaphysical description is not the whole of what can be said.


30.7     The Open Questions: Conceptual
The framework’s principles make visible a set of questions that the framework does not settle.
The questions are metaphysical, and they are marked with the appropriate status. They fall into
three groups. The first group is conceptual: the questions about the framework’s concepts and
their relations.
    First question: the precise relation between the four kinds of necessity and the four strata of
Ω. The four kinds are derived in Chapter 14; the four strata are derived in Chapter 15. The
relation between them is stated in Chapter 15 as identity; the question of whether the identity is
exact, or whether one is a mode of the other, is left open. ((Q))
    Second question: the precise relation between the created modal space and the context of the
whole. The created modal space is derived in Chapter 28; the context of the whole is derived
in Chapter 20. The relation between them is stated in Chapter 15 as condition and order; the
question of whether the relation is one of containment, of condition, or of something else, is left
open. ((Q))
    Third question: the precise structure of the grounding of Ω in God. The grounding is stated
in Chapter 15 as a family of analogous relations; the question of whether the analogy is exact, or
whether it is a family of distinct relations, is left open. ((Q))
    Fourth question: the precise relation between transcendence and the four columns. The
relation is stated in Chapter 26 as condition; the question of whether the condition is the same
as the condition of the created order, or whether it is a distinct condition, is left open. ((Q))
    Remark. The four questions are open because the framework does not have the resources to
settle them at the strength its arguments support. The framework’s claim is that the questions
are real questions—that they arise from the framework’s principles—and that the framework’s
354                                                  Chapter 30. The Boundaries of Metaphysics


principles make them visible without answering them. A reader who settles one of the questions
has extended the framework; a reader who shows that the question is not real has shown a limit
of the framework’s formulation.


30.8      The Open Questions: Argumentative
The second group is argumentative: the questions about the framework’s arguments and their
premises.
    Fifth question: the relation between the minimality of the four columns (Chapter 2) and the
metaphysical minimality of the realms. The minimality of the four columns is an analytical
claim; the question of whether it entails a metaphysical minimality of the realms, or whether the
metaphysical minimality is a distinct claim, is left open. ((Q))
    Sixth question: the status of the modal-realist objection. The objection is stated in Chapter 15,
Objection 1, and the reply is given there. The question of whether the reply is fully adequate, or
whether the modal-realist objection can be restated in a form the reply does not meet, is left
open. ((Q))
    Seventh question: whether the doctrine of primitive thisness can be given further metaphysical
support. The doctrine is derived in Chapter 7; the question of whether it can be given further
support—by argument, or by showing that a framework without it explains the same things as
well— is left open. ((Q))
    Eighth question: the status of the free-will defence. The structure of the defence is stated in
Chapter 29; the question of whether the structure is sufficient to resolve the problem of evil, or
whether it leaves the problem untouched, is left open. ((Q))
    Remark. The four questions are open because the arguments for the relevant principles are
given at the strength they have, and the arguments do not settle the further questions. The
framework’s claim is that the arguments are given, that their premises are stated, and that
the further questions are questions that the arguments raise but do not settle. A reader who
strengthens an argument, or who shows that a premise can be given independent support, has
extended the framework; a reader who shows that an argument is invalid has shown a limit of
the framework’s formulation.


30.9      The Open Questions: Metaphysical
The third group is metaphysical: the questions about the framework’s ontology and its structural
claims.
    Ninth question: the problem of evil. The framework states the structure of the free-will
defence (Chapter 29); the problem of evil is not resolved. The question of why the amount of
evil is what it is, and of how the existence of evil is compatible with the divine attributes, is left
open. ((Q))
    Tenth question: the eternal destiny of the creature. The framework does not describe the
eternal destiny of the creature. The question of what the creature’s final state is, and of how it
relates to the creature’s choices, is left open. ((Q))
    Eleventh question: the precise mode of divine self-disclosure. The framework states that the
divine ground is the source of all light (Chapter 26); the question of how the divine self-disclosure
occurs—whether through revelation, through the created light, or through some other mode—is
left open. ((Q))
    Twelfth question: the relation between the modal space and the actualization chain in detail.
The relation is stated in Chapter 15 and in Chapter 29; the detailed structure of the actualization—
how the selection occurs, how the temporal order is established, how the configuration-dependence
of the manifestation relates to the actualization—is left open. ((Q))
30.10. The Open Questions and Book I                                                            355


    Remark. The four questions are open because the framework’s ontology is stated at the
strength its arguments support, and the further questions are questions that the ontology raises
but does not settle. The framework’s claim is that the ontology is stated, that its structural
claims are argued, and that the further questions are questions that the ontology raises but does
not resolve. A reader who settles one of the questions has extended the framework; a reader who
shows that the question is not real has shown a limit of the framework’s ontology.


30.10      The Open Questions and Book I
The present chapter’s twelve questions are not the only questions the framework leaves. Book I’s
Chapter 34 identified fourteen open questions, and the present chapter’s questions are related to
them. The relation is worth stating, because it shows the continuity between the two books.
    The conceptual questions. Book I’s Q1–Q4 (the joint realizability of viabilities, the singularity
of death, the relation between light and expression, the mode of the relation between light
and its divine source) are conceptual questions that the present chapter’s conceptual questions
(Q1–Q4) address at the metaphysical level. The present chapter’s Q1–Q4 are the metaphysical
counterparts of Book I’s Q1–Q4.
    The argumentative questions. Book I’s Q5–Q9 (the relation among self-awareness, con-
sciousness, awareness, and the subject; the conceptual foundations of the thresholds and the
balance criterion; the independent support for the contextual manifestational capacity and the
manifestational adequacy; the relation among the three aspects of cost; the bridge to normative
prescription) are argumentative questions that the present chapter’s argumentative questions
(Q5–Q8) address at the metaphysical level. The present chapter’s Q5–Q8 are the metaphysical
counterparts of Book I’s Q5–Q8.
    The epistemic questions. Book I’s Q10–Q14 (the ontological standing of realization in
the barzakhic realms; the particular direct relations among the realms; the further support
for the doctrine that identity is more than signature; the exact form of the impossibility of
complete knowledge of epistemic light for subjects who are not finite; the temporal structure
of self-awareness) are epistemic questions that the present chapter’s metaphysical questions
(Q9–Q12) address at the metaphysical level. The present chapter’s Q9–Q12 are the metaphysical
counterparts of Book I’s Q10–Q13, and Book I’s Q14 is left to a later volume.
    Remark. The relation between the two sets of questions is not one of identity; it is one
of correspondence. Book I’s questions are epistemological; the present chapter’s questions are
metaphysical. The two sets are related as the two books are related: the second presupposes the
first, and the first is incomplete without the second. The reader who has followed both books
has the whole architecture of questions; the reader who has followed only one has part of it.


30.11      The Future of Metaphysics
The future of the framework depends on the capacity of the system itself to pose, analyze, and
resolve metaphysical questions: to sharpen its definitions, strengthen its arguments, and remove
what does not cohere. It is not a future that waits upon developments in other domains. The
framework’s claim is that metaphysics’s development is internal to metaphysics; the framework’s
future is the future of its own capacity to refine itself.
    Remark. The framework is not a static hierarchy in which higher principles simply dictate
to lower ones. When a conceptual difficulty appears at one level, it can lead to refinement of a
principle at another, and the refined principle in turn changes what can be said below. This is
what keeps the system revisable. The framework is a living framework, not a finished monument.
    Remark. The framework’s future is not the future of science. The two are different undertak-
ings, each answerable to its own standards. The framework does not wait upon science to answer
its questions; science does not wait upon the framework to answer its questions. The two coexist,
356                                                Chapter 30. The Boundaries of Metaphysics


and each develops by its own methods. The framework’s future is the future of its own capacity
to pose, analyze, and resolve metaphysical questions; it is not the future of any other domain.
    Remark. The framework’s future is not the future of theology. The two are different
undertakings, each answerable to its own standards. The framework describes the relation
between the created order and God; it does not describe the divine essence, and it does not
undertake theological inquiry. The framework’s future is the future of its own capacity to refine
the metaphysical description; it is not the future of any other domain.


30.12      Limits and Continuations
Three continuations belong to Part VIII and to other inquiries, and they are indicated here so
that the reader knows where the present chapter’s account ends.
    First, the open questions the chapter identifies remain open. They are stated at the strength
the framework’s arguments support; the settlement of any one of them belongs to an extension
of the framework. A reader who answers one of the questions extends the framework.
    Second, the conclusion of the book is stated in Chapter 31. The present chapter has stated
the boundaries; the next chapter states the architecture and its open questions, and it closes the
book.
    Third, the relation between the framework’s boundaries and the boundaries of other metaphys-
ical frameworks, and between the framework’s boundaries and those of other inquiries—including
epistemology, science, ethics, and revelation—belongs to a comparative inquiry. The chapter
states the framework’s boundaries and its relation to other domains; the specific comparison is a
different question, and it is developed in the later volumes of the series.
    Remark. The chapter opens Part VIII, not the book. The book continues with Chapter 31,
which states the conclusion. The boundaries stated here are the boundaries of the framework
as a whole, and they apply to Chapter 31 as much as to the earlier parts. The reader who has
followed the argument to this point has the framework; Chapter 31 states its architecture and its
open questions, and it closes the book.

30.14      A Question for Reflection
Consider a question the framework raises but does not settle—one of the twelve open questions,
or a question of your own. What would it take to settle it? Would the settlement be a new
principle, a new argument, or a new concept? And consider a question that belongs to another
domain—a question of the divine essence, of ethics, or of revelation. What does the difference
between the two kinds of question tell you about the relation between the framework’s boundaries
and its future?

and it offers a final statement of what the framework is and what it is not. The present chapter has
stated the boundaries; the next chapter states the conclusion that the boundaries make possible.

Chapter 31

Conclusion: The Architecture and Its
Open Questions

Scope. This chapter concludes the book. It states what the framework has established, what
it has not established, and what it leaves open. It is a metaphysical and meta-philosophical
analysis: it says what the framework is, and what it is not. Its claims are metaphysical; where it
speaks of “architecture,” “open questions,” “core,” “axiom,” or “horizon,” these are structural
terms. The framework’s task is the description of structure; the questions of values, goods, and
ends belong to distinct inquiries that the framework is designed to serve, not to replace. The
chapter closes the book; it does not close the inquiry.

Presupposition from Book I and Parts II–VII. This chapter takes as given Book I’s
Chapter 42 (the epistemic conclusion), Book I’s Chapter E (the registry of axioms), the inherited
core of Chapter ??, and the metaphysical analyses of Parts I–VI. It does not reargue them; it
states the conclusion that they make possible.


31.1     A Scene
Consider a mountain range. The range has many peaks, each with its own shape, its own height,
its own relations to the other peaks. The range is one, the peaks are many. The range is not any
of the peaks, and the peaks are not the range. The range is the order in which the peaks stand.
    Now consider a cartographer who has spent a lifetime mapping the range. She has climbed
some of the peaks; she has surveyed the valleys; she has drawn the contours. Her map is accurate
in its own terms, and it is drawn for a purpose. But the map is not the range; the map has
a boundary—the edge of the sheet, the region it covers, the features it represents—and the
boundary is not a defect. It is what makes the map useful.
    The scene poses the question of the chapter. What has the framework established? What
has it not established? And what does it leave open?
    The chapter’s answer is a statement of the architecture, its boundary, and its open horizon.
It is the book’s closing, and it is the inquiry’s continuation.
Remark 31.1 (The Scene Is an Illustration, Not an Argument). The scene shows the question
at work in a familiar analogy. It does not prove the framework’s account; it makes the account
intelligible before it is stated. The account is stated and argued in the sections that follow, and
the scene carries no weight in them. The mountain range and the cartographer are examples;
the account is about the framework in general.
360                         Chapter 31. Conclusion: The Architecture and Its Open Questions


31.2     The Unfinished Inquiry
Philosophy has always been an inquiry, often a fractured one. This book offers a language for
part of it. Its architecture proceeds from the framework of metaphysical inquiry (Part I), to the
four columns of metaphysics (Parts II to V), to the integration in viability (Part VII), to the
divine ground and modal order (Part VI), to the boundaries and conclusion (Part VIII).
    The architecture is the book’s contribution, and it is offered as a contribution to an inquiry
that continues. The reader who has followed the argument from beginning to end has seen the
architecture built, part by part, each part presupposing only what has come before. The reader
who has entered in the middle has seen one part in its context. Both readers have seen the same
architecture, and both are invited to continue the inquiry that the architecture makes possible.
Remark 31.2 (The Inquiry Is Not Finished). The inquiry is not finished. The book states its
claims at the strength its arguments support, and it states the questions it does not settle. The
reader who finds a claim unpersuasive, or a question unresolved, has located a place where
the inquiry continues. The framework’s honesty about its incompleteness is part of what the
framework is.
Remark 31.3 (The Inquiry Is Not Fractured by the Framework). The inquiry is not fractured by
the framework. The framework offers a language for part of philosophy; the philosophical inquiry
has other languages and other voices, and the framework is one contribution among them. The
framework is offered in the hope that it helps; it is not offered as the final word.


31.3     The Central Question
The central question of Book I was: “How does an identity express itself in manifestations, in
many realms, while remaining one?” The central question of Book II is different, and it is the
question that Book I left open: What must being be, such that the framework of Book I can be
assigned to it?
    The distinction between the two questions is not small. The first asks for the structure of
cognition; the second asks for the structure of being. The first has been answered in Book I; the
second is the question the present book’s architecture is designed to answer, and its answer is
not a definition but an account of the relations among the realms, the fixed elements, the fluid
element, the governing dynamics, and the divine ground.
    The framework’s answer is that being must be structured in seven realms; that the realms
must be independently real and ordered; that the fixed elements (substance, essence, identity,
thisness) must be modes of being; that the fluid element (light) must be created; that the
governing dynamics (law, modality, the modal space) must be created; that the context (the
realms, the Throne-Domain) must be created; and that the created order must depend on God,
who is not a level of the architecture.
    This is a metaphysical result. It concerns the structure of being; the questions of value
belong to distinct inquiries that the framework is designed to serve. The reader who has followed
the argument has seen the result, and the reader who has not is directed to the chapters that
establish it.
Remark 31.4 (The Central Question Is Conditional). The central question is conditional. The
framework does not claim that being must have the structure described; it claims that, given
Book I’s framework, being must have the structure that the present book describes. The
conditionality is the framework’s honesty about what it is doing: it is a metaphysics in the service
of an epistemology, not a metaphysics in general. The reader who accepts Book I’s framework
should accept the present book’s account of the structure of being that the framework requires;
the reader who does not accept Book I’s framework will find the present book’s claims conditional
on a framework he does not accept, and the present book states them at that strength.
31.4. Three Conclusions                                                                           361


31.4      Three Conclusions
The book has established three conclusions. They are stated here as the framework’s principal
contributions, with their statuses.
     First conclusion: the framework of Book I extends to being itself. The four columns of Book I
are not only the analytical roles of an explanation; they are also the structure of being, when
applied to the metaphysical domain. The four columns are the analytical architecture; the seven
realms are the ontological architecture; and the two are distinct (Book I, Principle 1.1). But the
framework of the four columns applies to the seven realms, because the four columns are the
roles that any complete explanation must assign (Book I, Principle 3.1), and the seven realms
are what the explanation explains. The first conclusion is that the four columns of Book I are
also the four columns of metaphysics, and the present book has applied them. ((T) relative to
Book I’s Principle 3.1.)
     Second conclusion: the metaphysics of viability integrates the four columns. Viability is
the structural character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations in a realm
(Chapter ??); the metaphysics of viability is the account of the conditions under which this
relation can be what it is (Chapter 29). The conditions are the three components of metaphysical
viability (fidelity, sustainability, recoverability); the four columns integrate as the four aspects of
the conditions. The second conclusion is that the metaphysics of viability is the integration of
the four columns in a single account of the conditions of expression. ((A) as a commitment of
the framework; the argument is given in Part VII.)
     Third conclusion: the created order depends on God, who is not a level of the architecture.
The realms are created; the light is created; the modal space is created; the Throne-Domain is
the encompassing created order. God is the transcendent Creator and sustaining ground of the
whole; God is not a realm, a level, or a part of the sevenfold architecture (Book I, Principle 7.3);
God is not the light (Book I, Principle 12.2); God is not the modal space (Book I, Principle 37.2).
The third conclusion is that the created order depends on God at every moment for its being,
its intelligibility, and its relations (Chapter 21), and that the framework is not self-sufficient: it
points beyond itself to its ground. ((D) relative to Book I’s three commitments.)
     The three conclusions are not separate. They are three aspects of one result: being must
be structured in the four columns and the seven realms; the structure must be integrated in
viability; and the structure must depend on God, who is not a level of the structure. The first
names the extension; the second names the integration; the third names the ground. Together,
they state what the framework has established.
Remark 31.5 (The Conclusions Are Structural). The three conclusions are structural features of
the relation between the framework and being. They do not rank identity above manifestation,
or the four columns above the seven realms, or the created order above God; they state the
structural order through which the framework’s account of being is built. The framework’s
account of expression, viability, and the divine ground is built on these structural features.
Remark 31.6 (The Conclusions Are Relative to Their Premises). The three conclusions are (T)
or (A) or (D) relative to the premises on which they rest. The first is (T) relative to Book I’s
Principle 3.1; the second is (A) as a commitment of the framework; the third is (D) relative to
Book I’s three commitments. A reader who rejects one of the premises has a reason to reject the
corresponding conclusion, and the framework states the premises so that the reader knows which
conclusion is in question.


31.5      The Boundary of the Framework
The framework’s domain is metaphysics. Its subject is the structure of being: the seven realms,
the fixed elements, the fluid element, the governing dynamics, the context, the integration in
viability, and the divine ground. Questions of how anything ought to be, what is good, what is
362                         Chapter 31. Conclusion: The Architecture and Its Open Questions


right, and what is worth pursuing belong to ethics, value, and normativity—distinct inquiries
that the framework is designed to serve, not to replace.
    The boundary is not a deficiency. It is what the framework is: a description of structure.
Where the framework reaches its limit, the limit is marked, and the question is marked as open
((Q)), belonging to the inquiry that undertakes it. The boundary is what makes the framework
useful: it tells the reader what to expect, and what not to expect, from the framework’s claims.
Remark 31.7 (The Boundary Is Structural, Not Arbitrary). The boundary is structural, not
arbitrary. It follows from the framework’s method: the framework’s principles are established
within philosophy, from philosophical arguments, and they concern the structure of being and
knowing, not the norms of action or the values of life. The boundary is what the framework’s
method requires, not an arbitrary limitation imposed from outside.
Remark 31.8 (The Boundary Is a Distinction of Undertakings). The boundary is a distinction
of undertakings, not a ranking. Metaphysics and ethics are different inquiries, each answerable
to its own standards. The framework is one of them—a structural description of being and
knowing—and the ethical and normative inquiries belong to their own domains. The framework’s
claim is that the two are different undertakings, not that one is superior to the other.


31.6     The Humility of the Philosopher
The book ends in humility, grounded in the limits of the observer. It is a proposal. Even the
claim that there are four fundamental grades of multiplicity is an estimate. The inquiry continues
not because a final answer has been found, but because a precise question has been put.
    The humility is not a rhetorical gesture. It is a structural consequence of the framework’s
account of the observer. The observer is finite; the contexts are not finite in number; the
manifestations are products of identity and receiving realm; the effects are conveyed through
configurations. Together, these facts make exhaustive knowledge impossible (Book I, Chapter 27),
and they make every claim a claim at a certain strength, to be revised as the inquiry continues.
Remark 31.9 (The Humility Is the Recognition of a Structural Limit). The humility is the
recognition of a structural limit, not a denial that knowledge is real. The framework claims that
complete knowledge is impossible for a finite observer, and that partial knowledge, at a certain
strength, is what such an observer can achieve. The limit is structural: it belongs to the relation
between a finite observer and an identity, not to the identity itself, and not to the object of
knowledge.
Remark 31.10 (The Humility Is Not Despair). The humility is not despair. The framework claims
that the inquiry continues, and that each generation that works on the framework sees more
of what it is than the generation before. The humility is the recognition that the work is not
finished; it is not a denial that the work is worth doing.


31.7     Final Remarks
The book is offered as an independent philosophical system. Its worth is to be measured by its
coherence, by the discrimination its distinctions make possible, and by the strength of its own
arguments, and by nothing outside them.
   The framework is a description of the structure of being. The inquiry into how anything
ought to be, what is good, what is right, and what is worth pursuing belongs to ethics, value,
and normativity—distinct inquiries that the framework is designed to serve, not to replace.
   The reader who has followed the argument from beginning to end has seen the architecture
built, part by part, each part presupposing only what has come before. The reader who has
entered in the middle has seen one part in its context. Both readers have seen the same
architecture, and both are invited to continue the inquiry that the architecture makes possible.
31.8. A Conditional Architecture on a Core of Axioms                                          363


Remark 31.11 (The Book Is a Proposal). The book is a proposal, not a finished system. Its
worth is to be measured by what it makes possible: the questions it raises, the distinctions it
draws, the arguments it states. A reader who finds the proposal useful has found what the book
offers; a reader who does not has located a place where the inquiry continues.
Remark 31.12 (The Inquiry Continues). The inquiry continues. The book has stated what it has
established, what it has not established, and what it leaves open. It has also stated where the
whole architecture stands: the seven realms are levels of a created order, situated within the
Throne-Domain and grounded in God, who is not one of them (Book I, Principle 7.3); and the
light that runs between them is created light, whose source is God (Book I, Principle 12.2). The
structure is the book’s subject; the Ground is the one to whom the structure points. The open
questions are real questions, and they are invitations to the reader to continue the inquiry that
the framework makes possible. The book’s final word is not an answer but a question: what will
the reader make of the framework, and what will the framework make of the reader?


31.8     A Conditional Architecture on a Core of Axioms
A correction to the way the book may be read. A book that proceeds from principles to
consequences, with a table of contents that runs from the four columns to the divine ground,
invites the reading that it is a closed system: that its parts follow from one another, and that
to accept one is to accept all. That reading is not the book’s own, and the audit of Book I’s
Chapter E, together with the inherited core of Chapter ??, is the reason.
Principle 31.13 (The Book Is a Conditional Architecture). (A) The book is a conditional
architecture on a core of axioms. Its core consists of the thirteen commitments of Book I’s
Chapter E (C1–C13), listed in Chapter ??, together with a small number of stipulated definitions
that fix the vocabulary of the metaphysical concepts (metaphysical viability, transcendence,
creation and sustaining, the created modal space, providence and creaturely choice, and the four
kinds of necessity). Every other claim of the book is a consequence that follows from the core
and the definitions, or a hypothesis that can be revised without disturbing the core. The book
is not a closed system: it does not claim that its conclusions are necessary, nor that its list of
principles is complete, nor that its models are the only ones that fit the core.
    The principle is (A): it is adopted as a stipulation of the book’s self-description, and it is
stated at exactly that strength.
    The principle has three consequences, and each is worth stating.
    First consequence: conditionality is stated, not hidden. The dependency of each conclusion
on the core is stated in the chapters that establish the conclusion. A conclusion of the book
is asserted given the core commitments on which it depends, not unconditionally. Where the
dependency is a single core commitment, the reader can see that it is; where a conclusion has
several dependencies, the reader can see which.
    Second consequence: rejecting a commitment has a known cost. A reader who rejects a core
commitment has a map of what is affected: the conclusions that depend on the commitment
are placed in question, and the other conclusions remain. A reader who rejects a definition has
proposed another vocabulary. A reader who rejects a hypothesis loses only the hypothesis and
what is built on it. The cost of each rejection is stated with the commitment that is rejected.
    Third consequence: revision is expected. The book’s self-description as a conditional ar-
chitecture is a statement that the book is open to revision. The framework’s living character
(Chapter ??) is what makes revision possible; the framework’s core is what makes the revision
checkable. A reader who finds a claim unconvincing has located a place where the framework
can be revised, and the chapters that state the claim state what the revision would affect.
Remark 31.14 (The Core Is Not a Claim of Certainty). The core is not a claim of certainty. The
thirteen commitments of Book I are (A): they are adopted, not proved. Their justification is
364                        Chapter 31. Conclusion: The Architecture and Its Open Questions


coherence, explanatory power, and fruitfulness (Book I, Chapter 2); the framework’s honest
position is that these are the criteria by which the core is to be tested. A reader who rejects a
core commitment has a reason to reject the conclusions that depend on it; a reader who accepts
the core has a reason to accept the framework at the strength its arguments support.
Remark 31.15 (The Core Is Not the Only Possible Starting Point). The core is not the only
possible starting point. It is the set of commitments that the argument of the book cannot do
without; a different framework might start from a different core, and the comparison of the two
frameworks would be a different inquiry. The framework’s claim is that its own core is coherent,
explanatory, and fruitful, not that no other core could be.
Remark 31.16 (What the Core Is Not). The core is not a claim that its thirteen commitments
are certain, nor that they are the only possible starting point. It is the set of commitments
that the argument of the book cannot do without. The justification of each is its coherence, its
explanatory power, and its fruitfulness (Book I, Chapter 2); the book’s honest position is that
these are the criteria by which the core is to be tested.
Remark 31.17 (The Conditional Architecture Is Not a Weakness). The conditional architecture is
not a weakness. It is what the framework is: a structure whose foundations are visible, and whose
claims can be assessed at the strength the foundations support. A framework that presented
itself as unconditional would claim more than its arguments support; a framework that presented
itself as conditional is honest about what it is, and is assessable at the strength its arguments
support.
Remark 31.18 (The Conditional Architecture Is Not Relativism). The conditional architecture is
not relativism. It does not say that every framework is as good as every other; it says that the
framework’s claims are conditional on the framework’s core, and that the core is assessed by the
framework’s own criteria (coherence, explanatory power, fruitfulness). A different framework with
a different core would be assessed by its own criteria, and the comparison of the two frameworks
would be a different inquiry. The conditional architecture is the framework’s statement of its
own conditionality, not a denial of the possibility of assessment.

31.10      A Question for Reflection
Consider the three conclusions the book has established. Which of them do you find most
persuasive, and which least? What is the reason for your assessment? What does your answer
tell you about the relation between the framework’s arguments and its reader’s judgment?
    The answer is a model of the chapter’s account. The three conclusions are (T), (A), and
(D) relative to their premises; the reader’s assessment is an assessment of the premises and of
the arguments. A reader who accepts the premises should accept the conclusions; a reader who
rejects a premise has a reason to reject the conclusion that depends on it. The framework’s claim
is that the conclusions are coherent at the strength its arguments support; the reader’s task is to
assess them at that strength, and to decide what to make of them.
The horizon is open. The inquiry continues.

The Inherited Core: C1–C10

Purpose of the Appendix
This appendix states the ten core commitments that Book II inherits from Book I. The com-
mitments are stated in Book I’s Chapter 43 (the audit of the framework’s commitments), and
Book II’s body presupposes them in every chapter. The appendix collects them in one place, so
that the reader can see the core without interrupting the body’s metaphysical analysis.
    The appendix is a reference document, not a chapter with new arguments. Its claims are (A)
stipulated: they are the framework’s stipulations of its vocabulary and its commitments, and
they are stated at the strength that a stipulation can have. The reader who wishes to see the
arguments for the core commitments is directed to Book I’s Chapter 43. The reader who wishes
to see how Book II’s claims depend on the core commitments is directed to the map at the end
of this appendix, and to the Index of Cross-References to Book I at the end of the book.
       Note. Book II introduces three new ontological commitments (C11–C13) in Chapter 4
       (the bridge chapter). The three are derived from Book I’s framework, and they are
       not part of the inherited core. The appendix states the ten inherited commitments
       (C1–C10); the three new commitments are stated in Chapter 4, and they are marked
       (D) because they are derived from Book I’s framework.


.1      What a Core Commitment Is
A core commitment is a primitive commitment that is not derivable from the other entries of the
framework, and on which conclusions in at least two parts of Book I depend. The criteria are
stated in Book I’s Chapter 43, and they are restated here for the reader’s convenience.
     1. It is primitive. It is not derivable from the other entries of the framework. If it were
        derivable, it would be a consequence, not a core commitment.
     2. It is load-bearing. Conclusions in at least two parts of Book I depend on it. If only one
        part depended on it, it could be a local commitment, not a core commitment.
     3. It is either methodological or ontological. It is a claim about what counts as justification
        (methodological), or a claim about what there is (ontological). A claim that is neither is
        not core, however important it may be.
   The three criteria are the audit’s criteria, and the appendix uses them without rearranging
them. The reader who wishes to see the audit’s application to each of Book I’s claims is directed
to Book I’s Chapter 43.


.2      The Ten Core Commitments
The ten core commitments are stated one by one in the sections that follow. Each section gives
the commitment’s name, its statement in Book I, its status, what it presupposes in the order of
being, what depends on it in Book I, and what Book II does with it.
368                                                      Appendix . The Inherited Core: C1–C10


    The sections are grouped by family: the methodological commitments (C1, C2, C3), the
ontological commitments (C6, C7), and the structural-metaphysical commitments (C4, C5, C8,
C9, C10). The grouping is the appendix’s, and it is offered as an aid to the reader, not as a
claim about Book I’s structure.

.2.1   The Methodological Commitments
The methodological commitments are the commitments about what counts as justification and
what the framework claims. They are C1, C2, and C3.

C1: Finitude of the Subject
Definition .19 (C1: Finitude of the Subject). (A) Every cognizing subject is finite: at any time
it occupies finitely many contexts, and in any finite span it completes only finitely many acts of
reconstruction. (Book I, Principle 3.1)

     What it is. The commitment states that the subject who uses the framework is finite, and
that its finitude is a structural feature of its cognition. The finitude is not a contingent fact about
this or that subject; it is a condition of the framework’s being a framework for finite inquiry.
     What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that the subject is a being in the order
of reality, and that its finitude is a metaphysical feature of that being. The metaphysical
presupposition is the subject’s ontological structure: the subject is the kind of being that can
occupy contexts, complete acts, and be bounded in both. The presupposition is what Book II’s
analysis of substance (Chapter 5) and of the subject (Part V, if the book treats the subject) will
address.
     What depends on it in Book I. The impossibility of super-identity (Book I, Principle 27.1)
depends on C1; the theorem of unknownness (Book I, Theorem 19.1) depends on C1; the diagonal
argument (Book I, Chapter 27) depends on C1. The three are the most explicit dependencies,
and there are others.
     What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of the subject’s
finitude: what kind of being can be finite in the way C1 describes, and what the finitude requires
in the order of being. The statement is (D) relative to C1, and it is the subject of Book II’s
Part V (the context of the subject) and Part II (the fixed element of the subject, if the book
treats the subject).

C2: Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos
Definition .20 (C2: Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos). (A) Philosophy, as practiced
in Book I, describes the structure of what is: the relations among things, the rules that govern
those relations, and the frames in which both are posed. It does not, and by its method cannot,
establish the telos of what is. (Book I, Principle 4.1)

    What it is. The commitment states that the framework’s method is structural, not teleological:
the framework describes what is, not what it is for. The commitment is a boundary, and the
boundary is what makes the framework’s claims assessable at the strength they have.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that there is a distinction between
structure and telos—that the structure of what is is not the same as the end for which it is—and
that the distinction is real. The metaphysical presupposition is the distinction’s ontological
ground: structure is one thing, telos is another, and the two are related as the condition of
intelligibility is related to the good that the condition serves. The presupposition is what Book II’s
analysis of the good (Part VII, Chapter 25) and of the divine ground (Part VI) will address.
    What depends on it in Book I. The boundary of epistemology (Book I, Chapter 34) depends
on C2; the appendices (Book I, A, B, C) depend on C2, because they are offered as proposals
.2. The Ten Core Commitments                                                                  369


that do not establish telos; the book’s overall claim (Book I, Principle 43.1) depends on C2,
because the conditional architecture is a structure, not a telos.
   What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of the distinction:
what kind of being admits of the distinction between structure and telos, and what the distinction
requires in the order of being. The statement is (D) relative to C2, and it is the subject of
Book II’s Part VII (the metaphysical ground of the good) and Part VIII (the boundaries of
metaphysics, which inherit the boundaries of epistemology).

C3: Autonomy of Philosophical Justification
Definition .21 (C3: Autonomy of Philosophical Justification). (A) The validity of a philosophical
principle, within the domain of philosophy, does not depend on confirmation from outside
philosophy. (Book I, Principle 4.2)
    What it is. The commitment states that philosophical justification is internal to philosophy:
a philosophical principle is justified by philosophical argument, not by appeal to revelation,
authority, or empirical confirmation. The commitment is a methodological boundary, and it is
the condition of the framework’s claim to be a work of philosophy.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that philosophy has a domain of its
own, with standards of justification that are not reducible to the standards of other domains.
The metaphysical presupposition is the reality of the domain distinction: the domains are not
conventions, but structures of reality, each with its own standards. The presupposition is what
Book II’s analysis of the categories (Part II, Chapter 7) and of the domains (Part VIII) will
address.
    What depends on it in Book I. The framework’s claim to be philosophy (Book I, Chapter 34)
depends on C3; the framework’s silence on revelation’s truth (Book I, §34.6) depends on C3; the
framework’s use of empirical evidence as coherence test only (Book I, Chapter 17, and elsewhere)
depends on C3.
    What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of the domain
distinction: what kind of being admits of domains with their own standards, and what the
domains require in the order of being. The statement is (D) relative to C3, and it is the subject
of Book II’s Part II (the categories, which are the structure of the domains) and Part VIII (the
boundaries of metaphysics, which inherit the boundaries of epistemology).

.2.2   The Ontological Commitments
The ontological commitments are the commitments about what there is. They are C6 and C7.

C6: Openness of Relations
Definition .22 (C6: Openness of Relations). (A) For every cognitive context C and every
manifestation m that an identity has in C, there is a cognitive context C ′ in which m is itself
a fixed element, related by fluid elements and dynamics that are not available in C. (Book I,
Definition 11.1)
    What it is. The commitment states that every manifestation can become a fixed element of a
further context—that the process of re-contextualization never terminates. The commitment is
the first of the three load-bearing premises of Book I’s Part V (Book I, §27.8), and it is what
makes the infinity of contexts (Book I, Principle 11.1) and the impossibility of super-identity
(Book I, Principle 27.1) possible.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that contexts are not closed, and that
the process of contextualization is structurally open. The metaphysical presupposition is the
structure of context: what a context is, why it is open, and what the openness requires in the
order of being. The presupposition is what Book II’s analysis of the context (Part V) will address.
370                                                    Appendix . The Inherited Core: C1–C10


    What depends on it in Book I. The infinity of contexts (Book I, Principle 11.1) depends on
C6; the impossibility of super-identity (Book I, Principle 27.1) depends on C6; the diagonal
argument (Book I, Chapter 27) depends on C6.
    What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of the context:
what a context is, why it is open, and what the openness requires in the order of being. The
statement is (D) relative to C6, and it is the subject of Book II’s Part V (the context of
metaphysics).

C7: Trans-Categorical Character of Light
Definition .23 (C7: Trans-Categorical Character of Light). (A) Light goes beyond the existing
philosophical categories—substance, accident, process, relation. A new category is needed: the
trans-categorical substance. (Book I, Principle 15.1)

    What it is. The commitment states that light is not a substance, an accident, a process, or
a relation, but the condition of possibility of the distinction among them. The commitment is
Book I’s most original claim about light, and it is what distinguishes the framework’s account of
light from the physical and the metaphysical traditions.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that the categories of being are not
exhaustive, and that there is a kind of being—the trans-categorical—that precedes the categories.
The metaphysical presupposition is the structure of the categories themselves: what a category is,
what the categories are, and what the trans-categorical is. The presupposition is what Book II’s
analysis of the categories (Part II) and of causation (Part III) will address.
    What depends on it in Book I. The account of light (Book I, Part III) depends on C7; the
account of expression (Book I, Part VI) depends on C7; the trans-categorical triad (Book II,
C13, derived in Chapter 4) depends on C7.
    What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of the trans-
categorical: what kind of being is trans-categorical, how the trans-categorical relates to the
categories, and what the trans-categorical requires in the order of being. The statement is (D)
relative to C7, and it is the subject of Book II’s Part II (the categories) and Part III (the fluid
elements, where light is analyzed as the trans-categorical medium).

.2.3   The Structural-Metaphysical Commitments
The structural-metaphysical commitments are the commitments about how identity and manifes-
tation work. They are C4, C5, C8, C9, and C10.

C4: Identity Rigidity and Conservation
Definition .24 (C4: Identity Rigidity and Conservation). (A) Identity is rigid—it admits of
no degrees—and identity is conserved—it is invariant under all temporal transformations of its
manifestations. (Book I, Principles 12.1 and 12.2)

    What it is. The commitment states that identity is rigid and conserved: the manifestations
may vary, but the identity does not. The commitment is the foundation of Book I’s account of
persistence (Book I, Chapter 12), and it is what makes the account of death (Book I, Chapter 33)
possible.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that identity and manifestation are
distinct, and that the distinction is metaphysically real. The metaphysical presupposition is
the structure of persistence: what identity is, what manifestation is, and what the distinction
between them requires in the order of being. The presupposition is what Book II’s analysis of
substance and essence (Part II) will address.
.2. The Ten Core Commitments                                                                    371


    What depends on it in Book I. The account of death (Book I, Chapter 33) depends on C4;
the thread theorem (Book I, Theorem 12.1) depends on C4; the account of personal identity
(Book I, §12.11) depends on C4.
    What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of persistence:
what identity is, what manifestation is, and what the distinction between them requires in the
order of being. The statement is (D) relative to C4, and it is the subject of Book II’s Part II
(the fixed elements of metaphysics) and Part VII (the integration, where viability measures the
relation between identity and manifestation).

C5: Non-Duplicability
Definition .25 (C5: Non-Duplicability). (A) Identity cannot be copied. Signatures, pseudo-
identities, and information can be duplicated; identity cannot. A copy of a system reproduces its
signature. (Book I, Principle 12.3)

    What it is. The commitment states that identity is not duplicable: the copy of a system
reproduces the signature, not the identity. The commitment is the foundation of Book I’s
account of non-duplicability (Book I, Chapter 12), and it is what makes the verdicts on cloning,
teleportation, and fission possible.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that identity is more than its signature,
and that the more is primitive thisness. The metaphysical presupposition is the structure of
thisness: what primitive thisness is, what it requires in the order of being, and how it relates to
the signature. The presupposition is what Book II’s analysis of identity and thisness (Part II,
Chapter 7) will address.
    What depends on it in Book I. The verdicts on cloning, teleportation, and fission (Book I,
§12.9) depend on C5; the argument from the logic of numerical identity (Book I, §12.8) depends
on C5; the dilemma from the identity of indiscernibles (Book I, §12.9) depends on C5.
    What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of thisness: what
primitive thisness is, what it requires in the order of being, and how it relates to the signature.
The statement is (D) relative to C5, and it is the subject of Book II’s Part II (the fixed elements,
Chapter 7 on identity and thisness).

C8: Category-Relative Predication
Definition .26 (C8: Category-Relative Predication). (A) Epistemic predicates such as rigidity,
dynamism, unity, multiplicity, temporality, and atemporality are not absolute. They are defined
relative to a context and to a respect. (Book I, Principle 25.1)

    What it is. The commitment states that predicates are not absolute, but relative: the same
predicate can be true of the same thing relative to one context and false relative to another,
and the relativity is not a defect but a structural feature. The commitment is what resolves the
tensions of Book I’s Part IV (Book I, Chapters 25–26), and it is what makes the framework’s
claims coherent.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that the contexts are real (C6), and that
the respects are real. The metaphysical presupposition is the structure of the respects: what a
respect is, what it requires in the order of being, and how the respects relate to the contexts. The
presupposition is what Book II’s analysis of the categories (Part II) and of the context (Part V)
will address.
    What depends on it in Book I. The resolutions of Part IV (Book I, Chapters 25–26) depend
on C8; the distinction between the structural and the ontological (Book I, Principle 5.1) depends
on C8 in its application; the framework’s account of manifestation (Book I, Chapter 13) depends
on C8.
372                                                    Appendix . The Inherited Core: C1–C10


   What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of the respects:
what a respect is, what it requires in the order of being, and how the respects relate to the
contexts. The statement is (D) relative to C8, and it is the subject of Book II’s Part II (the
categories) and Part V (the context of metaphysics).

C9: Configuration-Dependence
Definition .27 (C9: Configuration-Dependence). (A) The manifestation of an identity in a
context depends on what passes through the epistemic light of the context, and this in turn
depends on the whole configuration of the context. (Book I, Definition 29.1)

    What it is. The commitment states that manifestation depends on the configuration of the
context: the same identity, in the same context, can manifest differently as the configuration
of the context changes. The commitment is what deepens Book I’s account of manifestation
(Book I, Chapter 27), and it is what makes the limits of super-identity structural.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that the context is real, that its configu-
ration is real, and that the manifestation depends on both. The metaphysical presupposition
is the structure of the context’s configuration: what a configuration is, what it requires in the
order of being, and how it relates to the manifestation. The presupposition is what Book II’s
analysis of the context (Part V) and of manifestation (Part III) will address.
    What depends on it in Book I. The strengthening of the impossibility of super-identity (Book I,
Chapter 29) depends on C9; the account of the cost of cognition (Book I, Chapter 39) depends
on C9; the structural ground of the singularity (Book I, §37.7) depends on C9.
    What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of the context’s
configuration: what a configuration is, what it requires in the order of being, and how it relates
to the manifestation. The statement is (D) relative to C9, and it is the subject of Book II’s
Part III (the fluid elements) and Part V (the context of metaphysics).

C10: Expression as Structural Necessity
Definition .28 (C10: Expression as Structural Necessity). (A) Every identity, by its very nature,
tends toward expression. Expression is not a contingent choice but a structural necessity. (Book I,
Principle 38.1)

    What it is. The commitment states that expression is intrinsic to identity: an identity that
never expressed itself would not be an identity. The commitment is the dynamical engine of
Book I’s framework (Book I, Chapter 38), and it is what makes Book I’s Part VI possible.
    What it presupposes. The commitment presupposes that identity and expression are internally
related, and that the relation is a metaphysical necessity. The metaphysical presupposition is
the structure of expression: what expression is, what it requires in the order of being, and how
the expression relates to the identity that expresses itself. The presupposition is what Book II’s
analysis of causation (Part III) and of the good (Part VII) will address.
    What depends on it in Book I. Part VI (the arguments) depends on C10; the account of time
(Book I, Chapter 32) depends on C10; the account of death (Book I, Chapter 33) depends on
C10.
    What Book II will do with it. Book II will state the metaphysical structure of expression:
what expression is, what it requires in the order of being, and how the expression relates to
the identity. The statement is (D) relative to C10, and it is the subject of Book II’s Part III
(the fluid elements, where causation is analyzed as the ground of expression) and Part VII (the
integration, where expression is measured by viability).
.3. The Structure of the Core                                                               373


.3     The Structure of the Core
The ten commitments are not a list; they are a structure, and the present section states the
structure.

.3.1   The Three Families
The ten commitments fall into three families.

         Family               Entries                   What it concerns
         Methodological       C1, C2, C3                What counts as justification;
                                                        what the framework claims
         Ontological          C6, C7                    What there is; the structure
                                                        of the contexts and the trans-
                                                        categorical
         Structural-          C4, C5, C8, C9, C10       How identity and manifesta-
         metaphysical                                   tion work; persistence, this-
                                                        ness, expression, predication,
                                                        configuration

    The three families are not arbitrary. They correspond to the three questions that the core
answers.
    The methodological family answers: what is the framework’s method, and what does it claim?
The three commitments (C1, C2, C3) state the framework’s method (structural description),
its boundary (silence on telos), and its autonomy (justification is internal to philosophy). The
family is what makes the framework a philosophical work, not a theological or empirical one.
    The ontological family answers: what is there? The two commitments (C6, C7) state the
framework’s ontology of the contexts: the openness of the contexts (C6), the trans-categorical
character of light (C7). The family is what makes the framework a metaphysics, not only an
epistemology.
    The structural-metaphysical family answers: how does identity work? The five commitments
(C4, C5, C8, C9, C10) state the framework’s account of identity: rigidity and conservation
(C4), non-duplicability (C5), category-relative predication (C8), configuration-dependence (C9),
expression (C10). The family is what makes the framework’s account of identity and manifestation
coherent, and it is the family that Book II’s Parts II and III will most directly address.

The ten commitments are the load-bearing part of Book I, and Book II’s parts depend on them.
The dependency is stated in the following table.
