marks the dependency.


.4    What the Core Does Not Include
The ten commitments are the core, but they are not the whole of Book I’s inheritance. The
present section states what the core does not include, so that the reader knows what Book II
inherits beyond the core.
    The definitions. Book I’s Chapter 43 identified twenty-four definitions, each of which is (A)
in the sense of stipulated. The definitions are not core, because they fix vocabulary rather than
make substantive claims. Book II inherits the definitions and uses them where it needs them;
the definitions are the vocabulary of the book, not its foundations.
    The consequences. Book I’s Chapter 43 identified fourteen consequences, each of which follows
from the core and the definitions by a one-line derivation. The consequences are (T) after the
audit. Book II inherits the consequences and uses them where it needs them; the consequences
are the framework’s arguments, not its foundations.
    The hypotheses. Book I’s Chapter 43 identified twelve hypotheses, each of which is a
substantive claim whose rejection would leave the core intact. The hypotheses are (E). Book II
inherits the hypotheses and uses them where it needs them; the hypotheses are the framework’s
modelling assumptions, not its foundations.
    The distinction between the core and the rest of the inheritance is the audit’s principal result,
and the appendix states it. The reader who wishes to see the audit’s full application is directed
to Book I’s Chapter 43.


.5    The Core and Book II’s Conditional Architecture
The core is the foundation of Book II’s conditional architecture. The present section states the
architecture, in the form that the Preface and Chapter 1 introduced.

Principle .29 (Book II Is a Conditional Metaphysics on the Inherited Core). (A) Book II is a
conditional metaphysics on the core of Book I. Its core is the ten commitments C1–C10; its body
is the analyses that the core requires; its (D) claims are the consequents of the core that the
analyses establish; and its (T), (E), (Q), and (S) claims are the analyses themselves, offered at
.6. What This Appendix Does Not Establish                                                        375


the strength that the book’s arguments support. The book is not a closed system: it does not
claim that its conclusions are necessary, nor that its list of principles is complete, nor that its
models are the only ones that fit the core.

    The principle is (A) because it is the book’s own statement of its architecture. Its justification
is the book’s practice: the (D) claims are the majority, the (T) claims are the analyses, and the
(E), (Q), and (S) claims are the estimates, questions, and speculations that the analyses produce.
The principle makes the architecture explicit, so that the reader knows what the book claims
and what it does not.
    The architecture’s three consequences. The architecture has three consequences, and the
reader is entitled to hold the book to each of them.

     1. The conditionality is stated, not hidden. The dependency of the book’s claims on the core
        is stated in the present appendix, in the Index of Cross-References to Book I, and in the
        (D) label of each claim. A reader who rejects a core commitment knows which (D) claims
        fall with it.

     2. The revision is expected. The book’s (E) claims are estimates, its (Q) claims are open
        questions, and its (S) claims are speculations. The book invites the reader to revise them,
        and it states the criteria by which the revisions are to be assessed.

     3. The core is open to challenge. The book does not claim that the core is beyond challenge.
        A reader who rejects a core commitment has a reason to reject the (D) claims that depend
        on it, and the book states the dependency so that the reader knows what falls with the
        rejection.

   The three consequences are the book’s contract with the reader. The book is offered in the
hope that the contract is honored, and that the inquiry continues.


.6      What This Appendix Does Not Establish
Four things that a reader might expect from this appendix are deliberately deferred.
    First, the appendix does not reargue the audit of Book I’s Chapter 43. It states the ten core
entries, but it does not argue that the audit is correct; the audit’s argument is Book I’s, and the
appendix takes it as given. The reader who wishes to challenge the audit is directed to Book I’s
Chapter 43, and to the appendix’s statement of the core’s families and relations.
    Second, the appendix does not analyze the metaphysical presuppositions of the core entries.
It states, for each entry, what it presupposes in the order of being, but the analysis of the
presupposition is the subject of Book II’s later parts. The reader who expects the analysis in
this appendix has misread the appendix’s scope; the analysis begins in Part II.
    Third, the appendix does not state the (D) claims that the core requires. The (D) claims
are stated in the chapters that give the analyses; the appendix states the core on which the (D)
claims depend, and it states the map of Book II’s parts to the core entries, but it does not state
the claims themselves. The reader who expects the claims in this appendix has misread the
appendix’s scope; the claims are stated in Parts II to VII.
    Fourth, the appendix does not settle the question of whether the core is exhaustive. It states
the ten entries that Book I’s Chapter 43 identified; whether an eleventh entry is needed, or
whether one of the ten can be derived, is a question the appendix leaves open. The question is
marked (Q) in the appendix’s status table, and it is addressed, where it can be, in Book II’s
Part VIII.

.8    A Question for Reflection
Consider a framework you know well—a philosophical system, a scientific theory, a legal code.
What are its core commitments? If you were to identify the entries that the framework cannot
do without, which would you choose? What does each commitment presuppose in the order of
being? And if you were to state the framework’s conditional architecture—the map of its parts
to its core—what would the map look like?
    The answer is a model of the appendix’s task. Book II is the metaphysics of a framework,
and the framework’s core is the ten commitments. The appendix’s task is to state the core, so
that the reader can see what the body of Book II presupposes. The model is offered as a way of
seeing the book’s project, not as a proof of its claims.

With this appendix, the inherited core is stated. The body of Book II begins with Chapter 5 (Sub-
stance), and the chapters that follow develop the derivation of the ontology from the epistemology.
The reader who wishes to see the core in its own place is directed to Book I’s Chapter 43; the
reader who wishes to see how Book II depends on the core is directed to the map in §.3 and to
the Index of Cross-References to Book I.

Mapping Table: Book I to Book II

Purpose of the Appendix
This appendix provides a single table that maps the concepts of Book I to the derived concepts
of Book II. The table’s purpose is to make the derivation visible at a glance: for each concept of
Book I, it shows the corresponding concept of Book II and the kind of relation between them.
The reader who wishes to see the derivation in detail is directed to the chapters that state it; the
reader who wishes to see it in summary is directed to this appendix.
    The appendix is a reference document, not a chapter with new arguments. Its claims are
(A) stipulated: they are the framework’s summary of the derivations that the chapters give, and
they are stated at the strength that a summary can have.

      Note. The mapping is not a claim of identity. Book I’s concept and Book II’s derived
      concept are not the same concept; they are related as the analytical role is related to
      its metaphysical condition. The table states the relation, not an identity. The reader
      who takes the mapping as a claim of identity has misread the appendix; the reader
      who takes it as a summary of the derivation has read it correctly.


.9    The Method of Mapping
The mapping uses three kinds of relation between Book I’s concepts and Book II’s concepts.
    Derivation. Book II’s concept is derived from Book I’s concept by a transcendental argument:
the Book I concept is the analytical role, and the Book II concept is the metaphysical condition
that the role presupposes. The derivation is marked (D) in the chapters, and it is the principal
kind of relation in the mapping.
    Extension. Book II’s concept extends Book I’s concept to a domain that Book I did not treat.
The extension is marked (D) when it is derived from Book I’s framework, and (E) when it is a
structural estimate. The extension is the second kind of relation, and it is used for concepts that
Book I introduced but did not develop.
    Correspondence. Book II’s concept corresponds to Book I’s concept without being derived
from it or extending it. The correspondence is marked (E) when it is a structural parallel, and
(A) when it is a stipulated analogy. The correspondence is the third kind of relation, and it is
used for concepts that are related by analogy rather than by derivation.
    The three relations are stated in the table’s right-hand column, and the reader can see, at a
glance, which kind of relation each mapping is.

.12      What the Appendix Does Not Do
Three things that a reader might expect from this appendix are deliberately deferred.
    First, the appendix does not reargue the derivations. It states the mapping, not the arguments;
the arguments are in the chapters. The reader who wishes to see the derivation in detail is
directed to the chapter that states it.
    Second, the appendix does not claim that the mapping is exhaustive. It maps the main
concepts of Book I to the main derived concepts of Book II; it does not map every concept, and
it does not claim that every concept of Book II has a counterpart in Book I. The mapping is a
summary, not a complete inventory.
    Third, the appendix does not settle the question of whether the mapping is the only possible
one. It states the mapping that the framework uses; a different framework might map the
concepts differently, and the comparison of the two mappings would be a different inquiry.

.14     A Question for Reflection
Consider a concept you know well from one domain—a scientific theory, a legal system, a
philosophical framework. What is the corresponding concept in another domain? Is the relation
one of derivation, extension, or correspondence? And if you were to map the two domains, what
would the map look like?
     The answer is a model of the appendix’s task. The appendix maps Book I’s concepts to
Book II’s derived concepts, and it states the kind of relation between them. The reader who
can state, for a concept he knows, what the corresponding concept in another domain is and
what kind of relation holds between them, has understood the appendix’s method; the reader
who cannot has found a place where the method is most difficult, and is invited to develop the
difficulty further.

With this appendix, the mapping from Book I to Book II is stated. The reader who wishes to see
the derivation in detail is directed to the chapters that state it; the reader who wishes to see the
core on which the derivation rests is directed to Appendix A and to Book I’s Chapter 43.

Bibliography

A Note on Citation
Citations in the body of this book are given in the text by author and title, with the passage
cited where the passage matters. The entries below are arranged by chapter, and each entry
is assigned a code of the form [B2-##-m], where ## is the chapter number of Book II and m is
the number of the source within that chapter. The same source cited in more than one chapter
receives a distinct code in each chapter, so that the reader can locate every citation in its chapter
context.
    References to Book I are given by the code [D##-m], where ## is the chapter number of Book I
and m is the number of the source or principle within that chapter. The Index of Cross-References
to Book I collects all such references in one place.
    The book cites three kinds of source. The first are the works that are used to make or assess a
claim in the argument: the classical, medieval, and modern philosophical works whose arguments
the book engages. The second are the Qur’anic verses that are cited as structural parallels, in the
sense fixed in the Preface: they are cited because they describe a structure that the framework
also describes, not because the framework’s structure is derived from them. The third are the
works that appear only in the coherence tests (Chapter ??), and they are marked as such.
    The comparative treatment of the philosophical traditions discussed in the Preface—Ibn Sina,
Suhrawardi, Ibn Arabi, Mulla Sadra, Plato and Plotinus, Proclus, Kant and Hegel, Whitehead,
the Upanishads and Buddhism, and Kashmir Shaivism—is given in a separate treatise, to be
published independently. The present bibliography lists only the works cited in this volume; the
separate treatise has its own bibliography, and its citations are not repeated here.

 A Note on the Separate Treatise
 The comparative treatment of the philosophical traditions is given in a separate treatise, Dialogues
 with the Philosophical Traditions, to be published independently. The separate treatise has its
 own bibliography, covering the primary and secondary sources for the comparative treatment.
     The two bibliographies are distinct. The present bibliography records the works cited in this
 volume; the separate treatise’s bibliography records the works cited in the comparative treatment.
 The reason for the separation is stated in the Preface: a comparison of structures is a different
 genre from a systematic reconstruction, and keeping them in one volume would encourage a
 misreading of the framework’s authority. The present volume’s arguments do not depend on the
 separate treatise, and the separate treatise presupposes the present volume’s framework.

Glossary of Metaphysical Terms

This glossary collects the technical terms that Book II defines or uses in a technical sense. Each
entry gives the term, a brief definition, and the place in Book II (or, where marked, in Book I)
where the term is fixed. The entries are arranged alphabetically. Where a term is defined in
Book I and used without redefinition in Book II, the entry points to the definition in Book I.


A
Accident A feature that does not belong to the essence of an identity, and that may vary among
     the manifestations of the identity without altering the essence’s determination. (Def. 5.2;
     Def. 22.25)

Actualization The realization of a possibility in a realm, according to the realm’s capacity.
    (Chapter 24, §3; Chapter 15, §7)

Analysis, analytical The reading of a claim or concept in terms of roles, as distinct from the
    ontological content that fills those roles. (Pr. 2.8; Book I, Pr. 1.1)

Architecture, conditional The structure of Book II as a body of claims that depend on a
    core of axioms inherited from Book I, rather than a closed deductive system. (Pr. 31.13)

Autonomy of philosophical justification The principle that the validity of a philosophical
    principle, within the domain of philosophy, does not depend on confirmation from outside
    philosophy. (Pr. 30.8; Book I, Pr. 41.1; C10)


B
Barzakhic, as category The mode of existence whose being is the passage between two other
    modes—not a being that passes, but the passage itself, considered as a level of being.
    (Def. 18.1)

Barzakhic realm An independently real ontological level whose mode of existence includes
    mediating, transforming, or regulating relations between other realms. (Book I, Def. 8.1)

Boundary The limit of the framework’s domain, fixed by the three principles of the boundary
    (autonomy, internal definition, non-export of meaning). (Chapter 30, §5)


C
Cause What produces an effect; the relatum of the causal relation from which the transfer
    proceeds. (Def. 9.2)

Causation The real transfer of effect from a cause to an effect through a medium. (Def. 9.1)
394                                                             Glossary of Metaphysical Terms


Cognitive context The frame in which something is cognized: the question asked, the elements
    held fixed, the rule applied, and the standpoint from which the partition into fixed and
    fluid is made. (Book I, Def. 10.1; recalled at Def. 21.6)
Condition, condition-conditioned The relation between a structural condition and what it
    makes possible; the relation that the analogical use of “substance” in Book I’s Pr. 12.1 was
    pointing at. (Pr. 11.1)
Context The frame in which the fixed elements, fluid elements, and governing dynamics take
    their specific content. (Book I, Def. 2.4; Def. 2.5 for metaphysical inquiry)
Context of the whole The encompassing order in which all the realms stand; not a realm,
    but the order of the realms, and the condition of their being together. (Def. 20.3)
Contingency The modal status of what could be otherwise; distinct from createdness, which
    concerns the grounding of a thing’s being, not its modal status. (Chapter 28, §6; Re-
    marks 28.13–28.14)
Creation The act by which God gives being to the created order; not a change in God, and not
    a change in a pre-existing material. (Def. 27.4)
Creaturely choice The selection by which a creature actualizes one possibility rather than
    another within the created modal space; the selection is the creature’s own, not determined
    by God’s knowledge. (Def. 29.16)


D
Dependent claim, (D) A claim whose truth depends on a specific principle, definition, or
    commitment of Book I, and whose argument in Book II consists in showing the dependency.
    (Def. 3.10; Pr. 3.11)
Disposition A power or tendency of a thing to manifest in a certain way; a candidate account
    of law and causation. (Chapter 9, §4; Chapter 13, §4)
Dynamic, governing The rule that explains how the fluid elements of an inquiry affect the
    fixed elements; the third column of the framework. (Def. 2.4; Book I, Def. 2.3)


E
Effect What a cause produces; the relatum of the causal relation toward which the transfer
     proceeds. (Def. 9.2)
Element, fixed An entity held invariant in an explanation of how things stand; in Book II,
    an entity, kind, or category held invariant in an explanation of the conditions of being.
    (Book I, Def. 2.1; Def. 2.2)
Element, fluid What conveys effect between fixed elements in an explanation; in Book II, what
    conveys the effect of conditions of being between fixed elements. (Book I, Def. 2.2; Def. 2.3)
Essence The constitutive what of a thing: the determination that makes the thing the kind of
    thing it is, and that grounds the features the thing cannot lose without ceasing to be the
    thing it is. (Def. 6.1; recalled at Def. 22.3)
Essential and accidental properties An essential property belongs to the essence of a thing
     and cannot be lost without the thing ceasing to be the thing it is; an accidental property
     does not belong to the essence and can be lost. (Def. 6.2)
Glossary of Metaphysical Terms                                                               395


Essentialism The thesis that things have essences: for every thing that belongs to a kind, there
     is a constitutive what that makes the thing the kind of thing it is. (Pr. 6.4)

Estimate, (E) A claim offered as approximate and subject to revision; typically a structural
     estimate, or a modelling assumption whose rejection would leave the core of the framework
     intact. (Def. 3.7)

Existential context The setting in which a manifestation is realized, with the capacity and
     the constraints of that setting; fixed by the identity and the receiving setting, not by the
     question. (Book I, Def. 10.2; Def. 17.2; recalled at Def. 21.7)


F
Fidelity The first component of viability: the extent to which the manifestation preserves
     the essential determination of the identity, in the mode that the receiving realm permits.
     (Chapter 21, §5; Pr. 22.13 for essence; Pr. 23.13 for causation; Pr. 24.12 for modality)

Four columns The four analytical roles that any complete explanation must assign: fixed
    elements, fluid elements, governing dynamics, context. (Book I, Pr. 3.1; Book II, Defs. 2.2–
    2.5)


G
Governing dynamics The rule that explains how the fluid elements of an inquiry affect the
    fixed elements; the third column of the framework. (Book I, Def. 2.3; Def. 2.4)

Grounding The relation by which one thing depends on another for its being, intelligibility, or
    relations; the relation of the created order to God, and of the necessary within the modal
    space to its structure. (Chapter 26; Chapter 15, §6)


H
Haecceity See Thisness.

Hub of Decree The barzakhic realm whose mode of existence is the apportioning of the measure
    from unity to form. (Book I, Def. 8.4; Chapter 5, §8.5)

Hub of Realization The barzakhic realm whose mode of existence is the actualization of
    meaning into matter. (Book I, Def. 8.6; Chapter 5, §8.7)

Hub of Signification The barzakhic realm whose mode of existence is the signification of form
    into meaning. (Book I, Def. 8.5; Chapter 5, §8.6)


I
Identity Invariance under a class of allowable transformations of manifestations. (Book I,
     Def. 9.1)

Identity conservation The principle that identity is invariant under all temporal transforma-
     tions of its manifestations. (Book I, Pr. 9.5; C5)

Internal definition The principle that the concepts of the framework are defined and justified
     within its own system, from its premises. (Pr. 30.9)
396                                                               Glossary of Metaphysical Terms


L
Law The structural pattern that grounds the regularity, necessity, and formality of a realm’s
    rules. (Def. 13.1)

Light, as metaphysical medium The structural condition under which causation and relation
     can function as the fluid element of an explanation; not a substance, not a relation, not
     a process, not an accident, but the condition of possibility of these. (Def. 11.2; Book I,
     Pr. 12.1; C7)

Logical necessity The modal status of a proposition that is true in virtue of its logical form
     alone; the necessity is grounded in the form of the proposition, not in what the world is
     like. (Def. 14.4)


M
Manifestation The contextually realized appearance of an identity in a receiving realm. (Book I,
    Def. 10.1)

Meaning is not exported The principle that the use of a word or concept in another domain
    does not determine its metaphysical sense here. (Pr. 30.10)

Mediation The structural regulation, conditioning, or transformation of a relation between two
    realms by a realm whose mode of existence includes that function. (Book I, Def. 8.2)

Mediation vs. itinerary The distinction between the hub’s presence as a condition and the
    identity’s traversal of the hub; mediation does not require passage. (Chapter 19, §6)

Metaphysical claim A claim about the conditions of possibility of what is; it asserts that, for
    some domain of beings or for being as such, a certain structure must obtain. (Pr. 3.1)

Metaphysical inquiry A form of explanatory cognition: it seeks to understand how some
    things stand to one another, and its aim is to make the standing intelligible. (Pr. 2.1)

Metaphysical necessity The modal status of a proposition, state of affairs, or thing that is
    necessary in virtue of essence; the necessity is grounded in essence, not in law and not in
    form alone. (Def. 14.5)

Metaphysical viability The structural character of the relation between an identity and its
    manifestations in an existential context (a realm), in three respects: fidelity, sustainability,
    and recoverability. (Def. 21.14)

Metaphysics of viability The account of the conditions under which an identity can be viable
    in the realms in which it is manifested. (Def. 25.4)

Modal space, Ω The stratified structure of possible configurations of essences and laws. (Book I,
   Pr. 37.1; C12; Pr. 15.1; Pr. 15.2 for stratification)

Modality The structure of the possible, the actual, and the necessary. (Def. 14.1; recalled at
   Def. 24.3)


N
Natural necessity The modal status of a proposition or state of affairs that is necessary in
    virtue of the laws of nature; the necessity is grounded in law, not in essence and not in
    form alone. (Def. 14.7)
Glossary of Metaphysical Terms                                                                397


Necessity The modal status of a proposition, state of affairs, or thing that cannot be otherwise;
    the sense of the “cannot” is fixed by the kind of necessity in question. (Def. 14.2)

Non-duplicability The principle that identity cannot be copied; signatures, pseudo-identities,
    and information can be duplicated, but identity cannot. (Book I, Pr. 9.6; C6)

Non-passage The principle that the presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm does not
    require that the identity pass existentially through every realm that lies between. (Pr. 19.3)

Normative necessity The modal status of a proposition or state of affairs that is necessary in
    virtue of the structure of the good; the necessity is grounded in the good. (Def. 14.9)


O
Ontological dependence The relation by which one thing depends on another for its being,
    in such a way that the second would not be if the first were not. (Chapter 26; Pr. 26.10)

Open question, (Q) A philosophical question that has no final answer yet, but can be examined
    within the system; it marks a place where the framework’s principles raise a question that
    the framework does not settle. (Def. 3.8)


P
Passage The existential traversal of a realm by an identity: the identity is present in the realm
     as such, in the course of moving from its realm of origin to a lower realm. (Def. 19.6)

Possibility The modal status of what could be; the complement of the necessary, in the sense
     that what is not necessary is possible (when the possibility is not excluded by another
     modal status). (Def. 14.3)

Presence The structural relation in which an identity is realized, or its effect is realized, in a
    realm; it does not require that the identity have been present in the intermediate realms.
    (Def. 19.7; Pr. 19.11)

Providence The governance of the created order by God; the act by which God orders the
    created order toward the ends that God wills, without determining the creature’s selection
    within the created modal space. (Def. 29.4)


R
Realm An independently real mode of existence within which a specific mode of manifestation,
    activity, and interaction is possible. (Book I, Def. 7.1)

Realm as context A mode of existence with a determinate capacity: a structural range of
    what can appear in it and what cannot; not a container (a “where” things are), but a
    condition (a “how” things can be). (Def. 17.1)

Realm as existential context The realm considered as the condition of the manifestation’s
    realization. (Def. 17.2)

Recoverability The third component of viability: the condition under which the identity
    retains its structural capacity to manifest in the realm; the singularity at which restoring a
    manifestation would cost more than producing a new one has not been crossed. (Chapter 21,
    §5; Pr. 22.21 for essence; Pr. 23.21 for causation; Pr. 24.20 for modality)
398                                                              Glossary of Metaphysical Terms


Relation The real connection between two or more terms, distinct from the terms themselves
     and distinct from the transfer of effect that causation names. (Def. 10.1)

Relatum A term of a relation; the terms that the relation connects. (Def. 10.2)

Rule A formulation of what must be the case in a realm; a law is the structural pattern that
    the formulation formulates. (Def. 13.2)


S
Signature The structural description of a thing’s invariance: what can be read off, compared,
     recorded, and reproduced about the pattern. (Book I, Def. 9.4; Def. 7.2)

Speculation, (S) A speculative extension, flagged for caution; the framework does not claim
    that the speculation is true, only that it follows naturally from the framework’s structure
    and is worth investigating. (Def. 3.9)

Stratification of Ω The internal structure of the modal space, whose strata are the four kinds
     of necessity: logical, metaphysical, natural, normative. (Pr. 15.2)

Substance The metaphysical ground of a thing’s being the same one through change, and of
    its being the subject of its properties. (Def. 5.1)

Sustaining The act by which God gives being to the created order at every moment; not a
     series of separate acts over time, but the continuous dependence of the created order on
     God. (Def. 27.8)

Sustainability The second component of viability: the condition under which the cost of
     producing and maintaining the manifestation does not exceed what the receiving realm
     can bear. (Chapter 21, §5; Pr. 22.17 for essence; Pr. 23.17 for causation; Pr. 24.16 for
     modality)


T
Thisness The non-qualitative individuating feature that makes a thing the particular thing it
    is, and that cannot be shared by another thing. (Def. 7.1)

Thisness, primitive The doctrine that thisness is primitive and non-qualitative: it is not
    derived from the thing’s qualitative features, and it is not a species of the qualitative.
    (Pr. 7.4)

Thisness and signature The distinction between the non-qualitative individuation that the
    signature cannot capture and the structural description of invariance that can be read off
    and compared. (Def. 7.2)

Transcendence The relation of ontological dependence of the created order on God; the created
    order depends on God for its being, its intelligibility, and its relations; God does not depend
    on the created order for anything. (Def. 26.5)

Triad of fixed elements The structure of substance, essence, and thisness, taken together, as
     the metaphysical content of the fixed element of Book I’s framework. (Def. 8.1)

Triad of fluid elements The structure of light, causation, and relation, taken together, as the
     metaphysical content of the fluid element of Book I’s framework. (Def. 12.1)
Glossary of Metaphysical Terms                                                                    399


Triad of governing dynamics The structure of law, necessity, and modal space, taken to-
     gether, as the metaphysical content of the governing dynamics of Book I’s framework.
     (Def. 16.1)

Truth, of a metaphysical claim Structural adequacy: the claim is true if the structure it
    asserts is the structure that the domain requires, and false if the structure is not required,
    or is incoherent with other structures that the domain requires. (Pr. 3.12)


V
Viable causation The causal relation whose expression in the realm satisfies the three compo-
    nents of metaphysical viability: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. (Def. 23.9)

Viable essence The essence whose relation to its manifestations in the realm satisfies the three
    components of metaphysical viability: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. (Def. 22.9)

Viable modality The modal relation whose actualization in the realm satisfies the three
    components of metaphysical viability: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability. (Def. 24.8)

Viability, structural The structural character of the relation between an identity and its mani-
    festations in a cognitive context, in three respects: fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability.
    (Book I, Def. 36.1; recalled at Def. 21.3)

Viability, metaphysical See Metaphysical viability.


W
Whole, context of the See Context of the whole.

The glossary does not restate the arguments that support the definitions; the reader who wishes
to see the arguments is directed to the chapter in which each definition is established. The
epistemic status labels (A), (T), (E), (Q), (S), and (D) used in the chapters are defined in the
front matter; the glossary does not restate them.

Index of Principles

A Note on the Index
This index lists every principle, definition, and theorem of Book II, in the order in which each
appears in the book. Each entry gives the number and name of the entry, its epistemic status,
and the section in which it is stated. The index is organized by part and by chapter.
    An entry is marked Definition where the book states it as a stipulation of vocabulary or as
a specification of a concept; it is marked Principle where the book states it as a claim that is
argued, estimated, or adopted; and it is marked Theorem where it has the form of a proved result.
The labels are the book’s own; they are retained here, even where the label and the status do
not align (a few “Definitions” carry (T) or (D) status, and a few “Principles” carry (E) status;
the book states the status, and the label is not always the same as the status).
    The status labels are those introduced in the front matter: (A) (axiom), (T) (argued), (E) (es-
timate), (Q) (open question), (S) (speculation), and (D) (dependent on Book I). The labels are the
book’s own; the reader who wishes to see them explained is directed to 3_Epistemic_Status_Labels.


A Note on the Numbering
The numbering of Book II’s definitions and principles is not uniform across the book, and the
reader should know this before using the index.
    In Chapters 1–18, the definitions and principles are numbered sequentially within each chapter:
the first entry of Chapter n is numbered n.1, the second n.2, and so on. Some entries in the
sequence are Definitions, some are Principles; the number does not distinguish the two. The
sequence is continuous within each chapter.
    In Chapters 19–31, the numbering is not sequential: there are gaps in each chapter’s
sequence (for example, Chapter 19 contains Principle 19.3, Definition 19.6, Definition 19.7,
and Principle 19.11, but no entries numbered 19.1, 19.2, 19.4, 19.5, 19.8, 19.9, or 19.10). The gaps
are not omissions; they correspond to entries that Book II cites from Book I, or to sub-sections
of the chapter that do not state a separate definition or principle. The book does not explain the
scheme, but the numbering can be read as continuous within each chapter’s reference sequence,
of which only some entries are stated as definitions or principles in Book II.
    The two schemes coexist. The reader who cites an entry should cite it by the number the
book gives it, and the reader who looks up a number should expect either the matching entry (in
Chapters 1–18) or a gap (in Chapters 19–31) that points to an entry cited from elsewhere.


Part I: Framework of Metaphysical Inquiry (Chapters 1–4)
Chapter 1: What Book I Established and What It Left Open
This chapter makes no new metaphysical claim and states no new definition or principle. It is
a structural inventory of Book I’s three ledgers (established claims, open questions, deferred
analyses), and it prepares the ground for the framework of Book II. The reader who wishes to see
402                                                                           Index of Principles


the chapter’s contribution is directed to its three ledgers (§1.3–1.5) and to the map of Book II’s
structure (§1.7).

Chapter 2: The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology
Principle 2.1 (Metaphysical Inquiry Is Explanatory Cognition). (T) Metaphysical in-
     quiry is explanatory cognition: it seeks to understand how some things stand to one
     another. §2.3.1.

Definition 2.2 (Fixed Element of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) An entity, kind, or cate-
     gory held invariant in an explanation of the conditions of being. §2.4.1.

Definition 2.3 (Fluid Element of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) A relation, process, or medium
     invoked to explain how the conditions of being of one fixed element bear on those of another.
     §2.4.2.

Definition 2.4 (Governing Dynamics of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) A rule that explains
     how the fluid elements affect the fixed elements of the inquiry. §2.4.3.

Definition 2.5 (Context of Metaphysical Inquiry). (A) The frame in which the inquiry’s
     fixed elements, fluid elements, and governing dynamics take their specific content. §2.4.4.

Principle 2.6 (Removal Test at the Metaphysical Level). (T, relative to the definitions
     of §2.4) If a metaphysical inquiry omits one of the four columns, the inquiry is incomplete
     as a metaphysical explanation. §2.5.

Principle 2.7 (Reducibility Test at the Metaphysical Level). (E) No fifth column is needed
     for a metaphysical inquiry: every candidate fifth column examined reduces to one of the
     four. §2.6.

Principle 2.8 (Analytical and Ontological at the Metaphysical Level). (D) The four columns
     of metaphysical inquiry are four analytical roles that any complete metaphysical explanation
     must assign; they are not four kinds of entity, nor four levels of being. §2.7.

Principle 2.9 (The Method of Book II). (A) The book’s method: for each metaphysical
     concept, ask what its fixed element, fluid element, governing dynamics, and context are.
     §2.8.

Chapter 3: The Epistemic Status of Metaphysical Claims
Principle 3.1 (The Nature of a Metaphysical Claim). (T) A metaphysical claim is a claim
     about the conditions of possibility of what is. §3.3.2.

Definition 3.2 (The First Criterion). (A) A metaphysical claim is (A) if it is adopted rather
     than argued; it is (T) if it is argued. §3.4.1.

Definition 3.3 (The Second Criterion). (A) A metaphysical claim that is (T) is either (T)
     by demonstration or (E) by structural adequacy. §3.4.2.

Definition 3.4 (The Third Criterion). (A) A metaphysical claim is (D) if its truth depends
     on a specific principle, definition, or commitment of Book I; otherwise it is (T) or (A)
     independently. §3.4.3.

Definition 3.5 ((A) Applied to Metaphysical Claims). (A) A metaphysical claim is (A)
     if it is a starting point that the book adopts, whose justification is coherence, explanatory
     power, and fruitfulness. §3.5.1.
Index of Principles                                                                             403


Definition 3.6 ((T) Applied to Metaphysical Claims). (T) A metaphysical claim is (T)
     if it is argued by demonstration from premises. §3.5.2.

Definition 3.7 ((E) Applied to Metaphysical Claims). (E) A metaphysical claim is (E) if
     it is offered as a structural estimate, whose justification is that a different structure would
     do the work less well. §3.5.3.

Definition 3.8 ((Q) Applied to Metaphysical Claims). (Q) A metaphysical claim is (Q)
     if it marks a question the framework does not settle. §3.5.4.

Definition 3.9 ((S) Applied to Metaphysical Claims). (S) A metaphysical claim is (S) if
     it is a speculative extension, flagged for caution. §3.5.5.

Definition 3.10 ((D) Applied to Metaphysical Claims). (D) A metaphysical claim is (D)
     if its truth depends on a specific principle, definition, or commitment of Book I, and its
     argument in Book II is the demonstration of the dependency. §3.5.6.

Principle 3.11 (The Signature Label of Book II). (A) The signature label of Book II is
    (D). §3.5.6.

Principle 3.12 (The Truth of a Metaphysical Claim). (T) A metaphysical claim’s truth
     is structural adequacy. §3.6.

Chapter 4: The Inherited Core: C1–C13
The thirteen core commitments are stated as Definitions 4.1–4.13. Each is (A), because each is
a commitment of Book I’s Chapter E that Book II inherits. The entries are grouped in three
families (methodological, ontological, structural-metaphysical), as Book II’s Chapter 4 groups
them.

Definition 4.1 (C1: Finitude of the Subject). (A) Every cognizing subject is finite. §4.4.1.

Definition 4.2 (C2: Philosophy Describes Structure, Not Telos). (A) Philosophy describes
     the structure of what is; it does not establish the telos. §4.4.1.

Definition 4.3 (C10: Autonomy of Philosophical Justification). (A) The validity of a
     philosophical principle does not depend on confirmation from outside philosophy. §4.4.1.

Definition 4.4 (C3: Independent Reality of the Realms). (A) Each realm is independently
     real. §4.4.2.

Definition 4.5 (C4: Transcendence of the Divine Ground). (A) God is not a realm, a
     category, or a level within the sevenfold architecture; God is the transcendent Creator and
     ontological ground. §4.4.2.

Definition 4.6 (C7: Trans-Categorical Character of Light). (A) Light goes beyond the
     existing philosophical categories; a new category is needed. §4.4.2.

Definition 4.7 (C11: Openness of Relations). (A) For every cognitive context C and every
     manifestation m in C, there is a cognitive context C ′ in which m is a fixed element. §4.4.2.

Definition 4.8 (C12: Totality of Possibility). (A) There is a space Ω of all possibilities,
     and it is real. §4.4.2.

Definition 4.9 (C13: The Trans-Categorical Triad). (A) Light, identity, and self-awareness
     are three trans-categorical conditions of possibility. §4.4.2.
404                                                                           Index of Principles


Definition 4.10 (C5: Identity Conservation). (A) Identity is invariant under all temporal
     transformations of its manifestations. §4.4.3.

Definition 4.11 (C6: Non-Duplicability). (A) Identity cannot be copied. §4.4.3.

Definition 4.12 (C8: Expression as Structural Necessity). (A) Every identity tends to-
     ward expression. §4.4.3.

Definition 4.13 (C9: Category-Relative Predication). (A) Metaphysical predicates are
     defined relative to a realm and a respect. §4.4.3.

Principle 4.14 (Book II Is a Conditional Metaphysics on the Inherited Core). (A) Book II
     is a conditional metaphysics on the core C1–C13. §4.7.


Part II: Fixed Elements of Metaphysics (Chapters 5–8)
Chapter 5: Substance
Definition 5.1 (Substance). (A) A substance is the metaphysical ground of a thing’s being
     the same one through change, and of its being the subject of its properties. §5.3.1.

Definition 5.2 (Accident). (A) An accident is a property that a substance has and that can
     be removed without the substance ceasing to be the substance it is. §5.3.3.

Principle 5.3 (Substance as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Fixed Element). (D)
     Substance is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s fixed element. §5.6.3.

Chapter 6: Essence and Essentialism
Definition 6.1 (Essence). (A) An essence is the constitutive what of a thing: the determination
     that makes the thing the kind of thing it is, and that grounds the features the thing cannot
     lose without ceasing to be the thing it is. §6.3.1.

Definition 6.2 (Essential and Accidental Properties). (A) An essential property belongs
     to the essence; an accidental property does not. §6.3.3.

Principle 6.3 (Essence as the Metaphysical Consequent of Defining Invariants). (D)
     Essence is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s defining invariants. §6.6.3.

Principle 6.4 (The Essentialist Thesis). (T) Things have essences. §6.7.

Chapter 7: Identity and Thisness, Deepened
Definition 7.1 (Thisness). (A) The thisness of a thing is the non-qualitative individuating
     feature that makes the thing the particular thing it is, and that cannot be shared by another
     thing. §7.3.1.

Definition 7.2 (Thisness and Signature). (A) A thing’s signature is the structural descrip-
     tion of its invariance; a thing’s thisness is the non-qualitative individuation that the
     signature cannot capture. §7.3.3.

Principle 7.3 (Thisness as the Metaphysical Consequent of Non-Duplicability). (D) This-
     ness is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s principle of non-duplicability. §7.6.3.

Principle 7.4 (The Doctrine of Primitive Thisness). (T) Thisness is primitive and non-
     qualitative. §7.7.

Chapter 8: The Fixed Elements of Each Realm
Definition 8.1 (The Triad of Fixed Elements). (A) The triad of fixed elements is the struc-
     ture of substance, essence, and thisness, taken together. §8.3.1.

Principle 8.2 (The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Triad). (E) The triad of fixed
     elements is articulated differently in each realm (collapse, coincidence, distinction). §8.4.2.

Principle 8.3 (The Fixed Element as the Realm’s Mode of Being). (T) The fixed ele-
     ment of a realm is the realm’s mode of being as an articulation of the triad. §8.6.2.


Part III: Fluid Elements of Metaphysics (Chapters 9–12)
Chapter 9: Causation
Definition 9.1 (Causation). (A) Causation is the real transfer of effect from a cause to an
     effect through a medium. §9.3.1.

Definition 9.2 (Cause and Effect). (A) A cause is what produces an effect; an effect is what
     a cause produces. §9.3.3.

Principle 9.3 (What the Theories Share). (T) The four standard theories of causation
     share the notion of a transfer of effect. §9.4.2.

Principle 9.4 (The Framework’s Position on the Theories). (E) The framework does not
     adopt one of the four theories; it identifies the general structure that the four instantiate.
     §9.4.3.

Principle 9.5 (Causation as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Conveyor Principle).
    (D) Causation is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s conveyor principle. §9.5.3.

Principle 9.6 (The Material Manifestation’s Causality Is a Mode). (D) Book I’s causal-
     ity rule of the Material Manifestation is the Material mode of the general causal structure.
     §9.5.4.

Chapter 10: Relation
Definition 10.1 (Relation). (A) A relation is the real connection between two or more terms,
     distinct from the terms themselves and distinct from the transfer of effect that causation
     names. §10.3.1.

Definition 10.2 (Relatum). (A) A relatum is a term of a relation; the relata are the terms
     that the relation connects. §10.3.3.

Principle 10.3 (What the Theories Share). (T) The four standard theories of relation share
     the notion of a connection between the terms. §10.4.2.

Principle 10.4 (The Framework’s Position on the Relation Theories). (E) The frame-
    work does not adopt one of the four theories; it identifies the general structure that the
     four instantiate. §10.4.3.

Principle 10.5 (Relation as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Relational Manifestation).
    (D) Relation is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s account of the Relational Manifes-
     tation. §10.5.3.

Principle 10.6 (Bradley’s Regress and Light). (D) Book I’s Principle 12.3 (light as the
     condition of possibility of relation) is the framework’s response to Bradley’s regress. §10.6.2.

Chapter 11: Light as Metaphysical Medium, Reconsidered
Principle 11.1 (The Analogy of “Substance” in Book I). (T) The word “substance” in
     Book I’s Principle 12.1 is an analogical use, whose analogy is the analogy between the
     substance-accident relation and the condition-conditioned relation. §11.3.2.
Definition 11.2 (Light as Metaphysical Medium). (A) Light is a metaphysical medium:
     the structural condition under which causation and relation can function as the fluid
     element. §11.4.1.
Principle 11.3 (Causation Presupposes the Medium). (D) Causation presupposes light
     as the metaphysical medium. §11.5.1.
Principle 11.4 (Relation Presupposes the Medium). (D) Relation presupposes light as
     the metaphysical medium. §11.6.1.
Principle 11.5 (The Reconsideration of Light). (D) Book I’s Principle 12.1 is deepened,
     not revised, by the metaphysical analyses of Part II and of Chapters 9–10. §11.7.3.

Chapter 12: The Fluid Elements of Each Realm
Definition 12.1 (The Triad of Fluid Elements). (A) The triad of fluid elements is the struc-
     ture of light, causation, and relation, taken together. §12.3.1.
Principle 12.2 (The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Fluid Triad). (E) The triad of
     fluid elements is articulated differently in each realm. §12.4.2.
Principle 12.3 (The Fluid Element as the Realm’s Mode of Operation). (T) The fluid
     element of a realm is the realm’s mode of operation as an articulation of the triad. §12.6.2.
Principle 12.4 (The Relation Between the Two Triads). (T) The fixed triad and the fluid
     triad are related as the related and the relating. §12.7.2.


Part IV: Governing Dynamics of Metaphysics (Chapters 13–16)
Chapter 13: Law
Definition 13.1 (Law). (A) A law is the structural pattern that grounds the regularity, neces-
     sity, and formality of a realm’s rules. §13.3.1.
Definition 13.2 (Rule and Law). (A) A rule is a formulation of what must be the case; a law
     is the structural pattern that the formulation formulates. §13.3.3.
Principle 13.3 (What the Theories Share). (T) The four standard theories of law share
     the notion of a pattern that grounds the regularity of the law. §13.4.2.
Principle 13.4 (The Framework’s Position on the Law Theories). (E) The framework
     does not adopt one of the four theories; it identifies the general structure that the four
     instantiate. §13.4.3.
Principle 13.5 (Law, Causation, and Relation). (T) Law, causation, and relation are re-
     lated as pattern, transfer, and connection. §13.5.3.
Principle 13.6 (Law as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Rules). (D) Law is the meta-
     physical consequent of Book I’s rules of the realms. §13.6.3.
Principle 13.7 (The Unity of the Rules as a Consequence of Law). (D) Book I’s Prin-
     ciples 16.15 and 17.11 (the unity of the rules) are consequences of law. §13.6.4.

Chapter 14: Necessity and Modality
Definition 14.1 (Modality). (A) Modality is the structure of the possible, the actual, and the
     necessary. §14.3.1.

Definition 14.2 (Necessity). (A) Necessity is the modal status of a proposition, state of affairs,
     or thing that cannot be otherwise. §14.3.1.

Definition 14.3 (Possibility). (A) Possibility is the modal status of what could be. §14.3.3.

Definition 14.4 (Logical Necessity). (A) Logical necessity is the modal status of a proposi-
     tion that is true in virtue of its logical form alone. §14.4.1.

Definition 14.5 (Metaphysical Necessity). (A) Metaphysical necessity is the modal status
     of a proposition, state of affairs, or thing that is necessary in virtue of essence. §14.4.2.

Principle 14.6 (The Structural Laws Are Metaphysically Necessary). (D) Book I’s Prin-
     ciple 16.7 (the structural laws are necessary) is a principle of metaphysical necessity grounded
     in essence. §14.4.2.

Definition 14.7 (Natural Necessity). (A) Natural necessity is the modal status of a propo-
     sition or state of affairs that is necessary in virtue of the laws of nature. §14.4.3.

Principle 14.8 (Natural Necessity Is a Mode of Metaphysical Necessity). (D) Natural
     necessity is the Material mode of metaphysical necessity. §14.4.3.

Definition 14.9 (Normative Necessity). (A) Normative necessity is the modal status of a
     proposition or state of affairs that is necessary in virtue of the structure of the good.
     §14.4.4.

Principle 14.10 (The Relation Among the Four Kinds). (T) The four kinds of necessity
     are related as form, ground, mode, and posterior. §14.5.4.

Principle 14.11 (The Grounding of Necessity). (T) The necessary, within Ω, is not a prim-
     itive status; it is grounded in the four structures. §14.6.2.

Chapter 15: The Modal Space Ω Reconsidered
Principle 15.1 (The Framework’s Position on Ω). (D) Ω is a structure of possible config-
     urations of essences and laws. §15.4.2.

Principle 15.2 (The Stratification of Ω). (T) Ω is stratified, and the strata are the four
     kinds of necessity. §15.5.1.

Principle 15.3 (The Grounding of Ω Is a Family of Analogous Relations). (D) The ground-
     ing of Ω in God is a family of analogous relations, each corresponding to a stratum. §15.6.2.

Principle 15.4 (The Relation Between Ω and the Throne-Domain). (E) Ω is the space
     of possibilities from which the seven realms are actualized; the Throne-Domain is the
     encompassing created order in which the seven realms are situated. §15.6.3.

Principle 15.5 (The Relation Between Ω and Light). (D) Ω and light are related as the
     space of possibilities and the medium of actualization. §15.7.2.

Principle 16.2 (The Realm-Dependent Structure of the Governing Triad). (E) The triad

Part V: Context of Metaphysics (Chapters 17–20)
Chapter 17: Realms as Contexts, Deepened
Definition 17.1 (Realm as Context). (A) A realm, as a context, is a mode of existence with
     a determinate capacity: a structural range of what can appear in it and what cannot.
     §17.3.1.

Definition 17.2 (Realm as Existential Context). (A) The existential context of a mani-
     festation is the realm in which the manifestation is realized, with the capacity and the
     constraints of that realm. §17.3.3.

Principle 17.3 (The Capacity Is Structural). (D) The capacity of a realm is the structural
     range of what the mode of existence admits; it is not a quantitative limit. §17.4.1.

Principle 17.4 (The Existential Openness of the Realm). (T) The capacity of a realm is
     open in the sense that it is a structural range, not a finite enumeration. §17.4.3.

Principle 17.5 (Realm-as-Context as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Existential Context).
    (D) Realm-as-context is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s definitions of fundamental
     realm and existential context. §17.6.3.

Chapter 18: The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category
Definition 18.1 (The Barzakhic Category). (A) The barzakhic, as a category, is the mode
     of existence whose being is the passage between two other modes. §18.3.1.

Principle 18.2 (The Framework’s Position on the Category of Barzakhic). (E) The barza-
     khic is a category in the mode-of-being sense and in the structural-role sense; it is a category
     of passage. §18.4.2.

Principle 18.3 (The Barzakhic Is a Mode of Existence, Not a Function). (D) The barza-
     khic is a mode of existence, not a function. §18.5.2.

Principle 18.4 (The Barzakhic Is a Passage, Not a Relation). (D) The barzakhic is a
     passage, not a relation. §18.6.2.

Principle 18.5 (The Answer to Q10). (D) Identities are not realized in the barzakhic realms
     as they are in the fundamental realms; they are present through the barzakhic realms.
     §18.7.2.

Chapter 19: Non-Passage and Presence
Principle 19.3 (Non-Passage). (T) The presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm
     does not require that the identity pass existentially through every realm that lies between.
     §19.3.

Definition 19.6 (Passage). (A) Passage is the existential traversal of a realm by an identity.
     §19.4.

Definition 19.7 (Presence). (A) Presence is the structural relation in which an identity is
     realized, or its effect is realized, in a realm. §19.4.

Principle 19.11 (Presence as Structural Realization). (T) The presence of an identity in
     a realm is the structural realization of the identity, or of its effect, in the realm. §19.5.

Chapter 20: The Context of the Whole
Definition 20.1 (Self-Awareness). (A) Self-awareness is the mechanism of regulating the
     connection between a manifestation and its source. §20.4.

Definition 20.2 (Consciousness). (A) Consciousness is the intensity of the connection be-
     tween a manifestation and its source. §20.4.

Definition 20.3 (Awareness). (A) Awareness is the regulation of a manifestation for the
     reception of reflective epistemic light and intra-category epistemic light. §20.4.

Definition 20.4 (The Structural Limits of Self-Knowledge). (T, relative to the impossi-
     bility of super-identity) The structural limits of self-knowledge are the limits that follow,
     for any finite subject, from the impossibility of super-identity. §20.10.

Definition 20.5 (Two Levels of Structural Determination). (A) The two levels of struc-
     tural determination: the range of manifestations structurally available, and the accessible
     manifestations at the present stage. §20.11.


Part VI: Viability as Integration (Chapters 21–25)
Chapter 21: From Structural to Metaphysical Viability
Definition 21.3 (Structural Viability, Recalled). (A) The structural viability of an identity
     in a cognitive context is the structural character of the relation between the identity and
     its manifestations, in three respects: fidelity, sustainability, recoverability. §21.3.

Definition 21.6 (Cognitive Context, Recalled). (A) A cognitive context is the frame in
     which something is cognized. §21.4.

Definition 21.7 (Existential Context, Recalled). (A) An existential context is the setting
     in which a manifestation is realized, with the capacity and the constraints of that setting.
     §21.4.

Principle 21.8 (The Transition Is From the Cognitive to the Existential). (T) The tran-
     sition from structural to metaphysical viability is the transition from the viability of the
     relation in a cognitive context to the viability of the relation in an existential context.
     §21.4.

Principle 21.11 (The Three Components in Their Metaphysical Form). (T) The three
     components of viability are the same in their metaphysical form as in their structural form;
    what differs is the context. §21.5.
410                                                                            Index of Principles


Definition 21.14 (Metaphysical Viability). (A) The metaphysical viability of an identity
     in an existential context is the structural character of the relation between the identity and
     its manifestations, in three respects: fidelity, sustainability, recoverability. §21.6.

Principle 21.18 (The Relation Between Structural and Metaphysical Viability). (T)
     Structural viability and metaphysical viability are the same concept applied to two kinds
     of context. §21.7.

Chapter 22: Viability and Essence
Definition 22.3 (Essence, Recalled). (A) The essence of an identity is the structural deter-
     mination that constitutes it. §22.3.

Principle 22.6 (Essence Is Subject to Viability). (T) Essence is subject to viability. §22.4.

Definition 22.9 (Viable Essence). (A) The viable essence of an identity in a realm is the
     essence whose relation to its manifestations in the realm satisfies the three components of
     metaphysical viability. §22.5.

Principle 22.13 (Fidelity of Essence). (T) The fidelity of an essence in a realm is the extent
     to which the manifestations of the essence preserve its essential determination. §22.6.

Principle 22.17 (Sustainability of Essence). (T) The sustainability of an essence in a realm
     is the condition under which the cost of expressing the essence does not exceed what the
     realm can bear. §22.7.

Principle 22.21 (Recoverability of Essence). (T) The recoverability of an essence in a realm
     is the condition under which the essence retains its structural capacity to manifest in the
     realm. §22.8.

Definition 22.25 (Accident). (A) An accident of an identity is a feature that does not belong
     to the essence. §22.9.

Principle 22.26 (The Essence Is Subject to Viability; the Accident Is Not). (T) The
     essence is subject to viability; the accident is not. §22.9.

Chapter 23: Viability and Causation
Definition 23.3 (Causation, Recalled). (A) Causation is the structural relation in which an
     identity, through its manifestation in a realm, brings about a change in another identity’s
     manifestation. §23.3.

Principle 23.6 (Causation Is Subject to Viability). (T) Causation is subject to viability.
     §23.4.

Definition 23.9 (Viable Causation). (A) The viable causation of an identity in a realm is the
     causal relation whose expression in the realm satisfies the three components of metaphysical
     viability. §23.5.

Principle 23.13 (Fidelity of Causation). (T) The fidelity of a causal relation is the extent
     to which the effect preserves the essential determination of the cause. §23.6.

Principle 23.17 (Sustainability of Causation). (T) The sustainability of a causal relation
     is the condition under which the cost of the effect does not exceed what the realm can bear.
     §23.7.

Principle 23.21 (Recoverability of Causation). (T) The recoverability of a causal relation
     is the condition under which the cause retains its structural capacity to produce the effect.
     §23.8.

Principle 23.25 (Causation Is Not Mere Succession). (T) Causation is not mere succes-
     sion. §23.9.

Chapter 24: Viability and Modality
Definition 24.3 (Modality, Recalled). (A) Modality is the structure of the possible, the
     actual, and the necessary. §24.3.

Definition 24.4 (The Modal Space Ω, Recalled). (A) Ω is a stratified modal structure
     whose strata are the four kinds of necessity. §24.3.

Principle 24.5 (Modality Is Subject to Viability). (T) Modality is subject to viability.
     §24.4.

Definition 24.8 (Viable Modality). (A) The viable modality of an identity in a realm is
     the modal relation whose actualization in the realm satisfies the three components of
     metaphysical viability. §24.5.

Principle 24.12 (Fidelity of Modality). (T) The fidelity of a modal relation is the extent
     to which the actualization preserves the essential determination of the possibility. §24.6.

Principle 24.16 (Sustainability of Modality). (T) The sustainability of a modal relation is
     the condition under which the cost of the actualization does not exceed what the realm
     can bear. §24.7.

Principle 24.20 (Recoverability of Modality). (T) The recoverability of a modal relation
     is the condition under which the possibility retains its structural capacity to be actualized.
     §24.8.

Principle 24.24 (Modal Status Is Not Modal Viability). (T) Modal status is not modal
     viability. §24.9.

Principle 24.27 (The Four Kinds of Viable Modality). (T) Each kind of necessity has its
     own modal viability. §24.10.

Chapter 25: The Metaphysics of Viability
Definition 25.4 (The Metaphysics of Viability). (A) The metaphysics of viability is the
     account of the conditions under which an identity can be viable in the realms in which it is
     manifested. §25.4.

Principle 25.7 (The Integration of the Four Columns). (T) The four columns integrate
     in the metaphysics of viability as the four aspects of the conditions. §25.5.

Principle 25.10 (The Three Domains Are Three Aspects of One Relation). (T) Essence,
     causation, and modality are three aspects of one relation. §25.6.

Principle 25.13 (The Metaphysical Conditions of Viability). (T) The metaphysical con-
     ditions of viability are the fidelity, sustainability, and recoverability of the relation between
     an identity and its manifestations in each realm. §25.7.

Part VII: Divine Ground and Modal Order (Chapters 26–29)
Chapter 26: The Metaphysics of Transcendence
Definition 26.5 (Transcendence). (A) Transcendence is the relation of ontological depen-
     dence of the created order on God. §26.4.

Principle 26.10 (The Ontological Mode). (D) The created order depends on God for its
     being. §26.5.1.

Principle 26.11 (The Epistemic Mode). (D) The created order depends on God for its
     intelligibility. §26.5.2.

Principle 26.12 (The Relational Mode). (D) The created order depends on God for its
     relations. §26.5.3.

Principle 26.15 (Transcendence Is the Condition of the Four Columns). (D) Transcen-
     dence is not one of the four columns; it is the condition under which the four columns can

Chapter 27: Creation and Sustaining
Definition 27.4 (Creation). (A) Creation is the act by which God gives being to the created
     order. §27.4.

Definition 27.8 (Sustaining). (A) Sustaining is the act by which God gives being to the
     created order at every moment. §27.5.

Principle 27.12 (Creation and Sustaining Are Two Modes of One Relation). (D) Cre-
     ation and sustaining are two modes of one relation. §27.6.

Principle 27.15 (Creation Is the Act That Establishes the Created Order). (D) Cre-
     ation is the act by which the created order that the four columns describe is given being.
     §27.7.

Principle 27.17 (Sustaining Is the Act That Maintains the Created Order). (D) Sus-
     taining is the act by which the created order that the four columns describe is maintained
     in being. §27.8.

Chapter 28: The Modal Space as Created
Definition 28.4 (The Created Modal Space). (A) The created modal space Ω is the strati-
     fied structure of possible configurations of essences and laws whose being, intelligibility,
     and relations are given by God. §28.4.

Principle 28.7 (The Createdness of the Logical Stratum). (D) The logical stratum is
     created: the form of propositions is given by God. §28.5.1.

Principle 28.8 (The Createdness of the Metaphysical Stratum). (D) The metaphysical
     stratum is created: the essences of things are given by God. §28.5.2.

Principle 28.9 (The Createdness of the Natural Stratum). (D) The natural stratum is
     created: the laws of the realms are given by God. §28.5.3.

Principle 28.10 (The Createdness of the Normative Stratum). (D) The normative stra-
     tum is created: the good is given by God. §28.5.4.
Index of Principles                                                                           413


Principle 28.12 (The Createdness of the Necessary). (D) The necessary is created: its
     being is given by God. The createdness is a claim about grounding, not about modal status.
     §28.6.

Principle 28.16 (The Created Modal Space Is Not Any of the Four). (D) The created
     modal space is not the modal realist’s plurality, not the Platonist’s abstract realm, not the
     divine ideas, and not a fiction. §28.7.

Principle 28.18 (The Created Modal Space Is the Order of the Four Columns). (D)
    The created modal space is the order in which the four columns describe the created order.

Chapter 29: Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered
Definition 29.4 (Providence). (A) Providence is the governance of the created order by God.
     §29.4.

Principle 29.9 (The Ordering Mode of Providence). (D) Providence orders the created
     order toward the ends that God wills. §29.5.1.

Principle 29.10 (The Sustaining Mode of Providence). (D) Providence sustains the or-
     der of the created order at every moment. §29.5.2.

Principle 29.11 (The Directing Mode of Providence). (D) Providence directs the created
     order toward its ends. §29.5.3.

Principle 29.13 (Divine Knowledge of the Created Modal Space). (D) The two kinds
     of divine knowledge (natural and free) are the knowledge of the created modal space, not
     of an uncreated abstract realm. §29.6.2.

Definition 29.16 (Creaturely Choice). (A) Creaturely choice is the selection by which a
     creature actualizes one possibility rather than another within the created modal space.
     §29.7.

Principle 29.19 (The Modal Status of the Future). (D) The future is the selected-but-
     not-yet-actualized part of the actualization chain. §29.8.


Part VIII: Boundaries and Conclusion (Chapters 30–31)
Chapter 30: The Boundaries of Metaphysics
Principle 30.8 (Autonomy of Philosophical Justification). (A) The validity of a meta-
     physical principle, within the domain of philosophy, does not depend on confirmation from
     outside philosophy. §30.5.

Principle 30.9 (Internal Definition). (T) The concepts of the framework are defined and
     justified within its own system. §30.5.

Principle 30.10 (Meaning Is Not Exported). (T) The use of a word or concept in another
     domain does not determine its metaphysical sense here. §30.5.

Chapter 31: Conclusion: The Architecture and Its Open Questions
Principle 31.13 (The Book Is a Conditional Architecture on a Core). (A) The book is
     a conditional architecture on a core of thirteen commitments inherited from Book I. §31.8.

A Note on the Dependency Map
The dependency map of Chapter 43 (in the Book I edition; not present in Book II’s own
Chapter 43, which Book II does not contain) is the authoritative statement of which conclusions
depend on which core commitments. The reader who wishes to see the dependencies of the
entries in this index is directed to that map, or to Book II’s own Chapter 4 (the thirteen inherited
commitments) and Chapter 43 (the ten core commitments and the map).
    The reader should know that Book II’s own Chapter 43 does not exist; the chapter with that
number in the Book I edition is the source of the dependency map, and Book II cites the map
from Book I rather than restating it.
