Index of Arguments

This index lists the arguments that Book II states, in the order in which they appear. Each
entry gives the argument number, its title, the place in which it is stated, its type, its conclusion,
and its epistemic status. The arguments are numbered by chapter (the argument A5.1 is the
first argument of Chapter 5), and the numbering does not coincide with the numbering of the
principles and definitions; a principle may be stated without an argument, and an argument
may be stated without a new principle. The type of each argument is one of the following:
direct proof (argument from stated premises to a conclusion by modus ponens or a chain
of deductions); reductio (argument that the denial of the conclusion leads to an absurdity);
transcendental (argument that the conclusion is a condition of the possibility of something
acknowledged); inference to the best explanation (argument that the conclusion explains the
phenomena better than its rivals); removal test (argument that the denial of the conclusion leaves
the explanation incomplete); reducibility test (argument that a candidate element reduces to one
of the established elements); three-step argument (argument that moves from an analytical role
to its metaphysical presupposition to the identification of the presupposition with a metaphysical
notion); demonstration of dependency (argument that the conclusion is a consequence of a
principle of Book I); and argument by analysis (argument that a set of positions shares a common
structure that the conclusion names).


Part I: Framework of Metaphysical Inquiry
Chapter 2: The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology
A2.1 Metaphysical Inquiry Is Explanatory Cognition. Chapter 2, §2.3.1. Direct proof (three
    premises). Conclusion: metaphysical inquiry is explanatory cognition in the sense of
    Book I’s Definition 1.1. Status: (T).
A2.2 Removal Test at the Metaphysical Level. Chapter 2, §2.5. Removal test. Conclusion:
    if a metaphysical inquiry omits one of the four columns, the inquiry is incomplete as a
    metaphysical explanation. Status: (T), relative to the definitions of §2.4.
A2.3 Reducibility Test at the Metaphysical Level. Chapter 2, §2.6. Reducibility test (three
    candidates examined: the standard of truth, the inquirer, the history of the inquiry).
    Conclusion: no fifth column is needed for a metaphysical inquiry; every candidate fifth
    column that has been examined reduces to one of the four. Status: (E).
A2.4 The Method of Book II. Chapter 2, §2.8. Direct proof from the definitions of §2.4, the
    removal test (A2.2), and the reducibility test (A2.3). Conclusion: for each metaphysical
    concept, the book asks four questions (fixed element, fluid element, governing dynamics,
    context), and the answers are the book’s analysis of the concept. Status: (A).

Chapter 3: The Epistemic Status of Metaphysical Claims
A3.1 The Nature of a Metaphysical Claim. Chapter 3, §3.3.2. Direct proof from the negative
    characterizations of §3.3.1. Conclusion: a metaphysical claim is a claim about the conditions
416                                                                              Index of Arguments


      of possibility of what is; it asserts that, for some domain of beings or for being as such, a
      certain structure must obtain. Status: (T).
A3.2 The Truth of a Metaphysical Claim. Chapter 3, §3.6. Direct proof from the nature of a
    metaphysical claim (A3.1) and from the kinds of truth distinguished in §3.6. Conclusion: a
    metaphysical claim’s truth is structural adequacy. Status: (T).

Chapter 4: The Inherited Core: C1–C13
A4.1 The Three Families of the Core. Chapter 4, §4.5.1. Argument by analysis of the thirteen
    core commitments. Conclusion: the core divides into three families (methodological,
    ontological, structural-metaphysical), and the division is not arbitrary but corresponds to
    the three questions the core answers. Status: (T).
A4.2 Book II Is a Conditional Metaphysics on the Inherited Core. Chapter 4, §4.7, Principle 4.14.
    Direct proof from the audit of Book I’s Chapter E and from the map of Book II’s parts to
    the core. Conclusion: Book II is a conditional metaphysics on the core C1–C13. Status:
    (A).


Part II: Fixed Elements of Metaphysics
Chapter 5: Substance
A5.1 Substance as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Fixed Element. Chapter 5, §5.6, Princi-
    ple 5.3. Three-step argument. Step 1: the fixed element presupposes a ground (D-claim,
    conditional on Book I’s Definition 2.1). Step 2: the ground is substance (T-claim, argued by
    analysis of the notion of substance). Step 3: the presupposition is a metaphysical consequent
    of the framework (synthesis). Conclusion: substance is the metaphysical consequent of
    Book I’s fixed element. Status: (D).
A5.2 Reply to the Bundle-Theory Objection. Chapter 5, §5.9, Reply to Objection 2. Reductio of
    the bundle theory: a bundle of properties is one only if it is collected, and the collecting
    requires a ground that is not another property; the ground is what the framework calls
    substance. Conclusion: the bundle theory presupposes substance even when it denies it.
    Status: (T).
A5.3 Reply to the Circularity Objection. Chapter 5, §5.9, Reply to Objection 3. Distinction
    between the defined notion (substance) and the notion in terms of which it is defined
    (identity). The definition defines substance as the ground of identity, not as identity.
    Conclusion: the alleged circularity is only apparent. Status: (T).

Chapter 6: Essence and Essentialism
A6.1 Essence as the Metaphysical Consequent of Defining Invariants. Chapter 6, §6.6, Princi-
    ple 6.3. Three-step argument. Step 1: the defining invariants presuppose a what (D-claim,
    conditional on Book I’s Definition 9.2). Step 2: the what is essence (T-claim, argued by
    analysis of the notion of essence). Step 3: the presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of
    the framework (synthesis). Conclusion: essence is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s
    defining invariants. Status: (D).
A6.2 First Argument for Essentialism: From Classification. Chapter 6, §6.7.1. Direct proof
    (five steps). Premises: to classify a thing is to identify the kind of thing it is; to identify the
    kind is to identify the constitutive what; the constitutive what is essence. Conclusion: to
    classify is to presuppose an essence. Status: (T), relative to the premise that classification
    identifies a kind.
Index of Arguments                                                                             417


A6.3 Second Argument for Essentialism: From Necessity. Chapter 6, §6.7.2. Direct proof (four
    steps). Premises: some properties are necessary to a thing; a necessary property requires
    a ground; the ground of the necessity is the thing’s essence. Conclusion: the necessity of
    the thing’s properties presupposes an essence. Status: (T), relative to the principle that
    necessity requires a ground.

A6.4 Third Argument for Essentialism: From the Determinacy of Change. Chapter 6, §6.7.3.
    Direct proof (four steps). Premises: a thing’s changes are determinate; the determinacy
    of change requires a determination of what the thing is; the determination is essence.
    Conclusion: the determinacy of change presupposes an essence. Status: (T), relative to the
    premise that the determinacy of change requires a determination.

A6.5 Reply to the Circularity Objection. Chapter 6, §6.10, Reply to Objection 3. Distinction
    between the word “essence” and the notion of the constitutive what. The definition
    defines essence in terms of the constitutive what, the kind-membership, and the necessary
    properties, and these are not the same as the word “essence”. Conclusion: the alleged
    semantic circularity is not a substantive circularity. Status: (T).

Chapter 7: Identity and Thisness, Deepened
A7.1 Thisness as the Metaphysical Consequent of Non-Duplicability. Chapter 7, §7.6, Prin-
    ciple 7.3. Three-step argument. Step 1: non-duplicability presupposes a non-shareable
    (D-claim, conditional on Book I’s Principle 9.6). Step 2: the non-shareable is thisness
    (T-claim, argued by analysis of the notion of thisness). Step 3: the presupposition is a meta-
    physical consequent of the framework (synthesis). Conclusion: thisness is the metaphysical
    consequent of Book I’s non-duplicability. Status: (D).

A7.2 First Argument for Primitive Thisness: From Numerical Distinctness. Chapter 7, §7.7.1.
    Direct proof (six steps). Premises: two things can share all their qualitative features; they
    are distinct; what distinguishes them cannot be qualitative. Conclusion: what distinguishes
    them is a non-qualitative feature, which is thisness. Status: (T), relative to the possibility
    of qualitative duplicates.

A7.3 Second Argument for Primitive Thisness: From the Logic of Identity. Chapter 7, §7.7.2.
    Direct proof (five steps). Premises: identity is strict sameness; an exact qualitative duplicate
    of a is not a; the distinctness cannot be qualitative. Conclusion: the distinctness is grounded
    in a non-qualitative individuator, which is thisness. Status: (T), relative to the doctrine of
    non-duplicability.

A7.4 Third Argument for Primitive Thisness: From the Possibility of Indiscernibles. Chapter 7,
    §7.7.3. Direct proof (five steps). Premises: there are possible worlds in which two things are
    exactly similar; in such a world, the two things are two, not one; what distinguishes them
    is a non-qualitative individuator. Conclusion: thisness is primitive and non-qualitative.
    Status: (T), relative to the possibility of indiscernibles. (The argument is the framework’s
    response to Black’s two spheres.)

A7.5 Reply to the Bundle-Theory Objection. Chapter 7, §7.10, Reply to Objection 2. Reductio
    of the bundle theory parallel to A5.2. Conclusion: the bundle theory presupposes thisness
    even when it denies it. Status: (T).

A7.6 Reply to Black’s Two Spheres. Chapter 7, §7.10, Reply to Objection 3. Direct proof : the
    two spheres are individuated by their positions, and the positions are individuated by their
    thisness; the spatial separation thus presupposes thisness. Conclusion: Black’s two spheres
    illustrate rather than refute the doctrine. Status: (T).
418                                                                          Index of Arguments


A7.7 Reply to Quine’s Skepticism about de re Modality. Chapter 7, §7.10, Reply to Objection 4.
    Distinction between the critique of necessity in rebus and the doctrine of primitive thisness.
    The doctrine is about individuation, not about necessary properties. Conclusion: the
    doctrine does not inherit Quine’s critique. Status: (T).


Part III: Fluid Elements of Metaphysics
Chapter 9: Causation
A9.1 What the Theories of Causation Share. Chapter 9, §9.4.2, Principle 9.3. Argument
    by analysis of the four standard theories (regularity, counterfactual dependence, powers,
     process). Conclusion: the four theories share the notion of a transfer of effect from the
     cause to the effect; the transfer is what the framework calls the causal medium. Status:
    (T).

A9.2 The Framework’s Position on the Theories of Causation. Chapter 9, §9.4.3, Principle 9.4.
    Inference to the best explanation: the general structure (transfer through a medium) is
    visible in all four theories and does the same explanatory work without committing the
    framework to any one. Conclusion: the framework does not adopt one of the four; it
    identifies the general structure that the four instantiate. Status: (E).

A9.3 Causation as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Conveyor Principle. Chapter 9, §9.5,
    Principle 9.5. Three-step argument. Step 1: the fluid element presupposes a transfer
    (D-claim, conditional on Book I’s Definition 2.2). Step 2: the transfer is causation (T-claim,
    argued by analysis of the notion of causation). Step 3: the presupposition is a metaphysical
    consequent of the framework (synthesis). Conclusion: causation is the metaphysical
    consequent of Book I’s conveyor principle. Status: (D).

A9.4 The Material Manifestation’s Causality Is a Mode. Chapter 9, §9.5.4, Principle 9.6.
    Demonstration of dependency: Book I’s Principle 16.12 (the causality rule of the Material
    Manifestation) is the Material mode of the general causal structure. Conclusion: the
    causality rule is a mode of the general causal structure, not a different relation. Status:
    (D).

A9.5 Reply to the Circularity Objection. Chapter 9, §9.8, Reply to Objection 3. Distinction
    between the transfer (primitive notion) and the relata (cause and effect). The definition
    does not define the effect as “what the transfer produces”; it defines the effect as the
    relatum of the causation that the transfer produces. Conclusion: the alleged circularity is
    only apparent. Status: (T).

Chapter 10: Relation
A10.1 What the Theories of Relation Share. Chapter 10, §10.4.2, Principle 10.3. Argument by
    analysis of the four standard theories (realism, anti-realism, trope theory, structuralism).
    Conclusion: the four theories share the notion of a connection between the terms; the
    connection is what the framework calls relation. Status: (T).

A10.2 Relation as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Relational Manifestation. Chapter 10,
    §10.5, Principle 10.5. Three-step argument. Step 1: the Relational Manifestation presup-
    poses a connection (D-claim, conditional on Book I’s Definition 7.7). Step 2: the connection
    is relation (T-claim, argued by analysis of the notion of relation). Step 3: the presupposition
    is a metaphysical consequent of the framework (synthesis). Conclusion: relation is the
    metaphysical consequent of Book I’s account of the Relational Manifestation. Status: (D).
Index of Arguments                                                                              419


A10.3 Bradley’s Regress and Light. Chapter 10, §10.6.2, Principle 10.6. Transcendental
    argument: the regress presupposes that a relation is a thing that needs to be connected to
    its relata; the presupposition is false, because light is the condition under which relation is
    possible, and the condition does not enter the regress. Conclusion: Book I’s Principle 12.3
    (light as the condition of possibility of relation) is the framework’s response to the regress.
    Status: (D).

A10.4 Reply to the Deus ex Machina Objection. Chapter 10, §10.9, Reply to Objection 2. Direct
    proof : light is introduced by Book I’s Principle 12.1 (the trans-categorical character of light)
    and Principle 12.3 (light as the condition of possibility of relation), and the introduction
    is justified by the argument of Book I’s Chapter 12 (the deadlock of the four categories).
    Conclusion: the regress’s solution is a consequence of Book I’s account of light, not a
    motivation for it. Status: (T).

Chapter 11: Light as Metaphysical Medium, Reconsidered
A11.1 The Analogy of “Substance” in Book I. Chapter 11, §11.3.2, Principle 11.1. Argument by
    analysis of Book I’s Remark 12.6 and of the definition of substance in Chapter 5. Conclusion:
    the word “substance” in Book I’s Principle 12.1 is an analogical use, whose analogy is the
    analogy between the substance-accident relation and the condition-conditioned relation;
    light is the structural condition under which the categories can be what they are. Status:
    (T).

A11.2 Causation Presupposes the Medium. Chapter 11, §11.5.1, Principle 11.3. Demonstration of
    dependency (two premises). Premise 1: causation requires a vehicle (Chapter 9). Premise 2:
    the vehicle requires a condition (the present section). Conclusion: causation presupposes
    light as the metaphysical medium. Status: (D), relative to Book I’s C7 and to Chapter 9’s
    analysis of causation.

A11.3 Relation Presupposes the Medium. Chapter 11, §11.6.1, Principle 11.4. Demonstration
    of dependency (re-examination of Book I’s regress argument in the light of Chapter 10’s
    analysis of relation). Conclusion: relation presupposes light as the metaphysical medium.
    Status: (D), relative to Book I’s Principle 12.3 and to Chapter 10’s analysis of relation.

A11.4 The Reconsideration of Light. Chapter 11, §11.7.3, Principle 11.5. Demonstration of
    dependency: the reconsideration deepens rather than revises Book I’s Principle 12.1, by
    giving the positive structure that the analogical use of “substance” gestured at. Conclusion:
    light is the metaphysical medium, the structural condition under which causation and
    relation can function as the fluid element. Status: (D).


Part IV: Governing Dynamics of Metaphysics
Chapter 13: Law
A13.1 What the Theories of Law Share. Chapter 13, §13.4.2, Principle 13.3. Argument by
    analysis of the four standard theories (regularity, necessitation, disposition, best system).
    Conclusion: the four theories share the notion of a pattern that grounds the regularity of
    the law; the pattern is what the framework calls law. Status: (T).

A13.2 Law as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Rules. Chapter 13, §13.6, Principle 13.6.
    Three-step argument. Step 1: the rules presuppose a pattern (D-claim, conditional on
    Book I’s Principle 16.1). Step 2: the pattern is law (T-claim, argued by analysis of the
    notion of law). Step 3: the presupposition is a metaphysical consequent of the framework
420                                                                          Index of Arguments


      (synthesis). Conclusion: law is the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s rules of the realms.
      Status: (D).
A13.3 The Unity of the Rules as a Consequence of Law. Chapter 13, §13.6.4, Principle 13.7.
    Demonstration of dependency: the unity of the rules of the fundamental realms (Book I,
    Principle 16.15) and of the barzakhic realms (Book I, Principle 17.11) is a consequence of
    law. Conclusion: the rules are related because they are the articulations of a single pattern.
    Status: (D).
A13.4 Law, Causation, and Relation. Chapter 13, §13.5.3, Principle 13.5. Argument by analysis
    of the three elements of the fluid triad. Conclusion: law, causation, and relation are related
    as pattern, transfer, and connection; the three are distinct, and the distinction is what
    makes the fluid element a triad. Status: (T).
A13.5 Reply to the Circularity Objection. Chapter 13, §13.9, Reply to Objection 3. Distinction
    between the pattern (primitive notion) and the formulations (rules). The definition does
    not define the rules as “what the law grounds”; it defines the rules as the formulations of
    what must be the case. Conclusion: the alleged circularity is only apparent. Status: (T).

Chapter 14: Necessity and Modality
A14.1 The Structural Laws Are Metaphysically Necessary. Chapter 14, §14.4.2, Principle 14.6.
    Demonstration of dependency: Book I’s Principle 16.7 (the structural laws are necessary)
    is a principle of metaphysical necessity grounded in essence. Conclusion: the laws are
    necessary because they are grounded in the essence of the realms, and the essence is what
    makes the laws necessary. Status: (D).
A14.2 Natural Necessity Is a Mode of Metaphysical Necessity. Chapter 14, §14.4.3, Principle 14.8.
    Demonstration of dependency: the physical laws are the Material mode of the structural laws,
    and the natural necessity is the Material mode of the metaphysical necessity. Conclusion:
    natural necessity is a mode of metaphysical necessity. Status: (D).
A14.3 The Relation Among the Four Kinds. Chapter 14, §14.5.4, Principle 14.10. Argument by
    analysis of the four kinds (logical, metaphysical, natural, normative). Conclusion: the four
    kinds are related as form, ground, mode, and posterior. Status: (T).
A14.4 The Grounding of Necessity. Chapter 14, §14.6.2, Principle 14.11. Argument by analysis
    of the four kinds and of the modal space. Conclusion: the necessary, within Ω, is not a
    primitive status; it is grounded in the four structures (form, essence, law, good). Status:
    (T).
A14.5 Reply to Quine’s Critique of de re Modality. Chapter 14, §14.9, Reply to Objection 1.
    Reductio of the premise that necessity is a property of propositions alone. The framework’s
    premise is that necessity is a status that things have in virtue of their essence. Conclusion:
    Quine’s conclusion—that de re modality is unintelligible—does not follow. Status: (T).
A14.6 Reply to the Circularity Objection. Chapter 14, §14.9, Reply to Objection 3. Distinction
    between the “cannot be otherwise” (primitive) and the definiendum (necessity). Conclusion:
    the alleged circularity is only apparent. Status: (T).

Chapter 15: The Modal Space Ω Reconsidered
A15.1 The Framework’s Position on Ω. Chapter 15, §15.4.2, Principle 15.1. Demonstration of
    dependency: Ω is a structure of possible configurations of essences and laws. Conclusion:
    the framework adopts configurationalism. Status: (D), relative to Book I’s Principle 37.1
    and to the framework’s accounts of essence and law.
Index of Arguments                                                                           421


A15.2 The Stratification of Ω. Chapter 15, §15.5.1, Principle 15.2. Direct proof (two premises).
    Premise 1: the four kinds of necessity are distinct, each grounded in a different structure
    (Chapter 14). Premise 2: if Ω were flat, the four kinds would be indistinguishable within it.
    Conclusion: Ω is stratified, and the strata are the four kinds of necessity. Status: (T).
A15.3 The Grounding of Ω Is a Family of Analogous Relations. Chapter 15, §15.6.2, Princi-
    ple 15.3. Demonstration of dependency: each stratum is grounded in a different structure,
    and each structure is grounded in God through a different mode. Conclusion: the grounding
    of Ω in God is a family of analogous relations, not one relation. Status: (D).
A15.4 The Relation Between Ω and the Throne-Domain. Chapter 15, §15.6.3, Principle 15.4.
    Argument by analysis of Book I’s Principle 36.1 and Principle 37.2. Conclusion: Ω is the
    space of possibilities from which the seven realms are actualized; the Throne-Domain is
    the encompassing created order in which the seven realms are situated. Status: (E).
A15.5 The Relation Between Ω and Light. Chapter 15, §15.7.2, Principle 15.5. Demonstration of
    dependency: both Ω and light are grounded in God, and the two groundings are analogous
    modes of the same grounding relation. Conclusion: Ω and light are related as the space of
    possibilities and the medium of actualization. Status: (D). (The argument answers Book I’s
    Q4.)


Part V: Context of Metaphysics
Chapter 17: Realms as Contexts, Deepened
A17.1 The Capacity Is Structural. Chapter 17, §17.4.1, Principle 17.3. Demonstration of
    dependency: the capacity of a realm is the structural range of what the mode of existence
    admits. Conclusion: the capacity is a set of kinds, not a count of instances. Status: (D),
    relative to Book I’s Principle 7.2 and to Definition 17.1.
A17.2 The Existential Openness of the Realm. Chapter 17, §17.4.3, Principle 17.4. Direct proof
    from the definition of capacity and from Book I’s Principle 7.2. Conclusion: the capacity is
    open in the sense that it is a structural range, not a finite enumeration. Status: (T).
A17.3 Realm-as-Context as the Metaphysical Consequent of the Existential Context. Chapter 17,
    §17.6, Principle 17.5. Three-step argument. Step 1: the existential context presupposes
    a condition (D-claim, conditional on Book I’s Definition 10.3). Step 2: the condition is
    realm-as-context (T-claim, argued by analysis of the notion). Step 3: the presupposition is
    a metaphysical consequent of the framework (synthesis). Conclusion: realm-as-context is
    the metaphysical consequent of Book I’s definitions of fundamental realm and existential
    context. Status: (D).

Chapter 18: The Barzakhic as a Metaphysical Category
A18.1 The Barzakhic Is a Mode of Existence, Not a Function. Chapter 18, §18.5.2, Principle 18.3.
    Direct proof (three steps). Premises: a function is what a thing does; a mode of existence
    is what a thing is; a thing can lose its function without ceasing to be the thing it is; the
    barzakhic can lose its function of mediation without ceasing to be the barzakhic, but cannot
    lose its mode of existence without ceasing to be the barzakhic. Conclusion: the barzakhic
    is a mode of existence, not a function. Status: (D).
A18.2 The Barzakhic Is a Passage, Not a Relation. Chapter 18, §18.6.2, Principle 18.4. Direct
    proof (three steps). Premises: a relation connects terms; a passage transforms terms; the
    connection and the transformation are distinct. Conclusion: the barzakhic is the passage,
    not the relation. Status: (D).
422                                                                              Index of Arguments


A18.3 The Answer to Q10. Chapter 18, §18.7, Principle 18.5. Direct proof from the definition of
    the barzakhic category (Definition 18.1) and Book I’s Definition 8.1. Conclusion: identities
    are not realized in the barzakhic realms as they are in the fundamental realms; they are
    present through the barzakhic realms. Status: (D).

Chapter 19: Non-Passage and Presence
A19.1 Non-Passage. Chapter 19, §19.7, Principle 19.3. Direct proof (four steps). Premises:
    each realm has a determinate capacity (Chapter 17); the form an identity takes in a realm
    is fixed by the identity and the realm’s capacity, not by what the identity became in the
    intermediate realms; the hubs mediate the relation without requiring the identity’s traversal;
    the manifestation of an identity in a realm is the product of the identity and the receiving
    realm. Conclusion: the presence or effect of an identity in a lower realm does not require
    that the identity pass existentially through every realm that lies between. Status: (T),
    relative to the accounts of realms, barzakhic realms, and manifestation.

A19.2 Presence as Structural Realization. Chapter 19, §19.5, Principle 19.11. Direct proof from
    the framework’s account of realms and of the manifestation relation. Conclusion: the
    presence of an identity in a realm is the structural realization of the identity, or of its effect,
    in the realm, according to the realm’s capacity. Status: (T).

Chapter 20: The Context of the Whole
A20.1 The Whole Is Not a Realm. Chapter 20, §20.4, Principle 20.6. Direct proof (four steps).
    Premises: a realm is an independently real mode of existence with its own capacity and
    rules; the context of the whole is the order in which the realms stand; if the context of
    the whole were a realm, it would have a mode of existence of its own, and the realms
    would stand in a realm among realms. Conclusion: the context of the whole is not a realm.
    Status: (T).

A20.2 The Context of the Whole Is the Condition of the Contexts of the Parts. Chapter 20,
    §20.5, Principle 20.9. Direct proof from the definition of the context of the whole and from
    the framework’s account of realms. Conclusion: without the context of the whole, the
    contexts of the parts would not be a plurality of ordered realms. Status: (T).

A20.3 The Whole Is the Order of the Parts. Chapter 20, §20.6, Principle 20.12. Direct proof
    from the definition of the context of the whole and from the framework’s account of realms.
    Conclusion: the whole is the order of the parts, not the sum of the parts, not a part of
    itself, and not a stage that comes after the parts. Status: (T).

A20.4 The Context of the Whole Points Beyond Itself. Chapter 20, §20.7, Principle 20.15. Direct
    proof from the definition of the context of the whole and from the framework’s account of
    the divine ground. Conclusion: the context of the whole is created, and the created order
    points beyond itself to its Creator. Status: (T).


Part VI: Viability as Integration
Chapter 21: From Structural to Metaphysical Viability
A21.1 The Transition Is From the Cognitive to the Existential. Chapter 21, §21.4, Principle 21.8.
    Direct proof from the definitions of structural viability and of the two kinds of context.
    Conclusion: the transition from structural to metaphysical viability is the transition from
    the viability of the relation in a cognitive context to the viability of the relation in an
    existential context. Status: (T).
Index of Arguments                                                                              423


A21.2 The Three Components in Their Metaphysical Form. Chapter 21, §21.5, Principle 21.11.
    Direct proof from the definition of metaphysical viability (Definition 21.14) and from
    the distinction between the cognitive and the existential context. Conclusion: the three
    components are the same in their metaphysical form as in their structural form; what
    differs is the context. Status: (T).

A21.3 The Relation Between Structural and Metaphysical Viability. Chapter 21, §21.7, Princi-
    ple 21.18. Direct proof from the definition of the two concepts and from the distinction
    between the two kinds of context. Conclusion: structural viability and metaphysical
    viability are the same concept applied to two kinds of context. Status: (T).

Chapter 22: Viability and Essence
A22.1 Essence Is Subject to Viability. Chapter 22, §22.4, Principle 22.6. Direct proof (five
    steps). Premises: the essence is the structural determination that constitutes the identity;
    the essence is expressed in manifestations in a realm; the viability is the structural character
    of the relation between the identity and its manifestations; the essence is the identity that
    the relation is between. Conclusion: essence is subject to viability. Status: (T).

A22.2 Fidelity of Essence. Chapter 22, §22.6, Principle 22.13. Direct proof from the definition
    of metaphysical viability and from the definition of essence. Conclusion: the fidelity of an
    essence is the extent to which the manifestations of the essence in the realm preserve the
    essential determination of the essence. Status: (T).

A22.3 Sustainability of Essence. Chapter 22, §22.7, Principle 22.17. Direct proof from the
    definition of metaphysical viability and from the framework’s account of the cost of cognition
    (read in its metaphysical form). Conclusion: the sustainability of an essence is the condition
    under which the cost of expressing the essence in the realm does not exceed what the realm
    can bear. Status: (T).

A22.4 Recoverability of Essence. Chapter 22, §22.8, Principle 22.21. Direct proof from the
    definition of metaphysical viability and from the framework’s account of the singularity.
    Conclusion: the recoverability of an essence is the condition under which the essence retains
    its structural capacity to manifest in the realm. Status: (T).

A22.5 The Essence Is Subject to Viability; the Accident Is Not. Chapter 22, §22.9, Principle 22.26.
    Direct proof from the definitions of essence and accident and from the definition of viable
    essence. Conclusion: the essence is subject to viability; the accident is not. Status: (T).

Chapter 23: Viability and Causation
A23.1 Causation Is Subject to Viability. Chapter 23, §23.4, Principle 23.6. Direct proof (five
    steps). Premises: causation is the structural relation in which an identity brings about
    a change; the causal relation is a relation of expression; the viability is the structural
    character of the relation between an identity and its manifestations; the causal relation is
    the relation of expression. Conclusion: causation is subject to viability. Status: (T).

A23.2 Fidelity of Causation. Chapter 23, §23.6, Principle 23.13. Direct proof from the definition
    of metaphysical viability and from the definition of causation. Conclusion: the fidelity of a
    causal relation is the extent to which the effect preserves the essential determination of the
    cause. Status: (T).

A23.3 Sustainability of Causation. Chapter 23, §23.7, Principle 23.17. Direct proof from
    the definition of metaphysical viability and from the framework’s account of the cost of
424                                                                           Index of Arguments


      cognition. Conclusion: the sustainability of a causal relation is the condition under which
      the cost of the effect does not exceed what the realm can bear. Status: (T).

A23.4 Recoverability of Causation. Chapter 23, §23.8, Principle 23.21. Direct proof from the
    definition of metaphysical viability and from the framework’s account of the singularity.
    Conclusion: the recoverability of a causal relation is the condition under which the cause
    retains its structural capacity to produce the effect. Status: (T).

A23.5 Causation Is Not Mere Succession. Chapter 23, §23.9, Principle 23.25. Direct proof
    from the definition of causation and from the definition of viable causation. Conclusion:
    causation is the relation of expression; the succession is the temporal ordering of events; the
    viability of causation is the character of the expression, not of the succession. Status: (T).

Chapter 24: Viability and Modality
A24.1 Modality Is Subject to Viability. Chapter 24, §24.4, Principle 24.5. Direct proof (five
    steps). Premises: modality is the structure of the possible, the actual, and the necessary;
    the modal relation is the relation between a possibility and its actualization; the viability
    is the structural character of the relation; the modal relation is the relation between the
    possibility and its actualization. Conclusion: modality is subject to viability. Status: (T).

A24.2 Fidelity of Modality. Chapter 24, §24.6, Principle 24.12. Direct proof from the definition
    of metaphysical viability and from the definition of modality. Conclusion: the fidelity of a
    modal relation is the extent to which the actualization preserves the essential determination
    of the possibility. Status: (T).

A24.3 Sustainability of Modality. Chapter 24, §24.7, Principle 24.16. Direct proof from the
    definition of metaphysical viability and from the framework’s account of the cost of cognition.
    Conclusion: the sustainability of a modal relation is the condition under which the cost of
    the actualization does not exceed what the realm can bear. Status: (T).

A24.4 Recoverability of Modality. Chapter 24, §24.8, Principle 24.20. Direct proof from the
    definition of metaphysical viability and from the framework’s account of the singularity.
    Conclusion: the recoverability of a modal relation is the condition under which the possibility
    retains its structural capacity to be actualized. Status: (T).

A24.5 Modal Status Is Not Modal Viability. Chapter 24, §24.9, Principle 24.24. Direct proof
    from the definition of modality and from the definition of viable modality. Conclusion: the
    modal status is a status of the possibility; the modal viability is a character of the relation
    between the possibility and its actualization; neither entails the other. Status: (T).

A24.6 The Four Kinds of Viable Modality. Chapter 24, §24.10, Principle 24.27. Direct proof
    from the four kinds of necessity (Chapter 14) and from the definition of viable modality.
    Conclusion: each kind of necessity has its own modal viability, and the four kinds are
    related as the four kinds of necessity are related. Status: (T).

Chapter 25: The Metaphysics of Viability
A25.1 The Integration of the Four Columns. Chapter 25, §25.5, Principle 25.7. Direct proof
    from the four-column framework of Book I and from the definition of the metaphysics of
    viability. Conclusion: the four columns integrate in the metaphysics of viability as the
    four aspects of the conditions under which an identity can be viable (fixed elements: the
    subject; fluid element: the medium; governing dynamics: the form; context: the setting).
    Status: (T).
Index of Arguments                                                                            425


A25.2 The Three Domains Are Three Aspects of One Relation. Chapter 25, §25.6, Principle 25.10.
    Direct proof from the applications of viability to the three domains and from the definition
    of the metaphysics of viability. Conclusion: essence, causation, and modality are three
    aspects of the relation between an identity and its manifestations (essence: what the
    identity is; causation: how it reaches its manifestations; modality: whether and how it can
    be manifested). Status: (T).
A25.3 The Metaphysical Conditions of Viability. Chapter 25, §25.7, Principle 25.13. Direct
    proof from the three components of metaphysical viability and from the applications to
    the three domains. Conclusion: the metaphysical conditions of viability are the fidelity,
    sustainability, and recoverability of the relation between an identity and its manifestations
    in each realm. Status: (T).


Part VII: Divine Ground and Modal Order
Chapter 26: The Metaphysics of Transcendence
A26.1 The Ontological Mode of Transcendence. Chapter 26, §26.5.1, Principle 26.10. Demon-
    stration of dependency: God is the Creator of all that is not God; the created order is all
    that is not God. Conclusion: the created order depends on God for its being. Status: (D).
A26.2 The Epistemic Mode of Transcendence. Chapter 26, §26.5.2, Principle 26.11. Demon-
    stration of dependency: the modal space is the order of the possible; the order is given by
    God; the intelligibility of the created order is the intelligibility of the order. Conclusion:
    the created order depends on God for its intelligibility. Status: (D).
A26.3 The Relational Mode of Transcendence. Chapter 26, §26.5.3, Principle 26.12. Demon-
    stration of dependency: light is the medium of relation; light is created and given by God;
    the relations of the created order are carried by the light. Conclusion: the created order
    depends on God for its relations. Status: (D).
A26.4 Transcendence Is the Condition of the Four Columns. Chapter 26, §26.6, Principle 26.15.
    Demonstration of dependency: the four columns describe the created order; the created
    order depends on God; the transcendent relation is the condition under which the four
    columns can describe it. Conclusion: transcendence is not one of the four columns; it is
    the condition of the four columns. Status: (D).

Chapter 27: Creation and Sustaining
A27.1 Creation and Sustaining Are Two Modes of One Relation. Chapter 27, §27.6, Prin-
    ciple 27.12. Direct proof from Chapter 26’s definition of transcendence and from the
    definitions of creation and sustaining. Conclusion: the relation is one (the dependence of
    the created order on God); the modes are two (the establishment and the maintenance of
    the dependence); the modes are modes of the relation, not separate relations. Status: (D).
A27.2 Creation Is the Act That Establishes the Created Order. Chapter 27, §27.7, Principle 27.15.
    Demonstration of dependency: the four columns describe the created order; the created order
    depends on God for its being; creation is the act by which the dependence is established.
    Conclusion: creation is the act that establishes the created order. Status: (D).
A27.3 Sustaining Is the Act That Maintains the Created Order. Chapter 27, §27.8, Princi-
    ple 27.17. Demonstration of dependency: the four columns describe the created order; the
    created order depends on God for its being at every moment; sustaining is the act by which
    the dependence is maintained. Conclusion: sustaining is the act that maintains the created
    order. Status: (D).

Chapter 28: The Modal Space as Created
A28.1 The Createdness of the Logical Stratum. Chapter 28, §28.5.1, Principle 28.7. Demonstra-
    tion of dependency: the modal space is created; the logical stratum is a stratum of the
    modal space. Conclusion: the logical stratum is created. Status: (D).

A28.2 The Createdness of the Metaphysical Stratum. Chapter 28, §28.5.2, Principle 28.8.
    Demonstration of dependency: the modal space is created; the metaphysical stratum is a
    stratum of the modal space. Conclusion: the metaphysical stratum is created. Status: (D).

A28.3 The Createdness of the Natural Stratum. Chapter 28, §28.5.3, Principle 28.9. Demonstra-
    tion of dependency: the modal space is created; the natural stratum is a stratum of the
    modal space. Conclusion: the natural stratum is created. Status: (D).

A28.4 The Createdness of the Normative Stratum. Chapter 28, §28.5.4, Principle 28.10. Demon-
    stration of dependency: the modal space is created; the normative stratum is a stratum of
    the modal space. Conclusion: the normative stratum is created. Status: (D).

A28.5 The Createdness of the Necessary. Chapter 28, §28.6, Principle 28.12. Direct proof (three
    parts). Part 1: createdness is a claim about grounding, not about modal status. Part 2:
    the necessary is the form of the created order. Part 3: the createdness of the necessary does
    not make it arbitrary. Conclusion: the necessary is necessary (in its stratum) because it is
    the form of the created order; it is created because the form is given by God. Status: (D).

A28.6 The Created Modal Space Is Not Any of the Four. Chapter 28, §28.7, Principle 28.16.
    Argument by analysis of the four false conceptions (modal realism, Platonism about
    possibilities, the doctrine of divine ideas, fictionalism). Conclusion: the created modal
    space is not any of the four; it is a created structure of essences and laws. Status: (D).

A28.7 The Created Modal Space Is the Order of the Four Columns. Chapter 28, §28.8, Princi-
    ple 28.18. Demonstration of dependency: the four columns describe the created order; the
    created order is possible in the modal space; the modal space is the order of the possible.
    Conclusion: the created modal space is the order in which the four columns describe the
    created order. Status: (D).

Chapter 29: Providence, Knowledge, and Choice Reconsidered
A29.1 The Ordering Mode of Providence. Chapter 29, §29.5.1, Principle 29.9. Demonstration
    of dependency: God creates the order; the order is the structure of the created order.
    Conclusion: God orders the created order toward the ends that God wills. Status: (D).

A29.2 The Sustaining Mode of Providence. Chapter 29, §29.5.2, Principle 29.10. Demonstration
    of dependency: God sustains the created order; the created order is ordered; the sustaining
    is the maintenance of the order. Conclusion: God sustains the order of the created order
    at every moment. Status: (D).

A29.3 The Directing Mode of Providence. Chapter 29, §29.5.3, Principle 29.11. Demonstration
    of dependency: God wills the ends; the ends are the orientation of the order. Conclusion:
    God directs the created order toward its ends. Status: (D).

A29.4 Divine Knowledge of the Created Modal Space. Chapter 29, §29.6.2, Principle 29.13.
    Demonstration of dependency: Ω is created; the two kinds of knowledge are the knowledge
    of Ω. Conclusion: the two kinds of divine knowledge are the knowledge of the created
    order; the knowledge is distinct from the creation. Status: (D).

A29.5 The Modal Status of the Future. Chapter 29, §29.8, Principle 29.19. Demonstration of
    dependency: the future is part of X; X is selected within Ω; the selection is the creature’s.
    Conclusion: the future is the selected-but-not-yet-actualized part of X; it is real, and its
    reality is the reality of the selected chain. Status: (D).

Index of Formalizations

A Note on the Index
This index lists the formalizations of Book II: the symbolic notation, the formal expressions, the
formal structures, and the tables that carry the book’s analytical apparatus. Its purpose is to
make the framework’s formalizations visible in one place.
    Book II uses formalization even more sparingly than Book I. Where Book I formalized a
small number of definitions and principles, Book II formalizes almost nothing: its apparatus
is almost entirely prose, and its precision is carried by the definitions, the status labels, the
enumerated arguments, and the tables. The formalizations that appear in Book II are few, and
each is offered at the strength of a summary: the prose carries the principle, and the symbol
or the table abbreviates the prose. A reader who has followed the prose has the framework; a
reader who has followed this index has the shorthand.
    The index covers the metaphysical body of Book II only. It does not cover Book I, whose
formalizations are indexed in Book I’s own Index of Formalizations. Where Book II uses a symbol
that Book I introduced (notably Ω, X, and the core commitments C1 –C13 ), the entry states
that the symbol is inherited and points to the chapter of Book II in which it is used.


A Note on the Sparsity of Formalization in Book II
Book II’s subject is metaphysical: the fixed elements, the fluid elements, the governing dynamics,
and the contexts that the four-column framework of Book I presupposes. The subject is
structural, but it is not mathematical, and the framework’s precision in Book II is philosophical,
not computational. The book uses:

  • the status labels (A), (T), (E), (Q), (S), and (D), defined in the front matter and used
    throughout;

  • the reference codes [B2-##-m] and [D##-m], defined in the front matter and used through-
    out;

  • the four-column framework in the form in which Book I stated it, used throughout as the
    analytical scaffolding;

  • a small number of symbolic abbreviations, chiefly the modal space Ω, the actualization
    chain X, the structural order R, and the core commitments C1–C13;

  • the triads of the fixed, fluid, and governing elements, stated as tables in Chapters 8, 12,
    and 16;

  • the dependency map of Chapter 43, stated as a table;

  • a family of argument forms (reductio, transcendental argument, three-step argument,
    removal test, reducibility test, argument by analysis, demonstration of dependency, diagonal
    construction), named in the prose and used in the chapters.
430                                                                       Index of Formalizations


   The formalizations in Book II are the labels, the codes, the symbols, the tables, and the
argument forms. There is no formal proof in the book, in the sense in which a proof is a derivation
from axioms by inference rules. The book’s arguments are given in prose, and the tables and
symbols are summaries of the prose, offered at the strength the arguments support.

Front Matter: Epistemic Status Labels
The six labels. (A) Axiom or foundational commitment; (T) Argued; (E) Estimate; (Q) Open
epistemic question; (S) Speculation; (D) Dependent on Book I. The labels are stated in prose in
3_Epistemic_Status_Labels, with a summary table. The labels are not formal symbols in the
mathematical sense; they are abbreviations of the kind of claim each carries.
    The reference codes. [B2-##-m] for Book II sources; [D##-m] for Book I references. The
codes abbreviate a citation of the form “chapter ##, source number m” of the respective book.

Chapter 2: The Four-Column Framework as a Method of Ontology
The four columns of metaphysical inquiry. Stated in prose in §2.4 as four definitions (Defs. 2.2–2.5).
No symbolic notation is used; the four columns are named, not symbolized.
    The removal test at the metaphysical level. Stated in prose in §2.5 as Pr. 2.6. The schema: a
metaphysical inquiry that omits one of the four columns is incomplete. The schema is a summary
of the argument in prose; it is not a formal inference rule.
    The reducibility test at the metaphysical level. Stated in prose in §2.6 as Pr. 2.7. The schema:
no fifth column is needed; every candidate fifth column reduces to one of the four. The schema
summarizes the case-by-case examination of the candidates.
    The distinction between analytical and ontological at the metaphysical level. Stated in prose
in §2.7 as Pr. 2.8 (D). The distinction is the metaphysical application of Book I’s Pr. 1.1; no
symbolic notation is used.

Chapter 3: The Epistemic Status of Metaphysical Claims
The three criteria for assigning status. Stated in prose in §3.4 as Defs. 3.2–3.4 (A): the first
criterion (adopted vs. argued), the second criterion (demonstration vs. structural adequacy), the
third criterion (independence vs. dependence on Book I). No symbolic notation is used.
    The six labels applied to metaphysical claims. Stated in prose in §3.5 as Defs. 3.5–3.10. The
definitions are prose; they specify what each label means when the claim it labels is metaphysical.
    The signature label of Book II. Stated in prose in §3.5.6 as Pr. 3.11 (A): (D) is the book’s
most common label. No symbolic notation is used.
    The truth of a metaphysical claim. Stated in prose in §3.6 as Pr. 3.12 (T): the truth is
structural adequacy. No symbolic notation is used.

Chapter 4: The Inherited Core: C1–C13
The thirteen core commitments. Stated in prose in §4.4 as Defs. 4.1–4.13 (A), one per commitment.
The commitments are named C1 through C13 and grouped in three families (methodological,
ontological, structural-metaphysical) in §4.5.1. The notation C1–C13 abbreviates the names of
the commitments as Book I’s Chapter E identified them.
   The relations among the families. Stated in prose in §4.5.2. No symbolic notation is used.
   The map of Book II’s parts to the core. Stated as a table in §4.5.3. The table is the
formalization; it maps each part of Book II to the core commitments on which it depends.
   The book’s conditional architecture. Stated in prose in §4.7 as Pr. 4.14 (A). No symbolic
notation is used.

Chapter 5: Substance
The definition of substance. Stated in prose in §5.3.1 as Def. 5.1 (A): substance is the metaphysical
ground of a thing’s being the same one through change and of its being the subject of its properties.
No symbolic notation is used.

    The definition of accident. Stated in prose in §5.3.3 as Def. 5.2 (A). No symbolic notation is

    The three-step argument. Stated in prose in §5.6 as the argument for Pr. 5.3 (D). Step 1: the

Chapter 10: Relation
The definition of relation. Stated in prose in §10.3.1 as Def. 10.1 (A): the real connection between
two or more terms. No symbolic notation is used.
    The definition of relatum. Stated in prose in §10.3.3 as Def. 10.2 (A). No symbolic notation
is used.
    What the theories of relation share. Stated in prose in §10.4.2 as Pr. 10.3 (T). Argument by

    The framework’s position on the theories. Stated in prose in §10.4.3 as Pr. 10.4 (E).
    Relation as the metaphysical consequent of the Relational Manifestation. Stated in prose in
§10.5 as Pr. 10.5 (D), argued by the three-step argument.
    Bradley’s regress and light. Stated in prose in §10.6.2 as Pr. 10.6 (D). The argument is the
framework’s transcendental diagnosis of the regress’s premise: the premise is that a relation is

relation, and the condition does not enter the regress.

Part III: Formal Structures
Book II uses a small family of argument forms. Each is named in the prose and used in
the chapters; none is presented in symbolic notation, because the book’s arguments are prose
arguments. The forms are listed here so that the reader can see what kinds of argument the
book gives.

The Reductio
The reductio proceeds by supposing the negation of what is to be proved, deriving a contradiction,
and concluding that the supposition is false. Book II uses the reductio in the following places.

The Three-Step Argument
The three-step argument is Book II’s most characteristic argument form, used throughout Part II.
It proceeds in three steps: (1) the analytical role presupposes a ground; (2) the ground is
identified with a metaphysical notion; (3) the presupposition is identified as a metaphysical
consequent of Book I’s framework. The conclusion is a (D) claim.

         Three-step argument                      Ch.   Conclusion (D)

         Thisness as the metaphysical conse-      7     Pr. 7.3

The Removal Test and the Reducibility Test
The removal test and the reducibility test are inherited from Book I’s method and applied at
the metaphysical level in Chapter 2. The removal test shows that each of the four columns is
necessary (T relative to the commitment that we can recognize an explanatory failure); the
reducibility test shows that no fifth column is needed (E).

The Argument by Analysis
The argument by analysis proceeds by examining a set of positions and showing that they share
a common structure, which the framework then names. Book II uses the argument by analysis
in the following places.

         Argument by analysis                     Ch.   Common structure named
         What the theories of causation share     9     The transfer (causation).
         What the theories of relation share      10    The connection (relation).
         What the theories of law share           13    The pattern (law).
         The four theories of modal status        15    The stratified configuration.
         (via the framework’s position on Ω)

The Demonstration of Dependency
The demonstration of dependency is the argument form of the (D) claims. It proceeds by
showing that the conclusion follows from a principle of Book I. Book II uses the demonstration
of dependency throughout, wherever a (D) claim is established. The principal instances are the
seven three-step arguments listed above, and the arguments for the principles that are (D) but
are not three-step (e.g., Pr. 9.6, the Material Manifestation’s causality as a mode).
440                                                                          Index of Formalizations


The Diagonal Construction
The diagonal construction is used in one place: the second argument for the impossibility of
super-identity (Chapter 27, §27.5). The argument proceeds by constructing, from any finite list
of contexts surveyed by a subject, a context outside the list. The construction uses the list’s
own content as a fixed element of a new context, and the new context is outside the list. The
construction is stated in prose, not in symbols.


Part IV: The Status of Formalization in Book II
Book II uses formalization at a specific strength, and the strength is stated here, in parallel with
Book I’s statement of the same point.
    Formalization here means brief notation, enumerated tables, and epistemic labels. It does not
mean full formal proof, axiomatic derivation, or mathematical formulation. The book’s aim is
precision of presentation, not justification; the precision is carried by the prose, and the tables
and symbols are summaries.
    Three consequences follow, and each is worth stating.
    First consequence: the prose is primary. Every principle appears first in full philosophical
prose. The tables and symbols abbreviate the prose. The prose can stand without the symbols;
the symbols cannot stand without the prose. A reader who has followed the prose has the
framework; a reader who has followed only the tables has the framework’s summary.
    Second consequence: the tables carry the analytical structure. Book II’s analytical structure
is carried chiefly by the tables: the table of substance in the seven realms (Ch. 5), of essence
(Ch. 6), of thisness (Ch. 7), of the triad of fixed elements (Ch. 8), of causation (Ch. 9), of relation
(Ch. 10), of light (Ch. 11), of the fluid triad (Ch. 12), of law (Ch. 13), of necessity (Ch. 14), of
Ω (Ch. 15), of the governing triad (Ch. 16), of capacity (Ch. 17), of the barzakhic (Ch. 18), of
the four strata (Ch. 15), of the three modes of transcendence (Ch. 26), of the three modes of
providence (Ch. 29), of the four modes of the createdness of Ω (Ch. 28), and of the four-column
structure of the metaphysics of viability (Ch. 25). These tables are Book II’s formal apparatus
in the primary sense; the symbols are secondary.
    Third consequence: formalization summarizes, and the argument justifies. The tables and
symbols summarize the principles and the arguments; the argument is the place where a principle
is assessed. A principle is justified by its argument, and the table or symbol is a way of seeing
the principle.

The count is small, and the smallness is the point. Book II uses formalization where it aids
precision—chiefly the tables of the seven realms, the tables of the triads, the tables of the
strata, the table of the dependency map—and it withholds formalization where formalization
would substitute for understanding. The tables are Book II’s formal apparatus; the prose is its
substance.


A Note on the Absence of Symbolic Proof
Book II contains no symbolic proof, in the sense of a derivation from axioms by inference rules.
The book’s arguments are prose arguments; the tables and symbols are summaries of the prose.
This is a deliberate choice: the book’s subject—the metaphysics of viability—is structural but
not mathematical, and the book’s precision is philosophical, not computational.
    The reader who wishes for symbolic proof is invited to provide it where the prose admits of
it. The framework’s claim is that the prose is assessable on its own, and that the tables and
symbols are a help, not a substitute. Where the prose is not assessable without the tables—as in
the dependency map of Chapter 43—the tables are the formalization, and they are offered at the
strength of the audit’s method.

End of the Index of Formalizations.

Index of Cross-References to Book I

A Note on the Index
This index collects every reference that Book II makes to Book I. Each entry gives the Book I
principle, definition, theorem, or remark; a one-sentence summary of it; the place or places in
Book II where it is used; and the kind of use (presupposition, dependent claim, coherence test,
or structural note).
    The references are stated in the form in which Book II states them: Principle X.Y, Definition
X.Y, Theorem X.Y, Remark X.Y, and the core commitments C1 through C13. The Book I
chapter numbers are given in parentheses, and the reader who wishes to see the principle in its
own place in Book I is directed to that chapter.


A Note on the Version of Book I
The reader should know that Book II’s citations do not all correspond to the text of Book I as it
currently stands. Book II was written against an elaborated version of Book I that included,
at the time of writing, the seven-realm ontology, the modal space Ω, the Throne-Domain, the
Divine Ground, the trans-categorical triad, and a core of thirteen commitments. The version of
Book I currently in circulation presents the purely epistemological framework, with a core of ten
commitments (C1–C10 in Chapter 43) and an explicit deferral of ontology to later volumes.
    The entries below record what Book II cites. Where the citation cannot be matched to
the current text of Book I, the entry says so. The mismatch is a fact about the two books’
composition, not about the reader’s understanding, and it is stated here so that the reader is not
misled by a citation that points to a chapter that does not say what Book II says it says.


Part I: Foundations and Method (Book I, Chapters 1–5)
Definition 1.1 (Explanatory Cognition). Cognition whose aim is to understand how some
     things stand to one another. (Book I, Ch. 1.) Use in Book II: Ch. 2, §2.3.1; Ch. 7.
     Kind: presupposition (the four-column framework applies to metaphysical inquiry because
     metaphysical inquiry is explanatory cognition).

Definition 2.1 (Fixed Element). An entity held invariant in an explanation of how things
     stand. (Book I, Ch. 6; cited by Book II as Def. 2.1.) Use in Book II: Ch. 5, §5.6.1; Ch. 8,
     §8.3. Kind: presupposition for the (D) claim that substance is the metaphysical consequent
     of the fixed element.

Definition 2.2 (Fluid Element). What conveys effect between fixed elements in an expla-
     nation. (Book I, Ch. 6; cited by Book II as Def. 2.2.) Use in Book II: Ch. 9, §9.5.1;
     Ch. 10, §10.5.1; Ch. 12, §12.3. Kind: presupposition for the (D) claims about causation
     and relation.
444                                                         Index of Cross-References to Book I


Definition 2.3 (Governing Dynamics). The rule of the conveyance. (Book I, Ch. 6; cited
     by Book II as Def. 2.3.) Use in Book II: Ch. 2, §2.4.3. Kind: presupposition.

Definition 2.4 (Context). The frame in which cognition occurs. (Book I, Ch. 6; cited by
     Book II as Def. 2.4.) Use in Book II: Ch. 2, §2.4.4. Kind: presupposition.

Principle 3.1 (Four-Column Principle). Every explanatory cognition requires the four columns;
     they are jointly necessary (T) and jointly sufficient (E). (Book I, Ch. 7; cited by Book II as
     Pr. 3.1.) Use in Book II: Ch. 2; Ch. 4 (C1–C13); Ch. 25, §25.5; Ch. 31. Kind: presupposition
     and (D) source.

Principle 3.2 (Distinctness of the Four Roles). No role is supplied by another. (Book I,
     Ch. 7; cited by Book II as Pr. 3.2.) Use in Book II: Ch. 2. Kind: presupposition.

Principle 4.1 (Conveyor Principle). No explanation of how one fixed element bears on
     another is complete without a fluid element. (Book I, Ch. 8; cited by Book II as Pr. 4.1.)
    Use in Book II: Ch. 4 (C8); Ch. 9, §9.5. Kind: presupposition; (D) source for the claim
     that causation is the metaphysical consequent of the conveyor principle.

Principle 4.2 (Non-Sequential Connectivity). The conveyor need not pass through every
     intermediate element. (Book I, Ch. 9; cited by Book II as Pr. 4.2.) Use in Book II: Ch. 9,
     §9.5.4; Ch. 11, §11.6. Kind: presupposition.

Definition 5.1 (Openness of Relations). Every manifestation can become a fixed element
     of a further context. (Book I, Ch. 11; cited by Book II as Def. 5.1, C11.) Use in Book II:
     Ch. 4 (C11); Ch. 11, §11.3; Ch. 27, §27.5. Kind: (A) core commitment C11.

Principle 5.1 (Context-Dependence). Fixedness and fluidity are roles, not essences. (Book I,
     Ch. 10; cited by Book II as Pr. 5.1.) Use in Book II: Ch. 2; Ch. 8, §8.2; Ch. 10, §10.3.
    Kind: presupposition.

Principle 5.2 (Infinity of Contexts). The contexts are not finite in number. (Book I, Ch. 11;
     cited by Book II as Pr. 5.2.) Use in Book II: Ch. 4; Ch. 11, §11.4; Ch. 27. Kind:
     presupposition.

Principle 6.1 (Impossibility of Super-Identity). No finite subject can know all manifesta-
     tions in all contexts. (Book I, Ch. 27; cited by Book II as Pr. 6.1.) Use in Book II: Ch. 1;
     Ch. 27. Kind: presupposition for the derived impossibility arguments.

Definitions 6.2–6.4 (Three Criteria of Context Validity). Cross- checkability, minimal-
     ity, consistency. (Book I, Ch. 21; cited by Book II as Prs. 6.2–6.4.) Use in Book II: Ch. 21.
     Kind: (A) presupposition.

Definition 6.2 (Viability). The structural character of the relation between an identity and
     its manifestations, in three respects. (Book I, Ch. 36; cited by Book II as Def. 6.2, C11 in
     the C-list.) Use in Book II: Ch. 21, §21.3; Ch. 25. Kind: (D) source for the metaphysical
     account of viability.

Principle 1.1 (Cognitive/Ontological Architecture). The four columns are analytical roles,
     not ontological levels. (Book I, Ch. 5; cited by Book II as Pr. 1.1.) Use in Book II: Ch. 2,
     §2.7–2.8. Kind: (D) source for the distinction between analytical and ontological.

Principle 1.2 (Finitude of the Subject). Every cognizing subject is finite. (Book I, Ch. 3;
     cited by Book II as Pr. 1.2, C1.) Use in Book II: Ch. 4 (C1); Ch. 27. Kind: (A) core
     commitment.

     Ch. 4; cited by Book II as Pr. 1.3, C2.) Use in Book II: Ch. 4 (C2); Ch. 30. Kind: (A)

Principle 41.1 (Autonomy of Philosophical Justification). The validity of a philosophi-

A Note on the Version Mismatch
The reader is again directed to the note at the head of this index. Book II cites Book I in the
form given above. Several of those citations cannot be matched, in the current text of Book I,
to a principle or definition that says what Book II says it says. The mismatch is a fact about
the two books’ composition. The index records what Book II cites, not what Book I currently
contains, because the index’s purpose is to make Book II’s dependencies visible. Where a citation
cannot be matched, the entry says so or gives the closest match in the current text of Book I.

End of the Index of Cross-References to Book I.
